en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues*.

During the fifty years that Śākyamuni Buddha turned the Great Dharma Wheel, there was no scripture more ultimate or supreme than the two sutras of the *Lotus* and the *Nirvāṇa*, which constitute the unsurpassed treasury of jewels.
This is because [the *Lotus*] expounds the revelation of the provisional means, while [the *Nirvāṇa*]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the extant portion.)
The discourse on the manifestation of the original [truth] is not yet clearly elucidated; these two sutras alone hold this distinction.
It is for this very reason that our school judges these two sutras to be identical to the *amṛta* (clarified butter).

Although the texts and meanings regarding the manifestation of the original and the revelation of the reality are vast and manifold, when their essential conclusion is examined, they do not transcend the infinitesimal mind of each person. The Venerable Jingxi said: "The Wondrous Dharma is simply..."

The three virtues in one mind. Again it is said: "If one understands that the three virtues reside within the single mind, then the entirety of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra dwells within the square inch of the heart.
How profound these words! This is truly what those who study the meaning [of the teachings] should most earnestly take to heart.

Furthermore, although all scriptures may be established in peace and share the same flavor, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* upholds the Vinaya and discusses the Eternal; it universally benefits the final age, and thus in these present times—

This is a matter that students ought to investigate with urgency. However, while the Great Master Zhiyi’s propagation of the sutras was limited to his commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and did not extend to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, this is indeed to be regretted.
Nevertheless, the Venerable Zhanran, relying upon the meaning and intent of the Great Master, composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Thus, the two commentaries circulate together like a pair of precious jade disks. Furthermore, the Venerable Jingxi’s composition of the *Ji* (Records) likewise...
However, he only commented on the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) and did not reach the *Niepan shu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra). Is this not a deficiency?

Although there are the two commentaries by Xian and Man, they do not satisfy the minds of people; many are those who debate this. Furthermore, in recent times, these have been lost and no longer transmitted.

Therefore, students of antiquity and the present alike have suffered from this commentary, as its language is archaic and its meaning profound, making it difficult to understand and comprehend. Master Yuan of Mount Gu in the Song dynasty—
Relying on his transcendent talent and following the teachings of Master Dao’an, he composed the *Sande zhigui* (The Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues) in twenty fascicles.
Consequently, those points that were difficult to understand and obscure were all dissolved like melting ice and became as bright as the sun;

it was of great benefit to the world and may truly be called complete. Furthermore, he titled it with the "Three Virtues" (*sande*) in order to enable students to achieve thorough understanding through memorization.
The Commentary states: "By means of this commentary, one harmonizes with the Sūtra and thereby awakens to the One Mind and the Three Virtues; its intent is indeed excellent.
However, it is regrettable that its author was a master of the 'Mountain-Outside' (Shan-wai) school, and thus occasionally presented his own lineage of transmission.

Consequently, the Three Virtues he demonstrated seem not to have reached the ultimate perfection. Siming said: "If the Three Virtues were not manifested by being identical to the three realms of existence (the three paths), [then they would not be truly perfect]."

This is what has been taught in the Way of the Buddha. How rich these words are! They are sufficient to distinguish the divergent views outside the mountains and to manifest the true orthodoxy of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun).
Only after the wise and accomplished have gained thorough and penetrating faith in this can they read this book;
then, the purport of the secret treasury of the three virtues (sande) will likely not be mistaken. This book was not included in the Mingzang (the Japanese Tripitaka).
Furthermore, this work has not been widely circulated in our own country, a matter scholars have lamented for a long time.
In the past, I requested from the Great King Lunwang (Cakravartin) several dozen Song editions from the ancient collection at Chōtaku-ji Temple in Nōshū; this book was one of them.
I examined it with joy, only to find that the fifteenth fascicle was missing. Although I regretted its incompleteness, [the remaining portion] was as vast as a tree with arms-spanning girth.
This work has been revised and corrected according to the *Shichu* (The Standard Measure). It is intended for circulation among like-minded colleagues throughout the four quarters.

Consequently, I have requested that two or three disciples add annotations in the vernacular language (*guoyu*) and entrust it to the "Forest of Books" (*shulin*). Recently, the carving of the woodblocks has been completed; the Forest of Books has now requested a preface from me.

I rejoice deeply that this work may be transmitted for a long duration. Furthermore, I pray that those who preserve the complete canon in the future will take pleasure in supplementing its deficiencies.
[Omission]. Thus, taking up my brush, I have recorded this directly to serve as a preface at the beginning of the fascicle.
Written respectfully by the aged bhikṣu Guāngqiān in the spring of the year Yǐwèi of the Zhèndé era.
Preface to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues*.

This commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* was indeed composed by my ancestor, Master Zhang’an, based upon the fundamental tenets of Nāgārjuna and employing the Dharma-gates of Master Zhiyi, in accordance with the Sūtra.
He discerned and elucidated the profound meaning of the three virtues. Subsequently, after Master Zhāng'ān had passed away, Master Jīngxī took up the task of editing this text;

he refined it again and again, and by means of the established precedents, he revealed new insights—for instance, adding personal comments beneath various passages and changing the title of the *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary) to *Shū* (Commentary). Thereafter...
This is truly the ultimate perfection. In recent times, these empty texts have existed in mere fragments with no one to transmit them.
The śramaṇa of Qiantang, Shi Zhiyuan, whose style name is Wuwai, is the tenth-generation dharma-grandson of Jingxi.

Lamenting that these subtle words were on the verge of falling into oblivion and deploring that later students did not hear them, he composed this record to clarify and propagate them. He compiled them into twenty fascicles, titled... [title follows].

The *Three Virtues: Pointing to the Goal* (Sande zhigui) states: "Whenever there are passages where the phrasing is lofty and the intent far-reaching, or where the words are concise yet the meaning subtle, [the commentator] shall set aside divergences, reconcile differences, trace the deep currents, and analyze the layered points to bring them back to this single focus:

so that future readers may recognize that the essence expounded by the sutra and the principles established by the commentary are entirely contained within the principle of the three virtues of the one mind, wherein sentient beings and Buddhas are without distinction. Thus, there is no need for further wandering."

For those lost in the mazes of delusion, I have for the time being undertaken the task of lecturing and expounding upon the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*). Only those who cherish the Way will understand my intent.

At this time, the eighth month of the fourth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era of the Great Song dynasty, the year of Xin Hai, on the day of the full moon at West Lake in Qiantang, I began the work of editing and revision in the lecture hall of Chongfu Temple.
Six years later, on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month of the year of Gui Chou...

First, regarding the general title of the commentary, there are two levels of subject-object correspondence. First, the character "commentary" (*shu*) is the subject, which refers to that which understands; the remainder...
The two sutras to be explained are the means of expression (*vācaka*), and *nirvāṇa* is that which is expressed (*vācya*).

Since the specific name of a sutra is derived by taking up its expressed content, I shall now likewise take up the content to be explained as the specific title of this commentary (*ṭīkā*) to distinguish it from general works.

This clarifies that this commentary is not a commentary on other sutras. "Commentary" (*shu*) means to clarify (*shū*) and to resolve (*ju*). It elucidates the intent of the sutras and discerns the meaning of the Buddha’s teachings.
In the old edition of Zhang’an, the title was called *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis), reflecting a sense of humility that it merely provides a structural analysis and sectioning of the sūtra text.
After Jingxi’s revision and finalization, it was changed to *Shu* (Commentary), signifying that it decisively penetrates the meaning and intent of the entire sūtra without obstruction.
This was also Jingxi’s skillful way of conveying Zhang’an’s original intention; for example, the *Zhiguan* was originally titled *Yuantun* (Perfect and Sudden).

Regarding the fact that Zhāng'ān standardized the text and changed the title to *Mahā*, since there is a sound principle underlying this, the revision is not erroneous. Question: Since Zhìzhě provided exegesis for the scriptures and explained their titles—calling them *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning)—and his commentary on the text was called *Wénjù* (Textual Phrases), and since Zhāng'ān’s own master-disciple lineage is well-established, is this not merely an expression of further humility? Answer: It is precisely because Zhìzhě was humble that Zhāng'ān followed his example. Furthermore, it is also because Zhāng'ān was humble. Thus, he did not dare to call it *Xuányì* himself; instead, he named it *Shǒuxí* (Hand-Copied). It was only after the text had been transmitted to the capital that it was subsequently titled *Xuányì*. As for the *Wénjù*, it was originally named *Jiàoshì* (Instructional Commentary) by Zhìzhě. Zhāng'ān later revised it and renamed it *Wénjù*. This is how it came to be. It is not that Zhāng'ān lacked the authority to do so; rather, it was simply that he deferred to his predecessor. This is similar to how former scholars explained the *Shu* (Book of Documents), where some referred to it as a *zhuan* (commentary), taking the term to mean "transmission" (*chuanshu*)—

either because they personally received the Sage’s instructions or because they were transmitted by successive teachers— as in the *Kongshi zhuan* of the *Shangshu*. Others referred to it as a *zhu* (annotation),
meaning that out of humility they did not dare transmit their own interpretations, but merely annotated them directly beneath the text— as in the *Liji* of Zheng Xuan.

This is correct. For example, the titles *Shu* (Commentary) and *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) carry meanings that are either humble or non-humble. Thus, when Jingxi composed the outline for the *Zhiguan*, he also titled it *Wenju*;
was this not simply because he used the phrase "outlining the sentences and dividing the text" to refer to it as *Wenju*?

Question: If that is so, the name *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) should not be considered humble. Answer: Indeed it is so; it is called thus because the title is explained through five meanings as being "wondrous" (*miao*).

Because it accords with the Buddha’s intent, it is called the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Thus, Jingxi merely changed the title of the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), while the *Xuanyi* retained its original designation.
Therefore, we know that Zhan’an’s intention was such that the two—humility (*qian*) and non-duality (*buer*)—manifest each other.
As the *Miaole Ji* states: "The reason one cannot hastily explain the title is that the principle of providing a separate explanation beneath the title is not something undertaken lightly."

The Great Meaning of the Title has been explained in full detail; therefore, regarding the main text of the sūtra, I have merely made a rough division into sections and titled this work "Wenju" (Words and Phrases).
This is precisely for that reason. Question: Since ancient times, many masters have titled their commentaries on the sūtras as "Shu" (Commentaries).

Is it not the case that they all lacked humility? Would this not violate the rules of propriety? Answer: Whether one is humble or not depends entirely on the intention of the author. In principle, there may be a justification for either approach. Although [the title] is... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
To receive praise is also without fault, as the Master said: "Since King Wen has passed away, does not the culture now reside in me?
Yan Hui replied, "What kind of man was Shun? What kind of man am I? This means that because their moral character and virtue were equal and uniform, he compared himself to King Wen and Yu Shun;
who would dare to criticize him for this? If he were not of such a caliber, even a child three feet tall could laugh at him.
Furthermore, it is like the Great Master himself, who claimed that even the great treatises of India were not his equal; how much less need one mention the teachers of the land of China?
Although this is not an act of humility, as he lacked a sense of shame, the intent behind titling this work "Commentary" (Shū) is of this nature.
Some say that regarding the exegesis of the teachings of this school, there are distinct sections for the "General Exposition" (Gemyō) and the "Textual Commentary" (Monku).

If one were to treat these as a single unified work, they would be titled collectively as a *shu* (commentary), following the precedent of works such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śūtra-śu* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra-śu*.
Now that the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) has been assigned to each respective section, how can the *Wen-ju* (Textual Exegesis) be called a *shu*? Answer:

These are all established conventions from the past, not my own new invention. Were it otherwise, consider for instance the *Vimalakīrti-guang-shu* (Broad Commentary on the Vimalakīrti), which was previously [titled] only the first six fascicles.
The titles for the first twenty-eight volumes were designated as the *Xuanshu* (Profound Commentary), while those for the subsequent volumes were designated as the *Wenshu* (Textual Commentary).

Upon Jingxi’s revision and finalization, he excised the word "textual" (*wen*) and simply titled them the *Lueshu* (Abridged Commentary) for the first volume and so forth; these were then circulated separately from the six-volume *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).

As for those who stubbornly cling to the original title of *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) and refuse to follow this new intention—how are they any different from lecturers who re-treat the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) while discarding its revised version?
Does the title "Mahā" (Great) instead employ the terminology of the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]?

Furthermore, since Zhanran himself referred to his work as a *shu* (commentary)—as seen in the *Xuanyi* where it says "the origin of the *shu*" and "entrusting the *shu* to another's house"—his intention was one of humility;
moreover, when he titled his work *Wenju*, Jingxi revised it so as not to neglect the original intent of the Master.
"Volume" (*juan*) signifies "rolling up and unfolding. "First" (*di yi*) means the beginning; since this volume occupies the beginning, it is called "the first.
"Second," "compiled" (*zhuàn*), and "refined title" (*jiā hào*): first, it clarifies the name of the compiler, which is Zhāng'ān; next, it clarifies the name of the editor, which is Jīngxī.
The old text states: "Expounded by the Great Master Tiantai Zhìzhě; compiled by his disciple Guǎngdǐng."
This is Zhiyan attributing the merit to his teacher; he states that although this commentary was composed by him, it is entirely a compilation of the Dharma-gates taught by the Great Master (Zhiyi).

Thus, the *Xuanyi* says: "On the tenth day of the tenth month of the tenth year of the Daye era, while dwelling at Nanguan on Mount Tiantai, I have ventured to provide an explanation of the meaning and intent of the Wenzhi [Zhiyi], looking through the narrow tube [of my limited understanding]. Furthermore, below, he explains the *Chang'an*.
The initial commentary on the "Chapter on Longevity" states: "Even Bodhisattvas of Diligence cannot know [this]; how could it be that an ordinary person with a darkened mind could fathom it?
I have merely recorded what I have heard. This is all done out of humility regarding one's own lack of talent and to attribute excellence to the wise;
thus, the original text under the title simply says, "Spoken by the Wise One. It was only when Jingxi re-edited it that he directly revealed his own contribution. Therefore...
The title of "Wise One" (Jñānin) has been omitted, and it is stated that this was composed by the Dharma Master Ding.
According to the ritual rules regarding the avoidance of names, one does not avoid both parts of a two-character name; thus, he may be referred to as "Ding" without mentioning "Guang.

The significance of his name, the excellence of his conduct, the reasons for the composition of these commentaries, and the dates of their writing are all fully detailed in the *Xuánjì* and the *Jiàoxiàng Zhāngshū Yuányǐqǐ*.

Regarding the title "Dharma Master" (*dharmabhāṇaka*), the *Brahmacarya-varga* states: "Because he knows the Dharma, he is called a Great Dharma Master; because he knows the meaning, he is called a Great Dharma Master," and so forth.

These [definitions] are explained according to the seven types of excellence (*saptavidha-kauśalya*), all of which reside in the Buddha; thus, the designation "Dharma Master" applies to both cause and fruit.
The current commentator (*śāstrakāra*) is a Dharma Master in the state of cause. As Yangzi’s *Fayan* says: "A teacher is the model for humanity..."

The *Famofa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts through the Dharma Seal) and the *Guansin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) both clarify the three masters—namely, the Vinaya Master (*vinayadhara*), the Dharma Master (*dharmabhāṇaka*), and the Meditation Master (*dhyānācārya*).
One who is thoroughly proficient in observing what constitutes an offense and its non-offense is called a Vinaya Master; one who is deeply versed in the sutras and śāstras is called a Dharma Master;

and one who cultivates the mind through meditative concentration is called a Meditation Master. The commentary on the *Guansin lun* clarifies that each of these three masters has ten faults. Regarding the ten faults of the Vinaya Master: [The text continues with the enumeration of the ten faults.]
1. Because they cling only to external discipline and fail to recognize internal precepts, they are rebuked by Vimalakīrti. 2.

Because they cling to the names and characteristics of the Vinaya, they dispute over right and wrong, failing to recognize that suffering and its origin are rooted in the mind. 3. Since morality, concentration, and wisdom support one another, one can only advance on the Path;

"If one does not grasp at signs and speaks with a mind free from attachment, there are nine ways of causing others to read, uphold, and correctly recollect [the teaching]: first, to illuminate that which is unknown so that it may be known."
Second, "opening up" is like opening a treasury of jewels so that one may take and use them as desired;

third, "indicating" is like showing the good and the bad to one with poor vision—since the eye of wisdom of the Hīnayāna is unclear, it indicates what is the path and what is not; fourth, "discriminating" refers to the mundane and the supramundane;
fifth, "manifesting" means that at times he disparages the wholesome to assist the unwholesome, doing so out of a desire to cause sentient beings to attain [liberation].
Sixth, because it provides clarification, it is the teaching of the Dharma and the Buddha’s intended meaning;

seventh, because it explains, it is like a sack containing treasure that people do not know of unless its mouth is opened—one should likewise open the sack of the Buddha’s sūtras to explain their principles;

eighth, because it analyzes the heavy to make it light, it uses various metaphors to make [the meaning] easy to understand; ninth, because it is shallow and easy, it is like making a difficult-to-cross ford easy by providing a bridge.
The profound waters of Prajñāpāramitā can be made shallow and easy to cross; although the current text cites only the eighth and ninth passages, its intent encompasses the preceding seven.
Thus, we know that since the *Śāstra* opens the way for explaining it for the sake of others, the ancient and modern classifications are perfectly appropriate.
Although the five chapters listed below differ, they are all termed "Nirvāṇa"; though their various meanings diverge, they all ultimately converge in the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The *pāramitās* do not transcend the three virtues (*triguṇa*), so how could Buddha-nature be separate from the three causes?

The "three virtues" is the name for that which realizes sainthood, while the "three causes" is the designation for those in the state of ordinary beings. Since the principle of ordinary and saintly beings is equal, how can cause and effect be different?

Therefore, one knows that the three thousand realms within the mind-ground are mutually pervasive; there is a fundamental reason why these three are without distinction. Thus, one must divide this chapter here to know in advance its great significance.
To grasp the essential meaning as entering into one's own nature is what is called "expounding the sutra. The three virtues and three causes are precisely the three truths of the mind;
they are illuminated by the three contemplations and verified by the six stages of attainment. For one who acts thus, what need is there to explain the meaning according to the literal text?

To conceal the essence while speaking of the words, or to speak of the mind while seeing only the phenomena—the principle is not far removed from this. Since this sutra is so, all other scriptures are likewise; furthermore, the One transforms into the Five.
The time and function unify the ten directions and the three periods of time; the Way is equally present here, and its original nature is without distinction.
I entrust these words to future worthies, who must apply themselves with even greater diligence. Because there is this profound purport, I have thus provided these annotations.

The term "Explanation" (*shì*) refers to the sequential explanation of the names of the five chapters within the following section. First, in explaining the names of the assemblies, there is first a statement on the intent of the invocation, followed by the explanation of their names.
The phrase "The Way does not operate in isolation," etc., serves as a general heading; it means that the Way—which upholds the Vinaya and discusses the Eternal—is not solitary or self-existent.

The destiny [of this teaching] necessarily awaits the time when the conditions for its extinction are about to end; it is at the site of the Kuśinagara Forest, with the assembly of fifty-two followers as its companions—these three factors meeting together—that this teaching arises.

Therefore, such matters as the discourse on the five fruits being without distinction, the doctrine of the Buddha-body’s eternal abiding, the principle that even icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, and the ultimate meaning of the perfect *I* (the three characters of the *Īśvarapratyaya-hṛdaya*), have all been taught in the various sutras prior to this assembly.
Because it has not yet been revealed, it is said that it does not operate in isolation.
The phrase "now, at the time of Nirvana," and so forth, explains the preceding meaning. "The time of Nirvana has arrived" means waiting for the proper occasion;
"the face-gate [emitting light] down to being moved" means waiting for its companion; and "Kuśinagara" means waiting for its location.
"Face-gate" (*mianmen*) refers to the mouth. "Illuminating" means that the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the Tathāgata, during the early morning, emitted various kinds of light from his face-gate."
Regarding the emission of sounds according to each type, the Sūtra says: "By the Buddha's spiritual power, a great sound is produced;

that sound pervades everywhere, even unto the Peak of Existence. In accordance with the voices of each species, it universally addresses all sentient beings, saying: 'If there is anything you doubt, you may now ask about it all.'"
Regarding "startled awakening" and "being moved": the Sūtra states that when sentient beings encounter this light, all their karmic defilements and afflictions are completely eliminated;
this is what is meant by "startled awakening. The Sūtra further states that after sentient beings have seen or heard this, their minds are filled with great distress and even their bodies tremble;
this is what is meant by "being moved."
The Sūtra clarifies that all the assemblies proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara to reach the place where the Tathāgata was; therefore, it says they "assembled here at Kuśinagara.

Regarding the names of the two groups of followers summoned by the conditions of the occasion: the first group consists of those who practice through reality (*satya-caryā*), for whom the conditions for ripening the seeds have been drawn forth, and thus they must be summoned to initiate their influence and response.
The second group consists of those who practice through skillful means (*upāya-caryā*), for whom the vessel is being forged by the hammering of the anvils, and thus they must be invited.
Therefore, it is said that "the multitudes possess both the provisional and the real," where "to reach" (zhì) means "to arrive at.

Regarding the phrase "all for the purpose of manifesting and developing," this is because those with the capacity for the true practice have matured; thus, they come to hear the Dharma and realize the Truth, which constitutes the manifestation of the Three Virtues of Nirvana for themselves.
As for those of provisional practice who assist the Buddha, they arrive to respond to the teachings and benefit sentient beings, which constitutes manifestation for others.
The manifestation of the three virtues is *nirvāṇa*. If one who employs skillful means (*upāya*) fundamentally abides in the ultimate fruit (*phala*), they act solely for the sake of others;
if they abide in the true cause (*hetu*), it is not that they do not act for themselves—namely, by diminishing birth and increasing the Path—and this is precisely what is meant here.

Nevertheless, even when those at the stage of the ultimate fruit speak of what they have realized themselves, it is called "self-manifestation" (*svaprakāśana*); yet, because they establish this teaching so that the multitudes may awaken to the Path, it is necessary to invoke [the Buddha].

In the following explanation, the Buddha first clarifies that his own intention is without partiality; subsequently, he reveals how he establishes transformations according to the capacities of beings.
Regarding the initial passage: because the perfectly integrated *nirvāṇa* cannot be realized by those on the seven stages of expedient means, it is called "difficult to attain.

Furthermore, to realize this perfect *nirvāṇa*, one must pass through forty-one stages before reaching the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); since this treatise discusses the ultimate fruit, it is likewise difficult.
Attaining the essence of the quiescence of the three truths, which contains the three thousand [realms], is termed the "Treasury" (garbha).
Since the original intent of the supramundane [teaching] was to expound this very point, there is no secrecy or withholding. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"If I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed regarding the Dharma of the equality of the Mahāyāna."
However, it is not that [the Buddha] does not manifest wisdom or establish teachings according to the capacities of beings. It is simply that not all are able to receive them;
those of sharp faculties, namely the Bodhisattvas, have already attained entry into reality within the *Avataṃsaka* itself. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says:

"As soon as they see my body and hear what I preach, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. As for those of dull faculties and inferior capacities, who are like the deaf or the mute—
Because they receive great benefit, it is said that they cannot yet fully receive [the ultimate teaching].

Therefore, while wandering and transforming beings at the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma of the Small Vehicle’s non-self to destroy false notions of self, like applying poison [to a wound] first. Subsequently, through the Vaipulya (Prajñāpāramitā) sutras, he rebuked and corrected them, and through the Prajñā teachings, he refined their great capacities.
Once these capacities had matured, he then revealed the perfectly integrated True Self in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, like washing with water. Thus is the Tathāgata.

The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, in the Chapter on Nature (*Svabhāvavarga*), states: "For example, just as a woman, for the sake of her child, applies a bitter flavor to her breast, so too does the Tathāgata;
for the sake of cultivating emptiness, he declares that all phenomena are entirely without self.
Just as that woman, having thoroughly washed her breast, calls to her child so that he may return to suckle, so do I now declare the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, O Bhikṣus..."
"One should not give rise to fear, just as that young child, upon hearing his mother call him, gradually returned to drink milk.

Regarding the statement "the beginning is the same while the end is different," this explains the intent behind the [teachings on] anointing and washing. In the Deer Park, the teaching of the "small" was the "beginning being the same," because it was taught according to the specific capacities and conditions of those listeners.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the refutation of the "small" and the discourse on the "eternal" constitutes the "end being different"; all of these involve passing through the intermediate stages.
The two flavors [of the teachings] wait upon the opportune conditions and await the time of *nirvāṇa*, using figures such as Cunda as the catalyst for their manifestation;
they then preach the permanence and the discernment of nature through this perfect Dharma-gift, so that those of the partial vehicles may all enter the reality.
Following Cunda, the text proceeds through the sūtra to clarify the meaning of giving (*dāna*): first, it clarifies that making offerings is the cause for initiating giving;

because of making offerings, giving is established as a constant cause; because of requesting [the Buddha] to remain, the Truth is discussed; because of discussing the Truth, the inquiry is encouraged;
because the Tathāgata encourages it, Kāśyapa then poses thirty-four questions; therefore, the Buddha responds with sixteen chapters accordingly.
To ask and answer this is to expound the doctrine of the eternal [Tathāgata] and universally bestow it upon those with the capacity for it.
The "one who presents offerings" refers to Cunda, who at the beginning of the second sutra addressed the Buddha, saying: "I only pray that you will compassionately accept our final offering."
Regarding "bestowing the eternal and so forth," this refers to the Buddha’s response. The Sūtra says:
"If you now seek from me long life, physical form, strength, peace and happiness, and unimpeded eloquence, I shall bestow upon you eternal life, physical form, strength, and so forth."
Regarding the request for the Buddha to remain, as mentioned in the *Sārasamuccaya* (The Chapter on Lamentation), it says: "I pray only that you will remain for a long time and not enter parinirvāṇa.
In this regard, the Tathāgata rebuked the false discourse of the Hīnayāna and affirmed the truth of the Mahāyāna, stating in the sūtra:
"You should not now grasp at these deceptive things," and further: "Although you have gone forth [into homelessness], regarding this Mahāyāna..."
"Though they have generated longing and wear the dyed robes of the *kāṣāya*, their minds are still not yet imbued with the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna"—this immediately refutes the spurious.
When the Sūtra says, "One should cause all beings to dwell securely within the Secret Treasury," and then cites the *ī* character and the celestial eye as metaphors, this speaks of the True.
The "Exhortation and Inquiry" refers to the beginning of the "Chapter on Longevity," where it first exhorts the bhikṣus to inquire.
Next is the exhortation for the great assembly to inquire. Because the words of exhortation were repeated profusely, they are described as "earnest.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, reverently upholding the intent of the Tathāgata’s earnest exhortation, spoke twenty-two lines of verse consisting of thirty-four questions, namely:
"How can one attain long life? and so forth.

"Bestowing Answers According to Questions" refers to the Buddha’s responses to each of the sixteen chapters, beginning with "Longevity" and ending with "The Great Assembly," which fully answer the thirty-four questions posed by Kāśyapa; hence it is called "Bestowing Answers According to Questions."
Because all remaining doubts are severed, it is said that "nothing is left behind or obstructed"; because the entire assembly benefits, it is said that [the Dharma] is "overflowing," and so forth.

Now, the following section explains the practice (*xing*): "profound" (*yuan-shen*) means deep and still; it is "deep" because it vertically penetrates the three truths, and it is "still" because its essence is free from the three delusions.
Although the mind inherently possesses all phenomena and the three aspects (one and three) are mutually fused, were it not for the Buddha’s teaching, no one would be able to know this.
Therefore, it is called the "Secret Treasury. Although one knows that [the Buddha-nature] is inherently possessed, if one does not practice, there is no way to realize it.
It is like standing by a river and envying the fish; one must cast a net before they can be caught. Thus it is said: "One cannot reach it without practice. Practice refers to the five practices.

One should know that these five practices do not transcend the three contemplations: emptiness is the holy practice (*ārya-caryā*), the provisional is the Brahma practice (*brahma-caryā*), and the middle is the celestial practice (*deva-caryā*).
Simultaneously illuminating the two types of goodness is the "infant-like practice"; simultaneously illuminating the two types of evil is the "sick person's practice.

The dust-and-sand [delusions] are the evils of the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatā-anta*), while ignorance is the evil of the limit of the provisional (*prajñapti-anta*). When these three and one are mutually identical and the five practices are fused together, it is called the "Tathāgata practice"—this is precisely what is meant.
Therefore, one must begin from the stage of names and cultivate the five practices until reaching the first dwelling (*prathamā-bhūmi*), where they are partially realized.
The fact that realization is manifest and not reached through practice makes its meaning all the more evident.
"Causing those who are before" means causing sentient beings to practice so as to reach the secret treasury of the three virtues.
The following section correctly clarifies how the Tathāgata’s meritorious deeds initiate the Dharma-gate of the five practices.
Regarding the phrase "lying on his right side," etc., it refers to the end of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly, which states:
"In order to subdue all sentient beings, he manifested illness and lay down on his right side.

Regarding "Kāśyapa’s exhortation," it refers to the beginning of the Chapter on Manifesting Illness, where the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa exhorted the Buddha regarding his own practice and his transformation of others.
Regarding the three proofs of his freedom from illness: since [Kāśyapa] requested the teaching on all three occasions, it is called "inviting by urging.
As for the full-lotus posture and so forth: because Kāśyapa had already urged him, the Tathāgata immediately manifested the sign of being free from illness.
The subsequent scripture states: "He immediately rose from his reclining position and sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), his countenance serene and joyful like a mass of molten gold.
Therefore, it says "molten and joyful"; "joyful" (*yì*) means delight. "Three" refers to the Holy One (*ārya*), Brahmā, and the Infant (*bāla*);

since each speaks one chapter, it is called "speaking the three. "One" refers to the Celestial Practice (*deva-caryā*); because it is specifically indicated within the *Avataṃsaka* at the conclusion of the Brahma-conduct, it is called "indicating the one."

The section beginning with "Bodhisattva" clarifies that the five practices (*pañca-karma*) belong to cultivation based on the teachings, while the ten virtues (*daśa-guṇa*) belong to realization; this is precisely what is elucidated in the "Chapter on the King of Virtues.

However, the section beginning with "Nirvāṇa" explains the meaning: the wondrous significance of the three virtues (*tri-dharma*) is universally pervasive across all phenomena and encompasses everything without exception; therefore, it is described as "vast."
Nevertheless, regarding the appearance of this inexhaustible and vast great water:

although the meaning encompassed by *nirvāṇa* is all-encompassing and extensive when one intends to raise and correctly expound the purport of the text, nothing surpasses *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) as the definitive pointer to its essential core.
"To cite one and thereby encompass all" refers to the concealment of abundance. Confucius said, "Of the three hundred poems, one phrase may summarize them all: 'Thoughts are without depravity.

Thus we know that although the literature of the *Feng* and *Ya* is vast, its essential aim lies in being without depravity; and although the meaning of *Nirvāṇa* is manifold, its sole intent is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
It is like the depth and breadth of the ocean: by pointing to its saltiness, one encompasses its depth and breadth; so too with *Nirvāṇa*.
Yìfēng points to the analogy of salt to illustrate the essential principle of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Thus, although the Tathāgata raised eighteen general topics—such as the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths—to offer encouragement and inquiry, Siṃhanāda addressed his questions solely in terms of the single dharma of the Buddha-nature across six successive layers;
therefore, it is said that he "exclusively questioned," and so forth.
However, when the Buddha subsequently explains the application of the names "good" and "evil," he does not depart from the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) to distinguish their general and specific meanings;

this can be understood through their essence, which is precisely emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, they are neither good nor evil. Emptiness is itself the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the principle of inherent inclusion (*liju*) is perfectly manifest.

It is precisely because of this inherent inclusion of the principle that there is phenomenal function; since all phenomena do not transcend the ten realms and their function pervades these ten realms, it is said to be "non-existent" [in terms of fixed substantiality].
Regarding "yá" (涯), the *Erya* states that "sì" (涘) is "yá" (厓); Guo Pu’s commentary explains this as meaning "the water's edge.

Regarding "nánguò" (囊括), it refers to a "náng" (囊), which is a bag or pouch. The *Zitong* says: "That which has a bottom is called a náng; that which lacks a bottom is called a tuò (pronounced tuō)—it is a wind-instrument implement."
The poem says, "In the bag, in the bag," which refers to tying it up. The *Yi* says, "The fourth line: a tied-up bag; no blame and no praise. This is a rough summary.
It means that the present sutra clarifies the function of subsuming the two realms and encompasses the breadth of the ten realms.
This constitutes tying up the bag of this entire sutra, thereby obtaining a concise clarification of its two functions. However, these two chapters on clarifying the functions do not... [text ends].

In one instance, the Kāśyapa-parivarta subsumes "evil," which refers to the subsuming of Puṇyaprabha; in another instance, the Cunda-parivarta subsumes "the heterodox," which refers to the subsuming of the ten non-Buddhist schools.

Since evil must be contrasted with good and the heterodox with the orthodox, and since Rāhula and Cunda have already attained the Way, their inclusion in this assembly as they return from the Small Vehicle to the Perfect [Vehicle] constitutes the subsuming of the goodness within the realm of the Śrāvakas. Furthermore, the Buddha prophesied that Puṇyaprabha would fall into hell.

Those who do not rescue the heterodox followers and external paths—none of whom are anything other than seeds for the hells—are now all gathered here; this refers to the inclusion of the evil of the hell realm within these two realms.

By using these two realms as an illustration, the remaining eight are implied; by using *nirvāṇa* as an illustration, the four periods are implied; therefore, it is said that "the concise encompasses the extensive."
The "Excellence of the Lower" (Shan-xia) section of the Kāśyapa Chapter comprehensively encompasses the ten realms.
Regarding the "two sons," this refers to Rāhula and Sunakṣatra, both of whom were sons of the Buddha.

As for the phrase "the rest are all equal," it means that since both the good and the evil among one's own children are included, how could the many sentient beings possibly exist apart from these two categories?
The categories of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) and "inclination" (*āśaya*) can be understood by analogy with this.

Furthermore, the section below on "substance" (*tattva*) clarifies that the *Caitanya* (or *Caitika*) chapter vertically encompasses the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching]. Regarding "the heterodox and the orthodox": the heterodox is identical to evil and the orthodox is identical to good;

because the principle-substance (*li-ti*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is neither heterodox nor orthodox. Since emptiness is itself the provisional (*prajñapti*), it is able to employ both simultaneously.
The "initial gathering" refers to the teaching of the Small Vehicle at the Deer Park, wherein Cundabhadrā and the other four companions realized the fruit of enlightenment.
The "final inclusion" refers to this sutra clarifying how Subhadra and the other nine sages attained the Way.
The beginning and the end serve as examples for the concluding sections; the middle—namely the Vaipulya and Prajñā sūtras—encompasses both the heterodox and the orthodox.

This discourse transcends the sequential stages: although from the Deer Park onward the Buddha employed provisional teachings of the Small Vehicle, according to his original intention, he intended for all beings to return to the Secret Treasury.
Thus, in this present assembly, they equally awaken to the perfect and eternal. One should know that the entire pedagogical system of his single lifetime is the functioning of *nirvāṇa*.
He was also asked why, in his summary, he did not mention the *Lotus Sūtra*. He replied: "The scriptural divisions and the flavor (*rasa*) of both sūtras are identical;

however, the *Lotus Sūtra* addresses those with residual capacities, whereas this sūtra gathers in those who have been left behind. Following the primary intent, I have set aside the *Lotus Sūtra* for now.

Nevertheless, these four chapters constitute the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle. 'Teaching' refers to the eternal teaching; 'practice' refers to the eternal practice; and 'meaning' refers to the eternal principle. By receiving the teaching..."

The three meanings—the practice of cultivation (*pratipatti*), the perfection of conduct (*caryā-sampad*), and the realization of principle (*tattva-adhigama*)—arise in a sequence that is never disordered.

"Assembly" (*gaṇa*) refers to those who receive the teachings, practice them, and realize the principle; "function" (*vṛtti*) refers to the power of these three to gather and transform, meaning that the perfect, eternal teaching, practice, and principle are all capable of universally encompassing both the heterodox and the orthodox, as well as the good and the evil.
Subsequently, one gathers these five and three back into one’s own mind, contemplating the mind itself.

To contemplate that the mind is itself provisional is the practice of bestowing *nirvāṇa*; to contemplate that the mind is itself empty is the practice of *nirvāṇa*; and to contemplate that the mind is itself the Middle Way is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
One who contemplates in this manner is called a member of the *nirvāṇa*-assembly. To destroy delusions by relying on such contemplation is the function of *nirvāṇa*.

These three aspects—provisional, empty, and middle—are mutually identical, yet the six stages are clearly distinguished; they comprehensively encompass the entire sutra without departing from the square inch of one’s own mind.
In the section on "Arising," there is first the sequential arising in both reverse and direct order, followed by a summary that returns to the fundamental tenet.

The phrase "because sentient beings possess giving and so forth" refers to the sequential arising. Here, "sentient beings" refers to those who are the recipients of the teaching (the *ālambana*), while "giving" refers to the teaching itself which is capable of reaching them (*upāya*).

Since the teaching is established in accordance with the capacity of the recipient, it is said "because sentient beings possess [the capacity for] giving. Because they receive the teaching and practice accordingly, it is said "because of giving."
To practice and abide in this is precisely what is called the stage of "semblance contemplative practice" (*nāma-sadṛśa-bhāvanā-caryā*).

Because one enters stages such as the First Abode (*prathamavihāra*) through these semblance practices and realizes the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), it is said that "through practice, one sees the meaning. Within the First Abode, one internally realizes the wondrous meaning of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and externally one is able to initiate the transformation and teaching of others;
thus, it is said that "realizing the meaning has utility. This constitutes the sequential arising of the five chapters. Furthermore—

Based on this, "arising" refers to the transformation of others through one's own practice; what is the intended meaning of "agent" and "object"? The first three chapters represent the causes of one's own practice:
in terms of meaning, they are proximate as the partial realization of the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*), and remote as the ultimate perfection of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).

This constitutes the fruit of one's own practice. Furthermore, "function" refers to the capacity to transform others. If there were no objects to be transformed, by whom would the methods of subduing and gathering be applied? This is precisely the transformation of others.

The "other place" (*parārtha*) can likewise summon the assembly, for it is a transformation for the sake of others; thus we know that from beginning to end, this single scripture does not transcend cause and effect, or the agent and the object.
This is entirely consistent with the five meanings of the *Miaoxuan* and the ten chapters of the *Zhi guan*; they correspond to one another in every detail.
The interpretation of our school’s teachings is beautiful in its very core.
This also clarifies the reverse order of arising below. Regarding "functioning by means of the meaning and so forth":

it refers to the ability to subdue and gather [beings] through the realization of the meaning, up to the bestowing of the eternally abiding Dharma because there are those with the karmic conditions; thus, it is said that "bestowing" occurs due to the assembly of the multitude.

The section "Without Beginning" concludes by directing the intent toward the fundamental source. The wondrous principle of *nirvāṇa* is inherent within the mind; though it is truly without beginning or end, sentient beings are fundamentally deluded.
Thus, through the movement of their faculties, they invoke the Buddha as the beginning, which is why there is the practice of summoning and requesting.

Through the realization of this principle, the teaching arises as the end, which is why there is the function of subduing and gathering. Once the beginning and the end are established, the middle is naturally formed.

Below, the meaning of "application" (*yòng*) is extensively clarified. Using the present Śākyamuni—who has already realized the wondrous principle and is preaching the Dharma to benefit others—as the primary example, this section precisely elucidates the meaning of application;
hence it is explained at length. "Evil exhausted" (*è jìn*) refers to Icchantikas who possess the Buddha-nature. "Perversity vanished" (*xié wáng*) refers to the ten seers (*ṛṣi*) receiving the Way.

"Good perfected" (*shàn qióng*) refers to Rāhula obtaining his prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). "Correct cessation" (*zhèng xī*) refers to Kauṇḍinya understanding the eternal. "Evil exhausted" and "perversity vanished" [refer to the aforementioned].

Therefore, having ceased and brought rest to the conditioned, one exhausts the ultimate stillness; thus, by gathering and resting, the bird is lost and the bow is hidden, for when the trigger is exhausted, the response ceases.

Hence it is said, "Ultimately," and so forth. This is what the Sūtra means when it says: "I have placed my children within the secret treasury, and I too shall not long remain outside, but will abide therein myself."

Regarding the general and specific [classifications], "general" means that the meaning and intent of the five chapters encompass both the beginning and the end; "specific" means that the text is divided according to its predominant themes, each receiving a distinct name.
As for the term "inquiry and conditions," it refers to Kāśyapa; because the Buddha answers based on his inquiry, it is said that he grants [the teaching] in response to a request.

"Ruler and Square" refers to using the ruler and square to explain the practice of righteousness. The circle is defined by the compass and the square by the carpenter’s square; as Mencius said, "A master craftsman instructs others by means of the compass and the square.
In a separate discussion below, the Five Phases and Ten Virtues are taken as the ruler and square. The compass can be used to illustrate the analogy of the single mind.
The square shape of the fivefold compass is a metaphor for the sequence of the five practices; the ten virtues are likewise so.
That the Buddha-nature is not "one" means that whatever is "one" must necessarily be contrasted with "two," yet the wondrous principle is empty and harmonious, transcending all such contrasts;
therefore, it is said to be "not one. This is just as the sutras clarify that the great void does not derive its name from a small space.
Since even "one" does not exist, how could there be the name "five"? Therefore it is asked: "How can there be five?

That this sutra text establishes the names of the five is because it provides different designations according to the capacities of beings, so that they may recognize the principle through the teaching; thus it says "to cause understanding," which means [the names] are not five.
The five names are the teaching, while "not five" is the principle. Furthermore, since the principle is the teaching, it is not one; and since the teaching is the principle, it is not five.
This is what is meant by liberation through the five characters.
*Śūraṅgama*—in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is translated as "Mighty Aspect" (*kian-xiang*)—is precisely the King Samādhi of the Middle Way.
Within this text, because it is explained from the perspective of expedient practice, it says "all abide," and so forth.
I interpret "private" (si) here as referring to private matters or hidden details; furthermore, the *Yupian* states that what is not public is called "private.

This is because when Jingxi re-edited [the text], there were instances where he provided supplementary assistance in secret; since he was separated from the author of the commentary by a great distance in time, these were not cases of formal, face-to-face consultation and resolution.
For all subsequent instances where "private" is used, one may understand it by analogy.
Regarding the increase in the number [of assemblies], it should be stated as twenty-one; some versions that read "ten" are erroneous. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The various types of practices and categories are all known; this is called 'all-aspect wisdom' (*sarvākārajñatā*). This refers to the three wisdoms of the Buddha-fruit.

Contemplating the ten realms and so forth is termed "universal illumination. The distinction between the provisional and the real in their various aspects is called "capacity" (*indriya*), while their lack of differentiation in the three [wisdoms] is called "principle" (*tattva*).
"Xiánjiè" (纖介) means "minute and weak. The *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* says, "Sorrow, regret, and parsimony reside in the *jiè*.
Han Kangbo’s commentary states that *jiè* refers to "the minute and subtle" (*xiánjiè*). Therefore, the character *jiè* should not be written with the radical for grass.

The "Treasury of Awakening" (*bodhigarbha*) is the "Treasury of the Buddha" (*buddhagarbha*); the meaning of "treasury" is as explained previously. To expound the eternal teaching and reveal the Buddha-nature is metaphorically described as "excavating.

If one proceeds from below to correctly demonstrate this, the reason the chapter on the "Perfection of Giving" (*dānapāramitā*) is established under the name of "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is precisely because there is wisdom within, which then manifests externally.
The *Śākyamuni-sūtra* states: "If one wishes to know wisdom, it lies in its exposition. Thus, by means of internal wisdom (*adhyātma-jñāna*), one is able to verify the meaning of external teachings.
Regarding the "five practices": these are not sequential; because the five are identical with the one, they are called the "five practices.

The subsequent text states: "Furthermore, there is one practice called the Tathāgata-practice. Because it is not the counterfeit of the Two Vehicles, it is true; because it is not that of external paths (*tīrthika*), it is authentic.
Because it is free from such perversions, it is correct; because it is not the gradual, winding path of a bodhisattva, it is harmonious and direct;
and because it is the eternally abiding Middle Way, it cannot be tilted or moved by the two extremes. The above clarifies the essence of practice.
Furthermore, the following clarifies that practice possesses the function of destroying delusions, just as a vajra can shatter and disperse all things.
The phrase "if one follows the [textual] connection" indicates the intent of citing the scriptural evidence; the term "meaning" (*yi*) refers to the underlying principle or purport.
Thus, regarding "Nirvāṇa" and so forth: Nirvāṇa is the name of a single sūtra, while Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is the meaning explained therein.

Since this meaning is both that which is explained by the teaching (*nāma-dharma*) and that which is reached through the gate of practice (*pratipatti-mukha*), this section on "Meaning" (*Artha-varga*) belongs to the latter category, whereas the preceding two belong to the former.
Yes. This meaning will be clarified below: the three virtues are sovereign liberation, certainty, and prajñā.
The fearless Dharma-body is likened to the lion’s roar; as the king of beasts roars with sovereignty and certainty, he is without fear.
This illustrates the three virtues.
If one concludes from below by showing the intent of citing evidence:
as for the identity of essence and function, it is like waves and water; first, it clarifies that through function, the essence of all phenomena is realized.

The functional joy of the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—is the very substance of the three truths of one’s own mind; since the environment and inhabitants are solely the mind, they are the function while being the substance.
Therefore, it is said that all things "exist" and "do not exist," and are neither equal nor unequal. Next, regarding "functioning while being the substance":

although it is eternally merged with the ultimate reality, it manifests through activities according to the capacities of beings, subsuming the evil and heterodox of the nine realms back into the correct goodness of the Buddha-realm.

It should be understood that the following section provides a concluding indication of the intent behind the cited evidence; the text here is abbreviated, but following the preceding pattern, it should have stated:
"If considered from the perspective of essence, it is *buddhadhātu*; if considered from the perspective of function, it is termed 'subduing and gathering' (*saṃgraha-vinaya*)."
Regarding the phrase "it should be known," since essence and function are mutually identical, it is appropriate to use the term "Buddha-nature" to refer to the chapter on the realization of function.
As for the supporting evidence, as cited previously, many passages—and indeed every single one—contain the meaning of all five chapters;
this is based upon the sūtras and is not a hollow application of one's own whimsical fabrications.
Regarding the statement that "it may be so after midday," the character "after" (後) is likely an error; it should read "before midday" (中前).
The original text says "at dawn when the sun rises," but Jingxi merely changed "sunrise" to "before midday.

This is the Master of the Commentary’s initial concession to Emperor Liang’s division of the day into "before midday" and "after midday," as seen at the beginning of the sutra: "At the early morning, at the time when the sun first rises... [the sound and light].
It would be reasonable to say that the assembly was summoned to gather together for the meal offered in the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" as the midday portion;
however, it is not tenable to claim that the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was recited after the assembly had departed as the afternoon portion.
This is because the divisions of "midday" and "afternoon" are based on the day itself; furthermore, the Tathāgata continued his teaching until midnight before finally entering parinirvāṇa.
Because the text of the *Madhyāpararātra-bhāga* (The Latter Part of the Middle) does not exhaustively include the entire sūtra, it is criticized by saying "at dusk," and so forth.

Below, the householder cites the sūtra again to offer a further critique: even if one were to include [the events] from the middle of the day through the latter part until midnight, according to the meaning of that sūtra, it would still be inconsistent.
The first fascicle of that sūtra states: "In the first year, on the fifteenth day of the second month, he proclaimed his parinirvāṇa. The second [fascicle]... [text continues].
Since he entered parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month of that year, we know that this account describes the passage of one full year.

Furthermore, because the Great Sage’s responses to conditions vary, there are differences in the length of time compared to other sūtras. Now, I cite that text to refute those who restrict the sūtra’s meaning to a specific duration.
Since this sūtra specifically addresses a particular karmic condition, if it were taught as lasting for one week, then [the meal] would have to be before midday.
Since there is no affiliation whatsoever after the midday meal, we know that the division of the sutra is based solely on the Dharma and cannot be based on time.

As for the phrase "now following," etc.: now, following the dharma-meanings of what has been taught, they are divided into five chapters; since this does not rely on time, the aforementioned difficulty does not apply.

Regarding the "Partial Application Chapter" (*yòngzhāng shǎofèn*): the present Master takes both the chapters on Kāśyapa and Cundī as the "Application Chapter," whereas that [other] tradition takes only the chapter on Cundī as the "Circulation" (*liútōng*), hence it is called "partial."

Since this occurs in a subordinate section and the questions and answers pervade the entire sutra, the remaining portions of the text concerning the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) are quite diffuse and prolix;
in the texts of Hexi, the meaning of the opponent's position is first presented, followed by the exposition of the current refutation.
Regarding the first two fascicles: the commentary composed in Hexi explains the forty-fascicle Northern Edition;
since the "Chapter on the Lifespan" spans two and a half fascicles, what is here called "two fascicles" refers to the entirety of the two sections comprising that "Chapter on the Lifespan."
Those who possess a karmic affinity from the past and present are precisely those in this assembly;
those who have newly entered are those from the Deer Park onward who received the provisional teachings—the fifty-two assemblies are exactly these people.
Because all are summoned by sound and light, it is said they are "drawn in.

The following section now refutes this. If one claims that there is a specific condition for being drawn in, one must simply accept the Master’s intention regarding the summoning of those of true practice (*shinjitsu-gyō*).
One who fully encompasses both the provisional and the real: when practicing the real, one summons the provisional; when practicing the provisional, one requests the real.
The third fascicle also relies upon the Northern Edition. Reaching the "Questions of the Great Assembly," it concludes with the tenth fascicle, comprising four and a half chapters in total:
namely, the three chapters on the Life Span, the Vajra Body, the Names and Merits, the Tathāgatagarbha, and the Great Assembly.
This is the question.
Regarding the brief and extensive sections: the thirty-four questions posed by Kāśyapa constitute the brief section (*saṃkṣipta-mukha*);
the subsequent detailed answers to those thirty-four questions constitute the extensive section (*vistara-mukha*).
Since both are within the causal stage, the ten virtues as partial fruits are themselves the true cause.
To avoid redundancy in the text: since the five practices and the ten virtues are both causal practices, they are now combined into one, thereby eliminating the fault of repetitive complexity.
"Fan" (煩) is synonymous with "fan" (繁); in the *Zhouyi*, both are written with the character "fan."
Regarding the "mixed and difficult-to-discern" [section], among the final three chapters, only the *Siṃhanāda* (Lion’s Roar) chapter explicitly clarifies the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The two chapters on Kāśyapa and Cūḍapanthaka represent the functions of subduing and gathering; since these are collectively treated as a single section, they are termed "mixed.
As for the "Master of the *Bhūmi*," the *Bhūmi-śāstra* was also composed by Vasubandhu; because this master lectured on the *Bhūmi-śāstra*, he compiled this commentary.
Since this returns to the school of Vasubandhu, the preceding text refers to it as the "Seven Parts of Vasubandhu.

Regarding the first fascicle, that treatise states that the section from the beginning "Thus" up to "the blood flowed and drenched the ground," which is named the "Division of the Manifestation of Inconceivable Supernatural Powers," constitutes the first part.

Regarding the term "reverse manifestation" (*fǎnshì*): entering from the state of an ordinary being into the state of a sage is called "conformity" (*shùn*); concealing one's sagehood to manifest as an ordinary being is called "reverse.
This refers to the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body who conceal their spiritual virtues and manifest in the forms of ghosts, animals, and so forth.
Since all fifty-two classes of beings are categorized under this, it is now refuted by saying they "attain the provisional while losing the real."

Regarding the second fascicle, the Treatise states that the two chapters titled "Cunda’s Lamentation" are named "The Section on Accomplishing the Seed-Nature" (*gotra-sampadana*) and "The Section on Dispelling Attachment.
Here, "seed-nature" refers to Cunda’s offering of food as the seed-nature for the five fruits of permanence. "Arising" is termed "nature" because the name does not change;
the offering of food is the seed of the five fruits, and permanence is the very nature of that offering of food. Therefore, it is so called.
This refers to the "spiritual lineage" (gotra).

The phrase "dispelling doubts and eliminating attachments" refers to the *Śokavinodana-parivarta*, which dispels the doubts and attachments regarding the inferior practices of former teachings by means of the three superior practices of giving and so forth.
Regarding the third fascicle, the treatise states that from "After the three proclamations" down to the end of the "Questions of the Great Assembly," the term "three proclamations" refers to:
first, in the *Cīvaravastu*, the initial exhortation for the bhikṣus to eliminate doubt; second, the exhortation to accept deposits; and third, the exhortation to receive benefits.
As for the true meaning of the True Dharma, it consists of the thirty-four questions posed by Kāśyapa, all of which inquire about the authentic Dharma, and to which the Buddha [responded] with...
This is the response that reveals the definitive meaning of reality.
Now, for those below, the "Cunda Chapter" uses the five fruits of permanent abiding to respond to the diverse assembly of this land;

the "Sorrowful Lamentation Chapter" uses the three superior cultivations to respond to the śrāvaka assembly of this land; and from the "Longevity Chapter" through the fourteenth chapter, [the Buddha] responds according to their questions.
Since this practice of giving is directed toward the assembly of bodhisattvas in this land, the present chapter on giving encompasses both of those two parts;
thus, it also constitutes the skillful means of the five practices and the accomplishment through cultivation of the ten virtues.
Regarding the term "heedfulness" (*apramāda*), the treatise states that it is the abandonment of all forms of negligence.
While the previous section [of this work] refuted [the opposing view], here we merely refute the judgment that the passage on the Lion’s Roar (*siṃhanāda*) is incorrect.

Since the meaning of "practice" (*caryā*) is already established through the cultivation of skillful means (*upāya*), there is no need for further refutation here, as the subject matter of this chapter on practice is closely related to that meaning.
Regarding "Kāśyapa and others," the *Śāstra* states that this is the section on the skillful maintenance of compassionate light;

what is here called "the compassionate maintenance" refers to the Kāśyapa Chapter, which reveals the Buddha’s compassionate skillful means in maintaining the evil of the icchantika Sunakṣatra while maintaining the goodness of the Buddha-nature.

"Revealing the characteristics" refers to the *Caitika-parivarta* (Chapter on Cunda), which reveals the false characteristics of the ten sages and restores the correct characteristics of the Buddha-nature.

"Holding evil and turning toward the good" explains the meaning of the "Abiding and Sustaining" (zhuchi) chapter; "revealing the false and returning to the correct" explains the meaning of the "Revealing Characteristics" chapter.
When these two meanings are integrated, they do not go beyond the Great Function of *Nirvāṇa*: subsuming the evil and subsuming the good.
Because it is erroneous, I have now combined these into the "Chapter on Function" (*yòng zhāng*).

However, when comparing these seven sections with the original treatise, only the first, second, fifth, and sixth [sections] show slight differences in wording, as pointed out previously; this is merely because the masters of the Di school made alterations according to their own convenience.
Among the eight gates of Xinghuang, seven gates are modeled after the Hexi tradition, while only the second gate follows the Di school.
The divisions of the sūtra text can be understood from the preceding section.

As for the "gate of the five stages" (*pañca-avasthā-mukha*), it refers to the "gate of meritorious qualities" (*guṇa-mukha*) of Hexi; because these ten qualities constitute the stages of entry into realization (*praveśa-sākṣātkriyā-avasthā*), they are termed the "gate of stages."
Regarding the distinction between the "opening" and "closing" [of the gates]: in the Hexi tradition, three categories were combined into a single Middle Way Buddha-nature gate;
here, however, we open them up, establishing Kāśyapa as the seventh, the Gate of Expedient Means, and Cunda as the eighth, the Gate of the Non-duality of the Erroneous and the Correct.

"Name and flavor are not different" means that flavor is the text. The ancient scriptures and treatises speak of "name, phrase, and flavor," while the new [translation] speaks of "name, phrase, and text.
In the Gate of the Middle Way, this is no different from Master Lang’s "name.
Although seven or eight gates are opened, they are still merely the scriptural texts within Master Lang’s Gate of the Middle Way; thus, the flavor is not different.

Second, the detailed explanation of the five sections begins with the invocation of the assembly. According to the sequence of the meaning, one should first explain the title and then interpret the main text;

however, since the profound meaning of the four-character specific title has already been exhaustively discussed in the *Fahua Xuanshu* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), and that work refers back to it, the author of this commentary does not provide a separate topical analysis of the title here. As for the lecturer, should they... [text ends]

To briefly explain the categories of this section: it should be called the "Preface" (*xu*). "Preface" means "to narrate" (*xu*); it is so called because it narrates the origins of the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
If one considers the meaning of the characters, it is identical to the character *xu* (thread/twine). The *Erya* states: "To unfold an activity in proper sequence is 'order' (*xu*).

Furthermore, "thread" (*xu*) refers to the thread of a cocoon; whenever a cocoon is unwound for silk, one first extracts its thread, and only when the thread is exhausted does the [silk] become visible.
The threads [of the text] are like a formal exposition that possesses a sequential order; once the sequence concludes, one sees that formal exposition.

The three intermediate chapters correspond to the "Chapter on the Exposition of Textual Categories" (*Zhengshuo Wenpin*); "categories" (*pin*) takes "classification" as its meaning, and because those with identical categories of meaning are gathered into a single section, it is called a "chapter.
The Northern Version merely titles this the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Shòumìng Pin*); Master Xié revised and finalized the text, opening it up to serve as the introductory prose.
One should know that at the beginning of this thirty-six-fascicle sutra, the titles of the chapters are listed directly, such as "The Preface Chapter, First" (*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Chapter One).
As for the numbering of the fascicles, they are merely noted in small characters beneath the titles;

this is because all subsequent chapter titles incorporate the name of the sutra itself, a practice common to many sutras, with the sole exception of the six hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Because the volume number was recorded directly at the beginning of each scripture, the individual chapters within the text were titled solely by their chapter names without a title for the entire scripture.
The versions currently in circulation—such as those stating "The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume One, Chapter One:
Introduction"—are the result of later generations' arbitrary alterations; they clearly failed to consider the structure of the internal chapters. If this were indeed the case, it should...

To call this alone the "Chapter on Sorrowful Lamentation" (the third) raises the question: how can it be so when all chapters share the title of the sutra? Although this is a minor matter, many people are confused by it;

therefore, in recent times, the tradition of copying the Tripitaka has generally involved arbitrarily altering the ancient texts. Yet, as many original versions still survive, they can serve as evidence.
Once the source of such confusion is resolved, it cannot be restored. If this is the case for a minor matter, how much more so for those that are far greater than this?
How tragic! As for the "compiler of the sutra," this refers to Ānanda, who was the compiler of the sutras.
Regarding the general and specific prefaces, there are three meanings of "preface" (*nidāna*): first, it means sequential order; second, it means the source or basis.

Third, "sequence" (xu) is taken as the meaning [of *nidāna*]. The first [of these three] refers to the general sequence (*sāmānyanidāna*), which means that the six matters are arranged in order at the beginning of the sutra.

The remaining two refer to the specific sequence (*viśeṣanidāna*). In this present sutra, the listing of the assembly—including the terms for summoning, responding to the invitation, requesting the Buddha to remain, and so forth—all describe the sequence.
Since these expressions are scattered throughout the various records, the three are condensed into two, referred to simply as the general and the specific.

Regarding the section on the three periods of time, the meaning is demonstrated through two pairs of examples. First, the initial pair shows that while the openings of all Buddhas' sutras are identical in being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are distinguished by the different teachings given according to the capacities of their respective audiences.
Second, the subsequent pair shows that while the openings of the sutras of the five periods are identical in being conditioned, they are distinguished by the different events that initiate them.

Regarding the identity of the path across the three periods of time, the *Śāstra* clarifies that when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked the Buddha what words should be placed at the beginning of the sūtras.
The Buddha replied: "The Dharma-treasury accumulated by me over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* should initially be stated thus: 'Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, together with such-and-such a great assembly. This is not unique to my own Dharma."
Since the beginning of the sutras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is likewise thus, it is said that "the path of the three periods is the same.
The latter portion of this sutra also speaks in accordance with this.

As for the distinction between the capacities of the teaching gate: this sutra addresses those whose capacity is to support the Vinaya while discussing the eternal; the Lotus Sutra addresses those whose capacity is for the revelation of the provisional.
Because they are the vehicles for those whose faculties are suited to the manifestation of reality, the specific events that initiate the assembly at its beginning differ.

"One period" refers to the five periods, which are vertical in terms of the ritual of transformation; "the Small and so forth" refers to the four teachings, which are horizontal in terms of the dharma of transformation.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* includes the Separate [Teaching], and even this present sutra applies these [teachings] repeatedly; all such various sutras are thus established.
This is precisely the meaning of "penetrating through.
As for "by means of the scriptures," it refers to relying upon provisional supports. When the Great Sage expounds the teachings, he must necessarily rely upon such supports;

therefore, he manifests auspicious omens to inspire the wholesome minds of sentient beings. Taking these as his basis, he is able to expound the teachings, just as this sutra uses sound and light to summon [beings].

The rain of flowers from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the shaking of the earth, the merging of canopies by Vimalakīrti, the manifestation of lands, the radiance, and the appearance of the four Buddhas—all these are established teaching gates tailored to specific capacities; thus, the scriptural sources and the texts vary accordingly.

Regarding "the combination and separation of the subject and the locus": "subject" refers to the Lord of Transformation, which is the Buddha; "locus" refers to the dwelling place, such as Kuśinagara, Rājagṛha, and so forth.
When the subject and locus are combined, there are only five [categories]; when the subject and locus are separated, they become six.
The present commentary follows the interpretation based on their combination because it is more convenient for correlating them with the five chapters.

Regarding the principle that is transmitted: Ānanda pointed to such a Dharma, saying, "This is what I heard directly from the Buddha. Thus, he designated what was heard as "the transmitted" (*śruta*).

Question: What was heard is the teaching (*dharma*); why then is it called "principle" (*tattva*)? Answer: The teaching is expounded based on the principle; the teaching fundamentally elucidates the principle.
It is only by using the principle as a seal to verify the teaching that one can understand its partial or universal aspects. Therefore, what is elucidated is designated as "the transmitted."
"Being able to transmit what was transmitted" means that Ānanda is the person who transmits and the Dharma is that which is transmitted.

"Convergence" (hui) means that the teaching now re-applied below accords with the faculties and conditions of sentient beings; thus it is said that it "converges with their capacities" (ji) and above it "converges with the Buddha."
Because it is the nature [of reality], it is called "converging with principle" (*li*). The convergence of principle and capacity (*ji*)—the unification of these two meanings—is found herein.
