That which is "received and inherited" refers precisely to the Lord Śākyamuni as the transformative master.
Regarding the phrase "the place where one hears," one should say "the place where the hearer hears"; since a "place" must necessarily correspond to a "hearer," the term "hearer" is retained here.
In brief, the auspicious assembly of the principal and its retinue must have its specific location, which is the Śāla grove.
As for those who heard it directly as companions, this means that it was not heard by me alone; there were indeed associates, namely the great bhikṣus.

Regarding the phrase "mutually verifying one another" and so forth, it means that the Tathāgata understood according to the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and spoke according to the true nature of phenomena; what he taught is authentic.
Because the truth must be trustworthy and followed, the initial establishment of such and such teachings is essential.

If these were transmitted through hearsay from others, errors and distortions would frequently arise; however, since they have now been heard directly, they are trustworthy. Thus, the entire assembly receives them with no cause for doubt.

Therefore, it next says, "Thus have I heard," and further cites the occasion when the fourfold assembly was moved by the teaching and attained the Way, thereby assisting in the accomplishment of this trustworthiness.
Therefore, it is said that "at one time," and furthermore, it is raised that the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One spoke these truthful words when preaching this wondrous Dharma in Kuśinagara;
since what was received is so supreme, it is revered by all sentient beings, hence the phrase "the Buddha dwelt in Kuśinagara," etc.
Moreover, it points out that the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as devas and nāgas, heard this together with me—how could this be a mistaken transmission?

"Desiring to cause [others] to be equal" means that these five meanings are intended precisely to encourage the attainment of Buddhahood, so that future generations who see or hear them may have their doubts stilled and their faith increased.

Regarding "the various scriptures of the Small and Great Vehicles": the Small refers exclusively to the Tripiṭaka, while the Great encompasses the three teachings; subsequently, there are no distinctions between Small and Great, nor between Common, Separate, and Perfect.
The distinction lies in the fact that the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) alone receives this grand name, as it is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna.

This is as indicated by the subsequent inquiry in the text. Within the text, the four teachings differ according to their respective meanings: the *Zang* (Tripitaka) teaching is distinguished by its doctrine and principle;

the *Tong* (Shared) teaching by two kinds of *nirvāṇa*; the *Bie* (Distinct) teaching by the distinction between self and others; and the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching by the pervasiveness of the nature. Regarding the *Zang*, it is said that "two matters are similar."
That which Ānanda transmitted is no different from what the Buddha taught; because his words accord with principle, they are said to be "without error.

As for "understanding merging with the truth": understanding is the wisdom that contemplates, while truth is the principle that is contemplated. When one understands in accordance with the principle, understanding and principle merge in profound stillness.
This takes *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder) as the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*).

Regarding "the body becoming ash," this refers to taking *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) as the goal. The "ten practices" involve emerging into the provisional realm and universally employing the four teachings according to the capacities of beings;
this explains "conformity" (*rū*) in terms of transforming others. When matters appear contrary, it refers to the sequence of the three contemplations;
when the principle is harmonious, it refers to the realization of the path where all is identical to the Perfect [Teaching]. This explains "is-ness" (*shi*) in terms of one's own practice.
If one says that the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is explained in this way solely from the perspective of principle, [it is because] only in the first three teachings do demons and Buddhas differ;

it is not because [in those teachings] form and fragrance deviate from the Way. This is not what is being clarified here. We clarify that while the myriad objects differ, the single principle returns to the same source.

The Dharma-body pervades all, so how could there be any difference between demons and Buddhas? The nature of the mind encompasses all, including form and fragrance. It is not that the Perfect and Sudden teaching lacks such pervasive integration.

It is said thus: furthermore, one should know that form and fragrance are but a small portion of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); the Middle Way is but another name for Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).
How much more so when form encompasses both the internal and external—the external being the Buddha-land (*buddhakṣetra*) and the internal being the physical aggregates (*skandha*).

If one realizes that the Middle Way within form and fragrance is precisely the presence of nature in insentient things (*niṣceṣṭa*), then one deeply understands that the three thousand realms are contained within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), and that those with this nature shall attain Buddhahood.

To explain in a manner that is harmonious and logically consistent—meaning those passages that can be understood through analogy—I shall apply this same method of interpretation across the four teachings to the sections from "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) up to "those who heard it together.

This will be done in detail within the subsequent section on the specific interpretation of the text, where the passage beginning with "Thus have I heard" will be fully analyzed according to each of the four teachings. However, [the current section] is restricted [to a general overview].

The commentary on this has already been explained in detail; therefore, these [points] are seen both before and after [one another] to save on brush and ink, demonstrating the artistry of the composition.
Thus, the Dragon [Master] below cites the *Śāstra* (Treatise) to establish and encourage the meaning of faith. The *Śāstra* says: "In the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is..."
"Being able to enter and being thus" are terms of virtuous faith; such a believer says, "This matter is thus," and so forth.
If one believes [the passage] below, it serves as a general conclusion that both the provisional and the real are entered through faith.

Since this sutra emphasizes the bestowal of the four teachings, we know that these five points encourage faith in both the provisional and the real. However, their meaning is eternally different from the previous four flavors (*pañcarasa*); whereas previously...

If the provisional and the real are not yet integrated, then one now knows that all things are eternally abiding (*nitya*). When compared with the *Lotus Sūtra*, there are both differences and similarities:
in terms of repeated application, they differ; in terms of realizing the reality, they are the same.

As for the phrase "in detail as follows," the *Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra* explains this extensively by means of four principles for each: the principle of causes and conditions (*nidāna*), the principle of teaching (*yoga*), the principle of the original and the trace (*mūla-vyañjana*), and the principle of the fundamental and the manifest (*mūla-vyañjana*).
The "Contemplation of the Mind" (*Guānxīn*) is pointed out in that [previous] text, so it is omitted here; however, regarding the interpretation of the teachings within this school:

when explaining the various sutras prior to the *Lotus Sutra*, there are only three interpretations, because the fundamental [truth] has not yet been revealed, thus lacking the distinction between the Fundamental and the Traces (*benji*), or explaining them by way of essence and function (*tǐyòng*) as a general approach.
When explaining the present sutra, however, the four categories of meaning are complete, as they follow the revelation of the Fundamental; therefore, [this section is provided].

Because of this "gathering up," the present explanation of the final five chapters— which accord with the meaning of the introduction— clearly demonstrates that the division of sections within this school perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intent.

Regarding "not different" and so forth, these terms indicate the meaning from the perspective of principle. "Not different" means that Māra and the Buddha are of one suchness; "not not" means that form and fragrance are both [the Dharma].
If one does not descend to cite delusion to manifest awakening, there is no understanding of "no names" and so on; therefore, it is said that one must not thus cling to the traces.
Because one is deluded regarding the fundamental, there is a fixed attachment to phenomena; because one forgets the principle, there is a fixed denial of it.

One who penetrates this meaning realizes that the five [aggregates] are identical to the arising of understanding, for the realization of the principle is ultimately one; thus, it is called "penetrating the meaning."
From "Arranged in rows" (*liè*) downward, the text correctly raises the point of summoning the assembly to clarify this meaning.
Regarding the *qiūqiāng* (dung beetle), the *Erya* states it is the *qiāngláng*. Cui Bao’s *Gujīn Zhù* says it is able to encase dung in soil and roll it into balls;
the *Zhuangzi* says, "The wisdom of the *qiāngláng* lies in rolling its ball. The subsequent scripture says: "Then..."
Even venomous snakes whose gaze can kill, dung beetles (*kīṭaka*), scorpions (*vṛścika*), and all sixteen kinds of evildoers gathered together;
the dung beetle is mentioned here because it is the most minute among the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).
Those who have returned include five groups of beings, from nāgas, ghosts, māras, and Brahmās up to bodhisattvas, totaling fifty-two assemblies.
They are strange and extraordinary; the distinctions among the various realms of existence—whether based on the correct or the dependent—are chaotic and intermingled.

In the *Dhvaja-ma-hā-sūtra*, the assembly of the upper realms is enumerated: it states that the lowest of the banners reaches as far as the realm of Maheśvara, and that the shortest of the streamers is suspended in the Brahma palace;
therefore, it is said that they reach the Brahma world (*brahmaloka*).
The *Sūtra on Covering the Great Trichiliocosm* further states that even a small precious canopy can cover a great trichiliocosm;
[the bodhisattvas] came to the Buddha's presence bringing such articles of offering as these.

The "large" and "small" refer to the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*); the "refined" and "coarse" refer to the secondary environment (*bhājana-loka*). "Small" refers to creatures such as dung beetles, mosquitoes, and gadflies;

"large" refers to beings such as the Bodhisattva Anantagātra. Regarding "mutual displacement," this means the large displacing the small; for example, when the Bodhisattva Anantagātra arrived, the hairs on the bodies of all the devas stood on end.
The upright one sees his own body as lacking radiance and so forth; this is like reducing the minute to the vast and then overturning it.

Among the various assemblies preparing offerings, there are differences in quality, alternating between the refined and the coarse; because the refined supersedes the coarse, it is said they "outshine" one another.
Thus, the subsequent sutra states, "twice as superior as before," and so on.

If one uses the following analogy—mistaking a cow for a sheep due to confused vision and failing to recognize the cardinal directions—it illustrates how deluded followers fail to comprehend the relationship between the provisional (迹) and the fundamental (本).
This is why it was said previously, "If one does not [attain] such [realization]," and so forth; thus, they merely perceive the various discrepancies and contradictions among the multitudes.
How could they know that although the manifestations differ, they share the same single principle without duality? Therefore, it is said, "How could they attain such [realization]?"
"Attaining such [a state]" below clarifies that the realization and vision are identical.

This means that those who have awakened to the principle know that the fifty-two assemblies are all Bodhisattvas of partial truth (*bhūta-ārya*) who manifest according to the capacities and benefits of beings; though their traces differ, their fundamental essence is the same.
Since the phenomena appear different while the principle is fundamentally one, one knows that such a meaning accords with the various chapters. Question: If it is said that there are fifty-two...
If all members of the assembly were Great Beings (mahāsattva) of the Dharma-body, then they would have attained the provisional while losing the real;

if there were those with actual practice, such a principle would contradict [the premise] and the two meanings would be mutually exclusive. How can this be explained away? To answer: let us first clarify the provisional. Since the provisional must lead to the real principle, the Great Being likewise dwells in the *Śūraṅgama*;
though the traces differ, the essence is the same. Thus, the ice melts away and the three—ordinary beings, sages, and the Buddha—are seen to be without distinction.
Because it is as it has always been, one who has not yet awakened the mind is called a bodhisattva. As for what was said previously regarding "original and trace" in terms of essence and function:

when Ānanda says, "In the past I did not hear [this]," he is referring to his own admission that during the four periods of the Dharma-taste, he had not heard that the two kinds of giving are without difference, nor had he heard of the *Amitābha* (New I), the *Guhyaka* (Secret), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "seeing eight *hu* [measures] and so forth," this refers to seeing the presentation of offerings as the cause for hearing the Dharma; thus, by seeing it, one hears it.

The *Dàzhòngwèn pǐn* (Chapter on the Great Assembly’s Questions) states: "At that time, the refined rice and matured foods brought by Cunda, which filled eight *hu* according to the measure of the kingdom of Magadha, were all made sufficient for the entire great assembly through the Buddha’s spiritual power."
Regarding the two types of giving and so forth, the *Cunda-parivarta* states: The Buddha said to Cunda, "There are two fruits of the gift of food, which are equal and without distinction.
What are these two? First, having received it, one attains *samyak-saṃbodhi*; second, having received it, one enters *nirvāṇa*.
By my accepting your final offering, I cause you to fulfill the *dāna-pāramitā*. This is the intention of the Buddha.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, when the body of Vairocana was first perfected, the Buddha’s light was poured upon him as a consecration (abhiṣeka), which is termed "receiving food.
Therefore, there is no difference between this and the present sutra regarding the fruition of having received [the meal] and entering Great Nirvāṇa.

If one were to refer to the Lesser Vehicle’s initial reception of the milk from the cowherd girl as "receiving food," then there would indeed be a distinction from the present case. Thus, Cunda immediately contrasted the small-scale beginning with the great-scale conclusion.
Regarding the difficulty of distinguishing [the characters] (and so forth):

Shin, I, and the others were lamenting when the Buddha raised the three dots of the character *i*, neither vertical nor horizontal, as a metaphor for the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*)—which are eternally blissful, self, and pure—and thus called it the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyakośa*), the Buddha-nature. Therefore, it is said: "The secret treasury is the Buddha-nature."

The "various flavors of the Dharma" refers to the fact that within the *Āyuṣparyanta-parivarta* (Chapter on Longevity), Kāśyapa posed thirty-four questions, to which the Buddha replied one by one across fourteen chapters; hence they are called the "various flavors of the Dharma.

Since these were all teachings that Ānanda had not previously heard but now hears for the first time, it is known that the meaning of "I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) should be applied within the introduction concerning the practice of the sequence.
In the Separate Teaching (*bīe-jiao*), one cultivates the five practices sequentially and realizes the ten virtues at successive stages; this is called "different times" rather than "one time.

Regarding the phrase "returning to the body" (*gui-shen*) and so forth in the section on the Prologue (*xu-yi*): this combines the transforming subject (*hua-zhu*) and the dwelling place (*zhu-chu*) into one. "Body" (*shen*) refers to the Buddha-body (*fo-shen*).
Buddha-nature (*foxing*) is the principle (*li*) that is realized, while the ground (*di*) represents the wisdom (*zhi*) that realizes it; thus, the principle is taken as the body.
When one reaches the ultimate limit, wisdom ceases; when one finds the place of rest, the body returns [to its source].
Regarding "driving out the heterodox," this refers to expelling the various non-Buddhists from the six great cities so that they all turn toward Kuśinagara.
Regarding "neither withered," etc., the space between the eight trees symbolizes the Middle Way.
If it were another, one would bind the upper [gate] to expel the heterodox and draw in the evil;

if it is oneself, one binds the upper [gate] because the intermediate [state] and the secret treasury of quiescence (śānti-guhya-kośa) return to the same source. Thus it is said that one stops at the ultimate limit. This is as the Sūtra says:

"I shall place all my children within the secret treasury, and I myself shall not long remain outside, but abide therein. Therefore, we know that the dwelling place is the sequence for realizing the principle.
The introduction uses the term "zhì" (螫), which is also read as "hū" (呼) or "gè zhī liè" (各知列)—the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "the movement of poisonous insects.

Regarding the "three sons" and so forth: at the beginning of the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, Kāśyapa questioned the Buddha, saying, "Why did you not first preach the Dharma for Śunakṣatra, and only later for the Bodhisattvas?
If you cannot save Śunakṣatra, how can you be said to possess great compassion? Therefore, the Buddha cited three [cases].
In the *Upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, it is said: "Suppose, for example, a father and mother have three sons:
the first is faithful, compliant, and respectful toward his parents, possessing sharp faculties and wisdom; the second is disrespectful and lacks faith, yet possesses sharp faculties and wisdom;
the third lacks both. If the parents wish to instruct them, whom should they teach first? Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha: "They should first teach the second son."
First, as for the second and third [sons], although those two sons lacked faith, obedience, and a heart of reverence, he taught them next out of compassionate concern.
As for the third son, the first [son] is a metaphor for a bodhisattva, the middle for a śrāvaka, and the last for an icchantika.
Next, three fields are raised as metaphors, saying: "It is like three kinds of fields with a single irrigation channel."

First, the soil is easy to cultivate and free from saline alkalinity, such that one seed yields a hundred or two; second, although there is no saline alkalinity, the irrigation channels are difficult to manage, so that even if the harvest is gathered, it is reduced by half;
third, the irrigation channels are difficult to manage and the soil is largely saline, such that one seed yields only one.

Furthermore, the analogies of the three vessels, the three diseases, the three horses, and the three men all share the same intent as the first case. The meaning of the current text is that [the realms] are like those of ghosts and animals.

The third son, Icchantika, is illustrated by the analogy of the evil destinies (durgati). Based on their causes, they are likened to ghosts and animals; based on their results, it is because of being Icchantikas that they receive the bodies of ghosts and animals.

Now, listing them together with those who hear [the Dharma], we know that the combined application of the teachings—namely, the functions of subsuming the evil and subsuming the heterodox—is consistent with the principles of the examples.
As for "shudang" (屬當), the pronunciation is "zhudang."
Now, regarding the initial clarification of the assembly at the beginning of the text, it is thus complete with five parts, the first being the assembly.

As for the "eight Buddhas," six are the present Buddhas, making six; the past Buddha makes seven; and the Buddha from another direction makes eight. The fifty-two assemblies are not outside these eight.
Of these, the first four are those of actual practice (*satyavādin*), and thus they are summoned; the latter four are those of expedient practice (*upāya-vādin*), and thus they are invited.
At this point, it is known that these eight [Buddhas] exist among all classes of beings—devas, humans, ghosts, and animals. Question: Why are future Buddhas not included? Answer:
Future Buddhas are identical to the previous five; they are simply humans. Question: Since past Buddhas and those of other directions are already ultimate, there should only be six Buddhas.
Answer: That is indeed so. However, we now include the present ones because within the current assembly, there are those who increase in the Path and those who diminish in it.

Birth refers to newly entering the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment from the position of Equal Enlightenment as the ultimate; this specifically indicates those who attained Buddhahood prior to this assembly, namely those of the past in other lands.
The present Buddha is Śākyamuni, together with his retinue. Since the principle of self and others is identical in their nature, it is said they are "not different.
Although ordinary beings and sages differ, all six are Buddhas; therefore, it is said there is "nothing that is not [a Buddha]."
Second, regarding the sequence of the two types of giving: the sequence of giving to the Tathāgata and the sequence of practice are identical; the meaning of this sequence can be seen as follows.
Because evil and the sequence are one, and because evil itself is the Buddha-nature, it is called "non-duality. Because it transcends partial principles, it is said to be "without fault.
Next, regarding the five chapters of the "I Heard" (Evam mayā śrutam) formula, the first character of each of the five texts says "I [heard] in the past," all of which refers to the Deer Park.

Whether referring to the past or the present, this convention merely concerns the relative distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles. For instance, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is called the second turning of the Dharma wheel, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths; now you again turn the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma.
These passages may also be understood as collectively referring to the four preceding flavors (the four periods of teaching) as the "past."
The fourfold assembly consists of two groups each for the laity and the ordained. Within these four assemblies, there are further four categories:

those with whom one forms a karmic connection (*karmabandha*), those who are the primary audience (*pratyarhita*), those who inspire and influence others, and those who are the "echoes and shadows" (*pratibimba*). Those with whom one forms a karmic connection are, in principle, Buddhas.

Those who are the primary audience are Buddhas in terms of their names, their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), and their stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*). Those who inspire and influence others include those who have attained partial realization (*viśeṣa-adhigama*) or ultimate realization (*niṣṭhā-gata*), as well as others from the past.
Since they are the Buddhas of the ten directions, it is said that the eight Buddhas are the fourfold assembly.

Regarding the sequence of offerings, it speaks of "superiority and inferiority between the beginning and the end": "the beginning" refers to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), where [the Buddha] first received the milk from the cowherd woman;

this is inferior because it was a body of mixed food (*miśrāhāra*). "The end" refers to the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), where he later received the offering of Cunda; this is superior because it was the eternally abiding body (*nitya-kāya*). This is as stated in the *Cunda-sūtra*.
Cunda raises the initial objection at the beginning of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
"Migration" (*qiānyí*) means that the food offered by Cunda at the beginning results only in the five fruits of impermanence; hence it is called "migration.
"Now he hears" and below is the text of the Buddha’s response to Cunda. The Buddha relies on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as the initial [teaching], whereas the present [teaching] is the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Because it is seen by those of great capacity in the future, and because both the beginning and the end are eternal, there is no distinction between them.
In the *Preface to the Practice* (*Xuxing*), it says that the winding course of rivers is a metaphor for the practices of the partial and the small;

that which is like a straight cord refers to the great river of golden sand flowing directly into the ocean, which is a metaphor for the practice of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*). These are all...

Regarding the text of the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Āryacaryā-varga*), it states in the section on the meaning of the introduction: "Even emptiness is not yet seen. This refers to the teaching of the sequential stages of the former [Hīnayāna] teachings: the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) sees coarse forms; the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) sees subtle forms;

the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) sees empty phenomena (*śūnya-dharma*); the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) sees the provisional (*prajñapti*); and the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) sees the middle. It should be stated that the fleshly eye sees coarse forms.
If the eye cannot yet see even subtle forms, how can it now perceive emptiness? This is merely a provisional explanation based on the sequence and relative depth of the three truths.
Since the eye cannot even perceive the shallowness of true emptiness, how much less could it perceive the profundity of the Middle Way?

The reason the fleshly eye is called the Buddha-eye is that it is so designated based on the meaning of "identity" within the two stages of the name-stage (*nāma-bhūmi*) and the contemplative practice-stage (*manasikāra-bhūmi*);
thus, it is clear and distinct. However, if distinguished according to the six meanings of the true [Buddha-eye], it is not yet fully clear.
The preface states in the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean): "Jing and Wei are the names of two rivers located in Chang'an;
the Jing River is turbid like the evil of Sudarśana, while the Wei River is clear like the goodness of Rāhula."
"Tracks" refer to wheel-ruts; the heterodoxy of the ten celestial immortals and the orthodoxy of Cunda are like two chariots traveling on divergent tracks.
As for "Dīpamāla" and others, this refers to the parable of the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Ganges River spoken by the Buddha in the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*:

first, those who are perpetually submerged, such as large fish that have received bodies due to great evil karma and dwell in the deep; second, those who emerge briefly and then return [to the depths].
First, "submergence" means that when the body is heavy and situated in shallow water, it sinks back down because of the light.

Second, "staying after emerging" means that the *timi* fish, being in shallow water, delights in seeing the light and remains there after surfacing. Third, "observing the four directions after emerging" refers to the *cakra* fish, which surveys all four directions in search of food.
Fourth, "walking after surveying" refers to the *cakra* fish, which, having seen [something] from afar...
"Other things" refers to edible food; one hastens toward it—this is the sixth. "Having walked, one then stands still" refers to the fish, which, once having obtained edible food, immediately stops.
"That which moves both on water and on land" is the tortoise.

By means of these seven analogies, from the first regarding the *icchantika* up to the seventh, the Buddha illustrates the differences between the three vehicles, the Buddhas, and the seven types of persons, yet the Buddha-nature is [the same].
Just as the seven classes [of beings] coexist within the river water, so too do good and evil, the heterodox and the orthodox, follow no different paths.
As for *dīmī*, according to the *Sāncāng* (Three Cang), its phonetic transcription is *dīxià* (lower tone); it refers to a fish with a massive body.
The divine tortoise is called "divine" because it can know good and ill fortune;
the *Baïhùtōng* says that it is an object of longevity within heaven and earth, and thus it is questioned. The word for "tortoise" (*guī*) signifies "long-lasting."

Regarding the "one time" (ekasmin samaye) at the beginning of the text: the first "one time" is the sequence for the assembly; the second "one time" is the sequence for the prostration and reverent practice;

and the phrase "dwells in the secret treasury" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is the sequence for the meaning. The passage "hearing that [the Tathāgata] eternally abides," etc., is the sequence for the function.

Each of these passages can be seen by referring to the original scriptural texts they cite. Within the descriptions of the dwelling places, the term Kuśinagara is used throughout to represent the principle of Buddha-nature.

Regarding "sound, light, and so forth," this means that by means of the sound of the Buddha-way and the light of wisdom, one summons those of perfect capacity toward the dwelling place of the Middle Way within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
From the word "Buddha" onwards, it is called "bestowing" because he explains and demonstrates the realization to others.

From the Buddha’s descent, one relies on principle to give rise to practice; by analytically breaking through ignorance and seeing the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), one is said to see the Buddha’s dwelling place.
By subsuming all phenomena through principle, even the wicked and evil are not omitted, thereby manifesting the great function.

All of these are explained according to the signified (*lakṣya*) to clarify the five meanings of the signifier (*lakṣaṇa*) regarding Kuśinagara. Within the introductory section of the "Those Who Heard Together" (*saha-śruta*), the meanings of the five chapters are all established with "those who heard together" as the basis.
At the beginning of the passage:
"As for 'hearing and seeing,' etc., hearing sounds and seeing light both manifest the eternally abiding and unchanging; this is the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness), not anything else.
Regarding "all others," the three teachings and four flavors are all termed "others"; they are all skillful means (*upāya*), and "others" implies that they have not yet reached ultimate realization.
The meaning of "expedient means" (*upāya*) is a designation for that which is indirect and skillful; since this is not an expedient means, it is the ultimate truth (*bhūtatathatā*).
"Hearing together," etc., refers to the sequence of giving. The questions and answers refer to the inquiries made by Cunda, Kāśyapa, and others, and the Buddha’s responses.

Regarding the Western Sea, the *Xi jing* (Western Scripture) states: "For example, the great river of golden sand flows directly into the Western Sea. Here, the sea is used as a metaphor for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
As for "evil and so forth," all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; in the mere stirring of a thought, the three thousand realms are fully present.
Therefore, even non-Buddhists, heterodox persons, icchantikas, and those of extreme evil all possess Buddha-nature; because they possess this nature, they have the capacity to achieve Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the following addresses the essential meaning of this sutra.

Regarding the "three points," in the *Śokavarga* (Chapter on Lamentation), the Buddha employs the three points of the letter "i" as a metaphor for the mutual fusion of the Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation.
These three dharmas are eternal because they do not undergo transition through emptiness or conventionality;

they are blissful because they are not oppressed by the two extremes; they are self-sovereign because they universally encompass all; and they are pure because their nature is free from delusion and defilement. Each possesses these qualities.

For these four reasons, they are called "virtues" (*guṇa*). Thus, the *Fameng xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) states: "Because of the dharmakāya, prajñā, and liberation, they are called the 'Three';
because of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, they are called 'Virtues'. This is the pivotal essence of the correct teaching and the compass for the present doctrine;

therefore, by further correlating the five meanings with the three and four [categories], it is clearly shown that this introduction and the main body [of the sūtra] are not empty, but serve to encourage faith.

Regarding "not allowing [the strokes] to run vertically" and so forth: in the Western Regions (India), the new *i* (ī) is like the cursive script (*cǎoshū*) of this region, where the lower character has one dot above and two dots below, with a fine line connecting them.
The large dot represents the "one" that is three, and the fine lines represent the "three" that are one;

thus they differ from the vertical stroke of the water radical (*shuǐ*) and the horizontal stroke of the fire radical (*huǒ*). "Parallel" refers to the meaning of verticality, while "distinct" refers to their differentiation.

Regarding the meaning of "transverse" (*yōng*), this general introduction contrasts it with the "longitudinal" (*zòng*) arrangement of the three virtues in the partial and limited vehicles; thus, they are not equivalent.

From the passage beginning "I have heard," wisdom arises from hearing the teachings; therefore, it corresponds to *prajñā*. Furthermore, the "Chapter on the King of Virtues" clarifies that... [text truncated].
Because hearing, hearing, and hearing are themselves *prajñā*, they are set in opposition [to the other two].
That the three delusions below are severed simultaneously and the two deaths are destroyed simultaneously is precisely liberation;
it is not a process of severing and destroying through successive stages at different times.
The "dwelling place" refers to the lower dharma-body, which is the principle realized; it is the dwelling place of wisdom and cessation.
In this passage, the three virtues are all explained according to the meaning of being attained through cultivation.
As for "not false," the three dots represent the wondrous teaching that is true and without error; the intent of the "witnessing and believing" by those who hear together lies herein.

Regarding the general introduction to the four virtues: if one relies on their distinct meanings, the Dharma-body possesses the two virtues of permanence and self, while Prajñā possesses only purity, and Vimukti only bliss;

thus, they are not as such [in a complete sense]. Now, because these three dharmas are perfectly interfused, each and every one of them possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, it is called "Thus."

Regarding the sequence of "joy" (*sukha*): upon hearing the teaching, one awakens to the principle that *nirvāṇa* (quiescence) is joy; furthermore, as the Sūtra below states, "The joy of much learning and discernment," it is therefore sequenced by "hearing" as joy.
First, because the Middle Way is free from the defilements of the two extremes, it is sequenced by "purity" (*śubha*) at this stage.
Because it abides without shifting, it is sequenced by "permanence" (*nitya*). Because both self and others hear it together and freely receive its benefit, [it is sequenced by "self"]...
Those who heard it together [recorded] this preface to extol my virtue.
Following this pattern, the conclusion serves as a model for further elaboration;

let others reflect upon the remaining examples. Now, I shall tentatively consider one point to demonstrate to future students: furthermore, regarding the five practices and ten virtues— [The text continues with the specific analysis of these categories.]
This is the essential core of this sutra. If one wishes to provide a preface, one should know that such a general preface consists of five lines;
because these five lines are identical to the One, there is no fault in their lacking a sequential order. Thus, the "I have heard" preface refers to the Noble Practice:
having heard the Vinaya Piṭaka, one cultivates the Noble Practice of Precepts; having heard the Sūtra Piṭaka, one cultivates the Noble Practice of Concentration; having heard the Abhidharma Piṭaka...

The section on the sequence of the noble practice of cultivated wisdom refers to the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), meaning that compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity do not distinguish between enemies and kin, but provide equal salvation at all times.

The section on the sequence of the dwelling place refers to the celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*); this means the principle of natural spontaneity, which is the dwelling place of wisdom. Because one gives rise to practice based upon this principle, it is called celestial conduct.

The section on the sequence of those who heard [the teaching] together refers to the two types of "sick children," meaning that among the fifty-two assemblies, both the virtuous and the non-virtuous are included.

If those among the assembly of ghosts and beasts who hear [this teaching] immediately enter the stage of the sick, and those among the assembly of humans and devas who hear it immediately enter the stage of the infant, then since this is the case for these five practices, the ten virtues can be understood accordingly;
how much more so when Guangzhai’s interpretation states that the fifty [virtues] are merely matters of expansion and contraction.
Furthermore, the four phrases such as "the non-arising of arising" and the three causes of the five Buddha-natures are all essential meanings, as illustrated in the third section.
The meaning of this point is as clear as pointing at one's palm, so it will not be discussed further.
Second, regarding the detailed explanation according to the text: within the five prefaces of the sutra, the commentary lacks an explanation for the term "thus" (*evam*).
This is because the previous section has already provided an explanation of it in terms of the four teachings; therefore, it is not clarified here.
In the opening section of "Thus Have I Heard," four phrases are listed at the outset to correspond to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).

Regarding the term "self" (*ātman*): the first instance of the word "self" refers to the delusively grasped self of non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings, which generally serves as the object of contemplation for all four teachings;

here, it is specifically clarified as the object of the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) teaching. The second instance of the word "self" refers to the wisdom of contemplation that investigates and seeks out [the nature of] the self.
According to the Sarvāstivāda, the self exists only as a name; according to the Saṃmitīya, there is a provisional self;

and the Vātsīputrīya clarifies that the self is in the fifth category (*pañcama-koṭi*). Although these views differ, they all refute the externalist conception of a substantial *ātman* by explaining it as a merely nominal self.

Therefore, the character "self" (*ātmā*) in the following phrase belongs to the wisdom of contemplation. This fourfold analysis of the self is the "Pure Name" (*viśuddha-nāman*) from the *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light).

All of these texts exist, yet commentators provide different interpretations of their meaning. Some say that the "upper self" (*ūrdhva-ātman*) is the object of grasping (*grāhya*) and the "lower self" (*adhaḥ-ātman*) is the subject of grasping (*grāhaka*).
Others say that the upper self has not yet distinguished between the true and the false, while the lower self is the deluded self of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If this were the case, there would only be objects of perception and no contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*); since such wisdom is absent, these would simply be the six classes of ordinary beings. How, then, could one take the former [the upper self] as...?
Is this phrase a "repository" (pitaka)? Now, in our explanation, we should select the best [interpretation] and follow it.
Regarding "self and non-self": the self that is universally grasped as a delusion is empty by its very nature; therefore, it is called "self and non-self.

"Non-self" is precisely the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). An ordinary person, at the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*), destroys the delusively grasped self and enters true non-self.
In the "Ten Practices" (*Daśabhūmika*), the True Non-Self is negated to bring forth the provisional designation of Self; the text is shown here in brief, referring simply to "Non-Self" and "Self.

Furthermore, according to the intent of the teachings, bringing forth the provisional to transform others is considered primary. Thus, for those of the Perfect Teaching (*Vairocana-yāna*), they realize that the self clung to through delusion is itself emptiness.

Therefore, it is not that "non-self" is emptiness, but rather that while non-self is emptiness, the perfect nature of the provisional is nonetheless fully present. Emptiness and the provisional are thus spontaneous and natural.
Within the unmoving nature of the mind, the Middle Way’s nature of mind is the dual negation of the two extremes. Ānanda’s fourfold understanding refers to this fourfold teaching.
Regarding the phrase "hearing what is heard," some interpret these two characters as referring to the faculty of hearing and the object of hearing; however, I say this is not so.

Since the "object of hearing"—the teaching—is already established in the initial introduction, the current statement "I have heard" carries the meaning of the "faculty of hearing. To penetrate this faculty of hearing through its fourfold understanding is not [merely] to understand the four teachings.

Because they are the same, four teachings are established. It should be understood that "superior hearing" refers to the convergence of the three—ordinary beings' faculties, objects, and consciousness—which enables hearing;

"inferior hearing" refers to the contemplative wisdom of the Tripitaka Teaching, wherein the ear, relying on the convergence of various conditions, has a hearing that is empty and false, unlike ordinary beings who cling to it as fixed and real.
The two phrases regarding the "Shared" and "Distinct" [teachings] may be understood by analogy with the [discussion on] the self.

Regarding the phrase "not hearing, not not hearing," some commentators explain that the character "not" (fēi) above does not function as a negation but serves to connect to the subsequent phrase, meaning "neither hearing nor not hearing.
If one applies this same logic to the four propositions concerning the self (*ātman*), this interpretation is somewhat superior;

it means that because the sense organs and their conditions are empty, there is no hearing, yet because the nature of hearing is inherently present within the principle (*li*), there is no non-hearing. This clarifies the meaning within the context of the indeterminacy of the true and the conventional.
Question: Why does the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) not say "neither hearing nor non-hearing"? Answer: This fourfold formulation of "hearing" appears in the text of the Sūtra below.

Since the Sūtra itself says "not hearing, not hearing," why must it be altered? Interpreting the meaning according to the occasion and training [the reader] to understand what is not [explicitly stated] is without fault.
As the Confucian texts say, "Do not let the letter obstruct the meaning," and as the Sūtra says, "Rely on the meaning, do not rely on the words"—this is precisely what is meant.

Furthermore, as the *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) contrasts "hearing" and "not hearing" with the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching), while the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) contrasts them with the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching), we know that the interpretation of meanings does not necessarily follow a single path.

Regarding the three types [of flavors] below: although this present sūtra bestows the four teachings, they all ultimately converge upon the Perfect; therefore, it is judged that the three flavors of the past are all subsumed within it.
The same applies to the subsequent sections as a matter of course.
This explains the methods of counting and the directions within a single moment. First, there is the method of worldly counting;
this serves as the common object of observation for the three contemplations.

Regarding the meaning of the Two Vehicles: because the subsequent sutra clarifies that by contemplating the realm of causes and conditions with inferior wisdom one attains the fruit of a Śrāvaka—this is the meaning of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka)—and by contemplating it with middle-level wisdom one attains the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha—this is the meaning of the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā)—one may alternatively say there are two vehicles according to the two teachings;
however, following the sutra is the correct interpretation.

Regarding the unification of the ultimate and the conventional: within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi*), the provisional is identical to emptiness; because their essences are mutually identical, this constitutes the meaning of "unification.

For those of the Shared Teaching who rely on habitual tendencies, this is not the meaning of unification. Since this phrase stands alone within the Distinct Teaching, it serves as a verification that the previous two vehicles possess the meaning of partial correspondence.
Specifically, in the Tripitaka Teaching, all three vehicles are termed *śrāvaka*; in the Shared Teaching, all three vehicles are termed *pratyekabuddha*.
The four lines following "Awakening" (etc. reveal the interpenetration of the three truths, which is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

1. "One" is emptiness; "all" is provisionality. Since the first line is emptiness while being provisionality, it says "one. 2. Since the second line is provisionality while being emptiness, it says "all one.
3. The third line clarifies the Middle Way as the non-duality of both. 4. The fourth line clarifies the Middle Way as the simultaneous illumination of both.

Regarding the explanation of the dwelling place, *buddha* in Sanskrit is translated here as "the Awakened One" (*jùzhě*). This means one who has awakened by oneself, awakened others, and whose practice of awakening is perfected.
The commentary states that because he has attained clear and great enlightenment regarding the mundane and supramundane, the permanent and the impermanent, and so forth, he is named Buddha.

Regarding the three bodies and four meanings: when Ānanda says "this is my self" and uses his faculty of hearing to hear, he personally receives the teaching from the Buddha of the sixteen-foot form who maintains the Dharma of analyzing emptiness;

this is common. When Ānanda says "this is not my self" and uses his faculty of hearing to not hear, he personally receives the teaching from the Buddha of the combined form of the sixteen-foot and the special body who maintains the Dharma of the identity of emptiness; this is distinct. When Ānanda says "this is not my self" and uses his faculty of not-hearing to hear, he personally receives [the teaching].
The Buddha of the Honored Distinct Body (Prabhūtaratna) upholds the sequential Dharma, while Ānanda upholds the non-sequential Dharma-treasury.
Because this is neither "self" nor "non-self," and because it functions through not hearing yet hearing, one personally receives [the teaching of] the Dharma-body Buddha.

Since the Universal sees the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya), the Individual sees the Retribution-body (Sambhogakāya), and the Perfect sees the Dharma-body (Dharmakāya), it is said that there are three bodies and four meanings.

Regarding the subsequent meaning found in the passage below the sutra: "My present body is itself the Dharma-body," and the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* which states, "When Śākyamuni is named Vairocana," these sections open up the assembly [of teachings] wherein the three bodies are all eternal.

Question: If this is so, do all three bodies equally preach the Dharma? Answer: There are differing doctrinal positions regarding whether they preach or do not preach. For instance, one school, that of Nāgamitra, holds... [the text here is incomplete].
In the Nature School (Xingzong), it is held that the three bodies do not all preach the Dharma, because wisdom and principle are quiescent and beyond verbal expression.
Rather, through the power of the Buddha’s compassion and vows, sentient beings of the three vehicles and five natures are moved;

within their own consciousnesses, the aspects of words and meanings arise. This arising based on conditions is termed "preaching the Dharma. It is further said that these aspects are transformed within the consciousnesses of sentient beings themselves.
The manifestation of the Buddha-body is not inherently existent; since the Buddha-body is a transformational arising, the teaching of the Dharma likewise arises from the mind.

Therefore, it is said that to claim "the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma" is to slander the Buddha. Regarding the second point, the school of Dharmapāla and Prabhākaramitra maintains that all three bodies teach the Dharma.
Question: Since the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) reality, how can it teach the Dharma? Answer: Teaching the Dharma consists in generating understanding.

In meaning, for now, from the perspective of generating understanding, it is also called "preaching the Dharma. Furthermore, when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), one attains awakening and understanding of *asaṃkhyeya* dharma-gates;
this is the Dharma-body preaching the Dharma for its own enjoyment-body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*). Regarding the self-enjoyment-body preaching the Dharma within the reward-body (*sāmbhoga-kāya*):
this means that when fundamental wisdom causes subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to generate understanding, it is then the self-enjoyment [body].

The Dharma is preached by means of the body. Since the two schools hold views that are as opposed as water and fire, it is truly difficult to provide a coherent explanation unless one adopts the perfect meaning of our own school.
Therefore, in the tenth fascicle of the *Myōraku-ki* (Record of the Profound Joy), Jingxi harmonizes these positions, stating:

"Thus, while the three bodies are established, it is fixed that the *dharmakāya* does not preach; the *saṃbhogakāya* admits of both meanings [preaching and not preaching]; and the *nirmāṇakāya* definitely preaches. However, if they are mutually identical (*sō-soku*), then both preach and both do not."
To say that it arises solely from principle—neither speaking nor not speaking—is to align phenomenon with principle such that non-speaking is itself speaking, and speaking is itself non-speaking;
when the mind penetrates this wondrous resonance, both grasping and rejecting are entirely lost.

Regarding the second explanation of the phrase "the place of residence," the *Sūtra* states, "The Buddha was at Kuśinagara. The *Xianji* (Record of Xian) says: "To 'dwell' (*zhu*) implies residing for a long time;
to 'be at' (*zai*) implies a temporary visit. For example, because the Buddha preached the *Lotus Sūtra* on Vulture Peak for eight years, it is said that 'the Buddha dwelt in Rājagṛha.
Now, however, as the Buddha was at the Twin Trees from the early morning until midnight to preach this sūtra, it is said [he was 'at' Kuśinagara]."

The Buddha is present. To "revere such a person" means to hold them in deep honor. Regarding the term *míng* (名): the first character is pronounced in the level tone (*shēng*), while the second is pronounced in the departing tone (*qù*).

Concerning "violence and chaos," the *Lunyu* states: "To look for success without prior preparation is called violence. Ma Rong commented: "It means to demand results without having observed the precepts overnight."
Those currently regarded as disorderly are said to be ministers who kill their lords and sons who murder their fathers; thus, the *Lunyu* states, "One does not dwell in a state in chaos.
Now, although these powerful men lack a sovereign, they maintain themselves by means of ritual and law and do not commit the evils of superiors.
"Vertically firm" refers to the establishment of virtue. "Five *zhang*" is measured according to the scale of the Ji-Zhou period.
Regarding "joined stems," the *Foguo zazhuan* (Miscellaneous Records of Foreign Countries) states that "joined stems" means the branches and twigs are interconnected.

Regarding "mutual yielding," the *Bowuzhi* (Records of the Wondrous and Extensive) says that in Andu County there were two trees growing side by side as one; after one withered the following year, the other grew again.

When one tree flourishes while the other withers, it is called the "Mutually Yielding Tree" (*jiaoràng zhīmù*). The "Connected Stems" (*liǎnlǐ*) and "Mutually Yielding" trees both exist in this region;
therefore, they are cited here as points of comparison.
Regarding its leaves, the *Xīyùjì* states: "The shape of the tree resembles that of the *huái* (juniper), its bark is greenish-white, and its leaves are highly lustrous."
The four trees were particularly tall and lush; furthermore, at Xian'an Temple in Ba'ling of this region, there was once such a tree.

According to the *Jingnan ji*, in the first year of the Yongkang era of the Jin dynasty, a tree suddenly grew from beneath a monk’s bed. It continued to grow in this manner for many generations, not just once.
As the tree grew, it healed illnesses, and everyone marveled at it. They left it as it was without pruning, and within ten days, it had taken root.
Ke Jidong subsequently moved his quarters to avoid it; from that time on, the tree’s growth became slow, but it bloomed very late, bearing flowers and leaves only during midsummer.
Its leaves fell in autumn no differently than those of other trees, and despite many years passing, no one recognized it.
Later, a foreign monk saw it, climbed upon it, and wept, saying, "This is a śāla tree; the Buddha sat beneath it."
"I wept because I was reflecting on my past deeds regarding Nirvana; however, the blossoms that opened were small and white, not worth viewing or collecting.
In the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, a flower suddenly grew with a form and color like that of a hibiscus; this too is a miracle of this region.
"Arising and ceasing" explains the meaning established above. This means that if one observes earth, stones, trees, or wood, they must inevitably cease once they arise;

because this is the law of transmigration and decay, it is impermanent (*anitya*); because it is oppressed by transmigration and decay, it is suffering (*duḥkha*); and because it ultimately returns to annihilation, it is empty (*śūnya*). As the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* says:

"The kalpa-fire blazes forth, and the great trichiliocosm is destroyed together. Because this is what is perceived by the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, it is said that "the two vehicles abide [therein]."
Question: Why does it not say "non-self"? Answer: "Non-self" is for the purpose of destroying the subjective observer; here, the forest is merely the object of observation.

Next, the Bodhisattva is explained, which refers to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth," this briefly cites meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so on, implying the inclusion of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Observe this great trichiliocosm; there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not a place where a bodhisattva has sacrificed their body and life.

This next point concerns what is perceived by those with the capacity for the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). As for "showing people through compassion," it means that one fundamentally abides in the four virtues, employing compassion.
Therefore, he manifested his traces at the City of Reed (Kuśāvatī) so that sentient beings might realize the principle through phenomena.
At the base of the City of Reed, the initial [features] symbolize the four virtues: because the city of reeds is firm and solid, it symbolizes the permanence of the Buddha-nature’s immovability;

because the Mallas are valiant and fierce, they symbolize the self-mastery of the Buddha-nature; and as for the non-Buddhists' reckoning that entering the auspicious river to bathe extinguishes sin—[this is likewise shown].
Thus, the shade and coolness among the trees represent the purity of the Buddha-nature free from defilement, as they remove the suffering of heat and exhaustion.
The "reed city" (or "reliant city")—where "reliant" may alternatively be read as "entrusted"—should have the character "entrusted" (*ji*) applied throughout the following three points;
that is, it represents our entrustment to the Mallas.
Next, each represents four virtues. Because it is indestructible, it is eternally present and abundant, and thus there is no poverty or suffering.

Because it is free from arrogance toward neighbors or enemies, it carries the meaning of sovereignty (*vaśitā*). Because it is free from the calamity of hostile thieves, it carries the meaning of purity (*viśuddhi*).
Because it has no one to whom it is subject, it is not demoted; therefore, it is never afraid of others. Because the mind is at peace, there is bliss (*sukha*). Gold and sand do not become mud.
Because it is defiled by water, it manifests purity.

As for "Auspicious and Blessed," since bathing therein extinguishes transgressions and generates merit, it is called the "Auspicious River. To bring about the mastery over birth and extinction is precisely my meaning.

Regarding the fact that the East symbolizes permanence (*nitya*): it should be understood that each [direction] symbolizes permanence, impermanence, and so forth; however, this is merely an abbreviation of the text, and furthermore, they are described as "permanence" and so on based on their predominant characteristics.
The East presides over generation, hence it is permanent; the South presides over growth and maturation, hence it is bliss (*sukha*);

the West is golden and decisive, hence it is self (*ātman*); the North is like water that washes away [impurities], hence it is purity (*śubha*). Furthermore, because the two pairs [of trees] grow long and flourish, it is permanent; because they provide cool shade, it is bliss.
Because they are sovereign, they are "I"; because they are fresh and pure, they are "Flowers"; because they are abundant and satisfy hunger, they are "Fruits," and thus they represent bliss.

One must clearly understand that the meanings of permanence and so forth regarding the city and other things are intended to manifest the four virtues of Buddha-nature; it is not appropriate to cling to the literal events or to misinterpret the text until one forgets the correct principle.
To merely set up superficial correspondences is truly to fail the Master of the School.

Regarding "if one can be equal": if one knows that the environment and its inhabitants (the *sāmbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*) are none other than the Buddha-mind, fully endowed with the four virtues, and that this Buddha-mind is the three truths—this is called the "place of abiding.
Since the Buddha-mind is thus, my own mind is likewise so. If one is deluded regarding one's own mind, one needlessly observes external objects;
if one recognizes one's own mind, the self is the other, and the other is the self. Although the present text explains this in terms of the fruit of Buddhahood, it is shown [here].
The intent is for the practitioner to personally recognize their own abiding place; therefore, the *Zhiguan yili* clarifies three types of contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), namely:
relying on phenomena (*toshi*), attaching to dharmas (*fufa*), and according to practice (*yexing*). Within this school, the elucidation of contemplation does not go beyond these three.

For instance, in the *Zhi guan*, the contemplation of the ten realms where the nature of the mind is eternally one is an example of "according to practice. Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* subsumes the dharma-characteristics of the Four Truths and the five practices.

When the text enters the mind and forms contemplation, it is called "contemplation based on phenomena" (*fufa guan*). In the *Fahua shu*, the names "Rājagṛha" and "Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain" are established according to their literal meaning;

grasping the phenomena to realize the principle is called "contemplation based on events" (*fushi guan*). In the present text, using the city, trees, and so forth to symbolize and correspond to the four virtues is precisely "contemplation of the mind based on events.
However, the practice of explaining the meaning through contemplation of the mind originated with the Master of Mount Sa (Zhiyi), who attained the wondrous realization of his own mind.

Because it deeply accords with the Buddha’s intent, the *Lotus Sūtra* contains three admonitions regarding clothing, seats, and dwellings; this scripture uses the term "East" to signify constancy and so forth.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of weeding out the weeds of craving, while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states that the Dharma-joy is one's wife. Such passages pervade the entire course of the Buddha's teaching.
Furthermore, it is not only the Buddhist scriptures; the Confucian texts are likewise so. For instance, in the *Liji*, when Confucius addressed Duke Ai of Lu, he spoke of the "Ru."
There are those who take loyalty and trustworthiness as their armor (the *dōmu* or helmet) and ritual propriety and righteousness as their shields (small and large bucklers).

Wearing benevolence upon their heads as they walk and embracing righteousness as they dwell, even if there were a tyrannical government, they would not change their station; such is the way they establish themselves.
Furthermore, Master Xun Qing said: "When Confucius was observing the water flowing eastward, Zi Gong asked him, 'The gentleman, upon seeing great water, [reflects its qualities]...'"
"Why must one observe it? The Master said: "Water is universally bestowed upon all living things yet remains non-active; water resembles Virtue (*de*).
Its flow downward is humble and deferential, always following its natural course; it resembles Righteousness (*yi*). Its vast expanse has no end to its exhaustion; it resembles the Way (*dao*).
Its plunging into valleys a myriad *zhang* deep without fear; it resembles Courage (*yong*). Its reaching its destination with a level measure; it resembles..."
The Dharma is full yet seeks no measure; it is upright yet appears relaxed; it is subtle yet reaches far; it is discerning yet its source is vast.

It must flow eastward, as if determined to emerge and enter, so that all things may achieve transformation through goodness. For this reason, when a gentleman encounters great water, he must observe it;

thus one knows that the Confucian way takes the Five Constant Virtues as the essential means for governing a state and establishing one’s person—never to be abandoned even in moments of haste or distress.

Since one forgets [the truth], one must constantly maintain mindfulness throughout all activities; how much more so for the Great Hero (Mahāvīra), whose intent in bestowing the teachings was to enable the realization of the fundamental and the recognition of the mind?
Thus, the school we follow has a basis for its transmission of the essential doctrine; since others do not accept it, upon whom else could the blame be laid?
Regarding the "those who heard together," there are two parts. First, the initial section briefly illustrates this by analogy with the preceding [text].
As for the "nine Buddhas and so forth," including Śākyamuni makes nine; Śākyamuni is the presiding teacher, while the other eight are the audience.

Second, from "as for those who heard together" onwards, the sūtra is explained in detail. Regarding "the bhikṣus were at the beginning," furthermore, "those who heard together" belongs to the general category.
The introduction states that since all fifty-one assemblies are distinct introductions, it refers to the bhikṣus merely as the "co-hearers.

Those who are "equal to the Buddha" are so called because, according to the Tripiṭaka, their fruit of Buddhahood and their severance of delusions are equal to those of an Arhat; thus, seven matters are identical.
For this reason, in the Hīnayāna, the five bhikṣus and the Buddha are referred to as the "six arhats. This, then, concerns the Buddha and the bhikṣus...
"All these" refers to what Ānanda has pointed out.

The *vinaya* precepts (*śīla*) refer to the five categories and seven groups of offenses. The path to *nirvāṇa* refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; these constitute the path leading toward *nirvāṇa*.

"Residual liberation" means that although the fetters and afflictions have been eliminated, the physical body which serves as the basis for suffering still remains; thus, it is called "liberation with remainder."
[This refers to] liberation.

Next, within the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the name "Shared" is used in contrast to the "Treasury" (Zang) teaching; thus it is called "Shared and Distinct. *Mahāyāna* is translated here as "Great Vehicle" (*Dacheng*):

it is called "Great" because it encompasses all, and it is called a "Vehicle" (*Cheng*) because it transports [beings]. It is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) that are empty, which the three types of persons cultivate in common.
"The narrow path" is like a narrow road that cannot accommodate two people walking side by side; this excludes the three vehicles of the Tripiṭaka Teaching and their distinct studies.

Next, the seven meanings of the Distinct Teaching are eternally different from those of the two teachings. The "Exalted Body" (Zhunteshen) refers to that which is attained by Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*).
Because it is seen, it is the *parabhogakāya* (enjoyment body for others).
Regarding the "seven [factors] such as time and place," there is a textual error; it should read "the two, namely time and place.

As for the phrase "the former two...?"—it refers to the fact that for individuals of specific capacity (*pudgalaviśeṣa*), they see only this [body] as the locus where the arousal of the bodhicitta and so forth unite the ultimate and conventional truths.

At this first stage, the two previous teachings and the two vehicles are forever severed from their respective destinies; furthermore, since this concerns the phenomena of time and place within the mundane world, it is illustrated by the analogy of a blind person.
The candle represents the Separate Teaching, while "being without eyes" is a metaphor for those whose faculties lack the Dharma-eye;
thus, although the Great Matter is manifested, it provides no benefit to those of a lesser capacity.

Regarding "precepts and so forth," this refers to the Brahma-net precepts, the nine kinds of great meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and the sequential realization of the distinct stages of the path leading to liberation.
Because these five [faculties] cannot be seen with the eyes as described previously, they are dismissed by reference to the deaf; their pleasure is as explained elsewhere.

The "teaching the deaf" is a metaphor for those of small capacity; to speak of the Great [Vehicle] to them is ultimately of no benefit, as they would be like those who are deaf or mute at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Furthermore, the phrase "even lower" uses the superior to illustrate the inferior. In the two teachings, the fruit-stage merely eliminates the residual habits (*vāsanā*), whereas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, even a bhikṣu...
Because ignorance has been shattered, one does not share [in its defilements].
Next, regarding the seven aspects of the Buddha within the Perfect [Phase]: first, the three contemplations are fused such that the four virtues are simultaneous;

mind-only abides where phenomena and principle are non-dual; the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is the foremost of precepts; the mind is perfected without succession; and one perceives the path of non-action, which is inconceivable.
This discusses liberation.
As for manifesting the appearance of a bhikṣu, it means appearing in the body of a bhikṣu for those who are to be delivered by means of a bhikṣu’s body.

Regarding the statement "not shared with the three previous Buddhas," if one refers to the path of realization according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is identical to the Perfect Teaching; thus, the seven [aspects] are all shared.
This is now based on the teaching path from beginning to end.

All these are great provisional [expedients]; their fundamental abiding is in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, while their manifested traces serve as bhikṣus of the first three teachings. This is an exposition based on the provisional person’s attainment of realization.

As for "having completed the revelation": even those of actual practice who have already passed through this assembly will have their provisional teachings opened up and their Buddha-nature fully revealed.
Therefore, when the compilers of the sutra established the preface, all seven meanings were perfected; this is the conclusion shown from the perspective of those of actual practice.
Regarding the term *mahā* (translated as "Great" or "Vast"), because the Sanskrit word *mahat* possesses multiple meanings, the single name *Mahā* contains these three senses.

The section beginning with "The Heavenly Kings" provides a distinct explanation according to the specific teachings; the first part concerning the *Āgama* and *Abhidharma* teachings is still from the treatise itself, though with slight differences, while the following three sections are the Master of the Commentary’s own inferences based on the meaning of the treatise.
As for what is called "slight differences," the treatise states that the number reaches five thousand.
Thus they were called "many" (bahu). The present term "proficient in the four Vedas and so forth" refers to those who externally understand the Vedas and internally master the Tripiṭaka.

That [previous] account defined "many" in terms of the number of people; here, "many" is defined by the universality of their understanding. In terms of people, the number is restricted to one person per scripture;
in terms of understanding, the meaning applies across all teachings. The treatise states "ninety-six," while the present text says "ninety-five"; however, it is indeed ninety-six.
The one path within [the ninety-six] is the correct one, namely the Buddha-way; all others are merely heterodox. Thus, the *Treatise* (Shi'er men lun) states in chapter twenty-five:

"Among the ninety-six [paths], the real one is the Buddha. Furthermore, because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Lun jie da pin) correctly clarifies the meaning of the "common" (tong), it also denounces the Buddha-way of the Tripiṭaka as heterodox.
Therefore, it says that [the Buddha-way] is superior to the ninety-six paths. The present text, however, restricts its teaching to correctly clarify the meaning of the "Treasury" (zang).
Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha's teachings] surpass those of the ninety-five [heterodox schools].
As for the four Vedas: first, hymns of praise; second, sacrificial rites; third, chants; and fourth, exorcisms.

One Veda contains three hundred and twenty thousand verses, totaling one million two hundred and eighty thousand verses across one thousand seven hundred fascicles; these constitute the "Outer" [teachings].
The "Dao" refers to the scriptural texts.
"Worthy and Holy Ones" refers to those within the Three Baskets who are among the Seven Worthies and Seven Sages—bhikṣus who revere the essence of the Dharma.

Those who have "thoroughly mastered both the analysis of phenomena and their essence" are those who internally cultivate the essence of the Dharma while externally mastering the analytical method; they excel in both the superior and the inferior.
Regarding "those in training" (śaikṣa) and "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa): the Buddha also belongs to the category of those beyond training within the first two teachings.

Regarding "small" and "great": "small" refers to the Hīnayāna teachings (the Tripitaka), while "great" refers to the Mahāyāna teachings (the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect), which transcend the two vehicles of the first two teachings.

Regarding the seven kinds of skillful means (*upāya*): humans, devas, and those of the two teachings and two vehicles constitute four; together with the bodhisattvas of the three teachings, they form seven.
Since all seven serve as skillful means for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), they are collectively termed "skillful means."

Regarding the provisional and real dharma-gates: the first three are provisional, while the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is the real. Those who see the Buddha-nature are called the "definitive assembly" (niyata-rāśi).

The phrase "great provisional" at the end follows the previous pattern for the conclusion; one should follow the previous example by stating: "What is now called 'great' refers entirely to the great provisional."
This concludes the section on the opening and manifestation [of the meaning].

Regarding the three meanings of "bhikṣu" (monk) mentioned below—namely, the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), the destroyer of evil (*bhikṣu*), and the terrifier of Māra—the *Śāstra* (Treatise), in its fourth fascicle, states: "There was a Brahmin woman named Viśākhā who came to see Śāriputra."
He asked, "Śramaṇa, do you eat? He replied, "I eat. Viśuddhamati said, "Do you eat with your mouth turned downward? He replied, "No. [The question was repeated] up to:
"Do you eat with your mouth turned toward the four intermediate directions? He replied, "No. Viśuddhamati said, "There are four ways of eating.
I have questioned you and you say 'no' to each; I do not understand you. You should explain: what is eating with the mouth turned downward? He replied, "There is..."
For a renunciant to compound medicines, sow grains, plant trees, and so forth—such impure means of livelihood—is called "food from below" (adhomukha-bhikṣā).
For a renunciant to observe the stars, the sun, the moon, wind, rain, lightning, and thunderbolts—such impure means of livelihood is called "food from above" (ūrdhvamukha-bhikṣā).
For a renunciant to flatter those of high status and power, act as a messenger between the four quarters, and seek much through clever speech—[this is called "food from the side"].

Those who maintain a pure livelihood are said to have their "mouth [of sustenance] directed toward the four quarters. There are renunciants who study various incantations, divination for good or ill fortune, and minor arts that are not upright;
such impure means of livelihood are called "having one's mouth directed toward the four intermediate directions" (caturvidig-mukha).
I do not fall into these four kinds of impure food; I sustain my life by begging for pure alms. As for the term "not toward the intermediate directions," it refers to the four [impure modes].

"Directions" (fang) refers to the four cardinal points; "interstices" (wei) refers to the four intermediate corners. "Interstice" signifies that which is not the right path, meaning the pursuit of profit through minor arts.
Regarding those who beg for alms in successive order, according to the Vinaya, they are permitted to go to seven houses at most before stopping.

Regarding the meaning of "breaking evil" as explained through the three trainings (*śikṣā*)—starting from the lower level of precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata*): the precepts break the evils of body and speech; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) breaks the scattered mind;
and wisdom (*prajñā*) breaks the evils of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Since there are three types of bodily action and four types of vocal action, they are called the "seven branches.
As for meditative concentration, it is like a lock, whereas a scattered mind is like a monkey; thus, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* says, "The mind is like a monkey."

"Feeling fear toward impermanence and so forth" clarifies wisdom (*prajñā*). This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka, who do not sever their afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus speak only of "subduing" them.
Here, the general term *bhikṣu* common to the Three Vehicles is being employed; therefore, one may cite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says:

"Although this Bodhisattva possesses the five supreme sensual desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), he does not give rise to attachment because he maintains contemplations such as impermanence. It is, for example, like..."
The king had a high minister who concealed his own transgressions. When the king wished to punish him, he said to him:
"If you can obtain a fatless sheep, I shall pardon your crime. The minister was wise; he tied up a sheep and raised it on water and grass, yet three times every day he terrified it with a wolf.
Although the sheep was well-fed and grew fat, it remained devoid of fat. The Bodhisattva is likewise: he perceives the wolf of impermanence and emptiness.
This causes the fat of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be consumed and the body of merit to grow plump; thus, one destroys evil through the wisdom of the contemplation of impermanence.

Therefore, the Treatise says: "Furthermore, 'bi' means to destroy, and 'qiu' means afflictions (*kleśa*); because he can destroy afflictions, he is called a *bhikṣu*. 'Afflictive poison' refers to suffering.
Māra delights in birth and death, and since he seeks liberation therefrom, he opposes that delight; therefore, he is vexed."

The *Dulun* (Toxic Treatise) states: "Furthermore, 'bi' (comparison/inference) is named *bhī* (fear), and 'qiu' (seeking) is named *kṣama* (capable). It is so called because it is capable of terrifying Māra and the people of Māra’s realm.

Its essence is to thoroughly understand the lower [teachings], thereby clarifying the meaning of 'pervasion. However, in the three lower vehicles, one proceeds directly through contemplative wisdom to clarify these three meanings.
