The reason for this is that the objects of the spheres of morality (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are no different from those of the *Āgamas*; it is only that the internal understanding differs, and thus the objective sphere shifts according to that understanding."
There are four distinct teachings; yet in this world, those who study the Mahāyāna disparage the minor aspects of phenomena—how erroneous this is!

Those who are not like [the aforementioned] rely on the universal human body and penetrate that which is to be abandoned: the four perversions. Being able to abandon [them], they regard begging for food as being like an illusion or a transformation;

both the primary and secondary elements are empty. To observe the objective realm in this way is called the "contemplation of begging for food. When the wisdom of observation does not cease, it is called "sustaining life."
Therefore, it is said that this serves to sustain the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).
Regarding "knowing evil" and so forth: the emptiness of the delusions to be destroyed is called "evil," while the emptiness of the wisdom capable of observing them is called "non-knowing.

One should neither fear nor rejoice; for [the former] causes the Māras of householders to rejoice, while [the latter] causes the Māras of those who have left home to fear. Thus, both the laity and the clergy are capable [of this].
Regarding "one who fears joy":
one who is without fear or joy refers to the Māra who is the object of fear and joy. As long as there remains the duality of subject and object, one still dwells within the realm of Māra;
now, realizing that both are empty, one truly fears Māra.
Regarding the phrase "passing through the stages in succession" and so forth: for an individual practitioner, one first realizes the Middle Way;

in order to manifest this Middle Way, one realizes the Truth (*tathatā*) during the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*), realizes the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) during the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), and cultivates the Middle Way during the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*). It is at the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) that the food of the joy of seeking the Middle Way is first manifested;
therefore, it is called "begging for food."

Regarding the five abodes: the views of the three realms are combined into one, while the thoughts of the three realms are expanded into three; thus, there are four abodes, with ignorance being the fifth abode.

The obstacles of *rajas* (dust-like afflictions) are set aside without discussion because the ten abodes destroy views and thoughts, the practice-toward-attainment destroys *rajas*, and ascending the stages destroys ignorance; hence they are said to be sequential.

By means of "afflictions" (*kleśa*), the text briefly explains the breaking of the four *māras* to clarify the meaning of "fear. Because afflictions can moisten karma, and because when afflictions are destroyed, karma collapses, it is said:
"Because of the fear of afflictions, there is the fear of karma. Because karma can summon results, and because when karma ceases, the result perishes, it is said:

"Because of the fear of karma, there is the fear of the aggregates (*skandha*). Because the cause is extinguished and the result perishes, one is not reborn within the three realms; thus it is said: "Because of the fear of the aggregates, there is the fear of the celestial *māra*."
This is also for the purpose of establishing the meaning of sequence; thus, by means of mutual dependence, the meaning of "perfection" (*pari*) can be understood.
Following the examples below, the meaning of "assembly" (*saṃgha*) is clarified.

That which is called an "assembly" is so named because it is gentle and patient (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), and because it is harmonious through yielding. As the fourth chapter of the *Śāstra* states: "The *saṃgha*..."
The Qin (Chinese) term for "a great multitude of bhikṣus in harmony" is *saṃgha*. This is the formal citation from the *Śāstra* (Treatise).

The *Śāstra* states: "There are four kinds of *saṃghas*: the *hrīmanta-saṃgha* (the modest *saṃgha*), the *ahrīmanta-saṃgha* (the shameless *saṃgha*), the *eḍamūka-saṃgha* (the sheep-like mute *saṃgha*), and the *tattvika-saṃgha* (the true *saṃgha*). What is the *hrīmanta-saṃgha*?

It refers to those who uphold the precepts without violation, whose bodies and speech are pure, and who are able to distinguish between the good and the foul, though they have not yet attained the Path.
Those called "shameful monks" are those whose bodies and speech are impure due to broken precepts, committing every kind of evil; they are called "shameless monks.

Although they have not broken the precepts, they are of dull faculties and lack wisdom; they cannot distinguish between the good and the ugly, nor do they know what is light or heavy, nor do they know what constitutes an offense.
If there is a monastic matter and two parties are disputing, they are unable to resolve it, remaining silent and speechless—just like white sheep, and so forth.
Those who have been killed by others and cannot utter a sound are called "dumb sheep" monks (*mūka-eḍaka-bhikṣu*).

Whether they be learners (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), those who abide in the four fruits and practice the four paths are called the "True Saṃgha. Among these two types of Saṃgha, one may perform together with them the *karmavācanā* (formal acts), the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the observance of the *varṣā* retreat, and various other rites.
Herein, the sequence is rearranged in order to point toward those who possess a sense of shame (*hrīmat*).

In reality, it is because it serves as the basis for the latter two; *karmavācanā* is translated here as "action" (*karman*), just as the four classes of people in secular society each have their own occupation, so too the Sangha takes such matters as the recitation of the precepts as its occupation.

"101" is a general designation and not necessarily fixed to that specific number; for instance, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* explains that there are 184 *karmas*, whereas according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, they are definitively 101.
Thus, that Vinaya states: Upāli asked the Buddha, "How many *karmas* are there? The Buddha replied, "There are 101.
He asked again, "How many are *jñapti* (motions) and how many are *karma-vācanā* (formal acts)? The Buddha answered, "There is one *jñapti* and two [types of] *karma-vācanā*."
There are fourteen *jñapti-dvitīya* [karmas], forty-seven *jñapti-caturtha* [karmas], and thirty; thus, they total one hundred and one.

In the three lower teachings, such as the *ūṣmagata*, the "inner ordinary person" (*antarāpudgala*) is taken as possessing shame and remorse; this is generally termed the "phase of dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), which follows along with the preceding stages and correctly takes the "ground of nature" (*prakṛti-bhūmi*) as its basis.

Since this is present in every teaching, one should clarify it by tracing it through successive stages, even down to the sages and saints of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), who fail to realize that the provisional teachings are themselves the Dharma-realm;
they are thus termed "those who break the precepts. As the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* says: "Only the Buddha alone possesses pure precepts;

all others have defiled precepts and cannot reach a definitive resolution. Furthermore, because they do not realize the Perfect Teaching, they are termed "mute sheep. Thus, the subsequent scripture speaks of "such disputes."
This is the realm of the Buddha, not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; since it is called the "Buddha-realm," it is also not something known by bodhisattvas of the partial teachings.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), those who lose their minds and give rise to attachments are designated as the two types of saṃgha.

Regarding "initiating [the teaching]" and so forth: it is like the various bhikṣus who, weeping with grief, entreated [the Buddha] to remain, thereby initiating the teaching on the permanence of the Dharma.

Regarding "influences and echoes": this refers to the Great Beings of the Dharmakāya in other lands who, while internally concealing their great practices, externally manifest as followers of the Hīnayāna to benefit and assist sentient beings;
they support the Dharmakāya like a shadow following a form, or like an echo responding to a sound.

Those who are "ready for the teaching" refers to those who gain benefit from hearing the Dharma, such as the bhikṣus who, upon hearing the discourse on the three dots, abandoned the Lesser Vehicle and entered the Great Vehicle.

Fourth, those with whom one forms a karmic connection refers to those whose conditions in the past or present are shallow; although they hear the teaching, they do not understand it, yet it serves as the cause for their awakening to the Way in the future.

This gradual explanation is made solely with reference to the two types of monastics—the *zàng* (Āgama) and *tōng* (Vaipulya)—and does not concern the true path of realization of the *biéjiào* (Distinct Teaching), which is identical to the *yuán* (Perfect Teaching) and thus beyond such discussion.
To clarify this by synthesizing the points: previously, the "four persons" were taken as the assembly; now, these four meanings likewise constitute the sense of an assembly.
Regarding the note "and so forth": First, this is discussed from the perspective of the most prominent cases, and it defines the fourfold assembly by way of the latter two types of monks.

Second, when speaking generally, even those who have broken the precepts—those who are like "dumb sheep"—are all included in the discourse on the four assemblies. This is analogous to the case of the six groups of bhikṣus, who originally followed the Buddhas of the six directions;
since they constituted the initial transgressions that gave rise to the Vinaya, their influence can be taken as a precedent for other cases. Furthermore, it is as follows:

The householder Jīvaka committed a grave offense yet left the household life, encountered the Buddha, and awakened to the Way; this is precisely what is meant by "responding to the occasion. It is likewise evident that the karmic connection was established.

Furthermore, how could these four assemblies consist of only bhikṣus? Among the fifty-two assemblies, every group contains those who invited [the Buddha], those who were summoned through expedient means, and those who came with sincere intent—this is easy to perceive upon reflection.
Regarding "counting," there are those who count only persons; this refers to the worldly sense of counting people.
As for "counting the emptiness of persons and dharmas": when one counts persons, the sixteen views are empty;
when one counts dharmas, the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen realms are empty—this is the meaning of the *Zang* (Treasury) and *Tong* (Penetrating) teachings.

Alternatively, "numerous dharma-gates" refers to the four teachings and four gates used for emerging into the provisional to transform sentient beings; each gate and each teaching applies the four *siddhāntas* to the ten realms.
These numerous dharma-gates constitute the meaning of "numerous," which is precisely the sense of "distinct."
Alternatively, regarding the enumeration of the true reality (*dharmatā*), it is as when one says that "a single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way," and so forth.

Furthermore, the three—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are mutually fused to form nine; yet these nine are merely three, and the three are merely one. Since even "one" does not exist, how could there be "nine"?
This enumeration of the true reality is precisely the meaning of the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*). The word "or" (*vā*) used throughout is a term of indefiniteness.

This reveals that while the numerical categories are one, the ways they are understood differ; specifically, these numbers refer to phenomena produced by causes and conditions, which are observed as being simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.

In the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) by Cien [Zhiyi] regarding the *weiyi* (dignified deportment), it states: "To turn around is called *wei* (encircling); to sit all around is called *rao* (surrounding).

However, the interpretation of our own school (*jinjia*) states: "The ritual movement is called *rao* (circumambulation). Indeed, since ancient times, both the characters for *juanyao* (entangling) and *xingrao* (walking around) have been written with the radical *mi* (silk/thread), which has led to these differing interpretations.
Herein, we express that the sense of the sentient being’s movement—circumambulating—is stronger.
Regarding "dignified demeanor" (*vīryāpatha*), the *Zhuozhuan* states: "To have dignity that inspires awe and to have decorum that may be emulated.
Alternatively, it may be understood by correlating the sequence below with the realms of humans and devas, as well as the four teachings.

"Fullness signifies perfect permanence" refers to the ultimate perfect permanence of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) downward, one possesses only partial permanence;

as long as *pariṇāmika-vedanīya-karma* (transformative karma) has not been exhausted, it remains impermanent. The *Renwang jing* clarifies the "fourteen patiences" (*caturdaśa-kṣānti*), which are the causes of patience.

This combines the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*) into three groups, opens the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) into ten, and includes Equal Enlightenment to form fourteen—just as there are fourteen [lunar phases].

The "Sun and Moon of Wondrous Enlightenment" refers to the fifteenth day of the month; furthermore, because the completion of a single cycle of transforming others is like the full moon, the fifteenth day represents both self and others.

Regarding the term "approaching" (*lin*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "To approach the honorable and adapt to the humble. Thus, the meaning of "approaching" the humble in response to the honorable capacity is clearly established.
"Not waiting and not passing beyond" means that if one waits, the capacity (*tāki*) has not yet matured; if one passes beyond, the capacity has matured but is not yet transformed.

Now, it is revealed that when the capacity matures, transformation occurs immediately; hence it is said "not waiting and not passing beyond. When the water is clear, the moon appears—how could there be before or after? Question:

If this is so, why did the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sit at the site of enlightenment for ten *kalpas* waiting for the capacity to mature? Answer: It was because the conditions for the capacity were appropriate [to wait].
That Buddha, in truth, does not depend [on external causes].
Regarding "divine power as the foundation": "divine" (shen) means the unfathomable; "power" (li) refers to the capacity for transformative function.

That which is unfathomable is the profound principle of spontaneity (tianran), while the transformative function is the great power of transmutation. Thus, the pervasive response of the Dharma-body is termed "divine power."

Regarding the phrase "causing one to awaken, etc.," while awakening to principle through phenomena still pertains to phenomena because it awaits a counterpart, here, by means of phenomena, one awakens to and realizes the fundamental principle;
therefore, both are negated. Awakening, when considered from the perspective of partial truth (*vibhāṣika-satya*), also encompasses the three identities (*trīṇi samatāni*).
The phrase "taking the wisdom of emptiness as the foundation" incorporates the meanings of both teachings; the following two phrases distinguish between the Separate and the Perfect [Teachings].

Within the context of "responsive resonance," the expression "by means of non-duality and so forth" refers to the passage in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* where the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind.
The phrase "exclaiming so as to inspire veneration and admiration" (*kantan ryōsō*) and so forth is a restatement of the intended meaning.
Regarding "Yun-tong" (*yuntong*): *yun* means "to believe. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that one comes by riding upon the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*) to achieve perfect enlightenment;
since all Buddhas of the three periods of time come from within this path, Śākyamuni is said to be "in accord with truth" (*yuntong*), thereby causing sentient beings to revere and admire him.

The *Classic of Filial Piety* states: "In serving their parents, filial sons manifest the utmost reverence when at home. Thus, "reverent admiration" (*jingyan*) explains the meaning of "accomplishing the father.
The Tathāgata gives birth to my Dharma-body; just as a worldly father transmits his physical form through continuity, he is therefore called the "Worldly Father.
"Field" (*kṣetra*) takes the capacity to produce as its meaning. The Worthy One (*Arhat*), who is worthy of offerings, gives birth to my wholesome karma, enabling me to be born into liberation.
Death is like a sovereign of the world, for it can produce my official rank and emolument, enabling me to emerge from poverty and lowliness; therefore, it is called the Sovereign of the World.
Perfect and Universal Knowledge destroys my fetters and delusions, producing my prajñā, just as a worldly teacher awakens a child’s ignorance and produces worldly wisdom;
therefore, it is called the Teacher of the World. In sum, it is simply to cause [me] to...
Entering the secret treasury of the three virtues, the Father gives birth to the Dharmakāya, the Lord commands liberation, and the Master awakens Prajñā.
Although these are manifested through phenomena, their reality is that the three are mutually integrated. Without one who reveres this principle, there is no teacher.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (yún yún): because the Blessed One here utters three titles to announce his parinirvāṇa—namely, as the Lord of the World, the Kinsman, and the Teacher—the subsequent passage on lamentation employs the metaphors of a lord, a kinsman, and a teacher for the great assembly to entreat the Buddha to remain; thus the textual meaning corresponds exactly to this.
Therefore, the commentary states "and so forth."
The former three are categorized as internal because they are one's own names; the latter four are categorized as external because they are practices for transforming others.

Regarding "original fathers, lords, and teachers," this means that the conditions and opportunities of those in this assembly were all established during their original time [of practice], when they acted as lords.

The father, the teacher, and the intermediate [disciples] were all matured and delivered today through these three; this sūtra follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and thus it clarifies the meaning of the long eon.
Below, Kāśyapa asks, "How does one obtain long life?"—this is precisely asking about the long-lasting lifespan of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa, saying: "When I first attained perfect enlightenment, as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges came forth."

The question that "this meaning is no different from yours" also refers to the primordial establishment from long ago. Thus, when this present sutra is compared to the *迹门* (Trace Gate) of the *Lotus Sutra*, there is one point of agreement and two points of difference:
first, the agreement that we now know the remote origin; second, the difference in that the provisional teachings are now bestowed.
As for the revelation of the reality (*實*), the principle is the same. However, when compared to the *本門* (Origin Gate), there are two points of agreement and one point of difference.
The fourfold equanimity is also called the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). "Immeasurable" refers to the object, while "equanimity" refers to the mind.
Because the preceding objects are not one, they are termed "immeasurable"; although the objects are many, because my own mind remains ever-one, it is termed "equanimity."
Regarding the phrase "now [the four immeasurables]": one now employs the four immeasurables to fulfill one's original vows; these vows consist of two aspirations:

the aspiration to uproot suffering and the aspiration to bestow happiness. The mind of the four immeasurables does not transcend uprooting and bestowing; compassion (karuṇā) uproots suffering, while loving-kindness (maitrī) can bestow happiness.

Sympathetic joy (muditā) rejoices in others' attainment of happiness, and equanimity (upekṣā) abandons attachment and aversion. Thus, the latter two mental states accomplish the former acts of uprooting and bestowing.
The "three bonds" refer to the father relying on the son, the sovereign relying on the minister, and the teacher relying on the disciple.
The "four equalities" refers to the four minds of the Tathāgata as the refuge for sentient beings, like a house in the world; through wisdom, one can sever [afflictions].
Because there was doubt regarding compassion, the questioning was permitted.

The aforementioned doubt refers to the passage in the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Chapter on Lamentation) where, following the request of the great assembly for the Tathāgata to remain, the Tathāgata then provided his response.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, monks, if you have any doubts, you should now all ask them—whether it be concerning emptiness or non-emptiness, and so forth."
"If there be any doubts, you should now inquire of me, and I shall, in accordance with the truth, sever them for you.
These were all doubts prior to [his] parinirvāṇa; therefore, they are called "prior doubts" (*pūrvaka-vicikitsā*).

"Must listen to the subsequent questions" means that "must listen" (聽) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*) and signifies permission; "subsequent questions" refers to the thirty-four questions posed by Kāśyapa in the *Cīvaravastu* (Chapter on Longevity).

"Expounding the Way" (*jiàodào*) means to unfold and propagate widely, and to explain thoroughly. It is because of Kāśyapa’s inquiries that [the Buddha] provided a complete exposition through fourteen chapters.
The answer extensively expounds and clarifies its meaning; this is provided in accordance with the questions asked.
Regarding the passage "discarding the false and attaining the true" and so forth, this refers to the section on lamentation and exhortation to sever doubt.

Following this, the Buddha exhorts [the disciples] to abandon the false practices of the former Hīnayāna and to cultivate the true path of the Mahāyāna; thus the Sūtra says: "Now you have encountered this precious city of the Buddha-dharma."

One should first take up these deceptive objects and then explain for them the secret treasury of the three virtues; using the "new *ī*" and the "heavenly eye" as metaphors to cause them to awaken to and understand this is equivalent to "obtaining the truth.
Thus, the establishment of the teaching corresponds to the chapter on "Bestowal" (*śīla*).

Since the severing of doubts and the raising of questions accord with the meaning of the chapter on "Bestowal," we know that the invocation by sound serves as the introduction to the chapter on "Bestowal."
Next, "summoning by light" is categorized under the chapter on Practice (*xing*), while "summoning by movement" is categorized under the chapter on Meaning (*yi*);
since the chapter on Function (*yong*) consists merely of the application of the aforementioned three, it has no separate correspondence.
This is because "Great Awakening" (*dàjué*) is the "Perfectly Universal Knowledge" (*zhèngbiànzhī*), as their meanings regarding awakening and knowing are one and the same.

That which is both the Master and the Father refers to the fact that once wisdom and understanding have arisen, one will necessarily produce wholesome karma and manifest the Dharma-body, because the substance of the three virtues is identical.
"Great Awakening" (Mahābodhi) is the subsequent title; "Buddha" is translated as "Awakened. This scripture explains the ten titles in its later sections as follows:
The eleven phrases are largely consistent with the *Benyeyingluo jing* (Sutra on the Necklace of Original Karma); that sutra states: "First, the Tathāgata...

up to tenth, the Buddha," being endowed with these ten titles and named the Honored One Among Men. In the third volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the title "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara-puruṣa*) and "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*) are combined into a single phrase, continuing thus up to the tenth title, "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*). Here, we follow the sutra as our basis.
Because it is correct, it is called "Great Enlightenment," which is the final title. In the praise, one praises the first three titles; in the address, one addresses the final title.
Since the beginning necessarily includes the end, and the end necessarily includes the beginning, it is said that its meaning is all-pervasive.
Regarding the clarification of the four meanings in each section: "each section" refers to the six textual segments invoked by the sound [of the title].

Furthermore, concerning the elucidation of the four teachings through the expressions of praise and address, as previously discussed regarding the three—the sovereign, the father, and the teacher—these are identical to the Buddhas in their ability to generate wholesome karma and produce wisdom and understanding;

thus, all may be discussed in terms of the four teachings. This means that the Buddha possesses both provisional and real karmic functions, distinguishes between the internal and external realms, and his wisdom is applied accordingly.
Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle. Thus, writing does not exhaust speech, and speech does not exhaust meaning; if one grasps the essential intent, why rely on the accumulation of writing?
*Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary: Pointing to the Return to the Three Virtues*, Scroll One.
*The Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues*, Fascicle Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiandang. Regarding the "convergence of darkness and light":
this refers to the end of the night when the signs of dawn appear, as described in the *Book of Documents* as "the dim clarity of morning. The rising sun...
This means "clarity.
Regarding the phrase "manifesting wisdom," the arising of wisdom is like the appearance of light, and the extinction of delusions is like the end of the night.
As for "the power of nirvāṇa," it is because one contemplates nirvāṇa that one is able to sever delusions and give rise to wisdom.
For these reasons— and because this assembly’s karmic conditions were such that they required this manifestation to enable them all to realize the principle through the very facts—
it was at the juncture between dawn and dusk, when darkness and light meet, that he emitted light.
Regarding the "six colors," the Sūtra states that "its radiance is of variegated colors," which is a general designation; blue and the others are precisely these six colors.
The "six dharmas" refer to the five aggregates (skandhas) and the self (ātman). These six dharmas are false phenomena, whereas Buddha-nature is the true reality.
This reality and its phenomena are neither identical nor separate, just as ice and water are not distinct from one another.

Furthermore, the three phrases below the blue heading are an explanation. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), both principle and teaching are real, and it is thus called "according to one's own intention" (suiziyi).

In the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (Zangtong), both principle and teaching are provisional, and it is thus called "according to the intentions of others" (suita yi). In the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the teaching is provisional while the principle is real, and it is thus called "according to the intentions of both self and others" (zita yi).

The two phrases indicated by the sutra encompass these three, because "according to one's own intention" and "according to the intentions of others" together constitute two categories. Although the four teachings differ, [the classification remains consistent].
All things ultimately return to the Buddha-nature.
*Pho-li* (頗梨) is also called *sphatika*, which means "ice-jade"; it refers here to rock crystal (*śuddha-sphaṭika*).

Because its substance is translucent and pure, it changes color according to the objects it reflects; coral (*musāragalva*) is also like this. According to this, the color of this jewel may resemble coral, and for that reason [it is so named].
This is for the sake of the name.
Furthermore, the passage below that explains *nirvāṇa* cites the subsequent scriptural text to show that its meaning accords with this "emission of light.
*Nirvāṇa* is like the ocean; the metaphor of the "great body" refers to the Buddha, while the nine realms are differentiated. Therefore, it says "various [realms] equally rely upon *nirvāṇa*."
Since they all dwell within the ocean, and the current text states that "their radiance is of variegated colors," how does this differ from the "various" [rays]?
Furthermore, since they all emerge from the face-gate, how are they different from those dwelling in the ocean? Therefore, it is said that [the text] should precisely indicate this.

Furthermore, in his *Ji Xia Biao* (Explanation Below the Surface), [Jizang] interprets the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*) by pairing them with the six [objects], their numerical correspondence being identical.

He argues that one should not explain the meaning based solely on form (*rūpa*). He states that within the six destinies there is a distinction between the internal and external realms, and regarding the pure six sense organs, there is a distinction between the real and the semblance, and so forth.
Regarding the extent of the light’s illumination, which encompasses three thousand great thousandfold world systems, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"One thousand sets of four continents, suns, moons, Mount Sumeru, desire-realm heavens, and Brahma-worlds is called a small thousandfold world system.

One thousand times this small thousandfold world system is termed a medium thousandfold world system. One thousand times this medium thousandfold world system is termed a great thousandfold world system."

Regarding the mutual manifestation of height and breadth: whereas the preceding sound was described only as reaching the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the present light is described only as pervading the ten directions.
This is the sūtra-author’s way of mutually manifesting the text; one should understand that the sound likewise pervades the ten directions and the light likewise reaches the Peak of Existence.

Sound and light are thus the inconceivable functioning of phenomena. Because the nature of the mind is all-pervasive, its phenomenal functioning is all-pervasive; yet the nature of the mind and its phenomenal functioning are one and the same.

Question: Sentient beings also possess this nature; why then do its sound and light not pervade everywhere? Answer: Sentient beings dwell in delusion; though their nature is not limited, they are as if limited.
For example, although wood possesses the nature of fire, how could it burn everything everywhere? The Buddhas have already realized [this nature];

though it is not something that must be made to pervade, it is like striking wood to produce fire, which then burns everything. Although delusion and awakening differ, the nature of the mind is no different. If one can reflect back upon oneself, [it will manifest].
One’s own mind alone knows that the function of phenomena has its source and their ultimate aim lies herein; yet later students still remain deluded.
Regarding the phrase "others and so forth," this refers to those previously explained who were universally addressed as the "old assembly" of sentient beings;
since this passage identifies them as the "new assembly" within the six realms of existence, it is clear they are none other than the multitude summoned by the preceding sounds and lights.
One must not arbitrarily distinguish between "new" and "old.

Those who eliminate the three obstructions do so because these three obstruct the three virtues; thus, they are collectively termed "obstructions. The six realms of existence are the obstruction to the fruition-retribution;
the defilements of transgression are the obstruction to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*; and the afflictions of the three poisons are the obstruction to the *prajñā* (wisdom) of liberation.
Question: Regarding the three [karmic obstacles] following the obstacle of karma, what is the distinction between them and the afflictions (*kleśa*), given that they are the three poisons? Answer:

The *Guangming shu* states: "That which is spontaneous and constant is the affliction; that which arises from a determined mind and moves the body and speech, necessarily drawing forth a future retribution, is karma."
Regarding the passage "the sutra says 'all are eliminated,'" the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* states that eliminating the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) and being free from all evils is its meaning;

this refers to the elimination of the two kinds of obstacles, those of the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) realms. Furthermore, "leaving behind the obstacles to manifest virtue" is the distinct meaning, while "leaving behind the obstacles to manifest virtue" is the perfect meaning.
That which is easily seen in the text is as follows: mental anxiety is the mind; raising one's voice and so forth is speech; and raising one's hands and so forth is bodily action.
In the sutra, "Alas" (āḥ) is a sound of lamentation.
Regarding the phrase "obstacles removed" and so forth: because they were illuminated by light, their three obstacles were extinguished and the three virtues arose;
having deeply felt the Buddha's profound grace and heard that his parinirvāṇa was imminent, they yearned with their three karmas and hastened to Kuśinagara to behold the World-Honored One.

Regarding the phrase "referring to the equal," the five practices and ten virtues are merely for the purpose of destroying obstacles and generating goodness; therefore, they are indicated by the sequence of the "Light Invocation. As for "at that time" (*tadā*), *tad* means "this.
"Land" refers to the earth and mountains; "water" refers to the great ocean. "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) refers to the delusions among the obstacles;
"craving and views" refer to the delusions regarding reality. These two rely upon one another: if one discusses ignorance, it is the root of both views and thoughts.
While these branches are merely dependent upon their root, here, because the substance of ignorance pervades both the views and thoughts, it is the case that the root depends upon the branches;
this is like water and earth depending upon one another, and thus they are said to be "mutual."

Regarding "delusion and craving": delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*), and craving is the view of attachment. For those whose faculties are to be matured, these afflictions must be overturned and destroyed;
thus, the movement of the earth is a manifestation of retribution. To say "overturn" rather than "destroy" means to reverse. Reversing the false is the true, and reversing delusion is wisdom.
Since the essence of the true and the false is identical—like turning over one's palm—the intention is to manifest a perfect destruction; therefore, it is called "overturning."
Furthermore, it is said below that this indicates [the distinctions]: "movement" (*iṅgana*) refers to physical trembling, while "shaking" (*prakampa*) refers to sound;

therefore, they are distinguished by means of six types. Regarding "rising," "surging," and so forth, the new [translation] says: movement (*iṅgana*), surging (*utsarpaṇa*), shaking (*prakampa*), striking (*nirghāta*), roaring (*nirghoṣa*), and bursting (*prapāta*).

Here, the old names are used: "movement" (*iṅgana*) refers to swaying and instability; "rising" (*utthāna*) refers to ascending from below to a higher level; "surging" (*utsarpaṇa*) refers to the formation of ridges, mounds, depressions, and elevations; and "rumbling" (*ghurghura*) refers to having a low, resonant sound.

The name "zhèn" (震) refers to a thunderous crash (*péngkài*, with *kǎi* pronounced as *gài*). To emit such a sound is called "roaring" (*hǒu*). To cause sentient beings to awaken is called "enlightening" (*jué*).
A new commentary states: "To strike is like a blow; to burst forth is like the sound of fire."
"Extensive and equal" refers to the six types listed above; this present sutra briefly mentions only the two categories of form and sound.

Regarding the eighteen kinds of movement, each of the six is further divided into three—namely, movement (*calana*), pervasive movement (*pracalana*), and equal pervasive movement (*sampracalana*)—as well as shaking the four continents, shaking the great chiliocosm, and shaking the trichiliocosm; the remaining five cases follow this same pattern.

The six movements symbolize the overcoming of delusions through the six sublime stages of abiding, practice, progress, and realization; they may also symbolize the purification of the six sense organs, for the attainment of purity in the six organs necessarily depends upon the overcoming of delusions.
Regarding the eighteen movements, the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) uses them to symbolize the purification of the eighteen realms (*dhātu*);

here, they symbolize that each of the six stages overcomes three types of hindrances, and further symbolize that each of the six sense organs overcomes three types of delusions—thus, by means of this sūtra...

To clarify the meaning of the three virtues, following the precedent of what has come before, one should state that this refers to the sequence of the meaning of *nirvāṇa* within the earthquake; the text here is merely abbreviated.
The proof of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) arises from the destruction of ignorance; since the earthquake already signifies the destruction of delusions, it accords with the *Yìzhāng*.
The reason for not including the section on "function" is as previously explained.
The phrase "yet the sound" below clarifies that [the teaching] follows the capacities of beings according to the sequence of before and after.
"Ocean of sorrow" means that the suffering of grief is as deep and vast as the ocean.

"Great kalpa" refers to the eighty cycles of increase and decrease comprising the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; here, it refers to the twenty cycles of increase within the kalpa of abiding.
From the tenth *kalpa* of decrease until Maitreya’s appearance in the fifteenth *kalpa*, there will be nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas who appear in succession;
if one were to calculate by means of a great *mahākalpa*, this would contradict that [reckoning].
"Gradually shortening" refers to the period from eighty-four thousand years ago when the lifespan decreased by one year every hundred years until it reached ten years.

Since Śākyamuni has now appeared during the ninth such reduction at a time when the human lifespan is one hundred years, he requested that this kalpa of reduction continue until the human lifespan reaches ten years;
therefore, there is no impediment to the appearance of future Buddhas.
"Both afflicted" (*juying*) means being entangled in suffering.
"Orphaned and exposed" (*gulü*)—as Mencius said—"one who is young and without a father is called an orphan; 'exposed' (*lù*) refers to having lost the protection of a canopy.
"A diverse multitude" (*zazhong*) refers to the presence of both ordinary and sage beings, as well as those of the Great and Small Vehicles.
One who practices the Middle Way is identical to what this sutra says: "Ordinary persons and those of the Two Vehicles are empty, whereas Bodhisattvas are neither existent nor empty.

Regarding the terms *jì* (the last) and *mèng* (the first), the commentary on the *Yueling* (*Monthly Ordinances*) states: "*Mèng* means 'long' (the eldest); *zhòng* (the middle) means 'medium'; *jì* means 'small' (the youngest). Thus, "between the last and the first" refers to the middle.
The middle group consists of those who were present.

As for their inclusion, it was based on the degree of intimacy as evidenced by their physical presence. The Śrāvakas are listed first because they left the mundane world, personally witnessed the sutras, and thus shared a close relationship with the Buddha.

The devas and humans are listed last because their forms differed from his and their attire was distinct; since their roles were not that of personal attendants and they did not personally witness the sutras, their connection was more distant.

Furthermore, the form of a Bodhisattva is not constrained by formal discipline, and their traces have no fixed location; they differ from the laity yet are distinct from the monastic community, dwelling between the positions of the "eldest" and the "youngest," thus occupying the middle rank.
As for those who manifest themselves, the Śrāvakas rejoice in Nirvāṇa while devas and humans cling to birth and death—each has its own partiality—but the Bodhisattva is not so.

Joy does not abide in clinging; because one seeks the Middle, it exists between the two extremes. Furthermore, the *śrāvakas* represent the real, the *bodhisattvas* represent the provisional, and the miscellaneous assembly represents the false.

Regarding the reduction in the number of those listed: others see them as being of the same number within the assembly. Among them, first ten trillion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges) are listed, followed by two.
The "ten sands of Ganges" (daśagaṅgā-vāluka) refers to the reduction of the number of divisions.

Regarding the first division, "monastics and laity": within the context of increase, "monastics" refers to śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, while "laity" refers to the twenty-one assemblies beginning with upāsakas.
The intention here is as previously stated: one does not take another’s portion or division.
"To startle" (hài) means to cause subsequent questioners to be startled; this is the dual invocation of light and movement. "Causing subsequent questioners" refers to the invocation by sound.
As the Sūtra says: "If there is anything you doubt, you may now ask all at once; this is the final questioning. The meaning is that even though [the Buddha] was on the left, [he remained present].

The above merely describes how the movement of light causes alarm and the utterance of sounds, thereby eliciting their response; this is what is meant by "summoning" (*zhào*) their latent capacities (*jī*).
Regarding "following the majority," it means that while those near the Buddha are few and those summoned are many, the term is used according to the majority;

thus, it is generally termed "summoning. In truth, however, for those already at the Buddha's side, there is no need for summoning. Previously, the term "summoning" was used because their latent capacities were being activated; therefore, for those at the Buddha's side, [it is not necessary].
Furthermore, because they are summoned in sequence and arrive by name through their physical presence, the convention follows the majority.
As for the phrase "at that time," it refers back to the previously established number in the introductory section;
why then is it now said that there were "immeasurable" bhikṣus, numbering eight hundred billion? This is what is being asked.
The phrase "no answer below" means that because the preceding individuals were listed as the foremost, their number was fixed.

Regarding the passage from "like a younger brother" to "between the two pillars": *yíng* refers to pillars. This means that the disciple provides support through respectful service to the teacher as if to a father;

thus, the disciple is called a "son. The teacher’s humility consists in viewing the disciple as a younger brother. Being situated between these two states of respect and yielding is like standing between two pillars.

Therefore, although the title "disciple" (śrāvaka) relates to two meanings, it is applied specifically to those who provide support; thus, while the term encompasses multiple senses, it is used here to designate a single matter.
Regarding this, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "A junior monk addresses a senior monk as 'Venerable One' (bhadanta), and a senior monk addresses a junior monk as 'Life of Wisdom' (jñānajīvita)."
To "praise one for their virtue and deeds" means that one is not considered an elder (*sthavira*) merely on account of advanced age.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it means that even if one is a senior, if they lack virtue and deeds, they are still called a youth; as the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:
"Ānanda’s hair was white, yet Kāśyapa called him a youth," and rebuked him, saying: "The assembly wishes to lose [the distinction of] your age."
Regarding young bhikṣus who do not properly restrain their sense faculties, are greedy, and lack contentment, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
those from one summer retreat up to nine summers are called junior seats (*hīnāsana*); those from ten summers up to nineteen summers are called middle seats (*madhyāsana*);
those from twenty summers up to forty-nine summers are called senior seats (*vṛddhāsana*); and those of fifty years or more are [honored] by all śramaṇas and kings.
"Veneration" refers here to seniority based on the number of years since ordination (*vassa*); this definition of "elder" differs from that in the *Āgamas*.
"The fan and the cord" means that a mother, out of attachment to her son, refuses to remarry, as if the fan were tied to the cord.

"Good Appearance" (Sunong) was so named because his physical features were upright and handsome. At the age of one hundred and sixty, he was free from illness and untimely death, and he possessed knowledge of future events.

Knowing that [the King] would surely die and be usurped from his great throne by the Demon King (Māra), he manifested himself in the form of an Arhat, displaying supernatural transformations to entice him into leaving the household life.

"Preserving goodness" refers to the longing and devotion of the three karmas. "Passing through the body" refers to the turbidity of the body and mind; "passing below" refers to the turbidity of the mind;

and "emitting sound" refers to the mouth. Regarding the question about the mind—where sorrow and grief are afflictions of volition (*cetanā*) that have already been severed by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—the answer clarifies this by means of the four teachings.
Regarding "residual habits" (*vāsanā*) and so forth: although the afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*) have been exhausted, residual habits remain; therefore, there is sorrow and grief.
For example, Śāriputra had much anger, and Pilindavatsa had much pride; this is the meaning of the *kṣudraka* (Miscellaneous) Piṭaka.
Furthermore, it is shown that once one has reached the realization that [all things] are empty, sorrow and grief naturally cease;

however, this is merely presented as a model and paradigm so that sentient beings may emulate it and know how to aspire toward the Buddha—this is the general meaning. "Specific delusions" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*);

specifically, these are what Bodhisattvas eliminate. "General delusions" refer to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which are eliminated by those of the three vehicles; therefore, [the text speaks of] the ignorance of Arhats.

If it has not yet been shattered, there is sorrow and lamentation outside the realm (*dhātu*), such as when Kāśyapa was moved by grief throughout the great trichiliocosm, or when he rose to dance upon hearing the lute;
this is a distinct meaning.
That which is the Buddha’s *dharmadhātu* involves sorrow and lamentation manifested through the mind; since the mind consists of the three truths, sorrow and lamentation are likewise so.

Since the Truth (satya) universally encompasses all that is named, it is called the Buddha-dharmadhātu; therefore, the sorrow and suffering of an Arhat are nothing other than the dharmadhātu—what is there to marvel at?
This is the meaning of "perfection" (yuan).

As for "kindred" (lei), since the class of those bhikṣus who have exhausted their outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) is identical, they naturally form a community. The *Zhou Yi* says: "By means of the directions..."
This is a thematic compilation.

One who has mastery over the mind is one whose mind is concentrated (*samādhi*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one whose mind attains excellent liberation is a person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), while one whose wisdom attains excellent liberation is a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
A person of wisdom may regress, which means that delusions may arise again.
Because of this meaning, there is no virtue that is not produced; now, because this is the fruit of both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*), one does not regress and afflictions do not arise.
Thus, "mastery over the mind" is a praise of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Regarding "having already accomplished what was to be done": because one has already destroyed the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and has attained the wisdom of non-arising, it is said that this praises the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Wisdom is also a field of merit because, by possessing wisdom, one is worthy of offerings; this is the meaning of "one who should be honored. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because self-benefit has been completed, it is called 'that which has been done' (*kṛtakṛtya*); because of benefiting others, it is called 'one who has accomplished their task' (*kṛtārtha*)."
One who is "free from affliction" (vīta-rāga) is so called because afflictions harm wisdom; thus, "removing" (vi-) has the meaning of "killing.
That the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are also "thieves" means that when the six faculties are defiled by sensory objects, various afflictions arise.

Therefore, one must subdue the six faculties in order to be free from affliction; being free from affliction and subduing the six faculties are mutually constitutive. Thus, they share the same meaning of "slaying the thieves."
Because the name "Arhat" encompasses three meanings, the author of the sutra praises them in this sequential order.
There is no room for [the term] *wei* (awe/vigor) to mean self-majesty; it is called "awe" (*wei*) only because it causes others to stand in awe.
As for "awe-inspiring virtue" (*weide*), it means that by virtue of possessing inherent merit, one causes others to stand in awe.

Regarding the term "elephant" (*hastin*) and so forth, many versions of the sutra text read "great dragon king" (*nāgarāja*). According to the present commentary, this should be amended from "king" to "elephant.

Appearing as one who travels on land is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*) that illuminates and understands; being submerged and hidden like water is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that is tranquil and still.

These, then, are two distinct entities: the dragon and the elephant. Since these represent meditative concentration and wisdom, they pertain to one's own practice (*svacaryā*). However, if we consider the elephant’s capacity for transport and the dragon’s capacity for [flight], [they may also be understood in terms of benefiting others].
When it causes rain, it transforms others; as another sutra says, "Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings by means of this.
Alternatively, although it is merely a single object among elephants, it is praised as a "dragon" (nāga); thus it is called a "dragon-elephant" (nāga-hastin).
Therefore, the example of Śakra’s precious elephant is cited as proof.
"Brahma" (*brahman*) should be translated as "pure" (*viśuddha*), since the term "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is translated as "one of pure conduct"; thus, it refers to a "pure jewel-elephant.

Because its power of transformation while walking in the void is like that of a dragon, it is called a "dragon-elephant" (*nāga-hastin*). As the *Dongdu fu* (Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital) in the *Wenxuan* states:

"Ascending the jade carriage, he rides the seasonal dragons," with the commentary noting that "seasonal dragons" are horses whose colors correspond to the cardinal directions; generally, anything termed a "dragon" refers to a magnificent horse.
These words mean that one also names a horse a dragon;

this is more in accord with transforming others. To laboriously establish two categories [of practice] is analogous to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which, taken as a single direction, pertain only to one's own cultivation.

Now, to designate a precious elephant as a dragon is to suddenly manifest a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to delight the various devas, serving as a metaphor for the three wheels of Dharma acting upon sentient beings.

Therefore, "Great Accordance" (*mahā-anuvartana*) signifies the meaning of transforming others. The "void-walking" (*gaganagañja*) and transformation of the body metaphorize the wheel of the body manifesting supernormal powers;

the playing of music for the sake of delight metaphorizes the wheel of speech preaching the Dharma; and transformation arising from the mind metaphorizes the wheel of the mind discerning the capacities of beings.

Regarding the scriptural text, the "Dragon and Elephant" come first, followed by "Majesty and Virtue" (*tejas*). Now, the explanation of "Majesty and Virtue" comes first, either because it is more convenient or because the versions of the sutra differ.
One who has accomplished the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) is called "accomplished" only upon reaching the ultimate state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

One who has attained their own benefit (*ātma-hita*)—where "attained" (*dai*) means "reached" according to the *Shuowen* dictionary—is so named because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Eightfold Noble Path and the fruits of the śramaṇa constitute the Arhat’s own benefit. This refers to the attainment of the Way by the immeasurable great disciples.
Because both the cause and the fruit are attained together, it is called "one's own benefit.
Sandalwood from the lower sandalwood groves is fragrant and lush like the fragrance of the precepts; the majesty of the king of beasts [the lion] is like wisdom severing delusions.

Although "concentration" (samādhi) is not explicitly mentioned, since wisdom arises through concentration, one must know that concentration is present whenever wisdom is raised. Furthermore, previously, by means of the dragon...

The analogy of the elephant concludes the section on meditative concentration and wisdom; furthermore, it is presented by the compiler of the sutra as a mutual illustration. "Pure assembly" refers to those who have received the precepts and wisdom.
Regarding the "true sons of the Lesser Vehicle": the term "Lesser" is used because Bodhisattvas are considered "semblance sons," while those of the Two Vehicles are "true sons";
in the Mahayana, those of the Two Vehicles are considered "semblance sons," while Bodhisattvas are "true sons."
Regarding the phrase "by means of great merit" and so forth, the scriptural text reveals the fundamental nature and explains that this is precisely the Dharma-body Mahāsattva;
therefore, it serves to conclude the virtues of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. If one were of the Hīnayāna, there would be a deficiency in the transformation of others.
This is the intended meaning of the note "and so forth."
"Leaving one's usual place" means that when chewing a *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick), one must go to a secluded spot, thereby departing from one's ordinary location for meditation and recitation.
"Manifesting the beginning of superior practice" means that the movement of the Mahāyāna capacity first manifests the perfect practice.
"Having washed and rinsed" means rinsing the mouth and washing the hands; the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "rinsing" (*shòu*) is to cleanse the mouth, while "washing" (*zǎo*) is to wash the hands.
"Discarding the trivial and superficial" refers to the Middle Way, the emptiness of the primary meaning, which is not the partial emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle.
Question: The "Ultimate" refers to the Buddha-nature, which is the most supreme principle.

Now, those who respond to this summons will once again become sentient beings; this serves as the condition for the reversal of their vision. Therefore, the subsequent scripture immediately speaks of the "conditions for subduing."
"Following movement to summon" means that going forth because of movement is called "summoning in accordance"; the one who can summon is the Buddha, and those summoned are the great disciples.
"Profoundly perceiving and understanding" refers to being able to wondrously comprehend the Buddha's intent and recounting his words, thereby responding to the three summons.
Who else but one who has personally realized the provisional practice of the Dharma-body could reach such a state?
Only those of partially perfected true wisdom can understand the intent of the person of wondrous enlightenment; it is like a snake seeing the feet of a snake.
"Those who are served" refers to those summoned for service.
"Ayyā" (Ācāryā) and so forth are terms used when addressing one another among ordained *bhikṣuṇīs*.
Examining this sūtra, the initial reference to a "woman" (*nārī*) is likewise a general designation for an ordained *bhikṣuṇī*.
Regarding the mention of "separate treatises" and so forth, this is a provisional classification made according to the conventions of this land;
however, if one considers that "bhikṣuṇī" is a term from the Western regions while "nǚ" (woman) is a term from this land, then there is no distinction between the two.
The phrase "the stages can be known" refers to the passage from the *Sarvāstivāda-mahā-āgama*.
As for the phrase "as above," the lecturer should take up the preceding text to explain the sūtra so that the listeners encounter no impediments.
Regarding the "Three Invocations," the ritual manual follows the established ordinances.

As for the term "Bodhisattva" used to describe those with penetrating speech—whether their teaching be partial (*pian*) or complete (*yuan*)—those at both the initial stage and the higher stages are all designated as Bodhisattvas.
Among worldly beings, those who are like dragons are described in the *Jia Yu* (Family Sayings) as: "Of the three hundred and sixty species of scaly creatures, the dragon is the sovereign."

Regarding those of long standing who possess virtue surpassing the masses, they are compared to dragons. The *Hanshu* states that Song Xian, styled Ling’ai, lived in seclusion on the Southern Mountains of Jiuquan;
when the Prefect Ma Ji visited him, he did not appear, whereupon Ma sighed and said, "The Master is a dragon among men.
The *Shiji*, in the "Biography of Laozi," records that when Confucius traveled to Zhou, he intended to inquire about the rites from Laozi.
Zi-laozi said: "A skilled merchant hides his goods deeply yet appears as if empty within; a gentleman of abundant virtue has a countenance that seems foolish.
Cast away your haughty air, your many desires, and your licentious ambitions, for these are of no benefit to your person.
Confucius said to his disciples: "Laozi is like a dragon; I do not know how he mounts the wind and clouds to ascend to heaven. This.

All of these are merely like dragons among worldly people; however, those praised in this sutra are the Perfect and Sudden Bodhisattvas who transcend the worthy and sages of the three teachings—they are truly dragons among men.
The phrase "abiding peacefully and immovably" refers to the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi) being eternally quiescent.
The phrase "the Sūtra acts for the sake of transformation" means that one manifests in a female body when it is necessary to attain liberation through a female form.

Regarding the phrase "How does the trace descend?": this indicates that after presenting the scriptural text, the preceding [meaning] is now explained. It is because [the Buddha], through the four [immeasurables], responds to sentient beings by manifesting a female body;
thus it says, "by means of the four immeasurable minds."
What is its essence? Because one attains mastery by understanding the bonds of the two deaths and dwells in immovability, it is called "attaining the samādhi of mastery.

The phrase "capable of even becoming a Buddha" and so forth cites the superior to illustrate the inferior, demonstrating the breadth of its traces. This is how other schools and our own school [distinguish them].

To designate the general stages (*sāmānya-bhūmi*) as the "original" (*hon*) and the "traced" (*seki*) is somewhat plausible; however, to simply state that the general stages inherently include both the original and the traced—while separately designating the higher stages as cause and fruit—is not entirely consistent with the meaning.

If one were to claim that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the cause and attaining Buddhahood is the fruit, this contradicts the Sūtra, which states that one can manifest as a Buddha through transformation (*nirmāṇa*);
thus, we know this is the fruit of provisional bestowal (*jiseki*) rather than the fruit of one's own practice (*jigyō*). Therefore, it is rejected.
It is said that it is difficult to see.
Regarding the phrase "for the two lower [realms], etc.," this follows the previous classification of those summoned and those respectfully summoned.

As for the explanation of the numbers, such as "many people" and so forth, because they possess great knowledge, they will surely rejoice upon hearing [this teaching] and will obtain merit, thereby giving rise to wholesome states.

The "large breaking the small" refers to the destruction of evil; the Buddha was born in the city of Kapilavastu, and this river is near that city, sharing the same region as the Buddha—it signifies his dwelling place.
When entering into the principle, there are these four meanings; therefore, the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras all employ numerical metaphors.
Within the phonetic transcription, the Western (Sanskrit) sounds are fully preserved; it should be *bodhisattva*. The translator has abbreviated this by omitting the two characters *ti* and *tuō*.

*Bodhi* means "Way" (*mārga*), *sattva* means "mind" (*citta*), and *mahā* means "great. Master An translated it as "Opening Being" (*kaishi*) or "Beginning Being" (*shishi*). It is also translated as "Great Way-Minded Being" (*dàodàoxīn zhòngshēng*).
In the old translation of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, it was rendered as "Noble Being" (*gāoshi*); the new translation calls it "Bodhi-essence" (*pútízhì*).

*Devatā-sattva* is translated here as "Awakened Sentient Being" (*Jue Youqing*). This arises from the differences between Eastern and Western phonologies, which lead to divergent interpretations by people;
since the translation is not fixed, the Sanskrit term is retained.

The *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) explains the meaning of "Bodhisattva" below. First, it cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and next, it cites the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

One is designated a Bodhisattva only when they can fully possess ten meanings; based on these meanings, the explanation is applied broadly across the four teachings (*catvāra upadeśāḥ*). However, they are distinguished by the breadth or narrowness of their transformation of others (*parārtha*) and the distance or proximity of their own practice (*svārtha*), which is clearly visible.

In the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) and *Shared* (Sādhāraṇa) teachings, the scope of transformation is limited to the six realms of existence, thus being narrow; [in the Distinct Teaching], it extends to...

The "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura) is named "near" because it distinguishes the Separate [Vehicle] from the Perfect [Vehicle]; "transformation" encompasses the ten realms, thus its name is "broad," and it extends to the "Precious Abode," thus its name is "far.
The primary intent of the Sub-commentary lies precisely in the Perfect [Vehicle], for the Sub-commentary below states: "In this text, there is much praise for the virtues of the Perfect Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the reason why the ten meanings in the sutras and treatises all take "benefiting sentient beings" as their foremost principle is that Bodhisattvas maintain the aspiration to provide universal salvation. First.

Regarding the "all sentient beings" among the ten meanings in the *Śāstra*: they refer to the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*). Question: How does a bodhisattva teach and transform those within the Buddha-realm? Answer:

Bodhisattvas of partial realization (*bhūmi-prativedha*) teach and transform those who are Buddhas in name only (*nāma-mātra*), and so forth. Furthermore, among those who are "Buddhas in name," there are differences in the depth of their understanding;

among those in the five grades of the practice of contemplation (*kuan-hsing wu-pin*), there are distinctions of high and low; and among those in the ten stages of semblance faith (*xiang-si shi-xin*), there are gradations of superiority and inferiority—all of which are categorized as the higher positions.
The "teachings below" refers to the sentient beings within the realm of the transformation Buddhas. "All Buddhas" refers to those of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
"Gathering and transforming beings in the four lands" is called "purifying all. "Universally studying both the partial and the perfect" is called "fully upholding.

"Ensuring the Buddha-seed is not severed" means transmitting the lamp of the teachings through successive instruction. "Discerning the Buddha-lands" means clearly understanding the pure and the defiled. "Knowing the assembly of disciples" is difficult.
To harmonize and easily transform the distinct minds of sentient beings, one must know that all possess Buddha-nature; to sever delusions, both the branches and the root must be toppled;

and to know the faculties, one must understand the provisional and the real, as well as their differences. These ten meanings do not transcend the two categories of "self" and "other": numbers one, three, five, seven, nine, and ten pertain only to the self;

numbers two, four, six, eight, and ten pertain only to the other; while numbers six and eight pertain to both self and other. Since the primary intent lies in the Perfect [Teaching], they are all so designated.
All things.

Furthermore, although the gates of the downward-pointing broad finger are innumerable, how could they transcend self and other? Since self and other are not the same, how could they transcend the ten realms?
A single thought-moment possesses the ten [realms]; how do self and other differ from the four lands, the four teachings, the three delusions, the three truths, and the ten realms?

Having gathered [these points] exhaustively without omission, and having already explained the Bodhisattva’s state of mind, one must clarify that the Way is not far off; by looking back within oneself, it is immediately present.
This can be seen by applying the ten gates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as an analogy.
In Nāgārjuna’s commentary, the phrase "not calculating" and so forth means that by means of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), one universally covers the dharma-realm;

from the attainment of Buddhahood until the cessation of activity, one benefits sentient beings and delivers them from the suffering of the two deaths, dedicating the merit of this transformative work to oneself, which is termed "Great Adornment."

The two categories of "noble" and "base" refer to the noble being one's kingdom, city, wife, and children, and the base being one's slaves, servants, and attendants. "Internal" refers to the primary retribution (the direct fruit), while "external" refers to the environmental retribution (the indirect fruit).
Body and life constitute the primary [retribution], while nobility and baseness belong to the environmental [retribution]. The term "all things" does not exceed these four categories.
It is the nature of ordinary people to love and treat kindly those who are close to them, while hating and treating harshly those who have wronged them.
Now, because the Bodhisattva practices compassion throughout the nine grades of practice and causes all beings to attain happiness equally, it is said that [this benefit] is entirely impartial.

Although those of the four lower vehicles know that the Buddha-nature is without distinction, because their habitual tendencies differ, they expound the three vehicles according to their respective original inclinations;
subsequently, as the provisional is unified with the ultimate, it is said that they all arrive together at Nirvana.

The five lower [fetters] do not mean that "I am able to deliver sentient beings"; that Bodhisattva cannot be so named, for he neither attains "self" nor "other," nor does he perceive "I am the one who delivers sentient beings" or "these are those to be delivered. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says in brief:
"Although immeasurable sentient beings are brought to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa."
"Pure and unmixed mind" refers to the pure wisdom of the Middle Way that is not mixed with the two extremes.
"Sarvajñā" (all-knowledge) is translated here as "fruition-wisdom. "That which is created by the world" refers to the causes and effects of the ten realms.

Regarding the "one, two, etc.": first, "one" refers to mind-only; second, "two" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); third, "three" refers to ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; fourth, "four" refers to the Four Noble Truths and so forth.
Thus, among these ten gates, the first five concern transforming others, while the latter five concern one's own practice; other meanings may be inferred by analogy with what precedes.
As for the separate explanations, they are as found in the commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and so forth.

If one were to clarify the meaning of the Four Teachings (*catur-yāna*) through the ten meanings of the current text’s sūtras and śāstras: for instance, the first, the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka Teaching), involves teaching and delivering sentient beings of the six realms;

continuing thus up to the tenth, which involves knowing the faculties (*indriya*) regarding the four gates of analysis (*vibhaṅga*), understanding the methods of increasing the numerical categories of the teachings, and penetrating them universally.
[This is] a separate example (and so forth).
Within the text, the latter part reveals the present intention; since we are now situated within the Perfect [Teaching], the preceding teachings are abbreviated.
Those in the stage of expedient means refer to the worthies and sages of the three vehicles.
Regarding the transformation and benefit through the Dharma-realm of the lower stages: it refers to manifesting the bodies of the nine realms and preaching the fourfold teachings.

As for the "Ocean of Merits," the fifth chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma within the Great Jewel Enclosure, situated between the desire and form realms.
At that moment, the great trichiliocosm was filled with vast waters, just like a great ocean."
In all worlds, cities, towns, houses, mountains, forests, and trees, up to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there was no harm whatsoever, and everything appeared exactly as it had been before.
At that time, immeasurable *puṇḍarīka* lotuses emerged from the water, with stalks of blue lapis lazuli and leaves of pure gold.
Then, the great assembly each saw themselves sitting beneath these flowers, and these flowers emitted a great light.
A light shone universally throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
The great assembly asked the Buddha, "By what causes and conditions is this world filled with vast waters, like a great ocean?
The Buddha told Maitreya, "Below this world, past as many lands as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm, there is a world named Ratnavyūha. In that land, there is a Buddha named Sāgarajñānadeva."

It is because the Bodhisattva named Sāgaramati intends to come here that the Tathāgata has manifested this auspicious sign. What is now called Hai-de (Sea-Virtue) is none other than that same Sāgaramati;
it is merely a difference in name. If we consider them from the perspective of contemplative understanding, there is no lack of both similarity and distinction:

Hai-de is established as a name based on the object of contemplation, while Hai-hui (Sea-Wisdom) is established as a name based on the subject of contemplation. Because these three virtues are like the ocean, it is so called.

The three wisdoms of the ocean-like mind are called the "Ocean of Wisdom" because they resemble the sea; this "Ocean of Wisdom" has three meanings: profundity is like the depth, vastness is like the breadth, and the simultaneous illumination of both is like containing all streams.

Profound truth (paramārtha-satya) is like the depth, conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is like the breadth, and the middle truth (madhyama-satya), which illuminates both simultaneously, is like containing all streams.
Regarding the eight inconceivables: the first involves gradual and deep entry up to the eighth, which is neither increasing nor decreasing;
this refers to the text in the thirtieth fascicle of the sutra below.
As for the citation of eighty dharma-gates, the thirty-first fascicle of that same sutra states: "The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: 'In the eastern direction...'"
Beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Animiṣā (The Unblinking).
In that land, there is a Buddha named Samantabhadra Tathāgata. There, a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati resides.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Akṣayamati: "I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will explain the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattvas."
"O sons of good family, how should the Bodhisattvas who have attained the inexhaustible Prajñāpāramitā practice it?

How do they enter into the inexhaustible intention and speech? They practice according to what they have heard and skillfully enter into contemplation. Śāriputra asked: "How does one practice according to what has been heard?
One who hears [the Dharma] possesses eighty modes of practice, namely: the desire to practice, and a compliant mind..."
The practice of the ultimate mind; the practice of constant arousal of effort; the practice of drawing near to virtuous friends; the practice of being free from arrogance;

the practice of non-negligence; the practice of reverence; the practice of compliance with instruction; the practice of following wholesome speech; the practice of frequently visiting the teacher; the practice of listening to the Dharma with a sincere heart;
the practice of reflecting well upon good and evil; the practice of an undistracted mind; the practice of a diligent and energetic mind; and the practice of giving rise to the perception of reality.

The practitioner who possesses the thought of medicine, practices the removal of all diseases, and even attains the practice of all Buddha-dharmas, being well-entranced in contemplation, is endowed with the thirty-two marks.

This refers to: being well-entranced in the upholding of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), being well-entranced in the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā*), being well-entranced in the gentleness of mind, and being well-entranced in the solitary wandering of the body.
Regarding the perspective of contemplative understanding, these are inexhaustible within both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and conventional (*saṃvṛti*) truths.
This is because the three are mutually integrated.

"Inexhaustible" refers to the object (*viṣaya*), and "intention" (*abhiprāya*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). Since wisdom accords with the object, the object and wisdom are referred to together as the "inexhaustible intention."

Regarding the "Four Great Vows encompassing both upward seeking and downward transformation": the first two [vows] refer to upward seeking, while the latter two refer to downward transformation; they are said to be "encompassing" because they are contrasted with the previous [section], which praised only one aspect.

This is explained according to principle (*li*): within the text, principle is used to verify wisdom (*zhi*), and phenomena and teaching (*shi-jiao*) are used to explain the scriptural passage; the latter two [points] are self-evident.

Regarding the first three meanings, one should know that, in terms of principle (*tattva*), they refer solely to the object of contemplation; in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*), they refer solely to the subject of contemplation;

and in terms of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), they discuss both subject and object together, because it is by means of wisdom that one realizes the principle. Through this analysis, their meaning becomes clear.
That which one takes as a teacher is the Dharma, for the Dharma is the Teacher of the Buddha;
therefore, it must be revered and honored. There is nothing that surpasses Prajñā; this refers to the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Nevertheless, because this wondrous principle serves as the essence of both cause and fruit, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "The true reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the cause of the Mahāyāna; it is the fruit of the Mahāyāna."
Furthermore, the true reality (*dharmatā*) is the very essence manifested by the true cause that is now being extolled;
however, the text cites the Buddha as "Teacher" and "the one who first attained the Way," citing him merely for the sake of using the term "Buddha" to refer to the stage of partial fruition.

Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is cited because its meaning is identical to this: it states that one is called "abiding in the Great Vehicle" (*mahāyāna-pratiṣṭhita*) by means of realizing the principle through wisdom, and thus establishes the secret treasury (*guhya-nidhi*).
As for the phrase "that which can produce," the Great Vehicle is that which produces wisdom, while [wisdom] is the object produced; it is the profound object that gives rise to wisdom.
Because it is vast, wisdom is also profound and vast. To be profound means to penetrate vertically through reality; to be vast means to extend horizontally throughout the Dharma-realm.

This is what the *Lotus Sūtra* means when it says, "The wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable. The analogy of the box and the lid illustrates vastness, while the analogy of the well and the rope illustrates profundity.
The box and the well represent the objective realm (*viṣaya*), while the lid and the rope represent wisdom (*jñāna*). The rope is the cord used for drawing water from a well.
