Since each relies on only one side and does not accord with the primary intent of the present sutra, they are collectively rebuked by saying: "How could they comprehend the perfect principle? Now, let us attempt...
To speak of it is to bring forth what follows.

Now, the Buddha descends specifically to clarify the present interpretation. First, within the world-system, he demonstrates that the "Great Matter" (mahā-vastu) elucidated in the *Lotus Sūtra* is precisely this very sūtra’s teaching of permanence.
Initially, the "Great Matter" is explained according to the principle of response and resonance (*saṃgati*), wherein the "one who responds" is the Buddha.
Having realized this great matter, one transforms sentient beings by means of this very Dharma;

because there is no distinction among the three [truths], it is called the "Eternal Dharma" that encompasses all from its own cause to its fruit. Because the principle of the three thousand realms is manifested, it is called the "Eternally Established" of all dharmas.
This refers to the Buddha of the Fruit, who, because the principle of the three thousand realms is fulfilled, is able to respond accordingly.

In the *Changji*, the section explaining the meaning of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) by way of the capacity to evoke [response] states: because sentient beings are endowed with the three thousand [realms] by principle, they are able to evoke [the Buddha's response].
Thus, although the living being and the Buddha differ, the three thousand realms are both eternally present.

"Constantly non-existent" is explained in terms of object and wisdom; "constant response" refers to the mutual discourse between the Buddha and sentient beings. Regarding object and wisdom, we shall first discuss the two aspects of the responsive [Buddha].

Because the single principle of non-duality subsumes them into a single unity, it is said that they are "constantly without distinction. Yet, because they are non-dual while being dual, and because both object and wisdom are equally constant, they are said to have "distinction.
To explain this constancy, the following passage is cited as proof to establish that both object and wisdom belong to all Buddhas.
That which is the teacher of the observing wisdom is precisely the object of the three truths.
Regarding "teacher and disciple," the teacher is the object and the disciple is the wisdom; the object serves as the model for the wisdom, just as a teacher instructs a disciple.

That which is called the "Eternal World" refers to the fact that while responses to stimuli differ and the realms and wisdoms are distinct—meaning they are mutually exclusive—it can nevertheless manifest various responses according to the capacities of beings and speak of eternity in differentiated ways to cause sentient beings to rejoice; therefore, it is called the "World."

The passage beginning with "I now" refers to the section on the person; the citations from the sūtras therein are all intended to generate wholesome qualities regarding the permanence of the Tathāgata.
The passage beginning with "If one wishes" refers to the section on antidotes;

the meaning of "I am the Buddha" and so forth signifies that the awakened and sovereign Dharma-body is eternally abiding in nirvāṇa and blissful Right Dharma, free from false defilements. Furthermore, this constitutes both the collective and individual aspects of the Three Virtues.

It should be understood that what is called "Buddha" is precisely Prajñā, and the True Dharma is precisely the Dharmakāya of Liberation; thus, because these three virtues are perfectly complete, it is named Nirvāṇa.
The subsequent passage stating that "Prajñā is also not [existent]" and so forth conveys this very meaning.
Those for whom these causes and conditions exist are the ones destined to remain permanently within this assembly.
Regarding the "non-dual yet dual functioning": while the eternal principle is non-dual, its dual functioning according to conditions manifests as distinctions;

this refers to such things as using impermanence to shatter permanence and using permanence to shatter impermanence. Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is pointed out directly that function is itself the essence.
Since there is no differentiation and they are not led by mutual destruction—like two birds that take flight together yet rest together—it brings about the benefit of human principles.

One should know that the following [passage] concludes by demonstrating the refutation of attachments; "interruption" refers to the world, while "tranquility" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The arising of fetters is countered by [the realization of] persons, as explained in the text; below this, the Master correctly refutes the partial attachments and counteractive errors of ancient teachers.
As for those who disparage various sūtras and śāstras, since they all teach in accordance with the four *saṃgrahavastus*, how could one alone be right while the many others are wrong?
Is this not a harmful tumor?

Furthermore, the latter part clarifies that "permanence" (nitya) does not refer to the future or the present; the former part clarifies that it is taught as being in the future or the present in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, whereas in its true ontological essence, it is actually neither future nor present.
Therefore, he cites the verses from the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* (or *Amitābha-sūtra*) as proof to refute the masters of the Di-lun school.
Furthermore, the following section clarifies that the eternal is not something abruptly manifest. First, the teaching is cited to establish the general position;
next, the passage beginning with "Formerly concealed" (*xi fù*) explains and reveals the meaning of the esoteric teachings. Initially, the intent is stated briefly:

it is argued that the nine realms were formerly covered by impermanence, whereas the Buddha-realm was eternal; now, the opening of the nine realms reveals they do not transcend the Three Thousand Worlds, all of which return to the Buddha.
Because the realms (*dhātu*) are not distinct, it is said that "now" and "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth are inseparable.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "I," it investigates the sequence of experience to reveal that the opening of the nine realms is precisely the meaning of the eternal nature of the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*).

The fourfold slander of the Dharma, the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and the icchantikas constitute the four miserable destinies (*apāya*); these are impermanent evil causes that necessarily induce impermanent evil fruits. Now, this is understood.
The mind’s offenses are fundamentally empty; this is called repenting of grave transgressions. Because one solely penetrates the Dharma-realm, slander of the Dharma is eliminated.
Because one accords with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the sins of opposition are exhausted. Since Buddha-nature is immutable, even icchantikas are extinguished.

All these four evil karmas and fetters are themselves liberation; liberation is itself permanence, and permanence is Buddha-nature. When the cause is extinguished, the fruit perishes, leaving only the single realm of the Buddha; the two vehicles [are likewise subsumed therein].

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*), the two teachings [the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Lotus Sūtra*] collectively clarify the Bodhisattva realm, while the two teachings [the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*] each individually distinguish it; both are based on the revelation of the ultimate truth, as can be seen in the texts.

As for "with remainder" (*sa-upadhiśeṣa*) and "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*), these are the provisional teachings of the three vehicles that do not fully realize the ultimate meaning; thus, the nine realms are provisional, whereas the realm without remainder is not.

Since this is the teaching of the definitive meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya), the Buddha-realm is the reality. Now that the provisional has been opened to reveal the real, the three teachings are themselves the Perfect, and the nine realms are themselves the Buddha-realm;

therefore, it is said that the esoteric teaching is revealed and manifested. Since all have shattered ignorance and fully manifested the three virtues, it is said that they are "placed within the secret treasury."
Furthermore, this section below explains the three aspects of the perfect conditions (*pariniṣpanna*) according to the five natures (*pañca-gotra*), as is commonly explained.
"Object" (*viṣaya*) refers to matters of cause and effect, good and evil; these phenomena are themselves the principle, and are thus called Buddha-nature.
The "direct cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers exclusively to the principle within the causal state, while the "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) discusses only virtuous matters. This [latter] is...
To distinguish them: the nature of the fruit (*phala*) is precisely the two virtues of ultimate wisdom and cessation (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) as partially realized.
If one follows the subsequent praise and refutation, within that praise it refers back to the previously established "eternality" and "discernment of nature," which is what this meaning signifies.

That is to say, if one follows the opening statement that all nine [realms] are eternal and equally manifest the Buddha-nature, then the five [aggregates] of the nominally designated persons of the nine realms—[are likewise so].

The teachings of the partial and limited [vehicles] regarding the reality of the aggregates (*skandha*), the practices of the Three Vehicles, the stages of severing and subduing [afflictions], and all functions of antidotes—all these are precisely the Buddha-nature because they are eternally abiding;
thus it is said that they are not "not eternal. Know that this eternity is itself the Middle Way;
therefore, it is asked: "What dharma is neither non-eternal nor eternal? This phrase "what dharma" refers collectively to the dharmas of the superior person.
This refers to the function of the stages of teaching and practice.
How could it be otherwise? Below, the conclusion demonstrates that these are all equally the Buddha-realm, with no further distinctions of the nine realms;

that is, the six destinies together with the three vehicles constitute the nine realms. Because the path of language is cut off, they cannot be deliberated upon; because the sphere of mental activity has ceased, they are beyond conceptualization.

Inconceivable and vertical, its depth penetrates to the ultimate principle; horizontal and vast, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm. Because it is vast, it is boundless; because it is deep, it is bottomless.
To accord with the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) is called "establishing great significance.

Since its essence is fundamentally all-pervasive, it fills the Dharma-realm—this explains its horizontal vastness. Because the three truths are mutually identical, they cannot be exhausted. To speak of this again is an expression of praise.

This is the ultimate point; it is also a concluding phrase for what precedes, meaning that the establishment of the Great Meaning is inexhaustible and its fulfillment throughout the Dharma-realm is inexhaustible.
How can one conclude below by refuting the three schools? To briefly contrast with the four schools: the three schools are those being refuted, while our own school is the one establishing the truth.
This is because it discusses both the subject and the object together, and thus speaks of "four" [perfections]. "In general" (*genggai*) means roughly or in broad outline.

Next, regarding the "correct subsequent treatment," this is an added explanation; therefore, the initial mention of "constant" uses the character for "constant" to run through the following five dharmas.
As for "without beginning or end," this refers to the principle realized in fruition; since this principle is neither cause nor effect, it has no beginning or end.
To take that which is non-form as form is the principle of the eternal form; this form is precisely the mind, not a material obstruction, but rather true, virtuous, and wondrous form.
Its inexhaustible function is to respond universally according to conditions, like a mirror manifesting images; this is called "eternal power."
That which is stable and immovable means that although the essence is active in responding to changes throughout the entire day, it never departs from the *dharmakāya*;
therefore, it is called "immovable," and this is termed "constant tranquility."

Regarding those who are "responded to by their capacities" and so forth: the single utterance of the perfect voice is understood differently by various types of beings; because the nature of speech is empty and letters are liberation, this is called "constant eloquence.
As for "life being the secret of the mind": equal great wisdom is precisely the secret of the mind; since wisdom is taken as life, the mind is therefore [the secret].
The constant life-force of body and speech is easy to understand.

It is also called "Below": having already matched the five fruits with the three mysteries, one further uses the three mysteries to form the four virtues, thereby manifesting the principle realized by the fruit-virtue.
Great Wisdom is constantly illuminating; thus, the intention is the virtue of permanence. The Dharma-body is quiescent.

Cessation is bliss; being sovereign and omnipresent, it is designated as "I. Therefore, the Body-secret (kāyaguhyaka) corresponds to these two qualities, while the Wheel of Speech (vākcakra) preaches the Dharma to cause all beings to become free from defilement;
thus, this is the quality of purity. These are correspondences made according to conventional phenomena (*dharma*).
If one discusses the ultimate principle (*tattva*), however, the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are non-dual, and the four qualities are fundamentally integrated.

If one attains the lower fetters and demonstrates that their essence is pervasive—having already known that the five fruits are precisely the three mysteries and four virtues—one realizes that these three and four categories do not exclude anything;
only then does one know that the five fruits universally encompass all dharmas of cause and effect, self and other.

Regarding the explanation of the beginning and end: the "beginning" refers to the attainment of enlightenment at the site of tranquility (Vajrāsana), and the "end" refers to the entry into *parinirvāṇa* at this assembly.

Since the sutra has already explained these two—the beginning and the end—it can be understood that the three flavors of the intermediate period reveal the eternal. While the Deer Park [teachings] were exclusively esoteric, both [the middle and final] flavors are manifest;
thus, throughout the five periods of the Buddha’s entire life, the permanence [of the Dharma-body] is clarified in all of them.

Regarding the phrase "since [the means] have been raised," the teaching is that which expresses; since that which expresses is eternal, then that which is expressed—such as the practices (*caryā*) and so forth—is entirely eternal.
Therefore, it is said, "it is likewise thus. The principle of eternity is like a seal that stamps all phenomena; because all phenomena are thus sealed, they are eternal.
The Sūtra states: "The myriad phenomena and all images are sealed by a single Dharma.
This final section establishes the meaning of permanence. As for "the Dharma is permanent," "Dharma" here refers to the principle of permanence.
If this is so, how does it differ from "realization"? One should know that "realization" is discussed in relation to wisdom, whereas "Dharma" is spoken of solely in terms of principle.

In the section "Explaining Without Difference," first the Buddha’s response is cited, followed by a general reference to sutras and śāstras, and finally a specific demonstration through the corresponding text.

One must understand that the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is like space, while the *Śāstra on the True Reality* (Tattvasiddhi) refers to the permanent nature; although their names differ, their underlying principle and substance are no different.

"The elderly and the young" (*qishao*)—the term "elderly" (*qi*) refers to those aged sixty, as stated in the *Book of Rites*: "At sixty, one is called an elder. This is used as a metaphor for the nature of directing others, just as "the elderly and the young" [are distinguished].

The sixth is the analogy of the practitioner of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which refers to the realization of the five stages through the perfection of contemplative practice. If one begins to cultivate contemplation at the initial stage, this belongs to the "name-and-word" (*nāmamātra*) level.
Therefore, that which precedes the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya*) is called the "present," while from the stage of partial realization (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkriyā*) onward is called the "future."
Because this permanence has existed as the fundamental nature of sentient beings from time immemorial, it belongs to the past;

yet, since the six identities (liù jí) encompass the stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuán wèi) throughout all sutras, how could they be the same as the "permanence of the present" (dāng xiàn cháng) pointed out by those of the Earth-Stage (dì rén), which exists only within the teachings of the present?
Regarding the translation of names and the explanation of meanings: *A* means "non-"; *nuttara* means "supreme"; *samyak* means "correct"; and *sambodhi* means "true.
Taken together, it is called "Supreme, Correct, and True Enlightenment," which signifies the Supreme, Correct, and True Path.
While the meaning applies to all four teachings, the intent of the sutra lies in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

The perfection of the Dharma-principle consists in the completion of the teachings throughout the five periods; this is the perfection of the Dharma. To abide together in the secret treasury is the perfection of the principle.
Receiving offerings at the time of his passing is called the final [act].
Regarding the phrase "you who have heard" and so forth: hearing the Dharma and seeing the body are both eternally abiding;
by practicing the final gift in reliance upon this principle of eternal abiding, the gift itself is the Dharma-realm, and thus it is said that *dāna* (generosity) is necessarily perfected.

As for the general refutation: we clearly observe that what is inferior at first becomes superior later; how then can it be said that there is no distinction in giving? Therefore, this claim is incorrect. Regarding Yecheng (Yizheng):
according to the *Treatise on Geography*, it was originally a place where the Wu kingdom produced bronze and cast metal, and thus received its name. Wang Dao served as the Minister of Works (*Sili*).
The smelting works were relocated to the west of Shitou City, where the land was used as the Western Garden (*Xiyuan*);
thus, when the *Book of Jin* records that Emperor Cheng visited the Prime Minister’s residence (*Situ fu*) to tour the Western Garden, it refers to this very place.

In the fifteenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Liang dynasty, Emperor Wu established a temple for the monk Faxin of Jiangling on this site, naming it after the smelting works (*Yecheng*). What is currently called Yecheng refers to this location.
The Dharma Master Zhixiu also explains this as in the beginning of the first fascicle of the *Kaishan* [commentary].
Since the terminology differs, he refers to that commentary, hence the note (etc.).

Regarding the "five difficulties" below, the present master provides the formal classification. As for the passage beginning with "First, there is... and so forth, the sutra proceeds from the point where afflictions have not yet been exhausted.

The "Noble Name" refers precisely to the "God among Gods. The "four bodies" refer to those such as the one who eats solid food (*kavadīkāra-āhāra*). The "five bodies" refer to those such as the one free from afflictions (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the "four possessing inferior eyes," this refers to the five eyes; since the sutras clarify that [the Buddha] does not possess [all of them], the two eyes of *Dharmadeva* are omitted here, hence it is so stated.
As for the practice of listing the names in order from superior to inferior, one should have said "the Buddha-eye" down to "the deva-eye";

that the "wisdom-eye" (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is mentioned here is because the Buddha-eye perceives phenomena within the middle [reality], while the two eyes of the devas both pertain to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since the wisdom-eye perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is used as the point of reference.
Regarding the sequence from the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) to the "wisdom-eye" found in the sutras, this is a scribal error.
One should also say "the Buddha-eye" up to "the wisdom-eye. Therefore, the *Yuanshu* (Distant Commentary) explains: "Possessing the Buddha-eye and so forth manifests his possession of understanding.
Among the eyes of the sages, one proceeds from the highest downward; thus it says 'possessing the Buddha-eye' down to the 'wisdom-eye.
The divine and fleshly eyes are not considered [in this context]. (The above is from that text).

Regarding the phrase "attaining the five fruits and so forth," it means that one will not receive food thereafter; there are no mundane five fruits here, as this is based on the perspective of the Hīnayāna.
In the sūtras, it merely says "attaining life" and does not say "attaining eternal life. This is because the objection is raised regarding the initial five fruits of the outflowing (sāsrava) state.
Thus, "attaining life" refers only to mundane retributive life, and "peace" refers to the peace of the five aggregates.
The swift eloquence is the worldly wisdom that proclaims the power of form (*rūpa*) so that it may be known.

Regarding the phrase "since the first has already been fully set forth," this uses the first case as an example for the subsequent ones; since the merit for others can be understood [thereby], there is no need for further elaboration. If one were to apply this analogy to the [Buddha] himself, it should be stated:
"Furthermore, he was not yet able to cause sentient beings to be endowed with the 'God among Gods' (*devātideva*). All other instances should be understood according to this principle.
The characters *huā* (呼瓜) and *hù* (呼覇), with the second tone, signify "to explain" (*shuō*) and "to transform through culture" (*wénhuà biàn*).

Regarding those points that are difficult to resolve due to their angularity: *jì* (芰) is pronounced *qí* (奇) or *jì* (寄). The *Wèidū fù* (Wei Capital Rhapsody) states: "Following the *jì* plants, they float upon the surging waves and soak into the deep pools" (*tán*).
The commentary notes: "*Jì* refers to the water chestnut (*líng*). What we call 'slanting difficulty' (*xié nán*) resembles the corners of that water chestnut. If one uses... [text breaks off].

"Difficulties regarding the beginning of the small versus the beginning of the great, and difficulties regarding the end of the small versus the end of the great"—these are called "parallel difficulties" (*ping-nan*) and are not "oblique difficulties" (*ji-jiao*).

If one were to use the beginning of the small to challenge the end of the great, or the end of the small to challenge the beginning of the great, this would be an oblique difficulty, termed an "oblique difficulty.
Now, Pureṇa’s five difficulties all use the beginning of the small to challenge the end of the great; therefore, they are explained as "oblique difficulties. However, [the first...]
Although this was difficult to understand previously, if one explains the beginning and end by distinguishing the two types of capacities—the great and the small—the meaning becomes very easy to see;

therefore, the Master of the Commentary has exhaustively demonstrated the characteristics of the Great and Small Vehicles, citing the sutras and defining them according to their teachings to distinguish between them.

Regarding the statement that "conditions have sharpness and dullness," if one distinguishes between the internal and external realms based on the capacities of the four teachings, then the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings constitute the sharp and dull capacities within the internal realm, while the *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) and *Nirvana* (Perfect) teachings constitute the sharp and dull capacities outside the internal realm.
Thus, the Tripitaka teaching is termed "Small" (*Hīnayāna*), and the other three teachings are termed "Great.

Now, following the scriptural text, Cunda specifically uses the initial attainment of the Tripitaka to challenge the entry into extinction of the Perfect Teaching; therefore, he speaks in terms of "sharpness."
This refers to those of dull faculties who belong to the *hinayāna* vehicle; the same applies to the *mahāyāna*.

To clarify the beginning of the *mahāyāna* and *hinayāna*, it is said that he first received the milk-gruel from the cowherd girl; this is the initial sign of his attainment according to the *tripiṭaka*.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it clarifies that he received three *dō* and six *shō* of milk-gruel from the girl who tended the cattle.
Regarding "the one filled with the ten powers": because he has severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) after eating and attained the Way, he has obtained the ten powers.

His initial sitting upon the lotus pedestal and so forth represent the characteristics of the Separate and Complete [teachings] being accomplished; however, the present intent lies in the fulfillment of the Complete [teaching], as clarified in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
Regarding the "Flower Petals" up to the "Response Body Buddha": upon each of the thousand flower petals is a *vairocana-sambhogakāya*, also called the Great Transformation Body (*mahā-nirmāṇakāya*).
Within the billion lands is the Inferior Response Body, also called the Small Transformation Body;
this is the one seen by those of lesser capacity as previously explained, who accepted the milk gruel.

Regarding the phrase "milk gruel (up to) forever different": because the Buddha on the lotus pedestal takes in only light through the crown of his head as food, he differs from the inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) which eats milk gruel.
This is seen after the explanation of the distinctions between the lower and higher [realms].

Regarding the *candana-karṇa-sūpa* (sandalwood-ear soup), the third fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that when the Buddha arrived at the city of Pāvā in the Jeta Grove, there was an elder named Cunda who invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
He prepared the *candana-karṇa-sūpa* specifically for the Buddha; because it was a rarity in the world, he offered it exclusively to the Buddha.
Ānanda said to the elder, "Providing such an offering brings no merit," and [the Buddha] was the very last to partake of it.
As he entered parinirvāṇa, the Buddha said: "Do not speak thus. This householder has now obtained great benefit and merit;
his life span, physical strength, and good reputation have flourished, and with abundant wealth and treasures, upon death he shall be reborn in the heavens... (and so forth).

Regarding "the palanquin headed toward the Twin Śāla Trees": the character for *yù* (轝) is pronounced with the *zhǎn-fǎn* (諸反) tone; the *Fúzhì* (服志) states that the ancient sages observed the whirling dandelion puff and thereby conceived the wheel and the carriage.
Furthermore, "carrying [him] in a palanquin" refers to using a carriage to carry him from the house of the Elder to the Twin Śāla Trees;
all of this is what was seen by Cángjī (藏機).
If one observes the following passage, the present sūtra’s description of the marks of extinction is precisely what is seen by those of the perfect capacity (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).

By analogy, when the conclusion below establishes five pairs regarding the attainment of enlightenment and entry into extinction—since the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ eternally, it follows that the five aspects, such as wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), are likewise identical from beginning to end.
Therefore, Cunda’s adherence to the Hīnayāna and his difficulty with the Mahāyāna serves as the catalyst for the Tathāgata’s discourse that follows.
The response is given by answering that both the beginning and the end are great.
Those who raise the objection regarding distinctions do so by challenging the Buddha on the grounds that the small and the great are different.
That the Jing and Wei rivers are clearly distinct means that one knows Pureṇa (Cuntuo) clung to the small to challenge the great; thus, these distinctions are like the turbidity of the Jing River.
The Buddha, based on the five fruits of the great conditions at the beginning and end, explains that there is no difference between them, just as the clarity of the Wei River;
this exposition of the sutra’s intent can be seen, hence it is called "luminous.

Now, to further clarify the meaning of the objection, I shall provide a specific analysis according to the sutras and teachings, for what was previously stated was only a general discussion of the Great and Small Vehicles. Therefore, I shall proceed further.
Approximately four teachings are clearly elucidated: first, citing two sutras to prove the initial manifestation of the Buddha’s image;
second, using the *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* to resolve doubts regarding the final extinction; each of these possesses four teachings, as can be seen in the text.
Since the Teacher has already cited two sutras to clarify the four views of the beginning and the end, he now further correlates the fruit-Buddhas of the four teachings to explain the present sutra.

Generally, as long as a phenomenon has not yet transcended [delusion], prior to becoming the King of Trees (Bodhimaṇḍa), the fetters and afflictions remain entirely intact; therefore, there is no Sage who is the "God among Gods."
Regarding the title:

"Practicing Austerities" (Kuxing) refers to the six years at the Snow Mountains when he consumed only one sesame seed and one grain of wheat. His physical form became so emaciated that there was a fear he might be identical to the self-mortifying non-Buddhists (tīrthikas);
therefore, he accepted the milk-rice. Thus it is said that externally he required various kinds of food.

Regarding "the bondage of fruition" and so forth: since the beginning of the three great eons, one has not yet escaped birth and death. This present body in the royal palace is the retribution for past afflictions and is thus called the "bondage of fruition.
If this body perishes, one immediately enters the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*);
because this body is the final limit of birth and death, it is called the "final body" (*paścima-deha*).

There are none who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and clear vision (*vidyā*), because they have not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, they have not yet attained the three clarities (*traividyā*) and the six supernormal powers.

Since they lack supernormal powers and clear vision, they lack the four eyes; as there can be no divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and since there is no untainted supernormal power (*anāsravābhijñā*), they lack the three eyes beginning with wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one discusses Bodhisattvas who have first attained the five supernormal powers, they already possess the divine eye; however, this present discussion concerns those who have not yet attained the untainted [powers].

The celestial eye (*divyacakṣus*) that has been produced is also inferior in its function; just as the celestial eye of Brahmā is inferior to that of Kauṇḍinya, it is completely withdrawn from him, and thus it is said that he lacks the four eyes.
Therefore, according to this Tripiṭaka master, there is only the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).

Each of these five meanings should be applied one-to-one against the five pairs of positions held in the sutra regarding the initial attainment. The lecturer should explain them with precision so that they are properly reconciled.
The commentary by Master Shu at the end of the "Pure" section concludes by demonstrating the intent of the sutra.
Having already fulfilled the three absences [of giver, gift, and recipient], the three factors—the donor, the object given, and the receiver—are all empty.

According to the teachings of this school, upon entering the seventh stage one enters emptiness, possessing the three insights and six supernormal powers, having already attained the wisdom-eye and the divine eye; in the eighth stage, one emerges into the provisional [to benefit others].
Because he has already attained the Dharma-eye but has not yet severed residual habit-energies, he has not yet attained the Buddha-eye.
As for the demonstration of digesting morsel-food—where "chuai" (揣) is pronounced "tuan" (團), as in Jia Yi’s *Fengniao Fu*: "How can it suffice to control and grasp?

this refers to that very character—the statement that he "demonstrates digestion" actually means that he has long since severed afflictions and brought birth-and-death to an end; he does so only to transform sentient beings.
"Supporting habituation and receiving retribution" refers to the demonstration of eating *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (solid food), which enters the abdomen and is digested.
Regarding the passage on "Cunda," this concludes the intent of the non-criticism; for Cunda merely took the initial stage of the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness) as his point of contention.

Because the store-consciousness does not sever delusions, it contradicts the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching] (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), and thus he takes its existence as a difficulty. In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), the meaning of the five pairs of [teachings] regarding immediate emptiness is somewhat... [text fragment].

Because it is identical with the Perfect [Teaching], it is not considered difficult; yet, it merely accords with capacities, for since the capacity for grasping and storing [the teaching] is not perfect, there are four types of benefits [to be provided].
Thus, as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, even Zhijī (Jñānakuṭa) clung to a distinct meaning and challenged the Dragon Girl—how much more so would this apply to the Universal [Teaching]?

If one were to distinguish them separately below, since the path of realization through the Separate Teaching is identical to the Perfect [Teaching], they are combined and explained together to conclude the answer regarding the attainment of Buddhahood;
this reveals the meaning of the five pairs being without difference.

The phrase "as the Buddha answered" and so forth refers to the text and meaning of the Buddha’s response to Maitreya in the *Niyatāniyatagati-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Lifespan) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Now, when the Buddha answers Cunda by saying "already for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas," etc., this serves as a parallel instance.
The phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) is an abbreviation of the three intermediate pairs; it merely cites the beginning and the end. If one were to state them in full, they would be:

having long possessed the holy name, having long possessed the five bodies, and having long possessed the eye of deliverance—all of which use the term "long" (*cira*) to indicate that they were accomplished from the very beginning of time.

Since this sutra follows the explicit text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, those who claim it manifests the initial attainment of enlightenment should rather say it manifests the final extinction. To speak of "subsequent attainment" is a textual error;

it actually shows how the traces of today descend from the foundation of the distant past, manifesting the initial attainment at the site of tranquility (Bodh Gaya) and the final extinction at the twin śāla trees.

Later receiving the non-glutinous grain was a manifestation for the initial attainment of enlightenment at the Deer Park; later receiving the milk gruel in a layperson’s house was a manifestation for the final nirvana.
Whether great or small, whether occurring at the beginning or the end, all are manifestations within the traces [of his teaching].

How could it be that the inferior capacity of the concluding summary is the *zang* (concealed) mechanism, while the superior capacity is the *yuan* (perfect) mechanism, such that they are without distinction?
They are without distinction because both the beginning and the end are perfect.
Regarding the statement "the body has four or five [elements]" (*kāya-catur-ādi-pañca*): in the preceding difficult passage, there are four in the small [classification] and five in the large.

This is because in the large [classification], the "able-to-be-compared" (*upamāna*)—namely, the diamond (*vajra*)—is extracted separately; thus we know that "diamond" serves as the general metaphor for the large. Since the small and medium [classifications] do not extract the "able-to-be-compared," they have only four bodies.
If one were to extract them [from the small], one should say "non-diamond body"; in that case, both the large and small would have five.

If both are explained through their conjunction, then both the Great and the Small each possess four [attributes]. Now, because the Small is conjoined with the Great and opened up, there are four and five [attributes] respectively;

thus it is known that the body free from afflictions is not a body of minor afflictions, and the Dharma-body is not one of mixed food, for since the Dharma-body does not depend on solid food, it is eternally non-eternal, and boundless yet not bound—this constitutes the fourfold opposition between the Great and the Small. If...

Regarding the statement that each [element] is divided into five, it should be understood as meaning the adamantine body (*vajra-kāya*), which is neither the body of the Lesser Vehicle nor a perishable non-adamantine body;
thus, the answer was given in a transcendent manner because the eternal body is clarified among the five bodies.

Regarding the phrase "from the conditions of karma, etc.": the body is produced by karma, and karma arises from afflictions (*kleśa*). Speaking from the perspective of the fundamental cause, it is called the "body of afflictions.
The Buddha, using the five bodies (*pañca-kāya*) of the Mahāyāna, refutes the four bodies of the Hīnayāna;

yet, although the sūtra speaks of only three bodies within the Hīnayāna context, this is solely because the "limit" (*anta*) and "impermanence" (*anityatā*) share the same meaning. By merely stating that there is no "final body" (*paścima-deha*), it implies the absence of non-existence.
This is the eternal body (*nitya-kāya*).
You have raised [the objection] below; now, in the Buddha’s response, the sequence of the five "great" [aspects] is used to refute the four "small" [aspects].

Regarding "light" and so forth: this refers to what was previously explained concerning the distinct and perfect ways of attaining the Way, wherein all Buddhas emit light that enters the flower-pedestal and the crown of the Buddha’s head.
Furthermore,
to say that this is itself wisdom refers to the passage below where the Bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha, wishing to come to this assembly,
asks Mañjuśrī about the light that everyone perceives; Mañjuśrī then explains it by way of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and therefore it is so called.
"Radiance" refers to wisdom and so forth. Now, using this passage, it is established that the radiance of the lotus pedestal is also the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This is because radiance is form (*rūpa*), and form is a transformation of the mind; since form is itself the mind, it is said to be "wisdom.
That which is illuminated by wisdom is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which serves as an antidote to the "body of mixed food" (*āhāra-miśra-kāya*) of the Hīnayāna.
This statement that it is "eternally abiding" refers specifically to the *dharmakāya*; the eternally abiding body will be clarified below.
Furthermore, the phrase "light below" clarifies the body free from afflictions (*anāsrava-kāya*), which serves as an antithesis to the body of afflictions (*kleśa-kāya*).

The passage beginning with "If one first descends" clarifies boundlessness. The section following "the four great elements" clarifies the eternal body (*nitya-kāya*) in order to refute the impermanent body (*anitya-kāya*).
The statement "it is like a vajra" uses the vajra as a general metaphor; therefore, it concludes within the text concerning the eternal body.
In general, the five bodies are merely different names for the eternally abiding Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This refers to the first five bodies of the Great [Vehicle].

This refutes the first four bodies of the Lesser Vehicle. The Sūtra states that the *dharmakāya* is merely a reiteration of the aforementioned [body], contrasted with the "body that eats" (*āhāra-kāya*).

Regarding the phrase "Great conditions, etc.," this cites the cause to illustrate the fruit: if even those with the great capacity of the Bodhisattvas see only the five bodies of the Buddha, how much more so for others?
If those who have attained the fruits [of the path] have long since perfected their fundamental ground, how could there be four? The Sūtra states:
"There is no body of nutriment, nor a body of afflictions"—this constitutes a single phrase. Since the body of nutriment is the fruit of afflictions, it follows along with them;
thus, we know that the body of nutriment is itself that which is sublated by the Dharma-body. This is the same as the previous objection raised by Cunda: it refers merely to the five bodies.

Some claim that there are six bodies, but this is incorrect; moreover, since the *Śāstra* clearly states there are only five and not four, how can one falsely assert six bodies when it contradicts both the enumeration and the meaning of the preceding text?
At the end of the section on "Great" and "Small," the conclusion demonstrates their non-differentiation:
this is precisely the secret treasury, quiescent and real, which is not "great" or "small" but is manifested according to the capacities of beings.

Because the large manifests as the small, this "large and small" is itself neither large nor small; thus, principle and phenomenon are mutually identical, and cessation and illumination are simultaneous.

In this passage, first the "double negation" (both non-large and non-small) is clarified, followed by the "double illumination. If one were to fully enumerate the four or five pairs of negations, there would be nine propositions in total.

Among the four [propositions] regarding the small, the three names—affliction, the final limit, and impermanence—are identical to the three within the five [propositions] regarding the large: non-affliction, etc.
Since the three names—“affliction” (惱) and so forth—are mutually opposed, they are both negated; thus, there are only six phrases.
To respond to those below according to their capacities, he manifests accordingly; this is the simultaneous illumination of principle and phenomena across both the Great and Small Vehicles.

Although these phenomena are identical to principle, even though he is constantly engaged in activity throughout the day, the Dharma-body remains eternally quiescent; hence it is said, “yet for the Tathāgata,” and so on.

That which is profound and yet further profound refers to what was previously explained: that the beginning and end, as well as the great and small, accord with capacities is already profound and wondrous;

how much more so when the great and small are themselves the principle (*li*), for there is no difference between principle and phenomena—thus it is the most wondrous among the wondrous. As the *Laozi* says, "Profound and yet further profound, the gateway to all wonders.

Although we currently employ the phrasing of that text, the underlying meaning is worlds apart. This concludes the first section of the response concerning wisdom (*prajñā*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
I restate the previous objection:
regarding the phrase "receiving a consort" (*nàfēi*), *nà* (receive) means "to bring to" (*zhì*). "Bringing to" refers to the groom not personally escorting the bride to her family home.
The *Qūlǐ* states: "To receive a daughter for the Son of Heaven is called 'providing for the hundred surnames'; for a feudal lord, it is called 'providing for the wine.'"

Regarding the provision of beverages for a Great Officer (Dàfū), it is said that one prepares them with sweeping and sprinkling; the term "Officer" (Shì) is not mentioned because an Officer is of low status and must personally perform the welcoming of the bride, and thus cannot have the bride sent to him.
Since Siddhārtha was the Crown Prince, the phrase "taking a consort" (nàfēi) refers specifically to taking Yaśodharā as his consort, and the son born to her was named Rāhula.
"Abandoning the kingdom and renouncing kingship" refers to this very land:

on the eighth day of the second month in the forty-second year of King Zhou Zhao, he crossed the city of Kapilavastu at night, left the household life to enter Mount Gayā, and practiced the path to Buddhahood through six years of asceticism;

thus it is said "abandoning the kingdom," for while remaining a householder he would have become a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), and his departure from the household life was precisely the act of renunciation.
Regarding the throne and sitting under a tree upon grass and so forth: having completed his ascetic practices, he then accepted the milk-rice from a cowherd girl;

subsequently, he went to the Nairañjanā River to bathe, whereupon a precious tree bent its branches down for him, and the Bodhisattva climbed ashore by grasping a branch, causing the entire earth to tremble.
Thereupon, not far from the place of ascetic practice, there was a Pippala tree. Beneath it was the Vajrāsana (Diamond Throne).
Furthermore, the auspicious youth offered soft grass; the Bodhisattva accepted it and then, upon that seat, severed all afflictions with thirty-four moments of mind—this should be understood.
He arose, washed, and received food, then sat beneath the tree on the grass before him.

In the text, for the sake of convenience, the sitting under a tree is mentioned first; therefore, since even while sitting on grass beneath a tree one still possesses afflictions of both view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *bhāva-saṃyojana*), how much more so when receiving food?
Hence it says, "not yet severed by even a hair's breadth," and so forth.
The same applies to the Buddhas of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles.

Since the fruits of Buddhahood in these two vehicles realize only partial truth (*ekāntika-satya*) and have not yet perceived the Middle Way Buddha-nature, one should know that the statement "not yet having seen the Buddha-nature" simultaneously negates the causes and effects of both the *Zang* and *Tong* vehicles. Question: It is acceptable that they have not yet seen the Buddha-nature;

however, since those of the *Tong* vehicle have already severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), why are they still called "the body of afflictions" and so forth? Answer: This is based on the [absence of]... [text ends].
The "luminosity" (ming) being entirely present is also the body of afflictions and so forth.
If the "flower" (hua) represents the distinct and perfect [teachings], it signifies seeing the Buddha-nature.
Regarding "receiving the office of a Buddha," the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva attains that which was previously unattained... [one hundred...]
The thousand samādhis are called the stage of having already received the consecration;
they enter the realm of the Buddha, are fully endowed with the ten powers, and are counted among the Buddhas, just as the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch receives the royal position.
For one who has entered the Vajra-samādhi, even the most extreme grade of ignorance is difficult to shatter;

this samādhi is likened to a vajra, capable of destroying Mount Sumeru. As the Sūtra says, "Samādhi" means "right concentration. Therefore, the Vajra-like Samādhi is the virtue of liberation (vimukti-guṇa).
Attaining *sambodhi* through the Vajra-body is the virtue of wisdom (prajñā-guṇa); it is the eternal body, clearly perceiving the Buddha.
Because the virtue of the essential *dharmakāya* is itself the *dharmakāya*, it is called the "eternal body" (*nityakāya*). Although the *dharmakāya* is a vajra-body,

it is not designated as the "body free from afflictions" (*vītarāgakāya*) or the "body without end" (*anantakāya*), because these two bodies are merely named after what has been separated from the three qualities (*guṇa*).
They are called "the wise" because the three virtues illuminate together; thus, they all belong to wisdom.

As for the absence of the four kinds [of bodies] and so forth, since the body of impure food and the like is entirely ignorance, when ignorance is destroyed, it is precisely the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*);
therefore, one knows that the names and meanings of the four bodies are not restricted to the causal stage of the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

The Sūtra states that "when this food has been digested" refers to receiving the office [of Buddhahood] through the reception of light, thereby destroying the most supreme ignorance (*anuttara-avidyā*).

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent detailed analysis, each [body] possesses the aforementioned three aspects; however, these are generally categorized under the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) based on the three bodies as a whole.

Now, it is clarified that each of the three bodies corresponds to what is destroyed, such that each individually possesses the two meanings of wisdom and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). This is because the Vajra-body serves as the general metaphor for permanence (*nityatā*).
Because it abides, it destroys the impermanent body. If one were to discuss this in terms of opposition, one should say that the Vajra destroys what is non-Vajra;

that the Permanent destroys the impermanent is all as explained previously. However, because the five bodies are one in essence and that which is destroyed is no different, they are paired and refuted according to convenience;
there is no fixed principle [other than this]. Thus, the Dharma-body destroys afflictions, and the Permanent Body destroys the food-body (nirmāṇakāya). But...
In order to establish the wisdom that abandons what is to be destroyed, the term "the final limit" is not mentioned; the meaning is identical to that of impermanence.
Therefore, the conclusion below demonstrates there is no difference.
As for the distinction in the timing of their names: in the *Avataṃsaka*, the initial attainment is called the Vajra-samādhi, the Bodhi, and the Vision of the Buddha.
In this sutra, although it speaks of the final extinction of the nature, it also refers to the Dharma-body, the Eternal Body, and the Vajra-body.

Thus, while the two moments of initial attainment and entry into extinction differ, the designations established according to the capacities of beings are different; yet, in terms of wisdom and abandonment, their meaning is one.
Since the meaning perceived by those of great capacity is one, how can one raise objections based on the initial stage of the Lesser Vehicle?
Third, from the first section below, the previous objection is restated.

Regarding those who are "human among gods," as stated in the sutra, there are five kinds of gods: first, worldly gods (*loka-deva*), which the *Mahā-śāstra* calls "nominal gods" (*prajñapti-deva*), referring to worldly kings who are called "sons of heaven";
second, born gods (*upapatti-deva*), ranging from the Four Heavenly Kings...
Third, the Heaven of Non-Perception (asaṃjñisattva), which refers to the Pure Heavens from the first fruit up to the Pratyekabuddhas.

Fourth, the Heaven of Meaning (arthadeva), which refers to those from the first stage (bhūmi) and first abode (vihāra) upward who have partially realized the wondrous meaning. Fifth, the Heaven of Ultimate Meaning (paramārthadeva), which refers to the Buddhas who have seen their nature and reached the ultimate;
among these five heavens, they are the supreme heaven and are thus called the "God among Gods" (devātideva). Now, the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka [establish] the tree...
Previously, the King was merely a worldly deity; therefore, he is called "the god among men.

Now, the Buddha proceeds to provide the correct explanation for his current response regarding the four Māras—namely, the afflictions (kleśa), the aggregates (skandha), death (mṛtyu), and the son of heaven (devaputra).
Next, citing the *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra) to prove the initial accomplishment of the destruction of the four Māras:
"Attaining the path of Bodhi" and so forth refers to the transformation of afflictions (*kleśa*) into Bodhi;
"attaining the Dharma" and below refers to the transformation of the path of suffering into the Dharmakāya, thereby destroying the two Māras of the aggregates (*skandha*) and death.

Because one attains liberation immediately upon the non-arising of karmic bondage, the celestial Māra is destroyed; for the celestial Māra is the master of karma, causing people to perform demonic deeds.
Now, the following section of the sutra clarifies that what is taught here is identical to the *Śāstra*.
Regarding "the destroyer of the aggregates of affliction": the aggregates are the fruit of afflictions; to destroy them means to eliminate their cause and extinguish their fruit.
Regarding "the destroyer of the Māra of death": since death is impermanent, it is that which is destroyed by the eternal body.
Is it not the case that both the sutras and śāstras clearly explain that what the beings of great capacity see is the initial accomplishment of the destruction of Māra?
Now, the passage beginning with "entering below" clarifies that his current entry into parinirvāṇa likewise destroys the four māras.

Regarding "impermanence and so forth," this merely opens up the affliction-māra (kleśa-māra) into four inversions, which together constitute the seven māras, as explained in the section on the objects of demonic activity in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the "heavenly māra" (*devaputra-māra*), since cause and effect have already been extinguished, he is able to externally destroy the heavenly māra. Now, the lotus pedestal has just been formed.

Question: Since Māra has already been defeated, what more remains to be defeated now that the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is being expounded? Answer: It is said that he is defeated for the sake of providing a catalyst for those to be converted;
thus, it is called "already defeated" and also "defeated now. Furthermore, those who have partially attained the Buddha-eye are the Equal Enlightenment (Sambodhi) beings on the lotus pedestal;
although they have not yet reached ultimate perfection, they have already realized partial certification.
Now the Buddha descends to provide a brief answer as to why the scriptural text simply says "preaching the twelve divisions [of the canon]"; this refers to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Since the perfection of giving has three aspects—namely, the gift of Dharma, the gift of material wealth, and the gift of fearlessness—the other perfections are the five perfections.
Once it is understood that these are fully complete, one may know by analogy that the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) are likewise complete; therefore, the text is abbreviated.

Previously, although the initial accomplishment was not explained in detail, it had long since been extensively mastered; now, this sutra explains it once again in detail. Therefore, it is said that it "extensively reveals thorough mastery.
Here, "revealing" (*khyāpana*) means "explaining" (*deśanā*). Although the explanations may be extensive or concise, thorough mastery remains no different;

thus, there is no distinction. Question: Is the *Avataṃsaka* not an extensive explanation? Answer: It merely contrasts with the Perfect [Teaching] (*yuan*), yet even compared to the Distinct [Teaching] (*bie*), it still remains separated from the Two Vehicles (*er sheng*).
In this present sutra, the eight teachings are again bestowed so that all may return to the eternal; therefore, this is a summary.
Regarding the explanation of those with and without fruit, as for the two cowherd girls mentioned in the sutra, the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra) states:

"When the Tathāgata had completed six years of ascetic practice and his body was thus emaciated, he thought to himself: 'If I proceed toward the Bodhi tree in such a state, people of future generations will mock me.'"
He said, "I am famished; I would rather obtain the Way while eating soft food to restore my body, and only then achieve enlightenment.
At that time, there was the daughter of an elder who had married and given birth to a son. Her heart was filled with great joy, and she prepared a thousand oxen for the occasion.

They were made to drink from one another in succession, and from their pure milk she made a gruel intended as an offering to the tree deity. She sent her maidservant to sweep and clean, but upon seeing the Buddha, she did not recognize him. She returned and reported this.
Under the tree, there was a goddess, upright and beautiful; hearing this, she rejoiced and wished to take the congee away.

As she reached for it, the congee leaped out of the cauldron more than a zhang high, so that she could not reach it. The woman was greatly astonished. A deity in the sky said: "A Great Bodhisattva has already risen from his seat.

By the power of your original vow, you should first offer him food; only then will he attain Perfect Enlightenment. This is a brief account of the auspicious responses, similar to the *Sūtra on the Response of the Equal Enlightenment*.
In both cases, it is not stated that there were two women.
Since there was neither one who begged nor one who received, the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is serene and still; thus, begging and receiving are inappropriate.

Why does the Master of the Commentary (*Sūtra-vyākhyātṛ*) explain this by correlating it with the two conditions of the Great and Small Vehicles, given that the scriptural text merely cites the initial instance as a manifestation of receiving milk? Answer: It is because of Cunda.

Because [the disciples] grasped at the small as being difficult, the Buddha specifically cited the beginning of the small [vehicle] in his response; thus, the meaning of the words "I truly did not eat" has two layers.

If considered from the perspective of those with great capacity (*mahāyāna*), they saw only the crown of the head receiving the light and did not see the reception of the milk; therefore, it is said "I did not eat.

If considered from the perspective of the Tathāgata’s own practice, where phenomena are identical to principle (*dharmatā*), even the reception of light is not [a literal act]; therefore, it is said "I truly did not [eat]."
Because of this, we know that the Master [Zongmi] cited both conditions of what is perceived to clarify that principle is identical to phenomena;
this is the meaning of "not eating," and thus he has profoundly captured the Buddha’s intent. What was previously called "the profound within the profound" is indeed not a false claim.
In the section on "Arising," the first part concerns the cause for the request; "Pureṇa follows the intent" is below that; "The Buddha accepts the request" is below that;
"Obstructing the request for the eternal Dharma" is below that; and "The repeated request" is below that.
In the explanation by Master Xinghuang, the first part concerns the capacity and views regarding departure and abiding; the text contains four phrases, of which the first two cite the Buddha.

Regarding the statement "next, upon hearing 'cessation'... and so forth, the following two phrases clarify how the receptive capacity (the *ālambana*) gives rise to understanding according to the words.

As for the presence of the characters "furthermore" (*yòu*) and "first" (*chū*) before the word "cessation" (*miè*), it is not incorrect; rather, one should take the character "furthermore" as the opening of the subsequent phrase, meaning: "first, hearing 'cessation,' ...
and furthermore, hearing 'permanence' (*cháng*)."

Now, according to the principle of responding to conditions as explained below, there should be no coming or staying; that is, the Tathāgata’s body of responsive manifestation truly has no coming or staying—it is only when the conditions of sentient beings perceive it that there appears to be coming and staying.

If this is so, the Master [Zhizhe] now refutes Xinghuang’s interpretation, which, though claiming that the Buddha has no coming or staying, still asserts that the conditions perceive coming and staying.
If one does not clarify how the occasion and conditions bring benefit, and fails to clarify the four *siddhāntas*, then it would merely be a matter of responding to others' departures and arrivals,
providing no benefit to the assembly at that time.
Now, by clarifying the section below regarding "seeing [the Buddha] depart," the four benefits are explained.
Regarding those who yearn with the three karmas, because they manifest the goodness that gives rise to the three virtues, they belong to the category of humans.
As for the phrase "Even the Tathāgata departs," since even the Buddha is impermanent, how could we ordinary beings cling to permanence?
Those who enter the secret treasury realize that there is no characteristic of going or departing; they thus behold the three virtues just as Mañjuśrī does.

As for the phrase "to cite an example," it refers to citing Cunda as proof that a single person may possess four benefits. By analogy, cases where there are only three or only two [benefits] can be understood from the text.
His profound grief is the world-aspect (*loka-dhātu*), while his joy is the aspect for humans (*pudgala*). Thus, the Tathāgata does not pass into parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement that "the antidote and Mañjuśrī alike enter the principle," the question asks why this world is joyful, while the answer states that it is according to the specific purpose (*yathārtha*).
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Some feel fear, some feel joy, some give rise to weary detachment, and some sever their doubts.
The commentary on the text also applies the four *siddhāntas*; therein, "joy" is explained as having the sense of generating wholesome roots (*kuśala-mūla*).

If Cunda were not thus, it would mean that although he held a high position and truly lacked feelings of compassion and so forth, he merely used skillful means (*upāya*) to lead others toward the ultimate reality, enabling the multitude to obtain the four benefits.
"The whole land" (*shu lù*) means to follow or govern; as the *Shijing* says: "Among the guests throughout the land, there are none who are not subjects of the King."
Regarding the "ten acts of yielding" and so forth: this refers to how Cunda was placed after the assembly of fifty-two [bodhisattvas] when making offerings, yet received the benefits before them;
because he alone was immediately granted acceptance and attained the five fruits, he possessed this sequence of priority and posteriority, and thus it is said that he was "the one person."

Regarding the three characters "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth: this refers to the three characters "vow" (*praṇidhi*), "fulfillment" (*paripūri*), and "satisfaction" (*saṃtuṣṭi*) in the sutra text, which constitute the praise of the vow.

As for the statement that "fulfillment" (*paripūri*) extends upward to the preceding [terms], it means that although the two characters "fulfillment" fall under the category of "vow," their meaning extends upward to the [preceding] three—namely, fame (*yaśas*), benefit (*artha*), and virtue (*guṇa*)—because all four are fully complete; hence it is said, "the four are all sufficient."
The preceding section explains the meaning of "fulfilling vows," referring to how in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he once made a vow to offer worship and gather merit;

since that vow has now been realized, it is said to be "fulfilled. Although the structural analysis treats the character *de* (virtue) as a separate section, when reading the scripture, one should read it as a single phrase: "the fulfillment of virtue and vows."

Regarding the six difficulties: first, it is difficult for a human birth to arise; second, it is difficult to obtain the two kinds of spiritual benefit; third, it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world;

fourth, it is difficult for faith to arise; fifth, it is difficult to hear the sutras and the Dharma; sixth, it is difficult to achieve future offerings. In the text, these are explained sequentially:
first, both "human birth" and "spiritual benefit" are explained together as two difficulties.

Regarding the five signs of decline (*pañca-maraṇa-nimitta*), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that there are two types: the five great and the five minor. As for the great ones: first, dust and grime stain one's robes;

second, flower garlands wither; third, sweat exudes from both armpits; fourth, a foul odor enters the body; and fifth, one finds no pleasure in one's own seat. When these five signs appear, death is certain;

even if one encounters powerful external conditions, they cannot be averted. The minor signs are as follows: [the eyes become turbid, the skin loses its luster, the body emits a stench, sweat breaks out on the palms and soles, and food and drink lose their flavor].
First, one's clothing and ornaments produce sounds that are utterly unpleasant; second, the radiance of one's own body suddenly ceases to appear;
third, during the act of bathing, droplets of water cling to the body; fourth, one's naturally restless mind now becomes stagnant upon a single object;

fifth, the eyes, which were originally still and tranquil, now twitch repeatedly. When these five signs appear, although it is not certain that death will occur, one may still encounter superior and wholesome conditions.
Because of this transformation, Cunda is now born among humans as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of the Buddha who fully observes the five precepts; he is named a "perfected" (*pūrṇa*) upāsaka.

He has attained the unsurpassed benefit of the sutra, which means that by perfectly upholding the precepts of principle (*dharmatā-śīla*), he transcends the partial and limited [teachings]; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed and vast."
As explained in the chapter on the lay follower (upāsaka),

the passage beginning with "at the bottom of the ocean" explains the third difficulty of encountering a Buddha in the world; the passage beginning with "looking up at a needle" explains the fourth, fifth,
and sixth of the three difficulties, as the text states.
Regarding the "Flower Banner Wheel-Turning King" (Huabiao Lunwang): its full name is *udumbara*, which means "spiritual and auspicious.
Three thousand years before a Wheel-Turning King is about to appear, this flower manifests.
To be able to most fundamentally accord with the Dharma is to offer worship like that flower; thus, though it has not yet arrived, one shall obtain the eternal fruit as if by the wheel.
As the King was about to depart, the great assembly conferred upon Cunda the prophecy of his future Buddhahood; therefore, he is praised with the *udumbara* flower.

Thus we know that the Master of the Commentary (*Sūshuzhu*) correctly indicates that the *udumbara* flower in this scripture is a praise of Cunda, differing from other scriptures where the *udumbara* flower is used as a metaphor for the rarity of encountering a Buddha.
Hence, while the preceding scripture says, "Rare indeed is Cunda," here it says, "like the *udumbara* flower."
Since the phrase "rare in the world" is identical to the expression used for "rare," we know this is a praise of Cunda. [Question:
How could the great assembly bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon Cunda? [Answer: The great assembly verified the cause and thereby knew the fruit;

having seen the cause of Cunda’s offering of alms, they knew he would surely attain the wondrous fruit of Bodhi. It is like the case of Sadāparibhūta, who saw only that sentient beings possessed the correct cause (*samyak-hetu*).
The *Xingzhong* (Nature-Seed) already records: "If you all shall become Buddhas, how much more so now that Cunda offers this almsgiving? This is the causal condition for cultivating merit;
therefore, when the great assembly beholds it and offers praise, this itself constitutes the bestowal of a prediction [of enlightenment]."
"Calling out with the mouth is oral karma"—this "calling out with the mouth" refers to the act of crying out for salvation.
Regarding the phrase "the moon is the essence of Yin," the *Huainanzi* states: "The moon is the essence of the Great Yin."

Regarding the phrase "adorned in heaven and bright upon earth," the *Yi* states: "The sun and moon are adorned upon the King of Heaven. Wang Bi’s commentary explains that "adorned" (*li*) means "attached" (*zhu*).
Kong Yingda states that "adorned" means "clinging to" (*fu*) and "bright" (*jiao*) means "luminous" (*ming*).
Cunda’s section below corresponds to the Dharma; "the supreme and wondrous time" refers to the occasion of preaching the permanence [of the Buddha] at the time of Nirvana.
Cunda’s wondrous benefit accords with this time, like the moon meeting the autumn season.
In the "Praise of Names," the "Brief Praise" is also cited, which states: "To understand the wondrous meaning" refers to praising the realization of the single essence of the Triple Gem.
Since the "wondrous meaning" is the principle realized, it is the Dharma Jewel; since the Buddha-mind is the wisdom that realizes, it belongs to the Buddha Jewel.
Just as a father gives birth to a son, so too does the object give rise to wisdom; through the union of object and wisdom, there is the Buddha.
This "son" is the Jewel of the Sangha;
he is also of the lower category, which encompasses all dharmas. Although their names and numbers differ, the three virtues are no different, as explained above in the section on receiving offerings.
He praises him further by means of three names: he praises Cunda for attaining the wisdom of partial realization regarding the Master, the Friend, and the Teacher, which is like ultimate wisdom;
thus it is said that "his mind is the Buddha-mind," meaning that within a single stage he possesses all stages, just as a wise minister understands the King’s intent.
Therefore, because he has attained understanding through the Master, the Friend, and the Teacher, he understands the sublime meaning and has thus attained the Teacher.
Rāhula is the son of the Buddha’s birth-body (*janmakāya*), while Cunda is the son of the Buddha’s dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

although their births differ, they are equal in their status as sons. This is because they are both born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by the Dharma; thus, Rāhula is one who has attained intimacy.
The verse serves both as a request and as a restatement of the preceding praise; thus, while the praise is a "repeated verse" (*geya*), the request is an "independent verse" (*udāna*).
Regarding the "equality with the Brahma King": when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, the Brahma King of the First Dhyāna requested him to preach the Dharma.

Now, Cunda requests the Buddha to reveal the permanence of the Dharma-body, which is equal to that of the Brahma Lord. The Sixth Heaven is the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*); the Brahma world is situated above it.
Because he is above the six heavens of the desire realm, it is said that he has "already transcended.
Regarding the phrase "praise and fame" (*ślāghā-yaśas*), it should have been "praise and benefit" (*ślāghā-lābha*); the character *yaśas* (fame) is an error.

This means that since he already understands Cunda’s realization of the wondrous meaning and his mind is like the Buddha’s mind, he prostrates himself and is appointed as the host of the invitation; being one to whom the assembly turns for refuge, he is said to have attained great benefit, as explained below.
The verse states that the arrival of Śakra and Brahmā to make offerings is likewise for the sake of praising his merit. To summarize:

"To take one's life" means to demand it through a difficult ordeal; this refers to the fact that if Cunda had not entreated the Buddha on my behalf, my life would have been cut short—this is the meaning of "demanding through a difficult ordeal.
As the *Analects* says: "Though they say he did not extort [a gift] from his lord, I do not believe it."
"‘Sudden death’ (zúsāng) means to pass away (mò) and to perish (wáng); it is a brief term.
As for ‘the scripture mentions parents briefly,’ this refers to the fact that the sutra mentions the mourning for one’s kin only in brief. If one wished to provide a general analogy, one should say:
‘For example, suppose there were someone whose teacher suddenly passed away, or whose sovereign suddenly passed away,’ and so forth. Therefore, the commentary states [as follows]."
The "great joy" mentioned previously refers to what the sutra says: "The multitude rejoiced greatly, leaping for joy, and with one voice they praised," and so forth.
Now, Cunda’s joy occurs after the great assembly; therefore, it is said that he "rejoiced at the end."
Furthermore, this single act of yielding is an expression of joy; by yielding once more, he fulfills the ten virtues mentioned previously.

Since he previously offered his gifts while remaining at the rear of the assembly, and now expresses his joy while likewise remaining at the rear of the assembly, he diminishes himself to yield to others; from beginning to end, who is it but Cunda?

In the first section below, the commentary briefly conveys the general praise of the assembly. Within this, there is first a general and specific classification; the four characters "briefly conveying the three praises" constitute the general division.
The section beginning with "the first nine [lines]" constitutes the specific division, which conveys the text of the vows. It should be stated that the first six and a half lines are intended;
when the sub-commentary says "nine lines," it is an error for "two and a half lines."

The phrase "forming an analogy for the fetters" is also erroneous; it should read "half a line," referring to the two lines in the Sūtra that state: "Just as a blind turtle in the great ocean might encounter a floating yoke with a single hole.

Regarding the phrase "eliminating that which is to be abandoned": this means that greed and anger are the causes of origination (*samudaya*), while the three evil realms are the fruits of suffering (*duḥkha*); [the former] is the cause, and [the latter] is the fruit of cessation (*nirodha*).
The result of their extinction is that they are all free from what the Sūtra calls "greed, anger, and delusion" (the latter being "grasping").
According to the six-fascicle version of the Sūtra, this means they are now freed from the suffering of the *niraya* hells; here, the general [suffering] is concealed to highlight the specific.

When it says below, "they do not fall among animals," etc., this should also be understood as generally freeing them from the three evil realms, while concealing the general to highlight the specific—this is a matter of textual emphasis.
Regarding "fearless" and so forth: because one encounters a Buddha and eliminates delusion, one is freed from the animal realm.
"Rising" refers to the difficulty of generating faith; "descending" should likewise be understood as referring to the permanent cessation [of suffering] and so on, though the text is abbreviated.

Because one generates the seed of faith, performs wholesome deeds, and makes offerings that destroy stinginess, one is freed from the hungry ghost realm. Because one generates faith and removes doubt, one is freed from the asura realm.

Regarding the subsequent passage on the difficulty of making offerings, the first two phrases cite the rarity of encountering a Buddha; next, it clarifies that performing *dāna* (generosity) toward a Buddha is the most difficult of all acts of giving.
Because this *dāna* is identical to the *dharmadhātu* and is utterly without distinction, it is called "perfected *dāna*.
As an offering made as a constant cause, it shall surely yield a constant fruit, thereby delivering one from birth and death.
Regarding the passage "Hearing the Dharma is difficult," the sutra contains two lines. The first line praises the Buddha to show that hearing the Dharma from the Buddha is extremely difficult;

thus, by mentioning the Buddha, [the text] distinguishes him from all other persons. "Worldly dharmas" refers to the conditions of birth and death; that is, the four adversities and the four favors—the eight winds are these worldly dharmas.
Gain, praise, fame, and pleasure are the favors; loss, blame, defamation, and suffering are the adversities. This extends up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

The seeds are the cause and the flow of birth-and-death is the fruit. If one takes the delusions of the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" realm as the seeds of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the fragmented existence as the flow of birth-and-death, this refers to the Buddhas of the *Śrāvaka* (Treasury) and *Pratyekabuddha* (Penetration) vehicles.

If one takes the ignorance of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) as the seeds of the Peak of Existence and the transformational existence as the flow of birth-and-death, this refers to the Buddhas of the *Vaipulya* (Distinct) and *Vimalakīrti* (Perfect) vehicles.
Next, the half-line correctly clarifies the difficulty of hearing the Dharma, meaning that one must encounter a Buddha as a person.
Furthermore, it is difficult to hear the Dharma; the Sūtra does not state that one who encounters a Buddha necessarily hears the Dharma.

Therefore, the subsequent half-line serves as a concluding simile. According to the literal text of the Sūtra, this is merely a concluding simile for the difficulty of encountering a Buddha and hearing the Dharma.
However, according to the preceding structural analysis (*pīn-k'o*), it constitutes a general simile for the six difficulties.

Regarding the waters being the same color as the mountain: both the *Abhidharma* and the *Abhidharmakośa* state that each of the four sides of Mount Meru has a distinct color—gold on the east, lapis lazuli on the south, silver on the west, and crystal on the north—and that the waters correspond to the color of the mountain on each respective side.
When sentient beings enter into these waters, they all become the same color as the water.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha’s wisdom, etc.," it should be stated in its full form that the first half of the verse represents real wisdom (*jñāna*) and the second half represents expedient wisdom (*upāya*).
Now, to say simply that "half the verse is the perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*) is merely to cite the former to indicate the latter.
