"Dispersing chaos and so forth" means to dispel the rebellious incursions of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and restore the Buddha-nature’s correct path.

The *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu zhuan) states: "To disperse a chaotic age and return to the correct [order]—nothing is closer to this than the *Spring and Autumn*. The commentary on the "Lament for Shu" in the *Wenxuan* says:

"The Emperor, with his divine martial prowess and sagely wisdom, dispersed chaos and restored correctness. The note explains that "dispersing" (*bo*) means to eliminate; it refers to using sagely intelligence to remove [the disorder].
This rectifies the confusion regarding what exists and what does not.

That which exists even when there is no Buddha refers to the difficulty of being born as a human, the difficulty of obtaining the beneficial fruits of goodness, and the difficulty of hearing the sutras and Dharma.

That which exists only when a Buddha appears refers to the difficulty of encountering a Buddha in the world, the difficulty of giving rise to faith, and the difficulty of completing offerings in later times.
That even names are established in vain means that if one lacks the virtue of subsequent offerings, then the title "Cunda" is a name without substance.

Abiding within the Buddha’s realm is to exist when one dwells there and to perish when one does not; these three truths—the three virtues—are mutually exclusive and yet mutually inclusive, and this is called the Buddha’s realm.
Therefore, it is refuted by saying "it should not be so," because the Buddha’s realm of activity—his coming and going—is inconceivable.
Thus, the previous objection that one should not request the Buddha to remain long in the world is refuted.
Those who "know there are six kinds" refer to those like Cunda, who possess a partial realization of the Buddha’s realm but cannot yet attain its ultimate consummation.
Because he knows this, the Buddha prohibits it; thus, only the Buddha is called "holy" (ārya), while all other stages are considered ordinary (pṛthagjana).

Therefore, the "Treatise on the Five Ordinary Beings" (Pañca-pṛthagjana-śāstra) regards the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi) as holy, while regarding the wisdom of ordinary beings—even that of Samantabhadra—as ordinary. This is the same principle.
"Subordinating the high for the sake of the low" refers to subordinating the partial realization of the stage prior to abiding (*vyavasthāna-pūrva*).
"All three are entirely subordinate"—these four characters are an explanatory supplement added by Jingxi;

since it was previously stated "for the sake of the low," and it was not yet known what the lower stages were like, he points here to the three types of benefit prior to abiding, all of which are termed "subordinate. It is only when one enters into the principle that they are [fully realized].
Regarding the question of how the names of the first [stage], the "Abiding in All Questions," and the three preceding [stages] are established as corresponding positions, the answer is as follows:

The name [of the first stage] corresponds because hearing the name brings benefit through joy, as it causes one to recognize the essence of the dharma-body. The [second] five stages correspond because wholesome roots are produced and wholesome contemplative practices (*yogācāra*) are successfully accomplished. The [third] stage corresponds because it acts as a semblance-antidote that destroys coarse defilements and evils.
Regarding the "raising of two" and the "application": the sutra merely mentions impermanence briefly, yet its meaning encompasses the constant application.
If one were to say this is not so, why did the preceding text state that the five fruits are all constant? Therefore, we know that the preceding text also briefly raises the constant application.
The reason for this is that previously, when Cunda addressed the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and offered his gifts, the Buddha applied the constant [truth] to treat him; now it is likewise.

Because Cunda requested that [the Buddha] remain, the Buddha treated him with the medicine of impermanence. This was solely because his karmic conditions had not yet reached the point of understanding the dharma-realm of coming and going;
thus, the Buddha’s treatments were distinct for each. Although this is so according to the text, the meaning must necessarily encompass both aspects.

Furthermore, since the subsequent verses clarify two such applications, the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) categorizes this as "two applications. By blocking the request and following the text to illuminate the meaning, the confusion dissolves like ice melting.
Thus, we know that the Master of the Commentary (Suzhu) had a profound realization of this sutra, which he divides into three parts: first, [the Buddha] accords with capacities and principles;

second, the manifestation or concealment of the Buddha’s appearance differs according to the conditions of those capacities; and third, the Buddha’s dark secret treasury is eternally in accord with the Three Virtues.
In the past, using the lower-level covenant, the five-gate contemplation was explained and established as follows:
impermanence, suffering, non-self, impurity, and cessation are the reality, while provisional names are the realm of others.
Regarding the constant discourse on the five gates, these are the five gates of the eternal, blissful, self, and pure nirvana;
opening the provisional to reveal the real is called one's own realm.
If one employs the following conclusion to demonstrate the intent of the prohibition against requesting [further teaching]:
Regarding the passage "even kings who have attained mastery," although a king possesses mastery, how can he escape impermanence? Furthermore, the signs of impermanent death shift and extinguish life;
its momentum is as sovereign as that of a human monarch. Thus, the *Cittabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) states:
"The King of Death, like a golden-winged garuḍa, will before long swallow the life-faculty. This is precisely the same meaning; therefore, it was previously said that "life is prey to death."
"To swallow" means to undergo manifold sufferings, namely the five sufferings and the eight sufferings.
That which is impermanent within the three realms is suffering precisely because it is subject to the flux and passing away of impermanence.

Regarding the sūtra’s statement that "the nature and characteristics of the path of existence are equal," this means that the causes and conditions of the three realms of existence and the six destinies are mere fabrications;
when one seeks their intrinsic nature and characteristics, they are entirely empty.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement that [things] "are subject to destruction," they are empty because they can be destroyed.

Regarding the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*), Master Xiǎn says: "The meaning of 'self' (*ātman*) is sovereign mastery. Since one is already afflicted by old age and illness and entangled by afflictions (*kleśa*), one realizes through verification that there is no self.
In the sutra, the phrase "all these which are without limit" refers to the aforementioned terrors and various evils; "these" refers to those evils.
Because it is not ultimate, it is called "boundless.
Regarding the sutra’s mention of "yokes, bonds," and so forth: the substance of the fruit is impure, consisting of abscesses, ulcers, and various diseases that bind and constrain the body.
"Fundamentally lacking purpose and benefit" means that the seeds are impure; taking up that discarded physical remains is without purpose or benefit. (The auspicious sign.)
It should be understood according to the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Regarding "this shore" and "the other shore": birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is "this," and nirvāṇa is "that. To destroy existence and realize emptiness is to cross from this shore to that shore.
Furthermore, taking "this" and "that" as "this" refers to the Middle Way; to destroy extremes and realize the Middle is to take "that" [as the goal].
Therefore, it is said that the "other shore" is neither that nor this; though the words follow a sequential order, the meaning is in fact perfectly integrated.
Within the explanation of the Buddha’s realm, the identity of the three and the one results in the three truths (trisatya). To summarize and conclude:
the three and the one are no different. One truth is emptiness (śūnyatā), one truth is the conventional (saṃvṛti), and the truth that is neither one nor three is the middle (madhyamā).

The Way simultaneously negates both [existence and non-existence] while being one and three; this is the Middle Way. Simultaneously illuminating both emptiness and existence—what follows below merely explains and establishes the meaning of what precedes.
Only when it is thus can it be called "equality": the mutual fusion of the Three Truths and the non-duality of the living and the Buddha constitute what is called the realm of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, because in the concluding summary of the intent to reject the request, the provisional (假) is identical to emptiness (空), and since emptiness neither departs nor abides, how can one request that [the Buddha] remain?
Within emptiness, the provisional is identical to it; thus, there are only names. How can one request that he remain? The extremes are identical to the Middle; therefore, the Middle Way is level.

Regarding the non-duality of going and staying: why is it requested that [the Buddha] remain? The text is abbreviated because it relies on provisional meaning; thus it says, "up to the realm of the Bodhisattvas.

This refers to the distinct teaching of the nine and a half verses. Since these clarify the general purport of the five contemplations—that all things ultimately return to emptiness and are free from desire—and since the single verse states "because of right reflection," this is provisional meaning.
The single verse "I deliver" refers precisely to delivering [beings] to the Middle Way.
The Meaning of "The Other Shore":
Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues," Fascicle Three;
Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues," Fascicle Four.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang.

The Six Difficulties arise from the Buddha, as the Buddha himself directed and clarified them in response to requests. The Four Praises arise from the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, through which this teaching was obtained;
it is not false, but is indeed the Buddha’s own word.
Regarding the phrase "humbly expressing gratitude following the Buddha," one should change "gratitude" (xiè) to "therefore" (zhě), reading it as: "Humbly, [it] arises from the realm of the Buddha.
This clarifies that what follows below explains how gratitude arises from function; thus, the scriptural text begins from the words "From the World-Honored One... and so forth.
"Equal" means "level," signifying that his rank is level with that of Mañjuśrī.

As for the metaphors for wisdom (*jñāna*) and the abandonment of afflictions (*prahāṇa*): the dragon is a great metaphor for water, representing meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which can sever delusions; the elephant is a great [metaphor] for land-dwelling, thus representing wisdom (*prajñā*) which can illuminate the principle.
"Yuanquan" (Deep Spring) refers to a deep abyss. The *Guanzi* states: "When water emerges from the earth but does not flow, it is called a 'yuan'.

Regarding "xiaoyao" (the clouds), the *Wenxuan*, in the "Rudufu" (Rhapsody on the Wu Region), says: "Tearing through the layered clouds to hunt in the heights," with the commentary noting that "clouds" refer to the thin clouds near heaven;
this means that having emerged from beneath the aforementioned "deep spring," one now divides and proves oneself upon the heights of the clouds.
The expression "xiè wúcháng" (thank you for impermanence) means that it is through the Buddha manifesting impermanence that I have obtained benefit.
Regarding "rúlái wèirán" (the Tathāgata has not yet [done so]): the dictionary *Fānyán* states it is pronounced "mǎng yū rán"; Guo Pu’s commentary notes that these are all onomatopoeic sounds.
[The character is pronounced as *mǎng* (with the "huāo" rhyme) and *yū* (pronounced as *yú*).

First, the preceding analogy according to the explanatory text primarily illustrates the capacity (*jī*, the sentient being); next, the subsequent analogy according to the text of the citation primarily illustrates the response (*yìng*, the Buddha).
Now, the Sage dismisses the two preceding interpretations.

When it is said that the Sage’s words are "skillful and subtle," it means that although within the Dharma he selectively cites the capacity [of the sentient beings] and within the meeting of conditions he selectively cites the response [of the Buddha], though the language is partial, the meaning is mutually clarifying.
Therefore, this single metaphor encompasses both meanings: namely, that sentient beings are attached to the Buddha, and the Buddha...

Out of affection for the capacities of sentient beings, he responds to them without abandoning them; this is illustrated by the metaphor of one who, when starving, would not vomit out what they have eaten. Because the meaning applies universally to both [aspects], it is called "skillful and subtle.

That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is secondary, whereas making offerings is precisely the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*); thus, the gift of the Dharma through discourse (*dharmadāna*) is considered secondary.
This distinction between the secondary and the primary constitutes the meaning of the "worldly" (*laukika*).
When a treatise is composed for the sake of others, it is for the purpose of generating wholesome roots in those people; thus, it is "for the benefit of humans.
Regarding skillful means in question and answer: Mañjuśrī rebuked [Pureṇa] with impermanence to urge him to remain, while Pureṇa challenged impermanence with permanence;
this is the meaning of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*). The realm of the Tathāgata is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
In a contest between victor and vanquished, it is the vanquished who must carry the burden for the victor; thus, falling away from righteousness constitutes defeat.
As Zhuangzi said: "The strong man carries him off and runs with him, yet the deluded one does not perceive it."
To clarify what is irrational: because the notions of permanence and impermanence are mutually contradictory and do not accord with correct principle, they are termed "irrational.

As for the statement that this will be explained extensively later, it refers to the detailed explanation in the *Śoka-parivarta* (Chapter on Sorrow) concerning how neither permanence nor impermanence applies, as set forth by the Buddha.
The "is" of the "neither-nor" reveals that the biased attachments of the two individuals are "non.

Regarding Mañjuśrī, the Ancient Buddha, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that he currently resides in the world of Abhirati in the northern direction as a Buddha named Saṃkusumitarājendra (Flower-Blossom King),
and as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, in the past, for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas...
During incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, there was a Buddha named Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King (*Nāgottararāja*), who was none other than Mañjuśrī.
Regarding this matter from the perspective of principle and phenomena: by relying on the phenomenon of defeat to manifest the principle of the three virtues, the profound falls into defeat;

by relying on the phenomenon of victory to manifest the principle, the shallow attains victory. Victory is non-victory and defeat is non-defeat, thereby manifesting that the two extremes are identical.
The middle three truths are precisely the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the three rounds of analysis within this section, the first round analyzes existence and non-existence.

Based on the Sūtra’s statement that both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) shall be set aside for now, it follows that Mañjuśrī represents existence and Cunda represents non-existence; therefore, they are analyzed here.

Regarding "Mañjuśrī... the True Dharma," the sutra states: "One who practices contemplation in this manner and possesses the samādhi of emptiness, desiring to seek the True Dharma, should train in this way.
This passage challenges Mañjuśrī by seeking to establish the conditioned as the unconditioned.
For those who maintain the existence [of phenomena], one may arbitrarily take Mañjuśrī as existent and Cunda as non-existent;
yet, since the non-existence of Cunda is used to refute the existence of Mañjuśrī, this non-existence is itself established only in dependence upon that existence. As it is said:

"If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon is itself dependent. Now, the same principle applies here: if emptiness is established in opposition to existence, then this emptiness is itself established dependently.
"Because it exists, it should indeed be 'existence' (yu).
This is the conclusion of the refutation. "The explanation says" introduces the response and clarification.

Regarding "it is existence in relation to the Great [Vehicle]," this means that the principle of emptiness in the *Zang* and *Tong* [vehicles] constitutes the transformed birth-and-death (*pariṇāmanika-saṃsāra*) outside the realms; therefore, the *Bie* and *Yuan* [vehicles] are... [implied: distinct from it].

Because illusory existence and the emptiness of illusory existence together constitute the conventional truth, they are called the "repeated conventional. Thus, it is said that "in relation to the Great [Truth], there is existence";
this "existence" refers to the repeated conventional, while the "non-existence" discussed in the Middle Way refers to the non-existence within the discourse on existence.

"Existence is non-existence; non-existence is non-existence. Although existence is designated as such when established through mutual dependence, this very existence established by dependence outside the realm [of the teaching] further sublates the "non-existence" within the realm of the teaching.
Therefore it is said, "existence is non-existence"; this is explained in terms of mutual sublation.

Alternatively, the character "ke" (or) may be an error and should read "kyo" (to go/abandon); thus, "existence goes and non-existence is non-existent," meaning that once the "existence" to be sublated has vanished, the "existence" that performs the sublation [likewise vanishes].
Since even "non-existence" is severed when [existence] is destroyed, one knows that once the relative opposition has ceased, one returns to this very non-existence.

Furthermore, the following passage distinguishes between victory and defeat: Cunda’s practice within the six perfections is limited to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), and is thus called "shallow";

Mañjuśrī, an ancient Buddha whose myriad practices are already fulfilled, is thus called "deep. How can the shallow surpass the deep? It is because the shallow [in its ultimate sense] actually excels the deep.
Regarding the phrase "the reversal of defeat" in the response concerning the "suitable objects" and so forth: this refers to the suitability of the objects for the capacities [of the audience].
Thus, Mañjuśrī serves as the anvil and Cunda serves as the hammer; they manifest victory and defeat merely to bring sentient beings to maturity through the four *siddhāntas*.

Therefore, it is said that there is no fixed victory or defeat. Mañjuśrī is an ancient Buddha who fundamentally has nothing to lose; he manifests the acceptance of humiliation, yet even in his fundamental realization, there is no such thing.
The disparagement of Cunda’s shallow practice—which was originally unsurpassed—is manifested as a censure, yet there is no addition to his original realization.

Furthermore, the text below addresses right and wrong in mutual relation; first, regarding the present and the past, the meaning of what is appropriate is made clear: the teachings of the past were partial.

By employing impermanence to shatter permanence, impermanence is taken as correct; now, this Sūtra of Complete and Sudden Teaching employs permanence to shatter impermanence, and thus impermanence is taken as incorrect.
Next, regarding the four propositions, this is a transgressive articulation of meaning:

therefore, while the former teachings held that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, the present teaching holds that unconditioned phenomena are eternally abiding. Both are the function of the Great Nirvāṇa’s simultaneous illumination.

"Both are so" means that Mañjuśrī, by relying on the gate of existence (*yu-men*), penetrates the principle; thus, while he appears to have been attached to the past, that which he penetrates is precisely the essence of the Middle Way, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
Cunda, by relying on the gate of non-existence (*wu-men*), is likewise so.
Regarding "neither": if one clings to either [of the two gates], one is deluded regarding the principle; thus, both are "neither," because the essence is neither existent nor non-existent.
To cling to each individually then harms the essence.

The following section on "individually distinguishing" refers to the phrase "both yes and no"; it uses the function of existence to manifest the essence of double negation, taking function as the basis for what is "neither."
Regarding the essence, since it is likewise unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is said that "each has [its own]," and so forth.
This constitutes the third [point], as it is stated by contrasting the preceding two statements regarding what is and is not [the case].

This immediately clarifies the fourth point: since the function of the two extremes is itself the essence of the Middle Way, Mañjuśrī’s conditioned [nature] and Cunda’s unconditioned [nature] both accord with the secret treasury;
right and wrong are entirely stilled, and the exchange is as one.
If this is so, how could the incidental questions and answers deviate from the three virtues? The three virtues are but the single mind; if one can reflect back upon this meaning, it is not far off.
Thus we know that the four propositions reveal the principle to its ultimate depth and mystery.
That it is no different from the past or the present means that the Way of the three periods of time is uniform; from antiquity to the present, its Way has not changed.

Therefore, we know that the two characters "present" and "ancient" explain the meaning of "coming," while the two characters "not different" explain the meaning of "suchness. For this reason, all Buddhas...
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states that because one comes by means of the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*) to achieve perfect enlightenment, one is called a Tathāgata;

this is achieved by dividing the characters to correspond to the "True" (*satya*) and the "Response" (*pratipad*). What is explained here differs only in its treatment as a collective versus its individual components.

Now, the passage concerning the pure-minded Cunda’s reproach of Mañjuśrī intends to show that the title "Tathāgata" applies exclusively to the Ultimate Sage, whereas the designation of "various practices" is restricted to ordinary beings;
therefore, it is called a "lowly name for birth and death."

The "multitude of existences" refers to the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). "Exhaustion and toil" refers to the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), the fetters of birth and death, and the meaning of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).

Regarding "three seen and one heard": the matters of the water bubble, the wheel, and the village are what is directly perceived; the lifespan of the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) is what is heard.
Regarding the analogy of the chariot wheel as suffering: because the cycle of birth and death proceeds like the rotation of a wheel, this is the meaning of suffering.
As for "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," the lifespan of those devas is eighty thousand great kalpas.
Regarding the explanation of "losing dishonor" (*śīlavat*), "inferior" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), while "superior" refers to the title of "Venerable.

Because there is the reality of the four virtues within and the manifestation of the name of a "Divine One" (*deva*) without, it is clarified that "losing dishonor" names both the reality and the reputation together.

Regarding ranks, emoluments, fiefs, and rewards, the *Wen Jia* states: "The three grades of rank in the Yin dynasty and the five grades of rank in the Zhou dynasty each had their appropriate application.
The *Wang Zhi* states: "The system of emoluments and ranks established by the King consists of five grades—namely, Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, and Baron"—this refers to the Zhou system.

The *Bai Hu Tong* states: "Rank (*jue*) means 'exhaustion' (*jin*); it signifies that one's office is measured according to its requirements and one's talent is fully utilized. This concerns fiefs and rewards.
The term "feng" (feudal grant) refers both to a rank and a state. The *Wangzhi* states: "The territory of a Duke is one hundred li square;
that of a Marquis is seventy li; and that of a Viscount or Baron is fifty li.
Regarding those with skills and arts, the *Zhouli* states: "One instructs the sons of the nobility in the Six Arts: first, the Five Rites; second, the Six Music."
The third is the five archery skills; the fourth is the five charioteering arts; the fifth is the six scripts; and the sixth is the nine calculations.
Sentient beings attaining Buddhahood is like the following analogy.

The double exhortation to contemplate [the teachings] consists of three parts: first, the formal presentation; second, the traditional explanation; and third, the preliminary discussion of the general meaning.

In the "Narrative of the Past," the analogy of the man corresponds to the second analogy, that of the Far-Traveler; in the present treatise, this section is categorized as an exhortation to contemplation.
Within the text, the interpretations of four schools are largely identical with minor differences.

Traditionally, the analogy of the poor woman giving birth to a son represents the development of understanding from the objective realm (*viṣaya*), while the analogy of the man wrapping his body in clothing represents the protection of the True Dharma—meaning not asserting that the Tathāgata is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Yeshi also opens up the meaning of abandoning delusion; his intent is the same as that of Hufa, differing only slightly in its phrasing.
Regarding Yecheng’s interpretation of "protecting understanding" (*hujie*), because it arises from birth, protecting shame and remorse is in fact the meaning of abandoning delusion.

In the *Zhao ti shi* (Commentary by Zhaoti), it is explained that the Buddha’s unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is precisely the protection of understanding, which covers the Buddha’s conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nature—this is identical to the meaning of Hufa. Examining the sutras throughout, [this is evident].

In examining these four schools, one finds they have only grasped partial meanings; furthermore, as for the previous three—namely, the *xing* (practice), *zhao-ti* (Zhizhe), and *yue-jiao* (teaching)—although their explanations of the text and meaning are not without merit, they lack a definitive basis.
Moreover, since we have already criticized the biased [partial] teachings, it is now necessary to provide a dual exhortation toward this principle.

Thus, it is known that having already criticized the partial, the subsequent step is to exhort toward the Perfect (*yuan*). This is why the Master of the Commentary divided the parable of the poor woman to serve as an exhortation.
The analogy of the husband is taught as an exhortation to practice contemplation.

Now, regarding the "equality," because there is no objective referent in internal realization, one speaks for others externally; this speaking arises from compassion, just as a son is born because of a woman.
Thus, it is called the "analogy of giving birth to a son."
The "husband" is used as a metaphor for the resolute; this refers to transforming others, while the contemplation itself refers to one's own practice.

Because transforming others proceeds through compassion, it is represented by the feminine nature of softness; because one's own practice proceeds through wisdom—the unimpeded illumination of wisdom—it is likened to the fierce strength of a man.

The analogy of "traveling afar" refers to contemplation (*guan*); its principle is that "going to the ultimate limit" is the meaning of "traveling afar. The subsequent six "equivalences" clarify this contemplation.

Regarding the text of the analogy below, it refutes the positions established by various masters who merely grasp partial meanings without fully following the sequence; here, we rely on the dual [approach].

The exhortatory passage is clearly manifest; furthermore, following the text that "reproaches both," the sections are linked like a chain of hooks and locks. Having already received the Sage’s intent, how could one allow it to be a matter of mere personal conjecture?

However, regarding the phrase "facing the Sage" and so forth, it means facing the instructions of the supreme sage Mañjuśrī as conveyed through the text, directed toward the ordinary person who is the immediate recipient.
This causes [the audience] to realize the Middle Way, which is eternally abiding and not substantial;

it is a text of admonition addressed to Mañjuśrī. "Yuju" (寓寄) means to entrust or lodge. Furthermore, regarding the admonition below: those who are shown as the primary recipients (*dharmabhāṇaka*) are individuals from the stage of "name" (*nāmamātra*) upward.

"Ordinary ground" (*bodi*) refers to the stage of "principle" (*liji*), where one has not yet even heard the name [of the teaching]; what benefit would there be in admonishing such a person? "Ultimate Sage" (*jingsheng*) refers to the stage of "wonderful" (*miaoji*).
Since the principle is perfectly consummate, why labor over admonishing or encouraging through words? Mañjuśrī’s original ground is precisely this stage.
As for being "neither above nor below," it refers neither to the Sage who is above the Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue), nor to the ordinary person who is below the Principle-as-such (li-ji);

rather, it refers to those from the stage of "naming" the arousal of the mind (*nāmadheya-cittotpāda*) up to those whose realization is still insufficient compared to Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). This is the primary audience for whom admonition and encouragement are truly required. Thus he asks.

Question: Since those in the middle stage of the *maṇḍala* are already sages, why is it necessary to admonish or exhort them? Answer: Since ignorance still persists in the higher stages, there remains the clinging to impermanence;
thus, what harm is there in admonishing and exhorting them? Therefore, the treatise states: "In various places, it is taught that one breaks through ignorance by means of samādhi."
Third, first is the exhortation, followed by the formal explanation according to the text.

Regarding the sixth, "compassion" (*maitrī*): compassion is the wondrous principle of the three thousand realms, which universally covers and universally encompasses, yet does not cling to either extreme; this is called "unconditioned compassion" (*apratihata-maitrī*).
As explained extensively in the sutra, the principle is the same while the phenomena are different—thus there are six.

Using this analogy to explain the principle below: compassion is the nature of the true cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), which is neither cultivated nor attained because it possesses the conditions and the understanding (*pratyaya* and *pariniṣpatti*).

Thus, it is said that "there is no wisdom and no abandonment. This merges the nature into one; by using awakening to refute delusion, it causes the principle to be fully present. For now, this is discussed in terms of the true cause alone.

Regarding the statement "there is no abiding in a household" and so forth: the five fruits are merely the three virtues (*triguṇa*). These three virtues do not manifest because of the absence of wisdom and severance.
Furthermore, the *dharmatā* is itself ignorance; since *dharmatā* has no place of abiding, it is also "having no abiding in a household.
*Dharmatā* is simply a collective name for the three virtues.

Regarding those who have neither master nor kin, although the principle is inherently present, because there is no capacity to be awakened, they do not elicit the Buddha’s response; here, "master" and "kin" are metaphors for the Buddha.

As for the meaning of "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*), this refers precisely to the inherent *pratyaya* (condition) and *hetu* (cause) within nature: "explanation" is the *hetu* of awakening (*bodhi-hetu*), and "speaking" is...
Because the causal conditions are fundamentally inherent in principle, one is able to understand and explain them through cultivation.
Regarding the character *qǐ* (乞), the *Cāngjié piān* states: "To beg means to go forth and request.
The form of the character consists of the radical for "person" (*rén*) and the element for "absence" (*wáng*), signifying that when a person lacks wealth and goods, they go forth to beg and seek.
Those who are oppressed by delusion and distraction lack wisdom; because delusion is indeterminate and distraction is disordered, one hears that the essence of consciousness is awareness.
Since the nature of delusive obscurity is fundamentally luminous and the mind of distracted movement is fundamentally still, one seeks stillness and wisdom to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Stillness is *śamatha*; wisdom is *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding "white silk" (*su*) and so forth, the *Huainanzi* states: "Mo Di saw dyed silk and was moved to sorrow because it could be made yellow or black.

Now, when a loom is set in motion, it is like white silk; hearing the teaching and giving rise to understanding is like being easily dyed. The enumeration of names refers to the contemplation of reality (*satya*):

the number one is the single principle, while three represents the number of the three truths. That which is called "square" (*fang*) refers to the four cardinal directions, such as the central path; that which is called "corner" (*yu*) refers to the four intermediate directions.
Because the contemplative practice regarding the two extremes has not yet been perfected, it is said that one "knows [them] thinly and understands them subtly.
In the passage beginning with "stopping others," the explanation of contemplative practice is provisionally clarified by way of the auxiliary path (upāya-mārga);

thus, it mentions "inns" and so forth, but does not explicitly state that the aggregates (skandhas) are themselves the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Nevertheless, because the primary and auxiliary practices are unified and phenomena and principle are non-dual, the terms such as "stopping" and "sheds" are employed.

These five stages of practice (*pañca-vastu*) begin with the cultivation of the ten vehicles within the stage of names (*nāma-mātra*). These five stages refer specifically to those who have achieved progress through practice.
"Inn" (*ni-ye-lü*) means to welcome guests; it refers to a lodging for travelers, hence called an inn.
Because the body of the aggregates (*skandha-kāya*) has no master, it is used as a metaphor: birth is like gathering at evening, and death is like dispersing at dawn.

In the section on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the meaning is further clarified by means of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). While the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) differ only in their manner of classification—being either expanded or condensed—the "bases" refer to the internal faculties and the external objects.
Since the internal and external interact with one another, they are both termed "bases" (*āyatana*). Fundamentally, there is no sovereign master, like an empty village.

Yet ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) falsely conceptualize it; like a greedy man who does not realize the village is empty and searches for goods therein, they do so regarding the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Because the external invasions of the six sense faculties cause harm, sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are like bandits; because one is foolish, one is greedily attached to them, just as failing to avoid bandits inevitably leads to being harmed.

Observing in this way, one understands that the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are created by the mind, and that their very substance is the mind itself, which is the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*).

This is explained at length in the "Object of Meditation" section of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Out of compassion for one's own past delusions and pity for others who have not yet awakened, one feels deep sorrow.
It is as if one were being scorched and burned.
This section concludes the preceding three points: internally understood and externally explained, yet neither is fully manifest. It is like a child within the womb;
the principle is entirely unknown and not yet visible. Although there is understanding through the contemplation of names and practice, the actual function has not yet been manifested.

Therefore, the *Ten Gates of Non-duality* states: "Because the three thousand realms have not yet been manifested and verified, the essence remains obscure; thus, at the stage of semblance, the six sense organs achieve universal illumination.
Consequently, the preceding three [stages] are collectively categorized as belonging to the period when [the reality] has not yet been revealed.
The arising of pure understanding refers to the emergence of an understanding that resembles the Buddha-nature of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
"Compassion has already been manifested" means that compassion is the object; because understanding arises based on this object, understanding is also called "compassion.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "Only I alone am clearly aware of it; others do not see it"—this is the manifestation of compassion. This is because internal understanding is luminous.

Externally, she is able to preach the Lotus Sūtra; it is said that she desires to pervade the trichiliocosm with a single voice, and she is able to reach there at will—this is what the text clarifies.
Her fundamental nature is like a mother, while her exposition is like a son.

Because she gives birth from the rational nature, the meaning of "mother" is fully manifested through the birth of the "son. One must know that compassion is the direct cause, while exposition is the realization.
This means that the continuous sequence of the text’s meaning does not exceed the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
This serves to connect with the preceding section to correctly demonstrate the intent of the scriptural passage using the analogy of the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*).

While the aforementioned three [stages] all possess these three obstructions, the reason the scripture specifically discusses them within the stage of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is that by the time one reaches similarity, the obstacle of the mundane realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra-pratibaddha-āvaraṇa*) has already been shattered.

The compassion of the same essence (samatā-karuṇā) involves all things being mutually dependent and subject to transformation. Because the three obstacles (trividha-āvaraṇa) constitute difficulties, they are forcibly suppressed;

because [the obstacles] are weak, the three contemplations (trividha-vipaśyanā) are weak when faced with these difficulties, yet they become strong as they shatter those obstacles. Therefore, it is said that they are "mutually interactive" (genghu).

Therefore, in the section below, within the stage of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), because the three obstacles are about to be destroyed and their relative strengths contend with one another, the sutra text provides a detailed set of analogies;
yet in reality, these three obstacles pertain throughout all three stages.
Regarding the phrase "entrusting one son to another," Faya says that "delivering from the entrustment of the shadow" means giving birth to the True (zhen), and that this non-duality is called "One.

As for the "householder" and so forth, since the obstacles of retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*) are nothing other than the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the householder is used as a metaphor for them; thus, compassion and deliverance share the same essence.
The state where object and wisdom are identical as one, which is the true principle of the first stage (prathamabhūmi), is called the city of Nirvāṇa.

As for the phrase "the provisional names of the five grades and the ten stages of faith following [the stage of] 'Compassion' (*maitrī*)," this refers to the five provisional grades and the ten stages of faith collectively as the "middle path," because these three are situated within the interval between the state of total delusion (*sarvamoha*) and the partial fruit of the first stage.
From the fifth grade of the "Names" stage down to the sixth stage of "Faith," one still possesses karma within the realm;

this karma is coarse and powerful, capable of drawing forth the karma of segmented existence, and thus its harm is as severe as wind and rain. From the seventh stage of faith onward, one possesses karma outside the realm;
this karma is subtle and weak, only inviting the karma of transformation, and is thus likened to mosquitoes and gadflies whose damage is but slight. Furthermore, internal karma is...
Regarding the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), external karma consists of the realms of body and speech; within the internal and external realms, all three types of karma are fully present.
As for the character *shè* (螫), it is pronounced with the initial *shū* (舒) and the final *yì* (亦). The *Shuowén* states that it refers to the movement of a venomous insect.

Furthermore, it is also read as *gēzhīliè* (各知列) with the second tone on the final syllable. Master Xuán says: "According to Dharma Master Yán’s *Jīngyīn* (Phonetics of the Sūtras), *shè* is the name of a distinct type of insect; therefore, [the text] first mentions the mosquito."
The phrase "poisonous insects" concludes the section following the mention of gadflies and bees.
Regarding those who traverse the Ganges: it is by means of the cause that they do so; they cross by way of the river. As the *Lunyu* says, "Who can go out without passing through the door?
because afflictions moisten karma, the river is used as a metaphor.

Regarding the phrase "carrying children and so forth," crossing the river is merely a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*); yet, it speaks of the "three obstacles" (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) because those being driven across the river all carried their children.
Thus, by taking the carrying of children as the point of reference, it clarifies that the obstacles themselves are the realization of principle. Internally, one has already attained realization;

externally, one further transforms others through speech. What were obstacles are now virtues; the three virtues are fused into a single essence without distinction, where permanence and impermanence are non-dual.
The constant bondage and liberation, as well as clarity and darkness, are all explained by means of the two extremes to reveal the three virtues, all of which are the Middle Way:
first, retribution is the Dharma-body; next, karma is liberation; and finally, afflictions are prajñā. One should know that these three obstacles pertain both to the internal and external realms.
The following passage clarifies the mutual relationship between strength and weakness: since compassion and understanding are strong, coarse defilements naturally fall away;

because the obstacles of the分段身 (fen-duan-zhang, *bhavāgra* or limited existence) are destroyed, it is said that "obstacles cannot obstruct. This means that understanding is strong while obstacles are weak.
Regarding "drifting swiftly" and so forth: "drifting" (piao) means the current is rapid. Although the segmentation [of the body] is broken, the barrier of transformation is strong;

within that which resembles [the previous state], it is easy to give rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), which is termed "falling from the Peak" (*mūrdha-pāta*). This affliction of attachment to dharmas acts as a hindrance, moistening and binding karma to draw one into the Land of Expedient Means (*upāyabhūmi*) as a karmic retribution; this is termed "violent seizure."
Regarding the "wondrous essence": by reflecting back upon the source of the mind, attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is immediately extinguished; this is called "not being bent.

Because one is thus able to relinquish the stage of semblance and enter the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*), the term "sinking together" (*ubhayavilaya*) symbolizes the relinquishing of the stage of semblance.
Those born in the Brahma Heaven do so because the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the cause for that heaven;

it is the natural principle manifested by the ultimate reality of the celestial marks. By entering the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) through the three types of similar loving-kindness, one generates the merit of compassionate mindfulness and is thus born in the Brahma Heaven.
The general introduction below clarifies that the text as a whole integrates the four types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

From "already arrived" onwards refers to the five stages of the name-attainment (*nāmāpti*), the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), and the three positions. Because they have not yet realized the principle (*tattva*) and are unable to observe the capacities of others (*sattvāśaya*), their own practice and transformation of others rely solely on perfect interfusion;
therefore, it is necessary to employ the three types of loving-kindness and cultivate the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) in a perfect, simultaneous manner.
The three truths are taught in their perfect unity to preclude any partiality; therefore, it is said that they "should not" be taught partially.

Regarding the phrase "partial teaching is not the true protection," etc.: partial teaching holds that the Tathāgata is identical to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which is not the true protection of the perfect Dharma for those on the stages prior to abiding.
If it were the true protection, one ought to teach the three truths perfectly to others, namely:
The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), neither being existent nor non-existent, are the identity of the three and one; this is called the teaching that is not partial.

For those who lack the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), this eye of wisdom is none other than the Buddha-eye. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "I pray that I may obtain, like the World-Honored One, the foremost purity of the eye of wisdom.

Because this has not yet been realized prior to the stage of Abiding [in the Dharma] (*vihāra*), the Sūtra states: "One does not yet possess the eye of wisdom. Therefore, the three contemplations must be perfected.

If one practices only after [the initial stage], one will realize [the fruit] later; if the external is explained in a biased manner, then the internal will lack perfect understanding. This implies that one should not hold a biased interpretation.
Since the correct principle is the perfect fusion of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), explaining the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) in a biased way would contradict the three truths.
This implies that one should not apply [the practice] in a biased manner, because the three types of compassion are themselves the three truths.

Regarding the extensive refutations, each passage individually counters and refutes the three teachings as being partial rather than correct, non-protective, lacking the eye of wisdom, and contrary to the true principle;
this is because they fail to grasp the meaning of the extensive exposition. Therefore, the commentary states "and so forth" (*yathāvistara*).

All [stages] possess both the partial and the perfect. Although there are differences between the stages prior to abiding (*purvabhūmi*) and those upon abiding (*vihāra*) in terms of understanding and realization, they are perfect because the three truths are fused and identical;
they are partial because they dualistically illuminate the two extremes.

Those who have not yet perceived the capacities and principles of others cannot yet transform others according to the four types of capacities, and in their own practice, they have not yet attained true realization.

It is appropriate to permit only the complete teaching and not the partial teaching; therefore, it is said that "stopping the partial" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifying the practice of blissful ease (*sukha-vihāra*).
When there are questions or difficulties raised, one does not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but explains them solely by means of the Mahāyāna.

Question: Why is this so? Answer: If one were to forcibly preach the Great Vehicle to those who originally possess only the capacity for the Small Vehicle, it would conflict with their capacity and fail to achieve its purpose.
Having already aroused the great capacity [of beings], to speak only of the Small Vehicle causes them to lose the benefit of the Great;
this is the first reason for not yet seeing their capacity, as it causes one to preach only the Perfect-Small (the *yuan-xiao*), which, though they have not yet received it, serves as a distant seed.

Furthermore, because one’s own practice has not yet realized the principle, one preaches only the Perfect to internally support the contemplation of the principle; thus it is said that "one has not yet seen the capacity or the principle. Since he thus reproached himself...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to the total presence of delusion.

When one subsequently perceives [the truth] below, it is the stage of partial realization (*vibhāga-satya*), wherein delusions are ultimately destroyed and the principle is perceived. According to the capacities of beings, the teaching is established;

whether partial or complete is taught, all are caused to obtain benefit. Since the scriptural text uses the partial to illustrate the complete, it mentions only the "partial right view," which corresponds to the stage of partial realization (*vibhāga-prativedha*).
It is wisdom (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, the subsequent section provides a layered explanation of this passage, establishing it as a perfect teaching (*pariniṣpanna-deśanā*). Thus, the perfect realization of the three truths is termed "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*);
since this right view is the Middle Way of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the term "unconditioned" may superficially appear to suggest a partial or biased meaning.
Regarding the meaning, since it follows from both words and names, it is said to be a "partial teaching.
As for "opening up the partial" according to the text: "opening" means to permit; that is, based on the initial interpretation, it takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the partial teaching.

To show that those who perceive the primary meaning (paramārtha) skillfully distinguish between phenomena and principle, the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata is identical to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
This was spoken by Cunda specifically to counteract the view of the conditioned (saṃskṛta) held by Mañjuśrī;
yet, while the intent was partial, the unconditioned itself is perfectly complete as the very nature of reality (dharmatā).
Within the Middle Way, that which is conditioned is impermanent, while that which is unconditioned is eternally abiding;
because it is taught that this eternal state serves as the cause, one is able to attain and realize the ultimate fruit of eternal Bodhi, and thus it is compared to the Brahmā Heaven.

For one who does not seek liberation through the sūtras, because the two extremes are themselves the middle, there are no bonds of the two extremes to be abandoned, nor is there a middle way of liberation to be sought;
one who contemplates in this manner naturally arrives at liberation.
This exhortation to contemplation: the previous exhortation to discourse was based on the teaching (*śāsana*), whereas this exhortation to contemplation is based on practice (*pratipatti*).
The six-fascicle version translated by Zhu Fahu is titled the *Panniehuan jing* (Sūtra of Parinirvāṇa); it differs from the present sūtra only in its degree of detail.
Although the current text does not contain the word "man," since it likewise does not mention "woman," we know that the passage in the sūtra stating "like a person traveling far" refers to this.
It is the Great Man (puruṣa).
Because the principle is quiescent yet illuminating, within emptiness and the provisional there is the three thousand [realms] in their full manifestation; thus it is said "yet illuminating.
Furthermore, because the principle is neither one, three, nor both, yet one, three, and both are fully manifest; thus it is said "yet illuminating."

Regarding "the two intervals between the beginning and the end": "beginning" refers to the principle (li), and "end" refers to the ultimate realization; "intervals" refers to the four stages of identity (sijie).
Therefore, the analogy of "passing through the middle road" is used to illustrate these four stages of identity.

When those practitioners at the lower level of the stage of names (mingzi) hear of the Perfect Teaching and give rise to understanding, they know that [rebirth] is summoned by the causes of the exhaustion and toil of afflictions.

The fruit of being constrained by birth and death is thus to draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), humbling oneself and seeking instruction to resolve doubts, thereby illuminating one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
The *Book of Rites* states: "One rises when requesting the lessons; one rises when requesting further benefit. Kong Yingda explains:

"Lessons" refers to the scriptural volumes; "further benefit" means that when what one has already received as a lesson is not clear, one requests a more thorough examination of it. This is the way to honor the teacher and revere the Way.
This is the meaning.
Since the false defilements of the five desires are not the inherent nature of the three truths, the five desires are treated as an external principle;
because they constitute delusive obscurations, they are said to be "suppressed."

Those who are mired in deep delusion, though their contemplative practice (*guanxing*) may be accomplished, remain entirely possessed by the three delusions; thus it is said they have not "awakened. This refers to what is stated in the *Fahua Wenju* (The Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), specifically the "Gate of Non-duality" (*Fubimeng*), which says:
"The three thousand realms are not yet manifest, and while verifying the essence, one remains deluded. "Awakening" (*wu*) means to be alerted or awakened.
"Understanding and delusion exclude one another" means that similar understandings and the ignorance of delusion mutually cancel each other out.

"Entering the sea and seeing level ground" refers to what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one wishes to see the sea but does not see trees, mountains, or forests, one knows from these prior signs that the sea is not far away.
Why? Because the great ocean is a level place where there are no trees; such are the prior signs. Now, by means of the sea...

The true cause is likened to the aspect of equanimity, while the semblance-understanding is likened to that which is not yet dead, because ignorance still persists; thus, the white dharmas constitute semblance-understanding.

That which does not fully illuminate the object is like the stage of the Ten Abidings for an individual practitioner, who can only illuminate the True and cannot illuminate the False or the Middle; this refers to the Ten Practices.
Illuminating the conventional truth is likewise so; the perfect contemplation of the three truths is all-encompassing, like a garment that covers everything.

Regarding the explanation of "the end of life," it first refutes the interpretations of others: others claim that when a practitioner contending for the Dharma is challenged by an opponent and their argument is defeated, they die, thereby corresponding to the "end of life."
However, this has now been refuted by our Master. For how could those whose position has fallen into logical error be born together in the Brahma Heaven?
Since the other masters merely used difficult challenges to subdue [the opponent] while disregarding the statement regarding birth in heaven, the Commentator used this as a refutation.

Now, regarding the phrase "the present teacher," the Master’s primary interpretation—explaining the meaning by way of entering the holy from the worthy—establishes both the sense of passing away and being born in heaven.

From "thirty-two" onwards, it clarifies the meaning of using heaven as a metaphor for the true stage; this is identical to what is explained in the subsequent scripture concerning the thirty-three [gods].

The celestial nectar is consumed by both the ministers and the sovereign; this principle is the same as the thirty-two [stages]. That is to say, the stages of practice—*śuklavidarśana*, *gotra*, *aṣṭamaka*, *darśana*, and *tanu*—are opened up into thirty, while the ten *bhūmis* are combined with Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) to form one.
Thus, there are thirty-two. The "one sovereign" refers to the ultimate state of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

Since it is subsequently stated that he is a "king," we know that this is merely a metaphor for Wondrous Enlightenment. Furthermore, the three contemplations (*san-guan*) pertain to the stage of partial truth (*fen-zhen*), while that which is transcended by Wondrous Enlightenment is the subject at hand.
The "three evil realms outside the boundaries" refers to the three destinies of the Śrāvaka path: those of the seeker (*śaikṣa*), the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the view-based practitioner.
The phrase "place of peace and bliss" in the sutra reveals the wondrous principle of the three virtues.
In the section of the sutra containing the repeated exhortation, Mañjuśrī is rebuked for being identical to those externalists and those who have violated the precepts.

The scriptural statement that [the two] are alike in being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) represents the meaning of the Hīnayāna; to use the Great Vehicle to refute the Small is to equate it with heterodox outsiders because of its false speech.
This false speech is the cause of transgression, and hell is its fruit.
"Merely uniting [the faculties] until the end of life" refers to what the Sūtra says: "One should abandon ignorance and seek right knowledge.
This means that one abandons the ignorance of the stage of semblance and seeks the true, authentic knowledge; this ignorance is precisely *avidyā* (ignorance).
He who is equal to others and his teacher uses this passage to correlate the thirty-two marks with the birth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
that is to say, just as the thirty-two heavens share the honor of having Śakra as their sovereign, so too do the thirty-two marks collectively adorn the body of the Buddha.
The principle that the Lord may be combined but the ministers may not is because the thirty-two marks reside precisely in the Buddha;

thus we know this refers to the combination with the celestial lord at the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), and does not refer to the combination with the thirty-two ministerial marks at the stage of partial truth (*fen-zhen*).
If that is so, since the subsequent scriptural passage correlates the thirty-two marks with rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
it should likewise correlate the eighty minor marks with the preceding eighty instances of acting as a Brahmā king and so forth.

The "Unconquerable One" (Ajitajina) is so called because his eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are not shared with those of lower stages, just as a golden wheel-turning monarch is unconquerable throughout the four continents.
This is based on the sense of being "unshared," and does not refer specifically to the number eighteen.

Although this section lacks the explicit names "eighty secondary marks" (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*) and "eighteen unique qualities," they are present within Mañjuśrī’s eulogy; therefore, they are extracted here.
This completes the meaning of the analogy.

Regarding the two exhortations, one exhorts through discourse and the other exhorts through contemplation; the same applies to the two censures. Right view is the Buddha-eye, and right knowledge is the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñatā);
these are all eye and knowledge that resemble those prior to abiding [in the stages]. Because they possess this eye and knowledge, they are able to protect internally and guard externally.

To explain: taking "seeing and knowing" as the cause and "protecting the teaching" as the condition, one uses external means to speak for others while internally relying on the wisdom of contemplation;
this constitutes the causal conditions for attaining partial realization of the eternal.
The previous combined analogy refers specifically to the analogy of the poor woman.

Regarding "well-covered" (*susaṃvṛta*) and so forth: within the stage of similarity (*sādṛśyāvasthā*), the complete contemplation of the three virtues is called "well-covered," just as clothing covers the body.
The subsequent metaphor refers specifically to the analogy of the long journey (*dūragamana*).
Regarding the phrase "constantly receiving peace and joy," the scriptural text should follow from [the section on] this virtuous mind; the current text merely extracts the essential points.

As for the single instance of "reproving and exhorting," it refers to Mañjuśrī’s one reproach and one exhortation in the preceding passage. The term "er-xu" (爾許) means "several" or "a certain number."
This refers to the preceding section where the dual reprimands and the dual exhortations regarding the contemplation each have their respective teachings and analogies.
"Di-rang" (抵攘) means to falsely accuse and rebuke; "rang" (攘) means to ward off with the hands. To roll up one's sleeves and extend the arms is called "rang";
as the *Laozi* says, "He rolled up his sleeves and brandished his arms."
Furthermore, the following refers to Cunda’s prior adherence to the provisional teachings, whereby he initially accepted that the five fruits of milk were impermanent;

this was used to challenge the present sutra’s teaching that the five fruits of receiving offerings are eternally abiding (*nitya*). This was merely a means of establishing doubt for the sake of the audience as an introductory device.
Regarding the phrase "obstructing equality," it means that Cunda feared those who adhered to the provisional teachings would contradict and obstruct the permanence of *nirvāṇa*.

The discourse on "abiding" was established as a hypothetical challenge, causing the Tathāgata to provide an extensive answer regarding the non-differentiation of the two types of giving (*dāna*) in order to refute the Lesser Vehicle and the beginners.
This was spoken incidentally for the new assembly and primarily for the sake of future generations.

As for the "new assembly," they refer to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet experienced the various flavors [of the Dharma] and have now, at the beginning of this assembly, realized the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle; they are thus called the "new assembly. If they were to pass through...
Those who follow the present sutra are called the "Old Assembly. Why?
To clarify below why they are not the "Old" [in the sense of being original]. "One lifetime" refers to the period from the beginning at the Deer Park up to the present sutra;

that is, from the realization of the Small Vehicle at the Deer Park, through the critique of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) and the refinement of the Prajñāpāramitā, until the opening and unification of the Dharma at the Lotus Sutra, where all have returned [to the One Vehicle].
Since even a single moment of minor goodness, such as snapping one's fingers, can become the cause for attaining Buddhahood, how could the practices of the Two Vehicles not be a wondrous path?

Therefore, it is said that they have already realized that even the slightest virtue is like this. As for the assembly of former followers who have come to this present sutra, they merely increase their realization of the Path while diminishing their remaining births, entering higher stages;
how could they still cling to impermanence as if suddenly equaling those at the Deer Park? Thus, we know that Cunda’s posing of doubts was solely for the sake of the new assembly.
This is specifically for the sake of those of dull faculties who, after my parinirvāṇa, cling to the Small Vehicle and slander the Great; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is cited as proof.

As the sutra says: "If there were one who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, such a thing would be impossible—except for the case after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before them.
This statement indicates that it is only after his passing that those who have attained arhatship might cling to provisional means and slander [the Mahāyāna].
"Truly listening" does not imply arrogance; here, Cunda is specifically intended for such a person.
If it were not so, it would conversely reveal that his status is high. "If it were not thus" means that one might say Cunda was not practicing through expedient means.
How could there be [a doubt]? Below, the text cites evidence extensively to demonstrate that, when verified through three meanings, one knows this is an expedient practice (*upāya*).

First, it concerns the power of the Buddha’s acceptance of offerings and the timing of the assembly; second, it concerns his ability to challenge the meaning of the Tathāgata’s non-differentiation; third, it concerns his ability to use Mañjuśrī’s profound stage as a collateral discussion.
These three meanings are present in the text. Therefore, we know that the following section concludes and demonstrates this point.
Regarding "those who accepted the exhortation," the Sūtra states that they likewise covered the Tathāgata;
this refers to those who, together with Cunda, accepted his exhortation and, like Cunda, covered [the Buddha] to manifest the essence. Therefore, it says, "they all manifested," and so forth.
Furthermore, as for your [objection] below, let us set aside for a moment the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Since the conditioned is the function (*vṛtti*) of the unconditioned, it is said that its function cannot be fully exhausted; since the unconditioned is the essence (*svabhāva*) of the conditioned, it is said that its ultimate essence cannot be fully described.
Because essence and function are mutually identical—just like waves and water—they transcend the reach of verbal discourse and are cut off from it.
To set it aside and forget words is to attain the true realization of the essence; it is like Vimalakīrti’s silence, which alone constitutes true entry.
This is precisely the meaning of the "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha) discussed in the following passage.

Regarding the point that "the detailed is set aside for the concise": since it was already indicated that the Buddha himself spoke extensively with lamentation, I have merely discussed the essence and function briefly with you;
thus, let this matter be set aside. That the concise and the detailed differ is clearly evident throughout the worlds.

"Neither essence nor function" means that the true essence is utterly quiescent and transcends all dependence and opposition; since essence and function depend upon one another, how could they accord with the true source?

Therefore, one must set them aside to truly enter into principle. To alternately affirm or deny them is like treating symptoms as the disease itself; one knows not which is correct and should instead set them both aside.
This is precisely for the purpose of making offerings to generate the goodness of sentient beings, setting aside the peripheral to grasp the central truth; hence it is called "setting aside."
The fourth [point]: "Thoroughly eliminating the literal text and establishing the meaning" truly accords with our own school’s exhaustive investigation of principle; does it not lie herein?

Regarding the phrase "pure giving," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One gives for the sake of the Path, generating a pure mind free from all fetters (*saṃyojana*), seeking no fruit or retribution in this life or future lives, and because of reverence and compassion—this is called 'pure giving. 'Pure' refers to..."
The provisions for the path leading to *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the ancient dharma of the Buddhas, the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* records King Bimbisāra’s question to the Buddha as to why the Buddha eats at midday.
The Buddha replied: "In the early morning, the devas eat; at midday, the Buddhas of the three periods of time eat; in the afternoon, the animals eat."

In the evening, ghosts and spirits consume [offerings], but the Buddha established the prohibition against eating at that time to sever the causes of the six realms of existence and to cause beings to become equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, as clarified in the *Píng Guānshìyīn Shū* (Commentary on Invoking Avalokiteśvara), eating at midday symbolizes the realization of the Middle Way.
When Mañjuśrī appears to see things as others do, he manifests what ordinary and Hinayana practitioners perceive.
This means that because the practitioners such as Cunda were of shallow capacity, the assembly at that time saw only his outward traces and failed to recognize his fundamental essence.

The Buddha, in order to shatter their temporal perceptions and inspire deep reverence, provisionally validated his discourse on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); yet, when discussing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is in reality neither existent nor non-existent.
Furthermore, because the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" mutually pervade one another, to gladden a single person is to gladden all beings.
This is identical in meaning to the principle that when Maitreya attains the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), all sentient beings likewise attain the prediction.

Regarding the simultaneous presentation of two gates: if one establishes the meaning of the first gate, the meaning of the second gate is not established; if one does not establish it, the meaning of the second gate is not excluded.
Regarding the Buddha’s likes and dislikes: he loves Pureṇa because he delights in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and he dislikes Mañjuśrī because he does not seal the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one differs from this, then Mañjuśrī’s engagement with affairs becomes difficult to reconcile logically, as it involves clinging to the particular and thus fails to achieve perfection;

for in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), principle and phenomena are separated, resulting in likes and dislikes, whereas in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), principle and phenomena are mutually integrated, such that self and other interpenetrate.
The Sūtra states that this is inverted perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*). If one clings to the notion of something being pleasurable, it constitutes an affliction (*kleśa*);
therefore, it is called inverted perception. Because afflictions serve as the cause that drags one toward the fruit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is said that this is birth and death.

One must understand that what is pleasurable arises from the mind, yet the mind is fundamentally devoid of anything pleasurable to which one could take refuge. Since the Tathāgata has eternally exhausted all inversions, he is free from love and hatred; thus, the Sūtra says "there is none."
There is a thought of loving-kindness.

That which is universally pure and pleasing refers to the Tathāgata’s impartial observation of the three [spheres] as undifferentiated; because ordinary beings and sages are one and the same, and self and others are extinguished in purity, it is called "universally pure.
This is like the natural affinity between father and son, which is fundamentally identical; thus the Sūtra says, "He regards all equally, as if they were his own children."
"Hou" means "not.
That which is not within the scope of what you know refers to "you" and "I"; that which is ultimately realized is not within the scope of true knowledge.
To use a metaphor for those who possess ignorance: the tortoise and dragon represent the partial realization of truth, while the water represents ignorance.

"Passing over soft-shelled turtles (*yuán*)—the upper character *yuán* is pronounced with the *yúan* rhyme; the *Sāncāng* says they resemble tortoises but are larger—and crocodiles (*tuó*)—the lower character *tuó* is pronounced *dúō*;
the *Sāncāng* says they resemble *jiāo* dragons but are large; the *Shǎnhǎi jīng* says there are crocodiles in the Yangtze River;

Guō Pǔ says they resemble large lizards, the largest reaching one *zhàng* in length, with scaly patterns whose hides can be used to make drums. In the ancient commentary, Kāishàn [Dàoshēng] interprets [the term] as "donkey."

The analogy of "the four horses" [not catching up] illustrates that those in lower stages do not know the fruits of higher stages; the analogy of the "Golden-Winged Bird (Garuda) surveying the ocean" illustrates that those in higher stages can know the lower stages.
This is based solely on the analogies; when applied to the scriptural text according to its combined meaning, both cases concern the inability of the lower to know the higher.

The interpretation by Ye Cheng is somewhat similar to my own, though they differ in that his subsequent analogy concerns the object (*viṣaya*) while mine concerns the afflictions (*kleśa*). Lingwei’s preceding point relies on the combined application of the text.

Regarding the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), based on the subsequent metaphors, it is divided into two bodies. First, because it is the subtle, secret, and profound of the Tathāgata, it is called the "Dharma-body.
Second, because the garuḍa sees its reflection, it is called the "Response-body" (*nirmāṇakāya*).

As for the application of these metaphors, since it is stated that the Tathāgata’s wisdom corresponds to the meaning of "retribution" (*vipāka*), this is the most appropriate interpretation. While the interpretations of the three schools are partial and restrictive, the literal meaning of the text can be clearly seen [in this way].
Because [the text] cannot be fully analyzed, the commentary states "and so forth. Question:

Since your school now explains the text by means of "wisdom" (*jñāna*) and "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), why does the initial analogy and its application speak of "subtlety, secrecy, and profundity," while the subsequent section’s application speaks of the "Tathāgata’s wisdom"?

Answer: "Subtlety and secrecy" refers to that which is illuminated by wisdom; since the capacity [to illuminate] is revealed through its object, it is still the meaning of wisdom. "Wisdom" refers to the capacity to abandon delusion; since...
The ability to manifest what is to be abandoned is the meaning of "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*); when the dharma and its analogy coincide, the meaning of abandonment becomes clear.
As for "highly extolling the realm of the Buddha," this refers to what Cunda previously said: "I and you, O worthy one, cannot fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the phrase "I," this refers to the subsequent scriptural passage beginning with "In this matter... This is because Mañjuśrī himself reveals his original station by manifesting his trace;
thus he says, "It is not that I do not understand, but I merely wish to test you."
"To sweep away us" means that Cunda sweeps away the meaning of self-grasping toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Since the Buddha-body is conditioned, it is merely the function of the impermanence of *nirvāṇa*; as even this is not its constant function, how could it be known as the essence of "neither [existence nor non-existence]"?
Thus, one knows that "conditioned" is not a universal teaching, and is therefore called a "single path."
If my text were erroneous, it should have read, "Because I test you," as Mañjuśrī said to Cunda: "Because I grasp at the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), I test you.
Since this "grasping" is merely a provisional assumption, the testing is not real.

Therefore, when I previously stated that the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) shall for now be set aside, I first placed the conditioned before me to brush away my own traces; thus it is said that the conditioned is non-existent.
"To 'examine' (tui) means to investigate thoroughly; 'tui-tu-hui-fan-xiang-shen' (推吐回反詳審) means to examine and scrutinize. This refers to what was previously said to Cunda:
'I and you, O worthy one, cannot fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Although Cunda spoke of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he himself [then] examined it."
Since it is not detailed [in the preceding text], we know that "non-conditioned" (asaṃskṛta) is not [simply] non-existence;

all of this is the Master of the Commentary (the *Śāstra-kāra*) taking up the previous text to establish the meaning of Mañjuśrī’s clearing away of traces. Thus, when both existence and non-existence are abandoned, the fundamental essence (mūla-tattva) is revealed.
The previous text below employs the simultaneous rejection of words and thought to manifest this fundamental essence.
Regarding "the path of language is cut off," it is said that they are "set aside together" because one speaks by not constructing existence or non-existence;
this refers to what the preceding sutra stated: "Whether conditioned or unconditioned, let us set them aside together."
"That which is the realm of the Buddha" refers to what Cunda previously stated: "It is the realm of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
"Not something known by me" is as the preceding sutra stated: "One cannot calculate the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the statement that "contemplation is entirely quiescent": previously, Cunda criticized the partial teaching on contemplation and urged the complete teaching on contemplation.

Now, Mañjuśrī reveals his true identity and states that the path of speech and thought is severed and all words are exhausted; therefore, he speaks of "quiescence. Since even the complete dharma of the exhaustion of thought is extinguished, how much more so the partial?
The "various auspicious omens mentioned above" refers to the nine omens found in the first fascicle.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī," it describes the underlying intention: since Mañjuśrī and [Śākyamuni] reside together on the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), he may reprove [the Buddha];
