Because of taking refuge, it is said that after his parinirvāṇa, he no longer serves as a place of refuge for others.
Regarding the fact that the physical eye does not see: although the tree has dark shadows, they are not seen by the physical eye because they are subtle;

this serves as a metaphor for the three bodies (trikāya), which are all eternally present, yet are not seen by those who lack the capacity (an-adhimukti). "Lacking merit" means having no such capacity. When the perfect capacity is awakened, the Three Jewels are eternal.

Is this not merely a matter of principle? In fact, it is also vividly so: while the assembly perceives the burning away of the mountain of spirits and other abodes, my land remains undestroyed—is this not what is meant by this?
Regarding the passage stating that parents are distinct from one another: because the bodies of male and female are separate, they are impermanent;
thus, the Three Jewels are of one essence, unlike parents who produce children and to whom one takes refuge.
As for the phrase "seven generations," since [the lineage] is opened back to the beginningless past, why stop at seven? It is merely spoken of as seven in accordance with worldly convention.

Furthermore, because the habits of affection from seven generations have not yet been abandoned and can thus be gathered through conversion, he speaks of opening [the way] for seven generations of parents, regardless of whichever realm they are born into;
Kāśyapa goes to all such places to convert them, just as when the Buddha ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma to his mother.
The sūtra’s description of frost and hail is used to rebuke and break the impermanent with the teaching of the eternally abiding, just as frost and hail destroy the sprouts of crops.

If one does not accord with people in this way, teaching them partial doctrines and distinct natures that do not correspond to their fundamental nature, and thus instructing others in such a manner, all such acts are termed deception.
— *Vajrakāya-parivarta* (Chapter on the Vajra Body)
The fundamental basis of the world is the vajra-wheel, which rests beneath the water-wheel and supports the world.
"That which is aimed at has no predecessor" means that all things aimed at are shattered; "having no adversary" refers to the blazing radiance.
These four meanings of the vajra are applied in sequence as metaphors for the four *siddhāntas*.

The application of the "descent of golden essence" clarifies that the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are equally present within the principle (*li*), unlike other passages where the first three pertain to phenomena (*shi*).
This is because the analogy refers to the *dharmakāya*.
Regarding the inclusion of all dharmas: the Dharma-body is the fundamental basis of all dharmas. From the perspective of that which is included, their meanings should be distinguished;
however, from the perspective of that which includes, it is "joy" because one rejoices at hearing of this inclusion.

Regarding the analogy of "firm and solid" as representing permanence and so forth: the principle of permanence is well-detached from the hundred negations and transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

The "stiff and sharp" below represents the evil of ignorance; it destroys the Great Enlightenment, for the non-awakening of ignorance is destroyed by the Great Illumination, which dispels the delusive darkness of ignorance.
The following section clarifies that the essential nature is non-obstructive and indeterminate, not bound to any single direction; is this not indeed entering into the principle?
Nevertheless, although the methods of "going" and "coming" apply to all four *siddhāntas*, they primarily take up the cultivation of wholesome roots.
Regarding "having a single intent" (*ekāśaya*): although various questions differ, they all converge upon longevity; therefore, it is said to have a single intent.
As for "longevity and so forth," it is because the *dharmakāya* is long-lived that it is likened to a vajra. Because it is a vajra, it is firm; because it is firm, it is indestructible.
Thus, while the names and meanings differ, their essence is one.
Regarding the Dharma-body: the Dharma-body is precisely the long-lived, eternal body; it is likened to a vajra because it is not sustained by coarse food, and thus it is firm and indestructible.
Because the various meanings of the Dharma-body are mutually interwoven and perfected, they are said to be "perfectly penetrating and without obstruction.

Because these meanings are perfectly penetrating and without obstruction, when one understands even a single thousand [verses], one follows the underlying principle; therefore, upon hearing only the chapter on Longevity, one immediately awakens to all that follows.
Regarding these various differing interpretations:
if one understands [the meaning of] the "Longevity" chapter and so forth, I shall now briefly extend the discussion for two chapters, as the remainder can be understood by analogy;
thus it is said "up to," meaning that all the meanings within the "Great Assembly Questions" chapter are fully contained within the "Longevity" chapter.

If [the Buddha] does not descend [to explain], it is because those who are deluded have not yet understood; therefore, he must answer by proceeding through the chapters. This also serves to conclude what precedes and introduce what follows.
What was previously explained as "understanding" concludes the preceding section on Longevity; what is now explained as "non-understanding" introduces the subsequent chapters.
If one were to use "Longevity" as a general title to comprehensively include the lower chapters, then it would be designated as the chapter named "Longevity."
It is not that there are no distinct meanings for the thirteen chapters;

rather, if one were to apply the specific names—ranging from the "Vajra Body" to the "Questions of the Great Assembly"—to each respective chapter, each individual name would encompass the meanings of all the chapters through mutual interconnection.
Therefore, it is said that there is indeed a universal meaning.
"Universal yet not universal" is because it contains a specific meaning;
"specific yet not specific" is because its meaning pervades all categories. "Not universal" is the provisional (prajñapti), and "not specific" is emptiness (śūnyatā);
the latter two phrases are merely the cessation and illumination of the Middle Way. Thus one knows that all categories do not transcend one's own mind.
Now, from below, the meaning of this chapter is correctly demonstrated.
"Vajra" refers to the person because the body is metaphorically likened to a vajra.
Regarding the essence and function of the person and the dharma: "person and dharma" are combined as the essence, and "power" is the function.
To distinguish between the general and the specific: first, life-force must be attached to a person, and a person must possess power;

since the Vajra-sattva possesses both human life-force and power, and power fundamentally relies upon a person, how could a person lack life-force? Thus, based on these three mutually inclusive meanings, they are judged as "general.
However, because their essence and function are distinctly different, they are judged as "specific."
Why does the author not criticize the ancient masters?
From the beginning, he indicates that the five fruits in the *Cunda* chapter are the brief [explanation], while the fourteen chapters on long life are the extensive [explanation].
The section on "Names" is placed below because one obtains the merit of hearing and retaining [the teachings].
Regarding the four characteristics: first, correcting oneself; second, correcting others; third, answering according to questions; and fourth, skillfully explaining causes and conditions.
The latter three all belong to the category of analytical exposition (*vibhāṣā*).
The subsequent "Extensive Lower" section refers to fourteen chapters following the "Four Reliances"; although their names and characteristics differ, their meaning converges upon a single principle.

As for "binding" and "dispersing," binding refers to the general (universal) and dispersing refers to the particular; when correlated with the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), their significance becomes evident.
Regarding "not long" (非長): the ancients' intention was that the lifespan of the *dharmakāya* is not the long life of the *saṃbhogakāya*, nor the short life of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
They arbitrarily designate its non-transmigration and immutability as "long life.

Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* is not something subject to destruction like the *nirmāṇakāya*, nor is it "indestructible" like the *saṃbhogakāya*; they arbitrarily designate its indestructible essence as the "vajra-body."
This, then, refers to the following: now [the text] refutes the ancients who claimed their own views were profound and deep;
since they have departed from the two extremes, this is merely one path of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), as explained in detail in the commentary on the "Three Dots" (sān diǎn) section.
Regarding those who enter extinction in a withered forest, they enter extinction because it is not an extinction; thus it is called "entering extinction.

Regarding those who enter extinction in a flourishing forest, they are extinguished yet not extinguished; thus it is called "entering extinction. While the terminology for "entering extinction" is the same, its meaning differs.
To refute those who hold to impermanence, and to refute the attachment to the impermanence of the *saṃbhogakāya*, he taught that the *dharmakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are eternally abiding;
thus, this "eternity" is neither eternal nor impermanent. Because the realm of wisdom and its object are in profound unity, the essence of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* is identical.
The space between the twin trees precisely symbolizes this.
"Flourishing is the True" means that flourishing represents the Permanent; since the Permanent is the Dharmakāya and Sambhogakāya, it is the True.
"Withering is the Conventional" means that both the extremes of emptiness and existence are termed conventional; this is the meaning of the "repeated conventional. Question:

If both emptiness and existence are conventional, what is the True within the Middle? Answer: The essence of the True Middle is non-duality of duality; the essence of the Middle is itself transcended.
By dissolving the provisional to establish the true, it is named "True Emptiness" (zhēn kōng); by dissolving the provisional to establish the mean, it is termed "Mean" (zhōng).

Thus, within this text, although the two names "Mean" and "True" appear distinct, their essence is unified. While conventionally they are established as different, in principle, the three truths are mutually integrated and fundamentally without distinction.
The realm of all Buddhas consists of three aspects: first, their integration and inclusion.

Because these three virtues are what the Buddhas have realized, they constitute not only the ultimate realm of all Buddhas, but also the realms of Buddhas at the stages of partial realization, and even those at the stage of the name.

Because the middle and the extremes are mutually identical, they cannot be destroyed; because the three truths inclusively encompass one another and the true and the responsive are non-dual, they are likened to a vajra.
The question posed by the Buddha regarding both [the body and the power] corresponds to the three lines of the first verse below;

these inquire into the cause and fruit of the *dharmakāya*. "Vajra-body" asks about the fruit, and "solid strength" asks about the cause. Since this chapter correctly answers these questions, it is divided into two sections: first the fruit, followed by the cause.
Furthermore, regarding the statement on the "four bodies," within the context of the five bodies, the vajra serves as a general metaphor for these four.

Although the scriptural text, when analyzed according to its dharmas, speaks only of four bodies, they mutually establish one another; thus, the text establishes two pairs of bodies based on these four: the eternal body (*nityakāya*) and the indestructible body (*avināśikakāya*).
Regarding the mutual relationship between the *dharmakāya* and non-mixed food:
the four subsequent phrases now clarified correspond to the four aspects of "corresponding to the essence" (*tattvārtha*) and so forth.

All of these correspond to the essence because they do not deviate from their essential nature, and thus they are called "eternally abiding"; they correspond to the essence because they are without movement, and thus they are called "indestructible."

Because its essence is inherently firm, it is called the "Vajra-body" (*vajrakāya*); because it is not subject to fragmentation, it is not a body sustained by diverse food. Because it maintains the path of conduct, it is termed the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*).

As for being "free from faults": it is eternally free from the fault of impermanence; it is indestructible, thus free from the fault of decay; and as a vajra, it is free from what is not [the true nature].
The Vajra transcends faults; it is free from the fault of eating mixed food and is free from the fault of a non-dharmakāya that is apart from mixed food.
Since all things are dharmas—whereby the metaphor is the basis and the dharma is what is illustrated—and because these are dharmas, they constitute the fivefold dharmas.

All these are "analogies" (*dṛṣṭānta*); since the four [qualities] can serve as analogies for the four [points], both the "analogizer" (*dṛṣṭāntaka*) and the "analogized" (*dārṣṭāntika*) are established under the name of "analogy.
What follows below explains the meaning of their mutual establishment. There are four "analogizers," namely the four such as the essence of gold (*suvarṇasāra*).
Regarding the four virtues: these consist of being eternally abiding and indestructible, not being sustained by food, and the dharma-body; together they constitute the four virtues.

The passage beginning with "the essence of gold" uses metaphors to correspond to the Dharma as explained in the text. Regarding the two kinds of relinquishment (*upekṣā*): non-abiding is the relinquishment of the ultimate (*paramārtha*), while not perishing moment by moment is the relinquishment of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
"One exists and one perishes" means that what is not the body perishes while this very body exists.

That which is not the Vajra-body is what the ancients called "the mind at the end of Equal Enlightenment" (samyaksambodhi) and all preceding stages; because these still belong to the realm of impermanence, they are termed "not the body."

This "excellent body" refers to a body endowed with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). "Māman" describes the appearance of vast waters; its meaning is as expansive as water, reaching to the infinite.
As for what constitutes the "non-[true]," it merely states that it is not the reality, without clarifying the magnitude of that reality.

What constitutes "this"? Since both Brahmā and Māra possess the marks and signs [of a Buddha], Xinghuang’s commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that, from the perspective of principle, there is neither "is" nor "is not";
yet, from the perspective of phenomena, the Dharma-body is the body, while its functional application is not the body.
Regarding the mutual formation through causes and conditions: because causes and conditions are false and the physical substance is fundamentally empty, it is said that "this body is not a body.
Yet, this does not preclude it from being a body; because the Dharma-body is omnipresent, it does not preclude the physical substance, and thus "that which is not a body is a body."
This emptiness is that which is detached from emptiness; this emptiness is precisely the Dharma-body, while detachment from emptiness is not the Dharma-body.

"Now, [the commentary] has not yet descended" refers to the humility of the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*), who, based on the previous judgment, maintains that there is still room for further refinement in his understanding.
Tiantai explains that what is being clarified now is precisely the determination of right and wrong by means of the three types of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Now, regarding the "complete sentence" (*jùzhū*) in the *Zhǎng'ān*: the first is the sentence complete with four [parts], yet it says "is, is, is, is.

The two upper instances of "is" are the fundamental sentence, while the two lower instances of "is" are the derivative sentences (*śākhā-vākya*). Since all are called "is, is," one should take the former as the standard.

First, the word "is" (shi) functions as a term of specification; furthermore, since the current commentary clarifies that it does not constitute a complete sentence following a compound construction, it says "this is," and so forth, including cases where the preceding is simple and the subsequent is compound.
Although Zhanran (Zhang’an) stated that he relied upon the *Mohe Zhiguan*, his comparative analysis of those texts did not reach full clarity;
therefore, Jingxi further compared and examined them in detail against the *Zhiguan*.

The manifestation of its characteristics is limited to the categories of existence and non-existence within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Here, "is" is substituted for "existence" and "is not" for "non-existence";

thus it is said, "in comparison. Now, the two commentaries by Zhangan and Jingxi are each arranged into diagrams so that later students may easily understand the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) when consulting them.
In the first chapter, Zhanran indicates that the single phrases are easily understood.
Regarding the two instances where he indicates the phrases within the "complete yet non-phrase" section, the first uses a single "is" and the second uses a repeated "is.
Although the underlying reason for this is not immediately apparent, it can be understood by following the interpretation of Jingxi.
Second, Jingxi’s presentation of the phrases: first, regarding the three kinds of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the single fourfold propositions are as in the text.
When the combined fourfold propositions and the fundamental fourfold proposition are added, they constitute twelve propositions. However, within these, two are opened up;

the first is the "same-as-the-original" phrase, not the "equal-opening" phrase, and the example for the latter is likewise. If this is the case, then according to the meaning, there are only eight propositions.

If one counts the factors (*aṅga*) together with their bases (*mūla*), there are twenty phrases. However, if one considers the phrases according to their constituent parts, every phrase shares one element with its base;

thus, in terms of meaning, there are only sixteen phrases. Furthermore, just as within a single [category], although views such as "not-equal" (*asama*) may arise, in principle they ultimately revert to the other three types, so it is with the compound phrases as well. For example, this is like the *piṭaka*, which—[though containing many elements]—...

Regarding the four gates: in terms of their ultimate meaning, they all converge on reality (*tattva*); though there are four gates, their meaning converges on emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Specifically, "both" refers only to the two [extremes], while "neither" is simply the negation of both.
Although each of these possesses all four aspects, they are layered one by one. However, the current four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) belong entirely to externalist calculations;

thus, using the profound to illustrate the shallow should also be without hindrance. Furthermore, although the phrases have four meanings, they are essentially only two; "both" also belongs to this category.

Since the "neither-of-the-two" (ubhayābhāva) is subsumed under non-existence, although there are thirty-six distinct variations when the branches and roots of the three types of fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are combined,
upon examining their ultimate destination, they are reduced to nothing more than the two propositions of "is" and "is not."
The phrase "and so forth" (而已) refers downward to the negations used to form the four propositions; their meaning is entirely the same.
Second, regarding the negations, three types of four-proposition sets are clarified: the single four-proposition sets are as they appear in the text.
As for the phrase "not 'is' and not 'is-not'," the character "is" (是) here is a term used for specification, similar to saying "if it were not 'is,' it would be 'is-not.'"
Regarding the phrase "to establish three and four," one should say: "It is for the purpose of establishing that 'is' and 'is not' each form three and four sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Because the text omits details, it simply says "to establish three and four.

The following section is the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) criticizing the superficiality of ancient interpretations; thus, he previously described the seven schools as "using the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as... [and so forth].

It is not that [the opponent] takes the "real" as being correct; rather, for the time being, we shall provisionally judge this according to the two truths. One must know that what is perceived has not yet transcended the single fourfold alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*);

even if it were to transcend the single fourfold alternatives, it would still not have transcended the combined fourfold alternatives. Therefore, the present critique asks: "How can it be non-existent?
The meaning of the following passage is that even if it were not these three types of fourfold alternatives, then the interpretation of that master would merely produce various... [omitted].

Fourth, regarding the "not yet emerging" and the "transcending of words": if this were so, it would be entirely delusive confusion and the cause of birth and death; how could it differ from the non-Buddhists?
Therefore, the conclusion and reprimand state: "How can that which is bound [to samsara] be established as the Dharmakaya, the fruit of virtue?"

Now, the phrase "that which is below" refers to the Master’s current correct interpretation of the meaning of "that which is not the body is the body. This means that, conventionally, it is taken as "not," while from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is taken as "is.
"Not" refers to the four [elements] taken individually, up to the point where words are transcended—all of these are delusive afflictions; these delusive afflictions are the cause of "mixed food."
Because the "equal body" (samatā-kāya) is the fruit, it is said that the Tathāgata’s body obtained through various views is not this "equal body"; therefore, it is called "non-body.

Based on this, these three types of fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi) apply not only to the heterodox calculations of ordinary beings, but the cultivation of causes in the first three teachings all fall within these four propositions, as will be explained below in the passage where Kāśyapa recounts his own experience prior to this point.
Those with false views distinguish between the two teachings, yet both are equally heterodox, for how could they be correct?

This is because that which is induced by the first three [teachings] consists entirely of bodies sustained by impure food and the like. The realization path of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is set aside and not discussed here; this is as explained below in the section on the four teachings and the hundred negations.
That which is "neither [so] nor not [so]" is as stated in the sutra: "This body of mine is itself the Dharma-body.
Is this not a reference to the fact that the assimilation of various foods is itself Vairocana? Therefore, it is said to be the Dharma-body and so forth.

However, regarding the Buddha’s descent [into the world], from the perspective of principle (*li*), he is neither real nor responsive; thus it is said, "neither is, nor is not. From the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), there is both the real and the responsive;

thus it is said, "able to manifest for the sake of beings," and so forth. One should know that principle pertains to internal realization while phenomena pertain to responding to capacities according to circumstances.
Furthermore, the subsequent explanation clarifies the exclusion of one dharma-characteristic.
"Non-duality" explains the meaning of the "one dharma. This corresponds to the passage in the Sūtra which states: "It is neither body nor non-body;
it cannot be proclaimed"—this is the characteristic of the one dharma. Therefore, it is said that the body of the Tathāgata is, in reality, the double negation (neither A nor not-A).

The statement "removing" (chu) here correctly explains the meaning of "excluding" (chu), because it excludes both the manifest [body] and the two [other bodies]. In relation to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) is distinct from it in terms of its relational counterparts;
this is for the sake of the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

In the lower section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, an example is cited: "Sarvajñā" (all-knowledge) is precisely the single characteristic of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Although the ancient masters cited this treatise as proof...

This does not accord with the meaning of "excluding one dharma. Because he does not cling to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) but preserves only the wisdom of the fruit, it is said that [the powers] are excluded.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), fascicle 45, explains: "The Bodhisattva, knowing that the self-nature of the supernormal powers is non-arising, does not cling to them;
yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he merely contemplates all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). This concludes the section from the ancient times up to the entrustment.
This is intended to refute the views of the ancients;
now, as I attempt to explain it, I am establishing the perspective of the present.
Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real: the three previous teaching masters represent the provisional, while the Perfect Buddha represents the real.

The "one hundred negations" refer to the teachings of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the "five minds": first is the lower; second is the middle; third is the upper; fourth is the upper-upper; and fifth is the upper-middle-upper.
The phrase "and so forth" is an abbreviation that omits the [remaining] eight precepts, such as non-stealing and the rest.
Regarding "one good deed being endowed with ten": for example, because a single act such as non-killing is adorned by the remaining nine [virtues], it is endowed with ten.
Yet, one does not commit killing on account of stealing, nor does one commit killing on account of sexual misconduct, and so forth, up to not committing killing on account of wrong views;
this applies analogously to all cases. Thus, through mutual inclusion, they form a hundred.
The phrase "attaining the three unconditioned [states]" clarifies that the Three Piṭakas possess the meaning of permanence and the diamond-like nature.
The eighty billion māras are those subdued beneath the tree, as recorded in the *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* (Ruiying jing).
Furthermore, the "Hundred [Verses]" and the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) both maintain that there is "existence within existence" (*yǒuyǒu*), because birth and death have not yet been extinguished;

thus it is called "existence within existence. Master Xuán’s commentary explains: "Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are constrained by the causes and effects of the twenty-five existences within the triple world, it is called 'existence within existence.
Since the Śrāvaka Bodhisattvas do not sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), the body born in the royal palace remains a cause for delusion."
Because it is a result of [karmic] retribution, it is censured by the worthies and sages of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna).
In the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), Nāgārjuna refutes Pūrṇāśa to clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s three great aeons (*tri-kalpa*). Thus, that treatise states:
"If one is fully possessed of the three poisons, how can one accumulate immeasurable merit? It is like a poisonous jar; even if it contains nectar, [it remains poisonous]."
The body of a Bodhisattva who does not eat midday meals is like a vessel; delusions are like poison; and the practice of the Dharma is like storing ambrosia.
Because he teaches others by means of this, he causes them to lose their life of permanence. Thus, the commentary connects the text, stating: "There is a mind that performs practices," and so forth.
Those who raise objections here do so precisely by adhering to the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) to challenge the ultimate perfection [of the Mahayana].
Now, as we preserve the sequential order of the Four Teachings and speak in contrast to the Shared Teaching, it is said that "the nature of merit is empty" is correct.
Furthermore, in the section on "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), the initial part specifically refutes the partial emptiness of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*).
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-body is like space," this clarifies the Middle Way as taught from the perspective of the path of realization (*darśana-mārga*);
because it enters [the truth] through a gradual sequence, it is subsequently refuted by the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).

"Realizing enlightenment at the wrong time" means not waiting for the *Avataṃsaka*'s perfect and sudden teaching—which does not rely on anything else—nor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*'s revelation, but instead realizing the minor fruits at the Deer Park;
this is called "realizing at the wrong time. It is as when Śāriputra himself recounted in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:
"I did not wait for the explanation of the underlying cause. Here, the minor vehicle is specifically criticized because [the practitioners] do not yet know the Middle Way.

To take partial emptiness as the ultimate is called "attaining realization at an improper time"; those so described are said to be "those who eat mixed food," for they do not wait for their proper cause, just as one eats at an improper time.
This taking [of realization] at an improper time is what is meant by "eating mixed food."

Furthermore, it is not that the initial refutation of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) of the Lower Perfect Teaching (Xia Yuanjiao) involves entering merit through non-evil, entering emptiness through non-merit, and entering the Middle Way through non-emptiness—while omitting mention of entering the Provisional (Jia)—for that would be an abbreviation. One should rather say:

"entering merit through non-emptiness" and "entering merit through non-evil. Although the term "merit" (fu) is the same, there is a difference between the realms of within and beyond the world (jie-nei wai).

By distancing [this teaching] from the aforementioned lower vehicles, it distinguishes, clarifies, refutes, and concludes that while other sutras carry partial (p’ien) meanings, this sutra is exclusively perfect (yüan).
Although it is said that "repeated giving" and "understanding the permanent" are of one principle, the fourth period is pointed out as the primary intent of the sutra.

Furthermore, by distancing itself from the errors of the first three teachings and clarifying the correctness of the Perfect Teaching, it shows that the partial and the perfect are separated; since this meaning resides within the four periods, it is said to be "the intent within other sutras."

This distinguishes it from the past; that which was previously partial is now understood as having the meaning of the Perfect, because it is revealed and made manifest. Therefore, it is said that the primary intent of this sutra lies herein.
This clarifies the present [teaching]. Although the subsequent explanation is superior, the former interpretation is correct.

"Since ancient times" [refers to] rejecting the old. "By no means considering" means that those who simplify fail to discern between internal and external, partial and complete, or the opened and the unopened.
This explanation concludes the preceding section. "Since this is already" divides the scripture into a general interpretation.
The first phrase concerning humans and devas refers to what the sutra calls "not the body of a human or deva"; this corresponds to the first phrase.
The phrase concerning nirvana refers to what the sutra calls "at the time of parinirvāṇa," and so forth; this is the hundredth phrase.

What is the meaning of the "mutual inclusion" [of the three truths] as presented in the lower [teachings]? The phrase "appears to be so" (*sìrú*) means that because the principles and meanings are perfectly interfused and the three truths are mutually identical, one provisionally distinguishes them according to the literal text; hence it is said they "appear to be so. This refers to how the text appears to be the Truth of Reality (*zhēn*), while the meaning must necessarily be the fusion of all three. Regarding the phrase "the text appears to be so," it is because the Sūtra states: "not human or celestial... nor those who eat mixed food. Since [the text] mentions humans, celestials, and those who eat mixed food, it appears to be the Truth of Phenomena (*jiā*). Furthermore, because it says "neither born of desire nor born of karma," it appears to be the Truth of Emptiness (*kōng*). Thus, although the text seems to present each truth separately, the meaning is actually their mutual inclusion. Therefore, it is called "appearing to be so. This is the meaning of the mutual inclusion of the three truths in the lower teachings. As for the meaning of mutual inclusion in the higher teachings, it is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "The Dharma-body is neither male nor female. Because it is not male, it is the Truth of Emptiness; because it is not female, it is the Truth of Phenomena; and because it is neither male nor female, it is the Truth of the Middle Way. This is the meaning of the mutual inclusion of the three truths in the higher teachings. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata’s body is the Dharma-body, which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Here, "eternal" is the Truth of the Middle Way; "blissful" is the Truth of Phenomena; and "self and pure" is the Truth of Emptiness. This is the meaning of the mutual inclusion of the three truths in the higher teachings. Moreover, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-nature is neither male nor female. Because it is not male, it is the Truth of Emptiness; because it is not female, it is the Truth of Phenomena; and because it is neither male nor female, it is the Truth of the Middle Way. Since this conventional reality is now negated, it is subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
For those whose understanding is harmonious, the ultimate is inherently endowed with all phenomena; thus, the conventional is neither dual nor different.
Therefore, one cultivates the inconceivable emptiness within the Middle Way, like the striking of a vajra; this emptiness is itself the wondrous Middle Way, just as reaching the limit [of reality].

Next, regarding the eight [sections] up to "the one who has left the mundane": the first of the eighty phrases in the sutra text states, "The body of the Tathāgata is not a body; it is a body. This is the heading.
Because it is the True (zhen) while manifesting as the Responsive (ying), it is said to be "not a body, yet a body.

Furthermore, this is the provisional (jia) within emptiness (kong). Because it is empty, it is "not a body"; because it is provisional, it is "a body. Thus, by means of these three contemplations (sanguan), one attains liberation.
Although the two bodies differ in terms of fruit, cause, and effect, they all manifest the meaning that [the Buddha] is not truly transcendent from the mundane;
therefore, the final phrase concludes by stating: "The body of the Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable merits.

Since the introductory and concluding statements are thus established, the intermediate questions and phrases constitute a detailed exposition of the meaning that he is not truly transcendent from the mundane. Because this mundane is itself the true, the sutra...

Within this, there are phrases such as "the dual negation of extinction" and so forth; these truly refer to emptiness within the provisional. Although there is no leisure to provide a detailed analysis, they may be contemplated through profound insight.
Although previous records contain explanations that correlate these phrases, they do not accord with the present commentary, and thus they have not been recorded here.

Regarding the passage "neither tranquil nor non-tranquil," the character "non" (wu) governs the subsequent terms, meaning neither tranquil nor non-tranquil; "neither feverish nor non-feverish" is treated in the same way.
The final seventeen phrases enter into the Middle Way as they appear in the text.

"Entering immediately and emerging immediately" means entering the Truth (the ultimate) and emerging into the conventional. This refers to the mutual fusion of the three truths (*trisatya*), with the sequence [of their interpenetration] as it appears in the text.
Regarding the hunter who eats meat, the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly" states: "In the past, in this city of Rājagṛha, there was a hunter who killed many deer;
he invited me to eat their meat. Although I accepted his invitation, I maintained a mind of compassion toward all living beings."
Regarding the fivefold dharmakāya, it is because the "eternal body" and the other three are all alternative names for the dharmakāya.
"Taking a similar cause" refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The passage concerning the *śakti* (lance) and *prāsa* (javelin) is as explained in the commentary on the introduction to the *Sūtra*.
Regarding the fundamental intent of his actions, since his original aspiration was to protect the Dharma, he did not accept the precepts of ritual observance;
rather, by upholding and protecting the Mahāyāna, he preserved the underlying principle.
As for the "nameless practitioner," his name was not widely heard and his conduct did not subdue others.
In the past, the four phrases were first listed below.

Regarding "past" and "present": in the past, that is, prior to the *Nirvāṇa*, all the various sūtras and vinayas exhorted laypeople to receive and uphold the five precepts, regarding receiving them as right and not receiving them as wrong.
This present sutra, however, establishes that if one does not receive the precepts, then not receiving them is [the standard].
This receiving of the precepts is for the sake of what is not [the case], which is why it says, "What was previously right is now wrong," and so forth.
Regarding the section on "In former times... below, this explains the meaning of the four propositions: the former teaching exhorted the upholding of the precepts;
this refers to an era of peace and stability when the Buddha-dharma was widely propagated. Since there were no evil people at that time, laypeople were required to observe the five precepts.

Regarding the present time, this scripture prescribes that those who do not receive the precepts are so designated because, due to the dangers and chaos of the age, evil persons create obstacles such that the Buddha-dharma is obscured and does not prevail;
therefore, for the sake of protecting the householders, it is prescribed that they do not maintain the precepts.
Regarding the passage "In the past...": If at times both were perilous, the teachings of the past were not so; if at times both were level, the scriptures of the present do not differ.
If this is the case, although the words of the ancient teachings and the present scriptures appear to be contradictory, their essential intent is identical.

"Taking and discarding as appropriate" means that the former teachings were provisionally established for times of peace, and thus they adopted the observance of precepts; whereas this present sutra is provisionally established for an age of peril, and thus it discards them.
The Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) has grasped the underlying intent beyond the literal text, which is why he concludes by stating that one must not adhere to a single-sided view.

The phrase "those who take the Sūtras as sufficient" refers to those who take the sound [of the words] as their goal, meaning they are satisfied with mere brevity. This clarifies that these are people of the Hīnayāna;
therefore, the Sūtra rebukes them, saying they "cannot roar the lion’s roar," which means they cannot rely on this Sūtra to discourse on the eternal and support the Vinaya.
Because they do not discourse on the eternal, they are not surrounded by those of the Perfect [Vehicle] (Ekayāna) capacity; because they do not support the Vinaya, they do not subdue evil persons.

In the sutra, following the passage "If there be any bhikṣu... and so forth, it clarifies that the Mahāyāna master first states that the nine divisions [of scripture] are capable of discoursing on the eternal.

Regarding these "nine divisions of the scriptures," this refers to the fact that each of the two vehicles—the Great and the Small—possesses its own set of nine divisions; these are the nine of the Mahāyāna.

As for the statement that each has nine: within the Dharma of the Small Vehicle, there are briefly lacking the *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy), the *apṛṣṭavyākaraṇa* (unasked discourse), and the *udāna* (inspired utterance).

Because the Vaipulya [sūtras] are vast, they contain only nine [categories]; for within the Śrāvaka vehicles, the principle of practicing the causes to become a Buddha has not been taught, and thus there is no *vyākaraṇa* (prediction of enlightenment).
Because they are shallow and easy to consult, there is no *svayambhū-kathā* (self-proclamation). Because they do not discern the extensive principles, there is no *vaipulya*.
Within the Mahāyāna, the *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa* are briefly absent, so there are only nine. This is because Mahāyāna sentient beings possess sharp faculties.
They are easily understood and do not depend on causes, conditions, parables, or formal debate for their explanation.

Alternatively, they may be fully discussed according to their meaning, with both the Great and Small Vehicles each having twelve [categories], or the Great and Small combined having twelve—meaning that the Small Vehicle has only eleven, as it lacks the Vaipulya (Extensive) category, because the Small Vehicle has not yet discussed the great principles;
thus, the Mahāyāna sūtra-dharma is combined as the Vaipulya to manifest the Great Vehicle.

The *Dali* (Great Principle) commentary states that among the eleven divisions of the scriptures, those held by the Two Vehicles consist of ten divisions, while the *Vaipulya* division is held by Bodhisattvas.

The scripture says "Dharmatā" (*duōjiā*), which is pronounced "Yue" (*yuè*) in the vernacular; the *Lotus Sūtra* says "Muktaka" (*mùduōjiā*) or "Muyin" (*mùyīn*). These are variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit term.
Furthermore, when the sutra proclaims such words, it serves to support the Vinaya.
"To disseminate" means to spread everywhere. As for "mutually completing," the absence of anger leads to joy, and because of that joy, there is no anger.
The previous passage in the six-fascicle version states that the King was the second disciple;
the present statement that he was the first is intended to refer to his being the first-born, thereby resolving the contradiction with the six-fascicle version.

Regarding the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*): the perfection of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) is the first reliance; from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) to the sixth stage is the second reliance;
from the seventh stage to the ninth stage is the third reliance; and the tenth stage is the fourth reliance. Other practices leading toward the stages (*bhūmi*) follow this pattern.

A detailed explanation is provided below in the commentary on the "Chapter on the Four Reliances. Since the second reliance is situated above the first reliance, the sixth fascicle states that "the virtue of awakening (*bodhi-guṇa*) serves as... [the basis].
First, because this is now discussed according to the sequence of the four [vehicles], it is called "the second. If this is so, then there is no contradiction between the two passages.
Those who are Mahāyāna śrāvakas are precisely those whom one causes to hear by means of the sound of the Buddha-way.
"Kāśyapa Buddha" is translated here as "Golden-Colored Sage"; he was the third Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa.
"Geng-geng" (brightly shining) describes the appearance of clarity and distinctness.

Regarding the phrase "still possessing the virtue of a teacher," it means that because [the practitioner] followed and guarded [the precepts], his traces appeared similar to those who had broken them; fearing there would be no one to act as a teacher, [he remained].
Because of his virtue, he asked this question.
A "dependent beggar" (kīṭaka) is one who has left the household life out of hunger and dwells among the Saṅgha seeking a livelihood.
In some versions of the text, the four characters "dependent beggar, bald man" (kīṭaka-tulapuruṣa) are omitted from beneath the word for the direct answer.
Regarding those who protect the teachings of the true and authentic renunciant, such as Jue-de— who guards those below him—
since he himself maintains the precepts and so forth, even if he were to encounter killing, he would not permit retaliation.
Now that the world is filled with many evil people, how can one carry out the work of conversion?
According to the Sūtras, one who ought not to take life must certainly lack the intent to kill even while holding a blade or a weapon.
Regarding the three types of intention, the first two are internal resolutions; these correspond to what the Sūtra calls "possessing right view" and so forth.
Holding [the text] and carrying it away refers to upholding the Vinaya. The last one is external application; this corresponds to what the Sūtra calls "not going for the sake of gain and offerings."
Regarding the statement that one who subdues evil persons does not do so for their own benefit, but rather for the sake of propagating the Dharma and crushing evil, they are associated with him.

As for the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices) chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, which does not permit such association, that refers to one's own practice (*jigyō*), whereas this refers to converting others (*keta*).
That concerns a time of peace, whereas this concerns a perilous age; thus, there is a difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited.
"Right View" below explains the meaning of the preceding three points.
"Encountering expansive conditions" means encountering the conditions for propagating the Way and transforming others; it is appropriate that its external application be manifested.
There is a variant text that reads "strong conditions," but this is incorrect.

Regarding the "monks mixed with those who associate": although one's own body does not commit an offense, to associate and dwell in the same place as those who have broken the precepts is called being a "monk mixed with those who break the precepts.
To be personally free of offenses yet, seeing that one's disciples have committed offenses, neither instructing them to repent nor abandoning such behavior is called being a "foolish monk.
To be pure oneself and to purify others is called being a "pure monk."
The term *tú-dēng-méng* (徒登瞢) is read as *tú-dēng-dìng* (徒登丁鄧, with the second tone). The *Yùnjí* (韻集) states that it means "losing one's sleep" or "extreme exhaustion.

In the scriptural text, it is sometimes written as *téng* (瞪), which is borrowed for the reading *tú-dēng*. *Méng* (瞢) is read as *máng-dēng-wǔ-dìng* (亡登武鄧, with the second tone); it means "confusion and stupor," referring to a state of darkened disorientation.
The explanation of the day for the *Poṣadha* ceremony is as previously interpreted.
Regarding the time for the *Pravāraṇā*: since it occurs at the conclusion of the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*), one may perform the *Pravāraṇā*.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, this generally refers to three days—namely, the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the seventh month. This is because one freely invites others to point out one's own transgressions.
Because of this, it is called *pravāraṇā* (self-indulgence).
Regarding the "unsurpassed Great Master who protects the Dharma," these are the four types of persons upon whom one relies; there is none superior to them in the world.
Because they serve as a refuge for the assembly and act as craftsmen who bring others to completion, they are called "Great Masters."
Regarding the "six kinds of five dharmas," this refers to the text of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) concerning the seven dharmas. The first of those seven dharmas states:
"From now on, it is permitted to confer the full ordination upon a co-resident disciple who has fulfilled the ten years of seniority and possesses the six kinds of five dharmas.
As for the five dharmas of spiritual discernment, the Vinaya says: "Furthermore, there are five dharmas: first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing..."

There are five points regarding the gravity of offenses: first, not committing them; second, knowing they are light; third, knowing they are heavy; fourth, knowing them; and fifth, knowing the extensive explanation of the benefits of reciting the *Prātimokṣa* training.
Herein, the following section clarifies these five dharmas of the present sutra; "divine understanding" (*shenjie*) may also be rendered as "clear understanding."
The four matters that accord with the Vinaya refer to knowing what is light and what is heavy; these are to be verified by the Vinaya, for what is not in the Vinaya cannot be verified.
These four points are identical in meaning to the Vinaya.
As for those that differ slightly: "if" (若) means "as if" (如); furthermore, when comparing these four to the textual passages of the Vinaya, they appear to differ slightly. Thus [it is said].

The Vinaya is defined as "knowing what constitutes an offense and knowing what does not constitute an offense. This refers to whether something is according to the Vinaya or not; though their names differ, their meaning is the same.

Therefore it is said that even if there is a slight difference—where some versions read "the questions and answers differ slightly"—this is likely a scribal error where the character *ruò* (若) was written as the characters *wèn-dá* (問答).
As the Master Bào Pǔ said: "Three transcriptions turn 'fish' into 'lù,' and 'emperor' becomes a 'tiger'; this truly has precedent."
As for this, when one matter differs, both the name and the meaning are distinct; this constitutes a great difference.
The Vinaya explains below the characteristics of these differences. "Teaching and transforming according to the times" refers precisely to the subduing of sentient beings.
Regarding "not making selections" and so forth: according to the Vinaya regulations, one may not enter a village after midday; this constitutes selecting a time.

One may not enter brothels and the like; this constitutes selecting a place. Now, because the Bodhisattva of the Four Reliances transforms beings whenever there is an opportunity, he does not make such selections.

Furthermore, as for not engaging in indiscriminate guidance (*màn-diào*), one must skillfully observe the capacities of others and know whether they are spiritually mature or immature before going to transform them;

therefore, this is not something that can be accomplished by those of shallow practice or mediocre character. If one wishes to emulate this, one should consider that one’s own stage of practice (*xing-wei*) might cause one’s own downfall—how bitter it would be!
Thus, the Commentary warns: "One must not engage in indiscriminate guidance," and the Sub-commentary provides further notes to this effect, the intent of which lies precisely here.

Furthermore, regarding the repeated statements, the sutra distinguishes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by requiring that one choose the proper time and place; thus it says, "What a Śrāvaka ought not to do.

As stated in the *Huìpúsà jīng* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva Huì): Ānanda said to the Buddha, "I recall that in the past, in the city of Śrāvastī, I saw the Bodhisattva Zhòngshèngwáng sharing a bed with a woman.
I thought he had committed an impure act, and my mind was filled with anxious deliberation as to whether this might be different [from what is taught]."

When those who study the holy life (brahmacarya) within the teaching of the Tathāgata were about to give rise to such views, perceptions, and conceptualizations, the Great Trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that moment, King Tiṣya, the most eminent of kings, suddenly leaped up from the ground and remained suspended in mid-air at a height of forty-nine feet.
He addressed Ānanda, saying: "How could one who has violated the prohibitions and is defiled leap up and stay suspended in the void? In the presence of the Tathāgata...
Ānanda came forward, prostrated himself on the ground, and immediately repented his transgression, saying: "How could I have harbored such biased views as to seek out the faults of the Great Dragon?
This was actually the Bodhisattva’s means of taming sentient beings; it was not something a Śrāvaka should have done. Thus, Ānanda had been in doubt.

Regarding precepts established due to specific events, as clarified in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the first precept was formulated because of the incident involving Sudinna engaging in sexual intercourse with his former wife, and so forth.
The first nine offenses for which there is no formal admonition refer to:
(1) the initial emission of semen; (2) physical contact; (3) speaking coarse words to a woman; and (4) [making advances] toward a woman.

1. Deprecating one’s own person; 2. Soliciting offerings; 3. The five types of intermediaries; 4. An ownerless dwelling; 5. A dwelling with an owner; 6. Groundlessly accusing another of a grave offense (saṃghāvaśeṣa);
7. Accusing another on false grounds; 8. The four [offenses] involving admonition, namely:
the tenth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha despite being admonished; the eleventh, assisting in causing a schism despite being admonished; and the twelfth.
Those who defile the family through the thirteen types of evil conduct, who reject the Sangha and disobey admonitions,
and who violate the Vinaya such that they should not be taken as witnesses— these are those who possess the eight kinds of impure wealth; thus the Sūtra says,
"One praises and speaks of impure things," and so forth.

As someone below [in the commentary] provides a sub-commentary on the Master’s reason, he states that it is not the case that the meaning is not proven by the sūtras, because the sūtras merely provide brief examples;
therefore, this is clarified here. Within the text, both sections first present the characteristics of what is "not [proven]," as follows:

below, one should know that the clarification of what is "not proven" shows that the Sage manifests in commonality with sentient beings, such that there are those who manifest their own origins and those who wait for others to manifest them.
The case of Master Fu (Fu Dashi), who manifested his realization through the inspiration of the ascetic Sengtou, serves as a precedent;

it is appropriate for the sake of sentient beings that this be so, yet it is not because he himself was unaware. Your claim that he "forgot" such things is a statement that contradicts the scriptures and is therefore not the word of a sage;

thus, I do not corroborate it. Furthermore, regarding your claim that he actually experienced the pain of being dismembered: if he truly experienced such pain, how could he have subsequently entered [samādhi]?
One should know that the Sage internally realizes the true and eternal, penetrating the dharma-realm of suffering; being without deliberation yet responding universally, how could there be any pain?
As for your statement, "Since it is not me, I do not realize it either," and thus you claim that all others must likewise reach [this state], is this truly so?
Furthermore, it is said that the following section reiterates the refutation of non-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the "five hundred," the *Ting Shui Jing* (Sutra on the Water of the Pavilion) states that Avalokiteśvara manifests five hundred bodies here to teach and transform beings;
the present mention of Maitreya should be understood as following this same principle. Alternatively, there may be wicked bhikṣus who claim, "I am one of the five hundred bodies of Maitreya."
As for this great falsehood, how could it ever be verified? Therefore, it is said that none can be verified. Regarding the single character "lü" (律):
in ancient times, the meaning of *vinaya* was translated as "lü. Because the Buddha established the *vinaya* to prohibit and prevent evil, it is like the laws and regulations (*fǎlǜ*) of this method.
The *Fēngsú Tōng* states: "Gāoyáo planned [the system] for Yù, creating the 'lǜ'; 'lǜ' is explained as 'to interpret' (*qián*)."

Because it instructs according to the Dharma, the name of the Vinaya (Lü) originated in the era of Shun. It was because Xiao He of the Han dynasty codified the Nine Chapters (*jiuzhang*) that the gradations of light and heavy offenses were gradually differentiated with exhaustive detail.

Regarding the five names: as in the *Zhiguan chijie qingjing* (Cessation and Contemplation on the Purity of Upholding the Precepts), one establishes the contemplation of the mind by means of these five names; they are not discussed here.
Regarding the meaning of "taking up the contemplation of the mind," this is merely an explanation of the Vinaya principles within the sūtras based on five names.
These five names are: first, *śīla* (precepts), which means restraint; second, *vinaya*, translated as "extinction," because it extinguishes the evils of body and speech;
third, *pratimokṣa*, translated as "attaining liberation"; fourth, *uddeśa*, which refers to reciting the text; and fifth, *svādhyāya*, which refers to holding it in memory through recitation.

"Vinaya" (律) is defined as that which discriminates between the gravity or lightness of offenses, and whether they have been committed or not. If one follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (四分律), there are only four names for its upper and lower sections;
however, according to the ancient commentaries, only three names are retained—namely, Śīla (尸羅), Vinaya (毗尼), and Vimokṣa (木叉).

Thus, Master Nanshan, citing the eighteen dharmas, states that the two terms "Vinaya" and "Lü" (律) do not appear concurrently, because they are distinct expressions from the Chinese and Indic languages respectively. Now, our school...

It is my view that although all names are based upon one another, they exist as four distinct designations; though these do not coexist simultaneously, it is nonetheless termed "Vinaya" and also "Pitaka.

Therefore, in the present text, both names are employed together. Furthermore, the name "Mūla-aṣṭaka-saṃghātikā" (The Fundamental Recitation in Eighty Sections) is derived from the fact that the Venerable Upāli ascended the seat eighty times during a single summer retreat to recite it;
thus it is so named. Consequently, the character "lù" (律, *vinaya*) fully encompasses its intended meaning.
The fifth name:
Following the example of the Vinaya, when a teacher of transformation sometimes expounds the Small Dharma and sometimes expounds the Great Dharma, it is called "according to the occasion.
Regarding "with remainder" and "without remainder": "with remainder" refers to the incomplete teachings of the Hīnayāna, while "without remainder" refers to the complete [teachings] of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the explanation of the four or five matters of meaning, they are as interpreted in the preceding commentary by way of the Vinaya text.

As for the section beginning with "the student" (*xué rén*): since the six kinds of fivefold dharmas were previously listed based on the Vinaya and contrasted with the Sūtra to clarify the five [categories] of spiritual understanding, and since the explanation of the Sūtra is now complete, this further demonstrates the characteristics of each of the five [categories] for the students and others.
Those offenses that may later be repented of are those from the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (monastic offenses requiring suspension) onwards.
One who wishes to master a single collection must explain one of the *sūtra*, *vinaya*, or *abhidharma*.
As for me, your disciple, I lack the capacity to interpret the meaning of these base, evil, and heterodox doctrines.
"Crossing over" refers to first breaking through the external to enter the internal, now breaking through the internal to enter the external, and finally breaking through both internal and external;
such a person is called one who has crossed over.
As for the "remaining two sets of five dharmas," they refer to the five admonitions and the six matters of application.

Regarding the five points of instruction, the Vinaya states: first, knowing the dharma of renunciation; second, being able to act as a preceptor (ācārya); third, being able to act as a master of precepts (upādhyāya);
fourth, being able to know the rules regarding reliance on a teacher (niśraya); and fifth, being able to know the dharmas that obstruct the path and those that do not obstruct the path.

Regarding the five practical functions, the Vinaya states: first, one can instruct disciples in the pure precepts; second, one can instruct them in the Abhidharma; third, one can instruct them in the Vinaya;

fourth, when disciples are distressed, suffering, or unhappy in other regions, one can cause them to come [to one's own place], or if one is unable to do so oneself, one can bring them through the power of others;
fifth, if disciples are ill, one can provide for their needs, or if one is unable to do so oneself, one can have others do so.
If he has provided these five things, completed ten years—or more—of service, he should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple;
this is recorded in the first fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, under the "Seven Dharmas."

In the introductory section of the commentary on the title of the "Chapter on the Merits of Names," it first mentions the mundane world. Regarding the statement that both are designations based upon a substance, the *Baihutong* says:

"Upon hearing the name, one immediately knows the style-name; upon hearing the style-name, one immediately knows the given name. For example, Zigong’s given name was Li, while his style-name was Gong.
Master Yu thus knew that both names and personal appellations (*ming* and *zi*) are designations for the physical person.

Regarding how a name summons the person, the *Baitong* (White Tiger General Discourse) states: "Why must a person have a name? It is so that they may express their inner sentiments, record themselves, and show reverence to others.
The *Lifufuan* (Tradition on Ritual Robes) says: "When a son is born, after three months, the father names him in the ancestral temple. This refers to summoning [the person].
Regarding their personal names (*ti*): Houji was named Qi because he was abandoned [by his mother], and Confucius was named Qiu because his head was shaped like Mount Niqiu.

As for the practice of using courtesy names (*zi*) to praise virtue, the *Baihutong* states: "Why do people have courtesy names? It is to crown their virtue and clarify their achievements, thereby showing respect for the perfected person."

Furthermore, the *Li* (Book of Rites), in the *Shi guan jing* (Classic on the Capping of the Scholar), states: "Once one has been capped, a courtesy name is given to show respect for one's given name. Moreover, the *Tan gong* (Coffin of Tan) says: "In childhood there is the given name; at the capping ceremony, there is the courtesy name.

Regarding the examples from the Buddhist Dharma, throughout the Buddha-dharma, those who possess merit are said to have "merit" (*gong*) because they extinguish evil, and they are said to have "virtue" (*de*) because they give rise to goodness.
As for these virtues, both the name and the characters of this sutra are established based on the principle that evil arises from cessation and goodness arises from cultivation.

Regarding the "goodness of speech," as the sutra says, "the beginning is good, and so forth. There are many ways of explaining this; however, following the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*), we shall interpret it according to the sutra:
practicing generosity is the "goodness of the beginning," maintaining the precepts is the "goodness of the middle," and attaining the retribution [of merit] is the "goodness of the end."

"Excellence in meaning" refers to what the sutra calls "profound and deep flavor"; it refers to the principle elucidated in this present sutra, which is so vast and subtle that its limits and depths cannot be fathomed, hence it is called "profound and deep."
Regarding "meaningful flavor" (*artha-rasa*): meaning can moisten the mind and cause people to find delight in it, much like a delicious worldly taste.

Regarding "excellent phrasing": this refers to what the Sūtra calls "its phrasing is also excellent. This means that the teaching which directly explains the principle through the assembly of the text is called "excellent phrasing."

"Purely complete" (*śuddha-saṃpanna*) means that it is not mixed with the partial or the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), and thus it is "pure"; it is "complete" because it encompasses the sublime principles (*saddharma*).
"Complete" (*saṃpanna*) and "fully endowed" (*saṃpūrṇa*) have the same meaning. Because it is pure, it is unique; because it is complete, it is called the "sole, singular excellence."
Purity (*pariśuddhi*) refers to the practitioner of good deeds; because they perfectly cultivate the five practices and remain unstained by the two extremes, purity is the practice of good.

The Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) refers to the practitioner of kindness; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are the conduct of the Brahma-heavens, as clarified in this sutra. There is no [other]... [end of fragment].
Because universal operation is the practice of the ultimate celestial realm (*paramārtha-deva*), it is called "benevolent charity" (*śubha*).
Because the two edges below the vajra are indestructible, it is called "vajra. Because it is fully endowed with the three thousand [worlds], it is likened to a "treasury of jewels.

How could it be the same as partial principles that are fragmented or deficient in their vertical and horizontal dimensions? Therefore, it is called "complete and perfect goodness" (*paripūrṇa-śubha*).
The ten wholesome actions are established as three by opening up [the first seven] into speech; these are further divided into two by opening up [the latter three] into pure and complete fulfillment.
Thus, "pure and complete" constitutes the single category of wholesome action, while "complete fulfillment" is termed "perfectly complete wholesome action."
Regarding the combination into eight virtues: among the ten [virtues] at Yecheng, the superior, middling, and inferior are combined into one "virtue of speech," thus there are eight virtues.
Now, although the commentators differ on whether to expand or condense [the categories], since the scriptural text contains only seven similes, we know that it is simply [seven].
It is said that regarding the seven virtues, the dharma and its metaphors are equally merged.
The first metaphor corresponds to the following section, which cites the subsequent seven metaphors in sequential alignment with the seven virtues.
The lecturer should take the text of the sutra and explain it by correlating it with these points.
The metaphor of the eight rivers entering the ocean illustrates that the words are excellent; all sutras converge in this teaching just as rivers flow into the sea.
When matters are perfected and principles reach their ultimate limit, how could anything be more excellent than this?
Regarding the profound and secret aspects of a single direction, the sutra says: "Furthermore, it is like a physician who possesses a secret prescription... and so forth.
It is said that the Tathāgata is likewise; because the sublime Dharma he expounds is secret and profoundly abstruse, we know that the metaphor of the "secret recipe" is excellent.
Previously it was said that its meaning and flavor are profound; now, combining this with the analogy, it is called "secret and profoundly abstruse. Is this not indeed an excellence of meaning?
Regarding the "permanent severance of longing," the Sūtra says: "For example, when a farmer sows seeds in the spring, he is constantly filled with longing;
once he has harvested the fruit, all such longings cease. This analogy is excellent. Therefore, the Sūtra provides a parallel to this analogy, stating:
"If one hears this Mahāparinirvāṇa, the longing for the flavors found in other sūtras is permanently severed. Furthermore—
Regarding the phrase "excellent in its meaning," according to the teaching, it should be stated as "hearing the Great Nirvāṇa. Is this not indeed hearing the teaching?

What is called the "elephant's footprint" refers to the Sūtra; just as among all footprints the elephant’s footprint is supreme, this metaphor represents that which is uniquely and solely good—namely, what was previously described as "pure, complete, and fully endowed. Therefore, the Sūtra concludes by stating that among all sūtras and samādhis, it is the most supreme.
First, is it not the case that "one" (*eka*) signifies "solitary"?
Regarding the statement that autumn plowing is superior, this is a metaphor for practicing virtue; thus the sutra states in conjunction:
"This sutra is the most excellent among all such sutras, for its five practices are cultivated in their full perfection, and therefore it is deemed superior."
"Greatness is the meaning of tranquility," and tranquility is precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Skillfully treating the distracted mind" refers to what the Sūtra says: "The *amṛta* (clarified butter) skillfully treats the feverish afflictions and distracted minds of sentient beings.

This is an analogy for how the benevolent mind, through the power of non-referential compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*) and meditative concentration, skillfully treats the distracted minds of those sentient beings caused by ignorance.
The phrase "endowed with the eight flavors" refers to the seventh simile, that of sweet cream; this illustrates being fully equipped with virtues.

While the preceding sutra spoke of the "vajra-treasury being complete and without deficiency," the present text speaks of being "endowed with the eight flavors"; thus, the meaning of the text is brilliantly clear.
In each and every instance, following the analogy and its application (*upanaya*), the text concludes by stating: "Therefore, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
These are all instances where the Buddha himself enumerates his own names within the analogies to correspond with the seven virtues;
thus we know that both the "Ten" of Yecheng and the "Eight" of Kaishan deviate from the scriptural text. This [text] consists of the seven virtues destroying the seven evils to give rise to goodness.
Because this merit destroys evil and constitutes virtue, we know that the seven types of goodness are merely the merits designated by the name "Nirvana.
Regarding the explanation of the merits of the title, three passages are cited: the first and last are from the initial exhortation to uphold [the teaching] at the beginning of this chapter;

the second is from the concluding summary of its upholding at the end of this chapter, which is the scripture stating: "If there are those who study and practice this sutra, they shall attain the gate of the True Dharma."
Since it is said that "cultivation and study" must necessarily depend on others, the *Bodhisattva Sūtra* now adds [the term] "this sūtra," which refers to the present teaching of the *Nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is now stated that "cultivating the Great *Nirvāṇa*" is intended to make the phrasing explicit and the meaning consistent; thus, this has been revised to read "Question. If one asks:

"Having already cited a Buddhist sūtra, how can you permit such arbitrary revision? The answer is: for those who engage in the editorial refinement (*pi-xiō*) of texts, they change only according to what is appropriate to the circumstances.
The principle resides therein; one follows the meaning to employ the phrasing. How could it be merely a matter of transcribing?
It is not only the case for our own school’s masters that all traditions are thus; even the former Confucian scholars were the same.

For example, the *Book of Changes* says, "Words and deeds are the pivot and trigger of the gentleman," yet when Zheng Xuan cited and commented on this in his explanation of the *Quli*, he stated: "The *Changes* says: 'Speech is the pivot of the gentleman.'"
It is a pivot; it is a closure.
Regarding the brief mention of "three points" and so forth: the first two concern the production of good, while the third clarifies the destruction of evil.
Furthermore, the first point clarifies the fruit, while the latter two reside in the cause.
When one side is mentioned, if that side mentions the person who upholds [the teaching], there must necessarily be the dharma that is upheld;

if this side mentions the dharma that is upheld, there must necessarily be the person who upholds it. If both sides were mentioned together, it should have been stated as "Receiving and Upholding the Chapter on Names and Merits."
"Reaching the other shore" refers to the ultimate perfection of wondrous enlightenment. "The middle stream among Bodhisattvas" refers to the various stages of partial realization (*viniścaya-satya*).
"Sentient beings who have set out" refers to those from the stage of the Name (*nāma*) upward.

That which is neither "this" nor "that" is because the principle (*li*) is one from beginning to end; yet that which is "this" and "that" is because the phenomena (*shi*) of ordinary beings and sages differ. Thus it is known.
Natures have no high or low, yet understandings have clarity or dullness. Jingxi said: "The principle is the same, but phenomena differ.
These words are indeed verified by the following.
To answer the question asked: Kāśyapa asked only about reaching the ultimate shore, yet the Buddha further added [the discussion of] this shore.
Because this serves as an answer to a flow [of inquiry], it is called "answering the question.

Those who have ascended to the stage of nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) refer to the second stage of nature elucidated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which corresponds to the present stage of penetration (*tongwei*).

Since the stage of nature is equal to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), and because *kṣānti* (patience) prevents one from falling into the evil realms, one takes up the name of hearing and practices until—
In this stage, one finally attains the state where one does not fall [into evil realms] merely by having heard the sutras in a superficial manner.

Rather, it refers to those whose discipline is lax while their aspiration for the vehicle is urgent; these are people who fall into evil states due to breaking the precepts, yet obtain liberation through hearing the sutras.
Within the evil realms, they rely on the conditions of the Dharma they previously heard to encounter a Buddha and attain liberation, thereby returning to awakening.
Because of seeds planted in previous lives, it is said that one returns to the source; the meaning of "non-arising" in the Sūtra lies herein.
Furthermore, it is said that once there is understanding below [the level of the senses], even if one encounters adverse causes, one will not fall.
"Correct understanding of non-arising" means realizing that names are nameless and sounds are soundless; internally illuminating the single suchness is called correct understanding.
"Even obstructing humans and devas" means that those who give rise to this correct understanding proceed directly toward Bodhi and do not even accept rebirth as humans or devas.
If one fails to attain even the pleasant fruits of death, how much more so the bitter retributions of the four evil realms?

Judging by this, those who hear the names [of the Buddhas] in a superficial manner without correct understanding will likely not escape falling into the evil destinies. Thus we know that the interpretations of various masters each rely on a single path and are not entirely perfect.
If one follows the approach of Bei Yuan, it is based on the three grades of hearing the sutra: first, the superior grade, where one recites the sutra while listening, yet does not... [understand].
Those who grasp at the characteristics of phenomena will ultimately not be born in the four miserable realms, except by the power of compassion and vows.

Among these two types, those of middle capacity, though they have not yet abandoned the grasping at characteristics, will not be born [in the miserable realms] for a time while listening to and receiving this teaching with a virtuous mind, yet this is not a permanent non-entry.

Those of lower capacity, with a slight and minor virtuous mind while listening to and receiving this sutra, will plant the causes and conditions for liberation in the distant future, but it is not that they do not arise [in the miserable realms] immediately. Now...
Since that which is being discussed here is of the highest grade, it is impossible for one to be born in the four miserable destinies;
this is superior in its remote meaning compared to other masters.
Now, all [other views] are refuted as being inferior. First, the refutation of Master Xinghuang and the third master concerns the meaning of generating understanding.

What does this have to do with the following? The sutra text simply states that by hearing the name of the sutra one is not born in the four miserable destinies; it does not distinguish between whether one has produced understanding or not produced understanding.
"But merely holding" [the name] directly refutes the first master while also refuting the second master, because the first master [relies on] the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Regarding the stage of the nature-ground (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), one does not fall into evil; however, the former master says that if one gives rise to evil, one falls.

This shows that by practicing virtuous conduct, one does not fall, and thus this view is somewhat similar to that of the first master, differing only in that the former is profound while the latter is shallow. Now, I am specifically refuting the first master:
why must one hear the sutras and practice cultivation? Merely observing the five precepts is sufficient for one not to fall.
Now, "the Great One" (*mahā*) correctly indicates the meaning of the present [title].
