Regarding the dove’s descent, he cites scriptural evidence to show that returning to the Saṃgha brings one closer to escaping Māra; yet because Śāriputra still possessed residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the dove fought and was terrified—these habitual tendencies are precisely the affliction-māra (*kleśamāra*).
The term "previously" (*qian*) refers to the preceding section, as this passage is presented in contrast to the subsequent discussion of doctrinal principles; hence it is called "previously.
Regarding the phrase "fearing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and so forth," this means fearing the two types of death and taking refuge in the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
This clarifies that the "three" are identical with the "one"—this is the meaning of the term "three."
Because the three descend into one, it is said that the "three refuges" (tri-śaraṇa) signify the meaning of "refuge" (śaraṇa).

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that the Buddha is named "Awakening" (bodhi), the Buddha is the wisdom of the subject who contemplates; therefore, he receives the name "Awakening. The Dharma is the object of contemplation, and is thus called "Non-Awakening.
When object and wisdom are in union, awakening is non-awakening, and non-awakening is awakening. The ten realms depend upon this.
I have now fully realized that the meaning of my own mind as the three jewels being of one essence is perfectly clear.

Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* which states "that which is named empty space is not good," Master Yuan (Yuán Fǎshī) said: "It does not refer to performing wholesome deeds within the practice of morality, concentration, and wisdom;

rather, it means that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—emptiness—is the ultimate good. Master Shè (Shè Bǎoshī) stated: "Because it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), it is spoken of in contrast to the Buddha."
Her name was Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, also known as Kauṭamī; this means "Great Lady of the Multitude" or "Mistress of the Assembly.
She left the household life for the sake of sentient beings and served as the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Seven days after the Buddha was born, his mother passed away.

After the Buddha had been raised by Queen Māyā and subsequently renounced the world, King Prasenajit was filled with longing and remembrance. He personally wove a golden-threaded woolen cloth and waited for the Buddha to return to the palace, intending to offer it to him.
When the Buddha eventually returned to the palace, the king presented it as an offering.

The Buddha then said: "A gift given out of affectionate attachment does not possess great merit. One should instead make offerings to the Saṃgha; for if one makes offerings to the Saṃgha, one is thereby making offerings to the Three Refuges."
Now, taking up the term "pāṣa" (波闍) as a sequence, I shall explain it by means of the Buddha’s subsequent teaching.
First, the one who grasps the essential meaning refers to the two characters "is" (是) and "meaning" (義) in the sutra.

As for the phrase "how is it that" (云何下), one should again cite the aforementioned two characters "is" and "meaning" and connect them with the word "how" (云何) to explain them; thus, there are two [aspects].
I have merely cited the wording for now.

If one considers the matter according to the sutras, this is not so; although the phrases "without arising" and "without ceasing" are identical, their meanings are entirely different, because liberation with cognition is contrasted with a dull emptiness that lacks cognition.
The *Kalandaka* Sūtra also refers to it as *Kalandaka*; the latter term, *Kalandaka*, is the correct one. It is the name of a bird whose shape resembles that of a magpie.

As for the claim that the bodies [of the birds] must also differ because the Buddha stated only that their voices differ, this constitutes a fallacious objection based on the assumption that the bodies must be identical.
Some say that "one and three" means that while they are one, they are also three; this refers to their former distinct characteristics (*bhedalakṣaṇa*).
Others say that "three and one" means that while they are three, they are also one; this refers to their present identity of essence (*ekasvabhāva*).

In the passage below from the *Haimeng jing*, the body is compared to emptiness: just as the gravity of a crime against a Buddha is established as empty and thus cannot be used as a metaphor for the indestructibility of the body.
The *Jīngǔ* (經糓) states that "zǐ" (子) is pronounced four times as "jī" (積); the *Pīcāng* (埤蒼) defines "jī" as accumulation.

Within the "Comprehensive Summary" (*jìnglǐngjiě*), all three meanings are fully encompassed: "the place where the Tathāgata arrives" summarizes the aforementioned realm of liberation; the correspondence between wisdom and its object is the "place.
If this place is inexhaustible, it is "transversely pervasive"; if one's lifespan is inexhaustible, it is "vertically exhaustive"—this summarizes the aforementioned [point].
The nature is vast and expansive, encompassing all without exception. Since both its locus and its duration are inexhaustible, all afflictions and burdens are entirely eliminated;

this is precisely what was meant by "being free from sores and blemishes" mentioned above. As the three meanings have already been explained at length, I shall now fully summarize their essential purport.
In the initial brief explanation of the title within the "Chapter on the Four Reliances," "all worlds" refers to the nine realms and the three types of worlds;
it means that the four types of persons derive benefit by relying upon the Buddha-realm.
Relying on this, the extensive explanation below fully sets forth the four *siddhāntas*, all of which contrast the past and the present:

the teachings of the past prohibit reliance on persons, whereas this present sutra relies on persons; therefore, they must be contrasted to establish these four meanings. "Relying on oneself" refers to the teachings of the past, while "relying on others" refers to this present sutra.

If it is argued that the former passage merely reveals what was incorrect in the past while the latter clarifies what is correct in the present—asking why the four original reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), such as relying on the Dharma and relying on the meaning, are not called "reliances" [in the latter]—the answer is:
they are indeed called the "four reliances," but they cannot be called the "four persons who rely.
This is because the "four" mentioned in the latter passage all refer to persons.

Regarding those who have attained both [the Dharma and its realization]: formerly, because there were no people who possessed the Dharma, they were not permitted to rely [on others]; now, because people possess the Dharma, they are able to rely [upon it].
As for the strength of the meaning of benefit: "immediately responding to the desires of others" refers to benefit within this world (*loka*).
The first part directly discusses the past; the second clarifies the present. If people of today were to obtain the Dharma, they would have something to rely upon;

since relying on a person ultimately means relying on the Dharma, such a person must possess the Dharma. Obtaining the Dharma is the very arising of the Principle (Li), and thus it belongs to the person.

Regarding the mixture of the true and the false among people: when the Deer Park was first established, non-Buddhist paths were still flourishing. Had one merely relied on the person, there was the fear of becoming intimate with a "thief" (a false teacher).

Therefore, one must rely on the true Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; since the teachings of those outside the Way are false, they are not accepted simply because their form is familiar, and if what they say is indeed correct, it is not rejected simply because their form is distant.

Regarding the confusion between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: in the past, the Hīnayāna was already taught, and now the Mahāyāna is being expounded. Although those who have realized the Mahāyāna are few, the teachings of the Hīnayāna still persist;

thus, the names "True Emptiness" and "Nirvāṇa" are conflated across both vehicles. Because beginners and new students lack the means to distinguish between them, they are led to rely on the person of the Great Man (Mahāpuruṣa) to discern what is not of the Lesser Vehicle.
Once a person has entered the Mahāyāna, that which they teach is no longer of the Lesser Vehicle.

Now, by relying on the present to contrast with the past, we reveal the distinction between the present and the past; this is not based on the person, which serves to exclude heterodox individuals, whereas here we require reliance on the person, which means relying on a correct individual.

Thus, such a correct individual must necessarily rely upon the Correct Dharma to attain understanding, thereby destroying heterodox and limited views; this is precisely the meaning of "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).
If the Dharma is also not pervasive, then having abandoned the person, one relies on the Dharma;

yet it is not only that the Dharma is absent where the person is, but also that the Dharma does not encompass the person—hence it is said to be "not pervasive. Furthermore, since the Dharma is true emptiness and emptiness is fundamentally of one essence, there is no duality or distinction.
If one abandons the person to seek the Dharma, how is this different from abandoning this empty space to seek some other emptiness?

The person is one who upholds the Dharma; when a person abides in the Dharma, its wondrous principle encompasses all. Since there is neither grasping nor rejecting, there is the benefit of entering into the principle.
This is used as the concluding summary below.
Regarding the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] being called "not the true person": they are termed "not true" because the Great [Vehicle] excludes the Small [Vehicle].

Regarding the image that cannot be attained: since this is after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, if one were to produce a form of the Buddha, it would merely be a spurious imitation of the Buddha’s appearance.

Regarding the objection concerning other images: if one says that creating images of the four fruits makes the practice of transformation easy, then creating images of the other nine realms should make the practice of transformation difficult.
If you say it is difficult, why does the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* explain that bodhisattvas dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi manifest various bodies to transform sentient beings?
Regarding the general discussion up to the four fruits: from a general perspective, he manifests bodies throughout the ten realms to benefit sentient beings without restriction;
specifically, he displays the forms of the four fruits to propagate the teachings after his parinirvāṇa.

In the section beginning with "From the perspective of one's own [attainment]," although it is permitted to discuss them collectively as being applicable to all, this follows the preceding question by correlating the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) with the four fruits of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-phala*), each forming four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) to yield eight permutations in total.

Although there are eight in number, there are actually seven, because the four fruits cannot themselves serve as the four reliances; thus, there is no permutation where the four fruits constitute the four reliances. Regarding the first four permutations:
The first phrase refers to the manifestation of the eight phases by the Wondrous Enlightenment; this represents both the fundamental and the manifested being lofty.
The second phrase means that while fundamentally the ultimate fruit, it manifests as a causal practitioner; this likewise represents the fundamental being lofty and the manifested being lowly.

For example, Mañjuśrī was originally an ancient Buddha, yet after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni, he presided over the compilation and propagated the teachings of the Single-Nature school; he is precisely such a person. (3)
The fourth phrase refers to the Bodhisattvas of the "divided reality" who manifest the eight phases of enlightenment;

this is like Avalokiteśvara manifesting a Buddha-body for those who are to be saved by a Buddha-body—this is also the case where the fundamental is low while the trace is high. These four phrases describe the stages and positions based on actual realization;
this is like Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, both of whom were titled "Bodhisattvas. Compared to the preceding [three], both the fundamental and the trace are present.
"High" should be understood as both the provisional (迹) and the real (本); this fourth phrase is also for the purpose of contrasting with the four fruits (*phala*).
Regarding the first phrase, it must be interpreted in two ways. Next, concerning the four phrases explained in contrast to the four fruits:
the previous fourth phrase becomes the first here, which is identical to the "Tathāgata as Tathāgata" phrase among the previous four. The second phrase is like Kāśyapa.
Ānanda, having already manifested the full revelation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, is yet still called a "lesser sage" (śrāvaka) during the period of propagation after the [Buddha’s] passing;
thus, this phrase precisely captures the intent of the present chapter. These four lines refer to the Hīnayāna masters after the passing.
Since the Hīnayāna cannot manifest the Mahāyāna, there is no third or fourth fruit as the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*); this is according to the literal text alone.

Regarding the six propositions: if one takes the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*) as the four reliance-propositions and considers them from two perspectives, there are seven propositions; taken collectively, there are eight.

Question: If it is said that the four fruits of the path cannot serve as the semblance of the four reliances, yet even Māra was able to transform himself into the form of a Buddha for Kūṭadanta, how could an Arhat’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) not be able to transform his body into that of a Bodhisattva? Answer: Although... [the text continues].
The supreme body capable of transformation cannot preach the Great Dharma; it is simply because this present chapter specifically relies on those who possess the dharma that it says they "cannot.
Now, if one adopts a single approach, it is because the path of transformation is easy to practice; however, if one understands this text, each [of these bodies] opens into four [categories].
Only through these phrases can one recognize that the twenty-four patriarchs of the *Dharma-paryāya-vaṃśa* were all Mahāsattvas who were the Four Reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).
Whether their individual status was considered "small" or "great," they were subsumed within the two phrases: "the Four Reliances as the Four Reliances" and "the Four Reliances as the Four Fruits.
Alternatively, if the Tathāgata himself is regarded as the Four Reliances, he is endowed with three phrases; furthermore, this applies to the ancient masters of this land whose fruit was realized.
The same principle applies to those who propagate the Great Dharma while adhering to the Hīnayāna.
From "now following" up to "the four reliances": *nirvāṇa* is the principle realized, while the four reliances are the persons who realize it.

Although the principle realized is the same, the stages of those who realize it differ; thus, it is said that "from *nirvāṇa*, [the teaching] is opened," because [the teaching] is based on the fact that it accords with the principle.

Regarding the emergence of the four reliances (*catvāri pratiśaraṇāni*): when combined, they constitute the state of being a Buddha. Although the stages of the four reliances differ, their principle is not distinct; all are termed "the Buddha," for the Buddha is itself *nirvāṇa*.
Thus it is said that when combined, they are still the Buddha. This is the principle realized within phenomena (*jiaoshi er li*).

Regarding the phrase "This Buddha... and so forth, the three characters "for the sake of the four reliances" (*catur-śaraṇa*) were likely added erroneously by those who were ignorant; the unrevised original text states, "If combined, it is simply 'it is the Tathāgata,' and there are no [additional] three characters for the four reliances.
Jingxi merely changed "Tathāgata" to "Buddha. Question: Regarding the section beginning with "What is...?

why does it first refer to the *Āgamas* (the teachings of the past) and later refer to this very chapter? Answer: In the initial response concerning the appearance in the world, it first refers to the *Āgamas*. This is because the *Āgamas* represent the former teaching, while the latter part refers to the present chapter. Thus, within the answer, the first section concerns his appearance in the world.
This refers to the period when the Bodhi tree was first attained.

Those called "people of the present" are those who are dull-witted during the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; because their faculties are not equal to those in the Buddha’s own time, he established the rule that they must rely on the words of others.

These "people of the present" are those who transform the world through the four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni) after the parinirvāṇa; since this is the subject discussed in this chapter, they are called "people of the present."
The text states that what follows clarifies that one should now rely on the Dharma rather than solely on the person; the "Dharmatā" is the Dharma, while the "Tathāgata" is the person.

Those prior to the thirty minds refer to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*); because they have not yet destroyed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), they are disciples (*śrāvaka*).
One who occupies the stage of the Teacher (ācārya) is so called because they have severed two categories of delusion through thirty moments of mind; this refers to the first reliance (pratiśaraṇa).
"All occupy the stage of the Teacher" means that all four reliances belong to the stage of the Teacher.
In the lower section of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the stages of teacher and disciple are divided into four phases based on the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) and ten practices (*daśacaryā*).
Those prior to the sixth mind—that is, those prior to the sixth abode—are disciples because they have not yet exhausted the abandonment of afflictions through reflection (*vitarka*).
The seventh stage below refers to the seventh dwelling (*bhūmi*), where one attains this rank of Teacher because the afflictions of thought (*vitarka*) are exhausted.
The "twelve minds" refer to the second practice.

The "final mind of the path-knowledge" (*mārgajñatā*) marks the ultimate limit of the position of emerging from the conventional (*prajñapti*). This is according to the first of the fourfold determinations established by the masters of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
The stages reach their ultimate limit at the tenth *bhūmi*, which is then correlated with the three subsequent bases (*āśraya*) via the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
Regarding the phrase "possessing afflictions in the first [base]," this refers to the Madhyamaka masters' interpretation of the sūtra;

since the sūtra states that the first base is "endowed with the nature of afflictions," they maintain that it is called "possessing" them because, although one has just begun to destroy the first category [of afflictions] at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), many still remain.
Because they possess a multitude of afflictions, there is no ultimate nirvana.

Since their subsequent existence will end in a lower nirvana before long, it is said that they "possess" [affliction]; because they possess only a single category of subtle ignorance, it is said that they "do not" [possess it].
Regarding the phrase "at the beginning and at the end," this is because the ignorance of the higher stages is already partially revealed throughout all forty stages.
Regarding the phrase "others," this is because two bases are established within the first stage.
In the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the destruction of ignorance by means of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) constitutes the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].
However, if one were to correlate the first dwelling with the stage of the initial reliance (*prathamāśraya*), it would not be entirely appropriate.
In the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, if the initial reliance were established within the thirty moments of mind, that interpretation might be tenable, as the initial reliance is complete [in those moments].

Because of these afflictions, the fourth meaning of the masters alone is correct: the first basis (āśraya) extends up to the ten stages of practice (prayoga-mārga), while the second basis corresponds precisely to the ten stages of dedication (pariṇāmana).
Since the ten stages of dedication still possess ignorance, how could they constitute the second basis?

It should be understood that because the Sūtra clarifies that the two bases have already eliminated distinct delusions, the statement "establishing the bases therein" is intended to refute the error of establishing those two bases within the thirty moments of mind.

Regarding the ear-discrimination (śrotra-vijñāna), according to the Separate Teaching (pratyeka-deśanā), it relies on the two [stages] and is situated in the first ground (bhūmi); according to the Perfect Teaching (pūrṇa-deśanā), it is in the first dwelling (vihāra). Since that [text] speaks of the "ten transferences" (daśa-pariṇāmanā), it contradicts the two teachings.
Now, we follow the current master’s judgment of the stages based on the lower [teachings].

Regarding "the stages from the Grounds up to the three reliances": this refers to the first through the sixth grounds as the second reliance, the seventh through the ninth as the third reliance, and the tenth as the fourth reliance.

Within the section on the Perfect [Teaching], the following demonstrates the common and specific aspects of the perfect stages. Regarding the "forty minds acting together," the ten levels of faith constitute the first ten.
"Abiding" constitutes two stages, "heading toward" constitutes three stages, and so forth, making four.
As for the distinctions, because the stage of destroying delusions through the Perfect [Teaching] is extensive, these are assigned to the respective stages.

The phrase "the rest are all analogous" means that the stages of practice (*caryā*), heading toward (*abhimukha*), and the grounds (*bhūmi*) are each individually correlated with the three bases; all follow the example of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*). However, [in this case], they are merely [analogous to] the ten abidings.
Initially, based on a single stage, it is fixed at the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), for the Sūtra states: "There are those who appear in the world who possess the nature of afflictions;
this is called the first. This stage is therefore fixed.
Initially, it relies solely on the disciple because the distinct delusions (*pṛthag-vikalpa*) remain entirely present.
Those who later rely solely on their teacher dwell at the summit of the "partially true" stage;
thus, one who is both teacher and disciple is called a "teacher" in relation to those below and a "disciple" in relation to those above.
"Not allowing external conditions to interfere" means not permitting demons, outsiders, ordinary people, or followers of the Small Vehicle to disturb one's practice, as was the case with Kūṭadanta.
Nāgārjuna’s subduing of Māra and refutation of outsiders was the protection of the Dharma where it exists;
his descending to the lower realms was like Kāśyapa Mātanga entering China or Kang Senghui coming to Wu, which was the establishment of the Dharma where it did not exist.

Furthermore, by establishing the Mahāyāna in places where there was only the "small" (Hīnayāna), he benefited others; meanwhile, because of the former [refutation of outsiders], he himself remained undisturbed.
Therefore, because others are brought to excellence through one's own manifestation, and because others see and hear through one's own maintenance, they rely upon that person.

As for not encountering afflictive events: when universal afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have been abandoned, there are no longer any manifest activities within the realm; as for specific afflictions (*kleśa*), [the same applies].

Question: When the distinct delusions (*bhedakleśa*) have been subdued, they do not arise; yet, because their nature remains present, one is said to "possess the nature of affliction. What, then, are these distinct delusions? Answer:
In principle, they refer to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who fail to understand their own minds and give rise to pervasive attachment;

this is what is meant by "distinct delusions. Now, within the stages of the inner ordinary beings of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, those who realize that all phenomena are none other than Buddha-nature are said to have "subdued the distinct delusions."
The non-arising of false attachments is called the "non-arising of phenomena.

Regarding the stages from the first to the sixth: according to what is discussed in the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), the first stage is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the second through the sixth are called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the seventh through the tenth are called the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
Therefore, in terms of their respective positions, the second [stage] and those following are all aligned within the path of cultivation.
Since the two lower bases (niśraya) are judged by way of commonality, one knows that the position of the first base lies within the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*).

Therefore, the judgment is made solely in terms of the three teachings, because the Sūtra clarifies that from the second base onward, all afflictions are destroyed; furthermore, as the afflictions of the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas remain entirely intact, they are not included therein.

Moreover, in the *Tripiṭaka* teaching, both principle and phenomena are provisional, whereas in the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), the phenomena are provisional while the principle is real.
Since the reality [of the teachings] penetrates the Shared, Distinct, and Complete [vehicles], the four reliances are explained as pertaining only to the latter three vehicles.

Regarding the "Ground of Seeing" (*darśana-bhūmi*), it is said that the Ground of Seeing is equal to the first fruit; because on the "Ground of Thinning" (*tanu-bhūmi*) one has already severed six grades of the afflictions of the desire realm, it receives the name "Thinning."

If one follows the explanation in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra* regarding the meaning of a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*) who can transcend and ascend to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in a single lifetime,

it is known by analogy that within the body of the desire realm there still exist those with the "tiger-root" (*tuhgen*) difficulty; likewise, it should be understood that in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*),

there are also those who reach the sixth stage of "Freedom from Desire" (*vītarāga*) or the seventh stage of "Accomplishment" (*kṛtāvin*) in a single lifetime, and thus there exist those who have not yet abandoned the physical body of the desire realm.
Regarding the person [described as] "such a one," the commentary’s repeated remarks have this meaning in mind. However, since the text is somewhat abbreviated,
it should state that from the stage of seeing up to the stage of freedom from desire constitutes the second basis, while the seventh stage belongs to the third basis.
Regarding this "eighth or ninth stage," it should be stated as "seventh, eighth, or ninth stage"; the text omits seven characters. The "eighth abiding" (*aṣṭamavihāra*) is likewise a brief citation.

Based on the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), since he externally manifests the appearance of an *anāgāmin* while relying on the three [stages], his status is provisionally determined according to the Hīnayāna.
Thus, the *anāgāmin*—here translated as "Non-returner"—is one who does not return to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, if we provisionally rely on the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*), at the seventh stage, which corresponds precisely to the third reliance, the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) are completely exhausted and equalized with those of an Arhat;
therefore, such a person does not return to the three realms.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": if one were to distinguish between the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) vehicles, they would not yet have returned from the flow of transformation.
However, since these three bases are explained according to the Great and Small Vehicles, the analogy for the first two and the last one should likewise apply.

For instance, while the first fruit of the stream-enterer's "flowing against the current" is understandable within the Small Vehicle, in the Separate and Perfect vehicles, it refers to flowing against the current of transformation.

The fourth section below concerns the general [classification], which refers to the eight stages (*bhūmi*) for the Shared [Vehicle] and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and ten abodes (*vihāra*) for the Distinct and Perfect [Vehicles].

Regarding the note "and so forth" (*yún yún*): as previously explained regarding the division into the forty positions of the "partial truth," each is treated as three bases (*āśraya*) to correspond with the stages prior to the [ten] abodes, such as taking the first base as corresponding to those prior to the abodes, and so on.

Regarding the two trainings of precepts and wisdom: the section from "If there be a person" up to "the training in the true Dharma and precepts" concerns the training in precepts; the section from "From the Buddha" up to "the wisdom of words and meaning" concerns the training in wisdom.

As for transforming others, this refers to what the Sūtra says regarding "turning [the teaching] for others," which is the instruction for generating goodness by explaining the eight great awakenings.
Causing [others] to repent and confess is the eradication of evil.
Generally speaking, the subsequent two phrases from the sutra, "skillfully knowing" and "removing," constitute a summary in terms of the provisional and the real;
that is, both self-cultivation and transforming others possess both the provisional and the real.

Regarding the *Śāsanāntara-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching), the *Śāsanāntara-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) by Aśvaghoṣa classifies it as Mahāyāna, whereas the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, in his *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), classifies it as belonging to the Hīnayāna. How are these two views to be reconciled? Answer: It is called "Mahāyāna" because it analyzes the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*);
it is called "Hīnayāna" because it does not discuss the eternal or discern the true nature (*dharmatā*). This is because, in the Initial Teaching, the three vehicles are collectively termed "Small."
Distinguishing the ordinary from the noble refers to the first two phrases; distinguishing the ordinary from the noble by means of the noble refers to the next two phrases;
and distinguishing the result from the cause refers to the final two phrases.

Regarding the three successive instances of distinction explained below, the meaning is that the first two instances clarify that the initial basis is that of an internal ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and not yet a portion of the noble ones.

The first [section] of the *Śāstrakāra* (the "Holy Author") clarifies that this initial basis refers to the person who is a Bodhisattva on the path of causes, not a person who has attained the fruit of Buddhahood;
there is an original basis for this, as the character "first" (*chū*) frequently appears above the character "ordinary" (*fán*) in the text, though it is an error.

Regarding the interpretation using the "Shared Stages" (*sādhāraṇabhūmi*), the Buddha explains this through the stages of the Shared Teaching; this is what is meant by the "Shared Meaning" being perfected.

The commentary on the "Eight Persons" has two meanings: first, it asserts that the Eight Persons are themselves the eight patiences (*kṣānti*); thus, they are called the "Path of Abandonment," which refers to the preceding fifteen moments of mind.
Furthermore, counting backward from below from the tenth Buddha-ground, one arrives at the stage of the eight persons (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi), which is precisely the eighth.
Regarding those who sever the distinct afflictions and so forth, this refers to the manifestation of the Middle Way through the destruction of non-existence in the first dwelling (prathama-vihāra).
If one considers it according to its name, in terms of its universal and perfect meaning, it is the stage of insight (darśana-bhūmi) of the eight persons.
The phrase "cultivating the path" refers to the partial realization of nirvana, which is attained by cultivating the path prior to abiding [in the fruit].
As for the mind being "purely dharma," this is because one naturally flows into it through the path of effortlessness; thus, there is nothing that is not dharma.

The ancient commentary provides two interpretations of the "two stages of the ancients": first, it correlates them with the three realms, taking the dhyāna of the desire realm as the first, the form realm as the second, and the formless realm as the third;

second, it correlates them with the four patiences (*kṣānti*), taking the combination of patience through suppression and patience through conformity as the first, patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas as the second, and patience regarding cessation as the third.
Regarding "distinguishing the latter by means of the former": by distinguishing the latter two bases (*niśraya*) through the first base, the *anāgāmin* is precisely the second.
Regarding "distinguishing the former by means of the latter" and so forth: the second [fruit] corresponds to the four bases, while the third corresponds to the three bases.
Following the minor examples cited from the Hīnayāna, such as the *Aśokarāja-sūtra*, which identifies Śāriputra as the second Buddha after the World-Honored One,
this person specifically refers to the second "person of reliance. However, the meaning already fully realized through the commentary master’s explanation is now complete and excellent.

With this limited perspective, I offer this brief assistance for interpretation: one should know that since the sutra text explicitly clarifies two types of reliance (*niśraya*), the fundamental stage (*mūla-bhūmi*) is taken as the first;
therefore, the third reliance excludes the fundamental reliance and becomes the second, while the fourth reliance becomes the third.
Since ancient times, the two masters from Hexi have repeatedly cited this meaning: that [the fourth] is named according to its cause upon the fruit;
thus, because it is attained by ascending from the third basis, the fourth is provisionally called the third. The same applies to the following two examples.
Master Guan, however, combined the four into three to interpret the scriptural passages in a circuitous manner.
Regarding the two types of persons—the ordinary and the noble: the "ordinary" refers to the first reliance (*āśraya*), and the "noble" refers to the second reliance.
As for "relying on the lower [stages] with increased intensity," this refers to the scriptural citations provided by the Master as a basis for contemplation.

Regarding "both being of functional application" (*yogakṣema*): these two are alike in that they have not yet exhausted the afflictions of desire and thought; thus, they are both termed "functional application. This concludes the third reliance.

To claim that being free from desire in the desire realm is called "effortless" (*anābhoga*) and that it should not be equated [with the fruit of non-returning] is precisely to refute the commentator; since the pervasive afflictions have already been refuted in the first basis (*āśraya*),
and one is still equal to an Arhat, how could one rely on the *Ekottarika-āgama* to explain the second basis as the actual practice of the first fruit and so forth?

Regarding the passage on "adventitious dust" (*āgantuka-rajas*) and so forth, Master Sengzong says: "The afflictions outside the triple world are 'old,' while the afflictions within the triple world are 'adventitious.
*Bùcáng* (不藏) is read with a level tone (*píngshēng*). The Sūtra states that 'true śarīra' is the Dharmakāya;
thus we know that the flesh and bones of the Nirmāṇakāya are called 'false śarīra.'"

The first part, "Flesh and Bone," explains how in the past he employed provisional means to conceal the ultimate truth; the second part, "Dharma," explains how now he reveals the ultimate truth by opening up the provisional.

The Sūtra states: "That which I call 'self' is precisely the false self; that which is called 'non-self' is precisely the Middle Way, the inconceivable emptiness, the self that is free from the two extremes."
The phrase "attaining bodhi before long" refers specifically to ultimate bodhi.
In the first section below, within the explanation of the characteristics of realization, the name "Arhat" is identified as containing three meanings.
If the fruit is lost, it is the meaning of non-arising; the rest is as in the text.

This is because it does not instruct Bodhisattvas to subdue [demons], for they are naturally able to realize that the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are of one suchness and without duality.

Regarding the meaning of the passage beginning with "I now do not rely on [the person]," it is intended to convey that if, as the Buddha previously taught, even Māra can manifest in the form of a Buddha, how much more so the case of the four reliances?
Therefore, since I now rely on the Dharma, what need is there to rely on these four persons?
Regarding the phrase "the facial features are full," the character *bù* (部) should be *fǔ* (輔). Later generations erroneously changed it to *bù*.

The *Zuozhuan* states: "The *fǔ* and the *chē* depend on each other; when the lips are gone, the teeth suffer. Former scholars explained that *fǔ* refers to the cheeks (*jiá-fǔ*) and *chē* refers to the jaw (*yá-chē*).
The *Zhouyi* says, "Its *fǔ*, cheeks, and tongue are moved. Kong Yingda remarked: "Both *fǔ* and cheeks are the flesh at the sides of the mouth."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states that this refers to the mark of broad jawbones (*pīnagaṇḍa*).
Regarding the scriptural instruction "you should examine," it means to examine according to the principles of the Hīnayāna dharma.

In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Four Noble Truths for the sake of Subhūti; he realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). After the Tathāgata had departed, Māra came to cause confusion and delusion, manifesting in the form of a Buddha.
He addressed the elder, saying: "I have taught you the Dharma, yet I have not exhausted the Four Truths; beyond them, there exists another truth, that of a divine self (ātman).
The elder investigated thoroughly but found no such principle. He then went to inform the Buddha, who immediately instructed him:
"If Māra manifests as a Buddha, you must examine him; once you have known him, you shall subdue him."
Cui Shiluo newly transcribes this as Jushiluo. First, regarding the term "ran" (然) in the question: "ran" signifies permission or assent.
Zhizhao issues an order that one should rely on the present teaching to employ actual wisdom and perfect faith.

Regarding the Buddha, we take him as the standard for Māra; since both the provisional and the ultimate teachings are spoken by the Buddha, one must still distinguish the provisional to believe in the ultimate—how much more so in the case of others, such as Māras and non-Buddhists?
Regarding "stealing dogs": "stealing" refers to a thief, and "dog" refers to a canine; these two things both prefer to enter people's houses secretly by taking advantage of the darkness.
As for the "five corpses," although no textual evidence has been seen, tradition transmits that they are a dead dog, a dead snake, a dead human, a dead pig, and a dead fox.
The five locations refer to the head and the two hands and two feet.

However, both the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu fǎzàng zhuàn) and the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra* state that three corpses were tied to his neck, rather than five being bound. Thus, the fifth fascicle of that sutra says:
"When Gupada preached the Dharma, the Māra King transformed himself into celestial maidens and performed heavenly music to distract the minds of those who had not yet attained the Way."

All were deluded and attached, such that not even a single person attained the Path. When Guptaka entered meditative concentration to observe, Māra immediately placed a flower garland upon Guptaka’s neck.
The Venerable One then perceived through his insight that this was the work of Māra and thought:
"Māra repeatedly ruins my preaching of the Dharma; why does the Buddha not subdue him? He observed that the Buddha’s original intention was to cause Guptaka to tame [Māra].
Upagupta then took three types of corpses—first, a dead snake; second, a dead dog; and third, a dead human—and transformed these three into flower garlands.
He went to the place where Māra was, and Māra immediately stretched out his head to receive the garlands.
Upagupta then tied the three corpses around Māra’s neck. Seeing the three corpses fastened about his neck, Māra spoke these words: "How can this be appropriate?"

"Are you seizing this corpse and placing it upon my neck? The Venerable One replied, "Just as a bhikṣu should not wear flower garlands yet you have worn them, so too do I know that you should not bind a corpse around your neck, yet I have bound it for you.

[The Māra] continued until, unable to release himself by his own power, he went to the Brahmā King to seek liberation. The Brahmā King answered, "He is the younger brother of the World-Honored One who possesses the Ten Powers."
The power of my strength is too weak to undo what you have done; I shall instead take refuge in Guptaka.
Guptaka said, “First, you must make a covenant with me, and then I shall release her. From this day forth until the end of the Dharma, I will no longer permit a woman to harass or disturb a bhikṣu.
Māra replied, “I shall accept your honorable instruction,” and even went so far as to manifest himself as a Buddha before Māra.
The Mara of the Body said, "In the past, I manifested in the form of a Buddha to deceive the elder Śūra; what I did then, I am doing for you now" (and so forth).
This is largely identical to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or the *Dharmakṣaya-piṭaka*).
The five impurities refer to the impurity of the seed and so forth, as listed in the *Śāstra on the Record of the Assembly*.
The five gates are the four truths of suffering and so forth, plus cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "if one can thus" in the Sūtra, it means that the Buddha has commanded one to examine Māra by relying upon the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
To approach *nirvāṇa*, why must one necessarily rely on others?
As for what is called "Great Parinirvāṇa," it is merely a case of clinging to the "emptiness of the void" (*śūnyatā*) of the past and designating it as "Great.
That the sutras are not necessarily trustworthy is because one fears that Māra may manifest as these four persons.

Although they are celestial beings, they possess bodies of flesh; thus, even if they have the divine eye that penetrates mountains, walls, and obstructions, they do not penetrate the principle of the nature of mind.
How does this differ from the ordinary person’s physical eye? For both fail to penetrate the principle.

Although he possesses flesh, he is a Buddha; for one who studies the Mahāyāna, although it is but the physical eye, because they have attained the wondrous principle, this very physical eye is the Buddha-eye.
Realizing that Māra is none other than the Buddha, and seeing that all marks whatsoever are entirely empty and illusory—one who contemplates in this manner cannot be harmed by Māra.
The commentary states that because śrāvakas have already attained the eye of wisdom (prajñā-cakṣus), they see only partial emptiness and do not see the Middle Way;

thus, their vision is no different from that of the divine or physical eyes, as it does not penetrate the ultimate principle. The scriptural text begins by citing the divine and physical eyes, then proceeds to explain the śrāvaka within the Buddhist context based on the teachings of the past;
one should not indiscriminately apply the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-yi).
Regarding the phrase "the brave and robust are like the Buddha-nature," the word "nature" (性) is superfluous; it should simply read "are like the Buddha.
This is because the Buddha is said to possess fearlessness, which is termed "brave and robust," and his ten powers that crush the heterodox are called "awe-inspiring and fierce."
The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are like a bow: for those of the lower vehicles practicing the path-factors, the foundations of mindfulness come first;

this is like how one who intends to shoot must first grasp the bow. The application of right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) should be likened to the time when it is drawn. The arising of the five spiritual faculties (*pañcendriya*) is like the release of an arrow.

Furthermore, because their roots are deep and difficult to uproot, they are also like arrows. Their movement and penetration in transforming sentient beings is like a spear piercing a person. When there is neglect or deficiency, a long hook should be used [to retrieve it].
This is analogous to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding "instructing and admonishing," one who upholds the precepts with rigorous defense has no fear of transgression.
Regarding "regarding others," this refers to what the Sūtra says about regarding humans and devas; through untainted samādhi, one treats heterodox and external paths as light and weak.
One who possesses the wisdom of instruction observes with true wisdom; this is called being courageous and robust.
Regarding "having passed through various weapons," the term *zhàng* (杖) is pronounced *zhì liàng fǎn* (直亮反); the *Zuozhuan* states: "He led the way, staff in hand and spear at the front."
The term "great calling" (*hù*) refers to calling out to what is empty; it is used here because one fears others and thus summons them—this "calling" (*hù*, level tone) is so named.
This is because, within the five truths (*pañca-satya*), apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), they all falsely conceptualize a divine self (*ātman*).
The sūtra passage regarding "not giving rise to sorrow or fear" is like the example of Surūpa examining the five bonds of Gopaka.
The sūtra passage regarding "inferiorly following the training of others" refers to those who, being inferior and cowardly, depend upon others to practice and maintain [skills] such as archery.
The internal reliance on the lower explanation refers to the second section, which interprets the scriptural passage on "not falling.
The external reliance on the Buddha’s power refers specifically to the scriptural passage beginning with "those who have already made offerings."
The Sūtra being like the power of that medicine means that by relying on the Sūtra to cultivate contemplation, one realizes that all things are merely mind;
thus, one does not fear various māras, just as medicine neutralizes poison. "Pie-è" (憋惡) is a dialectal term for "sple-miè" (脾滅); Guo Pu states it means "acute temperament."

Regarding the sūtras that mention "viewing with the eyes" and so forth, the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* states that there are four kinds of venomous nāgas: those that harm by viewing, by hissing, by sound, and by touch;
here, two are briefly cited.
As for those śrāvakas who are converted [by such means], examples include Ānanda being ensnared by Māra in this present sūtra and in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*. Sūtra.
The lions, tigers, leopards, and so forth are used as metaphors for the śrāvakas.

To "lose their lives" means that those of inferior capacity lose their roots of goodness in the Lesser Vehicle and are thereby converted; this is explained from the perspective of beginners. Question:

Previously, dragons were used as a metaphor for Māra, while lions and others were used as metaphors for the śrāvakas. Now, in the subduing of Māra, he is also subdued through the power of mantras. Why is this?

Regarding the statement that "the lion and others should be those who have subdued the śrāvakas," the answer is as follows: Having already been converted by the transformations of Māra, they were already subjects of Māra;
thus, through the power of Mahāyāna mantras, they are all made gentle and virtuous.

As for their returning to their original state and even generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), it is not merely a restoration of their former minor virtues, but also the generation of the Great Mind.
One who fears the deeds of Māra severs views, craving, and grasping; this is because one fears the Māra of afflictions, as the subsequent sūtra states:
"One gives rise to fear toward all afflictions. Abandoning birth-and-death to seek nirvāṇa is fearing the two māras of the aggregates and death.
Because one fears these three, one fears the Māra of devas.

That one experiences fear toward this sutra is the awakening of a great capacity; that one views the pit of the unconditioned with dread and delights in the level ground of the true mark is because they do not cling to the Small Vehicle and do not slander the Great Vehicle.
"At the time of his departure" means that at this very moment he has entered extinction; "afterwards, not at the proper time" refers to the era of the Buddha’s world.
Regarding "satiated with virtue," it means receiving the Dharma to achieve awakening, such that virtue becomes manifest and the Way is perfected—like being full or satiated.
In such an age, how could one rely on the four reliances? "No physician" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s extinction; "no medicine" is a metaphor for the decline of the Dharma.

Regarding the *saddharma*, *pratirūpaka-dharma*, and *paścima-dharma* (the True, Semblance, and Final Dharma periods): the True and Semblance periods each last one thousand years, while the Final Dharma period lasts ten thousand years; the meaning is as previously recorded.
The "beings of pure goodness" mentioned in the sutra refers to the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).
Although the various sutras present differing explanations, none of these divergent accounts exceed these five categories.
One interpretation states that the subsequent sequential listing arises from reconciling [the teachings] from below.

For those whose karmic conditions are profound, the periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) appear long; for those whose karmic conditions are thin, the periods of the True and Semblance Dharmas appear short.
According to the *Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra*, the ordination of women resulted in the extinction of the Dharma five hundred years early.
When the legal system enforces the Eightfold Respectful Precepts (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), the Dharma shall endure for another thousand years.
The *Upāli-rāja-sūtra* also states that Kṣemadatta thought to himself:
"Although I now behold the Dharma-body, I do not see the physical marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s form-body. There is a bhikṣuṇī, one hundred and twenty years of age, who ought to know it. Now...
When he was about to go and inquire, he sent a person ahead to announce his arrival. The nun then entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to observe him;
she knew that he wished to ask about events from the time of the Buddha. Having emerged from concentration, she filled her alms bowl with oil and placed it behind the door.

When the Venerable entered the room and pushed open the door, he did not notice that several drops of oil had spilled. After he had offered his greetings and requested a seat, she asked him about the days when the Buddha was still alive.
"How does your teaching of sentient beings compare to that of today? The nun asked, "Have you not heard of the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika)?

He replied, "They were coarse and violent men; what is there to say of them? The nun said, "Though they were coarse and violent, when the Buddha was present, he entered this room with them and never spilled so much as a single drop of oil.
It is clear that today’s arhats are no match for the group of six. Kuvula heard this.
Feeling deep shame, she said; the nun consoled her, saying: "Why do you grieve? On the first day after the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, things were not as they are now;

on the second day, they were worse; and by the third day, they had become even more degraded. How much more so today, over a hundred years later, when we are far removed from the time of the Sage—what is there to find strange in this?"
Regarding Upagupta’s inability to synthesize [the teachings], the postscript to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa compiled the Vinaya-piṭaka as the foundation of the Great Master’s school. Next came Ānanda, then Madhyāntika, and then Śāṇakavāsin;

all of them fully maintained the eighty thousand dharma-treasuries. However, although Upagupta was prophesied by the World-Honored One as a "Buddha without marks" (animitta-buddha), he did not possess [them].
Holding eighty thousand dharma-piṭakas, there subsequently arose five schools. First, the Dharmaguptaka was established as a separate school;
next, the Mahīśāsaka; then the Kāśyapīya; and finally the Sarvāstivāda.

As these five schools were established together, they vied with one another in confusion, each asserting their own doctrine to be the truth. At that time, King Aśoka said: "How can I now fathom this?"
Regarding this matter of right and wrong, he questioned the monks on how legal affairs within the Buddha-dharma should be decided. They all said, "The Dharma should follow the majority.
The King said, "If that is so, then let us cast lots to know which side is the majority. Thereupon, they cast the lots; those who took the side of the original assembly were by far the most numerous.
Because they were the majority, they were called the Mahāsāṃghika. "Mahāsāṃghika" means the Great Assembly. This...
By taking the Mūlasaṃghika as the fifth in contrast to the preceding four schools, there are five.

If one follows the account in the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, there is additionally the Bhadrāyaṇīya school; thus, with differing origins, these five schools together with the Mūlasaṃghika constitute six schools.
This occurred one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. As for the present mention of "one hundred and sixteen years," it is...

According to this, due to the discord with Mahādeva, they were divided into two schools. That is to say, although they had previously been divided into five schools, these were all sages whose principles remained harmonious, and thus they still shared a single recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
Subsequently, however, because of the conflict arising over the matter of Mahādeva, they split into two schools;

consequently, both the persons and the Dharma were divided. These six preceding schools are all termed the Sthavira (Elder) school (because they were the disciples who participated in the council held within the cave, and thus followed the Elder Kāśyapa).

Regarding the title: that which Mahādeva calculated was called the Mahāsāṃghika (the name "Mahāsāṃghika" was established because Mahādeva was a descendant of those who convened the council outside the cave).
The king who held the great assembly was King Aśoka. "Diluted" refers to thin, weak wine.

It should be known that Kāśyapa and Ānanda each [served for] twenty years; these two personally witnessed the Buddha’s transformations and practiced the Dharma in a manner resembling that of the Buddha, thereby causing the Dharma to flourish.
As for their being sixty years of age, this is because the Buddha remained in the world for fifty years.
Those who uphold the Teaching for forty years would then be one hundred and twenty years of age.
Beyond this or below this, according to the Sūtra, regarding the statement that [the Teaching] subsequently disappears, these are people for whom the beginning and end are not seen.
As for the eldest son of Kāśyapa, all the sūtras and Dharma were entrusted to him; his faculties were sharp and his wisdom was unlike those of others.

Regarding the "Buddha-awakened Samādhi" (佛覺三昧): this is simply the power of the Buddha’s awakening being added [to the practitioner], whereby they are called "Buddha-awakened" because they are like the Buddha. Because one attains this samādhi, one can personally hear [the teachings].
As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Ānanda collected the Dharma on the day [of the First Council]," and he himself said that it was at the beginning of the Buddha's [teaching].
When the Wheel of Dharma was turned, I did not see it at that time; thus I heard it through successive transmission.
The passage regarding those who eat only millet is a metaphor for the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), who praise only the Arhat as supreme.

The passage from "If such a person of merit... to "...does not hear" clarifies that Mahāyāna practitioners, from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* down to the present sutra, have never heard even the names of impermanence, suffering, and so forth.
Non-glutinous grain is used as a metaphor for the permanent because it is the constant food of worldly people.

Rock honey is used as a metaphor for the self (*ātman*); because the nature of rock honey becomes soft when encountering warmth and hard when encountering cold, its hardness and softness being subject to one's will, it is used as a metaphor for the self.
Seeking that which possesses existence refers to the five kinds of faults mentioned in the subsequent scripture, such as seeking gain and sustenance;
furthermore, those of inferior capacity who abandon birth-and-death to seek nirvana, or who depart from words and letters to seek liberation, are all termed "seeking existence."
"Carrying it down by means of a vehicle" refers to what the *Sūtra* itself states: "to carry this sūtra and deliver it to that place.
Since the "vehicle" here is simply a worldly carriage and does not refer to its symbolic significance, it belongs to the literal (factual) interpretation.
"Those who understand through the wisdom of skillful means" refers to those who, through subtle and ingenious metaphors, cause others to awaken to the Mahāyāna.

"Those who instruct them in the Great Practice" means that they instruct and admonish them with the three contemplations within a single mind, saying: "The practice you all undertake is the path of the bodhisattva."

To seek profit for those beings in the hells by exchanging the Dharma for wealth is the cause for the hells. To seek empty fame through flattery is the cause for belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

To rely on one's own understanding to despise others out of arrogance and self-satisfaction is the cause for being a *asura*. To desire that others depend upon oneself is the cause for belonging to the assembly of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
If one uses this sublime scripture to trade for other sutras—whether they be minor or non-Buddhist (heterodox)—it is not [the cause for liberation].
Because the liberation of karmic labor results only in eloquence and intelligence, it is the karma of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Regarding the previous four [categories], some say that "karma" refers to "existence" (*bhava*) when viewed from the perspective of the fruit, and "labor" (*karman*) when referred to from the perspective of the cause; because one performs labor, these two may be explained interchangeably.

This is intended as a message for future sages, who should deeply reflect upon themselves in propagating this scripture. What kind of existence-karma can enable one to leave behind the four miserable destinies (*caturgati*) and...
When non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) finally encounter the causes for Buddhahood, they may give rise to a mind directed toward it; they should simply reproach themselves.

Furthermore, these five faults are the causes for the nine realms (*navadhātu*), and the four destinies (*caturgati*) should be understood according to the text. External karma contains those five realms, because the phrasing of other sūtras applies universally to all teachings.
If one substitutes the sūtras on the wholesome karma of the precepts, they become the causes for humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva*); if one substitutes the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, then...
If the causes of the Two Vehicles involve easy expedients, then the Mahāyāna is simply the cause of Bodhisattvas; the Buddha Vehicle rejects them all, collectively naming them "external paths.
Question: Since there are five faults [in this view], why does the sutra speak of "immeasurable bodhisattvas"? Answer: In principle, they are indeed bodhisattvas;
it is just as when one generally refers to all sentient beings as "sons of the Buddha."
The king’s arrival at the deep mountain borrows upon the previous textual metaphor to establish the present meaning.
"The ground" refers to the ground as the basis; thus it is likened to principle (li), while the person who can traverse the ground is likened to practice (xing).

Regarding the remaining eighty years, there are two interpretations for the lower-level ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The first interpretation does not concern the duration of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), but rather takes it that when the True Dharma is about to end, eighty years still remain.
The second interpretation first establishes the duration of its extension or contraction.

Regarding the mention of "one thousand five hundred," this refers to differing accounts in the sutras: some say the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years, while others say it lasts for five hundred years.
As for "eighty years remaining before its extinction," whether it be one thousand or five hundred years, this refers to taking the remaining ten years of those who have not yet passed away.
Regarding the phrase "to distinguish the dark hairs" (*xuan hao*): "dark" (*xuan*) refers to black, and "hairs" (*hao*) refers to the autumn hair (the finest tip of a rabbit's fur).
This serves as a metaphor for the profound and subtle meanings of the deep sutras; like the hidden depth of black and the extreme minuteness of an autumn hair, they are difficult to discern.

Regarding the south-pointing chariot, the *Boluozhi* states that when the Yellow Emperor fought Chiyou at the wilds of Zhuolu, Chiyou created a mist extending for a hundred li, causing his soldiers to lose their sense of direction.
A wise man then constructed a south-pointing chariot, upon which he placed a wooden hand that always pointed toward the south.
The *Gujinzhu* states that it was made by the Duke of Zhou and was carried by the Yuchang people.
Returning to Funan, he now uses the four reliances (*catur-pratisaraṇa*) to proclaim the meaning of the sutras, shattering delusion and pointing toward enlightenment, just like that chariot.
Regarding the term "universe" (*yu-zhou*): the *Zuan-yao* states that "the four directions, above, and below are called *yu*; the past and the future are called *zhou*.
Some say heaven and earth constitute the universe; today we say that when [the truth] is divided and proclaimed and then unfolded, it fills the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
When rolled up, its existence or non-existence is unknown; it is only when unfolded and expounded that it is found to reside herein.

[The character] "cong" (叢) should be corrected to "zhi" (恉); according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to contemplate," being composed of the radical "heart" (心) and the phonetic "miao" (苗), with the pronunciation "caidong" (才冬).

It is also read as "xion" (囟). To write it as "cong" (悰) is likewise an error. For such a great responsibility, there are only those who are the honored and wondrous "Four Reliances" (catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāni).

Regarding the turbidity of life caused by the violation of precepts: because one breaks the precept against killing, one receives the retribution of a short lifespan; furthermore, during the final dharma age when lifespans are diminished, people do not uphold the precepts.
As for the five kinds of Dharma-preachers, they are combined into a single category, thus constituting five types in total.
Among the four great rivers, the largest is the Ganges; it is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* long, forty *li* wide at its broadest and ten *li* wide at its narrowest.
Measuring one cubit across, if one were to descend straight down to the mud, one would find ten thousand *hu* of sand. This sand is as fine as flour.
If one proceeds according to the practice, this refers to hearing [the teaching] without slandering it; such is the practice that is to be performed.

Regarding the difficulty of reaching the fourth *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-samā* [kalpas]: according to the judgment of the present Master, the three *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-samā* kalpas still pertain to the first reliance (*prathama-āśraya*), while only upon reaching the fourth *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-samā* kalpa does one enter the second reliance (*dvitīya-āśraya*).

This second reliance corresponds to the stage of the first *bhūmi*, where one first shatters ignorance (*avidyā*), transitions from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into that of a sage (*ārya*), and thus "attains liberation by departing from delusion.
As the subsequent scripture states: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate [enlightenment] are not two; these two minds—the former mind..."
The difficulty arises precisely because liberation is produced from delusion; this is why the four *anāgāmins* add only one part, while the five *anāgāmins* likewise rely on two bases.
Having already realized the Middle Way and entered the higher stages, they derive further liberation from their prior liberation rather than from further delusion;
because they possess true liberation, it is called "derived from liberation. This is the path of effortlessness (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga*).
Because they flow in naturally, they are eightfold superior; compared to the previous [stages], they are seven times easier to attain.

Regarding the "six constant [attainments]" and so forth, one should first ask: "If the five constant [attainments] already add four constant [attainments] as seven times [the former], why do the six constant [attainments] only add five constant [attainments] as four times, and so on up to the eight constant [attainments] which only add seven constant [attainments] as two times? Since these are all derived from that [same principle].
How could it be that the former is superior and the latter inferior? Therefore, the answer states: "It is even more profound and subtle, making it difficult.

This means that since the revealed principle is profound, the delusions become increasingly subtle; thus, understanding the meaning is difficult, and for this reason, they are half as numerous as the preceding category.
Regarding the analogy of serving those below versus those above, the difficulty or ease is as follows:
As for the *taishǒu* (Grand Marshal), the *Qí zhí yí* (Rituals of the Offices of Qi) states that the *taishǒu*, *sītú*, and *sīkōng* were all ancient offices.

Yìng Shào stated that one who secures those above from those below is called a *wèi* (Marshal). Yú Huàn stated that the *taishǒu* oversees military affairs; in antiquity, the officials of both the military and the judiciary were [designated by this title].

*Wei* was taken as the name for the *Taishouwei* (Grand Commandant). It signifies a net (*wei*); it refers to the military, the judiciary, and the nets used to ensnare the wicked and the non-conforming.

Furthermore, Ying Shao stated that it means "a multitude. The *Siming* (Minister of Education) is the one who presides over the multitude; it also means a hollow. "Hollow" (*kong*) and "presiding over the earth" (*zhu tu*) are synonymous.

In ancient times, people lived in caves; the one who presided over them would dig into the earth to create dwellings for the people. During the Sui and Tang dynasties, the positions of *Taishouwei*, *Siming*, and *Sikong* were all established.
Regarding the Three Ducal Ministers:
as for the Chancellor (Xiang-wei), Master Guan said, "The Yellow Emperor obtained six ministers and the world was governed; spiritual brilliance arrived. Yao obtained Shun;
Tang of Yin obtained Zhong Hui and Yi Yin; Gaozong obtained Fu Yue; Zhou possessed the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao; Qin..."
King Dao appointed Chancellor, dividing the office between Gan Mao and Chu Li Ji; King Zhuang of Qin appointed Lü Buwei;
the Second Emperor appointed Li Si and Zhao Gao; and Han Gaozu appointed Xiao He, who was later succeeded by Cao Can as Chancellor.
During the Later Han, the position of Chancellor was held by three imperial princesses, and it was restored during the Jian'an era.

The office of Chancellor (Chengxiang) was established during the Song dynasty, and the office of Chancellor (Xiangguo) was established during the Qi dynasty; the title of Chancellor was used as a posthumous honor during the Liang dynasty.
During the Sui dynasty, it was called the Grand Minister (Dazhongzai), and later the Palace Secretary (Neishi), also known as the Censor-in-Chief (Nayan).

Furthermore, other officials would concurrently manage state secrets, either presiding over administrative affairs or deliberating on matters of great importance concerning the military and the state; all such individuals were considered Chancellors. As stated in the "Table of Officials and High Ministers" (*Han shu Baiguan gongqing biao*):

Xiangguo (State Chancellor) or Xiangying (State Associate): "Cheng" means to succeed to; "xiang" means to assist. He presides over the affairs of state and assists the Son of Heaven in managing the myriad matters of governance.
Now, the office of Taishouwei (Grand Marshal) is one through which various posts may be reached, and thus it is easily replaced by the post of Chancellor.
Because the appointment is selected directly from the Emperor's own mind, it is difficult to find an analogy for it; the great principle of the law can be understood from this.

This remains difficult to understand; although the former masters have interpreted the text by means of its difficulties and ease, they did not definitively determine its position, and thus it is said to be "difficult.
However, if one uses the present clarification of the stages of the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) to judge this, it is also easy to understand.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The four reliances (*catvāraḥ pratisaraṇāḥ*)... and so forth: Xuanchao established the stage of the disciple prior to the first reliance, as clarified in the previous explanation of the title and the determination of stages.

The two schools following Kaishan both employ the four types of spiritual natures (*gotra*) to determine the stages; thus, the stage of the *śikṣamāṇa* (cultivated nature) corresponds to the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), and the stage of the *gotrabhū* (nature-born) corresponds to the ten... [stages].
The path of cultivation consists of the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dedication, and the ten holy stages;
the nine [stages] are merely the first three, as they belong to the stage of the worthy prior to the [first] ground, and thus are subsumed under the first reliance.

If one were to entirely lower [the standard], the Master now raises objections against the two schools. Within the text, there are two types of difficulties—both advancing and retreating—which first cite [the opponent's position].

Regarding that meaning, the sequence now presents a challenge: since the nine [constituents] are always present from the very beginning, and because the Sūtra cites sixteen parts as the ultimate limit of number, these constitute one *liǎojīn* (one "full pound").
This one *liǎojīn* serves as a metaphor for the ultimate fruit (*phala*), while the causal dharmas serve as the metaphor for the cause.
If you proceed to take the ultimate fruit as being like the one *liǎojīn*, then it would follow that those prior to the stages of the *bhūmi* are already the final culmination, because of that.
Since the first of the nine *nitya-sahagata* [stages] is the basis (*āśraya*), and this has already been finalized, what further dharma is revealed by the latter three bases?
One should state that it reaches the second, third, and fourth bases; two characters have been omitted from the text. If one says "reaching one *jin*," it refers back to that meaning:
namely, that regressing to take the first basis is like a metaphorical "one *jin*" [of gold]. This is because both schools equate the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) with the first basis.
Therefore, this is now raised as an objection:
"How does this relate to the Buddha-dharma? Furthermore, the Sūtra states, "Do not slander these dharmas," which specifically points to the fruition-virtue of *nirvāṇa*.
If this dharma is already established as being solely what is understood through the first reliance (*pratisaraṇa*), how does it relate to the Buddha-dharma of the fruit?
Now, to clarify the following, our Master’s interpretation takes the "one *jin*" as precisely a metaphor for the dharma of the fruit;
thus, the stages of partial realization attained through the four reliances are fully encompassed within the nine [stages] across the four positions.

Regarding the "one part and eight parts" as the two bases: since the established position is thus, if one were to explain its meaning, it would follow the traditional interpretation—namely, that [the factors] such as grasping (*upādāna*) arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, because the ancient masters did not clarify their respective positions, the Master of the Commentary (*Śāstrakāra*) criticized them, saying, "It remains difficult.

Thus, we know that the ancient interpretations are not entirely incorrect; it is only that the three interpretations of figures such as Xuanhui have completely lost the correct sequence of the stages.
The text states: Since the subsequent scripture clearly says "complete," how could this not mean the entirety of the sixteen divisions?

Because [the Bodhisattva] has already reached the limit of the ultimate fruit through the Ten Grounds and Equal Enlightenment, entering it in a single lifetime, it is called "complete. Therefore, only by now determining the stages can the intent of the scripture be fully understood.
That which occurred prior to Xilian was the stage of Principle-Identity (Liri) and the entry into the stage of Name (Mingzi). Question: Can a person at the stage of Name possibly harbor slander?
Answer: If the practice of contemplation has not yet been perfected, one may give rise to slander when encountering specific circumstances.
Regarding the phrase "its solitary rejection and opposition," the subsequent text states "the three evils. It is likely that the text here is abbreviated.
Following "lack of faith" (*aśraddhā*), there is a summary: the first evil is lack of faith in the Buddha, hence it is called "destroying joy";
the second evil is lack of faith in the Saṃgha, hence it is "abandoning the precepts"; the third evil is lack of faith in the Dharma, hence it is "rejecting the Mahāyāna."
Regarding "characteristics of slander": because these three are clearly distinguishable upon examination, they are called "characteristics.
The "wooden staff and banner" mentioned in the sutra is a metaphor for uselessness.
As for citing one side or the other: the sutra clarifies that regarding one's own practice, it is only by being fully endowed with immeasurable merit that one can believe this.

In this Mahāyāna [text], the increase of wholesome states already arisen is presented; the Sūtra clarifies that in transforming others, it says, "When that person has heard [the teaching], their past evil karma is eliminated," which presents the elimination of evil already arisen. Since there is the increase of wholesome states already arisen, there must be the production of those not yet arisen;
since there is the elimination of evil already arisen, there must be the non-arising of evil not yet arisen. Each of these presents one specific case.

Therefore, it is said that these are mentioned alternately; furthermore, one’s own practice both eliminates evil and clarifies the production of goodness, while transforming others both produces goodness and clarifies the elimination of evil—this too is an alternating presentation.
The character *chou* (讐) in the scripture should be read as *qi* (隙), with the phonetic components *qiu* (丘) and *ni* (逆); it means a fissure or gap (*xian*).
Regarding the analogy of those who have not yet received the precepts, the Sūtra states that they have not yet received the ten śrāmaṇera precepts.

A śrāmaṇera is so called because he "rests from evil and practices kindness" (śamatha-karuṇā). The definitions and characteristics of these ten precepts are as explained in the Commentary on the *Amitābha-sūtra*.
Those who first give rise to the aspiration as ordinary beings are likened to those who practice the contemplation of names through the absence of precepts;

those who have ascended to the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) are those for whom the names are distinct but the meaning is perfect, such that the Ten Grounds are identical to the Perfect Ten Abodes, and the Thirty Minds are likewise so.
Because it refers to the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), the expression "Ten Abodes" (*daśa-vihāra*) specifically points to the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa-bhūmi*) regarding the six faculties.
Although one has not yet descended to the five provisional grades (*pañca-prajñapti-pañca-vidha*), and although coarse defilements have not yet fallen away, they will fall away before long;
therefore, it is said that the stage ranks with the Ten Abodes. This is precisely the second [point]: explaining the semblance fruit within the cause.
The three retributions of the lower realms are the result of the evil of the upper realm; thus, in one sense, these are the three horizontal obstructions.
In terms of sequential priority, they are vertical: those who are close to Bodhi are those who have first established themselves in Bodhi.
To provide a warning for those who follow with faith, since their wholesome fruits are profound, one knows that the retribution for slanderers is likewise grave;
thus, the exhortation to cultivate merit and the warning against sin are both reflected herein.
What is meant by "field of consciousness"? It refers to recognizing the characteristics of these four individuals as being excellent fields of merit.
Since one who seizes what is light by means of what is heavy would even renounce their own life and limb, let alone material wealth,
