The middle passage states: "The Buddha-nature within the body" specifically refers to the principle within the three bodies that is realized through correct contemplation.

It is called "Buddha-nature" because those at the stage of the cause possess the nature of one who has attained the fruit; since they already possess the nature of the fruit, they are the Buddha-treasure.
Although this is not the Buddha associated with the eight marks, it is the Dharma-Buddha of the three virtues; therefore, it is said that "this is the Dharma."
As for the body:
those who can expound this Dharma are those who teach this Dharma of Buddha-nature to others;
those who can receive and uphold it are I myself and the assembly that receives the teaching.
He does not even use others as a comparison for himself; that which "returns to my own person" refers to what was said in the sutra:
"I shall also cause sentient beings to conceive the notion of building stupas and temples within my own body," and so forth.

The reason I did not dare to apply the analogy of the Three Jewels [to the three vehicles] was that I intended to convey that while the three vehicles are provisional (*upāya*) and the one vehicle is real (*tattva*), both the provisional and real teachings possess the Three Jewels;
yet, there is also the principle that in certain cases not even a single jewel exists. Therefore, I did not venture to use the Three Jewels as an analogy for the three vehicles and so forth.

Master Guan applied this analogy, which is elegant and appropriate, by taking the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), and essence (*svabhāva*) as being eternally different, thus constituting the "three."

Because those of the same essence are designated as different essences yet are unified as one, the convergence of the three refuges into one is established by analogy with the meaning of the vehicles.

As the subsequent scripture states: "If there are those who differentiate the three refuges, I shall act as their single place of refuge. Is this not indeed the convergence of the three refuges into one?

Regarding the explanation of the distinctions among the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha: this means that while the Three Jewels are conventionally distinguished based on the single principle of *dharmatā*, their ultimate destination is in fact that one principle.
To cite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as proof:
although the names "śrāvaka" and "arhat" were the same as in the former sense of the Small Vehicle, their meaning now returns to the Great [Vehicle]; therefore, it is said: [with this...]

The voice of the Buddha-way universally receives offerings because it realizes the Three Jewels; although their names are the same, the meanings of the Great and Small Vehicles differ, hence the commentary states "and so forth.
To act as one body for others means to explain what one has personally realized to others, causing them to awaken and enter [the path].
It is also said that "the entire body" refers to the fact that this single mind-nature possesses these three meanings without contradiction; this is precisely the meaning of "harmony."
Ordinary worldlings who are blind from birth are called "blind from birth" because they are born with blindness; this serves as a metaphor for those whose fundamental delusion is beginningless.

Those whose predispositions consist of practicing the Lesser Vehicle will, upon hearing of distinct characteristics, [accept them], yet if they hear of the identity of essence, they will slander the Great Vehicle and fall into suffering.

Those of the two vehicles who have attained the state of a noble one have already realized the limited principle; though they encounter rebukes and receive empowerments until they reach nirvana, they all ultimately converge upon the single reality.

In the parable, the general is used as a metaphor for the Great [Vehicle] of the same essence; if the "enabling cause" (pariniṣpatti-hetu) is being illustrated, it means that wisdom is able to remedy delusions, just as a general is able to break [the enemy].

The analogy for the direct cause (*hetu*) is that sentient beings and the Buddha share the same principle of the direct cause, just as a crown prince and a great king are fundamentally equal by nature.
The analogy for the conditions (*pratyaya*) is that merit can support wisdom, just as a minister assists [a ruler].
Next, regarding the assignment of metaphors according to the Three Jewels: the Crown Prince is the sovereign of the people, and the Dharma is the teacher of the Buddha;
because the Buddha can destroy Māra, he is metaphorically compared to a great general, and because the Saṅgha can assist the Buddha, they are compared to high ministers.
The establishment of the intent by the great general below clarifies that each possesses the three [jewels] individually to manifest their mutual fusion and establishment.

Regarding the term "Crown Prince" (*taizi*): according to Han regulations, the Son of Heaven is titled *Huangdi*, his legitimate heir is titled *Huangtaizi*, and the legitimate heir of a feudal prince (*zhuhouwang*) is titled *Shixi*.
Regarding the phrase "succeeding to the hegemonic enterprise" (*jibayehuo*):

in the *Guoyu*, it says that Jin was still the hegemon (*ba*), and Jia Gui explained that "hegemon" (*ba*) is equivalent to "to grasp" (*ba*); it means to grasp and maintain [the leadership] over the various states.
The authority of the feudal lords is that of the sovereign; the service of the ministers is the way of subjects.

The original texts of the Classics all speak of the "achievements of the Hegemon and the King," though some versions read "Emperor and King. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "The Emperor is he to whom the world conforms;
the King is he toward whom the world turns."

Regarding the other princes who rely on analogies and conditions: the myriad virtues are collectively accomplished through conditions that act as causes, just as the other princes rely [on their king].
What was said above—that "all the troops rely on me"—has the same meaning.
The Sūtra states that one should not give rise to an inferior mind; if the Prince’s mind is not inferior, he can succeed to the royal enterprise.
Only when one does not harbor small aspirations will one see the identity of essence (*tongti*).

As for the analogy of "approaching the King" mentioned previously, this refers to the two characters "like a king" (*ru wang*) in the Sūtra, which serves to conclude and clarify that the Prince is the successor.

The "King" in this position represents one who succeeds to the ancestral enterprise; furthermore, it is said that he is the Crown Prince. Thus, the *Śāstra* commentary states: "It is like a former king.
As for the "Prince" mentioned below, this refers to the other princes, who are likewise great ministers.

Since the great minister is used as an analogy for the causal condition (*pratyaya*), and that condition also possesses the three aspects, if one were to apply the three metaphors to the explanation of the Crown Prince, one should take his "occupying the correct position" as the essence (*ātman*) and his "diligence" as the cause (*hetu*).
The labor of the royal household and the entirety of the hundred officials are all employed through these three matters to correspond with the three causes;
as the Sūtra says, "the great ministers are also like this"—is this not what is meant? Thus, each opens up into nine times nine, yet they are simply the three expanded as previously recorded.
The three matters combined therein are precisely the Three Jewels.
This "staircase" (*tadeng*) refers to the high and low levels, which are like steps or a flight of stairs.

Establishing the resolute mind is like the decisive severance of a vajra blade. If one takes the hidden state as being of one essence with oneself and practices meditative cultivation, the realization of the fruit is not far off;
however, if one takes it as a separate entity, one falls into the partial and narrow, grasping at another.
If the Buddha is of one essence, what does that matter to oneself? If one can reflect inwardly, the hundred deliberations are of one accord;

thus it is said that one does not grasp at separate essences. Within these praises, it is solely because the principles of cause and effect are identical within the nature of concealment and manifestation that Kāśyapa praises both meanings simultaneously.
The profound and sharp wisdom is "profound" because it is perfectly consummate and "sharp" because it thoroughly eliminates delusions; it observes only one's own self, like that adamantine blade.
Third, as for the "perfect observation," once one has recognized that one's own body is the single essence of the Triple Gem, if one wishes to manifest this, one must...
Because it concerns contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), the preceding passage clarifies the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*).

Regarding "entering the treasury through contemplation," both the stage of partial truth (*bhūtatathatā*) and the ultimate stage are termed "entering the treasury"; furthermore, in relation to the beginner's mind, there is also the sense of "entering" by way of a semblance of contemplative practice.
"Thus, there is no cultivation of causes or progression toward fruits" refers to the two phrases "understanding the sūtras" and "practicing [the path]," and so forth.
"That which is neither existent nor non-existent" means that because it is not existent, it is neither self nor suffering; because it is not non-existent, cause and effect are not forgotten.

That which is oppressed by the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) is called the suffering of formations because it is characterized by constant flux and instability; yet ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) falsely reckon it to be pleasure.

Therefore, the Treatise says: "Just as one does not perceive a single eyelash when it is placed upon the palm, but perceives it as an extreme injury and a source of great unease when placed upon the eye's pupil—ordinary beings are like the palm of the hand, failing to perceive the eyelash of the suffering of formations."
Regarding "both eternal and annihilated," the three pairs in the text consist merely of the two positions of annihilation and eternity;

when these are combined with the arising of conceptual calculations, they constitute the third [position], and when they are neither of these two, they constitute the fourth. These four views all deviate from the Middle Way;
although the text lists only two, the intended meaning necessarily includes all four.
Regarding "seeing the faults of what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation," this means either seeing the faults in one's own practice or seeing the faults in the practice of others. Question:
How does one see these faults? Answer: To know that the denial of cause and effect is a fault to be abandoned through seeing, yet to instead further cling to permanence;
and to know that the notion of a self dwelling within the body is a fault of the view of permanence, yet to instead further cling to annihilationism.
Regarding "in order to seek trust" (*yǐqiúxìn*): the pronunciation of *xìn* is *shēn*. Whether it is written simply as *shēn* or as *shēn* (with the radical for "stretch"), both are incorrect.
The *Cuǎnwén* states that the people of Wu call the silkworm cocoon "bùqū" (the character *hé* is read as *gǔhé*). The *Fāngyán* states that the "chǐwò" (the inchworm) is also called "bùqū."
The phrase "not necessarily all so" means that it is not necessarily the case that all [insects] are transformations of mulberry branches; there are also those born from their own species.
To cite an example from the roots of the mulberry, the cicada and the glow-worm also have their own species—how could they all be transformations of roots and grass?

The transformation of the mulberry root into a cicada is not clearly documented in extant sources; however, the *Lunheng* by Wang Chong states: "The quail-cou (qichao) transforms into the fuyu, and the fuyu in turn... [transforms].
Regarding the "Cicada Rite," the *Liji* (Book of Rites) states: "In the month of late summer, decayed grass transforms into fireflies.
One version says: "An error should state that one who practices the remaining dharmas is what is called the Tathāgata’s secret [teaching], and so forth."
The Sūtra states that "permanence" (nitya) is a scribal error; since the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*) says there are "three pairs and six phrases," one should adopt this interpretation:
first, suffering as medicine; second, non-self as self; and third, impermanence as permanence.
Regarding "eternal" as a general designation: the four virtues are called "eternal" because they do not shift and do not change.
Regarding "we" as specific designations: this eternity possesses sovereignty and is specifically designated as "self"; this eternity is free from suffering and is specifically designated as "bliss";
this eternity is free from defilement and is specifically designated as "purity."

Regarding the ten thousand virtues of the Buddha-fruit, these ten thousand do not transcend the four [attributes]. Since they are all universally termed "constant" (*nitya*), the sutra text uses "constant" to replace "self" (*ātman*).
This "constant" is precisely the "self"; thus, while the name is "constant," the meaning is "self. Therefore, it can be paired with "non-self" (*anātman*) to form a dyad.
Both interpretations possess their respective meanings, so there is no need for rejection or selection between them.

He then pointed out: "The Tathāgata below is the secret treasury of persons; this Dharma is the secret treasury of dharmas. These constitute the general Three Jewels, and these constitute the specific Three Jewels.
Because they are fully endowed with the three virtues, they are called the 'secret treasury. To enter this secret treasury is called 'right liberation.
One should know that person and dharma are non-dual, and both are identical to the eternal and so forth."
"Only the True Dharma" refers to the concluding text that establishes the meaning, specifically indicating the Four Virtues, the Three Jewels,
and so forth as the True Dharma.
Regarding "the two extremes are the remainder," since the conclusion states that one is "far removed from the two extremes," it is known that everything outside of the Middle Way is [the remainder].

It is called "the remainder" (*śeṣa*). If so, why does the Sūtra speak of "cultivating the joy of other dharmas" and so forth? The answer is: this clarifies that the extremes are themselves the middle.

Therefore, regarding the cultivation of joy and the self in other dharmas, it is known that the concluding statement—“being far removed from the two extremes”—means that by realizing the extremes as the middle, one attains the state where the characteristics of extreme and non-extreme are absent;
thus, one obtains the name “far removed.”

Regarding the phrase "doubt as the ford to liberation" (*jie-jin*): "ford" (*jin*) refers to a crossing point; because doubt serves as the means for crossing over toward liberation, it is called the "ford to liberation. As the subsequent scripture states:
"If a person conceives a mind of doubt regarding this [teaching], they are still able to shatter the afflictions (*kleśa*), even if they are as vast as Mount Sumeru."
The Middle Way is easy to understand because it abandons expedient means through straightforwardness; thus, even the foolish can understand it.

As the subsequent passage of the sutra states, "remaining far removed from the two extremes" is precisely the meaning of being clear and easy to understand. If that is so, why was the Lesser Vehicle first bestowed if the Middle Way is easy to understand?

The answer is that when the capacities of sentient beings were immature, it was difficult [for them to grasp], whereas now that their capacities have matured, it is easy. What was previously [difficult] is now...
Because they are now matured, what was difficult in the past is now easy; this also expresses the intent of earnest exhortation.

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who possess delusions are called "fools," while those of the Two Vehicles who have realized the Truth are called "wise. By citing that even ordinary beings can attain understanding, one encourages the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, the Lesser Vehicle is generally referred to as "ordinary folly" because one enters the Great from the Small and realizes the Perfect together; thus it is said, "one does not doubt [the Lesser], let alone the names of the Perfect Teaching."

Are the five stages [of the *pañcavasthā*] considered the stage of one possessing wisdom? Furthermore, can it be said that those dwelling in the preparatory stages (*prayogabhūmi*) are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while those who have ascended to the formal stages (*bhūmi*) possess wisdom?
If one follows the intent regarding delusion, then as stated previously, doubt is the gateway to liberation; since there is no doubt, there is no liberation.
Is this not entirely and utterly a perversion of delusion?
The "discrimination of fools" refers to false conceptualization (*parikalpita*). The meaning of the sixth fascicle, part two, is the same as that of the first school.
Regarding "existence is non-existence" and so forth: this means that existence is the existence of non-existence, and non-existence is the non-existence of existence;

because pointing to non-existence is itself existence, it is called "non-existence above existence," and because pointing to existence is itself non-existence, it is called "existence above non-existence. Thus, existence speaks of non-existence, and non-existence speaks of existence.
Existence and non-existence are non-dual because they are both absent. It is like flowers in the sky; where the flowers are and where the sky is—how could these two be distinct?

Next, regarding "non-duality," the duality of existence and non-existence is precisely non-duality, which is the Middle Way. Although the previous section showed that existence and non-existence are mutually identical to indicate the Middle Way, this was still a form of relative opposition;
thus, it did not yet qualify as attaining the true Middle Way. Therefore, it is now clarified that whether it be the center or the extremes, both are...
One cannot clarify the meaning of the "Middle" by severing it from its correlative opposites.

Furthermore, the three lower unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are clarified as follows, according to the previously mentioned three aggregates (*rāśi*): namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-rāśi*), the aggregate of mind (*citta-rāśi*), and the aggregate of that which is neither form nor mind (*naiva-rūpa-nacitta-rāśi*).
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are likewise: water and earth are used as metaphors for existence, while wind and fire are used as metaphors for non-existence.

"All diseases" refers to the four hundred and four diseases; since one hundred and one diseases arise when even a single great element is out of harmony, the four great elements collectively possess four hundred and four diseases.
Water-diseases are cold diseases, and fire-medicines are hot medicines; fire-diseases are hot diseases, and water-medicines are [cold medicines].
"Cold medicines.
"The same applies to earth and wind" means that earth-related illnesses are treated with wind medicines, and wind-related illnesses are treated with earth medicines.

Abscesses, swellings, and tumors (gallstones/lumps) are disorders of the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) and should be dispersed with wind medicines; palpitations and restlessness are disorders of the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*).
For illnesses that should be suppressed by earth-medicines to open the orifices and eliminate stagnation, these are called wind-medicines,
for wind has movement as its nature; those that settle the heart and viscera and benefit the tendons and bones are called earth-medicines, for earth has stillness as its nature.
An unskilled physician is like an ordinary teacher who fails to discern the student's capacity and circumstances, instead adhering dogmatically to their own doctrines to instruct others;
because the Dharma does not accord with the student's capacity, this is called "erroneous instruction.

The first observable point is that the Sūtras compare the Tathāgata to a skilled physician, and the essence and characteristics of afflictions are compared to the imbalances of the four great elements.
That which has arisen is eliminated through severance, and that which has combined is dissolved through cessation.

As for what should not be clung to with attachment, it is called "attachment" because grasping at existence gives rise to delusion; since the wise have no such grasping, it is said that one "should not."
Regarding the charge that [the Buddha-nature] pervades the entire body: when it is currently functioning, one perceives its location, which is precisely the root-body (*indriya-śarīra*).
The deluded do not understand this; they seek the Buddha-nature and claim it resides within the root-body.
In the latter part of the *Shenzhong lun*, two characters—"two" and "cloud"—are missing.

The presence [of these characters] indicates their absence; thus, the essence of wondrous function is precisely true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the provisional is precisely within emptiness—the intent of this is clearly visible.
There is certainly nothing that contradicts reason, for all sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature; therefore, to say it does not exist is to contradict the correct principle.
As for the phrase "you wise people," it means that one should not cling to existence while claiming it does not exist, for to do so is false speech. This is because, although it exists...
While rational in nature, it is devoid of functional utility; it is manifestly beyond words and not a false appearance.
What is termed "emitting light," "shaking the earth," and the "interfusion of the primary and secondary realms" refers precisely to such functional utilities.
The first interpretation holds that silence is used here because there is no [substantial] matter to address.
The second interpretation holds that silence means having no response; its intent is to say:
"Since Buddha-nature already exists within your faculties, when we investigate and examine it within you, why is there no response?"

The Sūtra merely seeks that which understands the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. One who knows that the essence of the four gates is one—seeing the principle through the gate of causes—is said to have understood the true nature.

If one recognizes that what our school venerates as the primary and secondary teachings is the mind-only of the three truths in their harmonious identity, then why seek the true nature of all phenomena elsewhere?
Since emptiness and existence are non-dual, how could there be any dispute? The three truths are themselves the four gates.
The meaning is as previously explained.

Regarding the third point, it should simply state "the third concerns the absence of self" (*anātman*); one should consult the sutra to see that the character "self" (*ātman*) appears frequently there.

As for the comparative analysis of delusion and awakening: in the initial section concerning suffering (*duḥkha*), there is only delusion; however, it says "not knowing that the body possesses [suffering]."

The nature of pleasure consists in not knowing what is right; to know it correctly is itself liberation (*mukti*). In the remaining four passages, the distinction between the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the wise person (*jñānin*) constitutes the characteristics of delusion and liberation.
By this standard, the nine realms are called "delusion" and all are termed "ordinary persons"; only the Buddha-realm is "liberation," and only then is one called a "wise person.
The meaning of the six stages (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*) can likewise be understood through this. However, these five meanings are all [merely] provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

Because one speaks of suffering as suffering and so forth, even speaking of the non-illusory as illusory, it is necessary to first realize suffering and then joyfully realize that illusion is eternally abiding;
only then is one called a person of perfect and sudden wisdom. All others belonging to the three teachings are termed deluded.
"Movement and stillness" means that movement is coming and going, while stillness is eternally abiding.
This summary of the object and wisdom is because it simultaneously concludes the preceding two [aspects], and thus possesses both the observer and the observed.
The sutra clarifies non-duality by means of causes and conditions, stating that "their nature is non-dual" because the true nature follows conditions to manifest as dual phenomena;
yet, because it remains unchanging while following conditions, the true nature is always identical.
Thus, from ignorance (*avidyā*) to clarity, and from white to black, although they differ according to their phenomena, their underlying principle is one and the same.

Because those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) have attained full realization, they are called "wise" (*jñānin*); those of the three provisional teachings, as they turn their backs on reality, are all termed "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).

First, regarding the mention of "ignorance" (*avidyā*), one should have said "wisdom-ignorance," but the character for "wisdom" (*vidyā*) is omitted; this, together with the following two sections, forms three pairs.
Regarding the traditional interpretations, the exegeses of the latter two schools both deviate from the Buddha’s intent. In his *Beiyuan shu*, the first master explains the dual meaning as follows:

"The listing of the two names, 'illumination' (*vidyā*) and 'ignorance' (*avidyā*), shows that illumination is still a form of volitional formation (*saṃskāra*). Because illumination is superior within the category of formations, it is singled out to manifest its distinct characteristics in contrast to ignorance."

Second, regarding the practitioner: previously it was clarified that causes and conditions are the objects of contemplation; now it is clarified that the three types of cultivation are the means of contemplation.

When both the contemplation of the object and the contemplation itself are perfected, they both accord with true nature (*dharmatā*). Although the sutra text mentions only suffering and so forth, suffering necessarily implies pleasure, and even non-self implies self;
since these are established through mutual dependence, emotional perceptions (*saṃjñā*) become firmly attached. Therefore, it is said: [as follows].
Ordinary people say that because the two [aspects] are identical in essence upon perfect realization, they are "non-dual.
Regarding the statement in the sutra that even the Tathāgata’s secret treasury is impermanent, Bei Yuan says:

when followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle heard the teaching of impermanence in the former teachings, they concluded that everything from birth-and-death up to the secret treasury is entirely impermanent—those followers of the Two Vehicles...

Although it was not explicitly stated in the ancient teachings that the secret treasury (guhyakośa) exists, they nevertheless said that "all things are entirely impermanent" without making any distinction;
since the secret treasury is also included within the limit of "all things," one may say that the secret treasury is impermanent.

I maintain that Master Song’s learning was vast, yet his adherence to the view that the Buddha-nature is subject to flux—was this not precisely what he meant by saying the secret treasury is impermanent?
The *Sūtra Praised by the Buddha* states: "I and the nature of non-self are not two.

This serves as proof that the previously explained meaning of the three cultivations (*tri-bhāvanā*) encompasses both [self and non-self], and that here too, suffering and happiness, permanence and impermanence, should likewise be concluded; the Buddha’s words are thus presented in an abbreviated manner.

Regarding the passage from "Now, by me, in this [sūtra]... up to "...have all been explained": the preceding section establishes the principle that enables sentient beings to rely upon it and accomplish virtue;
therefore, it is called the *Sarvaguṇasampad-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Accomplishment of All Virtues). This is a term of praise.
It means that all the meanings contained within the Tathāgatagarbha have been fully expounded within this sūtra; hence, it is said that they "have all been explained."
Regarding the *Avavādakāśayasamcodanasūtra* (The Sūtra on the Non-dual Dharma): "Dharma" refers to the principle that is explained, while "sūtra" refers to the verbal teaching that explains it.

Since one must turn back from delusion toward the true essence, one must practice the principle; therefore, [the Buddha] first exhorts the upholding of the Dharma. However, this practice of the principle is not elucidated without the teaching; thus, he next exhorts the upholding of the sūtra.
Fearing that future generations might grasp the words while forgetting the principle, he presented the Dharma first and the sūtra afterward.

Regarding the analogy of the lamp wick, it is explained in the "Chapter on the Lamp Wick" that neither the preceding flame nor the succeeding flame can burn the wick, nor does the wick exist apart from them.
The ancients referred to the preceding and succeeding flames as "two," while the fact that the wick is not separate from them clarifies "non-duality";
therefore, the Buddha pointed this out.
"Although it is not definitive" means that although it is not [the final word], by clarifying that "I am non-existent" and that "self and non-self are non-dual," the fact that form,
mind, seeds, and wisdom are all empty is precisely the meaning of non-duality; there is no further distinction between this and the clarification of the nature of non-duality.
The term "non-attainment" (anupalabdhi) refers back to the Prajñāpāramitā’s elimination of all marks; this is precisely the meaning of non-duality indicated here.
Furthermore, the phrase "the two" refers below to the teaching in that sūtra that both the faculties and consciousnesses are empty—this is the meaning of non-duality.

That "all dharmas are thus" means that, taking the meaning of the faculties and consciousnesses as an illustration, they are empty within the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) among the three categories [of skandhas, āyatanas, and dhātus].

By this analogy, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and even the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are all subsumed within emptiness; this is identical to what this present sutra clarifies regarding the non-dual nature.
Since the Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom and all interpretations are without error, there is nothing to be refuted.
Next, regarding the analogy of the four flavors, this refers to what the Sūtra says: "up to and including *tīrāma* (ghee).

The phrase "up to and including" (*nai-zhì*) abbreviates the inclusion of curd (*dadhi*) and the two types of clarified butter (*sarpis*), as these can be understood by analogy with milk; thus, it is categorized as the analogy of the four flavors.
One should know that from curd, the production of clarified butter and so forth also possesses both the meanings of "is" and "is not."
These "gateways" (chapters) refer to conventional designations based on causes and conditions; thus, it establishes that curd arises from milk, as the Sūtra says:
"In this way, the nature of curd arises from milk.
These are all "negation gateways" (non-gateways), meaning that curd does not arise from itself, nor from another, as all four positions are refuted; therefore, they are called negation gateways.
The Sūtra asks, "Does [arising] proceed from self or from another? These two gates are established as a fundamental basis for refutation.

If the Sūtra were to address arising from another, it would cite alternative views—such as the claim that water and so forth constitute the "other"—and one can understand the refutation by taking these as the objects of opposition.

Regarding the sūtra, if [the curd] were produced from itself, this raises a divergent view: namely, the calculation that the nature of curd already exists within the milk beforehand, and thus produces the subsequent curd.
"Produced from itself" (svayam-utpanna) refers, in the first instance, to a singular phenomenon; that is, the nature [of the curd] is inherently present within the milk from the very beginning.
Since curd is not produced from milk alone, one asks: "With what does it continue?

Now, seeing that curd resembles milk and continues from subsequent milk, and since it both resembles and continues [its source], it is clear that it is not produced from itself; thus, we know that the claim of "self-production" is merely a provisional expression.

If it were the case that the five flavors arise simultaneously, then if one were to say that the nature of curd already exists within milk as its self-arising essence, it would follow that the natures of the two types of ghee and clarified butter (māṇḍa) must also already exist therein; thus, all five flavors should manifest at once.
Why, then, do the five flavors arise in a sequential manner?

The inability to transform itself is explained below as arising through dependent conditions: since milk is sweet while curd is sour, and because the sweetness of the milk is superseded [by the sourness], it does not transform by itself;
rather, it requires the causal conditions of boiling and processing before it becomes curd.
Regarding those who raise objections to this discussion: below, Kāśyapa correctly challenges the notion that there is the nature of curd within milk.

However, since the Buddha has already refuted such attachment, he now speaks only by way of conventional designation; yet, fearing that the ignorant might still give rise to attachment, Kāśyapa further challenges him below.
That "knots" are the causes and conditions means that the cow is the cause and water and grass are the conditions; the milk having sweetness or bitterness is the dharma produced.
To transform evil into good is precisely to receive the teachings of humans and devas, as in the *Tie-wei jing*.

Those who receive the Great Teaching (Mahāyāna) receive both the Common and Distinct [teachings], while those who receive the Small [Teaching] receive the Tripitaka Teaching; this sutra, however, belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Vairocana-yāna).
Although the preceding sections are not without the Perfect and Sudden, they are not called "pure" because they are interspersed with other elements;
since this sutra reveals and clarifies the biased and small teachings to reveal the eternal, its perfection within these sections transcends the preceding teachings.

Regarding the passage stating that there are no fruits for śrāvakas, devas, or humans, the Sūtra clarifies five colors corresponding to the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*). Although the commentary (*śāstra*) preserves a brief account, one should understand them as follows:
the Bodhisattva is like white, the Pratyekabuddha like yellow, the Śrāvaka like red, the Deva like blue, and the Human like black.

This uses the brightness or darkness of these colors as a metaphor for the relative superiority or inferiority of the five fruits. However, the category of "Bodhisattva" encompasses all three [vehicles]; if they are expanded, [the classification becomes more detailed].

It is established that there are seven [vehicles], yet now there is only the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna); because there are no five fruits, it is said that "one purely attains [the fruit]," and so forth. As for the phrase "the text and meaning are perfectly clear":

when an ox eats water and grass, whether sweet or bitter, all belongs to the stage of Principle (li-ji); when the ox eats fatty and rich food, this is named the three stages of Equality (pingdeng-san-ji) and so on;
and when the clarified butter (ghṛta) emerges, this refers to the Stage of Manifesting the Fruit (fen-guo) and the Ultimate Fruit (ji-guo). The intent is to point out these six [stages].
The phrase "thus, following the sequence of stages to clarify the meaning of the text" is followed by the annotation "and so forth.

The passage from "grains, grasses, and weeds" (至) to "the differences in color and flavor" serves as a summary of the preceding text. The distinction between grains and grasses is a metaphor for the difference between the partial (p’ien) and the perfect (yüan) teachings.
The Sūtra clarifies that regarding the causes and conditions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and wisdom: when the conditions of ignorance are defiled, the characteristics of the nine realms arise;
when the conditions of wisdom are pure, the characteristics of the Buddha-realm arise. Thus, these two aspects—defilement and purity—are also the two aspects of delusion and awakening.
The *Sūtra on the Non-Duality of the Two* (the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*) shows below that ignorance is itself enlightenment and has no separate essence.
Those who find this view shallow or superficial claim that transforming evil into good is a matter common to humans and devas;

they argue that because it does not sever [delusion] and cannot be equated with the proximate realization of the Lesser Vehicle, they do not accept it. Instead, they explain "non-existence" (*amala*) through the Mahāyāna concept of the "conditions" and "causes" (*pratyaya* and *hetu*), whereby delusion is transformed into awakening.
To clarify the transformation,
only one example is cited; however, since grass and milk are listed together, it should be stated in full that there must also be milk within the curd.
"To explain by way of understanding" means to explain by way of worldly reasoning. It does not mean "to stir with a substance";
rather, one must stir with the hand. The character for *láo* (勞) in the sutra text is written with the radical for "wine" (*yǒu*), which is also pronounced *láo*.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Láo is the dregs of fermented juice; it is wine. The commentary (*shū*) says, "It is not the name of a type of wine," but this remains unclear.
Its meaning is as follows: "jiù" (救) with the *qiū* (酉) radical is pronounced "xiào" (孝), referring to wine yeast (*jiǔjiào*). It is used for brewing wine.

Regarding the analysis of the meanings of "opening" (*kāi*), "turning" (*zhuǎn*), and "severance" (*duàn*): "kāi" should actually be the character "guān" (關); it is an error to interpret it as having two meanings.
"Duàn" means differentiation; "zhuǎn" means roundness (*yuán*). This is as previously explained regarding the transformation of ignorance into clarity.

The sutra states that ignorance (*avidyā*) and clarity (*vidyā*) are the true nature (*dharmatā*) itself, which, according to conditions, transforms and constructs the ten realms; this is briefly as recorded previously.

One knows that because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is ignorance, it is said to coexist with all fetters (*saṃyojana*); and because it is the nature of phenomena that constitutes ignorance, it is said to coexist with wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
These wholesome dharmas are precisely the conditions for teaching and practice. Since the ten realms are one mind, they possess no dualistic characteristics.
Regarding the "four types of elephants" and so forth: first, the *padma* elephant; second, the *utpala* elephant; third, the *kumuda* elephant;
and fourth, the *puṇḍarīka* elephant. These are named because these various flowers arise when they hear thunder.
The "increase of the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) refers to the process of progressing through the stages (*bhūmi*) and attaining realization, which is termed "increase.

The phrase "pervading all sentient beings" does not exceed the nine realms; that is, it encompasses the six classes of ordinary beings, the fleshly eyes of devas, the two types of eyes of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, and the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), and the Buddha-eye of Bodhisattvas.
Among these, the four eyes belonging to the nine realms are entirely characterized by ignorance and thus do not see.
The Buddha-nature is likened to the blind.
As for the term "the common people" (*bǎixìng*), the *Báihùtōng* states: "Surname" (*xìng*) means "birth"; it is that which people receive from the heavenly breath so as to be born.
Why does the surname have "a hundred" (*bǎi*)? It is because in ancient times the sages blew the pitch-pipes to determine surnames in order to record them.
The clansmen combine the five constants to produce sound, which possesses five tones: gong, shang, jiao, zhi, and yu. These rotate and intermingle;
through five sets of five, making twenty-five variations, they further generate the four seasons. Thus, there are a hundred distinct forms.
"Attaining" (zào yì) means to arrive at or reach [the goal].

Regarding the "first teaching of one finger": traditionally, that which was taught prior to the twelve years [of the Lotus Sūtra] is called the first teaching; because it spoke only of existence with signs (sanimitta), it is likened to one finger.
Next, because it discussed signlessness (animitta), it is compared to two fingers. Finally, because it clarifies the meaning of eternal abiding (nitya), it corresponds to the third.

The analogy of the three fingers is used to clarify that patience does not refer to the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), because such quiescent extinction resides in the fruit [of the path].
Here, it is explained that the following section generally rebukes various masters for contradicting the scriptures and violating reason.

The single finger pointing downward correctly demonstrates the present meaning: entering the Truth (the True Aspect) without seeing is the realm of the Two Vehicles; not seeing the provisional is the realm of the Bodhisattvas.
Since even the Sages do not see it, how much less so the six classes of ordinary beings? The three fingers seeing slightly corresponds precisely to the Buddha-realm.

Since this is discussed according to the Perfect Teaching, there are various levels of "seeing" such as names and so forth; however, here we speak of the "partial truth," and thus the stages of the Grounds and Abodes are cited.
Since all the śrāvakas have attained realization and entered [the path], the textual divisions of the sūtra should treat "furthermore using two fingers" as a single phrase;

this is because it follows from what precedes. Thus, the sūtra text is abbreviated for conciseness, and the explanation of the meaning of the three finger-demonstrations belongs to the subsequent phrase.
*Jinbi* (pronounced *bī*): a small adze; it refers to the blade used for cutting through the film [of cataracts]. Master Ying states:
"According to Xun Kai’s *Gao You Wenzi*, the character should be written as *bì* with the phonetic *fāng xī*; the frequent use of *bó* in the canonical texts is merely a phonetic loan."
"Even after immeasurable bodhisattvas [have practiced] they are still unable to see," etc., refers to the bodhisattvas of the three previous teachings who fully practice the six pāramitās;

because they are those who have briefly attained penetration among the śrāvaka- and pratyekabuddha-bodhisattvas (the *zàng* [piṭaka] bodhisattvas), it says "even up to. The "ten abodes" (*daśabhūmi*) refers to the stage prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*);

thus, the persons of the three vehicles have all not yet seen their nature, and they alike undergo the cycle of birth and death through both the segmented (*prādeśika*) and the transformative (*pariṇāmika*) realms.
There is no confusion caused by a self.
Thus, for a bodhisattva who has ascended to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as described in the sūtras, there is no separate essence between the abider and the stage upon which they abide.

Regarding the nine subsequent analogies that may be investigated: at first glance, the text appears to correspond to the ten vehicles of meaning. First, "deciding the cataract to see the finger" is a metaphor for the three truths;
thus, contemplating the inconceivable realm means that the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the middle.

Next, observing the geese and wild geese in the empty sky from afar is a metaphor for the arousal of the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). Observing that the ignorance within the empty sky is the consciousness of the *dharmatā*—
that these very delusions are wisdom, that birth itself is extinction, and that the two aspirations consist of seeking supreme enlightenment above while necessarily transforming those below—
is precisely what constitutes the arousal of the great vow.

To perceive things vaguely and to claim that one’s vision is not clear or precise is like the three analogies of a drunken man traveling a long road. Ignorance remaining in its entirety is like the drunken man;

possessing two feet is like employing tranquil illumination (*jìzhào*) to practice in accordance with the principle of Buddha-nature; and traversing the distant path with those two feet is precisely this.
This is skillfully establishing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

The four similes are as follows: being driven by thirst while traveling through a vast wilderness represents the arising of delusion and attachment; being like a thirsty person seeking water represents the production of birth, death, and suffering;
knowing that delusion and attachment are erroneous is like the thirsty traveler turning back to reflect; and by contemplating with a single mind, one universally destroys the three delusions.
Realizing the Buddha-nature is like traveling everywhere in search of water; the three delusions are like the thicket of trees; and the three wisdoms are like the white herons.

Because the wisdom is inherent within the delusions, it is like the trees having the herons. Now, just as the herons originally dwell in the water, if the fruit-wisdom (果智) were in accord with the principle, it would be like the herons being in the trees.

This represents the causal wisdom (因智) residing within the delusions. When the attachment to delusion is heavy, it is like being dazed and confused, mistaking the false for the true—just as mistaking the trees [for the herons].
Regarding water, it is said that one cannot distinguish whether this is a tree or water; thus, one must discipline the mind through correct contemplation and diligent effort without slackening.

If one contemplates truthfully and does not cease, eventually delusion and wisdom will be realized as they truly are, and one will see the crane and the water—this is the "pervasive breaking of phenomena" (*dharmaparyāpti*).

The fifth analogy, regarding seeing a great ship from afar across the ocean: birth and death are like the ocean, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like the ship. Within this nature of phenomena...
When the open becomes obstructed and attached to—such as when one forms the thought, "Is this a watchtower?

or "Is this empty space?"—and after gazing for a long time, a mind of certainty arises, this is precisely the breaking of the obstruction to allow it to become open; this is what is meant by "knowing the penetration and obstruction.
As for the "great ship," according to the *Bai Cang*, it refers to a large vessel. A "large" ship is twenty zhang in length and can carry six or seven hundred people.
The "person" refers to this:
the six similes [illustrate] being born into the lineage of the Buddha as one who is weak like a prince; observing the subtle with a beginner's mind is like being weak;

to fully cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) within the ordinary mind is like playing throughout the night—this simile illustrates the harmonious adjustment of the factors of enlightenment.
*Yenuo*: "Nuo" (懦) has the phonetic component *nu* and the radical *ke*.

It also means weak. The seven parables concern officials returning home; being shrouded by ignorance is like being constrained by royal affairs. Observing the mind afflicted by defilements is like the principle of Buddha-nature.
Being pressed to return home at night is like the power of right observation being slight, as it is dark at night. Without observation, one must practice provisionally.

Contemplating phenomena (śubhānupaśyanā) serves as an aid to manifest the sublime principle; because one employs the contemplation of phenomena for a brief duration—like using a flash of lightning—the text says "temporarily manifested.

Just as an ox is capable of pulling heavy loads, so too is wisdom capable of guiding conduct; because the cause aids in the manifestation of wisdom, it is said "due to seeing the ox. The accumulation of afflictions obscuring the principle is metaphorically likened to being shrouded by clouds;

when these very afflictions become wisdom, it is like giving rise to the perception of an ox. This is precisely what is meant by "the aid of counteractive measures (pratipakṣa) in opening [the path]."

The eighth analogy concerns dust and insects: observing the precepts is likened to practicing contemplative cultivation; ignorance is like the dust, while the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is like the insect.

Since the essence of principle and delusion are identical, they are as difficult to distinguish as dust and insects; yet, by means of practice traversing the stages (*bhūmi*), there are degrees of depth and shallowness. This clearly elucidates the sequence of the stages.

The ninth analogy concerns seeing from a distance in the midst of darkness: this refers to those at the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*) who contemplate the principle of the dharma-nature within ignorance, like seeing a small child from afar.
Because the stage of contemplative practice is remote from the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), it is called "seeing from a distance.

The ox and bird represent objects that are contrary to one's nature, while the person represents objects that accord with one's nature; this is based on external factors of contrariety and conformity. Furthermore, the form of the ox is the largest, representing ignorance.
Human forms are next to oxen, while bird forms are as small as dust motes; these are the smallest. This is categorized according to internal opposition and compliance.
Through patience (*kṣānti*), one practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); thus, one endures both internal and external opposition and compliance.
Although one sees a small child, this immediately reveals the nature of reality (dharmatā) through its violation and compliance.

The tenth [analogy], "seeing a painted image in the dark," illustrates the stage of semblance (sādṛśya-avasthā), wherein there is no craving for dharmas; because ignorance still remains, it is called "night darkness.
It is said to be near the stage of partial truth (vibhāga-satya), not far from it. Seeing the image of a Bodhisattva is like true understanding; seeing the image of a deva is like semblance.
[The Master] explained:

"The meaning is that when one regards what appears to be a Bodhisattva image as being merely a semblance of understanding, one ceases to give rise to attachment toward it and enters the stage of 'partial truth' (*bhūta-ābhimukha*).

However, regarding these ten vehicles in relation to the three types of faculties: those of superior faculty contemplate only the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) and thereby directly penetrate the signless (*animitta*)."

When the various marks appear clearly, one enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), or for those of intermediate faculties among the ordinary beings (both internal and external), they reach it at the seventh stage;

for those of dull faculties, they must complete all ten. Although the scriptural texts all refer to "Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages," this is because they enter directly into the stage of partial truth (*viśuddha-satya*) by practicing each individual contemplation.
It is from the perspective of the ultimate fruit that the Buddha describes them as "not yet clear" and so forth in various passages.

Question: The preceding sutra states that even those in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) have not yet been able to see [the Buddha]; why, then, do the current analogies speak of "seeing a little" and so forth? Answer: The previous mention of the "tenth stage" refers to the period prior to hearing the Perfect Sutra—that is, the ten stages of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*). As for the current references to "seeing," they refer to all [stages] from the first stage onward. Thus, while the former passage speaks of "not seeing" based on the Distinct Teaching, the latter speaks of "seeing" based on the Perfect Teaching. This is because the Distinct Teaching posits that one does not see the Buddha until the tenth stage, whereas the Perfect Teaching asserts that one sees the Buddha from the very first stage. Therefore, there is no contradiction between these two statements. Furthermore, the term "seeing" here does not mean seeing with the physical eyes; rather, it means seeing through the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which is the true seeing. It is like the analogy of a person born blind who cannot see the sun, moon, or stars, yet upon being cured of their blindness, suddenly perceives them all. In this way, the analogy of "seeing a little" and so forth is established. Consequently, the meaning of the sutra is clear: although the Distinct Teaching says one does not see until the tenth stage, the Perfect Teaching says one sees from the first stage onward. This is the intended meaning of the scripture. Furthermore, the term "seeing" used here is synonymous with the term "attaining" (*prāpti*); thus, it is said that one attains the Buddha’s body from the first stage onward. This is the definitive conclusion. Moreover, the term "seeing" here is also synonymous with "entering"; thus, it is said that one enters the Buddha’s body from the first stage onward. This is the definitive conclusion. Furthermore, the term "seeing" here is also synonymous with "realizing" (*sākṣātkriyā*); thus, it is said that one realizes the Buddha’s body from the first stage onward. This is the definitive conclusion. Now, the *Ten Contemplations* (Shi guan) of this school is the essential pivot for entering the Way, and it accords with the present text like two halves of a tally.

Therefore, one must rely on this to develop understanding and rely on that to practice. For this reason, one should always apply one's attention to the practice gates of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* hereafter.
Question: How is it that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are the practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet one must rely on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* for understanding and cultivation?
Answer: The flavor of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is the same; though the sections differ, there is no distinction in their interpretation or practice.

Thus, the *Yìlì* (Exemplary Meanings) clarifies that the textual meaning of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* ultimately converges upon these two sūtras: first, relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to manifest the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*); second, relying on... [text fragment ends].
Since *nirvāṇa* manifests permanence, how much more so when [the teachings] have already been opened and unified? Thus, all sutras collectively constitute wondrous practice.

While the ritual procedures (*śīla-vinaya*) of the various sutras differ slightly, their principle-contemplation (*li-guan*) is without distinction. It is my hope that future students will apply themselves with greater diligence.
Question: Regarding these ten analogies set against the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*), is this based on a received tradition, or is it a mere conjecture?
This constitutes the response, which is precisely the intention of Jingxi. Thus, Master Man’s *Ji* states: "These ten analogies follow a similar pattern;
their textual content is identical in meaning to the 'Ten Dharmas that Form a Vehicle' in the *Zhiguan*.

Venerable Miaole spoke of them only briefly, while Masters Man and Xian each provided detailed expositions in their respective *Ji*, yet neither has fully exhausted the excellence of the meaning. In my current interpretation, one should perhaps select from among these.
It is well to follow this.
Regarding the four instances of praise and censure: these refer to praising the Tathāgata and censuring the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, those with discernment understand that this is not the consciousness of the two locations—emptiness and consciousness—but rather a subtle consciousness.

As for the presence of perception, it is not the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), nor is it the non-perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
rather, there is a subtle perception. Since this is what is taught in the Hīnayāna, the Sūtra says that it accords with the sūtras.

Ordinary beings within the principle refer to those who, according to the Perfect Teaching, are ordinary beings both internally and externally; because they are ordinary beings within the family of partial realization of the sages, they are called "sage-ordinary-beings.
The prince is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva, just as Śākyamuni was formerly one of the sixteen princes during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
To preach the Dharma of the Perfect Vehicle for those sentient beings is precisely like the mutual response and connection of the past,
such as the coming and going between friends.
The phrase "taking me into one's body" refers to clinging to a false self.
"Those who have not yet realized through vision" refers to those at that time who receive the Dharma but have merely entered the five stages of the name-stage;

these are solely cases of hearing and seeing, rather than the stage of semblance-realization or partial true-realization. If one enters the stage of semblance-realization, one no longer undergoes transmigration.

The Bodhisattva withdraws his response because the conditions [for it] have ceased; thus he withdraws his response from these sentient beings who have regressed from their understanding of the provisional names and, being attached to the five sensory objects, wander through birth and death.
Those who claim for themselves that they possess a self engage in false conceptualization of a distorted self.
"Naiyan" (寱言) means to speak while dreaming; the *Tongshu Wen* states that speaking in one's dreams is called "naiyan.
Regarding the reading "chan" (讇) in older editions, Master Ying says: "According to various dictionaries, the character 'chan' is identical to 'chan' (諂), meaning sycophantic speech."
Furthermore, regarding the character *zhì* (囈): this refers to false speech, hence it is called *zhì*.
The *Jīngdàngchù* (經摚觸) [reads] *zhǒu gēng fǎn* (紂庚反); the *Shuōwén* (說文) states that *zhàng* (摚) means "a pillar," while the *Cuǎnwén* (纂文) says *zhàng* (摚) means "to touch."
"In my treasury there is no such sword" means that within the treasury of the emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there is no "my sword" of heterodoxy.
As for the five expedient means, they consist of the four foundations of mindfulness together with the four roots of goodness, making five.
"Destroying the views of self and other" means destroying the false views of a self held by sentient beings during the stages of the true and the semblance.
Regarding "sentient beings facing the first fruit and so forth": the sentient beings with false views of a self are those to be transformed, like subjects;
the first fruit and so forth are the transformers, like rulers. The "five aggregates" refers to the five *skandhas*.
Those who have previously received this Dharma are those who in the past received the Mahāyāna teaching on the True Self.

"Wisdom through hearing" refers to the wisdom of names and words; "wisdom through reflection" refers to the five stages (*pañca-varga*); and "wisdom through cultivation" refers to the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
In both cases, one must not engage in contemplative cultivation because, although the Mahāyāna was heard in the past, it remained merely at the stage of names;
since the great elements (mahābhūta) were suppressed and there was only erroneous understanding, it is said to be "like the horns of a ram."

For example, one who is compassionate may transform those capable of only minor fruition, yet fail to discern their great potential; out of pity for their false views, they are said to be "compassionate and sorrowful.
Because these individuals' capacities are not yet fit to be broken from such false calculations, the transformation is temporarily suspended.
Regarding those who previously escaped [to attain Buddhahood], such as Śākyamuni, he ceased his bodhisattva transformation during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;

now that the capacities of beings have matured, he has returned to achieve Buddhahood and deliver them. This clarifies that the aforementioned teaching on the transformation of śrāvakas refers to the period between the end of the Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū kalpa and the present day, situated between these two pillars.
"Time-periods" (*shishu*; *shu* is pronounced in the departing tone) means "several days," hence it is called "time-periods. Three, four, and five are all referred to as "numbers" (*shu*).

As for "only clarifying [the teaching of] non-self and so forth": when the Buddha appeared in the world, he first used the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) teaching of non-self at the Deer Park to break [the grasping of self].
That "false self" was subsequently refuted and washed away; now, having reached Nirvana, one again awakens to the true self.
The present text is abbreviated and clarifies only the absence of self; the subsequent corresponding passage will fully encompass both meanings.

Regarding the statement that "the *upapāduka* (or *utpala*) deity is black," this refers to the calculation of outsiders (*bāhyaka*) who maintain that the four elements, the deities, and the self (*ātman*) each possess distinct natures, with varying degrees of nobility and baseness.

When the Sūtra says, "one does not see [their] marks," it means one does not perceive the principle of the non-self and true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Hīnayāna. As for the preceding... [text continues].
The statement "it clarifies only non-self" refers precisely to this passage.

There is one excellent sword because the true self is non-dual; it is "excellent" because it is free from the evil of the two extremes of existence and non-existence. It is called a "sword" because it is capable of destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"In the scriptures of the teaching of non-self within my own treasury, there is no such sword" refers to the previous analogy,
meaning that one does not see the true characteristic of my sword.

"But its meaning exists" means that in the Tathāgata’s method of transformation— first small and later great— the clear exposition of the initial small [vehicle] already contains the complete meaning of the later [great vehicle].
"Great!
As for what follows below, the preceding question concerned whether it is not a sage but an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who gives rise to the false self; now, the conclusion states:
'If there is an ordinary person, then this ordinary person is able to know the true self. The previous commentary explained the question by distinguishing between two types of ordinary persons."
This is indeed the intent.

Each character remains upon paper and ink so that it may not perish; by means of this imperishability, one may use it as a metaphor for the eternal.

This subsequently concludes the meaning by contrasting it with the half-letter.

"To be without obstruction and without attachment regarding all dharmas" means that which is free from dependence; that neither the partial nor the full exists is the meaning of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

He said, "The King wishes to leave the household life. My teacher is titled Buddha, one who has awakened to all things.
Now that he has accepted the invitation from the Lord of Devas to take a meal, he will return and bestow the precepts upon the King, the ministers, and the rest all at once. The *Liezi* states:
Formerly, the Grand Chancellor Pi of the state of Shang asked Confucius, "Are you, Master, a sage? Confucius replied, "I am merely one of broad knowledge and strong memory; I am not a sage."
The man asked again, "Were the Three Kings sages? He replied, "The Three Kings were skilled at employing wisdom and courage;
as for their being sages, that is beyond what I know. He asked again, "Were the Five Emperors sages? He replied, "The Five Emperors were skilled at employing benevolence and trustworthiness;

as for their being sages, that too is beyond what I know. He asked again, "Were the Three Sovereigns sages? He replied, "The Three Sovereigns were skilled at employing the opportune moment; as for their being sages—"
"Nor is this something I know. The Grand Chancellor was greatly startled and asked, "In that case, who then is the sage?
The Master moved his countenance and spoke, saying, "I have heard that in the West there is a Great Sage who does not govern yet is not in disorder;

he does not speak yet is trusted; he does not transform others yet they act spontaneously. Vast and expansive! The people are unable to give him a name. Based on these various texts, it is clear that...

The relationship between Confucius and Laozi as teacher and disciple is clearly evidenced by their relation to Śākyamuni. When Zhang Zhan annotated the *Liezi*, he provided convoluted interpretations of the words of the Western Sage;
though he claimed they were not those of the Buddha, how could one who wishes to exalt the Way avoid insulting the words of others?

Regarding the citations from the *Qingjing faxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Pure Dharma) in your commentary: is it an authentic translation, or is it suspected to be apocryphal? Answer: Tiantai.

The wise realize that one who dwells in the five stages of practice (*pañca-viśuddhi-bhūmi*) relies upon the first [refuge]. Regarding the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, all of these works cite it;
however, if there are errors or corruptions therein, they should not be cited. Therefore, the "Chapter on the Four Reliances" states:
"If these four persons were to say that what was spoken by the Buddha was not spoken by the Buddha, such a thing is impossible. For this reason, I declare that these four persons are..."
Because it is the basis for the world, Jingxi (Zhiyi) says: "According to various catalogs, this sutra is generally ranked among the suspicious and spurious;
yet since its text and meaning are correct, it may have been lost during translation. This is also the intention of what our own school cites regarding the *Xiǎngfǎ juéyí* and the *Miàoshèngdìng*.
For instance, the latter part of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was originally included in the list of spurious works until it was rectified during the Great Tang dynasty.

When entering the authentic scriptures, how can one simply dismiss them as spurious because people of the time have not yet reached a decision? The Great Master personally realized that his rank was in the first stage of reliance;
it should not be applied erroneously. If one were to harmonize this according to the following [passage]: [text follows].
Since the terminology of the non-Buddhists who claim [these teachings] as their own is actually a theft of the legacy of the former Buddhas,
Śākyamuni now claims them back, stating that they are all the Buddha’s words and not the words of the non-Buddhists.

Those who bestow through skillful means are the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body; concealing their true reality (*tathatā*) and manifesting provisional means (*upāya*), they appear in the bodies of non-Buddhists to preach their respective teachings, gradually inducing and leading them forward.
Therefore, it is said they "bestow. Now, the Buddha reveals his original nature; thus it is said that "all are the Buddha's teaching," and so forth.
If one opens up the lower [level], then one meets the convergence of phenomena with principle, saying: "This is what the Buddha taught.

One knows that the teachings on the great and small, as well as the scriptures of the inner and outer paths, all arise through the transformation of the mind; their very substance is the mind itself. That the mind is the Three Truths applies equally to all transformations.
Yangzi already knew that "words are the sounds of the mind" and "writings are the paintings of the mind"; although his words are mundane, they can serve as an analogy for this.

Yuan, you should know that when the contemplation of the mind is deviant and transgressive, heterodox teachings arise; by receiving these teachings, one establishes the causes and effects of the six destinies.
When the contemplation of the mind is true and correct, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings arise;

when contemplating the mind as empty, the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teachings arise, and by receiving these teachings, one establishes the causes and effects of the two vehicles. When contemplating the mind as provisional, the sequential (Distinct) teaching arises, and by receiving this teaching...
Thus, when one contemplates the mind as the Middle Way within the cause-and-effect of the Bodhisattva, the Perfect and Sudden Teaching arises; by receiving this teaching, one attains Buddhahood.

Furthermore, when contemplating the mind through the cause-and-effect of the Buddha-realm, there arise the teachings of gradual emptiness—contemplating the mind as empty—and both gradual and non-gradual contemplations of the mind.

These various Mahayana and Hinayana teachings arise solely because all teachings are inherently contained within the principle (*li*); they manifest according to the conditions of one's contemplation of the mind.

Because it is through this that [awakening] is initiated, one contemplates what arises and sees only the inherent principle (*li*). As the Sūtra says, "All are the Buddha's teachings"—the meaning lies precisely here.

Since it points to the single suchness (*tathatā*) of the mind-nature and states that all verbal expressions are the principle, we know that when the Sūtra says "all are the Buddha's teachings," this does not refer to the Tathāgata’s recognition of them as his own, nor is it a provisional bestowal;
it is a direct pointing to the essence of the principle itself, declaring it to be the Buddha.
Regarding the statement "it is said," the commentary notes:

"The basis of the principles of letters" means that the principles of the *half-syllables* (*ardhamātrā*) of the Hīnayāna serve as the basis for the principles of the *full-syllables* (*pūrṇamātrā*) of the Mahāyāna.
Because one enters the Great Vehicle by way of the Small Vehicle, this is identical to the preceding passage which first teaches the half-syllables and subsequently teaches the *vyākaraṇa*.
This is the *Luo-lun* (Treatise on Letters).
To specifically clarify the root of letters, the *Siddham* chapter is called "the root" because it explains the generation of sounds;
the remaining chapters, which fully explain the constituent characters, are called "complete. Furthermore, twelve of the chapters are all termed "half," while the rest [are termed "complete"].

The sūtras, śāstras, and treatises are established for the sake of completeness; it is only through these thirty-six phonemes that various characters arise, and thus the sūtras and śāstras come into being.
Since the sūtras state that one "upholds all śāstras and treatises," this clarifies that the "half-letters" (*ardha-kṣara*) are the basis of the śāstras and treatises.
Therefore, it is said that the fundamental nature of letters is explained separately; as the subsequent sūtra states: "For this reason, the half-letters [are the basis] among all sūtras."
The *Śāstra* (Treatise) regards literary composition as its fundamental basis.
Regarding those who have attained realization of the "Full Dharma" (*pūrṇa-dharma*), the Sūtra states: "Thereafter, one is able to know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma;

that which is Dharma is 'full,' while that which is non-Dharma is 'half. Therefore, the subsequent Sūtra says: "The half-syllables are all the root of afflictive speech, whereas the full-syllables..."
This is the very foundation of the language of all wholesome dharmas;
it is because the Tathāgata, by means of the "half" and "full" [teachings] of the mundane world, reveals the supramundane Dharma, leading from the small to the great.
"Following the sounds according to the letters" means that the twelve vowels enter into the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka* and *kha*.
"Following the letters according to the sounds" means that the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka* and *kha* follow the twelve vowels beginning with *a*.
Zhezhou says: "Among the chapters on Sanskrit phonology, there are twelve vowels; the *Siddham* chapter is considered the first, and within it..."
Altogether there are fifty-two characters; two *siddham* characters constitute the general title of the chapter, while the remainder constitute the body of the chapter.
These are what are called "A, Ā," and so on, up to "Lu, Lū. In the original foreign pronunciation, these are named *iṭ*, *li*, *bā*, *li*, and *tā*.
This is the first chapter. Within this chapter, from "Ka" and "Kha" onwards, there are thirty-four characters which constitute the primary phonetic forms.
The first twelve characters are the "generative" (janman) syllables, and the final four characters at the end of the chapter are the "invocatory" (āhvāna) phonemes.

When invoking the initial twelve [syllables] and the subsequent "generative" syllables such as Ka and so forth, there are both single and compound invocations. Regarding the single invocations, one relies on the two sounds indicated by the latter four [characters].
As for the compound invocations, one employs the two sounds "E" and "Li" from the latter [set], namely "E-ka-li. In both the single and compound invocations, [the procedure is] as follows:
Because there are distinctions between long and short vowels, there are four primary tones; when combined with the preceding and following [consonants], there are sixteen sounds.
Although the sutra speaks of fourteen sounds, this is because the latter two among the first twelve are auxiliary sounds (*anunāsika*) rather than primary tones, and thus these two are excluded.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of *dan* (single) or *chan-ju* (combined with *chan*), the character for *chan-yi* (chan-robes) in the *Dan-li-ji* (Book of Rites) follows the initial radical of "clothing" (*yi*). Below, various [explanations] are set forth.

The Master’s alternative interpretation of this passage is as follows: since these are Sanskrit verses, the teachers of this land were unfamiliar with that language, which led them to produce various explanations based on their own subjective sentiments.

Furthermore, Yijing’s *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) explains the phonetics and characters in great detail; I shall not trouble to cite it here for fear of confusing later students.
It suffices to have a rough understanding of the general principles so as to recognize what they signify. One should know that the Buddha cited the original Sanskrit characters.
The intent is to use this analogy to manifest that the Buddha-nature is all-pervasive. If one understands this principle, the meaning of the sutra becomes clear;

if one is muddled regarding its essence, disciples will merely split the sounds and characters. I entrust this to those who lecture: you may only provide a general explanation of the text, but you must not engage in forced interpretation.
Regarding the statement that "these are the fourteen vowels," although the sūtra lists fourteen, when explained by enumerating their names, there are only twelve;
consequently, various masters differ in how they interpret the meaning.
As for the fourth interpretation, the "single" [vowels], it simply adds to the previous twelve to complete the number fourteen.
Regarding the second interpretation of "repetition" (*fù*): this refers to taking the latter thirty-four characters and overlapping them so that they together form fourteen;
hence it is called "repetition.

As for the phrase "two characters are missing in the text," etc., this is based on the *Ruiying Benqi Jing* (Sutra of the Auspicious Response of the Prince's Past Deeds), which clarifies that the Prince rode a goat-drawn carriage to enter the schoolhouse to study.
When this was written, the original manuscript was missing two characters; the master did not understand them and instead questioned the Crown Prince about them.
This Master Ying stated that these two characters are the residual sounds (*yúshēng*) of the preceding *è* and *ā*.
If they were not residual sounds, then not all characters would be fully accounted for; therefore, he took these two characters again to complete them.
Exhausting the limits of words,
the *Jīngxià Kāishàn* school cites the text as proof: since the pronunciation "páo" correctly corresponds to the tenth [vowel], and it concludes with fourteen [vowels],
we know that the final two remaining sounds are not included.
Furthermore, taking the four subsequent vowels to supplement the preceding ten makes fourteen.
"Inserting them into the center" means that the four subsequent vowels are inserted among the ten vowels;
specifically, the letter *a* directly indicates the place of insertion, which is between the first six and the last four.
"A-ā" refers to the short *a* and the long *ā*; "i-ī" and "u-ū" are likewise so; these are the first six phonemes.
"Va-va" and so forth are the latter four phonemes. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the two phonemes *o* and *au*.

Regarding the statement that the first twelve constitute six phonemes: this means that "short *a*" and "long *ā*" constitute one phoneme, continuing in this manner until "*am*" and "*aḥ*" constitute one phoneme.
Regarding the subsequent five groups of five: this refers to selecting twenty-five characters from among the final thirty-four characters, with five characters forming each group.
When taken as a single sound, there are five sounds; together with the previous six and the upper [sound], they form eleven sounds.
Regarding the "three by three pairs," since the remaining vehicles consist of nine characters, it says "three by three.
However, only four characters are taken to constitute one sound to complete the preceding count; the remaining five characters then belong to the "slow" (chí) sound.
When the lower part of the character was missing from the manuscript, he cited the *Ruiying* [Sutra] to resolve it. Regarding the general name for *siddham*, it is as explained previously.
As for the fact that the Yecheng [edition] was also damaged, it was likewise because the characters were incomplete in their phonetic values.
