Regarding the phrase "a partial meaning" (片意) followed by "notes saying 'and so forth'": this is a detailed explanation of the twenty-five dharmas found within the "Excellence of Practice" (行妙) section of the *Fahua xuanyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
Now, based on that text, I shall briefly indicate their names and meanings.
Regarding the Sutra on the Stainless Samādhi: Hell is the place of retribution for heavy defilements;

the causes of retribution are "defilements," namely the defilement of evil karma, the defilement of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), the defilement of *paryavasthāna*, and the defilement of ignorance (*avidyā*). These are termed "sufferings and calamities.

The Bodhisattva first perceives these faults and, in order to destroy all defilements, cultivates the fundamental precepts clarified previously to destroy the defilement of evil karma, and cultivates [the subsequent practices] as before.
The concentrations such as the *pratisamvid* (liberations) explained previously suppress the defilements of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) through cultivation;

the wisdom of arising and ceasing and the wisdom of non-arising explained previously destroy the defilements of views and afflictions through cultivation; the immeasurable wisdom explained previously destroys the defilements of *pāṣa* (dust-like ignorance);

and the unconditioned wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-prajñā*) explained previously destroys the defilement of ignorance (*avidyā*). These are called the merits of the fundamental dharma, for the three delusions have been destroyed.
The three truths are manifested as the Samādhi of Stainless Purity; this constitutes the completion of the practice of these names.
When the Bodhisattva personally destroys the various defilements of the hells, every phrase contains vows of compassion.

If there are sentient beings in those hells who possess the karmic conditions for responding to compassion, he proceeds to meet them through the power of the King Samādhi, remaining unmoved within the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and causes the multitude to... [return to purity].
To destroy these three defilements upon arising is called "compassion destroying existence" (*bhava*). The following twenty-four instances can be understood by analogy with this.
Furthermore, this has been explained here according to the gradual sequence; thus, within each individual state of existence, the three delusions are each destroyed.

If one speaks in terms of the perfect and sudden teaching, the three delusions are subsumed within a single mind without exception. When the single mind is destroyed, all states of existence are simultaneously destroyed. Twenty.
The five kinds are non-differentiated yet differentiated; as previously recorded, they do not regress from the sūtras.
Regarding those who delight in the mind, because hungry ghosts (preta) suffer much, one overcomes them by means of mental delight.
Regarding those who delight in joy, because asuras (asura) are full of suspicion and fear, one overcomes them by means of joy.
The passages concerning the sun and moon are as previously recorded.

Regarding the passage on "hot flames," this refers to the northern regions where the ground is shrouded in shadow and ice remains frozen and difficult to melt; it serves as a metaphor for the northern continent (Uttarakuru), which clings to the notion of non-self.
Since there is no way to dissolve such clinging without the fire of knowledge and the flames of wisdom, the "hot flames" are employed to break through it.

Regarding the *Sūtra on Being Like an Illusion*: because the retributions in the Southern Continent of Jambudvīpa are mixed and lifespans are indefinite—just like magical illusions—it is refuted by means of "being like an illusion.
Regarding the *Sūtra on Being Immovable*: because the Four Heavenly Kings protect their realms and traverse the worlds, it is refuted by means of "being immovable."

As for those who are difficult to subdue, the Heaven of the Thirty-three is the pinnacle of the earth-dwelling heavens; because the three delusions of retributive fruition are difficult to subdue there,
[the Buddha] uses that which is difficult to subdue to overcome them.
Regarding "pleasing" (*manojña*): because the gods in this realm find pleasure in the absence of battle with asuras in the sky, they destroy [the asuras] by means of what is pleasing.
Regarding "blue-colored" (*nīla*): the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states that the karmic retribution of these gods consists of blue palaces, garments, and articles of enjoyment.
Because it is blue, it is refuted by the "blue of the ultimate sense," which is not blue.

The same logic applies to yellow, red, and white; these are all results of karmic retribution, and the samādhis of white and so forth should be understood as examples analogous to the samādhi of blue.
Regarding the "Sūtra on the Various": because the Brahmā King presides over a great trichiliocosm where the types of beings are manifold, he employs the "Various" to dismantle them.

Regarding the "Sūtra on the Pairs": the second dhyāna alone possesses the factors of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) and joy (*prīti*); as these two constitute a pair and the other factors are shared with the other dhyānas, he employs the "Pairs" to dismantle them.

Regarding "passing through the thunderous sound": this dhyāna-joy is so profound that it is like fish in ice or hibernating insects; therefore, the thunderous sound is used to startle and awaken them in order to break [the state of stagnation].
Regarding "passing through the falling rain": the fourth dhyāna is like the great earth, which possesses the seeds of all roots of goodness; only when it receives rain do they sprout.
Therefore, the sūtra uses the pouring of rain to break it down.
Regarding the sūtra’s comparison to space: because non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize nirvāṇa as being non-empty, the sūtra uses the analogy of space to break that down.

Regarding the sūtra’s comparison to a mirror: although those in the superior untainted heavens have attained pure form, they have not yet exhausted the emptiness of form; thus, they are like a mirror that has not yet [attained its ultimate clarity].

The "extremely bright" refers to the state where the form has not yet appeared, like a mirror that has no reflection; the "form within the unknown" refers to the state where one has not yet mastered the clarity of the mirror.
Therefore, one uses the act of looking into the mirror to break through it.

Regarding the "unimpeded" mentioned in the Sūtra, this refers to the gods who have attained the ability to exit the "cage of form"—that is, their karmic retribution is unimpeded—but this is not yet the unimpededness of the Three Truths.
Because it is obstructive, one uses non-obstruction to refute it. Regarding "permanence," it is as previously noted.
Regarding "pleasure" in the sūtra, because these gods are like those who are deluded and because they are [ultimately] suffering, one uses pleasure to refute [the notion of their suffering].
Those who have passed through my [teachings] consider the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to be *nirvāṇa*, yet because they still possess subtle afflictions and lack mastery,
[the Buddha] uses mastery to refute this.
The initial general statement regarding birth in various places refers to what the Sūtra calls "birth in whatever place one desires," which corresponds to the capacities of those to be converted.

Regarding the phrase "should be born in the ten realms," although the term "places of birth" does not explicitly list the ten realms, the general intent encompasses them because it does not discuss specific names and characteristics;
thus, it is called "birth in the general sense.
Next, regarding the "specific birth," within the ten realms, the hells are first explained as an illustration for the remaining nine, thereby revealing their specific names and characteristics.
Therefore, it is called "distinct arising.

Regarding the destruction of Mount Sumeru, the first [of the three sections] within the "Summary of Merit" and "Manifestation of Power and Function" concerns the subsuming of worlds by the environment and its inhabitants;
the second concerns the dispersal and reintegration of self and others throughout the ten directions; and the third concerns the few and the many.
The Sūtra says that "dividing one into many and combining many into one" is called "dispersing and uniting.
As for "being unstained," this refers to what the Sūtra says: "although performing such [actions], the mind has no attachment."

The function of taking birth in the lower realms of wandering existence is precisely the function of the stages (bhūmi). By means of being unstained and free from suffering, it manifests the function of fearlessness.
Regarding the phrase "the lower serves as a comparison for the high": "the lower" refers to the Bodhisattvas, while "the high" refers to the Buddhas.
Question: Regarding the intent of this inquiry from below: since these bodhisattvas have already entered this stage, their functions should be equal;

for what reason does the sutra clarify that the bodhisattvas differ in their relative status? For instance, when the Bodhisattva Anantagātra arrived, all these bodhisattvas were struck with trembling;
is this not due to differences in the power and function of their realizations?

The phrase "the former says 'the answer below explains that they are equal within the middle'" means that since the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) are equal and their dwelling grounds (*bhūmi*) are also equal—if both are in the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*), for instance—their functions are entirely identical; thus, they are all the same without distinction.

Regarding "equality within inequality": although they are equally designated as being within the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), they are called "unequal" because the first and second grounds differ in their levels of depth and profundity.
Therefore, the functions of the profound stages cannot be fathomed by those at the shallow stages.
If one discusses the "horizontal" (paryāya) perspective according to Xinghuang, then all merits are equal; this differs from the meaning of "equality within equality" mentioned previously.
Here, they are considered equal because a single stage possesses the qualities of all stages. Previously, they were considered equal based on the alignment of positions.
Vertically, however, this is not equal to the previous "equality within equality," though their meanings are somewhat similar.
It is also like a single object: first, taking up a metaphor to overturn [the previous position], as in "a single stage possessing all stages";
second, lifting it up, as in "the distinction between high and low positions. Since both explanations are essential, I employ them here.

"Vigor" (*vega*) refers to external application, which is the exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). "Virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to internal realization, which is the realization of the three virtues within.
Since great external function necessarily arises from internal virtue, they are called "vigor and virtue. This constitutes a general praise of the accomplishment of both the internal and external;
the mention of "supernatural powers" specifically praises the external application.
A mother can give birth to a child because she gives rise to wisdom by receiving instruction; thus, the Buddha is like the child.

Since the King of the Pitakas (Kṣemendra) praised [the Buddha] below in terms of "noble conduct" (*ārya-caryā*), which constitutes his own practice (*sva-caryā*), whereas the two types of conduct for the sick child pertain to the transformation of others (*parārtha-caryā*), he caused the King of the Pitakas to offer praise specifically regarding the Buddha's own practice.

Regarding the statement that other sutras cannot serve as analogies for this sutra and so forth: it is because prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, the partial and the perfect were separated;
consequently, their merits could not equal those of this sutra.
Regarding the analogy of the five-period teachings, beginning with the Āgamas and ending with the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, these constitute the five periods.
Traditionally, the *Avataṃsaka* was classified as "Sudden," while the five periods were categorized as "Gradual"; consequently, the *Avataṃsaka* was placed outside the framework of the five periods.
Furthermore, as for the statement that the *Prajñāpāramitā* precedes the *Vaipulya*, this is a misinterpretation resulting from the following:

because the twelve divisions of the teachings were said to have emerged from the Buddha as the *Āgamas*, and seeing that the *Vaipulya* was placed third, one then paired the *Tala* (i.e., the *Madhyama*) with the *Prajñāpāramitā*, thereby placing it before the *Vaipulya*.
Moreover, failing to realize that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the present sutra share the same flavor, one has failed to synthesize their textual content.

Emerging [from that state], one forcefully employs Prajñā to counter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; consequently, the teachings of this single lifetime—the great purport of this sūtra—become inconsistent and divergent.
Regarding the term *dharmapada* (法本): because in ancient translations *sūtra* was rendered as *dharmapada*, and because wisdom (*prajñā*) guides practice.

It is said that the movement of clouds fundamentally arises from wisdom; thus, movement is also called the "fundamental of movement. Since the meaning of "fundamental" is the same as "knowing," this knowing is *prajñā*.
Great Wisdom (*mahāmaitrī*), this is *prajñā*, for *prajñā* is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*).
Furthermore, it is said that the following section is the sequential explanation by Kaishan. The *Zhizhi jing* states: "Prajñā is the teaching of signlessness. Regarding the phrase "beginning at...
and so forth, this clarifies that Prajñā is precisely present at the initial stage; as the sutra says, "From the Buddha emerge the twelve divisions [of the canon].
Therefore, it is said that during the twelve years of the latter part, it borders upon Nirvāṇa; thus the sutra says, "From Prajñā... and so on.
If it is argued that they have emerged from *nirvāṇa*, this matter will be refuted later.
Regarding the citation of the "Ultimate Chapter" (*Paryavasāna-parivarta*) as proof, the *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 95, further states:
"Subhūti, having heard in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that even a small amount of merit performed toward the Buddha—even down to a single instance of 'Namo Buddhāya' uttered in jest—gradually..."
"One will certainly become a Buddha in the end. Yet, in the *Avivartika-parivarta*, one hears that there is regression; furthermore, one hears that all śrāvakas shall become Buddhas.
If this were so, there should be no regression. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the path] is certain, whereas other sūtras speak of both regression and non-regression.
Therefore, I now ask: is it certain or uncertain? He cites this passage [to address the doubt].
The realization of Prajñā occurs after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

If this is so, the following section again investigates and explains the meaning of the scripture: if one distinguishes between the prior and posterior portions based on the *Prajñā*, then the scripture states that the twelve divisions of the canon emerge from the Buddha—this is the prior portion—and that the *Dhāraṇīs* emerge from the twelve divisions—this is [the posterior].
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and other such sutras emerge from the *Vaipulya*; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* emerges from the *Vaipulya*;

and the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the latter portion of the *Prajñā*. Therefore, one proceeds directly from the *Prajñā* to the *Nirvāṇa*. This is the second interpretation of the Kaishan school; compared to the former, it is even more circuitous.
Not only does it fail to encompass the *Avataṃsaka*, but it also fails to encompass the "with-characteristics" (sanimitta) teachings, as it [only] takes the ten...

Because the two sections constitute the preliminary portion of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the first three clarify the teaching, as the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) are the teachings that can express [the truth]. The latter two clarify the principle (*tattva*), as cause and effect can manifest the principle.
Since the means (the teaching) follows from the end (the principle), it is said that they "rely on the principle."
Regarding the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], these refer to the twelve divisions of the Hīnayāna; thus it is said that the *sūtra* (契經) constitutes the Hīnayāna Piṭaka.
Because the term "sūtra" (經) applies to both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna, when discussing them together, they are termed the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka* (雜藏).
Furthermore, because the Vaipulya (方等) is the vast and impartial Dharma of the Mahāyāna, it belongs to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The meaning of "Buddhism does not go beyond these three" is that many sutras frequently expound upon these three;

by taking these as the triad, the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s career, encompassing both the Mahayana and Hinayana, are subsumed. Therefore, it is said that they do not go beyond them.
Regarding the latter two principles: the former [set of] causes manifests the principle, while the latter [set of] fruits manifests the principle; this should be understood.
Zhaoti attempts to explain the text through both scripture and principle, yet he not only fails to grasp the general purport of the sutra, but his interpretation also lacks consistency. Why is this?

Since the teaching fundamentally elucidates the principle, how can it be that while the teaching encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles, the principle exists only within the Great Vehicle? The rest shall be refuted below.
Xinghuang [Sengzong] explained solely by means of the sequence of arising and understanding; that is, he took the twelve divisions of the scriptures as the teaching.

He stated that *sūtra* translates as "the source of the Dharma" (*dharmamūla*), which is precisely the meaning of being "under the teaching. Although the "source of the Dharma" already exists within the twelve divisions, its name is general and its substance is comprehensive;
since it can be designated as a "sūtra," one comes to know the meaning of the sūtras through the study of the twelve divisions. Thus, the Vaipulya (fangdeng) constitutes the principle.

Having studied the teachings, one comes to know their meaning; by seeking the meaning, one attains the principle, whereby wisdom arises. Therefore, it is said that by penetrating the Vaipulya (fangdeng) scriptures, one gives rise to Prajñā.
Wisdom realizes the principle, thereby comprehending Nirvāṇa. This process—from the many to the few, from the extensive to the concise—is the "going" [of the practitioner].
"Many" and "few" are simply synonyms for "extensive" and "concise. According to the five phrases of the sūtra, each subsequent phrase is more concise than the preceding one.

Furthermore, among the twelve divisions of the canon, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is the most concise, while the others are the most extensive. When compared to the former, it is concise; when compared to the latter, it is extensive.
Moreover, "extensive" and "concise" merely refer to the universal and the particular; therefore, within the text, the meaning is explained through these universal and particular aspects.

Regarding the phrase "comprehensive of both Great and Small [Vehicles]," this refers to the fact that each of these vehicles possesses its own twelve [divisions]; thus, it is called "comprehensive. The meaning of the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) is as previously recorded.
As for the specific praise of the *sūtra* (*tāra*), this excludes the other eleven divisions and specifically points to the *sūtra* genre.

Furthermore, "Tara" (多羅) is also a term that applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as both are called *sūtra*; therefore, by clarifying it through the *vaipulya* (方等), one knows that it pertains exclusively to the Great [Vehicle].
As for "not yet being rare" (未為希有): the *vaipulya* constitutes the teaching, and it is only when wisdom is generated based upon this teaching that it may be called "rare."

Regarding the separate praise of *nirvāṇa*: *prajñā* (wisdom) encompasses both cause and effect, whereas *nirvāṇa* is exclusively the fruit. The three virtues of *nirvāṇa* are collectively termed "Buddha-nature.

Just as the subsequent citations of metaphors and their application to the meaning follow from the preceding [text], all [the arguments] below proceed to refute the four masters. First, the refutation of the Kaishan school’s theory of the five periods.
Regarding the meaning: below, the refutation is presented by contrasting the twelve divisions [of the canon] with the initial teachings of the Āgamas, revealing two faults.

First, since the names of the twelve divisions apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and given that this sutra specifically refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, its meaning must reside solely in the Mahāyāna;
yet for the moment, we concede the point by saying it applies to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Second, even if one concedes that the twelve divisions are explained according to the Hīnayāna...

If, according to the Hīnayāna, it were not initially taught there—since various sūtras and vinaya sections of the Lesser Vehicle state that the Deer Park was the beginning—it would be appropriate to make such a claim within the context of the Hīnayāna;
however, this present sūtra is a Mahāyāna teaching that universally concludes the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime of instruction.
The claim that the "First Teacher" (the Buddha) specifically refers to the *Avataṃsaka* is untenable because its meaning has no fixed point of reference.
As for the objection, "Do other sūtras not contain prose sections?"— it is because among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, those that consist of direct prose exposition are termed *sūtra*.
Regarding "inconsistency of names," the sutra states that the *Prajñāpāramitā* emerges from the *Vaipulya*, yet it subsequently refers to it as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
this is what constitutes an inconsistency of names.
"Suppose" and below refutes the second interpretation of Kaishan.

Regarding the statement that "Prajñāpāramitā is adjacent to Nirvāṇa," this is explained by reference to its later division; thus, if Prajñāpāramitā follows the Lotus Sūtra, it would constitute the fourth period of teaching.
Yet, in your own system of the five periods, you state: first, the teaching with signs (sanimitta); second, the signless (animitta), which is Prajñā;
third, the teaching of praise and censure (saṃstuti-nindā), which is Vaipulya; fourth, the convergence of all virtues, which is the Lotus Sūtra; and fifth, the eternal (nitya).
Since Nirvāṇa has already been placed first, and Prajñā is now positioned adjacent to Nirvāṇa, Prajñā consequently occupies the fourth place;
thus it is said that this again contradicts the sequence of the five periods. "Er" (爾) means "you."

He then laments that those who cite other scriptures do so because the first three [categories] constitute the Tripiṭaka; thus, by praising their teaching, they are effectively praising other scriptures.

The section beginning with "Xinghuang" (Xinghuang Monastery) first refutes this as not being the Tripiṭaka; the section beginning with "Wang" (King) cites textual evidence to demonstrate it is not; the section beginning with "Congjiao" (From the Teaching) concludes that it is not.
If one examines the preceding section, it first restates their established thesis.
The text states that the citation below demonstrates that for them, brevity is superior while the sūtra is superior through its extensiveness.
"Since this... concludes the refutation; as this sūtra is extensive, to now praise brevity would pertain to another scripture.

The concluding refutation of the various masters' views consists of three sections. First, the presentation of the various masters' intentions, wherein each establishes their own doctrine with the aim of being comprehensive and leaving nothing out.

Next, the refutation of the masters' errors, beginning with the words "Unaware," which criticizes their failure to grasp the great purport of the sūtra in their interpretation of these seven lines of text.
"Zhi chi" (a distance of eight inches) is called a *fu*; ten inches is called a *chi*. To say that this slight textual variation causes one to lose the essential meaning is an error.
The following citation from Handan concludes the category of "types of things. The pronunciation of Handan is *han dan*. The seventeenth chapter of the *Outer Chapters* of the *Zhuangzi* says:
A young man from Shouling heard that people in Handan of the state of Zhao were walking slowly with their feet set apart, so he went there to learn it;
however, failing to master it, he lost his original gait and returned crawling on all fours. Thus it is said that he gained nothing from either method.

Now, when various masters explain this sutra, they are like that man learning to walk in Handan: their interpretation misses the essential meaning of the sutra, just as the student failed to learn the new step.
This contradicts one’s own established doctrine as if losing a long-practiced path;

for instance, when Kaishan (Kai-shan) establishes five periods of teaching with the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the second period, yet in his commentary on this sūtra, he instead places the *Prajñāpāramitā* in the fourth period. Since this violates his own doctrine as if losing a traditional practice, other examples may be inferred.
A comprehensive refutation of various masters is provided in the "Chapter on the Characteristics of the Doctrines" (*Jiaoxiang Zhang*) of the *Fahua xuanyi*.
Now, within the explanation of the present understanding, there are two parts: first, explaining the meaning by means of a single sūtra; second, explaining the meaning by means of a single period.

Although these two explanations differ, they equally reveal that the initial parable of the five practices constitutes the five aspects of the one reality, where praise and description are simultaneously perfected.

Furthermore, the subsequent parable of the five periods shows that throughout the entire dispensation, the ultimate goal is *nirvāṇa*. Moreover, the former explanation is horizontal, applying to a single [lifetime].

Regarding the subsequent explanation of the sutra: vertically, it encompasses the entirety of the Buddha’s transformational activity (*ekāśraya-pariṇāma*), while horizontally, within that vertical scope, there are five sequential stages of practice (*pañca-krama*) proceeding from shallow to deep;

thus, within the vertical there is the horizontal. Since this present sutra’s "cream of cream" (*amṛta-ghṛta*) explains these five stages, these two interpretations exhaustively capture the essence of the text.
First, concerning the initial section of the single sutra: (1) raising the question based on the text and stating the underlying intent; (2) first clarifying the preceding section on the *piṭaka*.

The King’s lament regarding the two teachings and the assistance of the two Buddhas clarifies this section, which describes their mutual fulfillment through both sequential and non-sequential generation.
"Sequentially generating" refers to the meaning of sequence, while "exhausting the profound and reaching the ultimate subtlety" refers to the meaning of non-sequence.
The Buddha’s praise of "Excellent! (Sādhu) intends this very point; therefore, it is said that he further adds these terms to accord with the meaning.
The "cow" is explained according to the sequence of the lower [stages].

"Milk" refers to the training in ethics (*śīla-śikṣā*) being at the head, just as the flavor of milk comes first; since concentration (*samādhi*) is accomplished through ethics, it is like curds produced from milk.
The subsequent three flavors serve as analogies for the arising of the Abhidharma (*abhidharma*), following this same pattern.

Regarding the analogy that "produced butter" (*navanīta*) represents the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths and so forth: the Four Truths pertain to the stage of entering the chamber; the two truths pertain to the stage of the two provisional [truths];
and the one reality pertains to the stage of entering the middle. These are all provisional meanings intended to establish a sequential order through mutual interpenetration;
they do not take the meaning of mutual identity as definitive.
When the five practices unfold in depth, precept and concentration constitute two, while wisdom constitutes three aspects of practice.
When they reach the ultimate in the single reality, they culminate in the realization of the Middle Way.
If one explains them solely from the perspective of non-sequential application, they are categorized as follows.
That which does not proceed by stages means that there is no duality between the beginning and the end, as both are cultivated as the single reality.
The Buddha then cites the passage below, using the metaphor of all medicinal herbs entering [a single vessel] to represent the Dharma-realm and so forth.
Regarding the intermediate dharmas, according to the preceding sequential text: the Tathāgata is the Teacher of Nirvāṇa, like the cow at the beginning;

the actual Nirvāṇa is the Wisdom, like the clarified butter (sarpis) at the end; and that which is in between consists of the precepts, meditative concentration, the Four Noble Truths, and the Two Truths.

There is nothing that is not *amṛta* (clarified butter), for true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) fuses all things; there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is identical to the cow.

Just as when a cow eats, it produces pure *amṛta*, so too, because the one is without duality—revealing the single reality through the sequence, and because the single reality fuses with the sequence—one should know this to be "one practice" (*ekācāra*).
The substance of the five elements is no different [from the five flavors].
This concluding summary below uses the five flavors as a metaphor for the five elements, thereby establishing the meaning of their sequential correspondence.
Since this sutra is solely a teaching that elucidates practice, it establishes the significance of praising the teaching; thus, it is said that both meanings are established.

If one explains the meaning by looking downward and delimiting it to a single period [of a Buddha’s life], then regarding the Dharma heard by these three types of people, there is both that which is common and that which is uncommon: the "emptiness" (śūnyatā) is called common, while the "Middle" (madhyama) is called uncommon;

yet within this, there is the distinction between the "limited Middle" and the "unlimited Middle. Thus, we know that although the discourse involves both the general and the specific, its underlying intent lies in the Perfect Middle.

Therefore it is said that [the teachings] are exclusively directed toward the one reality; since the meaning of the Two Vehicles’ transformation of the teaching should constitute a distinct category, it is said that "the Small Vehicle is led back to the Great.

Because the Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct Teachings receive the benefit of the Perfect Teaching, it is said that "the partial is grafted to become the perfect. Within the Vaipulya section, this intention is not absent;
however, because the sense of "rebuking and censuring" is predominant there, it is explained in a partial manner for the time being.
"Those who abide in [the stages] up to the minor fruit" refers to the stages of the internal and external ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the Tripitaka Teaching (*zàngjiào*).

"Allowing them to study universally" means allowing them to study universally—that is, to realize that form is emptiness (*rūpaṃ śūnyatā*), thereby severing delusions and realizing the state of a sage (*ārya*).

Furthermore, it is accepted that those who study both vehicles have not yet entered the true state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dharmapada*), as they still belong to the stage of the seven worthies;

thus, it is permitted for them to turn their minds toward practicing the Bodhisattva path. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If those of the two vehicles can give rise to the bodhicitta, I rejoice in all of them.

This refers to those of the two vehicles at the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who are not yet "seeds that have perished"; therefore, the arising of [bodhicitta] is possible through the *Prajñāpāramitā*. However, if they are in the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), it must be...
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and this present sutra: while they were situated within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they could only lead one toward the accumulation of karma.

The section "The Great Parinirvāṇa" below clarifies this present sutra. It is called "Venerable" (*zūn*) because it transcends a single lifetime; it is called "Ultimate" (*jí*) because it reveals the eternal and manifests the reality.

Furthermore, it is called "Venerable" because its revelation of the eternal and manifestation of reality surpasses all other scriptures, and it is called "Ultimate" because it marks the conclusion of the transformation for this single lifetime.
Because it is honored, it is supreme; because it is supreme, it is honored.

Having already resided in the two lower vehicles, this [text] causes the seeds that were ruined to sprout again, thereby reviling and abolishing the three types of cultivation as described in the "Chapter on Lamentation" (Śokavarga).
If that is so, what is the intent of the subsequent question? Since the dharma and metaphors in this passage encompass all five periods, why is it placed after the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
One might then ask: why does [the Buddha] speak of *nirvāṇa* but not of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
To answer this question regarding the subduing of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), there are three points: First, concerning the identity of meaning in the cessation of the Lesser Vehicle:

since the *nirvāṇa* is now being correctly expounded, the Buddha spoke of it in brief and did not mention the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This is simply because their meanings are identical, and thus it was permissible to speak of one in place of the other. Furthermore, Kā... The latter two [teachings] are described as "ultimate proclamations" (jichō), and while their meaning as ultimate proclamations is the same, when they emerge from the Pure Land to discuss the eternal, that alone suffices;

thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* is already an alternative designation for *nirvāṇa*. In contrast, the teaching that "the characteristics of the world are eternally present" on Vulture Peak is roughly equivalent to the current Buddha’s teaching here in this defiled land, intended to protect the capacities of sentient beings.
Since this teaching extensively discusses the eternal, it must still rely upon and support the Vinaya in accordance with those [beings].

Because the capacities [of sentient beings] differ, these distinct names are established; thus, the designation "Nirvāṇa" arises. Although the names and meanings differ, the intent of the transformation is necessarily equal.
Therefore, while the Buddha’s words are brief in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it follows the three previous [teachings] by means of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

As for the subsequent [teaching], the two sets of conditions for the capacities differ: the former involves the *Prajñāpāramitā* purifying [the faculties], while the latter involves the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* bringing them to maturity.
Thus, by employing the *prajñā* to refine and bring the *nirvāṇa* to maturity, this present sutra follows immediately after the *prajñā* and leads to *nirvāṇa*.
This demonstrates that the sequence of the five periods culminating in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is explained according to a single set of karmic conditions for a specific audience.
However, if one considers that the transformation of beings never ceases, then even the Deer Park teachings lead to *nirvāṇa*; thus, the meaning of the five periods is mutually interpenetrating.
This point is fully explained as clarified in the tenth fascicle of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).

Regarding the commentary on the lower section, the *Fahua xuanyi* poses the question: "With what intention is it known that those of dull faculties do not enter the *Lotus Sutra*, but instead use the *Prajñāpāramitā* for further refinement?
The commentary answers: "Why does Subhūti ask again about the bodhisattvas who are fixed in their destiny (*niyata*)?"
He did not give a definitive answer, saying: "Subhūti heard that all bodhisattvas receive the prediction of buddhahood within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Now he asks further regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*; one should know that after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is elucidated even more clearly."
Furthermore, the following section praises the correspondence between the present teaching and its underlying meaning.
As stated in the text, this is as clarified in the previous "Noble Conduct of Precepts," where it was explained that the five branches and ten precepts encompass all phenomena;

thus, their meaning is identical to the principle in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the initial illumination for those of great capacity—that the Dharma-realm is all-pervasive. There are two points of identity: first, [the correspondence of the teachings]; second, [the correspondence of the realization].
The meaning of "the foremost" is the same as [the first] two; the meaning of "extensively encompassing" is the same as [the second].

Regarding the self-vow below, after the respectful invitation, let later students observe this self-vow and hope to emulate it. Alas! Human faculties are gradually dulling and the Great Dharma is about to be diluted;
people compete for fame and profit for their own sake, regarding the circulation [of the teachings] as mere child's play. This fate is the same as a passing error.
In a century, how much time is there? To die aimlessly and live in vain, passing from darkness into darkness—whenever I reflect upon this, it is truly a cause for sorrow.
Furthermore, I have not heard the name of a Mahāyāna sūtra concerning the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world; yet, though I have not heard its name, through the arousal [of the aspiration]...
Due to the influence of past habituation, one perceives the principle of the four virtues.
My cultivation of this lower scripture should be divided into two sections: first, the assembly praising the virtues; second, the deliberations of the three devas.
First, a son of heaven; second, a rishi-son of heaven; third, from "As you have said" onwards, Śakra.
Regarding merit and wisdom: the firm observance of the prohibitive precepts constitutes merit, while profound insight constitutes wisdom.
Just as a carriage requires two wheels to travel far, and a bird requires two wings to soar through the sky, so too must these two be present.

Regarding "disciplining the rebels" (*dǎozé*), the *Yìnyì* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings) to the *Hànshū* states: "To discipline means to eliminate. The *Lǐjì* says: "To discipline means to execute.
Regarding "the Way and the standards" (*dàojiǎn*), according to the *Cāngjiépiān*: "Standards refer to laws and measures. "Standards" (*jiǎn*) also implies "to restrain" (*shè*).

Regarding the phrase "not abandoning" and so forth, it is said that when one observes during the time of the final examination that the Bodhisattva possesses wisdom and fearlessness and is able to relinquish [the body], one knows that they have partially realized profound wisdom and that the five fears have already been eliminated.

Reaching the dharma-realm of suffering and being able to relinquish body and life reveals the subsequent stage, which is that of a partial realization of a true person (*satpuruṣa*). These three dharmas should be applied respectively to the meanings of burning, grinding, and polishing.
"Manifesting the meaning of transition and cessation" means that the meaning of impermanence is made manifest;

since impermanence is the meaning of transition and cessation, the phrase "the permanence of non-abiding," etc., acknowledges this principle. That is to say: because of impermanence there is no abiding, yet one falsely clings to it as abiding;
and because there is no abiding, there is impermanence, yet one falsely clings to it as permanent.
"Glancing" (經眄): the phonetic transcription is *wángjiàn* (亡見反). According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "to glance" (*miàn*) means to look askance.
In the *Tongshu Wen* (Explanations for Popular Use), it is stated that "a fleet of boats" (*fang*) refers to two boats joined together.
Regarding the phrase "finally obtained" (*hou zu de*) in the sutra, "finally" (*zu*) means "suddenly" (*cang zu*), as in the expression "obtained unexpectedly," and so forth.

The scripture, having been covered, gives rise again to doubt; "fu" (覆) is pronounced as "fu" (福), or perhaps the two characters "fei" (非) and "er" (或) are the beginning of the next line, and now it is also impermanent.
This meaning of "neither arising nor ceasing" precisely accords with the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, for this half-verse is the Great Nirvāṇa.

Because it serves only a single purpose, the interpretation of the first master who claims this is a "skillful means" (upāya) is entirely of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and contradicts the intent of the sutra.
Regarding the word *yanyan* in the sutra, according to the *Erya*, *yanyan* means "to scorch"; it refers to the parching heat of a drought that scorches people.
"Exhausting meager blessings" (*jīng bó zhòu*): in the *Erya*, "blessings" (*zhòu*) refers to the blessings of Heaven.

"The scripture opens the path of the dharma of emptiness" means that this verse reveals and clarifies the path of the dharma of emptiness; this specifically refers to the inconceivable emptiness of the Middle Way.
The text states that the following section explains the meaning of "nirvāṇa" (寂滅) in two parts.
First, it presents a counter-objection based on the essential nature [of phenomena]. The question, "Is the arising of tranquility (寂生) considered bliss? intends to inquire:

if all phenomena are non-arising while Prajñā arises, then its essence would not be wisdom and abandonment (智斷), yet wisdom and abandonment are clearly present. Since this refers to the virtue of abandonment, it is said that "nirvāṇa is bliss. This is...

Regarding the statement that "all phenomena are unborn," may it not also be understood in terms of the merit of wisdom—that the arising of quiescence is bliss? This is precisely the arising of *prajñā*.
Answer: Following the subsequent presentation of the meaning, the response is twofold: first, by way of concession and refutation.
Regarding the phrase "taking this as an example": if one follows the doctrine of unrestrained non-directionality, then it is indeed as you have juxtaposed;
thus, it is said to be "an example.

Regarding "not following the lower [approach]": if one does not follow the doctrine of unrestrained non-directionality in order to explain the verses by distinguishing between the real and the false, then...
Because they are parallel in this way, they are not comparable as examples.
Regarding the phrase "following the path," "following" means to let it proceed freely; "the path" refers to verbal expression.
The following section provides the formal response.

Regarding the phrase "correctly grasping the removal of arising and the removal of cessation," etc.: it means that nirvāṇa is the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇaguṇa*). This clarifies that [the opponent] cites past evidence to seek nirvāṇa;
thus, if one seeks nirvāṇa, one might say that the cessation of arising is bliss. However, since this [present discussion] concerns nirvāṇa itself, it is stated that the case is not analogous.
Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues, Scroll Eleven.
Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues, Scroll Twelve.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Holy Life" (Brahmacarya-varga), the four mental states refer to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the three categories refer to ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Citing a sutra, this master’s intention is that because the holy life is shallow while the noble practice is deep, the cultivation of the four mental states alone can only lead to [the attainment of] *srotāpanna*.
When one reaches the Brahma-heaven and contemplates the Four Noble Truths, one is able to penetrate the path to ultimate truth; this is precisely the meaning of "penetration.

Therefore, the cited scripture states that the Four Noble Truths are that which enables the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, which is the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). This proves that the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*) takes these three categories as its essence.
The "Twelve Gates of Dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; these are called the twelve gates.

Since the four immeasurable minds are among these twelve, [the text] now distinguishes them from the "Noble Practices" (ārya-caryā). First, it raises the inquiry by questioning the Noble Practices, as the three categories have already been clarified.

Now, as for the further clarification of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) by these three [factors], since what has been explained is the same, why is there a distinction between the "Noble" (*ārya*) and "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) chapters?

The answer below explains that precept (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) mutually support one another; that is to say, precept and concentration are the auxiliary supports that bring wisdom (*prajñā*) to fulfillment.
The subsequent phrases follow this same pattern.
Since the Way penetrates both the ordinary and the sagely, how could the sagely practice not penetrate the ordinary? To say that what the sages practice does not apply to the ordinary is incorrect.

Although the sequence of precepts and wisdom differs between the ordinary and the sage, the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) exists in both cases. As for "sagely practice" (*ārya-caryā*) and "pure conduct" (*brahma-caryā*), although there is a difference in the priority of precepts and wisdom, the practice of concentration is present in the middle of both.
The phrase "the wisdom of Brahmā first" refers to the seven wholesome factors as wisdom.
Regarding cause and effect, the subsequent noble practices are the same as those mentioned previously; since they take the three grades as their essence, they are not discussed here.
As for the meaning of the subsequent sections: now the initial statement is refuted by a general censure, while the four [subsequent points] refute the three masters individually.
All [of these] are said not to be the Great Parinirvāṇa because the preceding sutra states that there are five kinds of practices for a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Thus, the first master [teaches] only the path of birth and death within the Brahma-heaven; the second master [teaches] only the partial emptiness of the Two Vehicles;
and the third master merely attains the phenomena of cause and effect. None of these are the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*tri-dharma*) of nirvāṇa.
Regarding this path:
if it were not for the refutation of the lower fetters, who would [claim] "whose is this brahmacarya"?
Since the various masters' interpretations of this brahmacarya do not constitute the Great Nirvana cultivated by Bodhisattvas, it is therefore questioned: "Whose is this brahmacarya?"
Now, regarding the phrase "explaining below," this means that the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) is simply the initial mind’s cultivation of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).

To penetrate the principle of the three truths is called the cause of Brahma-conduct; to partially realize it at the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) is called the fruit of Brahma-conduct. Cause and fruit are not two, for the three truths are mutually fused.
There are three meanings of purity, which refers to the three truths themselves. Regarding "purity of purity," this means purifying by means of an objectless pure mind.

To cause the supramundane pure dharmas to accord with inconceivable emptiness, those who are "pure yet impure" employ a non-conditioned pure mind to emerge into the provisional for the benefit of others;
they purify the defiled dharmas of the six ordinary realms so that they become inconceivable provisionality.
Those who are "neither pure nor impure" employ a non-conditioned pure mind to simultaneously negate both extremes, thereby accomplishing inconceivable centrality, which is again pure.
Purity refers to one's own practice within the cause; impurity-purity refers to transforming others within the fruit. Non-purity is not purity, and purity is the negation of both;

this is the purity of both cause and effect, as well as self and other. Furthermore, purity is the pure dharma of the four noble ones, while impurity-purity is the defiled dharma of the six classes of ordinary beings.
The negation of both defilement and purity reveals the principle of the Middle Way.
The "Universal Purity" refers to the Great Nirvana which integrates the four types of noble purity.

It should be said that "this" refers to compassion; "this" is the unconditioned compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*), which is the means of purification, while "the four noble dharmas" are that which is purified.

Thus, all virtues are the branches and unconditioned compassion is the root; by taking the branches as the root, unconditioned compassion comprehensively encompasses the mind of loving-kindness. This being so, it is likewise for compassion.
Since all [beings] are likewise so, it was said previously that "now, by means of the pure Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), one is universally purified," and so forth.
Thus, we know that Brahma-conduct is simply the four minds of the Buddha-realm.

As for the fact that compassion has immeasurable gateways: from its essence, it gives rise to function, manifesting forms within the six realms to gather and transform beings according to their capacities; therefore, these [gateways] exist.
Immeasurable.
This refers to the brief enumeration of six kinds of immeasurable gateways for correct demonstration, all of which appear in the text of this chapter.

Regarding "taming the elephant," it means manifesting as a lion to tame a drunken elephant. Regarding "taming the mad," it refers to a case where a Brahmin woman went mad upon the death of her son, and the Buddha transformed himself into a son for her.
The woman recovered her original mind; the treatment of the eyes refers to a thief whose eyes were gouged out who, upon taking refuge in the Buddha, had them restored;
the healing of the wound refers to a woman who offered her own flesh when the Buddha applied medicine to her painful sore—all such occurrences were witnessed through the power of his compassion.
Regarding "Compassion in Practice" (*ciyou xia*), the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* praises it, saying: "I shall now praise with a single dharma, namely, the practice of a compassionate mind in the world.
Regarding "Compassion in Entry" (*beiju xia*), the Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva sees an icchantika falling into hell, he also vows to be together with them."
One is born in hell;
it is neither cause nor effect (up to) neither pure. That which is the Middle Way without conditions is not the meaning of the former two types, as explained above.
This section below concludes the integration of the three types of compassion.

Regarding the "three compassions": that which is pure and pure is the compassion with dharmas as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*); that which is impure and pure is the compassion with sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana-maitrī*);

and that which is neither is the compassion without an object (*anālambana-maitrī*). In the text, it first refutes the notion of pervasiveness, and subsequently, by means of "integration" and "one," it reveals the perfection [of the preceding three], showing that the essence of their purity is entirely identical.
The non-dual [principle] is manifested from the three as the basis for its name; since it is one and yet three, the three titles are established.
Since it is three and yet one, its ritual expression is eternally harmonious.

According to the Sūtra, by abiding in the seven wholesome dharmas, one attains the full observance of the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*); "fully endowed" should be stated as "abiding in the seven wholesome [dharmas] and the four minds."
The dharmas such as the precepts fully constitute the holy life (*brahmacarya*); for now, they are briefly indicated according to their respective contexts as the "seven wholesome [factors].

If one were to extend this further to clarify the secondary and primary meanings through these seven wholesome factors: because the holy life cultivates the four [immeasurable] minds, it primarily pertains to transforming others;

because the noble conduct (*āryacaryā*) cultivates the three grades [of practice], it primarily pertains to one's own cultivation. Thus, since these seven wholesome factors are already the holy life...
Because these are the primary factors, transforming others is considered the principal practice while cultivating oneself is secondary.

However, they also encompass self-cultivation: the seven wholesome qualities correspond to wisdom (*prajñā*), the four mental states correspond to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and maintaining the precepts corresponds to ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Since these contain all three categories [of training], they collectively encompass self-cultivation.

Because one knows the Dharma, the following demonstrates how it applies to both oneself and others: precisely by knowing the Dharma, one is able to advance one's own path internally and transform sentient beings externally.
Regarding the fivefold explanation of its meaning: because the name *sūtra* contains many meanings, it cannot be translated; it can only [be left as is].
It is explained through five meanings; as for these five meanings, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (*Zaxin lun*) explains the sūtras by means of five aspects:
first, the meaning of a gushing spring, because its flavor is inexhaustible; second, the meaning of manifestation, because it can reveal the true principle;

third, the meaning of production, because it can give rise to sublime goodness; fourth, the meaning of the carpenter’s line, because it establishes the correct and the erroneous; and fifth, the meaning of a string of garlands.
To ensure that [the meaning] is not lost or confused, this is not merely a direct translation of the name, but rather an explanation of *sūtra* through five meanings.

Alternatively, it is said that below there are two schools; the first holds that "Kie-ching" (契經) is a semantic translation, and thus it is said that this [term] is used here as a substitute for that.

The scriptures of the former sages of this land are called *sūtras*, and those composed by the worthy are termed *zǐshǐ* (sub-histories), serving as substitutes for the *buddhabhāṣita-sūtras* of that land.
As for the term "translation of meaning" (*yìfān*), since no Buddha has appeared in this region, there is no Buddhist teaching;

thus, these works can only serve as substitutes for them, which is why they are called "translations of meaning. If it were like *Sāgara*, which is translated as "sea," then it would be [a literal translation].

The "correct translation" (zhèngfān) refers to the fact that both sides—this [land] and that [Western land]—possess oceans; alternatively, it is said that "the correct translation" represents the interpretation of the second school of thought.

This means that since there is a Buddha in the Western land and there were former kings here [in this land], and since the words of these former kings are already termed "sūtra," it is precisely appropriate to translate *sūtra* by means of this term.
"Seal" (*qiè*) means to accord with principle (*li*), to accord with the capacity of the audience (*jī*), and to accord with the timing (*shí*).
Regarding the meaning of "correspondence" (*yoga*) as taught by the Buddha: it accords with these two [aspects], and there is certainly no empty bestowal.
As for the statement that "the general has no distinction," the intention is this: while the other eleven divisions (*aṅga*) have distinct entities, the *sūtra* division has no separate entity;
rather, the eleven divisions taken as a whole constitute the *sūtra*. This is because it begins from "Thus" (*evam*) and concludes with "Acceptance" (*pratipattavyam*).
Because it is called a "sūtra," this refers to both the verses (*geya*) and the prose (*gadya*); this clarifies that each has its own distinct essence.
That is to say, *geya* refers to the verses, while *sūtra* refers to the prose; the term "sūtra" here points to that which is being versified.
The citations in the lower volume of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun) merely use verses to explain the prose; thus, the treatise clearly indicates that the prose is the *sūtra*.

How can one then claim that it lacks a distinct substance? However, the extensive explanation of the meanings of the twelve divisions of the teachings is found within the "Excellence of the Dharma" section of the *Miaoxuan*;
those who require it should seek it there. Now, Kaishan and Zhuangyan each have grasped a partial sense of this. If...
Following the sequence of the sūtra and adhering to its general meaning, the sūtra states: "From these [beings]...
It should be understood that those of sharp faculties who arrived later did not require the extensive prose explanation because their faculties were sharp;
however, those already present in the assembly—without distinction between those of sharp or dull faculties—all heard the prose explanation.
The term *śaṅkha* is also rendered as *xiāngqū* (餉佉) or *shuāngqū* (霜佉), which translates as "conch shell"; it is merely another name for *ka*.

As for the title "Maitreya," according to the specific commentary within the sūtra, because it follows the general [principle], it says that he shall "bestow [the teachings] upon the six realms of existence" and so forth.
Know that there are two kinds of *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies). If one bestows the prophecy of Buddhahood upon a bodhisattva, it is a prophecy within the Mahāyāna;

if one records a proximate cause or proximate fruit, it is a prophecy within the Hīnayāna. The holy teachings refer to "bestowing" (*śāsana*) as the giving of a name, and "recording" (*vyākaraṇa*) as the naming of what the mind anticipates.

Alternatively, it is said that "receiving the prophecy" (*pratigraha-vyākaraṇa*) refers to the superior bestowing upon the inferior, which is called "bestowing," and the inferior receiving from the superior, which is called "receiving. Therefore, the sutra...
The two names [of the *geya*] appear interchangeably.
Regarding "unequal verses" (*visamagāthā*), this refers to those that are spoken in isolation, where both the words and their meanings do not correspond to the prose (*gadya*).
By this standard, the *geya* should also be called "equal verses" (*samagāthā*), because its words and meanings correspond to the prose.
The text below states that "verse" (gāthā) refers to both meaning and phrasing, because phrasing encompasses both long and short lines.
By excluding those with distinct characteristics that are set in long metrical lines, this specifically eliminates the *geya* (repetitive verses).
The same applies to the precepts (*śīla*): when there is no prose introduction (*gadya*), it is called "isolated" (*kevala*) because it is not a verse summary (*geya*).
When there is no verse summary to the prose introduction—meaning that if there were a verse summary below, the preceding prose would be termed *sūtra*.
If there are no *geya* (verses) and only the prose (*gadya*) exists, it is called *udāna*.
As the Sūtra states at its conclusion: "This sūtra is self-declared without being questioned; therefore, it is named *udāna*. Thus, one must rely on the words of the Sūtra.

Regarding "unasked spontaneous teachings" (*anupṛcchita-svayaṃbhāṣita*): these are proclamations made spontaneously without being prompted by inquiry. First, because the principles are profound and the meanings are far-reaching, no one is able to ask about them.

Second, it is not that they cannot be asked about; rather, it is because the listeners ought to hear them, and the Buddha, as the Teacher who does not wait for requests, speaks of his own accord without awaiting questions.
The term *nidāna* (因緣) is explained here as follows: it refers to verses such as "Do not underestimate even small evils," which appear in the first fascicle of the *Dharmapada*.
Here, the Buddha cites past events to clarify the meaning of *nidāna*; that is, because he proclaims teachings by relying on present circumstances and conditions, these are called *nidāna-sūtras*.
The *Śāstra* states: In the twelfth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it says that *nidāna* refers to the *Nidāna-sūtra*.
Why is this so? Because all the essential teachings spoken by the Buddhas and noble sages possess causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
These various causes and conditions are found either within the *Sūtras* or in other places; this is the explanation of the twelve divisions [of the scriptures].
Generally speaking, whenever the term *śāstra* (treatise) is used, it refers to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra).
As for the *Ava-dāna*, this establishes metaphors (*dṛṣṭānta*) to clarify the Dharma. *Itivṛttaka* means "thus it was said" (*itivṛtta*).

Regarding the term *jātaka*, [the school of] Kai-xian [Senglang] considers it inferior to this; here, the *Vṛttaka* (Past Events) and *Jātaka* (Birth Stories) are combined into a single category. Thus, the eighth [division] is translated as "Thus" (*evam*).

[The word] "ornament" (*vyūha*). Regarding the section below, if one opens it into two divisions based on the *Itivṛttaka* and *Jātaka*, then the *Itivṛttaka* would be the eighth and the *Jātaka* the ninth;
however, there is no such statement [in the text]. As for the *Itivṛttaka*, it proclaims the events of others in the distant past; therefore...
Because those who have been born speak of the events of their own past lives, each has its own distinct realm (*dhātu*).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of separation; that is to say, the matters and meanings spoken of are different from one another.
To clarify the subsequent explanation in the sutra regarding how each of the four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa established a distinct name for this fundamental narrative (nidāna),
it is like having different territorial boundaries and corresponding separate seals of authority.

Combining the ninth [case] as the Jātaka (Birth Stories) means that when past events concerning oneself or others are given the same name, they are collectively termed "Jātaka" without distinguishing between the two;
if one were to distinguish between the two as different, such a designation would not exist.
In the commentary on the *Vaipulya-mahā-śāstra*, the character is read with the initial *kǒu* (口) and the final *yè* (夜).
In the present scripture, "vaipulya" (*fāngguǎng*) refers to what the scripture calls "vaipulya-sūtras" (*fāngděng jīngdiǎn*). It is called "vaipulya" because its meaning is vast.

"Vaipulya" signifies that the principle is correct, while "vaipulya" signifies that it is comprehensive and rich. Furthermore, because the principle is harmonious and non-dual, it is also called "equal" (*fāngděng*). As for the principle being correct...

The oneness of the sentient being and the Buddha encompasses all; when "rich" is taken to mean the three thousand worlds, it is fully present. Because the teaching manifests from principle, it is called the Vaipulya Sūtra.
To directly expand upon what follows, this applies generally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, comprising twelve divisions.

Since the principle that pervades space is not manifest as the central [truth], it is not called "Vaipulya" (the Central). Within the six realms, it may be termed "Vipula" (Broad); this represents a partial negation, whereas a full affirmation would be...

That which opposes the false is called the correct, and it may also be termed "directional" (*diś*); if it were entirely exclusive, it would not pervade the ten realms and thus would not possess the meaning of "extensive.

"Unprecedented" (*āścarya*) refers to the Buddha manifesting various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), such that sentient beings marvel at what they have never before experienced, as described in the sutras.
"Taking seven steps without anyone supporting him," and so forth.

It is also said that "one who explains the meaning" (*arthavibhāga*) refers to the sense of "explaining" (*vibhāga*), meaning one who answers various questions by explaining their underlying reasons and expounding upon the various meanings.
Such question-and-answer exchanges for explaining the meaning are all termed *upadeśa*.
Within the Mahāyāna, this is explained based on the fact that there are only nine divisions (*navāṅga*), namely excluding the *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*;

this is because those with sharp faculties in the Mahāyāna do not require these three. In the Hīnayāna as well, there are likewise only nine divisions, and thus lack the *vaipulya*, *svayambhū*, and *vyākaraṇa*.

Alternatively, it is said that there are eleven [divisions], but they simply lack the *vaipulya*. These [distinctions] are all separate discussions concerning the specific characteristics of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; generally speaking, both [vehicles] share them.
The treatises each possess twelve [categories].

Guangzhai’s [commentary] follows this; it clarifies that Guangzhai merely translates *tīśā* as "discourse" (*lunyi*), yet asserts that the term for "explaining the meaning" belongs to the *vyākaraṇa* (prediction/prophecy).
He takes the character "jie" (解) to mean "thoroughly understanding," because it thoroughly understands the meanings of eons, lands, and so forth.
One should say that the subsequent passage clarifies the equality of the meanings of the three truths: "immeasurable" is emptiness, "limitless" is the provisional, and "ultimate" is the middle.
Since the scriptural text states that one must "comprehensively know" their meaning, it is only upon attaining the three truths that one can be said to have comprehensive knowledge.
To discern clearly between the wholesome and the unwholesome refers to what the Sūtra calls "faith and so forth" in this way: that is to say, such faith in the heterodox is called unwholesome;
such faith in the orthodox is called wholesome; partial faith is called unwholesome; and perfect faith is called wholesome. The same applies to precepts and other virtues.
One must conduct an internal examination to cause oneself to abandon the heterodox and attain the orthodox, to abandon the partial and return to the perfect.
The *Analects* records that Zengzi said: "I daily examine myself thrice: In planning for others, have I been disloyal? In my dealings with friends, have I been untrustworthy?
In transmitting what I have learned, have I not practiced it? This was Zengzi’s self-reflection, which resembles the Bodhisattva’s self-awareness;
thus, it may be cited as scriptural evidence to clarify self-knowledge. There are ten such phrases in total, of which the first five are as follows.

One knows the five grades of roots of goodness; subsequently, one knows the three types of action performed by oneself: the bodily actions of coming and going through right mindfulness and virtuous conduct;
the mental action; and the verbal action of knowing for oneself the questions and answers, victory and defeat, and right and wrong.
To provide a brief enumeration: "persons" and the "two vehicles" refer respectively to the realm of persons—namely the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriyas—and the realm of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, to briefly enumerate the body and speech: coming, going, sitting, and rising pertain to the body; preaching the Dharma and engaging in dialogue pertain to the speech.
A complete discussion should include all ten realms, yet since each realm possesses the three types of karma, the Buddha’s words have abbreviated them by citing only the essentials.

Those who employ their minds sparingly do so because they understand the opportune moment through mental karma before then applying physical or verbal actions; however, because the mind operates secretly and subtly, it is omitted from discussion.

As for the terms "Distinct" and "Complete," these refer to seeking the meaning of the Mahāyāna, which encompasses the four teachings (*catur-yāna*). In terms of the practice of the *pāramitās*, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is considered inferior [to the Perfect Teaching].

The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) takes principle and practice as supreme and principle and practice as inferior; the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) takes sequential progression as supreme and sequential progression as inferior—these three all belong to the realm of the Bodhisattva.
Sequential progression is inferior, while perfect fusion (yuanrong) is supreme, for perfect fusion is itself the realm of the Buddha;
thus it is said to be "the realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
The "perfect seven virtues" means that one realizes the preceding seven virtues are solely mind and are non-separate from the three truths; thus they are called the perfect seven virtues.
"One virtue is all virtues" means that the virtues of the three truths arise together.

Regarding "the extinction of all and everything": this refers to the extinction of the three delusions and evils, which occurs precisely at the stage of partial truth (*san-bun-shin*). Its meaning extends through the three stages [of the Separate Teaching].

Regarding "among the worthies, sages, humans, and devas": this means that from the stage of the Perfect Name (*en-myōji*) upward, although one still possesses afflictions, they are as if without afflictions;
because one is able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, one is thus included among the worthies, sages, humans, and devas of the preceding three teachings.
Because it is the most supreme and excellent, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) states: "The ultimate of that school is not as good as the beginning of my school.

That which is one category within the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*) refers to the seven meanings; among the three categories of precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), this is wisdom.
This is the chapter.
Regarding "the immeasurables [arising] from their objects," it is because the number of sentient beings who serve as the focal objects (ālambana) is immeasurable.

Regarding "the four immeasurables [arising] from the mind," it is because they bestow happiness and extract suffering equally, without discriminating between enemies and kin. Therefore, the subsequent commentary states:
"My mind is of a single characteristic.
As for "the object is also called 'equal,'" it is because the object follows the mind and both attain bliss together.
"The mind is also immeasurable" is because the mind follows the object and its various discriminations differ. The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: "Because..."
Because the sentient beings who are the objects of focus are immeasurable, the cognizing mind likewise becomes immeasurable according to those objects;
thus, they all receive the name "immeasurable minds.

As for the statement that "all three are the same": since the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—just like the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)—possess these three objects, it is known [that they are the same].

The three minds collectively fulfill the meaning of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). If it were merely the mind of loving-kindness alone, there would be only one and not four; therefore, it is said that it is difficult to make it "only one.

However, the passage beginning with "but with respect to the object" explains the aforementioned sense of being "only one. That is to say, although with respect to the object there may be sentient beings or dharmas, or even no object (*anālambana*), [the three minds together constitute a single category].

Although these differ, because the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is of only one kind, it is said that there is no distinction between them. If this were so, then the third [difficulty] would become identical to the first;
why then call it a "fourth" difficulty? The answer to the fourth would likewise be identical to the first, as all three equally fulfill the meaning of loving-kindness and thus ought to be one.
Nevertheless, this section clarifies the meaning of the three types of loving-kindness; if categorized according to the Three Truths, they exist only within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

As for how the five aggregates arise: it means observing that the aggregates of the four miserable destinies arise from unwholesome causes and conditions, while the aggregates of humans and devas arise from wholesome causes and conditions, and so forth.
To observe only such dependent origination is called "compassion conditioned by arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda-maitrī*).

Because the five aggregates are what is fundamentally required and are the basis [of experience], observing this basis and its manifestations is called "compassion conditioned by dharmas" (*dharma-maitrī*). Regarding "unconditioned compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*), its meaning can be understood in reference to the Buddha.
Therefore, these three conditions all converge upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
How much more so regarding other objects—namely, the nine realms (*navadhātu*)?
In the sutra, the phrase "this is called the wordless" (*amukha-pada*) precedes the two characters "compassion" (*maitrī*), which mark the beginning of the next line.
Third, this clarifies that the three conditions are identical to the three truths; thus, these "conditions of arising" encompass the previous three meanings because they are like close relatives.
Since one provides what is required, it is known that the Tathāgata does not depend on being supplied with anything;
as he merely remains among the laity, it is said that the realm of sentient beings is shallow.
Regarding the statement that "the emptiness of dharmas is profound," this refers to the sūtra’s teaching that one does not see parents and so forth;

because one sees only dependently originated phenomena whose very substance is empty, they are said to be "not seen. Since this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is said to be "profound."
When there is no object of perception and both [subject and object] are absent, one does not abide in the mark of dharmas, and thus there is no emptiness of nirvana;
one does not abide in the mark of sentient beings, and thus there is no conventionality of birth-and-death. Because the Middle Way negates both extremes, it is said to be "extremely profound."

There should be only three; since the essence of the three types of compassion is the three truths, and each of the [three] aspects of pity and so forth is established as the three truths, and these three truths are without distinction—relying solely on their essence there are only three—why is it necessary to discuss four?
Regarding the difficulty concerning the combination of the general and the specific in the designation of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*):

"four" is the specific designation, referring to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); "immeasurable" is the general designation, because these four states of mind are collectively termed "immeasurable.
Therefore, one raises the objection regarding the combination of the names by separating their general and specific aspects from one another.
The phrase "Since it is said... uses the general [argument] to refute the specific;
the phrase "Since it is its... uses the specific to refute the general. Because there are four that can be counted, they cannot be "immeasurable.

If [it were truly immeasurable], the conclusion would be established as follows: if one holds to the name "immeasurable" while asserting only one, it should logically be just one and cannot be called "four."
Regarding the single condition of "conditioned origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it subsumes those twelve factors as being solely the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
As for the conditions and fruits, among the twelve links, five links are causes and seven links are fruits; therefore, there are only these two categories of phenomena.

The threefold [classification] can be understood by assigning the twelve links to the three paths. The fourfold [classification] consists of: ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), which comprise the causes of the two past lives;
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), which subsume the present; and formations (*saṃskāra*), which comprise the present link of existence (*bhava*);

and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which subsume consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*). Alternatively, it is said that there are five types, wherein feeling (*vedanā*) is raised up to include consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth.

The mention of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) subsumes ignorance (*avidyā*); the mention of existence (*bhava*) subsumes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); and the mention of birth (*jāti*) subsumes old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
Alternatively, when six links are mentioned, this discusses cause and effect for each of the three time periods respectively.

When seven links are mentioned, the mention of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth subsumes birth and old age/death, while the mention of craving and grasping subsumes ignorance; this is a brief formulation that omits volitional formations and existence. Alternatively, eight links are mentioned.

The mention of "consciousness" and so forth subsumes birth and old age/death; the mention of "craving," "grasping," and "existence" subsumes ignorance and formations. Therefore, these are excluded [from the specific list].
Alternatively, it is said that there are nine types [of links], and that the remaining three branches are included within others; in that case, one should also speak of ten branches.
The *Mārga-vibhaṅga-sūtra* does not clarify this point as the *Tṛṇa-pura-sūtra* (茅城經) does; since that sūtra explains the causes and conditions in detail, it refers to it here.
