Regarding the term "leakage" (*lou*) in the sutra, it refers to falling into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). Regarding *kāmalā* in the sutra, this is translated as "leprosy.
As for "obstinate and aggressive," "shamelessness" means having no sense of shame within, while "lack of remorse" means not confessing one's faults before others.
The *Zhiguan yinyi* states that "lǔhù" (魯扈) is a term describing one who is dull-witted and ignorant.

The initial presentation of the physician’s excellence in the scripture has two parts: first, praising his own virtue; second, from "Great Compassion" (*mahāmaitrī*) downward, praising his benefit for others.

The first part [praising his own virtue] also has two sections: first, praising his physical virtues; second, from "Possessing the Ten Powers" (*daśabala*) downward, praising his wisdom-virtues. The praise of his benefit for others also has two sections: first, praising his benefit... [text continues].

Following the knowledge of others' minds, he next praises the practice of benefiting others through wholesome means. Within this practice, he praises the two types of conduct—bodily and verbal—just as a calf follows its mother.

First, he praises the Buddha’s bodily conduct; next, he praises his verbal karma. Regarding "knowing the proper time": it refers to being skillfully adept at discerning the capacities and conditions of others, administering medicine according to their ailments, and so forth.
"Truthful speech" means being free from false and deceptive words. "Pure speech" means being free from impure speech. "Sublime speech" means...
"Free from harsh speech" means that his words are meaningful; "free from meaningless speech" means that his words accord with the Dharma. "Single-syllabled speech" means that his words are non-dual.
Furthermore, "truthful speech" and "pure speech" clarify the absence of false speech; "exquisite speech" clarifies the absence of harsh speech;

and "meaningful speech" and "Dharmic speech" clarify the absence of frivolous speech. Speech that benefits others is called "meaningful speech," and speech that accords with the Dharma is [Dharmic speech].
Therefore it is said that a single word of the Dharma clarifies the absence of double-tongued speech.
Regarding "passing through the assembly of all Bodhisattvas," the term "Bodhisattva" generally refers to those who know both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
"Existence and non-existence are the two truths" refers here to the inconceivable ultimate and conventional truths.
Regarding these afflictions and nirvana: conditioned phenomena are afflictions, and unconditioned phenomena are nirvana.

As for the Four Noble Truths, they are the four aspects of non-activity; because suffering and its origin are the causes and effects of outflows, while the path and cessation are the causes and effects without outflows, they are called the Four Noble Truths.

That which is also the origin of suffering refers to the afflictions, which are the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*); the result is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are the result of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), and [the cessation of these] is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The eleven kinds of form refer to the five sense faculties, the five sense objects, and non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

Regarding that which is neither form nor non-form, others claim it refers to the single factor of "acquisition" (*prāpti*) among the fourteen formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
As for the fourteen kinds of form, they refer to the five characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the five sense objects (*viṣaya*), and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

That which has neither an agent nor a locus of action is the "non-associated formation" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* clarifies that there are seventeen types of non-associated formations in total;
this [category] corresponds to one of them: "non-manifestation" (*avijñapti*).

"Abandoning both" refers to abandoning form (*rūpa*) and abandoning mind (*citta*); this is the Middle Way. Regarding this, the Master [Zhiyi] now refutes it, stating that it is merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Master simply says that "abandoning both" is the Middle Way because it lacks intrinsic substance;

since the form and mind being abandoned are merely conventional truth, one knows that the "agent of abandonment" is nothing but partial emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*). How, then, could this constitute the Middle Way of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)?
By this, the disparagement and suppression of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* (Yuan jing) are resolved.
Now, to clarify the distinctions regarding the opening and closing of the two truths (*satyadvaya*) and three truths (*satyatraya*) as they appear in the following section:

if there are two dharmas, existence and non-existence, these are both termed the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), while the Middle Principle is termed the ultimate (*paramārtha*). As for the three truths, one opens up the conventional to reveal the ultimate, which is named the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
Because it is "middle," three are established: "not form" refutes the existence of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and "not non-form" refutes the emptiness of nirvāṇa.
For one who enters emptiness from the conventional, this entry into emptiness constitutes their own practice of destroying birth-and-death.
Emerging from emptiness into the provisional means that emerging into the provisional is for the purpose of transforming others and benefiting sentient beings.
That which is the Middle Way is the profound principle wherein the two extremes of action and reception do not exist.
In all such textual examples, one should interpret them by means of the three truths (*trisatya*).
Do not hold the past in high regard while disparaging the present; "the present" here refers to King Ajātaśatru.
The term "charioteer" (*yùchén*) in the sutra refers to the official who drives the chariot.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Kauśika," the Buddha answers by starting from the end.
As for the phrase "arising from doubt," it is because the Lord of Devas originally harbored doubts regarding his own life that he says, "It is truly as the Buddha has taught."
The passage concerning Mahāmaudgalyāyana cites his disciples to illustrate his teacher.
The passage concerning the king seeing the Buddha while among animals cites those of lower status to provide an analogy for humans.
The passage stating, "Great King, before the World-Honored One had attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," cites his causal practices to illustrate the fruit.

The term *anuttara* means "unsurpassed"; *samyak* means "correct" (*zhèng*); *sambodhi* means "equal" (*děng*). *Bodhi* means "awakening" (*jué*), which together constitute "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Awakening.
There are two meanings to "awakening": first, "perfect awakening," which refers to correctly contemplating the Middle Way;
second, "equal awakening," which refers to equally illuminating both extremes. Illuminating all three truths simultaneously constitutes [the ultimate].
Because it is ultimately beyond reproach, it is called "unsurpassed.
When the sutra mentions the "wilderness spirits," this reveals the Buddha’s universal compassion in saving all beings.
When the sutra states that "even the disciples of the Tathāgata still have such [limitations]," this cites the disciples as a means of illustrating the Master.

The *Jing* states that "to kill one's father"—the character for "kill" (*shā*) is sometimes written as "assassinate" (*shì*, pronounced with the same phonetic)—the *Zuozhuan* says, "To inflict violence upon one's ruler is called *shì*.
The *Zhouyi* says, "A minister assassinating his lord, a son assassinating his father; this did not happen in a single morning or evening, for what it leads to develops gradually.
The *Shiming* says, "When one below assassinates one above, it is called *shì*; *shì* means to wait (*sì*). One waits for an opportunity before being able to carry out the deed."
Also: *Bhindi-bi-min-zhi-ji-fan-zheng* (邠坻鄙旻直飢反正) says *Anāthapiṇḍada*. *Anātha* means "without support" (*wuyi* 無依) and is also called "the solitary" (*gudu* 孤獨).
*Piṇḍada* means "giver of alms" (*tuanshi* 團施). This indicates that this elder was fond of giving.
He was named "Poor" (Pín) because of his solitary poverty; his original name was Sudatta.

The sutras explain that "pàn" (pronounced as in *pǔ-dàn*) refers to a "contract" (*jiān*). According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, the Official of Marriages (*méi zhǐ*) "presides over the contracts of the myriad people. Zheng Xuan commented: "A 'pàn' is a half.
To join together when one has found a mate is called a 'pàn. This is what is meant in the *Sāngfú* when it says, "husband and wife are a joined pair (*pàn hé*)."
The *Shi'er you jing* (Sūtra of the Twelve Wanderings), which records the journey through the country of Daqin, states:

"Within Jambudvīpa there are sixteen great countries and eighty-four thousand cities, governed by eight kings and four celestial sons. To the east is the Son of Heaven of Jin, whose people are flourishing;
to the south is the Son of Heaven of India, whose land abounds in famous elephants; to the west is the Son of Heaven of Daqin..."
The land abounds in gold, jade, and precious stones; to the northwest, the territory of the Dayuezhi (Yuezhi) Heavenly Son is rich in fine horses.
"Jing" (經) here means to despise and lament—to feel shame for and sorrow over [one's failings].
"Jiè" (冑) [pronounced zhòu, with the radical for "clothing" and the phonetic "jiù" (救)] refers to a helmet; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, a "zhòu" is a *dōumóu* (a helmet).

Regarding the title of the sutra, "Because there is no pleasure in the intervals": the first "jiān" (間) is pronounced as *xián* (莧) in the upper tone, meaning "separation" (*jiàngé*); the second "jiān" (間) is pronounced as *xián* (閑) in the lower tone, meaning "the middle" (*jiānzhōng*).
This is the fifth section of the Brahma-Carya Chapter.

Regarding the statement that "only King [Mahāpraṇāda] has truly entered extinction": although King Mahāpraṇāda was included among the assembly in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, because his obstacles had not yet been removed and his spiritual capacity had not yet been awakened, he did not realize the perfect and eternal nature during that assembly.

Thus, even today, it is still said that he has truly entered extinction. Although this is an expedient teaching (*upāya*), it is only by interpreting it according to the ultimate reality (*tattva*) that the significance of the present sutra is revealed.
Regarding the six sections, the four middle ones all state: "Furthermore, the sixth section begins with 'Good son' and so forth;
this can be seen by consulting the sutra.

This passage itself explains that "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) refers to not being made into sentient beings; therefore, it is called "unconditioned sentient beings. Thus, because they are not produced as sentient beings, they are termed unconditioned.
Foguo explains this as follows:
"Sentient beings within the principle" refers here to the internal and external ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
However, this is not the interpretation of our own Master [Tanyan] presented below.
The fact that the sūtras are also not fixed is precisely because the sūtras explain "non-fixity" to refute the various masters' interpretations that fixate on the depth or shallowness [of practice].

However, according to the meaning of the scriptural text, it appears as if non-fixed; yet, based on the present Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*), there is a distinction between high and low, and a point of return.

Thus we know that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) corresponds to the stages prior to entering the [first] abode, while the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) corresponds to ascending into the abodes. Furthermore, from the stage of "Names" (*mingzi*) upward, all are termed unconditioned.
Because one knows that although the secret treasury contains afflictions, they are as if non-existent;
"for all" refers generally to both the good and the evil, while "for those who commit the five heinous crimes" specifically points to evil persons.
Although these cases differ, they equally return to the principle of suchness (*tathatā*); thus, even before the aspiration for enlightenment has been generated...

This principle is as follows: those who have already resolved their minds may either abide in conventional designations while failing to perceive the true nature, or they may universally abide prior to [the stages of] non-arising;
these distinctions refer specifically to the levels of partial realization and so forth.

Regarding the interpretation of King Ajātaśatru’s name—whether as noble or ordinary, deluded or awakened—it precisely clarifies the meaning of the provisional and the real. Its high and low are difficult to know and its secret words unfathomable; its beauty lies within.

He says that this clarifies that others generally accept the interpretations of the first three masters; his intention is to suggest that since these are esoteric teachings, what harm is there in having three different interpretations regarding the conditioned and the unconditioned?
Now, it is said that the following passage refutes the preceding arguments. As for the meaning of "esoteric" (*mi*), its heights and depths are difficult to measure;
how could it be definitively explained in terms of the relative profundity or shallowness, or distance and proximity, of the eighth stage, the first stage, and so forth?

Therefore, we know that others used the meaning of the esoteric to rescue the three previous schools, while the Master of the Commentary now uses the meaning of the esoteric to refute those same three schools. Since their [prior] depth and shallowness were incorrect, the rescuers [are likewise refuted].

This also refutes the four schools and clarifies that the present meaning is consistent with the sutra’s teaching on the "eight dharmas," which refers to the eight winds (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*). Before the King had resolved his mind [for awakening], he was constantly defiled by these eight dharmas;
killing his father corresponds to the four adversities, and coveting the kingdom corresponds to the four complacencies.

The Sūtra says, "This light has no roots. "Root" (mūla) signifies that which is capable of producing [something]. Because the Dharma-realm of the Middle Way is neither producer nor produced, it is said to have no roots.
The Sūtra says, "It is neither hot nor cold. When the King’s body is heated and is illumined by this light, he attains coolness; thus there is a benefit to his physical condition.
Although, in terms of its essential nature (*dharmatā*), it is neither cold nor hot,
the various phrases following "the sūtra says it is neither permanent nor extinguished" all explain this by way of the Middle Way.
When the sūtra states "it truly cannot be spoken," this means that light is the *dharmadhātu*, which is beyond description or perception.

Regarding those who are both ordinary beings and outsiders, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) constitute the stage of the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*). What was mentioned above as the "six abodes" (*ṣaḍvihāra*) refers to the internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*).

However, concerning these six abodes, there are two interpretations. According to the present school’s distinct positions, since the ten stages of faith have not yet severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), they are termed "sick."

Third, regarding the "lower" [stage]: if one looks toward the present school’s tenet, this is simply the stage of general penetration (*sāmānya-avasthā*). What is here called "external ordinary beings" (*bāhya-prthagjana*) specifically refers to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

As for "advancing or retreating," advancing means taking up the distinct teaching (*bheda*), while retreating means taking up the general teaching (*sāmānya*). Viewed from the perspective of the four teachings (*catur-deśanā*) that encompass all meanings, this [classification] does not exhaustively include them.
Now, following the correct explanation below: the seven stages of skillful means consist of the two vehicles of humans and devas, and the bodhisattvas of the three teachings.

Within their respective teachings, each considers its own path to be the ultimate reality; however, the present discussion concerns the Buddha’s intention, which aims to lead them to realize the Perfect [Teaching].
Although he speaks of the partial vehicles, they all serve as skillful means for entering the Perfect; therefore, they are called the "seven stages of skillful means within the Perfect family."
The commentary states: "Regarding the 'seven people who have not yet awakened to the Perfect *I*,' the Buddhas compassionately regard them all;
for should they commit the five heinous crimes while in the realms of humans and devas or at the stage of ordinary beings within the Three Teachings, they would fall into the three miserable paths.
Therefore, the Buddhas' compassionate heart is most urgent toward these individuals, likening them to a sick child—the meaning is as clear as day."

Regarding the sixth dwelling (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*), although there are two interpretations in the lower [traditions], both are distinct stages in comparison to the present [system]. The true understanding (*bhūta-jñāna*) is that of a distinct stage, while the semblance-understanding (*pratibimba-jñāna*) of the six minds pertains to the six dwellings.

Since these six dwellings belong to the internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already destroyed the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), they will never commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*); alternatively, they may be considered as belonging to the common stages (*sāmānya-sthāna*).

Regarding the sixth point, "as in the text": first, the blooming and bright clarity is a metaphor for the arousal of the bodhicitta; next, the ability to cause all those traveling on the road [to see] is a metaphor for cultivation.
This constitutes the pair of arousing the mind and cultivating practice. Next, the pair of wisdom and abandonment:

the gradual increase is a metaphor for the virtue of wisdom, and the decrease is a metaphor for the virtue of abandonment. These three constitute the pair of extinguishing evil and generating good, which eliminates the affliction of greed.
This cessation of evil is the flavor of ambrosia; this is the generation of goodness.

Regarding the "extinguishing of the mind's offenses," from this point downward, each question and answer reveals Jīvaka’s manifestation of the Tathāgata’s hidden response for the benefit of sentient beings.
Furthermore, each question and answer employs the icchantika as a parallel to King Ajātaśatru.
The King’s virtues surpass those of an icchantika because the King possesses the five virtues and is capable of generating the bodhicitta;
whereas the icchantika lacks goodness such that even the Buddha still feels compassion for him, the Buddha would never abandon the King who possesses the five virtues.
Therefore, you should go quickly to treat his mental illness.
Those with grave evil deny the existence of cause and effect;

they sever all wholesome roots of the present and the future because they regard the present as evil, and thus hold that there is no future wholesomeness. If one were to reform their evil and so forth, they would no longer be *icchantikas*;
therefore, we know that *icchantikas* lack both present and future wholesome roots.
Regarding "past minor virtues" and so forth: it is due to the five precepts observed in the past that this human body was obtained.

"Abandoning one and taking another" refers to abandoning [the view of] existence and adopting [the view of] non-existence, and so on; these are explained through successive permutations involving single, double, and complete [positions], as well as the inexpressible (*avyākṛta*).
"High observatory" (gāoguān): *guān* is pronounced with a departing tone; it is also a tower. The *Shiming* states: "An observatory (*guān*) is so called because one observes and gazes from above.
Regarding the analogy of the mountain: a mountain can produce grasses and trees, just as the precepts can produce manifold meanings.
Regarding the analogy of the trees: just as trees depend upon mountains, so too does meditative concentration arise from ethical discipline (*śīla*).

According to this principle, up to the point of "the three vehicles," we know that the elephant metaphor represents the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*), which is identical to the great white ox of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The metaphors of the horse, ox, and sheep represent the three teachings and the three vehicles; these are the sheep, deer, and ox of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If one considers them in terms of power and capacity:
Thus, the ox symbolizes the Bodhisattva, the horse the Pratyekabuddha, and the sheep the Śrāvaka; that the horse is placed first is merely for the sake of linguistic convenience.
If one were to judge by status, however, the horse would symbolize the Bodhisattva and the ox the Pratyekabuddha, which is why the horse precedes the others.

When discussing the four vehicles in terms of their partial or perfect nature, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* provides clear metaphors that correspond to the underlying principles, as traditionally maintained: "The three types of people [are like the sheep, the ox, and the horse]."
Regarding the obscurity of their sentiments,

these non-Buddhists calculate four distinct types of *ātman* because they infer that since caste is divided into four categories— noble and base— their divine *ātman* likewise possesses four different colors.
This is similar to what is clarified in the secular texts of this land [China], which state that the *hun* spirit is clear while the *po* spirit is turbid.

"Category" refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); because it is only when one clings to a self-body that the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) arise, we know that the view of a self-body is the root of all views.

Regarding "non-happiness" and below, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists in regarding what is not the fruit as the fruit; the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which is free from perception, is in reality not *nirvāṇa*, yet one falsely settles upon it as such.
Because they mistakenly conceive of what is merely a state of pleasure as being *nirvāṇa*, it is said that they lack pleasure and lack excellence; such is their false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

To grasp at what is inferior as superior is their prideful attachment to their own doctrine, claiming, "My path alone is true. Consequently, they cause all roots of mundane and supramundane goodness to be swallowed up and destroyed.
Their extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consist of calculating the self to be either annihilated or eternal; here, the metaphor of "falling" refers specifically to their adherence to annihilationism.

Because the view of extremes is particularly heavy, it is singled out for illustration. Regarding the clinging to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): this refers to reckoning what is not a cause as a cause;
although it is truly not the cause of *nirvāṇa*, one erroneously reckons it to be so.
As for "dog-precepts" (*śvavratika*), this means relying on dogs as one's precept in order to attain birth in heaven. Believing this constitutes the first stage, like resting one's head upon a dog.
I say that these five benefits below all involve conceiving views based on the aggregate-body;
therefore, among the nine kinds of aggregates, they are called the "defiled five aggregates" and are thus metaphorically likened to lying in excrement.
One who wears leaves as clothing, though dressed in such raiment, cannot avoid being naked; thus it is a metaphor for shamelessness (*ahrīkya*).
As for "the vehicle driven by evil dharmas": since the carriage is already broken, it is still drawn by a donkey; furthermore, the body [of the vehicle] is dilapidated and not level or upright.
Being both wicked and crooked—the intended meaning is found here.
Regarding the first of the three explanations for "directly south": it accords with the interpretation of the meaning here in this land.

As for the character *li* (離) being "separation from the earth," the *Zhou Yi* (Book of Changes), in its *Li* hexagram, explains that "two brightnesses create *li*. All instances of this character are written with the single radical;
those written with the simplified form *li* are later, artificial distinctions.

Regarding the loss of good and the arising of evil: the south belongs to Fire and the north belongs to Water. Fire is fierce, which is a metaphor for evil; water is gentle, which is a metaphor for good.

As for why the north is considered "above," it is because in the Western lands, the ruler and father face east; therefore, the north is the upper direction. This is explained in detail as recorded previously.
"Dark mechanism" (ming ji) refers to those who possess roots of goodness from past lives but do not yet realize it; hence it is called "dark mechanism.
"Dark knocking" (ming kou) refers to the fact that by virtue of these past roots of goodness, they evoke a sacred response; hence it is called "dark knocking."
Regarding the initial contemplation, all [practitioners] engage in darkened observation and silent assent.
As for the Fourteen Truths appearing in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, its thirty-sixth fascicle states:
"O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the fifth stage knows as it truly is: 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering.'"
"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

He thoroughly knows the conventional truth, thoroughly knows the ultimate truth, thoroughly knows the truth of characteristics, thoroughly knows the truth of distinctions, thoroughly knows the truth of establishment, thoroughly knows the truth of entities, thoroughly knows the truth of arising, thoroughly knows the truth of exhaustion and non-arising, thoroughly knows the entry into the knowledge of truths regarding the path, and thoroughly knows all things.
The Bodhisattva stages consist of the successive accomplishment of the truths, up to the truth of the perfect realization of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

This Bodhisattva knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) because he brings joy to sentient beings according to their mental inclinations; he knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) because he penetrates the single true mark;

and he knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*) because he realizes the specific and general characteristics of phenomena and understands the distinctions among the various states of all dharmas.

One knows the Truth of Differentiation because of skillfully discerning the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; one knows the Truth of Establishment because of awakening to the suffering and affliction of body and mind;

one knows the Truth of Phenomena because of awakening to the continuity of birth in the various realms of existence; one knows the Truth of Arising because of the ultimate cessation of all feverish afflictions;
one knows the Truth of the Knowledge of Exhaustion and Non-arising because of the emergence of non-duality; and one knows the Truth of the Knowledge of Entering the Path because of perfect awakening.
Because it encompasses all modes of practice, one thoroughly knows the sequential continuity and accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages, up to the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This is known through the power of faith and understanding (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*), and not through the power of ultimate realization (*niṣṭhā-jñāna-bala*).
Because those who are icchantikas lack the power of faith and understanding, they deny the existence of this goodness; this is termed "severing the roots of goodness" (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*).
Regarding "past roots of goodness," they are used as a metaphor for past roots of goodness because they inherently possess the foundation of merit.
The phrase "the mutual resonance of the Way" also implicitly contains this meaning.

As for "solitary and without companion," it means that although the Buddha wishes to respond to icchantikas, there is no one with the capacity to receive his appearance in the world or the seeds of goodness.
It is called "solitary" because it is capable of being received.
As for "going to the place of illness," although icchantikas lack the roots of goodness of the three periods of time, they are responded to in secret through the compassion that takes no object;
thus, it is said they "go" because their capacities and conditions are minutely examined.
Next, one contemplates the past: since the present lacks goodness, does the past—which has no beginning—also lack goodness?
To use an analogy for the five sense faculties: the five faculties lack goodness, being like bones and such, which are entirely diseased.
Regarding the phrase "desire will lead to pride and so forth": because desire is of a base nature while pride is an exaltation, pride only arises when one first gives rise to a desirous mind;
thus, the desirous mind prevents the proud mind from being exalted. The character *jiāng* (將) here has the sound of *yù* (禦), meaning to ward off or restrain.
For example, the two views of annihilationism and eternalism are compared to the two bodily excretions, urine and feces;
their mutual subversion when they do not flow together is used as a metaphor for the three karmas, which likewise serves as a metaphor for the absence of goodness.
The Sūtra asks: regarding those who tend to the sick who are icchantikas, though they take evil as their stimulus, they are called "those who tend to the sick.
What is their disposition? Is it that they possess past roots of goodness that can be aroused, or is it that they have none at all?
Regarding "the roots and their objects": this means that the roots and the objects they confront are both devoid of goodness.
Regarding the "seven outflows" (*āsrava*): these refer to the views, afflictions, roots, evils, intimacy, sensations, and mindfulness.
The Sūtra states "not fixed," meaning that for those who are about to die, the future time is vast; since there is the possibility of [wholesome] arising, it is said to be "not fixed."

Those things not prescribed by the Buddha are called "unprescribed" because, when wholesome conditions have not yet arisen, one may give rise to views of eternalism or nihilism and commit the evils of the three karmas.
Regarding the two statements in the sutra: first, upon hearing that Kāḷodāyin had entered prison; second, upon hearing that Cāṇūra saw the Buddha, their offenses were eliminated.
Although he heard these two statements, his mind was still not certain.
The Sūtra says "no certainty in certainty" because one who possesses certainty understands that there is no fixed certainty; thus it is called "no certainty in certainty.

This excludes those who take what is uncertain to be certain, for if the nature of a transgression were fixed, it could not be eliminated; it is only because the nature of the transgression is not fixed that it can be removed.
The Buddha possesses the wisdom capable of removing [afflictions] and is certainly able to remove them; therefore, it is said that he is "concentrated" (*samādhi*).
Regarding the eight kinds of voice, the *Brahmayu Sūtra* states: first, the most excellent voice; second, the easily understood voice; third, the harmonious voice;
fourth, the soft voice; fifth, the unerring voice; sixth, the non-feminine voice; seventh, the venerable and wise voice; eighth, the fearless voice.

Because they inspire fearlessness, the eight qualities of the voice are like the roar of thunder; although they are not listed separately here, they are identical to those sounds produced there, and for this reason they are cited.
Regarding the instruction to "constantly bind the mind" and so forth: these twenty matters cause ordinary persons to rely on concrete objects for observation, thereby subduing their afflictions.
When the mind penetrates phenomena and perceives principle, such that the primary and auxiliary practices are combined, only then is the wondrous contemplation perfected.
"Lacking the wisdom prior to the Way" refers to the absence of contemplative practice and its semblance of meditative concentration and wisdom;
herein, the stage of partial realization is taken as the "middle of the Way," while perfect enlightenment is taken as the "end of the Way."

Regarding the difficulty of attaining freedom from the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*): one is only distantly removed from the eight difficulties of the segmented birth (*bhavāgra*) by reaching the semblance stage (*tad-bhūmi*), whereas one truly leaves behind the eight difficulties of the transformational birth (*pariṇāmika*) only upon entering the stage of true realization (*bhūtārtha*).

Regarding the statement that "not a single dharma exists": within the supramundane dharmas, one has not yet attained even a small portion; therefore, one is unable to prevent [the arising of afflictions].
It brings to rest the cycle of birth and death within the twenty-five states of existence.

The sutra states that those who have crossed the ford of the five heinous crimes have not yet been able to construct the bridge of the Dharma of the six perfections to cross the long ford of the five heinous crimes;
these words apply directly to the person of the King.
Those who traverse the boundless cycle of birth and death may reach its limit upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the pair of emptiness and existence: if one does not undergo karma, one does not obtain its fruit; this is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty.
This is precisely what Vimalakīrti meant by "no self, no agent, and no recipient."
The phrase "there is no self that acts" and so forth clarifies that there is cause and effect; that is, the karmic actions of purity, evil, and name are not lost or destroyed.
This pair of cause and effect consists of the preceding line, which concerns the causes and effects of good, and the subsequent line, which concerns the causes and effects of evil.
The sūtra states that those in the cycle of birth and death due to ignorance are like a hand: whether it is turned palm-down or palm-up, both remain inseparable from the hand;
likewise, birth and death are minor states that never depart from delusion.
The two phrases concerning "Buddha-nature" refer to the fifth and sixth lines.

In the section on the paths of karma (*karmapatha*), it is stated that the preceding twenty matters are subsumed within the three paths, and these three paths are fundamentally the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the second, the detailed exposition: because the textual meaning of the preceding matters was both concise and brief, King Śreṇika’s attachments remained as they were.
To further elaborate on the contemplation of the principle of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-śamatha*) in order to eliminate and purge [delusions] and cause one to awaken to Buddha-nature:
the first two lines of the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sādhana* (Puxian Guan) trace the origin of karma. All karma—that is, the karma of the nine realms—arises from the mind of ignorance;
therefore, it is said to "arise from delusive thoughts" (*vikalpa*). The next line explains the method for destroying karma: sit upright and contemplate.
This indicates that by contemplating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) within one’s physical posture, one clarifies the object of contemplation;

since this is superior among the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), it is specifically mentioned here—one should understand that once one is seated upright, the same applies to the other three. Thus, whether in moments of haste or distress, in active life or retirement, in speech or silence, the mind remains suspended upon the wondrous principle without interruption.
Practicing in this manner, what transgression would not be extinguished? Contemplation itself—*nien ji* (念即)—is [the means].

The true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the three contemplations that are able to observe is precisely the true reality of the three truths (*trisatya*) that are observed. What is this? It is deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, observing deluded thoughts is itself the true Threefold Virtue (*triguṇa*); the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest, yet they vanish within emptiness.

This is called the "Perfect Operation of the Ten Vehicles" through mindfulness of the true reality. Thus, this single phrase is the grand framework of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the essential technique for the secret treasury.

(On Sound and Resonance) Therefore, the *Miaoshengding Jing* (Sūtra on the Sublime Victorious Samādhi) states: "To be able to sit in meditation with a straightforward mind is itself the foremost repentance.

A straightforward mind is simply the mindfulness of the true aspect (*dharmatā*). The two lines following "all transgressions" serve as a metaphor for the extinction of offenses when contemplation is perfected.

The lines beginning with "if one penetrates" conclude by clarifying the intent of the sūtra. Thus, the *Chanmen* (Gate of Meditation) says: "All phenomena without exception belong to the mind; the nature of the mind [is likewise...]"

If even emptiness is thus, how much more so the myriad dharmas? If there were no myriad dharmas, who would be the one committing sinful karma? If one does not encounter sin, one cannot encounter its absence.
By contemplating that sin is unborn, one destroys the fundamental nature of all sins;

because this nature is empty and intrinsically pure, one knows that when the Buddha showed King Ajātaśatru that there is nothing determinate, the essential point lies therein. Question: Since this is a perfect contemplation, why does the sutra...
Regarding the question of whether nature and characteristics are impermanent, the answer is that impermanence is itself permanence; how could this be the same as the dharmas of the Lesser Vehicle?

Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "I say that all dharmas are unborn; this is the meaning of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*). That which arises at the very first moment is simultaneously subject to cessation; I do not speak of this to the foolish.
To know this essence—that the impermanence of arising and ceasing is precisely the principle of the perfect and sudden non-arising—is to realize this intent. This realization depends solely upon...
Because the Buddha-realm is understood by the wise and not by the ignorant who rely on the seven stages of expedient means, it is not explained for their sake.
Regarding the statement in the sutra that "the natures of form and non-form do not harmonize": non-form refers to the four aggregates (*skandhas*).
The nature of form is obstructive, while the nature of the mind is empty and pervasive; since these natures are diametrically opposed, they do not harmonize.

Regarding the phrase "blending the minds of high and low": this refers to broadly inferring that there is no transgression in order to wash away clinging attachments. One should not differentiate by asserting that killing one's father is definitively a grave offense.

However, because these [attachments] all stem from clinging that has not been removed, the arrows of remorse enter the mind; since this obstructs right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), it is difficult to attain the fruits of the Noble Ones (*ārya-phala*).

Therefore, the Buddha extensively discoursed on the absence of transgression to demonstrate that [all things] are fundamentally empty. If one discusses how good and evil do not perish, one will accord with reality.
Alas! When those who have studied the Mahāyāna teachings in a superficial and reckless manner encounter this text, they fail to fathom its profound meaning.
Often they grasp it as their essential core and commit every kind of evil, claiming to have realized non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Yet, one who has truly realized non-arising would not even perform good deeds, let alone indulge in evil. You should know that for such people, the eight hot hells will arrive without even waiting for an invitation.
The path to evil is not reached by walking; yet to claim that one has attained the Way—how utterly deluded!
That which has passed cannot be remonstrated against, but that which is to come can still be pursued. Send word to those who have come to study: examine this and reflect upon it deeply.
The scripture states that "this person shall sit upright" and "lie down in compassion," which refers to the offense of sitting cross-legged; it means the offense of being implicated by association.
As the *Yantie Lun* says, this is like relatives being held jointly liable for crimes.
The scripture further clarifies that this does not apply to kings: a worldly king does not personally utter the command to kill, but merely orders that [the offender's] feet be lopped off.

That the Sūtra also mentions obtaining both good and evil fruits is because [the person] was killed now due to having killed a seer in the past, and obtained the first fruit of the path now due to having made offerings to a corpse in the past.
"Transgressing the law in every way" means acting wickedly at will.
According to my disciples, even those who have violated the precepts do so because they were insane; since they committed the offense without intentional malice, no formal charge of sin is incurred.
Indeed, life is of great value, and jewels are likewise of great value. The Preface to the Book of History (*Shangshu xu*) states that successive dynasties have treasured it, regarding it as supreme.
Regarding the correction of the term "bảo" (protector) in the title *Bǎofù* (Protector and Tutor), it is not incorrect.

For instance, concerning the practice of giving food, as a sutra states: "Suppose a person carrying food for themselves intends to go upon the path to the Tathāgata, but encounters a starving dog and gives it to that dog;
the merit of this is no different from making offerings to the Buddha. This arises because the nature of the mind toward animals and the mind toward the Buddha are one and the same.
Because the body is equal, it is said that they "share the same object and the same true mark.

This refutes those who fall into the error of clinging to extremes and losing the correct principle; for while the essence of karma is neither existent nor non-existent, the King [of Māras] clings exclusively to existence, and thus the Buddha refutes him.
Regarding the use of *nirvāṇa* as an analogy, a question is raised: "The meaning of killing one's father is shallow, whereas the meaning of *nirvāṇa* is profound;

how can the profound be used to illustrate the shallow? The answer is: Here, the easy is used to illustrate the difficult. By means of the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*, it is clarified that there is neither existence nor non-existence, which is easy to understand.
In contrast, when analyzed through the act of killing, its characteristics are difficult to discern. Therefore, the easily understood *nirvāṇa* is now cited [as an analogy].
How much more so regarding killing!

According to the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, the essence of nirvāṇa is neither existent nor non-existent: it is not existent because it is free from all marks, yet it is not non-existent because it possesses all virtues.

Furthermore, with respect to delusion it is not existent, and with respect to awakening it is not non-existent; yet it is also existent, because it can be realized. This clarifies its functional efficacy.

Furthermore, within the first section of the threefold synthesis, it should again be divided into two parts: the initial phrase is the general [statement], while the subsequent three sections beginning with "from having a sense of shame" (*hrī*) are the specific [explanations].
Although they are neither existent nor non-existent, they are nonetheless existent; this is the general [principle]—that which is neither existent nor non-existent.
When discussing the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of karma, it is also existent because its functional capacity (*śakti*) is manifest, as it is capable of producing results.

Regarding the subsequent section on shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*), this first part concerns their actual meaning: a person possessing shame and remorse is not "non-existent," for they possess the capacity to eliminate [unwholesome states];

conversely, one who lacks shame and remorse is not "non-non-existent," for they lack the capacity to eliminate them. Thus, this treatise establishes that the essential nature of karma receives its retribution.
It is named "existence" (*sat*) to manifest its functional capacity (*karmasāmarthya*), because it is able to attain a fruit;
next, the subsequent section proceeds to refute existence by entering into the emptiness of the view of existence, for the view of existence is not non-existent and thus cannot be extinguished.

This clarifies that the essence of the activity of one who possesses the view of existence is also called "existence," etc., to manifest its functional capacity, because it is able to attain a fruit. Within this, first, what is raised?

The following explains that those who perceive existence obtain retribution; thus, the correct understanding of the meaning of "existence" is that there is a name for existence because one perceives existence.
Those who do not perceive existence have no retribution; by citing non-existence, existence is revealed. In the subsequent section, emptiness is refuted to reveal reality.

For one who holds the eternalist view, [existence] is treated as non-existent because it can be annihilated; therefore, realizing and perceiving the principle of permanence is called [the realization of reality].

It is said: When one perceives the eternal through the realization of the eternal, one sees that phenomena are fundamentally quiescent and that no transgression can arise; thus, one is able to extinguish the view of impermanence.
To claim that this is not non-existent because it cannot be extinguished, and to grasp at the meaning of emptiness while calling it the "view of impermanence," is to fail to see reality.
This fails to permanently eliminate delusive thoughts and cause transgressions to cease. Therefore, it is not non-existent that this discourse addresses the substance of karma.

Regarding the phrase "those who constantly see [it]": they cannot avoid manifesting their karma and receiving its retribution. Within this context, the initial question "What is it? is raised, followed by the subsequent explanation.
To regard the constant nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as being fixed and eternal is called "the view of permanence.
The mind that grasps at this is entirely affliction (*kleśa*). Because it assists in the karma of killing and leads to the acquisition of evil retribution, it is said to "possess evil fruits."
Therefore, this concludes the section below.

Since those who hold the view of "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) also incur evil retribution, it was previously taught that those who hold the view of impermanence (*anitya-dṛṣṭi*) are not without [fault].
Now, based on a detailed analysis, the general category can be understood; thus, it is specifically stated that those who hold the view of permanence (*nitya-dṛṣṭi*) suffer evil fruits.
By this principle, the following section concludes the previous three sections.

"Great King, as for the multitude... and so forth clarifies that there is indeed the offense of killing; it gives rise to a sense of shame in the king, causing the king to feel remorse, thereby demonstrating that [the offense] is not non-existent.
Although there is no commentary on these three sections of the sūtra text, they must be carefully analyzed.
Exhorting one to cultivate the contemplation of eternal bliss and so forth, using the Perfect [Teaching] to shatter the partial, is termed "killing.
This is precisely the killing of the parents of ignorance, delusion, and craving.
As for the King’s resolve, this refers to generating the mind of self-cultivation and entering the first stage (*bhūmi*); thus, in the subsequent scripture, the King speaks.
"Jīvaka, I now cast off this impermanent body to attain an eternal body.
To "renew the resolve" means to give rise to the mind that seeks to transform others; therefore, it says, "May I always remain in hell," and so forth.

The section on "Truthful Speech" (*satyavāda*) below explains the secret of speech (*vāg-guhyaka*) as being free from the four faults. Although the text presents three meanings, one should know that it actually encompasses all four.

It should be understood that the three meanings of "truthful," "gentle," and "meaningful" pertain exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). Regarding "false," "harsh," and "frivolous" speech, these three terms generally refer to the three [lower] teachings.

Within the category of "gentle speech," the first two lines of the sutra clarify the concealment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and the provisional application of skillful means (*upāya*), stating: "For the sake of the multitude, I speak of the coarse. The subsequent two lines clarify...
Because the provisional is opened up to reveal the real, it is said that "all return to the primary meaning" (*paramārtha*).

Thus, the teachings of the four periods and three vehicles are all termed "coarse," whereas only the *amṛta* (nectar) of the perfect and integrated teaching is called the "language of the teaching's true meaning. These two phrases may be understood through analogy.
Regarding the meaning of the five types of repentance (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*), the sequence in the scriptural text is slightly disordered. According to other sūtras, one should first perform:

(1) confession (*deśanā*), (2) exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*), (3) rejoicing (*anumodanā*), (4) dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and (5) aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). Since all these are termed "repentance," they must serve to remedy transgressions; thus, there should be no lack of sequential order as found in the present text.

If one follows other sūtras and maintains the proper sequence, it serves a purposeful progression: namely, that if past offenses are not eliminated [through the preceding stages], [the subsequent ones will be ineffective].
Merely offering exhortations and requests, once the exhortations have been made, one observes the signs and hears the teachings, then practices in accordance with those teachings.

If jealousy is not eliminated, and one’s own virtues are weak and inferior, one will not even rejoice in the merits of others; how then could one perform dedication? When the four factors are complete, one should lead them with aspiration.

Regarding the destruction of transgressions, one should know that repentance destroys the three types of karma and the nature-based and prohibitory offenses, while exhortation and request destroy slander.
Regarding the sin of slandering the Dharma: having previously heard various teachings and given rise to slander, I now request the Buddha to speak so that all may hear;

thus, I am able to overturn the sin of slandering the Dharma. Regarding the sin of destroying through jealousy: whereas in the past I gave rise to jealousy toward specific objects, I now rejoice in everything;
thus, I attain the overturning of my former jealous mind. Regarding the dedication that destroys the sins of existence: as for the merit formerly performed...
Merely following the cycle of birth and death serves as the cause for all states of existence; one cannot escape it oneself, much less enable others to leave behind the causes of existence.
Now, by possessing both types of dedication, one escapes both for oneself and for others. Therefore, dedication follows the gate of Nirvana, and the making of vows destroys false aspirations.
These vows then guide the preceding four [perfections] to their respective destinations. Thus, we know that King Ajātaśatru’s address to the Buddha was clear and explicit.

How profound is the intent behind the five repentances! Thus, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "If one diligently practices the five repentances during the six periods of day and night, one can attain bodhi without relying on ascetic practices.
The phrase "the Three Jewels constantly remain in the world" refers to the request for them to abide in the world.
Regarding the phrase "I vow to shatter all [obstacles]": when sentient beings shatter Māra, I rejoice accordingly.

As for the vow that "all shall give rise to the initial mind," "initial mind" should be understood as referring to the first stage (the first bhūmi), because one first perceives the Buddha-nature therein;
it should also be understood as generally referring to the stages prior to the bhūmis.

Regarding the phrase "binding the mind with recollection and contemplation" and so forth: this refers to realizing that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and oneself have merged into one, such that the three are non-different;
when one observes in this way that the wondrous nature is serene and still, it is called "constant recollection."

Regarding the statement "ultimately seeing the Buddha-nature": Mañjuśrī and others have exhausted their delusions; since the ultimate fruit is not remote but is now manifest, it is said that they have "clearly realized" it.
Question: Why is Mañjuśrī alone singled out, while other sages are not mentioned? Answer: Mañjuśrī is the foremost among Bodhisattvas;
he has received the Buddha’s entrustment in this assembly; and he shares a karmic affinity with King Śrīgupta. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is directly revealed through him.
Because [other] names are [merely] conventional, the Bodhisattvas do not do so, and therefore it is not pointed out here. Mañjuśrī is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode);
because the Buddha-nature of the three virtues is neither vertical nor horizontal, it is called "wondrous."
The *Sūtra of the Adornment of the Great Assembly of All Buddhas* is so named because bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds on awakening vow to transform sentient beings;
thus, they are able to increase the assembly of the Buddhas, which is why it is called "Adornment.
Regarding *Vipaśyin*, this is translated as "Victorious Vision" (*Shèngguān*). He appeared in the world ninety-one kalpas prior to the present Bhadrakalpa. At Śrāvastī...
Since the King has long since resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he has never fallen into hell; how could he suddenly commit a crime of immediate retribution today?

Thus we know that the previous statement "he had not yet resolved his mind" refers to his manifested traces (*traces*), while the present statement "he has already resolved his mind" reveals his fundamental reality (*the source*).
The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (or *Lokarāja-sūtra*) has a separate text titled the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle, which fully elucidates these events.

It is like entering Piṇḍola’s [realm]: this demonstrates that cause and effect do not perish; rather, one merely repays them while in the state of a sage, which is equivalent to purifying a Buddha-land.
Just as it is not difficult for a wealthy man to repay his debts, there is no suffering involved. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is simply the *Huá* (Flower) [Sūtra].
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and its commentary refer to this as the *Acintya-sūtra*.
Regarding the term "infant" (*āraka*) in the "Chapter on Infant Conduct":
the *Cangxie pian* states that "male is called 'er' (child) and female is called 'ying' (infant). Here, the term "infant" is used to encompass both genders.
Furthermore, Liu Xi’s *Shiming* states: "An 'infant' (*ying'er*) refers to that which is before the chest; one holds it before the chest and nourishes it with milk.
This serves as a metaphor for the application of the fruit [of Buddhahood]: manifesting superior or inferior bodies to preach provisional or ultimate teachings is all termed "infant-like conduct.
Therefore, the meaning of the five kinds of infants is clarified here in the subsequent scripture.
The "Great" refers to the practitioner who is like a Tathāgata, namely the "Perfect Infant.
Therefore, it must take *nirvāṇa* as its essence in order to be able to give rise to both the Great and Small functions.

Regarding the "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*) that destroys the "yellow leaves" of other teachers—this refers to the "Infant of Human and Heavenly Beings. If one takes expedient wisdom as the essence, then...
It is simply that they can give rise to the functions of humans and devas.

When it is said that "both practices are thus," it means that both clarify cause and effect as well as the partial and the perfect; by analogy, one should know that this chapter ought to possess this meaning, which is why it is said that [this section] should not be absent.
Question: Since an infant is already a resultant function, why is it explained as a cause? Answer: [This is because... (The text continues with the explanation).
The fruit of the *yathābhūta* (ye-da) is produced from causes; through the cultivation of partial or perfect practices, one obtains the utility of the Great or Small vehicles.

Here, as the meaning encompasses both, it is subsumed under "cause" while its primary focus is on "fruit. It is also like the case of the "Noble Brahma," which primarily resides in "cause" but also extends to "fruit.
If that is so, although the "Heavenly Practice" (*devacara*) specifically resides in "fruit," in principle it also extends to "cause. This refers to the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka*.
It may be inferred accordingly.
From "the initial generation of the mind" up to "one who practices the path," this refers to the nominal generation of the mind (*nāma-cittotpāda*).

Regarding "the transformer and the transformed," the Buddha is the transformer; the four virtues of realized fruition and those of superior faculties are the transformed. [The latter] refers to cultivation.
Because of these four virtues, it is said that "all practice" refers to those who, being superior to the partial and small [vehicles], correspond to the highest faculties. First,
regarding the statement "those who are ultimately unable to speak," this refers back to the third category, "unable to come," from the scriptural text in order to establish the present meaning.

To follow the speech and sounds of others means to preach according to their capacities and conditions—speaking of the partial and the small, and discussing the permanent and the impermanent—and then to lead them from the provisional back to the ultimate;
thus the Sūtra says, "It also causes them to attain understanding through these causes."
Regarding the fact that the names of the objects in the sutra are not uniform:

because young children are fond of repeatedly calling out to objects, [the text] does not speak of "returning" while possessing the four virtues. This is because the preceding [section] on "not arising" and so forth corresponds to the four opposing virtues;

thus, "not speaking" is a metaphor for "joy. Now, since there are again four virtues regarding speech, it says "returning possesses [them]. By this analogy, each preceding case should likewise [be understood].
Although the words of the Buddha regarding these four are concise, according to their meaning they should be understood as being fourfold;
yet because their essence is mutually integrated and non-dual, this statement can be made, and thus it is said that "the other three should also be understood in this way."
"Bahe" is the sound of a child learning to speak.

If we take the character "he" alone, "he" is shallow while "ba" is deep; since the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka are contrasted with the teachings for the Two Vehicles to receive the name "Mahāyāna," and [the latter] is not yet untainted (anāsrava), the present text uses "ba" to correspond to the "Vaipulya" (Extensive).

The *Hehe wenzi zishu* (Self-Explanatory Notes on the Combined Text) states that according to the combined text, "harmony" (*he*) is named "impermanence. However, based on the combined text, which explains by approximating the provisional (*kai*) and entering it into the perfect (*yuan*), it says:

"Having heard [the teaching], one takes it as the Dharma of permanence," and so forth. The Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) merely points to what is opened up and judges it to belong to the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
The six characters mentioned—suffering and pleasure, day and night, father and mother—are those who are without hatred or love;
they do not hate the night nor cherish the day. One should take parents as a metaphor for object and wisdom (*ālambana* and *jñāna*).

The text is abbreviated and does not provide an explanation, but the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "Not knowing suffering and pleasure means the merging of sorrow and joy; not knowing day and night means the equalizing of brightness."

To be ignorant of the distinction between kin and stranger is to fail to distinguish between those one hates and those one loves; to make no distinction between the great and the small is to lose sight of the significant and the trivial.
This accords with the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others, for the Sūtra says: "One's mind is equal toward all sentient beings."
The initial analogy regarding "not committing great transgressions" and so forth explains that the illustrative text refers to the inability to perform various deeds,
whether great or small.
"Practicing the Middle Way" means remaining in the center, free from the two extremes.
The analogy for false permanence is that the willow tree remains ever-present. The analogy for false purity is that it is said to be gold.
The analogy for false bliss is that oxen and horses can be ridden, thus eliminating the suffering of walking on foot.
The analogy for false self is that men and women are human beings, and every person must possess a self.
Those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties give rise to delusions based on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
This is because both those on the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) and those on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) partially realize cessation.
Regarding the "nine grades of increased cultivation," this refers to the three grades each established for enemies, friends, and neutral persons.

Second, those who are "half-deluded" refer generally to Bodhisattvas; because they have only destroyed the afflictions within the realm (dhātu) while the afflictions outside the realm remain entirely intact, they are called "half-deluded.
Since delusion is defiling, it contradicts the meaning of purity.
However, because an infant gives rise to conceptual attachments, such a being is merely an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and not a manifestation through transformative power (*nirmāṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "because [the path] is accomplished through practice" and so forth: this refers to progressing from the shallow to the deep and entering from the provisional (*upāya*) into the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*).
Thus, beginning with the minor virtues of humans and devas, one ultimately returns to the Great Parinirvāṇa. One should know that everything prior to this stage is termed "weeping."
The meaning of weeping does not apply solely to the three miserable realms (*tricāṭu*).

Regarding the attainment of the fruit, [the author] below reproaches the ancients; the scriptural text clearly states that one has attained Great Nirvāṇa, yet they do not know it to be the fruit—how can this be?
This means he reproaches the ancients for failing to perceive the explicit text. As the poem says:
How is it that I have so much forgotten?
That which is also called "Great Nirvana" is partially attained at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). If this is so, then the present attainment of Great Nirvana is likewise the first stage;
its position is exactly equal to the two fruits of the previous sages, the *Arhat* and the *Brahman*.
The third section on single conjunctions refers to the three major divisions at the beginning of the "Chapter on Noble Conduct" (*Ārya-caryā-varga*).

Regarding the phrase "up to ninety" and so forth: because the remaining three are abbreviated, it says "up to.

To explain them fully, one should say that [the fourth] extensively clarifies the Brahma-conduct (brahmacarya), the fifth extensively clarifies the celestial conduct (devacara), and the sixth, seventh, and eighth extensively clarify the infant-like conduct (bālacaryā).
Taichang (the Emperor) decreed that the preceding two schools were judged by Master Zong;

as for the latter four, they extensively follow the final two categories. Regarding the seventh merit, from the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment up to the tenth merit, the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the realization of the Buddha-nature—these all constitute self-cultivation (*svayam-pratipatti*).
As for the "two practices" mentioned in the context of the "sick child," both are forms of transforming others (*parārtha*).
Therefore, it is said that they are entirely non-corresponding.
In the commentary by Guangzhai, there are two sections: first, the dual presentation; second, the dual explanation beginning with "Both being... First, the explanation of the identity of essence:

the five practices and ten virtues are both causal goodness and not the ultimate fruit; they represent the culmination of study for those outside the ranks of the ordinary person during the ten stages of faith.

The subsequent explanation of the meaning differs from the preceding one: if one considers the retributive fruit of the Sublime Enlightenment (Sugata-jñāna), then everything from the tenth stage downward is collectively termed the "cause," and within this cause there exists its own "habituated fruit" (vāsanā-phala).
Regarding "eliciting the subsequent fruit of cultivation": this refers to the causal stage of cultivation prior to the [ten] stages eliciting the fruit of cultivation on the [ten] stages;
therefore, the cause that elicits it is termed the "five practices.

Regarding "repaying the prior cause of cultivation": this refers to the fruit of cultivation on the [ten] stages repaying the five practices as the cause of cultivation; therefore, it is termed the "retribution."

If the fruits are taken as the merits, then the five practices are the preparatory causes (*hetu*) prior to the stages of the Grounds (*bhūmi*), and the ten virtues are the preparatory fruits (*phala*) on the Grounds;

this constitutes a difference in meaning. However, when viewed from the perspective of the Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), both are causes. The reason it was previously stated that their essence is one lies precisely here.
How can such an explanation of the beginning and end of the Path of Teaching according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) be reconciled with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjing*)? If...
This is not so; for how could those from the first bhūmi upward lack the eight attainments of the retribution fruit? Therefore, the following refutation states:
"This is the stage of the Bodhisattva.
As for taking the diamond-mind (*vajracitta*) as its essence, that refers to the sixth merit, which possesses the entry into the three stages of the diamond.
The statement "using the Golden Mind of Equal Enlightenment as the essence" refers to the two schools, namely Yao and Liang.
As for what they have said, it has been refuted by Taichang.
In the first section of the Kai Shan [commentary], the text first sets forth their doctrine; the subsequent citations of scriptural passages all serve to refute it.

As for the statement "Where is there no exhortation?"—since every passage following the five lines of prose contains an exhortation to practice, why wait for the King of Virtue (King De) alone to clarify such encouragement?

As for those who "examine the extant texts," this means they scrutinize the commentaries and interpretations left behind by various masters; [they find that] none of them withstand the refutations presented above.
Because this accords with the intent of the sūtra, I shall cite it to refute [the opposing view].
Now, based on what follows, I will clarify the present explanation. First, relying on the text to define the meaning, the five lines state: "Cultivation exists in the cause;
this refers to the ten matters prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Attainment exists in the fruit; this refers to ascending the stages."
The first three sections resolve doubts and clarify the underlying intent.
As for the text, that which explains the fruits of practice is not extensive;
this does not mean that the cultivation [of practice] is not explained, for as cited above, the initial undertaking of the five matters within the first of the nine merits is itself cultivation.
This is because one abandons the few for the many and leaves the peripheral to grasp the central; thus, his conduct and virtue are judged by means of cultivation and realization.

Regarding the explanation of the name "Virtue King" (*Guṇarāja*), the first part explains it through self-cultivation and transforming others, while the second part explains it in terms of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) to demonstrate that the aforementioned self and others do not transcend these three virtues.
As for the initial explanation, it states that "external transformation is extensive" because it universally illumines the ten realms.

Those who practice the profound internally occupy the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); thus, their position is adjacent to Subtle Enlightenment (*tathāgata*). Therefore, they are called "Noble" (*ārya*).

Because they have realized that which transcends the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they are titled "King of Virtue" (*Guṇarāja*). "Virtue" (*guṇa*) refers precisely to the three virtues (*triguṇa*) that have been realized.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage explains the names by way of the three virtues, as in the text.
As for the "Supreme Dharma-nature," it should be called the *dharmakāya*.
Regarding the titling of this chapter from a human perspective: if it were based on what is realized, it should be titled "The Chapter on the Ten Merits";
however, since it is currently based on the person who realizes it, the intent is to clarify that because the person has already realized the Dharma, the Dharma is not in vain.
Regarding the statement that "one who has thus practiced until reaching merit" practices by relying on the sutras to cultivate the preceding five practices and thereby realize these ten virtues:
Question: Since the "heavenly practice" (*deva-caryā*) is the fruit, why is it said that one cultivates the preceding five practices?
Answer: The five practices encompass both cause and fruit, though they differ in being either secondary or primary. Here, we speak in terms of their commonality as causes.
Furthermore, the meaning of the perfect contemplation of the three truths and the complete fulfillment of the five practices is as recorded previously.

Regarding the phrase "that which is not known by discriminative wisdom" and so forth: for Bodhisattvas of the Shared and Distinct [Teachings] who have emerged from the provisional to manifest in the world, discriminative wisdom is difficult to produce;

whereas for the two vehicles of the two teachings who have entered the *nirvāṇa* of emptiness, such wisdom is easy to obtain. The Middle Way Buddha-nature is not something that these two types of wisdom can know.
Therefore it is said that it is neither difficult nor easy.
That which is "without limit and without center" means that because the limit is itself the center, there is no limit; and because the center is itself the limit, there is no center.
Since center and limit are mutually non-existent, what form or characteristic could there be?

The "three kinds of wisdom resembling the Path" refer to the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) in the Lesser Vehicle; in the Shared Teaching, this corresponds to the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*).
It is still not equal to the realization of the Path at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching, which is identical to the Perfect Teaching.

Since even the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*) follow a sequential progression, and we do not yet employ them here, how could the ancients have used the three kinds of wisdom resembling the Path shared by the Shared Teaching to explain this? Therefore, it excludes the Perfect Teaching.
The meaning of the text becomes increasingly profound.
The commentary clarifies that the following section concludes the three preceding schools, collectively establishing ten errors.

Regarding the phrase "not hearing" (*aśruta*) and so forth in the commentary: the initial matter clearly states "not hearing," yet it is translated as "hearing-wisdom" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) when explaining the meaning. Thus, the error is evident.
This constitutes an error.
To interpret it as "conceivable" is because the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) of the Hīnayāna are indeed conceivable;
to interpret it as "manifest" is because these ten virtues in the present text are precisely the secret treasury of the Perfect Vehicle (*pūrṇayāna*), yet others have treated them as Hīnayāna.
To explain this explicitly:
those who interpret it as being partial or deficient [understand] that the three wisdoms of the Small Vehicle’s "partial truth" do not possess the three virtues in their perfect completeness.
As for the common interpretation: since the three wisdoms of the Small Teaching were already clarified in the past, how could they be considered "ordinary" now that they are heard?
On the contrary, this is even more startling and strange.
Those who formulate a discriminatory interpretation [fail to see that] the five dharmas are perfectly realized without distinction; how could they be mutually dependent and differentiated?
As for "exhausting the limits," it refers to the partial truth of the Hīnayāna, which is a limit of emptiness rather than the inexhaustible dharma of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "as stated in the Buddhist sutras, etc. in the text below, this refers to the resistance [of the mind]—that is, the ten previous faults.

To say that it "still involves the characteristics of causes" (*yōu cān yīn xiàng*) means that although one has heard these words, they are based on scriptural testimony; because, at first glance, it appears as though heard from another, it is said to "still involve the characteristics of causes.
"Involving" (*cān*) here means to be mixed with.

Furthermore, this refers to the practitioner within the realization itself; just as one who has attained the first stage initiates the practice of the second stage, this constitutes the true cause which is already a partial fruit.
Thus, we know that the ten virtues pertain exclusively to what is realized and attained.

If one seeks the meaning by following the literal text, as the masters of today do, they will recognize from the passage beginning with "having heard this chapter" that it refers to the characteristics of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).

However, if one judges the text according to its underlying meaning, as in the previous five lines which correctly concern the cultivation of causes, one knows that these ten virtues must clarify the attainment of realization;
therefore, one should judge the text based on this meaning.
Otherwise, this is a refutation of the ancients. "Simulacrum" (*xiàng*) may also be said to mean "resembling but not yet real.
It is not something to be grasped from another source; rather, it is as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The entire body of wisdom is not realized through another;

its teaching in lands and its teaching in atoms is inexhaustible"—this is precisely its characteristic. This, too, is a refutation of the ancients who relied on the understanding derived from the wisdom of hearing.
This refers to "hearing the hearing. Since one has already heard from another, there is both a subject who hears and an object that is heard; thus it is called "hearing the hearing.
How can one attain this? Not hearing is the principle, and hearing is wisdom; because wisdom is generated from the principle, it is called "not-hearing-hearing."

Regarding the brief enumeration of three types: although the full explanation is immeasurable, it does not transcend the three truths; therefore, this brief enumeration already encompasses the complete exposition.
As for the statement that all three truths are "heard by not hearing," this refers to the arising of the three kinds of wisdom based upon the principle of the three truths.
The following clarifies that although the preceding explanations appear sequential, the proofs necessarily occur simultaneously; thus it is said that the three dharmas reside within a single mind.

This is not the same as the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), which posits emptiness first, the provisional second, and the Middle third, nor does it share the view that the two contemplations are shallow while the Middle Way is deep.
Since it differs even from the Separate Teaching, how could it possibly be shared with the two vehicles of the Two Teachings?

Although they have attained the partial truth (pratisaṃvid-satya), they do not realize that the true void (śūnyatā) inherently possesses all phenomena, which are identical to the Middle Way in their very essence;
therefore, it is said that they "do not know the secret.

Regarding the nature and characteristics of the Three Jewels: because their characteristics are distinct, yet their three natures are identical, they are one; thus, they are called the "one essence" (ekakāya).
Regarding the Three Jewels:
from "all Buddhas" to "unchanging," the profound is cited to manifest the shallow;
this is because Bodhisattvas realize the same as the Buddhas, and thus the Buddhas are cited to manifest the Bodhisattvas.
The sūtra states that the Tathāgata’s entry into nirvāṇa means that one who has attained perfect enlightenment by riding the path of suchness comes without coming;

this is the meaning of "coming without coming," which corresponds to the beginning of nirvāṇa. That which is realized and entered is departing without departing; this is the meaning of "departing without departing," which corresponds to the end.
Thus, the beginning and the end are combined into a single phrase.
That each and every phenomenon is none other than the Middle Way means that since these five phenomena are all synonymous names for the Middle Way, each is capable of possessing twenty propositions.
To briefly explain the meaning of these twenty propositions found in the Sūtra: first, "neither existent nor non-existent" refers to the Middle Way, which is not the two truths;
"neither conditioned nor unconditioned" refers to [the fact that it] is not among the conditioned phenomena of the Four Truths.
