Suffering and its origin are neither conditioned nor unconditioned; this is not because they involve the realization or non-realization of truth.
They are neither form nor non-form; this is not because they pertain to matter or mind. They are not "names"; this is not because they consist of the four aggregates. They are not "not names";

this is not because they consist of the aggregate of form. They are not "characteristics"; this is not because they consist of the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. They are not "without characteristics."

That which is "not" is not the truth; that which is "neither existent nor non-existent" is neither the existence of the twenty-five realms of being (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) nor the twenty-five realms themselves.
That emptiness is "not a thing" means it is not what is perceived by the six sense faculties; that it is "not not a thing" means it is not the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
That which is "neither cause nor effect" means it is neither the cause and effect of the two states of *pariccheda* (segmented birth) and *pariṇāma* (transformative birth); it is "not dependent."
It is not that the two extremes are mutually dependent to manifest the "absolute beyond dependence," for even this "absolute" must itself be negated to be truly called absolute.
It is neither light nor darkness; it is not the luminosity of the Buddha’s fruit-intelligence, nor is it the delusive darkness of ordinary beings.

It is not "departing," as it is not the departure of the Two Vehicles from the triple world; yet it is not "not departing," as it is not the failure of humans and devas to emerge from birth and death. It is not permanent.

It is not the "provisional" bodhisattvas nor those of externalist heterodox views who hold to eternalism or non-eternalism; it is not the non-eternality of the two vehicles who are stalled in emptiness, nor is it the view of annihilationism;
it is not at the stage of severing delusions, nor is it at the stage of not severing delusions;
it is neither beginning nor end, nor is it like the externalists' calculation of a primordial darkness or the extinction that occurs after eighty thousand kalpas.
This "end" is not the dualistic reckoning of annihilationism or eternalism; nor is it the beginning of generating the mind or the ultimate end.
It cannot be understood as the past and so forth.
"The rest is also like this" means that the nine subsequent merits are likewise so.
What the Sūtra refers to as "all the scriptures of external paths" are, in fact, originally the inconceivable *saṃvṛti-satya* (conventional truth) of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, the preceding "Chapter on Words and Letters" states that these are what the Buddha taught and not the teachings of external paths;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says that even worldly speech accords with the True Dharma—this is precisely that meaning. It is only that external paths do not know this and instead cling to them.

Those of the two vehicles, being unable to penetrate the Dharma for themselves, claim this is a heterodox scripture; yet the Bodhisattva realizes that there is nothing therein that is not conventional truth.
Therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "The meaning of the secret [teachings] is now understood."
The *Zezhou Shu* (Commentary by Zezhou) on the *Sūtra of the Four Vedas* states: "In foreign lands there were four great masters of the treatises:
first, Vāyavya, who composed the *Caturveda-śāstra*, also called the *Veda*; this is translated as 'Treatise on Wisdom.

It contains one hundred million [verses] and elucidates the methods for fire-worship and repentance. Second, Yajurveda, which elucidates the methods for giving and sacrificial offerings. Third, Atharvaveda..."
The second treatise, known as the *Jñānaprasthāna* (Treatise on Knowledge), clarifies all methods of warfare;

it is called "Knowledge" because it provides knowledge regarding the military strategies of foreign lands and the arising of wisdom therein. It was composed by the second master, Pāṇini, and is titled the *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar);
this is called the "Explanatory Treatise" (*Vyākhyā-śāstra*) because it elucidates all phenomena concerning phonemes, names, sounds, and phrases. The third master was named Kātyāyana.
Vīra was a yellow-headed ṛṣi who composed the *Sāṃkhya-sūtra* (here translated as "Enumeration"); this is the name of the treatise he composed.

Within that treatise, twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are analyzed; its function pervades the great earth, and its essence consists of the enumeration of wisdom. The twenty-five truths are as recorded previously and will be set forth below in Chapter Four, "The Exposition of the Truths.
The master of this school is named Ulūka, a blue-eyed ṛṣi; he is the one who composed [the commentary].
The *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* is here named the most excellent exposition of the meaning of the six categories (*ṣaṭ-tattva*).
The commentary states: "There are three fundamental non-Buddhist schools. However, the calculations of all outsiders do not exceed those of two gods and three sages.
The two gods are Maheśvara and Viṣṇu—the latter is translated as *Pianjing* (Pervasive Purity)—as recorded in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
It is said that this is the third dhyāna, the Peak Heaven (*Bhavāgra*). The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "The Universal Purity Heaven (*Śubhakṛtsna*) has four arms;

he holds a conch and a wheel and rides upon a golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*). Possessing great supernatural power, he is prone to anger and harm; because people of the time feared his majesty, they came to revere him. Maheśvara is here called 'Great Sovereign' (*Mahādeva*);
he is the Peak Heaven of the Form Realm (*Rūpadhātu*), possessing three eyes and eight arms, and he rides [upon a bull]."
The White Ox holds a white fly-whisk and possesses great majestic power;

it can overturn the world and lift up the World-Honored One to serve as the basis for transformation, as detailed at length in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) commentary. Regarding the three sages: the first is Kapila, translated here as "Yellow Head," whose head is like the color of gold.
He preached one hundred thousand verses known as the *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*, which is here called "Calculation" (*shushu*). It employs two [principles].
The fifteenth is the *Satya-prakāśa*, which maintains the thesis that the effect exists within the cause (*satkāryavāda*). Second is the *Ulūka-sāṃkhya*; "Ulūka" is translated here as "Owl.
This sage hid in mountain valleys during the day to compose scriptures and wandered about preaching the Dharma at night.
Because he was like that bird, he received this name. His treatise also consists of one hundred thousand stanzas and is called the *Vaiśeṣika*. This...
The Ājīvikas (known as *Anuttara*) maintain that there is no fruit within the cause; they take the six truths as their primary tenet.
The Kṣapaṇakas (translated as "Asceticism") take calculation as their sacred dharma; they have composed a scripture of one hundred thousand verses called the *Nirgrantha*.

These people sever the fetters and take the six obstructions and four turbidities as their doctrine. They maintain that within the cause there is both fruit and no fruit, and that [the self] is both one and many.

Furthermore, the thesis regarding the six hindrances, the four turbidities, and the names and meanings of the six truths differs [from previous accounts] and is all as explained in the commentary on the eleventh fascicle.
It states: "As for the mere listing of Kapila and Ulūka, Vaiśeṣika is the treatise composed by Ulūka.
The present commentary, based on the three schools of non-Buddhists to interpret the sūtra, notes that within the sūtra only two rishis appear, and no *Lakula* is mentioned.
The term "śa-pa" is merely an abbreviation.
Furthermore, as for "ka," this is based on the calculations of the Le-sha school, which do not go beyond the two directions previously mentioned; therefore, the sutra does not clarify it.
However, if one considers the four great masters, the scriptural text is already sufficient, as in the explanation cited above from Zezhou.
That which was never heard before in the sūtras is not heard now; yet, by attaining and knowing it within this very sūtra, one hears it—this is what is meant by "hearing that which was not heard.
For those who hear the Dharma of the True Truth (*tattva*), the eleven divisions of the Hīnayāna merely expound partial truth; therefore, the sūtra says "ten."
Some know this to be the True Truth;

that is, those who have attained perfect realization understand that the empty truth of the Two Vehicles is itself endowed with the Three Virtues. What you all practice is the path of the Bodhisattva;

because awakening to the Small Vehicle is itself the Great Vehicle, it is called "perfect realization. Thus one knows that if one understands the ten realms as being within the single mind, then the three [realms]...
When both truths are fused together, what can cause delusion? The meaning of "not hearing what is heard" is as clear as parting the clouds.
The profound and secret meaning of the sutra was previously unheard; now, by means of this sutra, it is heard.
This is not merely an augmentation of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), but rather a thorough refutation of others' interpretations.
The text states that what follows below extensively explains the scriptural passages to prove the antiquity of [this] view as incorrect.
As for the phrase "near to Bodhi," it refers to the ten stages of partial realization (*bhūmi*) being close to ultimate Bodhi.
First, regarding the "causal conditions" (*nidāna*): this refers to the fact that hearing and receiving this sutra is precisely the causal condition for attaining true benefit;
because it is the cause and origin [of that attainment], it is called "causal conditions.

Regarding the phrase "contemplating phenomena through provisional wisdom": one asks, if provisional wisdom thoroughly realizes the inherent three thousand [dharmas] and is precisely the contemplation of principle, why is it termed "contemplating phenomena"?

The answer regarding the illumination of phenomena (*dharma*) arises from realizing that all things are inherently complete within one's own nature; because one thereby knows that all dharmas are entirely from within one's own mind, when observing external objects, one sees only the inherent completeness of nature.
Thus, it is said that "provisional wisdom illuminates phenomena. Indeed, in investigating verbal teachings, one must recognize their fundamental source;

one must not follow after names and become deluded regarding their essential meaning. Therefore, know that although the essence of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) is fused and identical, there is nonetheless no lack of distinction in their functional efficacy.

These distinctions collectively encompass all phenomena; yet when one brings them back to the realm of mind and objects, nothing surpasses the provisional as a means to dispel attachments and enter the state of non-arising.
Without departing from emptiness, through the three contemplations practiced as a perfect unity, the Buddha-way can be restored.
Regarding the statement that those who see the Buddha-way from afar "see the small as the great," what is meant by "afar"?
This means seeing the profound and far-reaching Buddha-way, rather than the shallow and near path of the two vehicles.
"Practicing the four dharmas" refers to: first, writing; second, reading and reciting until mastery; third, explaining them to others; and fourth, contemplating their meaning.

The first is physical action (*kāyakarman*); the second and third are verbal action (*vākkarman*); and the fourth is mental action (*manaskarman*). Furthermore, three of these constitute one's own practice, while the third serves to transform others through teaching.
In general, when citing these four pairs and eight items for comparative evaluation, one must understand that these four dharmas surpass the act of merely listening and receiving [the teachings].

The words regarding "listening and receiving" are all categorized under the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while the four practices such as "writing" and so forth belong to the stage of the noble one (*ārya*).

It is an error for other teachers who do not understand this to claim that these refer to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Regarding the four pairs in the sutra: first is the pair of principle and meaning; second, from the words "good son" (*kulaputra*) onwards, is the pair of name and meaning;
third, from the words "furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) onwards, is the pair of understanding and practice; fourth, from the words "good son" onwards, is the [pair of] phenomena...
The meaning is twofold:
"seeing" refers to seeing the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) by breaking through the portion of ignorance regarding giving;
"severing doubt" refers to external treatises, for by means of internal realization and benefit, one severs and abandons doubt regarding external objects.
It is said that this refers to external treatises.

Furthermore, regarding the term "wisdom and abandonment" (*jñāna-prahāṇa*): in the preceding chapter, the internal realization of benefit was the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while the severing of doubt here is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
This clarifies that the arising of the following analogy demonstrates that wisdom and abandonment are simultaneous.

Regarding the mutual clarification of the preceding and the succeeding: the former clarifies that the quality of wisdom must necessarily possess this quality of abandonment, while the latter clarifies that the quality of abandonment must necessarily possess the former quality of wisdom.
The analogy of light and darkness makes this easy to understand upon reflection.

Those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature do so because the stages of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*) in the Separate and Perfect Teachings (*bhedavāda* and *pūrṇavāda*) precede the stages of the Grounds (*bhūmi*) and Abidings (*vihāra*).
Yet, this current text states that one "comprehends that all possess Buddha-nature," and in the section on benefiting others, it says, "then one attains the vision [of it].

Since the meaning of "benefiting" implies the severing of doubt, their significance is mutually manifest; thus, we know that what is here called "comprehending" is identical to the aforementioned "seeing the nature. This must be understood accordingly.
How erroneous is the interpretation based on hearing and reflection according to the sequence of the scriptural passage!
Now, the following section correctly demonstrates the present meaning.

Those who suspect that the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is a perversion of impermanence do so because they believe the Buddha must certainly cease to exist, and thus it belongs to the category of impermanence.
Regarding "three singles paired with one double": the three singles refer to bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*); the one double refers to *nirvāṇa* and permanence (*nitya*).

As for the note stating "and so forth," it should be said that if one suspects whether the Buddha is true bliss or suspects whether he is suffering, and so on, there would logically be eight such points. However, this interpretation by the Master of the Commentary is itself one approach; if one follows the text and meaning of Jingxi, it is even more convenient: [The text continues: "If one suspects whether the Buddha is true bliss or suspects whether he is suffering, and so forth, then there are eight [points].
However, this interpretation by the Master of the Commentary is itself one approach; if one follows the text and meaning of Jingxi, it is very convenient."

I say that the following is correct: although the five phrases are divided into general and specific categories, once it is known that "Nirvana" is the general name and the "Four Virtues" are the specific designations, to harbor doubt regarding the general [name] constitutes a perversion.
Question: If one follows Jingxi’s interpretation of the text, then the eight perversions would be insufficient.
Answer: I shall now assist in the explanation. The initial doubt as to whether Nirvana is fixed is precisely a doubt regarding the four general [virtues].

The four doubts concerning the "withering" (the lower part) constitute the specific doubts; the eight inversions, through the analysis of the text regarding both the general and the specific, are fully accounted for.
Regarding the necessity of citing the Buddha-nature: at the end of the sections on the Three Vehicles, one should in all cases state, "Is there Buddha-nature?

Is there no Buddha-nature? The preceding doubts were abbreviated and simply stated as "Is there [Buddha-nature]? or "Is there not [Buddha-nature]? It is only upon realizing the true principle that one speaks of "Buddha-nature."
Therefore, it is said that they appear interchangeably.
The "sutra’s thorough knowledge of all sentient beings" refers precisely to those of the three vehicles.
Those who have abandoned doubts regarding substantial dharmas [realize] that impermanence is itself the four foundations of mindfulness; that is, observing the impurity of form.

Since these [terms] are based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they pertain to substantial dharmas (*dravya-dharma*). Yet, when the Sūtra speaks of "sentient beings" (*sattva*) and "non-sentient beings," it is because a sentient being is formed by grasping the aggregates;
thus, one should know that although there is the expression "sentient being," its true purpose is precisely to eliminate doubts regarding the substantial reality of the five aggregates.
The same applies to "life" (*jīva*) and "non-life" (*ajīva*).
Those who harbor doubts regarding the departure from conventional designations do so because they conceive a view of self based on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As for the term "Jing Yuanchen," "Chen" refers to a prophetic verification; it means that a divination made later proves to be effective and verified.

Regarding the passage concerning seeing an old man and so forth: this refers to the events of seeing an old man at the eastern gate, a sick man at the southern gate, a dead man at the western gate, and a śramaṇa at the northern gate, as recorded in the first fascicle of the *Śrī-samparigraha-sūtra* (瑞應經), as briefly noted previously.
To say that [the text] relies on existence and non-existence to express "neither existent nor non-existent" and so forth is to demonstrate the profound intent of the sūtra.

The text relies on existence and non-existence, while its underlying meaning lies in the "double negation" (neither-nor). When both the literal expression and the underlying meaning are complete, the principle of the Three Truths becomes manifest; because the expression and the meaning are thus unimpeded, both are described as "relying."
The concluding praise of the three truths cannot be reduced to two;
these two inconceivabilities above praise the True and the Conventional, while the further inconceivability praises the Middle Way, for since the three are mutually integrated, all are inconceivable.
When the profound (*xuan*) is followed by the mutual identity of existence and non-existence, this very profundity is itself the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "further profound" (*fu xuan*).

Regarding the meaning of "hearing what is not heard" in the Sūtra, it simply means "not hearing yet hearing. This is merely King De’s erroneous interpretation and does not reflect the true intent of King De.
For if one says "not heard," one should not say "heard"; if one says "heard," one should not say "not heard"—thus [the contradiction] is established.
This is a mistaken interpretation.

To divide [the subject] into two parts—where hearing is negated to establish the existence of a phenomenon, and non-hearing is negated to establish the non-existence of a phenomenon—is necessary because existence and non-existence are distinct categories.
Why, then, did the Tathāgata previously treat "hearing what was not heard" as a single meaning? Therefore, next...
The text refutes this with the concepts of arising and ceasing.
If arising and ceasing cannot be made into one, then "not hearing" is non-hearing, which is precisely "hearing";

yet existence and non-existence are fundamentally contradictory and are fixed as two distinct dharmas. Therefore, because "not hearing" cannot possess "hearing," the Sūtra says that what is non-existent should not arise. This is...
To cite "not hearing" is to negate "hearing"; since there cannot be "not hearing" apart from "hearing," the Sūtra says that what exists should not be extinguished.
This is to cite "hearing" in order to negate "not hearing.
Regarding the negation of "not hearing" by means of "hearing": the previous general discussion of existence and non-existence intended to attribute "hearing" to existence.
Since the argument that "hearing" is non-existent and devoid of characteristics has already been refuted, we now directly cite the Buddha’s teaching to refute it.
The sūtra establishes two distinct states because there is a difference between hearing and not hearing; thus, two [categories] are established.

It is certainly not the case that these are one and the same. Since we directly perceive that "not hearing" and "hearing" are different, how can it be said that "not hearing yet hearing" constitutes a single meaning?
Generally, three analogies are employed—namely, first, departure; second, birth; and third, attainment—and these three matters are used together to clarify the nature of hearing.

Hearing the *dharma* can also be illustrated by the analogy of "going" (*yāti*) and "not going" (*na yāti*), which serves to manifest the Buddha-nature through the analogies of the arising and non-arising of *nirvāṇa*. The analogy of "attaining" and "not attaining" manifests *bodhi*.

Regarding the section on the gate of "allowing" (*anujñā*) below, the logical force of the meaning should be understood accordingly. However, the commentary (*śāstra*) provides only a brief explanation of these three analogies;
if one wishes to analyze them in detail: in the first analogy, "going" represents hearing, while "not going" represents not hearing. As the scripture says: "It is like going."
The phrase "one who has already arrived" is a metaphor for the person capable of hearing [the Dharma]; "does not go" serves as an analogy to clarify the first clause.

Just as it cannot be said that a worldly person who has already reached their destination is "going," so too, when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already attained *nirvāṇa*, one cannot say they are "hearing the Dharma.
The phrase "having gone, one does not arrive" serves as an analogy to clarify the latter direction. Just as it is with those worldly people...
When one has traveled the path, it cannot be called "arriving"; likewise, for that which has already been heard according to the principle of correspondence, there can be no further hearing.
In the subsequent analogy, "arising" is used to illustrate "hearing," and "not arising after having already undergone arising" serves as a metaphor to clarify the latter phrase.

Just as when the characteristic of arising gives rise to all phenomena, one cannot say that it arises from what is not yet arisen; so too is the case with the principle of correspondence, where that which has already [been realized]...
When one has attained hearing, one must not speak of it; hearing that which is "not-hearing" does not give rise to the category of "arising.
As stated in the preceding phrase, just as the world's empty space cannot arise, it is correctly termed "non-arising" and cannot be said to arise. Regarding the correspondence with the Dharma:
the Dharma cannot be heard, and thus it is correctly termed "not-hearing" and cannot be said to be heard. In the third analogy, "attainment" is used to metaphorize "hearing."
Regarding the attainment of a metaphor: when one has attained [the state of] not hearing the sūtras, one cannot subsequently apply it as a category.

This is like the case among the fourteen dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), where there exists an "attainment" (*prāpti*) that is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), which is capable of attaining various phenomena (*dharma*). Taking this as a metaphor:

when those various attainments attain various phenomena, they cannot be called "attainment" with respect to the phenomena that have not yet been attained; this is because they have already attained them at the time of hearing.

One must not say that what is "not-heard" is "heard," nor that what is "not-obtainable" is "obtained. To clarify the preceding phrase, such things as the horns of a rabbit are dharmas that are fundamentally unobtainable;
their correct name is "unobtainable," and one cannot say that this "unobtainable" is "obtained.
As for dharmas that are inherently inaudible, their correct name is "not-heard," and one cannot say that this "not-heard" is "heard. These three analogies are cited to illustrate this point.
The two meanings of "not hearing" and "hearing" are clearly distinct; how then can the World-Honored One say that "hearing what was not heard" is a single meaning?
Therefore, the Commentary states: "In all cases, they are definitively determined as two."
The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "That which is 'non-arising and non-arising' means that one ultimately does not give rise to the dharma of non-arising.

Regarding the fact that the analogy cannot be unified: within the preceding section on dharmas, there were two parts—the first concluding that [the two] are established as distinct, and the second concluding that they should not be one.
In the analogy, it only illustrates the establishment of the two as distinct; therefore, it says, "When one arrives, one does not go," and so forth. Now, in the synthesis, however—
Because it is not logical for [the two] to be a single unity, it is said that "one hears what was not heard," and so forth.
In the analogy, the lower part indicates the omissions in the text of the analogy; this merely serves to harmonize the two passages below.

Regarding the mutual manifestation of opening and closing: "opening" refers to the analogy that clarifies both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), while "closing" refers to the analogy that merely brings them together as one;

this is called mutual manifestation. According to the scriptural text, both must necessarily be present. If, within the analogies, it is not appropriate for only one to be established—as in the first analogy below—it should state:

"How can it be said that [the light] arrives and then departs? and so on, up to the third analogy below, where it should likewise state: [how can it be said that the light arrives and then departs?]... [and so forth].
How can it be said that "attaining and not attaining" constitute a synthesis? If one relies on the current version of the scripture, it is precisely a synthesis of the two preceding fixed analogies.
The Commentator (*Sūshǔ*) says this is a synthesis of "not one," but I fear the current version of the scripture may be corrupted.
If one follows the Commentary and treats it as a synthesis of "not one," the scripture should simply state: "What was not heard before is likewise so. Let the wise examine this carefully.
Even if an opponent were to grant that "not hearing" is identical to "hearing," this constitutes one point.
As for the passage concerning the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes, it serves as a counter-argument. If one were to say that ordinary beings do not yet possess bodhi and have not attained nirvana...
If those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature possess it, attain it, or see it, then there would be no distinction between ordinary beings and Buddhas.

For what reason did the Tathāgata previously state that even those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) have not yet fully realized the nature? If even those in the ten stages are thus, how much more so for ordinary beings?
By this we know that "hearing the unheard" is twofold; why then do you say it is one?
Regarding the passage "As the Tathāgata in the past... and so forth: if [the teaching] were heard from another, it would mean that this [teaching] was heard;
this is a concession. Furthermore, the statement "without a teacher" is a counter-objection. Since it is said to be "without a teacher," one did not hear it from another;

thus, if one hears from another, it is hearing, and if one does not hear from another, it is not hearing. Therefore, one knows that these two dharmas are fundamentally different. For what reason, then, is it said [that they are not]?
Is "hearing" and "hearing it" one and the same meaning?
Since the two vertical lines [of the character for "two"] are distinct, and since the Buddhas who have already arisen are not identical, they must certainly constitute two separate dharmas.

Therefore, we know that hearing leads to attaining the Way and seeing the nature, whereas not hearing leads to not attaining it and not seeing it. All the scriptures present these difficulties as stated in the text; how much more so when considering the analogies involving form, color, and sound?
If even forms and sounds, which are phenomena that can be seen and heard, are yet beyond seeing and hearing, how much more so is the wondrous principle of Nirvana?
How could there be seeing or hearing of it, such that one speaks of "not hearing what is heard"?

In the first passage below, the meanings of "form" (*rūpa*) and "sound" (*śabda*) are explained: form is taken as that which exists within an obstruction and is moreover coarse and manifest, such that it can be seen;
sound is that which is in close proximity, such that it can be heard. The opposite of these cannot be perceived.

Alternatively, one may cite that form-dharmas are of three kinds—namely, visible and resistant (*sapratigha*), etc.—but this is entirely not the intent of the text. "Obstruction" refers to things such as mountains and walls; therefore, a pillar is cited in the text to illustrate this.
The character "質" (zhì) should be corrected to "秖" (zhǐ).
Regarding the second "response by praise" (*tàn-dá*) below, the ancient texts were incomplete.

Now it is clarified that the section below incorporates the subsequent text to form three responses together: first, the response by praise; second, the response by auspicious signs (*ruì-dá*); and third, the combined response.
The answer is as follows: the first point corresponds to the current text, while the second is found within the *Liu guang lun* (Treatise on the Flowing Light).

Regarding the "difficulty concerning fixed characteristics" (*dingxiang nan*): this refers to the fact that the meanings of "hearing" and "not hearing" are distinct; it is called a "fixed characteristic" because it raises a challenge based on the Tathāgata’s meaning of "hearing what is not heard."

Regarding the Buddha’s clarification of illusion and so forth: because the Buddha answers by means of illusion, emptiness, and the illusory nature of the provisional, he states that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
Thus, the three truths are mutually inclusive and mutually non-existent; therefore, all are like illusions.

Why do you dogmatically cling to the notion that there is a difference in meaning between "hearing" and "not hearing"? One should say: the provisional is itself emptiness, hearing is itself not hearing, and emptiness is itself [the provisional].
If one does not hear [the teaching], it is as if one hears it; thus, by clarifying that all is like an illusion, fixed attachments are naturally eliminated and all doubts are stilled.
That this constitutes a response through praise lies precisely herein.
The following section on "Liu-li" (Vaidūrya) clarifies the auspicious response.
It is not that one does not hear blue and so forth, but rather that one sees blue and so forth while hearing; therefore it is said, "Is it not that one hears what was previously unheard?

In the latter part, below, the response is explained through a combined answer; it should state, "The subsequent answer," but the text for the answer to the question of Vairocana’s Light is missing. The character "answer" (答) has been omitted.
"Answering both at once" means that while directly answering the question regarding the emission of light, he simultaneously answers the question concerning "not hearing what is heard.

The subsequent answer regarding the emission of light consists of two sections: first, clarifying the meaning of the "original" (hon) as being "not hearing," and second, clarifying the meaning of the "traces" (jaku) as being "hearing.
Thus, the original is the traces' "not hearing," which is "hearing," and the traces are the original's "hearing," which is "not hearing. This is the clear intent of answering both questions together.
However, this is clear.

Regarding the meaning of King Bimbisāra’s inquiry below: although King Bimbisāra had attained perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and truly had no doubts, he posed these questions for the sake of those of the three capacities, so that the Buddha might provide three answers to cause each to awaken to and understand the meaning.
Is the textual structure not like a chain of interlocking links?

Regarding the three grades of faculties being "relieved": those of superior faculty attain awakening immediately upon hearing the response of praise; those of middling faculty understand only after seeing the response of auspicious omens;
and those of inferior faculty achieve clarity only when hearing both responses together. Since their manifold doubts must be eliminated—likened to ice melting away—it is said they are "relieved."
The "separate answer below" refers to the distinction between answering specifically and answering inclusively.

"All [answers] refute fixed characteristics" means that they collectively refute King De’s doubt regarding fixed attachments; because this light does not belong to causes and conditions, it possesses no fixed characteristics.

The passage "the one who contemplates the Buddha contemplates the Dharma-body" means that all six sections of the sutra describe the essence of light; therefore, each and every one is said to be eternally abiding (*nitya*).
My personal view is that the following section explains the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). The commentary consists of two parts; first, the editor provides an introduction.
Next, following the intent of the text, the Master of the Commentary establishes a series of questions and answers.
Regarding the four Bodhisattvas' own practice of refutation and establishment: they personally destroy ignorance and personally establish the lamp of Bodhi;
since this is an internal realization, they all remain silent.

How could this be something eternally abiding? If one discusses partial eternity, the Bodhisattva has already attained it; however, if one refers to ultimate [eternity], even a Bodhisattva of the Golden Mind is still impermanent.

One interpretation states that the answer below contains two meanings: first, regarding the reception of empowerment, Jñānaprabha is identical to the fruit; second, regarding the original [status], he is superior.
If this is so, how can there be any doubt regarding its eternal abiding?

One should understand that while the profound conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is the fundamental essence (tattva), it is not heard [in its essence]; rather, it is heard [as the conventional] when functioning as a trace-manifestation (śeṣa-vyāpāra).

One should employ these trace-manifestations to suit the capacities of beings, without needing to obscure the fundamental essence; therefore, it is said: "Do not enter into ancient scriptures or commentaries."
The character for "liuli" (琉璃) is written simply as "liuli" (流離); the archaic forms are used interchangeably, and their meanings are as recorded previously.
Regarding the phrase "the armies raise banners and strike one another," the *Baïhùtōng* states: "Five men form a *wǔ*; five *wǔ* form a *liǎng*;
four *liǎng* form a *zú*; five *zú* form a *lǚ*; five *lǚ* form a *shī*. A *shī* consists of two thousand five hundred men. The *Zuǒzhuan* mentions the "bell" (*zhōng*).
The drum is called "striking.

When the harvest does not come to fruition for years on end, the *Zhou Li* states, "In accordance with the seasons of the year, [the grain] ascends" (*sheng*). Zheng Xuan says that "ascend" (*sheng*) means "to achieve completion.
Regarding the passage "These are named causes and conditions, etc.," because the manifestation of the traces descending from the source is perfectly manifest, it is said: "These are named as such."

Because the traces are rooted in phenomena and penetrate to principle, it is said that "neither is this [the case]. These two phrases collectively conclude the preceding discussion of the fundamental and the trace;
thus, they conclude that the traces are not [the ultimate] and conclude that the fundamental is not [the ultimate].
The inability to answer below is fully evident in the text through the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding this Buddha’s mention of that bodhisattva, it refers to what the sutra says: "The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: 'For what reason is there this radiance?
This is precisely Śākyamuni mentioning that bodhisattva.
Those who teach according to principle speak directly of the Great Truth without excluding the Lesser Vehicle.

Although that land lacks the lower [stages], this impure land possesses all four; pure lands possess only three. Based on these three benefits, both pure and impure lands are taught as being identical.

Regarding "responding to conditions without fixed form": the method of question and answer generally involves a subordinate questioning a superior; however, when the Buddha questioned Liuguang, it was a superior questioning an inferior.
This lack of a fixed formula is because he acted in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
This refers to humans and animals; above, Cunda had been debating with the Buddha regarding permanence, and Mañjuśrī came across to challenge him.
Thus it is said that he addresses "humans and animals," yet the dharma being discussed is still the dharma of permanence; therefore, it is said that "the dharma is not [limited to] animals."

This refers to those who are "adjuncts to the Dharma" (*dharmapratipakṣa*). They do not hear the correct discourse, yet they hear the Dharma and inquire about its past and future origins; thus, it becomes an adjunct.

This is called being an "adjunct to the Dharma" based on the difference in expression. If one considers the identity of the meaning, this adjunct is actually the correct [Dharma], because the Dharma of the past and future is precisely what is heard by not hearing.
"No one else intervenes" means that first the Buddha asks and Liuguang answers; next, Liuguang asks and the Buddha answers.
Because there is no other person to raise cross-examinations or objections, it is said that "no one else intervenes.
When you say, "I see that all dharmas have coming and going," this is your interpretation of the sutra: "You have come here. "Come" (zhì) refers to—
The question regarding "going from there and coming here" and the presence of the characteristics of going and coming is asked in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Because there is no going or coming, this interpretation of the sutra takes it to mean "not coming from elsewhere. "Not coming" means not arriving here from that place;
this is the question posed in terms of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In the first two rounds of the response below, where the light flows downward, these two [truths] are then addressed.
In the state where both truths are equally obscured, the Middle Way is likewise devoid of coming or going.

Regarding the "approaching the preceding object": because it comes from that [object] to this [point], it is precisely the preceding object; speaking directly in terms of this, it is called "approaching the preceding object."

As for the appearance of coming and going in its traces, "traces" refers to its functional activity; therefore, when the radiance reaches here, it is because this is a matter of phenomenal activity, and thus there is coming and going.
Now, in the response regarding the radiance, the Buddha speaks directly of the fundamental principle, and therefore, in both of these instances, there is neither coming nor going.
"Neither arriving nor not arriving" clarifies that arrival is itself non-arrival.
"Neither reaching nor not arriving" clarifies that non-arrival is likewise unobtainable, because both are the Middle Way within profound stillness (*mārga*).

Regarding the scriptural passage on whether conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are permanent and so forth: permanence is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), impermanence is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), and the identity of the ultimate and the conventional is the Middle Way.
Neither of these comes forth.
That "delusion and awakening are likewise" refers to the latter eight sections, which generally treat delusion and awakening; however, their meanings also differ slightly.

The first statement, "there is the nature of sentient beings," etc., refers to the fruit (*phala*); next, from "arrogance" (*māna*) onwards, it refers to the cause (*hetu*); and third, from "having grasping and formations" (*upādāna-saṃskāra*) onwards, it refers to... [the effect].
4. Those who have grasping or non-grasping, yet have not yet seen the principle of the Great Nirvana, are all termed those with "grasping conduct.

5. "If they see the Tathāgata... and below, this is explained in relation to the two vehicles' views of the past and future. 6. "They do not hear of Buddha-nature... and below, this clarifies the past and future by way of that which can destroy [delusion].
7. "If they see the Śrāvakas... and below, this again explains the past and future in relation to the two vehicles. 8. "If they see the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas... [and so forth].
The first section, "If one views the Tathāgata... and so forth, explains going and coming by means of the "double negation" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta).
Although the textual meaning of these eight sections differs, they do not transcend the distinction between delusion and awakening:
delusion involves going and coming, whereas awakening is devoid of going and coming.

In response to your question regarding both the noble and the "hearing what has not been heard": in principle, the fundamental (hon) is originally without hearing, yet in its phenomenal manifestation (ji), there is hearing because of awakening; thus, through non-hearing one awakens.

Conversely, through delusion there is hearing. One should know that both the fundamental and the phenomenal reside within the sage, whereas delusion and awakening are discussed in contrast between the ordinary person and the sage.
Furthermore, when an ordinary person clings to the phenomenal and is deluded regarding the fundamental, they are deluded regarding both the fundamental and the phenomenal.
The Sūtra says, "Setting aside this matter" means setting aside the matters of the past and future; I now wish specifically to inquire about the meaning of "hearing what has not been heard.
This is setting aside the peripheral in order to clarify the central point.

Regarding the passage "Liu Guang was originally in [his own land]," it means that while in his own country, he questioned the Buddha Pūrṇacandra, just as King Devarāja acted in the same manner. As for "taking away and letting go," it refers to the act of seizing and then releasing.
How much more so regarding the question of the three pairs!

"Realization" refers to the internal awakening; because realizing the principle is called "not hearing," while the arousal of wisdom is called "hearing," it is said that [realization] does not depend on external hearing.

"Cultivation within realization" refers to true cultivation; therefore, this true cultivation is "partial realization" (fen-zheng) when designated by its own stage, and it is called "cultivation" (xiu) when viewed from the perspective of initiating practice toward a higher stage.
"Increasing clarity in every thought-moment" means entering into what is heard and constantly accords with the principle of nature, which is termed "not hearing."

Regarding the phrase "resembling the Six Perfections," this is because the Buddha’s intention is manifold and not yet definitively determined; hence it is said they "resemble" them. As for their being "not in sequence":
if they followed the standard sequence, it should be first giving, second precepts, third patience, fourth vigor, fifth meditation, and sixth wisdom;
yet in this text, it begins with vigor and proceeds through to sixth giving. Therefore, it is said to be "not in sequence. This must surely be the Tathāgata’s [intention].
Because the six perfections are clearly and perfectly interrelated and mutually inclusive, their essential meaning is presented here out of sequence.
This is established based on the necessity of diligence; for if one were not diligent, how could one skillfully expound this without indolence?
Regarding those permitted by the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*): if there were no ultimate ethical discipline, how could one extract the poisonous arrows of the two extremes?
Since the meaning of ethical discipline is the cessation of evil, extracting the poison is precisely the cessation of evil.
The preceding passage refers to the sutra at the beginning of this fascicle, which asks, "What is it that one can hear though one has not heard before?
and continues up to, "the three true natures, characteristics, and the eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

Since it has been clarified that these four virtues are alternative names for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), this serves as proof that "hearing what was not heard" is a broad elucidation of the meaning of Buddha-nature; therefore, it is said that this is its significance.

The same applies to the noble ones: since the Buddha has now permitted that the radiating light constitutes the "attaining cause" (prāpti-hetu) for wisdom, he says, "I possess the torch of wisdom capable of providing illumination.
Therefore, we know that the noble ones also possess the attaining cause; for the question posed was identical, and the Buddha’s permission was likewise equal.
The following passage cites scriptural evidence to establish the "attaining cause" (lābha-hetu).
If one does not hear [the teaching], the term "Buddha-nature" is used as a general designation; however, because this general term encompasses specific distinctions, there are three distinct natures.
Therefore, the text now raises the general term in order to inquire into its specific details.

Not hearing this, [the author] now specifically employs four phrases to correspond with the three natures—which are actually five natures. Regarding these five natures, they are formed by adding two kinds to the three natures;

however, various explanations differ. Some say it is because of the "nature of the object" (*viṣaya-dhātu*) and the "nature of the fruit" (*phala-dhātu*), thus stating that the "nature of the fruit" and the "nature of the fruit-of-fruit" (*phalā-phala-dhātu*) are added.
Others say it is because of the "nature of the cause" (*hetu-dhātu*) and the "nature of the cause-of-cause" (*hetu-hetu-dhātu*). If...

To explain the meanings: the wisdom of emptiness (*prajñā*) is called the nature of the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*); the merits of such acts as bowing the head and raising the hands are called the nature of the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*);

the presence of the nature of peace and bliss within all phenomena is called the nature of the "causal source" (*hetu-hetu*); the distinction between good and evil deeds is called the nature of the "objective realm" (*viṣaya-hetu*);

when discussing only the merit of wisdom, it is called the nature of the "fruit" (*phala-hetu*); and when discussing both the merit of wisdom and the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa*), [it is called the nature of the fruit].

Nirvāṇa is termed *phala-phalatva* (the nature of the fruit of the fruit); this refers solely to the objective sphere of the twelve links of dependent origination as being the *hetu-tva* (nature of the cause).

When the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination is also included, it is termed *hetu-hetutva* (the nature of the cause of the cause). Although various explanations differ, the number must necessarily reach five.

If one treats *viṣaya-tva* (the nature of the object) as [the fifth], then *phala-phalatva* is subsumed under *phala-tva* (the nature of the fruit). If one distinguishes *phala-phalatva*, then *viṣaya-tva* is subsumed [under the other four].

Regarding those factors subsumed under the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*)—namely, the nature of the "disappearance cause" (*vigama-hetu*) and the nature of the "causal cause" (*hetu-hetu*)—the nature of the cause is subsumed under the "direct cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*), while the nature of the causal cause is subsumed under the "perceptual cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*);
their meaning may be understood accordingly. In the present text, for the sake of the five natures, this is stated as a general exposition based on one perspective.
"Hearing what has not been heard" is the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), because hearing belongs to wisdom; thus, while all phenomena remain unheard, it is *prajñā* that hears.

"Hearing what has not been heard" is the supporting cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), because conditions consist of the substance of merit rather than the illumination of wisdom; therefore, it is called "not hearing."
The true cause can indeed be seen.
As for this "object" (viṣaya), because the spheres of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena do not overlap, it is called "hearing what is heard.

If one were to distinguish between identity and difference by comparing the object to the true cause, the true cause resides in principle (li), whereas the object belongs to phenomena (shi); thus, all dharmas [are subsumed within these two].
The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is precisely the nature of bliss (*sukha-svabhāva*), which is the direct cause (*hetu*).

Since principle (*li*) is identical with phenomena (*shi*), and phenomena are identical with principle, one knows that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and five natures (*pañcasvabhāva*)—whether opened or merged, whether nature (*svabhāva*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—have much that can be elucidated. How could one possibly provide them all at once?
The meaning of the "et cetera" (*ādi*) in the sub-commentary below is also intended to convey this. If one understands that cultivation and nature are non-dual (*advaya*), [then this is realized].
The meaning of the term "gate" (mukha) is easy to understand.
Furthermore, because the two phrases "hearing what has been heard" and "hearing what has not been heard" below encompass both meanings, it is further contrasted with them.

As for the nature of the cause (hetu), the twelve links of dependent origination pertain to phenomena; thus, through hearing, one again gives rise to contemplative wisdom and realizes their true essence.
Because the three paths are fundamentally non-existent, they are "not heard"; yet, by hearing that which is not heard, the meaning lies herein.
"It is also thus" means that the three types of fourfold propositions—such as coming and not coming—are applied by analogy to the five natures.
Regarding the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*): if one does not endure the two types of death, how could one serve as a pilot of the ship of omniscience for others?

Regarding the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*): unless one abides in the Tathāgata-meditation and universally covers the Dharma-realm with the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), how could one regard all sentient beings equally as one’s own infant child?
Regarding the inclusion within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), it refers specifically to the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) among the three types of giving.

These six perfections are all established as distinct names according to their respective meanings based upon the single mind of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). As for the lack of sequential order in the text, it is due to their mutual interpenetration.
"Do not seek out their faults" means that those who cling to partiality destroy the perfect.
"Having explained 'covering over'" refers to the fact that if one gives rise to the three poisons, one does not advance in one's own path;

it is like an overturned vessel. "Not observing caste" means that in the Western lands there are four castes: Kṣatriya, Brahmin, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Among these, the Kṣatriya and Brahmin are considered noble castes, while the Vaiśya... [is considered inferior].
The Śūdra is of low caste; one should not hold high castes in esteem or look down upon low castes, but rather take up the Dharma, bestowing it solely based on virtue.
Thus, although the jackal preached the Dharma, Śakra paid him reverence.

This is also like King Wen being born among the Qiang of the West, Great Yu being born among the Yi of the East, Tai Gong originally being a butcher and fisherman, Fu Yue beginning as a laborer building embankments, and Ning Qi rising from the salt pans.
Qi Ke fed oxen and Chu Ping herded sheep; how could it be that their noble and sagely virtue was discarded simply because of the lowliness of their lineage?
This is true even among Confucians, let alone among Buddhists; therefore, the Buddha cautioned them not to regard caste.
"Do not leak into birth and death" means that because pride and the like are the minds of ordinary beings, if one does not give rise to such a mind, then true emptiness will be manifested;
thus, one does not leak into birth and death.
"Not falling into [premature] nirvana" means that because the mindsets of the two vehicles— such as seeking one's own liberation— are present, if one does not give rise to such a mind,

then the great vows will be fulfilled, and thus one does not fall into nirvana. As the Sūtra says, from "liberating oneself" up to "attaining nirvana for oneself," this can be understood in contrast to the Four Great Vows.
Do not defile the Mahāyāna: to put oneself before others is to defile the Mahāyāna; to discipline and liberate oneself alone is called "defilement.
If one treats [the Three Jewels] as separate entities, perceiving the distinctions and impermanence among them, this is to defile their single essence.
Those who cannot revere the Dharma are those for whom the Great Nirvana is the Dharma they have received.
If they give rise to the Lesser Vehicle, it is because the latter three defilements are likewise present within themselves; therefore, it is said that they cannot revere themselves.
Regarding the practice of these ten dharmas: first, there are three admonitions against concealment; second, two admonitions against leakage;

third, one matter concerning hearing and respecting the teacher, which in meaning opens into three but follows the text as it stands, thus remaining as one dharma; furthermore, within the admonition against defilement, there are five [sub-points], which together constitute the ten dharmas.
Moreover, for each individual dharma, there is first a prohibition and then the practice; taking the practice alone constitutes the ten dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "one who forms this most sincere mind," the scripture states, "If you can listen to the Dharma with such a sincere mind"; this is the concluding summary of the passage.
As for "the South," it refers to the region south of the Yangtze River.

Regarding the statement that the final two sets of four lines are metaphorical explanations, ancient scholars saw the character "ru" (如, "like") and immediately designated them as metaphors, yet they did not [further]...

The statement that "knowing the non-arising of arising" and so forth is a further explanation of "hearing what has not been heard," because the first four [phrases] pertain to the characteristics of the teaching.
This means that since it is said "hearing what has not been heard" and so on, one must necessarily hear the sound of the teaching.

Regarding the next two as the characteristics of realization (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*): it is said that *jāti-jāti* and so forth are the realizing practices (*sādhana*), while *jāti* and so forth are the realized principles (*sādhya*).
As for "the Dharma-body arising as response":
the Dharma-body is that which is not heard, while the arising of response is that which is heard.
That the *dharmakāya* is "loftily manifest" means that it does not arise in response to the times.

Regarding the phrase "the entanglements of birth and death": birth and death here refer to those severed through hearing and the cultivation of the path; they do not refer to those severed through not hearing [the Dharma].

That which is not the primary intention refers to the four propositions concerning "hearing-hearing," which serve merely as an introductory lead-in for the four propositions concerning "producing-production";
therefore, by explaining only "producing-production," the preceding meaning becomes self-evident.
Regarding the phrase "not hearing, not hearing is nirvāṇa" and so forth, it should properly be stated as "non-arising, non-arising.
The former masters, wishing to clarify the preceding clause, merely cited it; the subsequent three clauses directly refer to arising and so forth.
That which is without beginning and without end means that the essential substance (*dharmatā*) of the principle of *nirvāṇa* does not admit of beginning or end;
thus, it is not heard as having a beginning, nor is it heard as having an end.

That which begins though without beginning means that although the principle is without beginning, there is a beginning in the sense of its realization at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*); therefore, it is non-arising.
That which is beginningless begins precisely at its beginning;

that which is endless ends precisely at its end. Although in principle there is no end, because there is an end consisting in the realization of wondrous enlightenment, birth and non-birth are identical.
Since the wisdom of all seeds is already perfected and there is no further wisdom to be produced, it is called "non-birth."
The same applies to birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This means that birth and death are also explained in terms of beginning and end, and so forth;

one must understand that these are categorized according to three phrases each for both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa: "non-arising" and "non-arising" definitely belong to nirvāṇa, while "arising" and "arising" definitely belong to birth-and-death.
As for the remaining two phrases, their meanings are mutually applicable.
This birth and death is without beginning and without end because the cycle of saṃsāra has no boundaries; thus it has neither beginning nor end.
"Non-arising arising" refers to the arising of delusive afflictions through ignorance of the non-arising of true reality.

"Arising not arising" means that while there is the initial arising of birth and death, this is negated when one reaches the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) where [birth and death] are partially destroyed, culminating in the ultimate perfection of wondrous enlightenment; therefore, it is called "non-arising."
Because there is birth, there is an end to birth and death.

Now, the phrase "what is said below" refers to the refutation of the first proposition and a general critique of various schools. As for the phrase "how so? it introduces a sequential refutation of multiple interpretations.

To those who do not yet harmonize with the Perfect [Teaching], if various masters offer partial interpretations while wishing to explain the Perfect Sūtra, how is this different from grasping a square peg and trying to force it into a round hole?
This is why it is said that they do not understand.
To butcher and wound the body is [like] explaining the three rounds and four lines of the Dharma-principle through limited conceptualizations;
how is this any different from butchering the four limbs and wounding the physical body?
Regarding the explanation of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and so forth based on the single truth (*ekasatya*):

this refers to the view that one is able to "hear what has not been heard" and so forth, up to "hearing what has already been heard," solely by realizing the one true reality (*ekasatyatattva*). This interpretation was not presented in the previous commentary on the ancients;
it is cited here as an opportunity to refute various masters, hence it is described as "another teacher."

Although it is said that those who are "intimate" are compared to other masters because they lack the fault of "slaughtering," they are called "intimate" only because they cling exclusively to a single truth;
yet, since they do not understand the mutual integration of all phenomena, they are actually even more "distant and neglectful.

If this interpretation—which is already the most excellent—is still characterized by such distance and neglect, how much more so would interpretations based on the two truths and so forth involve "slaughtering" and wounding the essence?
Furthermore, the formulation of "mutual non-existence" is the explanation of the fourth master based on the beginning and the end;

that is to say, because nirvana lacks the three phrases within samsara, and samsara lacks the three phrases within nirvana, it is called "mutual non-existence. This refers to the distinct natures of principle and phenomenon (*dharmatā*);

since it merely captures the Mahayana sense of analyzing phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*), it still lacks even the Mahayana sense of the substantiality of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), and is therefore described as "insignificant."
This is merely a division of the mind.
Furthermore, these ten matters are themselves the ten virtues.

As for the "thousand paths and myriad tracks," they refer to what our current Master has categorized as the four dharmas, the five practices, the five natures, the three nirvāṇas, and the Great and Small Vehicles.
The commentaries of the Vinaya and Śāstra masters still fear they do not accord with the principle of internal realization of perfect penetration that universally encompasses all dharmas;
how much more so for various teachers who cling exclusively to a single meaning?

The phrase "flying brambles" and so forth is a metaphor for these teachers who cling exclusively to phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and have no reliance whatsoever upon the perfectly interfused principle (*yuanrong li*).
It is merely like a *péng* weed blown beyond the great wilderness, or a water-duckweed drifting upon the surface of the vast blue sea.

The "Northern Expedition Rhapsody" (*Beizheng fu*) by Ban Shupi in the *Wenxuan* states: "Like floating duckweed and whirling *péng* weeds," with a commentary noting that they are like duckweed and *péng* weeds, having no place of reliance or support.
"Penetrating all points of contact" refers to the explanations provided below concerning the five elements and so forth.

"One should support the Buddha’s words" means that since the Buddha himself provides explanations within the sutras, we now further extend and clarify those words so that their meaning becomes manifest;
because there is no separate path [other than what the Buddha taught], it is said that "one should support the Buddha’s words."

The intent here is that for those who practice through integration, because they attain entry into the true realization of the first bhūmi by means of preparatory cultivation (*prayoga*) prior to abiding [in the fruit],
such as "hearing what has not been heard," this must be discussed in relation to cultivation.

As for the sudden cessation of the path of cultivation, the wisdom and conduct prior to abiding are termed the "wisdom of the path of cultivation," which refers to the conduct at the stage of names (*nāmadheya*).

The third refers to the stage of similarity in contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā-sadṛśāvasthā*); now, as one turns from what resembles understanding to ascend to the true realization of the *bhūmis*, it is said that [the former] suddenly ceases.
Therefore, it is called "not hearing. That which is "not heard" is *nirvāṇa*, because it is devoid of the characteristics of a hearer or anything heard.
Regarding "hearing what is unheard": hearing that which was previously unheard is itself delusion; the arising of realization that cuts off this delusion is called "hearing what is unheard.

Because he responds according to the叩 (kǒu—knocking/impulse) by manifesting his response according to the capacities of beings and preaching the Dharma inexhaustibly, it is called "hearing what is heard.

Of these four phrases, the first three concern one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), while the last concerns the transformation of others (*parārtha*). Furthermore, within the first three, the initial phrase refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).
The first phrase refers to principle (*li*), and the subsequent phrases refer to the wisdom of cessation; that is, principle is the *dharmakāya*, and cessation is liberation (*vimukti*).
Regarding "the wisdom of realization and so forth," this refers to the wisdom of the one who realizes, up to and including the conduct of the one who realizes.
If one takes a lower matter as the subject, it can be understood through its corresponding counterparts such as "conformity to principle" (*yukti*).

As for "self and others," wisdom (*jñāna*), realization (*bodhi*), and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) constitute one's own practice (*svārtha*), while transformation (*nirmāṇa*) constitutes the practice for others (*parārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "resolving the doubts of two people," these two individuals are King Guṇarāja and Prabhāsa.
Furthermore, the following is explained by way of the five elements (*pañcadhātu*).
This is the realization of the noble practitioner (*ārya-caryā*); noble practice is the adornment of wisdom, which is "hearing what has not been heard.
This is the realization of the brahma-practitioner (*brahma-caryā*); brahma-practice is the adornment of merit, which is "not hearing what has been heard. All of these are one.
In the past, one distributed blessings and wisdom;
that which realizes the Celestial Path (devayāna) is the Path itself, yet the principle is neither blessing nor wisdom, and thus it is "not hearing what was not heard.
Because the infant-like [stage] shares in goodness and the practice of illness shares in evil, responding to capacities through manifestation, it is "hearing what was heard."
Furthermore, the following section explains this by means of the five Buddha-natures.

Regarding the phrase "hearing what was not heard" as being opposed to the *pratipakṣa-hetu* (antidote cause) and so forth: it is precisely because the *parijñāna-hetu* (understanding cause) is wisdom (*prajñā*), the *ālambana-hetu* (object-condition cause) is merit (*puṇya*), and the *prakṛti-hetu* (intrinsic cause) is principle (*tattva*) that this [phrase] is set in opposition to them.
However, when these five natures reach the stage of the first *vihāra* (dwelling), they are manifested simultaneously; thus, they are one.
This can be understood by reflecting on how the five are neither one nor five.

Furthermore, below, the three types of nirvana are explained: because the three—namely, intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and so forth—are all neither arising nor ceasing, they are called "nirvana.

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, being neither arising nor ceasing and neither defiled nor pure, is termed "intrinsic-purity nirvana" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*). Through cultivation...
Because delusions that accord with [the truth] are ultimately non-arising and wisdom is ultimately non-ceasing, it is called "Perfectly Pure Nirvana" (pariśuddha-nirvāṇa).
It is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; when conditions are met, it arises, yet this arising is not truly arising; when conditions cease, it ceases, yet this cessation is not truly ceasing.
This is called "Skillfully Pure Nirvana" (upāya-śuddha-nirvāṇa). The meaning of these paired terms is easy to perceive.
"What is meant by 'suchness'?"—this is the question that arises. "'The meaning of non-difference'"—this is the answer that explains it.

Regarding the verses such as "the Himalayas cut their own flesh" and so forth: the verse on the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the like is the "Himalaya verse," while the verse concerning the Tathāgata’s realization of *nirvāṇa* is the "cutting-of-flesh verse."
"Arising and non-arising are the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)," meaning that arising is the conditioned phenomenon itself, while non-arising is its impermanence.
"Non-arising arising is the nature of birth and cessation," meaning that non-arising is itself cessation.
This refers to the phrase "when arising and ceasing have ceased":
since "arising" is that which is to be extinguished, this is the Tathāgata’s realization of nirvāṇa. This is explained in terms of the wisdom that realizes it;
thus, in contrast to "non-arising," while all phenomena do not arise, prajñā arises.
To be born and not be born in the lower realms is the eternal cessation of birth and death, which is precisely non-birth.
This "birth of birth" refers to the very birth and death that was severed above; because one dies again after being born, and having died returns to be born, it is called the "birth of birth."
If one can bring down immeasurable bliss because it is the principle that has been attained, this is "non-arising and non-non-arising.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Purify one's own mind," etc., in the context of the Hīnayāna, these two lines of the verse serve to prevent the three types of action (*trividha-karma*);

the first two lines refer to the seven branches of body and speech, while "purifying the mind" refers to the three branches of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). If one unfolds the Hīnayāna to lead toward the Mahāyāna, then:
The ten realms that constitute all evils are the realm of the three unwholesome dharmas; the ten realms that constitute all virtues are the realm of the three wholesome dharmas;

and the pure mind is the realm of the four noble dharmas. This refers to the pure mind through the analysis of emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*), which is precisely the pure mind of emptiness, the pure mind of the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the pure mind of the Middle Way (*madhyama*).
"Large and small sūtras and vinayas" refers to the large sūtras and small vinayas cited above.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the Way," the sub-commentary notes "and so forth," which should also correspond to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages): namely, that emptiness and existence are non-dual, not different, and inexhaustible.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and so forth," various texts employ either the four propositions of "arising from arising" or the four propositions of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

Regarding the teachings, these are distinct categories and are not the intended meaning here; here, we are correctly clarifying the internal realization of the stage of partial truth (*bhūmi-prativedha*), wherein all four [teachings] are subsumed within the Perfect [Teaching].

Furthermore, if one relies on internal realization and perfect penetration, there is no contradiction with the teachings, for the nature of the four noble dharma-realms (*ārya-dharmadhātu*) is inherently complete.

Since even the Small Vehicle’s Vinaya pertains only to humans and devas—yet in the preceding passage it was already contrasted against the four phrases—how much more so must this apply to the four teachings?

Yes. Regarding the two meanings, they refer to external phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*) and internal phenomena (*ādhyātma-dharma*). External phenomena pertain to the birth and death of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while internal phenomena pertain to the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) by noble ones (*ārya*).

Alternatively, it is said that external phenomena pertain to the initial thought-moment of a noble one’s manifestation and response, specifically when taking conception in a womb—that is, being entrusted to a mother.

This interpretation is untenable. If one were to explain it according to external phenomena (*bāhya-dharma*) as in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), stating that at the time of death "merit and life-span are both exhausted," how could this mean that the Sage should undergo extinction?
One should know that this merely refers to the birth and death of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) as external phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "cultivating skillful means (*upāya*) and so forth," it means to dwell in the meaning through the cultivation of understanding.

As for "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because all distinct and discursive discriminations arise from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in conjunction with ignorance, it is called conventional truth.
What is now termed "cultivating skillful means" refers to establishing [the mind] in conventional truth through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, thereby bringing it to the state of the inconceivable.
Because the stages of objective realm, contemplation, and practice are perfected, it is called "abiding securely"; because of this secure abiding, it is called "entrusting oneself to the holy womb.

That which arises from cultivation and leads to realization refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*), where one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This is called "emerging from the holy womb" because one no longer perceives ignorance or conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and thus speaks of "non-arising," yet because one obtains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is called "arising."

It is said that "ignorance is suddenly shattered" and so forth; this phrase "the non-arising of arising" refers to the stage of the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*), which is the cause of one's own practice.

The scripture states, "there is no characteristic of arising," because the perfection of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) means ignorance does not arise, and the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) means *prajñā* does not arise.
Thus, it is called "the non-arising of non-arising"; this refers to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which describes the fruit of one's own practice.

Regarding the phrase "according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), at the time of death," and so forth: ignorance is its root. Since ignorance has been destroyed, it is said that there is "death in the world" (*loka-maraṇa*).

Because there is death in the world, it is called "the non-arising of birth. This explains the first phrase. In the phrase above, because the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) is perfected through reliance on principle (*li*), it is said "non-birth arises" (*anutpāda-utpāda*).

This phrase [refers to] the perfection of the quality of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) through the destruction of delusions (*kleśa*) in the subsequent phrase; therefore, it is said "birth does not arise" (*utpāda-anutpāda*). Not... [is not].
Although the term "birth" (*jāti*) is used in both cases, their underlying principles differ greatly. In the first sentence, the unfolding of wisdom is designated as "birth";
in this sentence, the activation of karmic bonds is designated as "birth of birth. Although the name is the same, there is a vast difference between bondage and liberation;
this latter case is merely the cause for one's own practice, corresponding to the first sentence.

Regarding the scriptural explanation that "all out-flowing (sāsrava) phenomena arise moment by moment," this clarifies the intent of the Bodhisattva in manifesting birth for the sake of transforming others.
Why does the Bodhisattva manifest birth when they do not truly arise? It is because the continuity of all out-flowing sentient beings is uninterrupted;
therefore, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion, manifests sovereign birth, and thereby delivers them.
The Sūtra re-explains the third phrase, stating that "the Bodhisattvas of the four abodes... attain mastery over birth.
While the previous explanation clarified the extinction of the delusions of one’s own practice, this re-explanation clarifies the manifestation of the transformative path. Why is this?

When a Bodhisattva severs the four abodes, they destroy the birth produced by fetters and karma and are thus able to manifest birth with mastery; how much more so when they sever the five abodes? By using the inferior to manifest the superior, the excellence is made even more evident.

Because those who transform the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) sever delusions and sink into emptiness, they cannot act in this manner; therefore, the term "bodhisattva" is specifically designated. This refers precisely to the capacity for transforming others.
Thus, these four phrases comprehensively encompass the causes and fruits of one’s own practice, as well as the capacities and objects of transforming others, all of which are fully complete.
Regarding the commentary on the bodhisattvas of the four abodes, first the ancient interpretations are cited, followed by the present interpretation, as per the text.

Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, its presentation of six stages (*ṣaḍ-vihāra*) is yet another distinct interpretation. Even when approaching Buddhahood, the text reveals the supreme perfection by means of the inferior and the general; how could it not also reveal the perfect through the distinct?
Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that from the first stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) up to the tenth stage, these are condensed into six stages:

(1) the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), (2) the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), (3) the stage of the pure mind (*śuddhādhyāśaya-vihāra*), and (4) the stage of the track of practicing the path (*pratipatti-mārga-vihāra*). [The remaining two are: (5) the stage of non-retrogression (*anivartana-vihāra*), and (6) the stage of the final birth (*carama-bhava-vihāra*).
Regarding the five stages of definitive abiding and the sixth stage of ultimate abiding:

as for the stage of abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), if a person lacks the spiritual lineage, even if they are born in the happy realms, they will repeatedly regress and repeatedly advance, and shall not be included among the ranks of the bodhisattvas. If one is established in the state of the spiritual lineage, there is no regression;
rather, one advances ever further. Such a person is one who has attained this. The practitioner who understands through practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) is [the stage of] the first ground (*bhūmi*).
