The "Abode of Purified Mind through Skillful Means" (*upāya-pariśuddha-citta-vihāra*) refers to entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), wherein one attains the supramundane mind and is freed from the obstacle of the ordinary person’s mark of selfhood;
thus it is called the Abode of Purified Mind. The "Abode of Practicing the Path" (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*) refers to the practice of the path from the second stage through the seventh stage.

The "Abode of Certainty" (*niyata-vihāra*) refers to the eighth and ninth stages; because one has already attained the practice of fruition and does not regress or turn back, it is called "Certainty."

Regarding "abiding in the ultimate consummation of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-paryanta-vihāra*): it is called "ultimate" because the practices and studies of the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) have reached their full completion.
Regarding "the four abidings corresponding to the fourth": the Sūtra refers to these four abidings as the very tracks of the path of practice (*pratipad-mārga*).

From the second stage upward, this is precisely the stage of entering into provisional [rebirths] to transform others; appearing in birth in various places, yet not being a real birth, is intended to be distinguished and revealed separately.

From the moment of his initial birth from the womb, he was already able to benefit others; as a spontaneously born being (*upapāduka*), he possessed mastery. This accords perfectly with the meaning of "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*), and thus it is said that "it corresponds to this meaning.
This is fully explained in the opening passage of the section "The Universal Destruction of Phenomena" (*dharmavyāpti*).

Regarding the detailed explanation of each phrase based on the arising of desire: "each phrase" refers to the three phrases of arising, non-arising, and so forth, as well as the four phrases each concerning "not hearing yet hearing," "not reaching yet reaching," and so on.
Regarding the statement that "conditioned phenomena with outflows (sāsrava-dharma) should not have this arising":

since conditioned phenomena with outflows are themselves produced dharmas, and it is established that such phenomena with outflows are necessarily impermanent, if the producer were permanent, then the produced phenomenon with outflows would certainly not have this arising.
Therefore, the Sūtra says, "then there is no arising. This is a refutation of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by means of the way they transform objects.

The characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) occurs first among the [four characteristics] because the notion of permanence (*nitya-saṃjñā*) easily arises; therefore, it is first described as "permanent.
The phrase "If there were no... cites the subsequent sentence of the sūtra. From "Arising is... onwards, the meaning of the sūtra is explained.
Regarding the characteristic of being able to produce that which cannot maintain itself: since it is impermanent and subject to decay and destruction, it cannot even maintain its own substance;
how then could it produce anything contaminated?

"That which is not produced by birth" reveals that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is naturally independent; since it is neither a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions nor is it permanent, how [could it be said to arise]?
"Since birth itself is that which is produced" explains the scriptural phrase "if birth were self-produced," which restates the opponent's position.
This means that if this characteristic of arising were itself the produced phenomenon, there would have to be something else distinct from it that acts as the producer.
This is not merely a further explanation of the scriptural phrase "the self-nature of non-arising"; rather, it constitutes a formal objection.
"Cannot further produce, etc. means that since it is itself that which is produced, how could it further act as a producer?
Since it is not a producer, one does not perceive a self-nature (svabhāva) of being a producer.
The second "cloud" (i.e., the second section) below explains the passage from the sutra beginning with "If it can produce another," which refers to the following text.
"In relation to itself, both, and another" means that in relation to the producer, it is "self," while that which is produced is "both" and "another.
"Not the six questions" refers to the three pairs previously mentioned, such as permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Regarding "six are not one": since the first six phrases all state that it "cannot be spoken," they are called the six non-ones;
only the seventh states that because there are causes and conditions, it can also be spoken of, and is thus named the one.
Regarding the phrase "the fourth, the difficulty of giving birth to others," the two characters "not born" (*busheng*) below refer to the non-arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it is the non-arising of the untainted, it is called "non-arising of non-arising.

As for the question "How is it that non-arising gives birth? the commentary below explains this in two sections: first, the direct explanation according to the text; second, [the explanation] based on...
Although the meaning is extensively demonstrated, these six phrases, taken as a whole, do not transcend the internal and external realms, nor the common and specific, nor delusion and awakening.

Contemplating the Buddha’s response, its significance is profound and far-reaching; only then does it become clear that what the transmitted light finds difficult to express is so mysterious and deep.

Regarding the two matters being mutually contradictory: "non-arising" refers to the permanence of the *dharmatā* (the true principle of phenomena), while "arising" refers to impermanence, which points to the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because the meanings of the real and the false are distinct, they are said to be contradictory.

This refers to the fact that while the Two Vehicles have already realized non-arising within the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*), as long as ignorance remains, they still undergo the birth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-jāti*). Therefore, it is said that "non-arising is itself called arising."
Beyond this realm of language, the delusions that adhere to the substance do not arise; thus it is called "arising. This arising is itself inversion, and inversion is itself non-inversion.

Because the sphere of mental activity has ceased and the path of language is cut off, it cannot be expressed—this serves as the answer to the challenge regarding the permanence of the *Sūryaprabha-samādhi*.

That which is produced by what produces it is precisely the Great Birth (mahā-jāti) that gives rise to the Small Birth; because it is a conditioned phenomenon (sāsrava-dharma) subject to transformation through the eight phases [of existence], it is impermanent.
This refers to the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and saṃjñā-kleśa) within the realm of desire.
Since these afflictions are phenomena that fully manifest from principle, it is said that their entire substance is birth. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Because there is the birth of birth, there is birth."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that which is extinguished by extinction," this extinction is precisely the principle of quiescent permanence.

Because phenomena produced through causes and conditions are empty and mean (the Middle Way), and because impermanence is itself permanence—such that the entirety of phenomena is the principle—it is said that "the whole substance is extinguished.
This corresponds to the sutra’s statement: "Because it is born again and again, it is unborn. Since delusion is itself the principle, and impermanence is itself permanence, [it does not arise].
One may say that this serves as a response to the objection regarding the impermanence of the "light-flowing" (*ābhāsvara*) concentration.
As for the phrase "originally taking up birth and death," this refers to the term "birth" (*jāti*) found in the sūtra; it is the birth of *saṃsāra*, not the birth of *prajñā*.
The purport of the commentary is that because all phenomena are non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is said that "birth does not arise by itself"; thus, this is the fundamental nature of birth and death.

There is nothing that does not arise from the four propositions; to briefly cite the single phrase "not arising from itself," since birth and death do not arise [from themselves], the principle of true emptiness is revealed—this is the understanding within the realm of desire (dhātu).
Because the understanding within the realm of desire eliminates and dispels the limited stages of existence (pariccheda), it says "arising is non-arising.
Since one does not perceive [birth] arising from the four propositions, it cannot be described by responding to the flowing light by definitively asserting that it arises from itself.

Regarding this difficulty: if the *Zhiguan* commentary on "birth does not arise from itself" is slightly different in its intent from that of the *Shu* (the *Fahua Wenju*), it is because both meanings are equally valid;
thus, each appears in the other. How could the Venerable Zhiyan (Zhang’an) have been refuting the Great Master?
As for the phrase "attained through the cultivation of the path," this means that the ultimate fruit is attained by relying on the causes of true cultivation;
this is the realization within the realm beyond (dharmadhātu), as clearly explained in the *Yi-shu* (Commentary on the Meaning) regarding the intent of the "flowing light."
This concludes the fifth section, which summarizes the refutation of the delusions regarding the internal and external realms.
That which arises within the realm is "arising," and that which does not arise outside the realm is also "arising. This is simply the arising of ignorance. Arising must depend upon conditions;

that which arises from conditions is itself emptiness and the Middle Way. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because arising does not exist. While arising from conditions is existence, this existence is itself non-existence.
This responds to the objection that there must necessarily be a flow of light.
This concludes the sixth [section], which refutes the interpretations of both the internal and external realms.

Since the realization within the realm is also attained through the path of cultivation, and the realization outside the realm is likewise attained through the path of cultivation, it is said that there exists an object that can be attained.

If one attains this, one immediately proceeds to principle; because principle cuts off both mind and speech, it cannot be expressed as a response to the difficulty regarding the "determination of non-existence" and the "passing of light.

Seventh, "that which can be spoken" below clarifies that "one is indeed so. The preceding six [points] are not [the truth], which refutes this "one"; being "one" is precisely the establishment and the refutation.

Therefore, it is not that "non-arising arises," nor is it established as "non-arising does not arise"; rather, according to those capacities and conditions, the four teachings are taught to resolve delusions, which is precisely "the arising of non-arising" up to "non-arising."
Excluding the final two links means excluding birth, old age, and death, because they have not yet arrived in the future.
Regarding their acting as causes and conditions for birth: in the past, within a mind of ignorance (*avidyā*), one performed formative actions (*saṃskāra*) such as giving and so forth;

within that mind of karmic action, the fourfold teaching and its conditions were already fully present. Furthermore, through the moistening of karma by ignorance, the present "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) is established.

From form (*rūpa*) up to grasping (*upādāna*), when the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are about to arise within the mind of craving and grasping, due to past virtuous conditions, one becomes a receptive vessel (*bhājana*) for the Buddha;

the Buddha then expounds for them the Dharma of the four teachings. Since these ten factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) act as the productive cause (*janakahetu*) for birth, it is said that they may also be explained [in this manner].

Regarding the phrase "the contemplation of non-arising" and so forth, that refers to the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas. Based on the teaching of non-arising in this present sutra, one cultivates the practice of the contemplation of non-arising;
thus, that contemplation and this teaching mutually accord with one another. Therefore, the principle is clear:

the specific indications for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* rely solely upon two sutras—first, relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to reveal the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), and second, relying on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* to reveal permanence (*nityatā*). This is the essential point.
However, the subsequent portion of the sutra text extensively demonstrates this according to its meaning.

As for "one phrase possessing four," it is as follows: "arising of arising" (*jātijāti*) represents the specific teaching of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) school. Furthermore, within that teaching there are four gates: the gate of existence (*astitva*), which is "arising of arising";

the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is "the non-arising of arising"; the gate of both, which is "neither arising nor non-arising"; and the gate of neither, which is "neither non-arising nor non-non-arising. Thus, [each phrase] possesses four aspects.

From "arising" and "non-arising," up to "by means of non-arising and non-non-arising," these four gates of the Perfect (Yuan) Teaching constitute the four phrases within the phrase "non-arising and non-non-arising.
How much more so, since within the Perfect, each of the four gates mutually fuses with one another, each further possessing its own four phrases;

and how much more so, since the provisional is identical to the real, and the three teachings are identical to the Perfect, such that every single element is interfused—how could one possibly speak of them in a partial manner?
The inner realization of clarity is fully exhausted in this. If one grasps this meaning, the subsequent explanation of phenomena and principle will be as clear as if before one's eyes.

Regarding "principle within phenomena," the four phrases refer to wisdom and abandonment, cause and effect, and the capacity to transform others and that which is transformed; therefore, they are called "phenomena" (*shi*).
If one knows [the principle] up to this point, it is precisely because the speaker has nothing to say; it is only when one understands this principle that it can be called true preaching.
Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Though there is no sound of speech in the mouth, one universally recites all the scriptures."
Regarding the categories of teaching, practice, and realization: "not hearing what is heard" and so forth pertain to the teaching; "the non-arising of arising" and so forth pertain to practice;
and "the non-arrival at arrival" and so forth pertain to the principle.
Although these meanings are not non-existent and are provisionally accepted as such for the time being, they are ultimately not employed [in this context].
The first two sections below provide the preliminary headings. Regarding pervasive and specific delusions: pervasive delusions refer to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realms;
specific delusions refer to the fundamental ignorance (*avidyā-mūla*) outside the realms.

Regarding pervasive and specific understandings: pervasive understanding refers to the wisdom of partial truth (*pratyekabuddha-jñāna*); specific understanding refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-jñāna*).
"Non-arising arising" is explained next. As for "single delusion," although its ontological essence (*tattva*) does not arise, the delusion itself arises;
therefore, it is called "non-arising arising. This delusion refers specifically to ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the "repeated arising of pervasive afflictions": the afflictions of other realms have already arisen from the primary arising afflictions; because afflictions arise again upon those [already] arisen afflictions, it is called "arising from arising" (*jñānajñāna*).
Since this refers to both the fundamental and derivative afflictions being discussed twice, it is termed "repeated" (*fu*).

Regarding the "single" interpretation of the general explanation: because it stops and dispels the *pariccheda* (segmented birth) within the realm, it speaks of "birth and non-birth"; this is the single interpretation of emptiness.

Regarding the "compound" interpretation of the specific explanation: because it doubly dispels both *pariccheda* and *parināma* (transformative birth) beyond the realm, it speaks of "non-birth and non-birth"; this is...
It is called "repeated" (*fù*) because above the understanding of emptiness there is further the understanding of the middle.
Next, regarding the latter two lines following the line on "arising," they merely conclude what preceded;

if one follows the text of the *Zhiguan*, the Master [Zhiyi] held that the first four lines constitute the understanding and delusion of the conceivable (*sīyì*), while the latter two lines constitute the understanding and delusion of the inconceivable (*bù sīyì*). This is consistent with the present commentary.
The distinction between these two explanations lies in their mutual application to both sides, as indicated previously.

When they are categorized [as] "permanent," it refers to the time when the four characteristics themselves, as distinct categories, each possess its own nature and have not yet been transformed by other characteristics;
because they exist eternally at that time, they receive the name "permanent."
The scripture’s statement that "arising is also permanent" specifically refers to the time when it has not yet been transformed by the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
The phrase "there is no... explains the meaning of impermanence, which is evident.

As for the statement that "there is also the meaning of both permanence and impermanence," this likewise refers to its respective parts, because they are permanent while undergoing transformation, arising, and abiding.
Because it is impermanent, the Sūtra says: "Since dharmas are impermanent, their differentiation is also impermanent.

That which has already arisen and that which is yet to arise undergo destruction; this refers to the characteristic of arising having already occurred, while the characteristic of destruction then follows, thus changing. Therefore, it is said that destruction cannot be permanent.
Destruction is originally non-existent, but because it has now arisen, it is what is presently existent.

Regarding the phrase "originally existing but now non-existent" and so forth: if one considers the characteristic of destruction as having existed originally, it is now non-existent because destruction has already occurred;

thus, this "now non-existent" characteristic is also impermanent. Although the scriptural text cites "originally non-existent but now existent," by extension of the meaning, it should fully include "originally existent but now non-existent";
therefore, the commentary clarifies this point.
That which is severed by Nirvana refers to the four marks as being false and Nirvana as being true.

To realize that birth-and-death is itself Nirvana and not perceive the four marks, but see only the single Nirvana—this is what is called "that which is severed. This is, therefore, severing without severing.
The latter four difficulties concern self-arising, other-arising, original existence, and original non-existence.

The fifth correct response addresses the objection that [the nature] exists inherently; the sixth addresses the objection that it does not exist inherently; the third and fourth can be understood accordingly.
Herein, the phrase "saying it exists" below explains the removal of obstacles. First, regarding the establishment of the obstacle:

one should ask, "Since the four characteristics are all non-existent, why did the preceding sutra itself state that there is the nature of arising? If this were so, would it not be an adherence to the notion of a fixed nature?

This is the subsequent explanation that resolves the objection: since the fixed attachment has already been dispelled, there is no loss in teaching that there is a nature capable of producing [results] according to the capacities of beings.
As before, the following passage cites the preceding sutra as an illustration.

The refutation of the attachment to intrinsic nature is concluded. Just as it was previously stated that all four positions are inexpressible, so now it is shown that the four characteristics are likewise non-existent.
Following this, the subsequent section establishes that there exists a generative nature.

The narrator of the sutra, having already described the characteristics of those who have heard the Dharma, shows that they have increased their Path and diminished their births, as the light of the Land of Quiescent Radiance is partially revealed;
thus, by leaping into the air, he manifests his internal realization.

To set forth the gateway through which this realization was attained: the superior root of Rūcīrāśmi attained awakening through what was heard and what was not heard, while the middle root among the great assembly attained awakening through hearing.

Regarding the state of non-arising arising, those with inferior faculties have not yet attained understanding; how much less so for those who have not reached the ultimate meaning, let alone the former two or four [categories]?

Thus, while the three types of *vaiśāradya* (fearlessnesses) and the fourfold sets (*catuṣkoṭi*) mutually encompass one another, the realization of them differs according to the three levels of faculty.

These two aspects are mutually constitutive: the first question, "this arises from that," asks about the cultivation of causes; the second question, "that possesses sharp faculties," asks about the attainment of the fruit.
Cultivating the cause necessarily results in the attainment of the fruit, and the attainment of the fruit proceeds from the cultivation of the cause. These two meanings converge in a single point;
it is like a single body which, though essentially without distinction, is divided into "this" and "that" through the movement of its limbs.
If one enters the truly pure land, it is superior, as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

when the bodhisattvas of the Fragrant Accumulation Land sit beneath the fragrant trees, they immediately attain the *Guṇagarbha-samādhi*. The same applies to the Land of Acala. Therefore, regarding the practice of entering reality, the pure land is superior;
this is the meaning of the sūtra’s statement that those with sharp and swift intelligence [attain realization].

Regarding the superiority of the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-lokadhātu*): if one excels in transforming others through skillful means and is fully conversant with the application of medicine according to the disease, then the defiled land is superior.

This is like one who must undergo the full training in both civil and military arts before entering the ranks of general or minister; as described in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, it is like the bodhisattvas from the Land of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*) who come to this land to study the practice of the two wheels [of wisdom and means].
The "Immovable World" (*acalā-loka-dhātu*) is the native land of Rūcīra. Its appearance of pure adornment is as described in the aforementioned scriptural passages.
Because the treatise does not discuss the meaning of "not reaching" and "reaching" from Rūcīra’s departure for this world, Vimalakīrti now raises this question to the Buddha;
this serves as an introductory prelude to extensively clarifying the meaning of "not reaching" and "reaching" for those of inferior faculties.
The phrase "furthermore, sending a subsequent question" refers to the second inquiry posed by those of sharp faculties.
Here, "stopping" (*śamatha*) refers to ceasing evil, such as refraining from killing; "practicing" (*caryā*) refers to performing good, such as releasing captive animals.
Although the preceding section of the sutra contains practice and the subsequent section contains stopping, they are distinguished according to their relative frequency and primary emphasis.
Each [of these] follows one specific good.

As for the non-difference between the general and the particular: the Four Great Vows are the general, while the Ten Wholesome Actions are the particular. The general and the particular support one another, whereby pure karma is accomplished.

Within the section on the "Wholesomeness of Cessation," the scriptural text concerning the Ten Practices is precisely the Ten Wholesome Actions; each practice clarifies one wholesome action in successive order.
Regarding the term "Zhāotí" (招提) in the text: it is a corruption and abbreviation of a Sanskrit word.

It is correctly called *cāturdīśa*, which translates as "the four directions," referring to a location where the Sangha from the four directions resides. Some say it means "inviting and leading," but this is an erroneous explanation.
Regarding the sūtra’s statement that not vexing sentient beings is superior, the *Siddhārthabuddhi-paripṛcchā* says:

"The sentient beings of this land, from dawn until noon, possess a mind free from anger and obstruction that surpasses the practice of the six pāramitās for hundreds of thousands of millions of years in a pure land.
This is because in this defiled land, the environment is so harsh that it is difficult to prevent the arising of anger.
"Sengman" (Saṃghāṭī) is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "offering face-to-face.
Regarding the "three kinds and six kinds," this refers to the aforementioned King Devarāja’s formulation of three pairs of challenges: first, taking away; second, letting go;
and third, comparison.
The Buddha taught six metaphors, namely that [phenomena] are like illusions, like mirages, and so forth.
If this is so, the meaning of the subsequent question is as follows:

since "non-arrival" (*aprāpti*) and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) are synonymous with *nirvāṇa*, why was "non-arising, non-arising" stated redundantly previously, whereas now it is simply called "non-arrival"? The intent of the answer is that the former was repetitive, while this...
A single condition (*pratyaya*) may be sufficient for this;

however, as for those who have not yet reached [the stage], they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This correctly explains the meaning of "not yet reached" (*aprāpta*) within the Sūtra. Since they have not yet returned [to the state of a noble one], it is said they have not yet reached it;

alternatively, there may be a scribal error, and it should instead be cited as "those who have not yet reached. One should know that the Sūtra says "not yet reached" (*aprāpta*) and "not reached" (*anuprāpta*).

This does not mean that [the stage] has not yet been reached; it simply refers to the principle of *nirvāṇa* as not yet attained. Thus, it is said that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet reached *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, one knows that the two characters "not yet reached" (*wei-zhi*) are spoken in reference to ordinary beings who have not yet cultivated the perfect cause.

The previous repetition of "non-arising, non-arising" refers to both aspects of *nirvāṇa*: wisdom (*prajñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), both of which are non-arising. What was previously stated regarding the meaning of the single and the multiple applies here.
Thus it is.
Regarding the alternating presentation of one side of birth and death: previously it was said that "the non-arising of arising" means that while all phenomena do not arise, prajñā arises;
this explained the character "birth" (*sheng*) in terms of the virtue of wisdom. Now it is said that "not arriving at arrival" means not arriving at birth and death.

As for *nirvāṇa*, *nirvāṇa* is the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Since this explains the character "to" (*zhì*) by means of the virtue of cessation, we know that the former [the arising of wisdom] was discussed in terms of *prajñā*, while this clarifies the death of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
However, because the arising of wisdom necessarily entails the death of delusion, and the death of delusion necessarily entails the arising of wisdom, it is said that each mentions only one side.
This is also an instance of mutual illustration. In the previous explanation of "arising and non-arising," there were two meanings:

first, it was said that at the time of death according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called "arising and non-arising"; second, it was said that a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage is called "arising and non-arising.

The former clarified the cessation of delusions through one's own practice (*svayaṃ-caryā*), while the latter revealed the perfection of the path for transforming others (*parārtha-mārga*). The present explanation of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) concerns only the perfection of the path for transforming others; thus, the Sūtra says: "For the sake of..."

Because he transforms and delivers others, he manifests within the world; since the path that enables such transformation of others must necessarily arise from one's own practice and the extinction of delusions, it is said "also" (*api*), which serves as a mutual illustration.
This explanation of the meaning of the character *zhì* (至) distinguishes its similarities and differences from the previous explanation of the meaning of the character *shēng* (生).
If one explains *bù zhì* (不至), its meaning is identical to the previous explanation of *bù shēng* (不生), as both refer to death according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, the Sūtra states that because those of the three vehicles have already attained permanent liberation, they are called "non-arriving" (*anāgāmin*).

Regarding the term *anāgāmin* in the Sūtra, it is because the afflictions of the upper realms still remain for those in the third fruit, and they still abide within the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*), that they are termed "arriving.

In the first section of the text, there are two successive divisions of the passage: the first is divided into three sections, and the second is divided into seven sections. This is intended to provide the response.
The textual basis takes the third [question] as primary.
Within that third question, there are again four distinct chapters; specifically, following the third question, the sub-sections consist of five chapters.

The first chapter correctly clarifies that "it exists," which shares the same title as the main section. The remaining four have distinct alternative titles, namely: the second is... (the text breaks off).

The passage beginning with "because it is visible" and continuing with "eternal," etc., constitutes the latter four sections among the seven divisions. In a comprehensive discussion, it should be said that there are five chapters;
however, as we are currently relying on the distinct titles, we speak of them as merely four separate chapters.
The initial inquiry also consists of three parts: the passage from "At that time, [the Dharma] cannot be heard" is the summary of the intent; "How so? and below is the abbreviated inquiry;
and "For what reason? and below is the extensive inquiry. The application of the dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis may be sought accordingly.
The fifth [section] contains two layers of analogies and their applications: first, the analogy of space, and second, the analogy of harming an enemy; each has its application as found in the text.
The sixth [section] contains both analogies and applications; the analogy of citing the past and its application can be understood accordingly.
"As the Buddha previously [taught] below" refers to citing a past scripture.
Regarding the phrase "all adornments and so forth," since these rely upon external embellishments and are not inherently possessed, they belong to the category of impermanence.
The *ānāpāna*—translated here as "sending forth and sending away"—refers to the inhalation and exhalation of breath; this is the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
Regarding the analysis of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "This body has no master; it is like the earth. This body has no... [text continues]
I am like fire; this body is without a life-force (*jīva*). It is like wind; this body is without a person (*pudgala*). It is like water; this body is like space, free from "I" and "mine.
Contemplating the great emptiness, one sees that this body is without cognition, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles.
Thus, by contemplating the six elements, one destroys the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). All of these are based on the causal practices of the Hīnayāna teachings to pose a challenge.
Regarding the scriptural analogy to space: space is equal and all-pervasive, such that it does not discriminate between the wise and the foolish;
yet nirvāṇa has those who attain it and those who do not, and because it is divided according to delusion and awakening, it is not the same as space.

Regarding the statement that "when one person attains [enlightenment], many should attain it as well," this is because the King of Virtue (the Buddha) does not perceive the nature of reality as being either different or identical;

rather, each and every thing is mutually pervasive. Thus, when one Buddha achieves the Way, there is nothing within the Dharma-realm that is not the support (the environment) or the supported (the body) of that Buddha—identical yet not identical.
While those are deluded and this is awakened, the distinction is manifestly clear, as can be understood through the analogy of a thousand lamps in a single room.
"Consciousness.
The section on "Stages and Persons" below is already present in the original text of the sutra.

"True cultivation" refers to ascending the stages (*bhūmi*) to manifest the principle; "conditional cultivation" refers to the practice prior to the stages. The "Three Treatises" refers to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*.
In the *Twelve Gates Treatise*, it is said that in ancient times the Three Treatises were widely propagated, and those who studied them were known as the "Mādhyamika Masters" (Sanlun Shis).

Regarding the passage "neither born nor emerged": it is "not born" because it is not the birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) of ordinary beings; it is "not emerged" because it is not the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
"Not falling and not dying": "not falling" means not falling into the pit of the three unconditioned states; "not dying" means not [subject to] the two kinds of birth-and-death.
"Neither round nor square": it is not "square" because it is not distinct, and it is not "round" because it is not pervasive; it is not "empty" and thus not "pointed."
Because it does not [previously] exist, it is not false.
Just as one who has been confined for a long time and finally emerges from the care of his parents— though he has emerged only after a long duration—
is never said by his parents to have only now come into existence for the first time.
"Simultaneously encompassing the other four" refers to the four questions concerning visibility, impermanence, and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the five causes resemble the four conditions and three causes," the intended meaning is as follows: the five causes in this sutra correspond to the four conditions and three causes in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. As for the four conditions in that treatise:

first, the condition of the cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), which consists of the [three] causes; second, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which refers to the mind and mental factors...

The dharmas of number arise in succession through three conditions: the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), such as when consciousness arises from the eye-consciousness; and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which refers to all other conditions. Regarding the three causes:
the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* does not establish them separately because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is identical to the dominant condition;

it establishes only the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), which corresponds to the present productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which corresponds to the present habitual cause (*abhyāsa-hetu*). The common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*) is [also included].
This is precisely what is meant by "relying on causes" now; thus, the five present [conditions] correspond to those four conditions and three causes. The *Śāstra* states:

"It is simply that the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is absent," because the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) fully possesses the three causes. Since the first three causes are already the causal condition, among the four conditions, only the sequential condition is lacking.
As for the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it says: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the co-existent [cause]..."

It is accepted that there are only six kinds of causes: the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), along with the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and [the remaining two].

Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states: "As for the so-called six causes: the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the self-seed cause (*svabīja-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The commentary explains: "The efficient cause is that which does not obstruct another; the associated cause refers to the mind and mental factors."

Simultaneous association (*sahabhū-hetu*) is so called because mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are mutually associated; it is like friends or acquaintances joining together to accomplish a task.

Common cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which arise together and mutually assist one another, just as brothers born at the same time support and aid each other.
Cause of its own kind (*sva-bīja-hetu*) refers to past wholesome phenomena [acting as the cause] for the present...
Regarding wholesome dharmas as causes, present wholesome dharmas and future wholesome dharmas are likewise [causes]. It is the same for unwholesome and neutral dharmas.
As for the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the eleven universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) within the Truths of Suffering and Origination are called the universal cause;

specifically, these are the five views under the Truth of Suffering, along with ignorance and doubt, making seven; and the four false views, view-grasping, and ignorance under the Truth of Origination.

It is suspected that these eleven proclivities (*anuśaya*) are the root of birth and death; because they can universally act as causes for the five categories [of defilements], they are called "pervasive proclivities" (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Regarding the "retributive cause" (*vipāka-hetu*): when one performs the causes of good or evil and obtains a neutral (*avyākṛta*) result, it is called a retributive cause;

its new name is "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*), meaning that it ripens as a different category [from its cause], hence it is called a ripening cause. As for the "four conditions" (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*), they are as stated above; the five causes are termed "causes."
Because the mind and mental factors arise dependent upon conditions, they are called "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*); this is a new term for what was previously termed the "object-condition.

When various phenomena arise, that which does not create an obstacle is called the "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Now, these five [conditions] are similar to the six causes and four conditions found in the *Mahā-śāstra* and other texts.
"That which is the cause of cultivation" refers to the cause of one's own seeds; it is newly termed the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Regarding the initial dual response concerning cause and effect: the Sūtra clarifies that the six perfections are the cause and Nirvāṇa is the fruit.
Because cause and effect are explained together, it is called a "dual response."
In this sutra, there are three sections: first, the cultivation of practice; second, from "from Great Nirvāṇa" onwards, the perfection of contemplation;
and third, from "at that time, attaining such signs" onwards, the entry into realization, which is the First Abode.
Regarding the first five [points]: the first concerns whether there is a petitioner or not; the second concerns whether the giving is occasional or constant;

the third concerns whether regret arises or not; the fourth concerns whether fear arises or not; and the fifth concerns whether one expects a reward or not. In the fourth section of the text, it is stated that only the arising of the four fears constitutes a *pāramitā*;
by this analogy, it is known that the non-arising of fear does not possess the meaning of "crossing over" (*tāraṇa*).
Those who attain a partial nirvāṇa have not yet realized that each and every substance of giving is signless and unattainable;
therefore, it serves only as a cause for a portion of nirvāṇa.
The latter [type of giver] is the one truly capable of judging and crossing over. The sutra states, "If for the sake of fear or fame... and so forth; there should be three [types of givers].

The section [beginning with] "First, it is stated that these two are not [perfections] from the perspective of practice" and continuing with "Thus, below, it is revealed that these three are [perfections]"—for example, "Suppose there were a person..."—first raises the analogy and then explains why the middle case is not [a perfection].
It says: "For one who is terrified. Question: Previously it was taught that practicing giving while generating fear constitutes a *pāramitā*.

Why is this [present case], which also generates fear, not so? Answer: Because the previous case concerned only a limited portion, it attained the name of "crossing over" (*tīraṇa*). Since that [limited state] already exists, [the present case is distinguished].

Because they are attached to marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it is now said that this is not so; thus the Commentary states: "If there are marks and there is attainment, then it is not the meaning of 'crossing over' (*tāraṇa*).
This also means that "existence is non-existence" and so forth, which clarifies that the four—namely, arising-arising (*utpāda-utpāda*) and the rest—are the meaning of the Three Truths.

Since arising-arising is the dharma produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), realizing this dharma is precisely inconceivable emptiness (*acintya-śūnyatā*); therefore, it is said that "existence is non-existence" and "arising is non-arising."

The phrase "arising" (生) is the point where emptiness is activated as existence; because the hundred realms are perfectly manifest therein, it is said that "emptiness is itself non-empty," which is the phrase "arising is itself non-arising.
The nature of the mind is unmoving, transcending both extremes; thus it is said that "it is neither empty nor non-empty," which is the phrase "non-arising is itself non-arising.
The three truths are perfectly interfused and the four phrases are fully present; profound and yet more abstruse, the meaning lies herein.
In this regard, the second part of the "Chapter on the Virtuous Kings" concerns the four types of offenders:

Regarding the statement that "Buddha-nature does not sustain," since all possess Buddha-nature, it should sustain these individuals so that they do not fall into hell.
The previous objection concerning Nirvana being impermanent refers to the passage from the end of the preceding fascicle where King Śrīgarbha raises a further argument.
Regarding the phrase "causing all to turn": if turning the ordinary into the holy is possible, then one should also be able to turn the holy into the ordinary;

if turning the small into the great is possible, then one should also be able to turn the great into the small. Therefore, it is said that it is difficult for all people [to understand]; this may be understood by consulting the sūtras.

One who has already severed their fundamental grasping is called an icchantika; this means that only after one has severed the wholesome qualities they have already attained is one designated an icchantika.

Since the constant principle of buddha-nature should be regained once it has been severed, yet it does not return to what was already possessed, it is said that "nature is not something already attained."
Furthermore, regarding the passage in the *Xiàxiāo jīng* (Sūtra on the Elimination of Defilements) which states,

"If [defilements] have been severed and attained," and "evil persons are not fixed," this means that whether one is evil or good, it all depends on the transformation of the mind; since the nature of the mind follows conditions,
how can it be fixed as either good or evil?

That the Tathāgata is not fixed is also because he has realized the nature of the mind; thus, he is able to adapt through skillful means according to the capacities of beings, remaining without a fixed [form].
Regarding "form and the characteristics of form": blue, yellow, and so forth are form; square, round, and so forth are characteristics.
Even within that which is indeterminate, there exists a determinate aspect: birth and death are indeterminate, whereas nirvana is determinate;
just as ore can become gold, yet gold does not become ore.

Within the path of skillful means (*upāya*), the Tathāgata is not determinate; "skillful means" refers to the manifestation of traces through provisional and ingenious methods, appearing to be born and appearing to pass away.
Therefore, it is not fixed.
For this reason, that which is not burned further involves the public interpretation: internally, one protects the body; externally, one wards off dust and grime.

This also symbolizes that the Tathāgata’s inner mind is firm and pure, while his external appearance is magnificent and beautiful. As for those who are ruined in the interim, all myriad afflictions are simultaneously extinguished. [Thus ends] the former masters and...

The interpretation by Xinghuang that "the ghost is not the ghost" is not without its various paths; however, because it does not achieve mutual fusion or account for the principles of concealment and illumination (*zhāozhào*), it is not adopted here.
Now, I clarify that the ghost is precisely the non-ghost: within the category of the ghost, the three truths (*sandi*) are fully present.
When "non-ghost" is placed below "non-ghost," it likewise possesses the three truths.
When "neither-ghost-nor-non-ghost" is placed below "double negation," it likewise possesses the three truths.

Since the ghost is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and non-ghost is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), while double negation is the middle (*madhyamā*), and because each of these mutually fuses with the others, each is discussed in terms of the three truths; therefore, the conventional is not fixed.

The meaning of the conventional being indeterminate within the true, the true being indeterminate within the conventional, and the conventional being indeterminate within the indeterminate is as clear as pointing at one’s own palm;
how could this possibly be compared to the old interpretations of Xinghuang?
This final conclusion demonstrates their mutual fusion. Question: Since the three truths are mutually fused, why does the sutra speak of cessation and cultivation?
Regarding the statement that "the two are illuminated simultaneously" to resolve [the doubt], it is precisely because the three truths are mutually interfused that they can be illuminated together.
As for the fact that [the Middle Truth] is placed last, Zhan’an clarifies the significance of its being situated at the end.
I say that the reason Jingxi provides such a clear and extensive explanation below is as follows:
the transformation of the three *āsravas* into the four *oghas* refers to the *kāma-ogha*, *bhava-ogha*, *dṛṣṭi-ogha*, and *avidyā-ogha*.
Regarding the clarification of the seven *āsravas*, the list presented in the text relies entirely upon the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

Regarding the statement that "opening up the extremes constitutes the views of annihilationism and eternalism": among the five views, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is opened up into the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;

therefore, there are six. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (or the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya*) states: "The sūtra text merely indicates six types [of views]. This is a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

'Self' refers to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); 'existence' or 'non-existence' refers to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, to cling to this inferior understanding while claiming it to be superior wisdom is also [a form of the view of extremes]."

The interpretation of Kai-she (Kai-hsien) regarding false views holds that the scriptural text provides both the heading and the explanation in full: first the number six is indicated by "self-view," and subsequently the six types are explained.
Thus, what he establishes is entirely different from that of Zhuang-yan; yet, although his six types are complete, their ultimate convergence is simply the view of self and its body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The "provisional self" (jātmaka) refers to that which is established as a sovereign by surveying the five aggregates (pañca-skandha); it is called the provisional self.
The "true self" (bhūtātman) is simply the spiritual self (puruṣa).

Regarding "suffering of conditioned existence" (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), it is as the Sūtra says: the suffering of conditioned existence experienced by those in the hells, among animals, or among hungry ghosts.

This suffering is the most pervasive because it exists throughout all three realms. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "For example, if one places a lash of hair upon the palm of the hand, one does not perceive it;

yet if it is placed upon the eye, it causes injury and extreme distress. Ordinary beings are like the palm of the hand, failing to perceive the lash of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

It cannot be considered as only one because it combines two matters—the impermanence of transience and the body as a mass of suffering—and is therefore called "suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This is not the "suffering of conditioned existence" found among the three types of suffering.
Regarding "the four beginning with afflictions" (*kleśa*), the term "etc. (*ādi*) includes the aggregates (*skandha*), death (*maraṇa*), and the sons of gods (*devaputra*).
What is encompassed here is extremely vast; "encompassing" (*gai*) means to pervade or include.
As for the phrase "merely auxiliary words," this is because [these factors] must be severed in order to realize *nirvāṇa*, and thus their meaning is identical to that of the preceding sentence.
Regarding the phrase "assisting words," the examples for "assisting phrases" can be understood by analogy with this.

As for "reaching the destination" (*shiki*), whenever one speaks of "sincere mind" (*shishin*), it means reaching the source of the mind; "source" refers to the wondrous principle of the three virtues (*san-toku*).

One aspires to the ultimate fruit (*kyokka*) so that it may be fully developed; since the ultimate fruit is the destination toward which one aspires, it is called "reaching the destination. Thus, it says: "reaching the destination, where? (*shiki ka sho*).
Regarding the passage "Now, birth-and-death is likewise afflictions," this is because karma and delusion are the causes of birth-and-death.
The phrase "I shall not explain further below, etc. refers to the preceding commentary.
Regarding the two lines beginning with "Directly corresponding," since they constitute a single meaning, it was previously stated that they cannot be divided.
Furthermore, these lines serve as proof for this Dharma; because they prove its permanence, there are no three periods of time.

However, since the meaning is already complete by contrasting the first half of the current verse with the preceding four lines, we know that the words "listen with a sincere mind" and so forth merely clarify the act of listening.
The present verse states that the four lines of the preceding verse merely expound the dharmas [taught therein].
Furthermore, regarding the "four [principles]," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 1, says there are four *siddhāntas*: first, the *loka-siddhānta*;
second, the *pratipuruṣa-siddhānta*; third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
The four *siddhāntas* encompass all twelve divisions of the scriptures and the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma;
they are entirely real and without contradiction.

Regarding the three contemplations that treat the three outflows: these are the three contemplations of loving-kindness, impurity, and dependent origination, which counteract hatred, greed, and delusion respectively.
Ignorance is the third outflow (*āsrava*), as explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* within the section on the therapeutic standpoint (*pratipakṣa-siddhānta*).

Alternatively, regarding those who claim that a self (*ātman*) exists, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this according to the worldly standpoint (*loka-siddhānta*): because there are persons and so forth within the world, there is a "first principle" (*paramārtha*);

yet because there is no dharma-nature or the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within the world, there is no "first principle. Thus, [the existence or non-existence of a self] is both existent and non-existent.
That each individual attains happiness is because this gives rise to the meaning of wholesome dharmas.

That *nirvāṇa* is merely a phenomenon of causes and conditions is as the Sūtra says: "Four dharmas are the proximate causes and conditions for *nirvāṇa," namely, associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth."
To say that "the meaning of being established as nature" is identical to the non-Buddhists' reckoning of spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*) is incorrect.

Regarding the four kinds of Buddha-nature mentioned below, where it says "excluding the direct cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), the subsequent correlation and explanation show they are: first, the fruit of the fruit; second, the cause of the cause;
third, the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*); and fourth, the nature of the fruit. Now, when it says "excluding the direct cause up to the four conditions of Buddha-nature," [it refers to these].
Fearing that the text might be erroneous, [the commentary] clarifies the attainment through verse; thus, there is no sense of a "causal factor" (hetu), for the causal factor resides in delusion.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also cutting off the twelve," the term "also" (yi) means "merely" (cai). Because one has merely exhausted the afflictions (kleśa), it belongs to the ultimate exhaustion of the cause, which is the fruit.
Regarding the distinction between shallow and deep: the preceding chapter still refers to Bodhisattvas at a shallow stage, whereas one who does not feel pain now is a Bodhisattva at a deep stage.

To alert others, [the text] uses the term *jìtuó* (警柝). This is the opposite of *tā* (他) in the sense of "each other. It refers to the practice of striking wooden clappers at double gates to await violent guests, as described in the *Zhouyi* and the *Zuozhuan* regarding the state of Lu striking clappers that were heard in Zou.
Zheng Xuan explained: "Holding two pieces of wood in the hands and striking them against each other is called 'striking clappers' (*jìtuó*), a means of maintaining defense and providing vigilance."

In the *Han shu*, it is recorded that within the palace guards and at the city gates, the *diao-dou* were struck to signal the five watches; the guards patrolled the perimeter and struck the willow-tree staffs.

The Sūtra states that for those afflicted by the four poisons, the four great elements become unbalanced and can harm one’s body and life; therefore, they are called "poisons.

As for the arising of the three afflictions based on the three feelings: this means that aversion arises based on painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*), craving arises based on pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*), and delusion arises based on neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*).

Because ancient scholars did not understand the illumination of the two extremes, they engaged in forced interpretations, attempting to resolve the matter through the categories of "two bodies" and "two wisdoms.

Regarding the distinction between the hidden and the manifest, others claim that for a person on the causal stage (hetu-pudgala), the principle is hidden and thus receives the name of "two wisdoms," whereas for a person on the resultant stage (phala-pudgala), the principle is manifest and thus receives the name of "two bodies."
To distinguish between two entities is precisely to differentiate their natures.

The commentary provides four meanings: first, firmness; second, the root; third, growth; and fourth, non-perception. These are to be correlated with the sequence as explained in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*).
"Attaining the nature of a noble one" refers to the Buddha-nature manifested by a noble person at the initial stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

"Extensively manifesting" (mízhù) means that when one illuminates [reality], it is profoundly vast and clearly evident; when one eliminates [delusion], both the horizontal and vertical dimensions are tranquil and still.

One does not flatter because of understanding dependent origination; that is, because one realizes that causes and conditions are empty and false.

Regarding the "five phrases," there is one phrase that gives rise to goodness and four phrases that eliminate evil, totaling five.
"Taking existence" refers to the new; because it is a present cause, it is called "new. "Ignorance" refers to the old;
because it is a past cause, it is called "therefore. "Non-arising arising" refers to the subsequent manifestation of the virtue of wisdom. "New conventional death" refers to affliction.
Because the preceding affliction has been removed, darkness departs and light arises; although there is no temporal sequence, in meaning it is as if darkness departs first and light arrives later.

As for "the new breaking the new," this refers to Prajñā breaking through grasping and existence (*upādāna*). As for "the old breaking the old," this refers to the abandonment of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and the absence of [defilements].

Because one serves as a vessel for others, extending grace to all beings, and because one propels the vessel oneself to repay that grace;
regarding the "great tree of causes and conditions," the two past links are like the roots, the five present links are like the trunk, and the three [future links] are like the branches.
The [eight] branches are like flowers, and because the [last] two branches are like fruit, they are compared to a tree.

Regarding the phrase "foreign lands such as those of the *zhàn* (war)," "foreign lands" refers to India (*Tianzhu*). There, as soon as one achieves victory in battle, one erects a banner; this "waving" (*huī*) is permitted as a reversal [of the enemy].
The *Shangshu*, in the "Mu Shi" chapter, states: "The King held a yellow battle-axe in his left hand and grasped a white yak-tail standard in his right hand with which to wave."
The *Kongzhuan* (Commentary by Kong [Anqing]) states: "The *yue* is an axe adorned with gold. Holding the *yue* in the left hand signifies having no concern for execution;
holding the *mao* (ox-tail banner) in the right hand signifies being engaged in instruction.
Regarding the passage from "If one can give rise to the mind" to "no longer called an *icchantika*": because one has already reformed their former evils, this is so.
Because a virtuous person who abides in the Buddha’s correct teaching cannot give rise to an evil mind, it is said that they do not deviate.
The Buddha-nature is distinct from the roots of goodness; the Buddha-nature is inherent goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*), whereas the roots of goodness are acquired goodness (*bhāvanā-kuśala*).

Because King Devarāja confused these two—acquired and inherent—the Master [Sengzhao] asked whether both goodness and the Buddha-nature should be considered uninterrupted. Now, the Buddha answers by distinguishing between the acquired and the inherent.
Thus, because icchantikas sever the cultivation of conditioned goodness, they lack it; yet because they do not sever their innate nature of goodness, they possess buddha-nature.

One should know that the distinction between cultivated and innate goodness and evil originates from our own school, which perfectly exhausts the source of the teachings and profoundly penetrates the intent of the Buddha. How could the various masters of past and present have fathomed this subtlety?
Therefore, the *Pumen xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Universal Door) states: "The Tathāgata does not sever his innate evil, and the icchantika does not sever his [innate goodness]."
Because the nature of goodness is uninterrupted, it is "good by nature. Regarding the text that further states: "Penetration (*prativedha*) is the adornment of wisdom through clear realization;
conditions (*pratyaya*) are the assistance of the adornment of merit. With these two as causes, the Buddha possesses the two fruits.

Fundamentally, this cause and fruit are originally inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*); these inherent virtues of penetration and conditions have existed from the beginning. The three thousand realms are, in their very nature, emptiness.

The three thousand [realms] as the *nirvedhabhāga* (the cause of realization) are the provisional nature; the three thousand as the *pratyaya-hetu* (the conditional cause) are the neutral nature; and the three thousand as the *mūla-hetu* (the fundamental cause) are the true nature.

Therefore, other interpretations only know that even an *icchantika* does not sever the fundamental cause, yet they do not know that it does not sever the conditional and realized causes inherent in its nature.
Thus, one knows that good and evil do not transcend the three thousand. He further asked: "If there is goodness within the nature, there must also be evil within the nature."
Question: Regarding the answer that both [the icchantika and the Buddha] possess [both good and evil], what kind of good and evil do the icchantika and the Buddha sever?
Answer: The icchantika severs cultivated good, yet the innate good remains; the Tathāgata severs cultivated evil, yet the innate evil remains.
Question: Why are the innate virtues of good and evil not severed? Answer: Because the innate virtues are merely the gates of dharma for good and evil; therefore, they cannot be severed at all.
In this world, there is nothing capable of destroying [the nature]; even if Māra were to burn the sutras, how could he cause the dharma-gate of inherent goodness to be exhausted?

Even if one were to burn the records of evil, one could not cause the dharma-gate of inherent evil to be exhausted. Question: Since icchantikas do not sever their inherent goodness, they will eventually give rise to goodness again;
likewise, since Tathāgatas do not sever their inherent evil, they ought to give rise to evil again at a later time. Answer: Icchantikas... [The text here appears to be truncated.]
Because one does not understand that inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*) is ultimately non-arising, later on, cultivated evil (*bhāvanā-pāpa*) arises again;

because one does not realize that inherent goodness (*prakṛti-kuśala*) is ultimately non-arising, later on, cultivated goodness (*bhāvanā-kuśala*) is defiled by it. Therefore, cultivated goodness can once again give rise to [defilement].

By using cultivated goodness to counteract cultivated evil, one ensures that cultivated evil does not arise. Although the Buddha does not sever inherent evil, he is able to fully comprehend inherent evil.
Yet, regarding evil dharmas, one attains mastery and is not defiled by the cultivation of evil; therefore, the cultivation of evil cannot arise.
Thus, the Buddha never possesses mastery over the cultivation of evil. If an icchantika can penetrate the gate of evil dharmas, they are no different from the Tathāgata.
Therefore, one knows that regarding both good and evil, it is only through thorough penetration of the cultivated and the innate that [one attains liberation].
Xiao now explains that the King of Virtue, based on the shared meaning of "wholesome," raises a difficult objection regarding the Tathāgata’s response according to the distinctions of cultivation.
As for those at the extreme limit of the most evil desires, they are called "extremes" because their evil is so absolute.
Skillful means are not non-existent because, by dwelling in the stage prior to [the first] and cultivating the attainment of conditions and understanding as one's means,
they manifest the rational cause of the true nature upon the arousal of that dwelling.

The performance of decadent music was likely a preference of the lords who had vacated their states; however, as this scripture cites it as a metaphor, such practices have existed in the Western Regions for a long time.
As for the mention of "one who scorns," the scripture refers to him as a person of ignorance.
This reckoning of the meaning of "nature" (svabhāva) is identical to the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) attachment to the view that the effect exists within the cause as an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

The Sūtra does not dispute this deficiency; rather, it reproaches [the practitioner] for it. The phrase "praising the excellence of self-sufficiency" praises the goodness of the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).

Thirteen. One who does not observe the precept against creating flaws does not refrain from [transgressions] below the thirty; one who does not observe the precept against creating impurities does not refrain from those associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sāṃvṛti*).
One who does not act as a Śrāvaka does not discipline or deliver themselves. All of these constitute evil precepts.
One who has attained the full precepts realizes the dharma-realm of cessation;

because they do not perceive the marks of upholding or violating the precepts, they do not treat the great with arrogance nor the small with pride, nor do they regard upholding as superior to violating.
Regarding the necessity of higher concentration: one must attain the four dhyānas before being born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for "white bones" being the *pratismukti-dhyāna* (meditation of liberation), it is because the first two liberations involve internal contemplation of a skeleton.

Regarding the statement that "loathing and revulsion constitute the practice of *prahāṇa* (abandonment) because it is easy," this means that loathing desire and abandoning attachment is the meaning of "loathing and revulsion.

yet the Tathāgata stepped upon the fire without being burned and ate the poison without being harmed. He then abandoned his false views and became a younger brother to the Buddha."
My son,
as for the twelve [categories], where there are many texts, one should say eleven; since the Vaipulya is selected from among the twelve, the two characters [in that context] are erroneous.
The reason why the *Vipula* (Vaipulya) division has few words but essential meaning is that it discusses sublime principles directly without engaging in other matters.
The reason why the twelve divisions of scripture have vast and extensive wording is that these twelve divisions collectively encompass all Mahāyāna sūtras.
Therefore, having now excluded the first three flavors (*rasa*), this sūtra—which incorporates the breadth of the twelve divisions—proceeds to reveal and expound upon the doctrine of the eternal.
"Abbreviated" means to set aside other twelvefold divisions of the sūtras so that one may receive and uphold these twelvefold divisions of this very sūtra.
Furthermore, regarding those that exclude the entire body [of a text], even if the beginning and end of a single sūtra have extensive wording, one takes only the essential words and sublime phrases—
such as four lines— that encompass the meaning of the entire Dharma-realm, like the "Four Pillars of the Snowy Mountain" verses and others.

If we simply take "permanently abiding" (nitya), even the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are still too elaborate; it suffices to say "permanently abiding," for in principle there is nothing it does not encompass, and in meaning there is nothing it does not include.

Furthermore, regarding the removal of "permanently abiding" and so forth: although previously we proceeded from the broad to the narrow, beginning with the twelve [links of dependent origination] and ending with "permanently abiding."
All [who] merely pursue names and words fail to awaken to the principle; they remain like those who count others' treasures while remaining ignorant of their own mind.

If one can realize that phenomena are themselves the principle and that speech is itself non-speech, then the cool pond will be reached and the treasure-site attained before long, for the mind encompasses all.
Therefore, it is said that one is "fully endowed with extensive learning."

Regarding the phrase "diminishing it again and again," the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) says, "By means of ultimate non-existence, there is no diminution. Zhaoming (Huisi) states that this refers to a change in practice; for now, we shall rely upon this.
"Diminishing it again and again" corresponds to the preceding four sections, which proceed from the broad toward the narrow. "Ultimately reaching non-action" corresponds to what is taken here:
simply maintaining silent stillness. Since the religious teachings of our school apply the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) to every passage, does this not indeed follow [that principle]?
Treading upon this has a profound basis that accords with the Buddha’s intent: if one does not contemplate the mind, one cannot peacefully accord with silent quiescence.

As for the statement that "dharmas have no nature," it is because they lack the four natures; thus it is said that there is no teaching of dharmas. This is identical to what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Know that dharmas are eternally without nature. It is the same as this.

Because they do not harbor attachments, having realized that the Dharma-realm is devoid of intrinsic nature, they do not conceive of difficult tasks as being difficult; this means they do not boast of their achievements.
Even the Confucian tradition holds that "one who benefits the world does not claim credit," and Laozi likewise says, "When the work is accomplished, one does not dwell upon it.
How much more so for a Great Being whose mind is the Dharma-realm itself—how could such a person be attached to the efficacy of their own efforts?
However, although the nature of what cannot be seen is empty, because one clings to it as being existent, one must cultivate emptiness in accordance with its fundamental principle.
As for "transcending form," since form is itself emptiness, it is not the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.

Regarding the statement that the sūtra does not depart from earth and so forth: because emptiness is itself form, it does not depart from form; and because the characteristics of emptiness and form mutually sublate one another, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the sūtra’s possession of the five matters: these are the first, faith, and the second, the straight mind, and so forth, making five in total.
If one does not obtain the direct vision of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one cannot become their immediate retinue.
To cite internal phenomena as an analogy:
"internal phenomena" refers to the primary retribution, namely all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). As for external [phenomena]...
"Dharma" refers to the conditioned environment (*pariṇata-niśraya*), for things such as salt and honey are all conditioned environments.
That which exists in relation to conditions is provisionally established in accordance with causes and conditions.
Greed is an existent dharma, not emptiness. As for that which makes it empty—the mind that is able to crave and the forms that are craved—they are [empty] in terms of delusion.
That which exists as real is non-existent now; because one immediately realizes the false as being the true, it is not emptiness that makes things empty.
This "dharma" refers to the mind of greed and its objective realm of form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the term *jāti*, Master Xian states that it refers to the Sāṃkhya heretics.
According to the Sūtra, one no longer perceives the nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-dharmatā*), because once the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is perceived, it is a seamless fusion of oneness;

thus, one does not perceive the distinct natures of various phenomena. This is due to two reasons: first, regarding the nature of phenomena as events (*vṛtti-dharmatā*), there is no differentiation in their essential nature;
second, regarding the nature of phenomena as reality (*tattva-dharmatā*), their essential nature is truly real. The Sūtra states: "The nature of all phenomena is the nature of events."
Furthermore, Prajñā is "without knowing" yet "there is nothing it does not know. Because it is devoid of deluded conceptualization and discursive cognition, it is said to be "without knowing";

because it possesses the knowledge that illuminates principle, it is said to "know nothing that it does not know. By analogy, emptiness is fundamentally without seeing, yet there is nothing it does not see.
This refers to the absence of the view that falsely imagines existence while possessing the view that illuminates emptiness.
The citation from the past to corroborate this concerns Ānanda’s grief and distress when the Śākyas were slaughtered by Virūḍhaka.

The rest are all visible: generosity (*dāna*) comprises two factors, namely, equanimity (*upekṣā*) and [the faculty of] mindfulness; ethical discipline (*śīla*) comprises three, namely, right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
patience (*kṣānti*) comprises four, namely, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of awakening of mindfulness, and right mindfulness;

diligence (*vīrya*) comprises eight, namely, the four right efforts, the faculty of diligence, the power of diligence, the factor of awakening of diligence, and right effort; and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) comprises eight, namely, the four bases of psychic power, the faculty of concentration, and the power of concentration.
The power, concentration, awakening factor of concentration, and right concentration are subsumed under wisdom;

these ten refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the awakening factor of investigation, the awakening factor of joy, right view, and right intention—these thirty-five factors are thus subsumed within the six perfections. Furthermore, there are two others:
faith, which is common to all thirty-five, because faith is the foundation of all dharmas; namely, the faculty of faith and the power of faith.

In the *Vibhāṣā*, the lower section subsumes the thirty-seven factors under eleven actual entities (*dravya*). First, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) encompass the remaining six categories:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga*);

the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*)—wherein "right effort" is [identical to] right exertion (*samyagvīrya*), which enters into the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) consist of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*), right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-sambodhyaṅga*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛti-indriya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-sambodhyaṅga*). These twenty-four factors are subsumed within the seven factors of enlightenment;

those not included are the two types of faith, which are counted as one, and right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), which is one mental factor, along with right speech, right action, and right livelihood, which are actually only two because they are the fundamental [paths of action].

The seven factors of enlightenment comprise thirty-seven [factors]; right livelihood is included within verbal action. However, among the seven groups [of the thirty-seven], joy is subsumed under investigation, and equanimity is subsumed under relinquishment.

Furthermore, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are only ten actual entities, because the three—verbal action, livelihood, and [right speech]—are combined into one as a single limb of morality (*śīla-aṅga*).

In the first section, "The Cloud of Merit" (*Guṇamegha*), the initial virtue is contrasted with the principle of the beginning and end being identical throughout the text; within the inquiry concerning this initial virtue, the *sūtra* is cited to demonstrate the three virtues.
