The meaning of "this interpretation and so forth" is that the ten virtues, from beginning to end, ultimately converge in the three truths. If discussed horizontally, each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses all ten;

if discussed vertically, there is no contradiction with the respective stages. Whether horizontal or vertical distinctions are made, the three truths remain unerring, because the ten stages of practice are merely partial realizations (*pradeśa-prativedha*) of the three truths.
Once this partial realization is understood, the stages prior to the [first] ground (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) can be known. Since it is already granted that they are horizontal...

In this treatise, we understand that the principle (*li*), names (*mingzi*), contemplative practice (*guanxing*), the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*), the partial truth (*fenzhen*), and the ultimate truth (*jiujing*) all fully possess the ten virtues.

Since these ten virtues are identical to the three truths, although there are two distinct levels—high and low—and differences between cultivation and realization, the sages and ordinary beings are unified within a single thread, and the essence of the principle remains without discrepancy.
Thus, we know that when the Master of the Commentary (*shuzhu*) explains the sutra, he probes the profound and seeks out the hidden; how could he be compared to those of antiquity?

To verify the text and substantiate the meaning, it was stated above that "both are endowed with the two adornments."

The oral secret (*kūmitsu*) consists of hearing the name and recognizing its essence, being able to explain the names to others through the oral secret, acting according to what is taught, teaching according to how one acts, and practicing through contemplative cultivation (*kan-gyō*).

Regarding the "secrecy of speech" (*mukha-guhya*): one can fill the trichiliocosm with a single sound. The similar secrecy of speech, the partial truth, and the ultimate secrecy of speech may be understood as follows:

the first five exist in the causal stage (*hetu*), while the last one is the fruition (*phala*). Now it is clarified that the questioner represents the true cause and the respondent represents the ultimate fruition;
these are the two locations.

Regarding the three secrets of body, speech, and mind, all are categorized according to the six stages of realization; however, following the title of this chapter, we shall here focus on the secret of speech.
This is because it pertains to the Worldly Stage (*loka-dhātu*), wherein cause and effect are distinct, and through the exchange of questions and answers, one brings joy to others.
This is "derived from being human" because disciples receive the Dharma from their teachers in order to produce wholesome states.

This refutes [your position] even if one were to resort to such a calculation.

Regarding the question "Who spoke of Buddha-nature?": since Buddha-nature was spoken by the Buddha himself, for what reason do you instead title this chapter after a Bodhisattva?
The explanations of the three masters contradict the meaning and deviate from the text; therefore, it is said they are "divergent" (guāi). Each [explanation] is at variance with the other.

Now, since the section below is clearly titled "Question and Answer on the Meaning of Nirvāṇa," it means that Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda asked about the meaning of Nirvāṇa, and the Tathāgata answered by explaining the meaning of Buddha-nature.
If one grasps this intent, there will be no other three errors.

"All belong to the revealing cause" means that while the myriad virtues fundamentally belong to the conditioning cause, it is through the single vehicle’s thorough realization that these myriad virtues are brought to fruition.
The myriad virtues also belong to the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*).

As the Sūtra says, regarding "there being a vehicle or there being no vehicle," this means that there is the One Vehicle which is wisdom, while the absence of the One Vehicle refers to the myriad virtues.
The other phrases, all speaking of "existence" and "non-existence," can be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the phrase "this refers to the nature of the fruit," it means that the category of "having the nature" (*sattvadhātu*) is the very nature of bodhi and nirvāṇa.

Regarding the citation of "the nature of the correct cause," this also includes sentient beings as having the correct cause; that is to say, whoever possesses a mind is endowed with the correct cause.
The explanation of the names and meanings of the five natures is as recorded previously.
Regarding "causes with and without results," this explains the meaning of the sixth section:
the phrase "cause with result" refers to the cause of cultivation (*abhyāsa-hetu*), and the phrase "result with cause" refers to the fruit of cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*).

Furthermore, the three phrases take existence with activity (*sābhisaṃskāra-bhava*) as the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*), and taking existence with retribution (*savipāka-bhava*) as the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*); these are the causes and fruits of cultivation and retribution.
The meaning is detailed as previously recorded.
Regarding "active" (*kṛta*) and "non-active" (*akṛta*), the following explains the meaning of these three phrases:
"It is the cause of afflictions" means that afflictions are able to produce karmic actions and their retributions.

Regarding "karma is not afflictions, etc.": because the three types of karma and the ten links [of dependent origination] are not themselves afflictions, the Sūtra states, "there is karma," thereby distinguishing it [from afflictions].

Regarding "retribution is the fruit of karma arising from afflictions": because karma is moistened by delusion (*kleśa*), these two together act as the cause that draws forth the retribution of birth and death.

The causes and effects of the world are the Path and Cessation: that which has a cause is the Path, and that which has an effect is Cessation. The causes and effects of the mundane world are Suffering and Origination;
the phrase "that which is conditioned and involves action" refers to Origination, while the phrase "that which is the retribution" refers to Suffering.

As for the statement "having a cause" and "lacking a cause," it means that when there is a supramundane cause, there is no mundane cause. These [terms] arise through mutual opposition, as do the remaining phrases.
For example:

based on the retribution of the environment (*i-bào*), when there is no [separate] retribution, one asks about the "correct nature" (*zhèngxìng*). This "retribution" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the five aggregates are themselves Buddha-nature, which is precisely the nature of the correct cause (*zhèng yīn xìng*).
As for the eighteen articles, it is sufficient merely to enumerate them in detail according to the six preceding sections.
Regarding their similarities and differences: "similar" means they do not depart from the Buddha-nature; "different" refers to the various points mentioned above.
Thus, they are the same yet not the same, and different yet the same.
I maintain that the subsequent section by Jingxi, which meticulously examines the meaning of the text,

However, this is not yet considered the "attainment of the intended meaning. When the Buddha enumerates the six gates, his intention lies in the Buddha-nature; thus, even if one exhaustively questions these six gates, though it may be called the Buddha’s word, one has not yet grasped the Buddha’s true intent.

The general exhortation below is an explanation that anticipates and addresses potential objections. One might object: "Since you allow for specific exhortations and general inquiries, why do you not provide a general [explanation]?"
Regarding the question of whether the Buddha’s exhortation to inquire into the distinct natures of the six gates is exhaustive, the current commentary explains that it is not so for two reasons:
first, if the Buddha had exhorted an inquiry into the Buddha-nature in its entirety, there would be omissions among the various names and characteristics; thus, it is said to be "not exhaustive.

Second, if a bodhisattva were to inquire separately into the six gates, since the Dharma is in reality boundless, how could it be limited to only six? Thus, it is said to be "not exhaustive. It is not as [some might claim].

To speak briefly, if one asks about the Buddha-nature, it comprehensively subsumes all specific meanings without exception; therefore, [the critique] states that this does not yet constitute grasping the essential meaning.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "conforming to the Buddha’s intent," it is because the Tathāgata’s intent lies in the Buddha-nature; thus, he generally exhorts Bodhisattvas to receive his instructions in a comprehensive manner.
Question: Although this accords with the Buddha’s intention, there is concern that if the assembly hears only the general [teaching], they may become confused regarding the specific;

therefore, the Buddha specifically exhorts [the disciples] below to open up the general to reveal the specific. Furthermore, because the Teacher’s Lion’s Roar asks about the general, the general and the specific are of one essence, allowing them to be elucidated through mutual reference so that the multitude may easily understand.

The characters "liǎn" (to gather) and "jiǎn" (to restrain) are used interchangeably; "liǎn" means to collect and "jiǎn" means to bind. Though the words differ, their meaning is the same, and either may be retained.

The *Hou Han shu* (History of the Later Han), compiled by Fan Ye, states that in the first year of the Zhanghe era, the kingdom of Anxi dispatched an envoy to present a lion and a *fuzhi* (auspicious branch);
the latter resembled a qilin but lacked horns.
This is because the ground of *śīla* (precepts) serves as the foundation for all wholesome virtues.
The sutra states that those who wish to destroy [the truth] but are not actually lions cannot perform the lion’s roar through the three preceding teachings;
thus, it says below that they "perform the lion’s roar for the sake of all sentient beings," which refers to preaching the Buddha-nature.

Regarding the phrase "purifying the place of dwelling" in the sutra, the subsequent text explains that this reveals the sphere of the Buddha’s practice, which is the secret treasury of the three virtues.

This is the place where the Buddha practices and dwells; now, by revealing it to sentient beings so that they may not be defiled by the three delusions, it is said that "the place of dwelling is purified."
The "mechanism for the extinction of evil and the arising of good" refers to the extinction of the three obstacles (trividha-āvaraṇa) and the arising of the three virtues (triguṇa);
this is precisely the perfect mechanism of the present sutra.

First, the non-appropriate [candidates] are cited, using the jackal as a metaphor for the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha): although they may attend upon the Tathāgata, they ultimately cannot...

Regarding the explanation of the Buddha-nature, a sutra states: "Although one follows a lion and so forth, [one is still called] a jackal. In the *Xiayu Fu* (Rhapsody on the Wild Geese), the term *shegan* is used;
"she" is pronounced as "ye," referring to an animal resembling a fox but smaller, capable of climbing trees.
The three types of beings are the noble Brahmā-devas.
Regarding the phrase "the Ten Powers, etc.," the application of other matters and dharmas may be understood by consulting the sūtras.
As for the four categories mentioned previously: first, those that move in water; second, those that move on land; third, those that fly; and fourth, the fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*).
The opening analogy concludes below by rebuking others for explaining the title of this chapter solely through the lens of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the first three questions concerning the Dharma and so forth: the former question concerns the nature that is perceived, while the latter question concerns the person who perceives.
First, regarding the nature of the fruit (*phala-svabhāva*): another passage in the sūtra asks, "What is called Buddha-nature? It is said to be the nature of the fruit.

Next, regarding the nature of the cause (*hetu-svabhāva*): the sūtra asks, "By what meaning is it named Buddha-nature? It is established as a name based on its meaning; that is, it is the nature of the cause.
The intention behind the "double question" is that the four virtues pertain to both cause and fruit; however, this interpretation deviates from the text, and thus Master Guan does not accept it.
Now, taking the essence and meaning of Master Guan’s approach, we shall establish the six stages by means of three [categories].

Regarding those who ask about the preceding dharma using subsequent terminology, one should bring the person capable of seeing from the latter section here to inquire about the differences in the high and low levels of the Buddha-nature they perceive.
First, one asks all sentient beings about the principle-Buddha-nature (*li foxing*);

this term "principle" encompasses the preceding four stages, as they have not yet manifested the pervasive reception of the principle and are thus termed "staying before" [the stages]. Next, one asks the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abidings.

Regarding the meaning of Buddha-nature in the "Section on Questions": subsequently, when the Tathāgata asks about the ultimate Buddha-nature, he speaks of its name, meaning, essence, and the three stages.

Now, setting aside the peripheral aspects to take up the primary ones, each is considered according to a single type: if it is inherently present but not yet manifested, then the name and meaning are not yet revealed;
once it is developed at the first stage (prathamabhūmi), its meaning begins to be distinguished; and only for the Buddha, who has reached the ultimate, is the name clearly and publicly proclaimed.

Regarding the nature and function of the eye: if one asks what constitutes the nature and function of that which is able to see, the answer is that the eye’s capacity for total vision is its "nature," while the eye itself is the "object" of that seeing.
If one were to exclude all capacities, the nature of the entity would fail to encompass all phenomena;
yet if everything were merged into a single unity, how could one distinguish between subject and object? I address future scholars: you must take this to heart.
The "praising and explaining the six meanings" refers to the aforementioned six questions.

In this land, those with superior merit and wisdom are considered "superior" because people in this defiled land generally have little merit, to the point where some lack sufficient food and clothing;
in contrast, those in the Pure Land possess such merit by default.
"Qi-shang" (企尚) means to aspire or look forward to.

From the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes up to those of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the "Abodes" (*zhu*) serve as the subject that relies, while the "Stages" (*di*) serve as the basis upon which they rely.

Because the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage of the Shared Teaching are identical to the Buddhas of the Shared Teaching in their ability to manifest the eight aspects of enlightenment (*baxiang*), it is said that the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are like [Buddhas].
The reason why Bodhisattvas are said to share with Buddhas in belonging to the adornment of wisdom from the ninth stage downward, while both belong to the adornment of merit, is as follows:
if one interprets this text, since these are Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka, why is it said that they abide permanently without obstruction?

Therefore, it is necessary to provide a secret interpretation of that initial teaching to dissolve its [limitations] through the perfect and eternal [truth]; for this reason, the Heavenly Son is cited as a witness.
If it is so even at the very lowest level, then since both devas and humans are permitted to enter the secret [teachings], how could the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas not be so?

Thus it is said, "The same applies to the others. Therefore, the instructor is cautioned that when interpreting the text, one must not dogmatically cling to the fact that the present sutra emphasizes the granting of [rewards].

Therefore, the Tathāgata established the three preceding teachings to explain the two kinds of adornment (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*). Next, by resorting to equality, he brings together the partial and enters the perfect;
since principal and attendant are of one suchness and Buddhas and sentient beings mutually pervade one another, he says: "Both you and I each possess the two adornments.
As for the question regarding why it is not the case that the two adornments are dualistic: if I possessed the two adornments, I should also be able to answer; I should not merely ask.

If the Buddha were fully endowed with both adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*), he should likewise be able to question; it would not be appropriate for him to merely answer. Since both [the Buddha and the interlocutor] would be equal in this regard, the dynamic of question and answer could not be established;

therefore, it is said that this is not the case. As for "one kind" and "two kinds": the principle of *nirvāṇa* is the same, hence it is called "one kind"; the phenomena of *saṃsāra* differ, hence they are called "two."
The various categories are as explained in the sub-commentary.
It is precisely because one understands that there is neither "one" nor "two"— that is, because one understands that birth-and-death is not false and nirvana is not real,
for their essential nature is identical— that it is said there is "neither one nor two."
Because the Bodhisattva’s understanding is the ultimate understanding of the Buddha, he is able to engage in question and answer so as to cause other sentient beings to also understand this Dharma;
thus it is said, "Sentient beings do not understand," and so forth.
This is not a concluding summary intended to reveal that the Buddha told me there are one kind or two kinds, nor is it a fixed calculation regarding birth and death.
Because it refers to the distinct characteristics of nirvāṇa, it is said that it is neither one nor two;

yet, regarding the one and the two, this is spoken of in terms of the non-differentiation of the single essence while discussing the distinctions between phenomena and principle. Therefore, it is said that there is "one-and-two" within the absence of one-and-two.
This also means that by using speech to explain and discern the principle of non-differentiation regarding that which is beyond speech;
it does not mean using speech to speak of speech, nor using speech to differentiate names and characteristics into the distinctions of one or two.
Regarding the text following the refutation of the previous objection, there is a commentary stating that the wording is erroneous.
"Craving and ignorance of the past and present" means that craving is a present delusion and ignorance is a past delusion.
One can know these two and their non-duality because one understands that the phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as defilement and purity, are distinct; thus it is said, "one can."
Because one knows these two and further realizes their identity in essence, it is said that "these two are not two. Since the objects known are distinct, there is no fault of being one;
since their essence is realized as identical, there is no fault of being two. The term "knowing" (能知) governs the subsequent phrase.
Now, the "Lion" section resumes the fundamental tenet to clarify its meaning. First, the Lion manifests by asking through the dual negation;
next, the Buddha responds by manifesting the Tathāgata through the dual illumination. This is truly because illumination is itself negation and negation is itself illumination;

since the essence of negation and illumination is one, the primary and the attendant each occupy one side. The subsequent text consists of three sections, which can be understood by following the headings and phrasing.
The statement, "If there were no 'one' or 'two,' how could one be free from 'one' and 'two'? means that only when 'one' and 'two' first exist can both 'one' and 'two' be simultaneously negated;
if there were no 'one' or 'two,' there would be no phenomena to negate.
Regarding the correct answers to five questions while simultaneously answering one: previously, there were six questions in total—five concerning the Dharma and one concerning persons.
These were: (1) the essence of the rational nature; (2) the meaning of the categorized nature; (3) the name for the ultimate state; (4) those who do not perceive the nature;
(5) which dharmas possess penetration or lack it; and (6) which eyes possess penetration or lack it. Now, the Buddha correctly answers the preceding [questions].

Regarding the second [set of questions], the third [question] is addressed within the explanation of understanding provided in response to the second question; it clarifies that one who possesses understanding is able to see, thereby simultaneously answering the third.

One should know that "emptiness and existence, neither emptiness nor existence" means that in terms of emptiness, the three truths are all extinguished, while in terms of existence, the three truths are all present.
Illumination is precisely illumination that has lost itself because wisdom is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); therefore it is said to be "not existent.

Precisely because it has lost itself yet illuminates, the emptiness of the ultimate truth is named wisdom; therefore it is said to be "not empty. This is fundamentally because emptiness and existence are identical in essence and do not depart from the wondrous nature;
thus it is called the Middle Way. Consequently, the three [aspects]—one and three—revolve and mutually fuse, and the three truths are simultaneously extinguished; hence it is so stated.
Because it exhausts all marks and illuminates the three truths simultaneously, it is said to "illuminate all objects.
Thus, regarding the phrase "within all," it is because the cessation of illumination and the illumination itself are of the same essence; the word "云" (yún) is redundant in the text.
Therefore, the following section cites the sūtra to demonstrate the meaning of the three truths.

That which is called "Buddha-nature" is precisely the Middle Way. Although in the sūtra text Buddha-nature appears first, here it is placed last in order to preserve the sequential order of the three truths;
thus, we know that the meaning of the three truths is complete within the sūtra text.

Regarding the phrase "not seeing the limit of emptiness" (*kō-hen*), this is a scribal error; it should read "the two limits" (*ni-hen*). The sub-commentary below states: "Emptiness (*kū*) refers precisely to the two limits.

One must understand that when the sutra speaks of "emptiness and non-emptiness," it does so by relating the middle to the two limits. Since the original text was not yet corrected, it reads "limit of emptiness";
one should know that this is an error for "two limits."

Regarding the observation of extremes within the middle: when both the middle and the extremes are observed simultaneously, this is called the perfect illumination of the three wisdoms, which is the wisdom of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
The following passage clarifies that because the three wisdoms are mutually integrated and fully present at once, they are not sequential; thus, the extremes are themselves the middle.
Because the non-shallow is not the extreme, it is not deep.
It is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Below, by means of the identity of the essence of stillness and illumination, the three contemplations are established. Emptiness is the stillness of all three truths;
wisdom is the illumination of all three truths. Now, taking stillness as emptiness and illumination as the provisional (*upādāya-satya*) is evident from the text.
Regarding those who lack the four virtues, the Sūtra says: "up to seeing that all things are without self.

Among these four [types of views], this briefly cites one case to demonstrate the incorrectness of seeing emptiness while lacking the four virtues, thereby revealing the correctness of seeing the Middle Way while possessing the four virtues.
As for the two types of non-seeing, they refer to ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles; as for the one type of seeing, it refers to Bodhisattvas.
Regarding those who follow their own inclinations, it is said that because Bodhisattvas perceive according to their own dispositions, they do not see clearly;
thus, the sutra concludes by stating that although the Buddha-nature exists, they simply do not perceive it.
As for those who give rise to views regarding names, they proclaim that one who sees the Middle Way merely gives rise to false conceptions upon the name "Middle."
The view of the Middle Way is not a view attained through realization; this applies equally to all three [vehicles]. Others claim that there is a single type of view, which is incorrect.

Ordinary beings and those of inferior capacity give rise to views of "middle" and "eternal" regarding the birth-and-death in which they are attached. Furthermore, the mundane world also clarifies the "middle," as the books say:

"With the virtue of the Mean, the people harmonize with it. As for the two vehicles (the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), they consider themselves to have attained [liberation] by departing from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

The Bodhisattva of the Middle Way employs the provisional emergence within the capacities of sentient beings as the very Middle Way; thus, these three types of persons are all not the Buddha-nature Middle Way.
One should know that while the name "Middle Way" is the same, their essential natures are eternally distinct.

Regarding "the practice of definitely experiencing suffering and pleasure": because the followers of the Two Vehicles loathe the suffering of birth and death and seek the bliss of nirvana, it is called the practice of definitely experiencing suffering and pleasure.
"Accepting suffering as if it were pleasure" means accepting that suffering as being like the bliss of the Third Dhyāna.
The Buddha next explains the three phrases of the sūtra in sequence: first, he explains the phrase from "all Buddhas" up to "supreme enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*);
second, he explains the phrase on the Middle Way; and finally, he explains the phrase on the seed. Regarding the first phrase, it is said that they "simultaneously attain the fruit of nirvāṇa.

This is because since they possess the merit of wisdom (*prajñā*) in the form of bodhi, they must necessarily possess the merit of cessation (*prahāṇa*) in the form of nirvāṇa; therefore, it is said that they "attain [it] simultaneously."

Regarding this fruit arising from a cause that itself arises from a cause: the realm of Buddha-nature serves as the causal nature of inherent possession (*prakṛti-prakṛti*), while the contemplative wisdom serves as the causal cause (*hetu-hetu*).
Through the causal cause of contemplative wisdom, the fruit of the wisdom of enlightenment is accomplished.
Regarding the statement that "this fruit of fruits arises from causes," it means that through the causal nature of merit and meditative concentration, the fruit of cessation—nirvāṇa—is accomplished.

The middle section explains the second phrase of the sutra; since the Middle Way is the rational, primary cause, it transcends both [existence and non-existence], thereby manifesting the fourfold negation.
The final section explains the last phrase of the sutra.
"Manifesting all" means that the four natures (catvāri svabhāvāni) manifest reality because they are fundamentally present as the primary cause within the minds of ordinary beings;
thus, all take buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) as their seed. This refers to the "seed of inherent principle" (*li-jù zhǒng*), not a seed acquired through cultivation (*xiū-dé zhǒng*).
Regarding the phrase "the seeds can produce [the result]," this is because the nature (prakṛti) gives rise to cultivation (bhāvanā).

Between these two, the "middle way" refers to taking that which is attained through cultivation as the seed; since cultivation illuminates the nature, the cause and fruit of what is attained through cultivation are designated as the seeds for manifesting the nature.

Regarding the statement that "each serves as the seed for the other": cultivation serves to manifest the nature-seed (prakṛti-gotra), while the nature-seed serves to give rise to the cultivation-seed;

thus, they are said to be mutually related. One cannot help but accept this text because the Sūtra states that bodhi is cultivation, it further states that the Middle Way belongs to the nature, and below it says that seeds encompass both cultivation and nature.
If one does not provide this mutual interpretation, there would be no way to reconcile these passages.
The purport of the sutra is that,
although in general the cultivated and the inherent are mutually interpenetrating, if one speaks of them specifically, one must take the inherent nature as the seed,
because the cultivated arises from the inherent nature.
Question: Regarding the intent of the subsequent inquiry into the Buddha-nature:

since the preceding sutra passage clarifies the distinctions among the four types—cause-of-cause, cause, fruit-of-cause, and fruit—and since the seed is the principle of the direct cause (zhengyin), it should be the seed for all four natures.

Why does the text specifically designate it as the seed for the nature of the Bodhi-fruit? Answer: The response contains two points. First, based on brevity, it is stated thus. Second, [the full explanation follows].

Precisely because the nature of the fruit (*phala-dharmatā*) is extensively clarified as being fourfold in its causal nature (*hetu-dharmatā*), there are four types of causal natures. Second, regarding the primary and secondary [causes], one should ask:
"If the first [category] is abbreviated, why is only the nature of the fruit retained while the other births are omitted? The answer is:

the direct cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) arises as the causal nature of the fruit, while it serves as the secondary causal nature for the others. Because the secondary is omitted and the primary is retained, this refers to *bodhi*.

As explained in the twelve [sections] below, this clarifies the correct meaning of the "auxiliary" (bàng) aspect. The three paths of the twelve links of dependent origination are, in fact, the three causes;

when combined with the nature (xìng), they are unified as the single "correct cause" (zhèng yīn). Since the principle of the correct cause also serves as the seed for the other natures, it is said that the auxiliary meaning is not absent.

However, because one penetrates the realization that the three paths are precisely the three causes, the correct contemplative wisdom (guān zhì) is generated; thus, upon reaching the fruit, it is termed Bodhi.
The reason the fruit is called "fruit" is precisely because its nature as a fruit is established by the seed; thus, its meaning is made manifest.
That which is primarily capable of producing heat also incidentally produces other diseases.
Therefore, it is neither identical nor different: the cause is not identical [to the effect], while the effect is not different [from the cause].

Now, it is clarified that what follows below pertains to the four categories; since they do not transcend the nine realms—which are themselves the Buddha-realm—they are all said to be the essence of all Buddhas.
As for your question regarding its meaning: you yourself are the lion’s roar.
Regarding the phrase "that which is above both sides," this explains the scriptural passage: "Why? Because it is superior.
This refers to the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), which transcends the two aforementioned categories of ordinary persons and non-Buddhists.

That which constitutes the fundamental limit of birth and death refers to the two types of afflictions— ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)— which are the root of birth and death in both the present and the future.
Regarding the "two causes enclosing one fruit," the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitute the fruit of the present.
"Excellence within the marvelous" refers to the realization that the fruit of suffering—birth and death—is itself *nirvāṇa* and Buddha-nature; therefore it is called "excellence within the marvelous.
Consequently, the two deaths are not destroyed [as external objects] but are destroyed [within the mind].
Regarding "clarity within the intermediate," the Sūtra says: "Neither eternal nor annihilated. This refers to the chapter on the Bodhisattvas, wherein the Bodhisattva contemplates.
Therefore, it is said that "clarity" refers to these Bodhisattvas of the Perfect [Teaching] and those individuals who have reached the Perfect through the Shared [Teaching].
Regarding the two causes and two fruits, they together constitute four natures: first, the nature of the cause; second, the nature of the cause of the cause; third, the nature of the fruit;
and fourth, the nature of the fruit of the fruit.
Now, to briefly distinguish and indicate this, there are four phrases in total: first, two phrases that exclude what is not [the object], and next, two phrases that reveal what is.
The first phrase states: "One must not take the cause of the causal stage as the cause. Here, "cause" refers to the wisdom capable of contemplation.

Since this wisdom is produced with respect to the causal object, the object is the cause of the wisdom; therefore, it is called "the cause of the causal stage. Thus, the object of contemplation is merely...

Since it is merely a single cause, it is said that it cannot function as a "cause of causes. The next phrase states that it cannot reach the "fruit of fruits. The text contains an extra character "fruit" (guǒ);
it should simply read "the fruit of the fruit-possessor" (guǒjiāzhī guǒ). To be called "fruit" means that the wisdom-virtue of bodhi is already a fruit;
to further add the cessation-virtue of nirvāṇa is to establish what is the "fruit upon the fruit. Therefore, it is called "the fruit of the fruit-possessor."
Because it is a fruit, one cannot take this heavy fruit as a single fruit;
the preceding phrase means that one cannot take a single cause as a heavy cause, and this phrase means that one cannot take a heavy fruit as a single fruit.

Reflecting on the meaning, one will realize that the text contains an error, or that "cannot" (*bùdé*) should be changed to "can" (*érdé*). Furthermore, the following two phrases clarify that these belong to the category of causes.
Regarding the result of this: if the object can give rise to wisdom, then the object is the cause of wisdom; since wisdom arises from the object, wisdom is the result of the object.
Furthermore, when this wisdom is viewed in relation to Bodhi, it is again termed a "cause"; thus, it is called the "result of the cause of the cause.
The preceding categories are easily understood.
The reason for this is explained below:

regarding the phrase "contemplative wisdom proceeds from cause to cause," it means that because the cause of contemplative wisdom is generated from the cause that is the objective reality (*li-jing*),
it is said to proceed from cause to cause.

If you maintain that *bodhi* (enlightenment) is solely the fruit, please examine this passage; only then will you verify that there is an extra word "fruit" (*phala*) in the preceding list of phrases.

Regarding the discrepancy between the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the principle (*dharma*): in the principle, two factors serve as two causes, whereas in the analogy, a single matter serves as two causes.
The same applies to the two fruits. Here, we simply take the names to be identical because both the principle and the analogy possess two causes and two fruits.

It is said "in part" for the sake of illustration; in the following text, the sūtra is cited to prove that each of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) universally functions as both cause and effect in relation to one another.
The same applies to the two fruits: awakening (*bodhi*) is itself a fruit, and it further serves as a fruit for contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Therefore, it is also [so].
The "fruit of fruits" (phala-phala) refers to *nirvāṇa* as being the fruit in its own essence and, furthermore, acting as the fruit for *bodhi*; thus it is called the "fruit of fruits.
This explains how, by taking the dharma and the analogy together, each of the two causes and two fruits is mutually designated as both "cause-cause" and "cause-fruit.
This is merely Jingxi’s provisional explanation based on the general meaning.
Regarding the claim that "sentient beings serve as the direct cause" for that [resultant] house and so forth: sentient beings are delusive phenomena, and these are certainly present within the cause.
To now say they are neither cause nor effect, but rather the true principle (tattva), is therefore inconsistent. This is truly because others do not understand that the delusive is itself the true;
thus, they merely point to delusive phenomena and designate them as the direct cause.
Now, regarding these five natures, the Master below provides the correct interpretation:
as for the two types of "conditioning-nature" (*pratyaya-svabhāva*), since the two dharmas of cause and effect can manifest the correct and pervasive, they are termed "conditioning-nature.
Thus, the "correct nature" (*samyak-svabhāva*) is principle (*li*), while the "conditioning nature" is phenomena (*shi*).
"To unify the two into one" means to unify cause and effect into conditions.
"To unify conditions into the primary" means that the phenomena of cause and effect are themselves the principle of the nature of mind.
"The primary has no further enumeration" means that the primary is the single nature; since even 'one' does not exist as a one, how could there be any numerical quantity?
That which is without knowledge and without vision cannot be known by the two types of wisdom nor seen by the four eyes;
rather, it is known through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) as having the characteristic of non-knowledge, and seen with the Buddha-eye as having the characteristic of non-seeing.
Regarding the extensive explanation of the profound: each of the six gates clarifies that the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Middle Way and Buddha-nature.

Although ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even partial Bodhisattvas possess this nature within their own bodies, they are unable to perceive it; only a Buddha perceives it with complete clarity.
Therefore, it is called "profound."
The sūtra has no beginning or end because it revolves through the three periods of time.

Here, the mutual manifestation of "disappearance" (mò) is explained as follows: from the perspective of the Buddha, it manifests the disappearance of the beginning; from the perspective of the Bodhisattva, it manifests the disappearance of the end.
To speak correctly of the "Ten Grounds" (shí dì) is precisely what the sūtra refers to as the "Ten Abodes" (shí zhù).
Regarding the phrase "the first turning" and so forth, this refers to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), which is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because one who has attained equal enlightenment destroys the final ignorance and thereby enters Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*), it is said that the "final place" is near. Based on this specific interpretation, the scripture states that the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) are the tenth stage.
That which was initially "profoundly obscure" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), because it has no beginning and is not known by the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*);
furthermore, because a single grade of subtle affliction still remains, it was previously said that the end-point is near.

If a Buddha has already reached the end, then upon seeing the end, one realizes it is even more profound; thus, this final [affliction] to be severed is actually the first to arise. This is merely explained according to the conventional sequence.
The arising of delusion is like the method of putting on clothes, proceeding from the inside out; the severing of delusion is like the method of taking off clothes, proceeding from the outside in.

Therefore, that which is finally removed is precisely that which was first put on. One should know that "seeing the end" refers to the severance of delusion, while "not seeing the beginning" refers to the arising of delusion.

Regarding the "Chapter on Destroying the Source in the Ten Abodes": this means that when the final mind of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) is able to destroy the delusions that first arise, the retribution of the transformation-birth (*pariṇāmika-vaipākika*) will ultimately never arise again.

"From self-nature [to] being easy" refers to the realization that phenomena are identical to principle (*dharmatā*); thus it is easy. "From conditions [to] being difficult" refers to the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*).
To trace back to the original beginning is difficult;
what is said now is an explanation following the sequence of the subsequent chapters.
What is referred to here as the "Ten Abodes" (daśabhūmi) points to each individual stage of abiding, wherein one successively breaks through ignorance in relation to its fundamental category.
Since all these are subsequent arisings, it is said that they "partially see their end.

My personal opinion is as follows: below, Jingxi reverses the scriptural explanation, stating that the Bodhisattva does not see the beginning; yet Jingxi provides an interpretation based on the sense of "seeing the beginning," hence he says, "It may also be said...
This demonstrates that the meaning is manifold and inclusive, and thus does not contradict the scripture.

"Because it cuts off its beginning" refers to the teaching on cutting off; thus, one attains the vision of the beginning. Since the *Jian-shi jing* (Sūtra on Seeing the Beginning) concerns the arising of afflictions, it only shows the end.
Therefore, "the stage of the worthy (*xianwei*) and so forth" refers to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds and prior to the [four] dwellings.
"Knowing that there is neither beginning nor end" means penetrating the delusive dharma-realm; "discerning its beginning and end" means penetrating the causal origination of phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Coarse and manifest" (*zhù* is pronounced with a falling tone): "original category" (*yuánpǐn*)—according to the *Erya*, "beginning," "ancestor," "primordial womb," and "commencement."

To clarify further: those who do not see [the Buddha] include all persons of the nine dharma-realms. If this were so, one might say that those from the stage of the "Provisional Name" (mí zì) upward in the Perfect Teaching (yuán jiào) also do not see;

however, because we wish to distinguish and exclude those in the ranks of the sages (shèng wèi), we place all the worthies (xián rén) of the Perfect Teaching within the category of those who do not see.
The preceding text is analogous to this.

Since the environment and its inhabitants constitute the three types of worlds, and each world possesses the ten suchnesses (*shí rú*) of cause and effect, they form the three thousand [realms].

Because they possess the ten suchnesses, they possess the twelve links of dependent origination; since the twelve links of dependent origination are identical to the ten suchnesses, it is said that the environment and its inhabitants are created by principle.

The "condition" (pratyaya) refers to the principle that the three thousand realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are fully contained within all beings, whether ordinary or sagely, with no increase or decrease in their number.

This "form" and the "name" of sentient beings refer to establishing the conventional designation of "sentient beings" based upon the substantial dharmas of form;

"The period after the five fruits" refers to the final stage of receiving these five fruits.

This refers to hearing the perfect Dharma, giving rise to perfect faith, establishing perfect practice, and entering the perfect stage.
Although it is not heard that such exists among the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*) of the sūtras, this refers to the twelve divisions of the former Hīnayāna.
Regarding the "three additional matters," these are as stated below: "What is the phrase for pleasure? There is only the single phrase of "neither-nor" (*ubhayānta-vinirmukta*).

According to the various phrases, there should be two phrases—suffering (*duḥkha*) and neither-suffering-nor-non-suffering (*aduḥkhāsukha*)—which would thus constitute thirty-six phrases. Furthermore, there are the topical headings (*mukhamukha*) and their explanations.

The general principle is that all sentient beings inherently possess this truth; all phenomena are fully endowed with the three truths and are no different from those of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—by practicing, one attains it immediately.

Now it is clarified that for one who practices with the mind of the Great Nirvāṇa, although the practice itself may be small, by perceiving it through the Perfect and Sudden contemplation, the small becomes great and the partial becomes perfect.
What was stated previously—that there is the transformation of others—indicates it is "great," yet it could not yet distinguish the partial from the perfect.
The "Preservation" (Bao) does not refer to the ultimate; the *nirvāṇa* of the "Transformation City" is not the final goal, yet it was grasped as such.
Regarding the name Lingwei Monastery, the former statement that "Lingwei refers to Bao Liang" was made by Master Lingzheng;
therefore, the present text uses "Lingzheng" to distinguish him [from Bao Liang].

To claim that "liberation" (vimukti) is translated as "freedom from entanglements" (wulei) lacks scriptural authority; since "liberation" is a term of this [Indian] region, how can it be further translated?
To say that "great bliss" (mahāsukha) is the "bliss of the renunciant" (pravrajita-sukha) explains one aspect of the sutra: first, the bliss of renunciation, because of renouncing the household life.
Because it is the supreme bliss, it is explained by means of great bliss; thus the Sūtra says, "To dwell at home is not joyful, being like a prison.
That which should be the joy of the precepts is that for those who have left the home life, the training in the precepts takes precedence.
Ultimately, that which is the joy of the Bodhisattva is so called because they perceive the principle of ultimate reality through partial realization;
furthermore, although the Bodhisattva is a person on the path of cause, they receive the name "ultimate" in contrast to those of provisional and limited capacity.
"There are only nine [stages] because there is no tenth; this is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings through *nirvāṇa*.

[The author] privately comments: "None of these are so. Since the present sutra takes the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* as its essence, how could one use a minor treatise to explain the causes and internal and external conditions?
One should take hearing the Dharma as the external condition and reflection and cultivation as the internal condition, relying upon the three types of wisdom (*tri-vidyā*)."

Through causes and conditions, one attains the bliss of future nirvana. Furthermore, ethical discipline (*śīla*) serves as the external condition, while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) serve as the internal conditions.
Since the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* is also titled the *Bodhisattva-śīla-śāstra*, its second chapter states:
"What is the meaning of 'bliss' (*sukha*)? There are five kinds of the meaning of bliss: first, the bliss of the cause."
First, practicing wholesome dharmas to obtain happiness in future lives is called "happiness as cause.
Second, experiencing happiness such that the body flourishes through causes and conditions and the mind attains tranquility is called "experiencing happiness.

Third, abandoning the experience of happiness by cultivating the Noble Path—because all feelings are severed and the Path increases until no feelings remain—is called "the happiness of abandoning feeling. Fourth, distancing oneself...

Being free from pleasure means being eternally free from afflictions, such that body and mind are without suffering; this is called the pleasure of seclusion (*viveka-sukha*). Fifth is the pleasure of enlightenment (*bodhi-sukha*);

because one constantly experiences bliss, it is called the pleasure of enlightenment. From the initial cultivation of causes until the final attainment of the Buddha-fruit, it is said to proceed "from shallow to deep.
Some texts read "the pleasure of the bodhisattva," but this is a textual error.

Regarding the statement that those prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) do not fully perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), this distinguishes the specific stages; it clarifies that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states the ten abodes (*vihāra*) are the perfect stages (*pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*), and since the abode is identical to the stage, they all equally perceive the Buddha-nature.
If one has studied the sutras yet cannot know that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, even a person at the stage of "name-only" (ming-zi-wei) knows that others have it;
how could a Bodhisattva of the ten abodes not know this? This [statement] is merely a suppression [of their realization], saying they are unable to know.
"Hearing and seeing" refers to hearing what the Buddha has taught and thereby attaining understanding.
The Second Part of the "Lion’s Roar" Chapter:
If there are those who wish to hear and see [the truth], they should be exhorted to cause ordinary beings to hear according to the teaching and see in accordance with the teaching.
As for those who receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this refers to the twelve divisions within this very sutra; thus, one should practice in reliance upon the teaching.
Regarding the statement that one "does not see" before attaining the realization of nature (*xing*), this refers only to the limited perspectives of the *Hīnayāna* and *Pratyekabuddha* vehicles.
As for the meaning of "seeing," if one can observe according to the teachings, the capacity for seeing arises;
furthermore, one must rely on the middle four [perfections] to clarify the practice of the seer in order to attain right vision.
Regarding the passage stating that sentient beings do not know the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s mind:

the deluded minds of sentient beings are agitated by the three delusions, whereas the true mind of the Tathāgata is quiescent in the three truths. How, then, can the real be known through the deluded?

In the preceding section, we contrasted the superior with the inferior by first contrasting the former volume; therein it was clarified that seeing with the eye is superior while hearing with the ear is inferior.

Now, we clarify that hearing with the ear is superior while seeing with the eye is inferior, and thus the underlying intent must be explained. Previously, the ultimate Buddha-eye sees the principle of nature (dharmatā), and thus it is superior;
[the stage of] partial true reality is inferior because it arises from hearing the teachings from others. Now, however, ordinary beings are able to awaken through hearing the Dharma.
Because it follows the Way, it is superior; because the physical eye sees only conditioned forms, it is inferior.

Regarding the distinction between those of superior virtue and those of inferior virtue, as explained in contrast with King De (德王): King De is one who clings to the traces and is deluded regarding the source, and thus falls into distorted views;
now, knowing that the traces manifest from the source, he is said to "see the Buddha."
The "wondrous basis" is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the Dharma-body is the basis and the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the trace.

To abandon both of these refers to the two preceding teachings: in those two teachings, one merely departs from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism and provisionally establishes the name "middle," yet there is no substantial essence of the middle.
Therefore, in the first stage, the various fetters are not destroyed, as they pertain to the abandonment of both [extremes].

That which constitutes "mutual accomplishment" (xiāngchéng) in the Separate Teaching (biéjiào) refers to the phrase "not saving sentient beings" and the phrase "not all are accomplished"; these two belong to the Separate Teaching.
This means that the two contemplations prior to the stages (dìqián) accomplish the Middle Way upon entering the stages (dēngdì), which is termed "mutual accomplishment."
Regarding "shining on both": this refers to the two phrases, "whatever is spoken" and "speaking not for the sake of profit," which belong to the category of shining on both.
As for the "six years of ascetic practice," the *Sūtra of the Twelve Wanderings* states that the Buddha left home at twenty-nine and attained the Way at thirty-five;
hence, it is said that he practiced asceticism for six years.
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* was translated at Vārāṇasī as the *Sūtra on the Deer Park*.
Regarding "right speech" (*samyag-vāc*) and so forth: speaking with gentle words that accord with the Dharma is called right speech; being free from falsehood and delusion is called truthful speech;
speaking according to the capacity of the listener is called timely speech; and speech that is without frivolous ornamentation and accords with the true nature of phenomena is called genuine speech.

Regarding the two kinds of causes and conditions: "hearing and seeing" refers to what is seen by the eyes; these two kinds serve as the basis for practicing according to the teachings, whereby one will certainly perceive the mental characteristics of the Tathāgata.
This means that when those who rely on the four reliances (catur-yoni-pudgala) inquire, they may say: "Whether it be the coarse or the subtle, we ourselves [still]..."
How can one know the mental states of those who have realized the fruit of the Tathāgata based on the teachings?

Regarding the first two [cases] being confused with the latter two: the person of the first stage is subtle and thus confused with the third, while the person of the second stage is confused with the fourth;
this is because sentient beings perceive only external traces and do not fathom the internal root, and thus they see the person of the first stage and mistake them for the person of the third.
Seeing the second person as being identical in essence to the fourth person in terms of the subtle and ultimate meaning, the Buddha’s skillful speech interweaves its phrasing;
furthermore, the second and third should be understood as the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*), while the first and fourth are not the four reliances.
Regarding the phrase "setting aside the Sangha-jewel and so forth," it means that even ordinary people find it difficult to distinguish [the Sangha] from these four reliances.
Regarding "relying on these two matters," it refers to seeing the Buddha’s form-body and hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma; how then can one know the characteristics of the Buddha’s mind?
The *Amalaka-fruit Simile* and other such parables illustrate that it is difficult to discern whether [the fruit] is ripe or unripe;
for it may be externally ripe while internally unripe, externally unripe while internally ripe, or both ripe and both unripe.
The passage concerning Śāriputra’s trembling shadow demonstrates the efficacy of the power of precepts (*śīla*) to verify ultimate realization.
It is not ultimate.

For those who seek gain and sustenance—even to the point of abandoning the borders to seek out the center, or discarding the ordinary to grasp at the holy—all such things are termed "gain and sustenance.
Therefore, it is said: "One should know that such persons do not perceive the Buddha-nature through these precepts."

If a sutra is for the sake of the True Dharma, it means that through the mind of Great Nirvana one reaches the limits [of reality] as being the Middle Way, wherein there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
This sutra is called "seeing with the eyes," which is seeing the form of the Tathāgata.
It is also called "hearing and seeing," which means that upon hearing of the Buddha-nature, one is able to understand it. The previous commentary stated, "Hearing and seeing are strong;
eye-seeing is weak," and this text refers to that.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of sentient beings" in the sutra: those who are able to see the Buddha-nature realize that the mind-nature of self and others is non-dual and without distinction. Only then...
To be able to benefit others in this way is itself to see the Buddha-nature.
Regarding the sutra’s mention of "meeting a teacher and monks": "teacher" refers to the three teachers, and "monks" refers to the seven witnesses.
As for the "various teachers," these are the *karmācārya*, the *śikṣācārya*, and the seven witnesses.
"Acting as one who makes a request" (yācanaka): "yào" (to request) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*).
"This is the method of market exchange" means that seeking the Holy from the ordinary is like exchanging the lowly for the noble.

"Spontaneous and natural occurrence" (*renyùn fǎ'ěr*) refers to the fourteen factors that mutually constitute this spontaneity, beginning from the observance of precepts up to the attainment of seeing the Buddha.
It is the nature (*dharmatā*).
"Dharmatā" means "it is so"; that is to say, it does not depend on artificial construction, for its dharma is inherently such.
It is what is called "spontaneity."
That one who upholds the precepts is not shallow is due to seeing the Buddha-nature; thus, the mind feels no regret.

Because upholding the precepts spontaneously accords with principle, these fourteen phrases explain one another in succession without distinction of depth or shallowness—the reason for what was previously called "mutual proximity" lies precisely here.

Nevertheless, although there is no difference in depth or shallowness, depth and shallowness nonetheless manifest clearly; therefore, upholding the precepts is the cause, and freedom from regret is the result.

Regarding the phrase "abiding equally in great nirvāṇa," and so forth: this refers to the fourteen phrases which indicate that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inherently complete and does not depend on cultivation for its realization.
Because one was previously ignorant of this, delusion and inversion arose; now that it is known, what further seeking could there be?
Therefore, the Sūtra says that it is "attained spontaneously."
Regarding the question of having causes but no fruits: the previous explanation of the fourteen phrases concerning *nirvāṇa* should correspond only to the eleventh phrase;
why then does the Sūtra clarify the twelfth phrase? It says: "Because one attains Great Parinirvāṇa, and because one attains the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Is it not the case that these four virtues are the fruits of *nirvāṇa*? Answer: The latter four phrases are merely [an elaboration of] *nirvāṇa*.

Because "parinirvāṇa" is a synonym [for the preceding terms], the Commentary states that it "resides at the end of all practices. Regarding the term "synonym": *nirvāṇa* must necessarily possess merit;

because it possesses merit, it is without arising or ceasing; and because it is without arising or ceasing due to the vision of the Buddha-nature, one knows that the final four [terms] are identical to *nirvāṇa*.
There is no further dharma beyond *nirvāṇa*, unlike the intermediate phrases which clarify each other through mutual reference.
Therefore, the charge that there is a cause but no result is raised by citing *nirvāṇa* as a difficulty; this is the intended meaning.
To "conclude one-sidedly" means to specifically conclude the difficulty based on *nirvāṇa* being impermanent. Although both were previously mentioned, the intent lies solely in the single statement:
"The precepts are permanent. This intends to challenge the Tathāgata’s four virtues by arguing that *nirvāṇa* is established as impermanent.
Regarding the meaning of this:
if one asks how it can be called "blissful," "self," and "pure" when it is both impermanent and lacks the three virtues, [the answer is as follows].
As for Śākyamuni’s short day, it lasts from dawn until midnight.
The passage beginning with "After the time it takes to eat" and so forth refers to what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*:

"At that time, those in the assembly who were listening were also seated in one place for sixty small kalpas, their bodies and minds unmoving as they listened to what the Buddha preached, yet they perceived it as being like the time it takes to eat.

This occurs because the capacity and conditions of the listeners have such a deep longing for the Dharma that, though long, they perceive it as short. Furthermore, this is due to the Tathāgata’s wisdom of extending and contracting time, which is appropriate to extend the long to make it short.
For example, because the conditions for this sutra were suited to a long duration, Śākyamuni skillfully extended the short to make it long, preaching for three hundred million years;

because the conditions were suited to a short duration, Śākyamuni shortened the long to make it short, concluding at midnight. One should know that Sudarśana’s [preaching] was also short while Śākyamuni’s was long;
thus it is said that "the Way of the Buddhas is uniform. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* is cited here as a general illustration.
The sūtra is both a cause and the cause of a cause. Faith is the cause, and hearing the Dharma is further the cause of faith; therefore, it is called "both a cause and the cause of a cause.
Furthermore, hearing the Dharma is a cause, and faith is again the cause of hearing the Dharma; therefore, it is called "both a cause and the cause of a cause.
This is because, due to the presence of faith, one hears the Dharma, and from hearing the Dharma, faith necessarily arises; thus, they mutually serve as causes for one another.
Regarding the sūtra being both the fruit and the fruit of a fruit: listening to the Dharma is the fruit of faith, and faith in turn is the fruit of listening to the Dharma;
this mutual explanation serves as an illustration by which the underlying causes can be understood.
Regarding the "three-wooded *kūṭa*": this refers to the externalist (tīrthika) ritual vessel, which is round like a gourd and lacks a handle;
it is lifted by crossing three staffs over it. In various sūtras, it is sometimes called a "three-pronged *kūṭa*" or a "trident-shaped *kūṭa*";
both terms refer to this same object.
Regarding "using supports for a single jar," the term "supports" (*zhī*) should be understood as *zhīzhǔ* (props or stays).
As for the "thirsty crow" (*kěwū*), this refers to the lever on a well; its upper and lower ends rise and fall like a thirsty crow drinking water.
It is also called *xunju* (pronounced *sǔn jù*). The *Shìmíng* states: "That by which bells are suspended: the horizontal beam is called *xun*, and the vertical post is called *ju*.
This is not an object found above a well. Furthermore, the character *jù* (拒) used here is not the same as the character for *xunju*;
it should rather be read as *juegao* (桔槹). It is likely a scribal error; some claim it is also called *lulou* (轆樓), but this too is an error.
"Alternately rising and falling" means that when one end is lowered, the other end is raised; being above is the cause for being below, and being below is the effect of being above.
This is explained by analogy with the preceding mutual relationship.

The Sūtra says, "Standing and pushing to lift the jar. According to the latter interpretation, this refers to a water-lifting device (a *ghaṭī-yantra* or well-sweep) where a jar is suspended from its end to draw water.
If one were to fixate on the three periods of time and so forth— taking two causes from the past and five fruits in the present,
or three causes in the present and two fruits in the future— it would not be convenient for clarifying the meaning of cause-and-effect as cause and fruit. Therefore,
we shall here simply take them as mutually conditioning one another to manifest and establish this meaning.
Regarding the explanation of the eightfold analogy, first the correct meaning is presented, followed by the refutation of the opponent's view. As for the correct meaning:

it refers to the Buddha himself citing the eightfold sequence from the former Hīnayāna teachings, wherein they arise in mutual dependence, in order to reveal the principle in this present sutra that they function as both cause and effect for one another.
The commentary on the *Mahājanma-nāman* (up to the point where it says "that which gives rise to arising") is still somewhat brief;

if one were to fully explain the sūtra, one should clarify the characteristics and causal origination within the eight aspects by taking the two types of birth—the great and the small—as the primary focus, as the other categories can be understood by analogy.
That which can produce through birth but cannot produce itself—namely, that great characteristic of birth—is only able to produce dharmas such as form and mind, yet it cannot produce itself;
it is just as, in the world, the eye does not see itself and a finger does not touch itself.

Because the *mahābhūta* (great element) does not arise by itself, it arises through the *bhūtabhautika* (derived from the elements); this clarifies that the great arising is produced by the small arising.

Since the small arising is uniquely capable of producing the great arising, it is called "the arising of arising" (*bhūtabhautika*). Because the great arising is that which is produced by this "arising of arising," it is called "the arising of the arising of arising" (*bhūtabhautikabhūta*).
The sutra states: "Birth after birth does not arise by itself; it arises because it relies on birth. This clarifies that the minor birth arises from the major birth.
Although the minor birth is capable of giving rise [to further births], the major birth cannot arise by itself. Because it does not arise by itself, it relies on the major birth to arise.
Thus, these two types of birth are both cause and causal cause, and both effect and resultant effect.

The author of the *Cheng lun* (Treatise on Establishment) refutes those who rely on the [Small Vehicle] treatises. The Master Cheng’s intention is that since this sutra is of the Great [Vehicle], one should not apply the eight aspects of the Small [Vehicle];
therefore, he establishes his own system of a single period and moment-to-moment transformation to explain this present sutra.
To say that this should not be so is to refute the established masters.

To refute while establishing according to the occasion means that although this present sutra refutes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to establish the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it does so by using the Lesser Vehicle as a metaphor for the Great Vehicle to enable sentient beings to attain awakening;
since this is perfectly suited to the timing of the occasion, why would proponents of [other] schools not allow the use of the Abhidharma principles?
The "great characteristic" (*mahā-nimitta*) is the cause because it can give rise to the "small characteristic" (*parīttaka-nimitta*); therefore, the small characteristic is the fruit.

As for saying that the "small characteristic" is the "cause of causes": since the great characteristic is already a cause, the small characteristic further acts as a cause for that great characteristic;
thus it is called the "cause of causes. Because the arising of the small gives rise to the arising of the great, it may also be said that the small characteristic is the cause.
The great characteristics are causes; their causal function can be understood through analogy, and the same applies to the meaning of their results.

Furthermore, while the great characteristics possess efficacy toward all eight [phases], citing even one characteristic suffices to encompass all eight; whereas the minor characteristics possess efficacy toward only one [phase], being able to produce only a single great characteristic.

Regarding this "fruit of cultivation" (*abhyāsa-phala*): it refers to the fact that the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is already perfected and the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are fully manifested;
therefore, it belongs to the fruit of cultivation. As for *śramaṇa* and *brāhmaṇa*, these refer to the Buddha himself: because all evils are eternally exhausted, he is called a *śramaṇa*;
because all virtues are universally assembled, he is called a *brāhmaṇa*. The sub-commentary states: "The fruit of Buddhahood is designated as the fruit of *śramaṇa* and *brāhmaṇa*."
To sever birth and death means to sever the two kinds of birth and death; both the partial realization and the ultimate realization are designated as the fruit of Buddhahood.
That which constitutes the essence of the cause of death refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), which are the cause of birth and death.

Regarding the absence of the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*): performing causes of good and evil and obtaining the fruits of good and evil is called the cause of retribution; now, in *nirvāṇa*, this does not exist.

Regarding the absence of the cause of production (*janana-hetu*): *nirvāṇa* is that which is realized through the cause of revelation (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*), whereas the cause of production consists of the adornment of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*), which draws forth the retribution of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Regarding the absence of a dependent cause: Nirvana is that which is produced by an absolute cause. Question:
If this is so, should Nirvana then be considered both a revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) and an absolute cause? Answer: Nirvana is definitely not a cause;
it is simply the fruit produced by what is properly termed a revealing cause and an absolute cause, and thus [the term "cause"] is used here without distinction.
However, as for the force of the phrasing, since there are six ways in which "non-existence" applies to the "meaningless," they are listed here provisionally;
how could it be a valid objection that this is identical to ultimate non-existence, which is like *nirvāṇa*?

Immediately following "taking [it] as correct," one takes up the concluding text of the previous section to express the present meaning, concluding below by stating: "Because at times there is no cause."
The name "nirvāṇa" indicates that although six absences are mentioned, it is specifically the absence of one [the self] that constitutes the difficulty.
If this is so, then not only is the ultimate absence [of the self] a matter of rhetorical emphasis, but the latter four absences are likewise matters of rhetorical emphasis.
Regarding the pond that has water during rain but lacks it during drought: when it rains there is water, but during a drought there is none.
Regarding the sun and moon being shrouded or dispersed: when shrouded by clouds they seem non-existent, but when the clouds disperse they appear.
The sense of mutual absence is like this: a *caṇḍāla* lacks the dharma of a *brāhmaṇa*, and a *brāhmaṇa* lacks the [dharma] of a *caṇḍāla*.
When the various categories of phenomena are examined in relation to one another, it is said that there is nothing that is not ultimately non-existent (*atyanta-abhāva*).
As for this "ultimate non-existence" being raised as a formal objection:

even if what you have cited—the six types of non-existence—were used as a formal objection based on ultimate non-existence, it would still not constitute the entirety of *nirvāṇa*, but would only possess a partial aspect of its meaning. Therefore, the Buddha provisionally proceeds on the basis of this specific meaning.
When they are rebuked, they ask, "Why do you not cite [the same] equality?
How much more so when, even though the ultimate and supreme [truth] is not entirely complete, how could your use of mutual non-existence as the primary objection ever accord with *nirvāṇa*?
Question: In what sense is there a partial correspondence? Answer: Because ultimately there is no self (*anātman*).
The reason why my nirvāṇa is without cause and both are equally quiescent is that the essence of my nirvāṇa possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which differs from "ultimate existence";
therefore, the subsequent text states that it does not correspond to any of the six metaphors.
Taking buddha-nature as the cause means that by realizing buddha-nature, one realizes nirvana. How is it possible to realize it?
It is through the threefold contemplation within a single mind.
The "lesser fruits of the śramaṇa" refers to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Regarding the two citations and three analogies: the passage in the sutra beginning from "that which can produce dharmas" constitutes these three analogies.
First, a lamp; second, parents; third, grain, earth, and water. Thus, the three pairs and six phrases within the sutra clarify the meaning of the two causes;
the initial phrase still pertains to the nature of dharmas.
That which can produce dharmas refers to merit (*puṇya*), for merit is able to attract retribution and is therefore called the "productive cause" (*janakahetu*);
merit is that which produces, while the superior retribution is that which is produced.

The lamp in the sutra that can illuminate objects is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*), for wisdom is able to illuminate and comprehend the fundamental principle; thus, it is called the "revealing cause" (*vyañjakahetu*).
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are called the "causes of production" because the fetters and delusions are able to produce the fruit of suffering; thus they are likened to the cause of production.
The parents are called the "causes of manifestation" because it is only through the union of the two kin that the fruit-body can be fully manifested and accomplished;
thus they are likened to the cause of manifestation.

Regarding "grain seeds and so forth": although grain is capable of sprouting, it must depend on the moisture of water; likewise, although merit can draw forth retribution, it must necessarily be guided by wisdom.
Therefore, the grain seed is used as a metaphor for the ground, and the water is used as a metaphor for clear comprehension (*vijñapti*).

Regarding the statement that all things take kinship as their cause of birth: this means that the principle of attracting retribution through merit and virtue is powerful, thus establishing kinship; wisdom is not so, and is therefore distant.

As for the correspondence between the horizontal and the vertical: the "revealing cause" (pariniṣpatti-hetu) refers to the eightfold right path, while the three types of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) are the result; the eightfold right path is the cause, and enlightenment is the fruit.

This is because fruit and cause stand in a relationship of mutual correspondence; thus, the "vertical" arising of the cause refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), while the "horizontal" cultivation occurs within those causes.
To clarify the taking of the fruit by means of the causes: if one takes the fruit of *bodhi* by means of the six perfections as causes, then the cause is the cause of the fruit;
if one establishes the six perfections as causes by means of the fruit of *bodhi*, then the fruit is the fruit of the cause.

Answer: "The result of arising" refers to the fruit that is the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while "the result of production" refers to the fruit that is the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). These two results—wisdom and abandonment—are established through the two causes of arising and production;
because they are designated according to their causes, they are called the "results of arising and production."
Regarding the statement that "produced fruits are impermanent, etc.," this raises an objection based on the distinct natures of the two types of fruits.

The intent is that birth (*jāti*) is merit (*puṇya*), which cannot accord with ultimate reality (*tattva*); therefore, it belongs to the category of the impermanent. Understanding (*parijñā*), however, is wisdom (*prajñā*), which is in profound union with reality;
therefore, it is permanent.

Regarding the term "yielding" (*qu*) used when these two sides debate: commentators all say that the proponent yields because they claim that produced fruits are impermanent, which contradicts the principle that *nirvāṇa* is eternally abiding;
thus, they yield. To "yield" means to be subdued. This is because they fail to understand that the principles of merit and wisdom are identical in their nature:
impermanence is itself permanence, and permanence is itself impermanence. This is the essential point.

This is because the Subcommentator (Sushu-zhu) cites the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* and the present sūtra, both of which clarify that while the phenomena of the two fruits differ, their underlying principle is the same;
this serves to reconcile the previous parallelism.

In the *Śūraṅgama*, the practitioner’s metaphor for the Buddha is that of a person who dies through an illusion and is immediately reborn—this illustrates that the eternal is identical to the impermanent.
Furthermore, the fact that they are born again immediately after dying is a metaphor for impermanence being identical to permanence.

The two birds below—the female representing impermanence and the male representing permanence—all clarify that while the fruit of *nirvāṇa* possesses these two functions, its essential nature (*tattva*) is one;
how, then, could this obstruct the arising of the fruit as impermanent, given that the realized fruit is permanent?
Regarding the passage "The Tathāgata’s liberation of form," etc., this section states that "form" refers exclusively to true, wholesome, and wondrous form.

As for the statement that "this is explained as the Middle Way," the Middle Way is a synonym for Buddha-nature; because Buddha-nature is described as being "neither of the two extremes," it is called the Middle Way.
Regarding the simile of the centipede: since it is said that [the mind] is not fixed within the body, one abandons the internal and takes up the external;

yet since it is also said that the conscious spirit itself attains Buddhahood, one abandons the external and takes up the internal. Thus, abandoning one and taking up another is like the movement of that insect.
The Master of Contemplation abandons both the internal and the external, like a bird shedding its wings.
What follows is a section that precisely demonstrates the meaning of "double negation" (*ubhayābhāva*) by means of the perfect interpenetration of the three truths.
