The "various flowers of awakening" (bodhi-puṣpa) are none other than the seven purities, which are called the "flowers of the purity of the seven factors of awakening.

This refers to those seeking the fruit; for the time being, it is explained in terms of the latter four [purities] as residing in the fruit. Furthermore, the meaning of "purity" (viśuddhi) pertains to the cause, while the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) pertains to the fruit;
thus, this is the corresponding explanation.

One who has left the household life should be one who has emerged from the river; the subsequent scripture states that "one who wishes to cross the great river of birth and death leaves the household life and shaves their hair.
Yet, in this analogy, it speaks of "emerging from the river" while referring to "entering"—why are these two contradictory? Therefore, the commentary explains:
because it seeks to clarify that the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is non-dual, it says they are not separated by a vast distance.
Regarding "about to stand and then withdraw": when about to enter within, one generally stands; here, "standing" refers to the present life, while "withdrawing" refers to the arising of evil.

This indicates that although one did not cultivate [the path] in the present life, one had already cultivated the five cessations and four foundations of mindfulness in past lives; now, lacking faith, one does not cultivate them again.
Thus, although the roots of goodness are severed, they emerge from the submergence; this means that after emerging from past lives, they submerge once more.
This refers to the present life.
As for those who have lost the sutras of the past, because they previously gave rise to evil before entering the stage of ordinary beings, they do not know the source of the Mahāyāna;
that is to say, they do not understand the Buddha-nature.
"To depart" means to depart by crossing over the river of birth and death.

"To follow from the side of the mind" means to settle the mind so as to benefit all beings; although there is birth and death, it is as if there were no birth and death, and for this reason it is called "shallow."
The sūtra states that the "five greats" (pañca-mahābhūtāni) refer to the great element of form (*rūpa-mahābhūta*) up to the great element of consciousness (*vijñāna-mahābhūta*).

Alternatively, it says that the claim of non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*) that the four great elements together with space constitute the five greats is not the intent of this sūtra; for the sūtra clarifies that the five greats are alternative names for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and thus it says they are "precisely named the five greats."
One interpretation states that the "five groups" refers to the five groups of renunciants.
Regarding the difference between the Mahāsāṃghika and the Mahāsāṃghika *mahājana*, the term "Mahāsāṃghika" here refers to the Sthavira school;
it signifies that within the Vebhāra Cave, the elders such as Kāśyapa and the five hundred arhats who were liberated from doubt held a council, which is thus called the "Sthavira."
Regarding the term "Mahāsāṃghika" (Great Assembly): at that time, there were members of the great assembly who were not included within the number of five hundred;

they held their council outside the cave, and thus they were named the Mahāsāṃghika. Now, since *mahāsāṃghika* translates as "Great Assembly," how does this differ from the name "outside the cave"? One should say:
the "Great Assembly inside the cave" and the "Great Assembly outside the cave" are distinguished like the Jing and Wei rivers. Thus, the distinction is self-evident.
The term "Elders" (Sthavira) is distinguished from Kāśyapa to manifest their specific title;

since the others—such as Tāmraparṇīya—are disciples of the internal council within the cave, they take the designation of "Elders" (Sthavira) along with Kāśyapa and his peers. As for Mahāsāṃghika, because they are the descendants of those outside the cave, they establish the name "Great Assembly" (Mahāsāṃghika).
Regarding the statement "King Aśoka established assemblies," the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (or *Śāsanodbhava-śāstra*) states:

"Thus it is heard that more than one hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Bhagavān, when the time since the Sage had passed like the setting sun, there was a king of Magadha named Aśoka who ruled over Jambudvīpa and whose transformation of both humans and spirits was pervasive.
At that time, the Great Sangha of the Buddha’s Dharma was subsequently split. It says "Great" because—
Devadatta, before his renunciation, had committed three heinous crimes—namely, killing his father, killing his mother, and killing an Arhat.

Having committed these three sins, he was deeply overcome with remorse and sought to extinguish his transgressions. Just then, he encountered the assembly of the Saṃgha gathered outside a cave for a formal recitation;
not knowing that he had committed such heinous crimes, they granted him ordination. After he had received full ordination, by virtue of his cleverness and sharp intelligence...
Later, he came into conflict with the Sthaviras. Mahādeva claimed that according to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, when settling a dispute, one should rely on the "majority opinion.
At that time, although the venerable elders within the Sthavira school were numerous, their followers were very few;
whereas within Mahādeva’s faction, although the venerable elders were few, their followers were very many. Consequently, King Aśoka regarded Mahādeva as being in the right.
The two schools proceeded in opposition.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* also pre-emptively indicated the five schools; the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, my disciples will uphold the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s sūtras, copying, reading, and reciting them, yet they will misinterpret their meanings."

Because they proclaim [the teachings] with inversion and thereby conceal the treasury of the Dharma (dharmagañja), this school is called Dharmaguptaka, which in Chinese means the "Dharma-Seal" (Famimibu).

The sūtras state that "concealing" (gupta) carries the meaning of "secret" (guhya); alternatively, it is said that "Dharma-treasury" (dharmagañja) implies that the "treasury" (gañja) itself has the meaning of "secret.

The Dharma is named after the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, and furthermore, they recite, transcribe, and study external treatises, accepting [the existence of] the three times as well as internal [doctrines].
They externally defeat non-Buddhists and are skilled in debate; they explain that all natures are fully capable of receiving the precepts, and they are able to answer all questions and challenges.
For this reason, it is called Sarvāstivāda (meaning "All-Exists").

This school maintains that the three time periods exist substantially and that all three natures are fully capable of receiving the dharma of the precepts. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "In discourse, there is no self."
Furthermore, the "receiver" (vedaka) who transmutes all afflictions (kleśa) like a corpse is therefore called Kāśyapīya; this is translated as the "Contemplation of Repeated Emptiness.
The followers of the Sāṃkhya school of non-Buddhists cling to the existence of a real receiver who experiences sensory objects, which is termed the "receiver. "Transmutes" means to discard;
thus it is likened to a corpse. This dharma is named Liberation (vimukti), and its precept manual (śīla-mūla) is identical to that of the Pañcavargika Vinaya.
To speak of not forming conceptions of earth, nor of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness, is called the Mahīśāsaka.

This [term] means "not adhering" to the contemplation of existence or non-existence; their sūtras are called the *Pañcavargika* (Five-Part Sūtra). They state that all things possess a self and do not speak of the characteristic of emptiness, being like small children;
therefore, they are named Vātsīputrīya. *Vātsī* translates as "Calf," and *putra* translates as "Son."
They are called the Vātsīputrīya school. This school maintains that the self (*ātman*) is neither identical to the aggregates (*skandha*) nor distinct from them, yet it exists as a real self.
The *Vinayamūla-sūtra* states that because they extensively and comprehensively collate the scriptures of the five schools, they are named the Mahāsāṃghika;
this translates as "The Great Assembly. Regarding this, the *Vinaya-śīrṣa-ṭīkā* states: "In total and in detail, there are six divisions of the Saṃgha."

This [Sammitīya school] is the general [category], whereas the previous five are the specific ones. Because the conduct and understanding of this Sammitīya community are vast and pervasive, they do not give rise to biased attachments and universally accord with the five views;
since they practice these views in common, it is known that this is the general category.
Regarding the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*, that treatise states: "In the second century, from within the Mahāsāṃghika school, three sub-sects emerged:
first, the Prajñaptivādins; second, the Lokottaravādins; and third, the Kukkuṭikas. As for the term "Prajñaptivādin," Paramārtha explains:

"This school maintains that both mundane and supramundane phenomena lack substantial reality and exist merely as single provisional designations (*prajñapti*); thus they are called 'Prajñaptivādins'."
Regarding the two assertions of the Saṃmatīya school concerning that which transcends the world (*lokottara*): this school clarifies that mundane phenomena arise from inversion and are all false;
therefore, they do not truly exist and are entirely mere designations (*prajñapti*). Phenomena that transcend the world do not arise from inversion;
there are both the path and its fruit, and the objects of the two emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) are real, as is the wisdom of the two emptinesses. This real object can give rise to real wisdom.
Because true wisdom can penetrate the true realm, it is substantially existent (*dravyasat*). Regarding the Kukkutika: in ancient times there was a rishi who mated with a hen and fathered sons;
this is the lineage of that clan. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that this is the surname of the master of the Vinaya.
Two hundred years later, another school emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika called the Bahuśrutīya (Much-Hearing School), named after the learning of its founder.
Because he had mastered the Tripiṭaka and profoundly realized the Buddha’s intent, he was called Bahusruta (Much-Hearing).

Two hundred years later, another school emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika, named the Prajñaptivāda (School of Designation). Master Daśabala Shīghra stated that according to the teachings of this school, worldly phenomena are both provisional and real.
When two hundred years were complete, there was a renunciant non-Buddhist who abandoned heterodoxy to return to the truth; he was also known as...

Mahādeva was not one who had committed a heinous offense (ānantarya). Having gone forth and received the precepts within the Mahāsāṃghika school, he became widely learned and diligent, residing on Mount Caitya.
Due to his repeated deliberations with the monks of that school regarding five matters, a schism arose, resulting in the division into three schools.

First, as for Mount Caitya, it is translated here as "Spiritual Shrine" (lingmiao), referring to the sites of the Buddha’s initial birth, attainment of enlightenment, turning of the wheel of Dharma, and parinirvāṇa.

This is because there were spirit temples for offerings at all four locations. Second, the Haimavata school is so named because their *caitya* mountain is to the west, hence "Western Mountain Dwellers.
Third, the Uttarīya school is so named because their *caitya* mountain is to the north, hence "Northern Mountain Dwellers.

When the primary and secondary divisions are explained separately, they form nine schools. Regarding the second, the Sthavira school: at the beginning of the third century, Kātyāyanīputra [resided] above...

The founder of this school was particularly devoted to propagating the Dharma of the Single Flavor (Ekayāna) and propagated the Sūtras and Vinaya only sparingly. Because this deviated from the specific intent of the Nikāya, it subsequently split into two schools.

First, regarding the Sarvāstivāda (the School that Teaches that All Exists), there are two aspects: first, conditioned phenomena exist throughout the three periods of time; second, unconditioned phenomena transcend the three periods of time.

These consist of space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Since their substance exists in all cases, they are called "All Exists" (*Sarvāsti*); they are also called the "School that Teaches Causes" (*Hetuvāda*).

"School" (*nikāya*) refers to the extensive presentation of the reasons for establishing the tenets of this school. Among the five aforementioned schools, the *Daśabhāṇaka* (Ten Reciters) is taken as the primary authority.
The two branches of the Sthavira school were subsequently renamed the Haimavata (Snowy Mountain School). The disciples of the Sthaviras originally propagated the Sūtra-piṭaka;

the Hetuvādins (Causalists) arose from them and primarily propagated the Abhidharma. Having become well-versed in its principles, they eventually eclipsed the Sthaviras, and as the Sthavira school declined, they [the Hetuvādins] subsequently shifted their position.

The name [Vātsīputrīya] is derived from the place where they resided while entering the Snowy Mountains to avoid [persecution]. Three hundred years later, it branched out from the Sarvāstivāda school as the Vātsīputrīya school.
In ancient times, there was a rishi who fathered a son by a cow; since then, those of that rishi’s lineage have all been called "Vatsiputra" (Calf-son).
This is a Brahmin clan name. They take the earlier Bahuśrutīya school as their fundamental tenet. Three hundred years later...
For a hundred years, four schools emerged from the Vatsīputrīya: first, the Dharmottarīya, so named because they possess a Dharma that can be ascended;
second, the Bhadrayānīya, where "Bhadra" is the name of the leader of the school and "Yāni" signifies lineage, meaning they are the descendants of Arhats;
third, the Saṃmitīya, which refers to those who weigh and determine [the doctrine] through authoritative standards.
It is called "Correct" (Saddharma) because it avoids the errors of the Saṃmitīya and Vibhajyavāda schools; this is the school followed by the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Next is the Ghosila-kaṇṭhīya school, which is the school of those who dwell near dense and thick forests; it is named after its location.
Three hundred years later, another school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda, named the Mahīśāsaka school; [this was] the school's founder.

In the past, he was a king whose transformative influence permeated the common people on earth; later, he renounced his kingdom to become a monk and was named after this legacy as the Mahīśāsaka (the School of the Earth-Pervader).

Taking the earlier Mahīśāsaka school as their primary tenet, three hundred years later, a branch emerged from the Mahīśāsaka known as the Dharmaguptaka, also called the Dharmaguhya or the Dharmarakṣita school. This [school] was established by an arhat.
This was the disciple of Maudgalyāyana; after Maudgalyāyana’s parinirvāṇa, Dharmarakṣa practiced what his teacher had taught and established it as five piṭakas:
first, the Sūtra-piṭaka; second, the Vinaya-piṭaka; third, the Śāstra-piṭaka; fourth, the Mantra-piṭaka; and fifth, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Within the Mahīśāsaka school, there were those who followed this same establishment of five piṭakas, forming a separate sect called the Dharmarakṣa school, which maintained the first four divisions.
According to the chronological sequence of the schools, at the end of the third century [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], a school named the Kāśyapīya branched off from the Sarvāstivāda.
In Sanskrit it is called Kāśyapīya; in Chinese it is translated as "Drinking Light" (Yǐnguāng). Kāśyapa is a clan name;
in ancient times there was a rishi whose bodily radiance was so intense that it eclipsed all other light, causing it to disappear. The founder of this school was a descendant of that lineage.
Taking the preceding liberation and discipline (*vinaya*) as their primary tenet, at the beginning of the fourth century, a school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda named the Sautrāntika.
These masters rely solely on the sūtras as their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not on the vinaya or the Abhidharma.
Whatever meaning they interpret, they take the sūtras as their proof; this name is derived from their founder. From beginning to end, these form ten distinct sections.
One school together with the aforementioned nine schools of the Mahāsāṃghika makes twenty schools in total.
Within the Sthavira school, although it divided into eleven distinct sects, each of these sects contained five sub-sects of doctrinal tenets;

among them, the Sarvāstivāda school specifically adhered to the *Sarvāstivāda* as its primary doctrine, while the Mahīśāsaka school specifically adhered to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda* (Five-Part) Vinaya as its primary doctrine.
The Vātsīputrīya school exclusively adheres to the *Mahīśāsaka* as its tenet; the Kāśyapīya school exclusively adheres to the *Kāśyapīya* as its tenet;
and the Dharmaguptaka school exclusively adheres to the *Dharmaguptaka* (the Four-Part Vinaya) as its tenet.
Although these sectarian divisions are not essential to the sūtras, students of later generations must nonetheless be familiar with them.
Regarding those who practice through faith, giving, and so forth, it is also because they believe in the single essence of the Triple Gem that this is not explained in detail in the *Sūtra*.
Since both the Small and Great Vehicles are contained within this [category], these third type of persons belong to the stage of ordinary beings within the four roots of goodness;

while they properly belong to the Small Teaching, they believe in the Tathāgata as eternally constant and unchanging, which negates the meaning of extinction. Therefore, it is said that they possess both.
The stages are identical for all three; since the two vehicles are "small" and the bodhisattvas are "great," it is said that these three persons share the same stage.

As for the differences in the Mahāyāna teachings, because the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) is the dharma of the solitary bodhisattva (*dú púsà*), it should not be equated with the stage of the two vehicles, let alone the fact that the fourth and fifth persons explained below are the two vehicles. Therefore, one must not interpret this according to the meaning of the distinct teaching.
Commentary:

One interpretation states that the following citation from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is intended to clarify the present meaning: since those within the Shared Teaching who are ordinary beings at the stage of the first practice have already attained faith in the permanence [of the Buddha-nature], they are not ignorant of the Dharma.
As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, its chapter on the One Vehicle says: "Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas transcend the fear of birth and death and successively attain the bliss of liberation.
They form this thought: 'I am free from the terror of birth and death; I shall no longer undergo the suffering of birth and death.
World-Honored One, when Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas contemplate, they perceive that they will not undergo further existence and observe Nirvana as the supreme place of rest."
Bhagavān Pṛthivī, regarding that ground previously attained, he is not deluded concerning the Dharma and does not rely on others;

he also knows for himself that there are further grounds to be attained, and that he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this? Both the Two Vehicles enter the Great Vehicle, and the Great Vehicle is itself the Buddha Vehicle.
Therefore, the Three Vehicles are identical to the One Vehicle. This is the profound and esoteric [teaching] of the Vaipulya.

Because it discusses how those of the Two Vehicles originally resolved upon the Great Mind in the past, it speaks of them as "beginners not deluded" or as having previously understood the permanence through esoteric means;

this is certainly not the same as the explicit teaching of the present sutra, wherein all three vehicles equally know the Perfect [Teaching], thereby causing all three vehicles to believe in the unchanging nature.

The reason there is so much relevance [to this teaching] is simply that this present sutra emphasizes the partial and small [vehicles]; therefore, the explanation of its meaning applies to all four teachings.

Since the previous section concerning the initial practice of the three vehicles already pertained to the *zang* (Āgama) and *tong* (Shared) teachings, the current section further explains it according to the distinct (*bie*) meaning;
thus, the significance of its broad relevance lies herein.
Regarding what appears to be a distinct meaning: it refers to an individual at the initial stage of the path who knows the principle of eternal abiding but is shrouded by delusions.
When one enters through the gradual stages and positions of practice with the Great [Vehicle]—that is, with the mind of the Perfect and Sudden—is this not merely a distinct meaning?
It is the same for the Complete (Zang) and the Shared (Tong); Subhadra attained the fruits of the Small Vehicle, which belong to the Zang and Tong, yet it is said that his cause was impermanence.
Furthermore, as for the fruit being permanent, it must be understood according to another meaning.

Since both texts are present, the Sūtra clarifies that the third person possesses both the Great and Small meanings, while the Commentary explains this through the categories of the general and the specific.
By means of this single passage, the seven sections from beginning to end are all consistently integrated; thus, they all pertain to both teachings.
One must not exclusively adhere to this [view], nor should one interpret the meaning by relying solely on a single teaching.

Now, for the time being, I shall provide an explanation according to the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-naya). Question: Since it has already been stated that "one must not exclusively adhere to this," why do you now provide an explanation solely through the Shared Teaching?
Answer: Because the sutra text clearly reveals the principle of the three types of people sharing the same stage; therefore, the subsequent passage...
It is said that the response to the question should be explained in this way:

"By means of the mind of the Great Nirvāṇa" and so forth refers to practicing the contemplation of the mind of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching while relying upon the stages and positions of the Shared Teaching.
If one emerges from the river of the mundane realm of birth and death, it is precisely equal to the stage of the purity of the six sense organs.

Answer: It should be explained as follows: since the previous question asked why, if all equally possess Buddha-nature, they should equally attain *nirvāṇa*, yet there are distinctions among the six realms of existence, this answer is now given from the perspective of the general stage (*sāmānya-avasthā*).
By means of the practitioners of the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-hsiao*), the meaning of the distinctions is fully manifested;

by their common realization of the ultimate truth (*tathatā*), the identity of Buddha-nature is fully manifested. However, while it is certain that one will attain it through cultivation, it is not attained if one does not cultivate it.
It is so. Regarding the citation of three analogies, there is a textual error; it should state five analogies: first, a skilled physician; second, a donor; third, the rising sun;
fourth, a river; and fifth, the great earth.

Regarding the phrase "relying on the existence of [intrinsic] nature" and so forth: there are those in the world who have studied the Mahāyāna in a superficial manner and claim that they are primordially endowed [with enlightenment].
Because they disparage the cultivation of the correct practice, this text deprecates them. Thus, the *Ten Gates of Non-duality* states:

"If one allows phenomena to not shift the mind, it will cause confusion regarding the completion of cultivation; therefore, one must unify confusion and realization, and through the illumination of nature, achieve cultivation—seeing nature is the cultivation of the mind."
Second is the simultaneous submergence of both cultivation [and non-cultivation].
To cause that which seeks to absorb to be absorbed, the stone remains motionless while the iron comes of its own accord; this is called "absorption.

This serves as a metaphor for the meaning of clinging to the existence of an inherent nature, whereby one realizes bodhi spontaneously without relying on the practice of the Path—this is what is meant by "absorption."
"Jing" (罐) refers to a water jar; "jing" (綆) refers to a bucket or drawing vessel. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "jing" is the rope used for drawing water from a well.

Regarding this "Prajñā appearing before one," Xian states that because the ancients matched the ten pāramitās vertically with the ten bhūmis, Prajñā corresponds to the sixth, the Bhūmi of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "that is within the principle" (*li-nei*) and so forth: the Middle Way, inconceivable emptiness, is termed "emptiness within the principle.
This emptiness within what is realized is used as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature existing amidst delusion.

Regarding the phrase "to create is like the initial mind" and so forth: the "initial mind" refers to the three stages of the name-position (*ming-zi-wei*), the understanding-position (*zhi-wei*), and the practice-position (*san-wei*); "cultivation" refers to the stage of contemplative practice (*guan-xing*).
The practice of the stage of semblance (sādṛśya-avasthā) is the third; the realization of the nature of seeing (darśana-svabhāva) is the third [stage] of partial truth (bhūta-tattva).
Regarding the six phrases, Zezhou’s commentary states: "That which has already perished and gone into the past body is called 'not internal' because it lacks a name;

that which belongs to the person who performed the action is called 'not external. When the karma has perished in the past or present, there is no substantial entity (dharma-bhāva), so it is called 'not having existence.'"

The reason why [the view that things] do not exist is incorrect is that what has already been produced is not something that was originally non-existent and only now comes into being for the first time.
Because things arise through production and because they exist, they are not without cause.
To claim that these aggregates and so forth have no cause other than a present condition, yet assert that there will be a subsequent result, belongs to the view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi).

"Human action and celestial reception" does not mean that one performs an action among humans and receives its fruit in the heavens; rather, it means that this person performs the action and that deity receives [the karmic result].
"Having the cause but lacking the fruit" refers to a case where a person performs an action but does not obtain its fruit.
Regarding the claim that there is an effect without a cause: those gods experience it because they lacked its cause in the past.
This is the view of eternalism, which holds that results manifest eternally without depending on the cultivation of causes.
This is the view of nihilism, which holds that the person is not the cause and thus does not bring about future results.
This view of annihilationism would also entail that karma performed by a being in a lower heaven is experienced by this person;
this is identical in meaning to the first proposition, which states that the agent and the experiencer are the same.

That is to say, if the aggregates (skandhas) that perform the action were the very same aggregates that experience the fruit, then there would be only one aggregate, and that one would be eternal. All other cases should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
"Harmony of time and season" refers to the moment when causes and conditions converge, at which point one must personally experience the retribution of one's karma.

Regarding amber attracting mustard seeds, this refers to its power to draw in mustard seeds. The *Xuánzhōng jì* states that pine resin sinks into the earth and, after a thousand years, becomes amber (*hǔpò*).
Soil and water act as the conditions for the sprout; the seed is the cause of the sprout, while soil and water are its conditions.
Thus, the seed and the soil/water are distinct phenomena (dharmas) in relation to the sprout.
Regarding the illustrations provided, the text states that there are six analogies, such as the magnet and the fierce fire, yet it mentions that "generally five are cited."
The character in the analogy is erroneous.
How could ignorance possibly "suck in" the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)? This refers to the fact that without conditions, nothing else arises; other cases are likewise so.
The Sūtra also speaks of "formative forces conditioned by ignorance" because one obtains the conditions for their arising; other instances should be understood by this same principle.
This clearly demonstrates that those who do not inhale [the breath] possess a rational nature that is without transition; thus, whether a Buddha appears or not, it neither increases nor decreases.
Is this not what the *Lotus Sūtra* means when it says: "This Dharma abides in the station of the Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant"?
If a sutra states that "the Buddha-nature dwells within sentient beings" and so forth, even to the point of saying it is itself impermanent,
how can those who claim that the Buddha-nature does not pervade insentient things escape this reproach?

Regarding the passage "passing through the twelve links [of dependent origination] without a fixed place of abiding," etc.: because the principle by which phenomena arise one after another has no fixed attribution, there is no characteristic of a fixed place of abiding;
yet, because the principle of arising is never for a moment absent, it is termed "constant. Thus, based on causes and conditions, the Buddha-nature is illustrated by this analogy.
The sutra states that there is no place of abiding whatsoever; this nature of non-abiding is possessed by all sentient beings.
"But those who rely on karmic conditions" means it is permitted—that is, it is granted that past karmic conditions collectively induce the present fruit-body of the four great elements.
Thus, the sutra says: "Furthermore, these four great elements are also devoid of karma."
"Manifesting when the time arrives" means that when the time for practicing the Path arrives, it manifests—just as the four great elements manifest when the time for receiving a body arrives.
Regarding the Mahāyāna teaching that wind has color: the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* mentions six-colored winds—black, red, blue, earth, heaven, and fire.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states, "Even if there be a black wind," and these are all Mahāyāna statements regarding wind having color.
Regarding the phrase "the autumnal air is white," the *Liang Yuandi Zuanyao* states: "Autumn is called 'White Treasury' (*Bai-zang*) because its air is white and it gathers and stores all things.

As for the phrase "because they belong to different dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*)," this means that since the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) differ, their names constitute different dharma-realms; therefore, [the qualities] such as hardness and so forth [are distinct].
It is not analogous.
When it is said that the Buddha-nature described in the sutras is also like this, it is because the Buddha-nature differs from the non-existence of a rabbit's horn;

therefore, when sentient beings cultivate the path, it immediately manifests. Furthermore, while false dharmas are extinguished upon reaching the culmination of cultivation, the Buddha-nature differs from them.
When cultivated to its full extent, it manifests as what is called the "distinct dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-viśeṣa*).
Regarding the term *lúfú* (radish) used in the *Erya*: the "Shicao" chapter of the *Erya* states, "The *tǔ* is the *lúyí*. Guo Jingchun’s commentary notes that *yí* should be read as *fú*;
thus, *lúfú* belongs to the category of *wŭqīng* (mustard greens), having purple flowers and large roots, commonly called *bó-tǔ*. The commentary cites minor variations from the *Xiaojie*.
Regarding the characters for "lu-bu" (radish): the upper character is pronounced as *li* with the tone *he*, and the lower character as *pu* with the tone *bei*.
Some editions of the classics have the reading *lai-fu*, which is identical to the former. Commentators sometimes pronounce them with the two sounds *lai* and *fu*; how extreme is such error!
That which cannot emerge from the two positions of "identity" and "separation" is such that one remains within the meaning of identity while the other vanishes into the meaning of separation;

yet the principle of Buddha-nature is neither identical nor separate. Therefore, know that your understanding has not yet emerged from these two positions of identity and separation—how much less could it emerge from the positions of "both" or "neither"?
Thus it is said: "How could one attain transcendence of the four propositions? This refers to the transcendence of the four conceptual extremes.
Thus, if one departs from the hundred negations, the four propositions do not perish; how could the hundred negations themselves be departed from?
Now, the Master correctly explains that "the non-existence of the six dharmas" and so forth refers to the five aggregates and the self (*ātman*), which together are called the six dharmas.

"Neither internal nor external" means it is neither the six internal sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) nor the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). The sense organs are the *pratyaya-vipāka* (direct retribution), while the sense objects are the *niśraya-vipāka* (supporting retribution).
As for those whom the various Brahmins slandered, it is as previously stated in the sutra: when Śyāma exhorted the Brahmin to generate the Great [Resolve].
As for that which is called the Mahāyāna, it is the mind-vehicle; since it is non-existent, O Great King, why do you cause people to equate it with empty space?
If you claim that Buddha-nature is separate from the six dharmas, you are entirely identical to those who slander it.

Regarding the phrase "neither identical nor separate," it is because they are realized through the path of cultivation that they are not identical; yet because they are precisely those six dharmas, they are not separate.
This can be understood by reflecting on how water is neither non-water nor yet is precisely water.
Each of these consists of three parts; while the preceding five all have three, the final one has only two, lacking the concluding text.
If we follow the pattern of the preceding five, it should read: "For this reason, I say that the self is the Buddha-nature."
Some say it is eternal and omnipresent, meaning that the self pervades empty space; this is the calculation that the self is large while matter is small.
Others say it is like a mustard seed; this calculates that matter is large while the self is small.
Regarding the formation of an army through the combination [of individuals], the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), in the section on the Grand Commandant of the Summer Office (*Da Sima*), states:

"In all cases of organizing an army, there are twelve thousand five hundred men. This refers to how a multitude of people combine to form an army, which serves as a metaphor for how the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) combine to constitute a self (*ātman*).

Regarding the claim that "provisional names have function while names have no substance," Kaishan maintains that although the provisional self has a name and the functional capacity of a sovereign, it lacks substantial reality because it is formed by grasping the aggregates (*skandhas*);
it is just as a fist has a name and a function but no substance, being formed by grasping the fingers. Zangyuan’s intention was to ask: since there are both name and function, how could this be so?
It is established that they lack intrinsic nature.
These two [positions] are now refuted.
Furthermore, if they are not provisional, then since they possess names and functions, they would be identical to real dharmas; how then could they be called "provisional names"?
The Master [Sthiramati] now cites the Master [Vasubandhu] as the correct interpretation.
He also refutes both "identity" and "separateness": by refuting identity, he shows there is no self; by refuting separateness, he shows there is no non-self.
That both are merely conventional designations means that both self and non-self are mere designations. Since even non-self is a mere designation, how much more so...
One should consider whether I possess a functional essence.
Regarding "distinct names and teachings," this refers to the fact that these four distinct categories of enumeration exist within various sutras.
As for the twelve links of dependent origination, they are merely the nature of causes for those who possess contemplative wisdom.

Regarding other sources where this is explained, such as the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), it clarifies that the three paths of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*);
thus, this principle may be further elaborated.
"The other two are as in the text" refers to the seventh and eighth passages. However, these eight passages begin with compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).
The "Ultimate Peak Samādhi" (Zhōngdǐng sānmèi) all refers to the fact that the rational nature of sentient beings is inherently complete, such that by practicing it, one will necessarily attain it.

Regarding the "Peak Samādhi" mentioned in the sutras: it is the ultimate principle of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Just as the crown of a person's head is the most honorable and noble part, observing this principle is therefore called the "Peak Samādhi."

Upon searching for this character, it was not found; however, according to Master Ying’s *Yinyi* (Commentary on Pronunciation and Meaning), it is read as "wang-pi" (亡皮反) and refers to a ripened grain.
Those in Guansi call it *xu*, while those in Jizhou call it *ji*.
The sutra states that one does not give rise to an evil mind, such as when eating the flesh of one's own son;

one does not harbor thoughts of greed, cruelty, or the intent to kill, but merely consumes it out of necessity to treat an illness, just as a person in dire hunger and poverty eats their own child with no joy in their heart.
Furthermore, those who joyfully extol the Triple Gem and propagate this sutra are the Saṃgha; thus, they constitute the Triple Gem.

While the preceding section was a general and concise praise, the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation. However, the sutra text contains only two sections—a general and a specific—and I fear that dividing the text into "concise" and "detailed" portions may lead to error.
Regarding the statement that the cause of the sūtra is also superior: this refers to the cause for birth in the Tuṣita Heaven, which is the cause of the desire realm.

This heaven is situated in the center because there are three heavens above it and three heavens below it; furthermore, the Buddha’s birth in the Central Heaven signifies his manifestation of the Middle Way.
Zhongsi is the name of a monastery located in Jianye. Wang Jian was the Chancellor of the Southern Qi dynasty.
When ancient people wrote the character for "jiao" (teaching), it should have been written as "jue" (awakening); thus, "jiao" is interpreted as meaning "to awaken from sleep."

Regarding those who provide a single, isolated interpretation: since the Sūtra states that it is "profound," this refers to the mutual identity of the three aspects (the essence, attributes, and functions), which is called "profound" because they are neither sequential nor horizontal.
If one were to explain it as merely a single horizontal or a single vertical relationship, that would be the meaning of being sequential or horizontal; such is shallow and not profound.
Regarding the fact that the ocean tides do not exceed their limits, many sūtras speak of this matter;
furthermore, according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, there is a sea named Mahābha whose breadth is five thousand yojanas.

When winds arise beneath the water due to the causes and conditions of sentient beings, waves emerge from all the great oceans and islands to a height of two yojanas, which the people of Jambudvīpa call "the sea."
The *Lunheng* (Discourse on Weighing Matters), in its chapter on "Tides," states: "Water is the blood and veins of the earth; it ebbs and flows in accordance with the qi to form tides.
When it moves in accordance with the wind, the waves and surges surge and stir, causing the great ocean to gradually deepen."
If it is asked why there is only one type [of birth], namely why only the womb-born (*jarāyu-ja*) exists, the Sūtra asks:
"How can there be *śarīra-dhātu* (bodily relics)? This is because those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) necessarily vanish upon being transformed;
as the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Just as when a lamp is extinguished, nothing more is seen."
The Sūtra on the Seed-Pod of Ignorance (Mūlapariyāya-sutta). *Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra:
Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues*, Fascicle Seventeen.
*Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues*, Fascicle Eighteen.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang.
From the beginning of the "Chapter on Kāśyapa" below,
this section concerning Kāśyapa and Cunda, along with the subsequent two fascicles, both belong to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and are divided according to their topical chapters.

The first two chapters of the *Duan* (Section) clarify the function of subduing evil and gathering the heterodox; the subsequent chapters clarify the function of universal transformation and the concealment of traces.

If this is so, why does the commentary on the latter section refer to it as the "Sixth Chapter: Universal Transformation and Concealment of Traces"? Answer: This refers to the specific enumeration of subsections within the chapter on functions (*yòng zhāng*).

According to that classification, it constitutes the sixth: namely, first, the invocation of the constant assembly (*cháng zhòng*), and second, the opening exposition of the constant bestowal (*cháng shī*).
Third, the manifestation of constant practice; fourth, the questions and answers on the meaning of constancy; fifth, the refutation of heterodoxy and the gathering in of the wicked;

sixth, the completion of transformation and the concealment of traces—thus there are six chapters. Now, the combination of the fifth and sixth is simply the "constant use," for it is the function of the "constant house";

thus it is called "constant use. This "constancy" is precisely the principle of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, one should know that although the later sections of the sutra were not yet extant during the time of Zhǎng'ān, the meaning of the doctrine was already present.

Because this is complete, the previous explanation—that the general introduction (sūtra-prologue) corresponds to the five chapters by means of five matters—is established; thus, one knows there is no further principle for establishing six chapters.
If it were otherwise, the meaning of the formal arrangement of the chapters would become incomplete.

Moreover, Dharmakṣema stated that while the meaning of this sūtra is sufficient, the text is not yet exhaustive; how could it be that the meaning of the sūtra does not emerge from these five chapters? Whatever else may exist [is contained therein].
The remaining text should be understood according to the [fourfold] inclusion.
Regarding "a good beginning" and so forth: previously, he posed thirty-four questions that accorded with the Buddha’s intention and led to the exposition of the constant practice;
hence it is called "a good beginning. Now, by further inquiring, he finally reveals the application of that constant practice; hence it is said to "bring it to completion," which is also "good."

Regarding the previous practice of titling chapters according to their subject matter: although it was Kāśyapa who initially posed the questions, because the meaning encompassed a broad range of topics, the chapters were titled according to their respective thematic categories—such as the fourteen distinct chapters beginning with "Longevity"—without any mention of Kāśyapa’s name.

Regarding the phrase "now following [the previous section]," the present inquiry concerns only the methods of subduing (*vinaya*) and gathering (*saṃgraha*); since its meaning is already established therein, the title of this chapter is based solely on the person [who taught it].

Regarding the phrase "the masters of the *Bhūmi*," this refers to the masters of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Dilun masters) who utilized Vasubandhu’s sevenfold classification to judge the sūtras; this chapter clarifies the Buddha.

Because compassion and skillful means sustain the evil of the icchantika Sunakṣatra within the goodness of the Buddha-nature, it is called the "section on sustaining through the skillful means of compassionate light.
As for the difference between their meaning and function:
"meaning" refers to self-realization, while "function" refers to transforming others.
Regarding the "seed of bodhi," its nature is both the seed of cultivation and the nature of cultivation; these two act as seeds for one another, as explained previously in the commentary.
Furthermore, that which is the "nature of the fruit" refers to what the sutra below states: "From ignorance, volitional formations, and various afflictions, one obtains the wholesome five aggregates;
this is called Buddha-nature. This means that one abandons impermanent form and attains permanent form, and so forth. One should know that this pertains to the preceding chapter.
Since this chapter clarifies both cause and effect—specifically how the transforming cause results in the fruition—it differs from what preceded.
This has been the interpretation of past scholars regarding the subsequent section.

As for the phrase "the Buddha-nature of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya)... and so forth, because the response-body conforms to the forms of the myriad classes of beings, it possesses the three periods of time; the dharma-body (dharmakāya), however, is quiescent.
Thus, it is not the case that the nature of the fruit of the sages of the three periods of time is already twofold;

since ordinary beings inherently possess these two [aspects], what was previously stated—that Buddha-nature exists in the three periods of time and does not exist in the three periods of time—refers to this inherent possession by ordinary beings.
This is not so; hereafter, the Master provides the correct interpretation.

If the Buddha-nature within the causal stage were subsumed under the three periods of time, then although the nature of the three bodies is all-pervasive and eternal, prior to the realization of the Golden Mind (*suvarṇacitta*), it is not yet ultimate and thus remains impermanent;
therefore, it would be subsumed under the temporal periods. However, because it is fully manifested upon reaching the fruition, it is not of the world.

Regarding the inclusion and synthesis: as for the synthesis of the three vehicles, previously they were distinguished because their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were subject to both diminution and exhaustion; now they are unified because they equally reach the other shore.

Furthermore, it should be stated that there is not only a difference between expansion and synthesis, but also a difference between the real and the false: the aforementioned river of birth-and-death is the false.
Now, the River of Nirvāṇa is the truth.
As for the statement that all beings in the six realms possess Buddha-nature, each and every one is endowed with the five types of Buddha-nature.

Regarding the specific reliance on the "enabling cause" (pariniṣpanna-hetu) of myriad virtues: the preceding chapter has already extensively clarified the meanings of the "generative cause" (janana-hetu) and the "enabling cause," and furthermore, it provides a broad refutation [of opposing views].

Fixed karma is shown to be indeterminate so that one may cultivate the factors of enlightenment and perceive the Buddha-nature; this is explained specifically in terms of cultivation and attainment, and thus belongs to the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*).
As for its general application to both good and evil: since this chapter clarifies both the cultivated and the innate, both good and evil are the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is said that the four lines of text from the following chapter are cited as proof.
Regarding the phrase "those with roots of goodness," this refers to virtuous persons who have cultivated and attained the provisional and ultimate conditions; however, icchantikas lack these.
Regarding the statement that "icchantikas have [the Buddha-nature] equally," while icchantikas cultivate evil, virtuous people do not; however, this merely cites two lines. One should rather say:

"There may be a Buddha-nature that both types of people possess," or "There may be a Buddha-nature that both types of people lack. Thus, four permutations are established: (1) both types of people possess the nature-virtue and the three causes;
(2) both types of people lack them; (3) [one type lacks it]; and (4) [the other type lacks it]. This is because those who have not yet entered [the path] lack the nature of non-retrogression.
Because they occupy similar stages.
Regarding the first intention, among the five differences, the title of this major section is given as "the function of nirvāṇa" because it differs in its functional meaning.
As for "by the power of delusion," buddha-nature is identical to the mind of ignorance; because it follows along with objects, it is able to give rise to evil.

Regarding the power of the Buddha-nature: because ignorance is the Buddha-nature itself, and because it is intrinsically endowed with the principle that internally perfumes [the mind], it can give rise to goodness and sever goodness.
The severing of goodness arises from turning one's back on the principle and giving rise to delusion; the arising of goodness arises from reversing delusion and attaining awakening.
"Alternating between two people" means that performing good and performing evil are each done by a different person;
that is, one person performs evil while the other performs good, or one person performs evil while the other performs good, alternating in their respective roles. Thus, they form a pair.
It is not said so because good and evil are discussed as occurring sequentially within a single individual; rather, it refers to their lack of mutual connection.
Furthermore, the first [section] below explains it according to a single person as the text states.
Now, to clarify that the two masters below each hold a position that results in error, while our own school takes both together as correct,
we cite the example of the seven people in the river to establish this meaning.
Those who have not yet given rise to the four abidings (catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ) are those who currently possess ignorance (avidyā) but have not yet developed views or afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa);
because their delusion is still shallow, they proceed toward Buddhahood from this intermediate stage.

Furthermore, for those whose karmic conditions involve transforming evil at once, because their capacities and conditions are such that they should hear [the teaching], it is merely a provisional skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) according to their individual circumstances.
It is said that because one's fundamental delusion is beginningless, there is no matter of the successive arising of afflictions.
If this were so, [the text] would generally criticize [this view] as being the same as those non-Buddhists;

for if it were claimed that a single grade of ignorance begins to arise and one becomes a Buddha upon being received by a Buddha, then one would naturally become a Buddha without relying on the cultivation of the path. By this analogy, it would likewise apply to the present time.
Even for those who have committed evil, when their wickedness reaches its ultimate limit, they must still be received by a Buddha; this would mean they do not need to cultivate the Path.

If that were so, it would be identical to the heterodox calculations of non-Buddhists, who claim that after eighty thousand kalpas one enters nirvana spontaneously—like a ball of thread that stops once the thread is exhausted.
Since this is the same as such heterodox views, how can it be considered the Buddha-Dharma?
If it is argued that [the text] refutes the unarisen by using the arisen as an example, then [the afflictions] should exist elsewhere—that is, they should exist where there are no afflictions.

If that were so, it would follow that the Buddha, who is originally a fruition-Buddha, would later gradually give rise to delusions and revert to being a sentient being. There could be no more absurd or confused statement than this.
If one follows the precedent of the "Chapter on Initial Arising" (*ādyutpāda-varga*) to refute the "Chapter on Subsequent Arising" (*paścādutpāda-varga*),
then regarding those subsequent chapters and so forth: since the various scriptural teachings generally state that ignorance consists of either twelve factors or forty-two factors,
and it is already granted that when the first factor initially arises, a Buddha comes to receive [the practitioner], then for all the subsequent factors that arise...

For example, if it were the case that ignorance (*avidyā*) should be interrupted when it arises, then since the four abidings (*catur-vāsana*) are also interrupted at that time, why is it said that they are interrupted only when [ignorance] arises in a single grade (*ekaprakāra*)? Therefore, it is asked: "Why are they not interrupted?"

If there were no lower [stages], one would use the "cave of ignorance" as an analogy for the "caves of the four abodes" to refute this; this is a refutation that proceeds even while conceding the opponent's position. To concede their calculation:
because the delusion is still slight when the first grade [of affliction] first arises, there is the possibility of being "taken up" and attaining Buddhahood;

however, because it gradually becomes heavier as it arises later, there is no such possibility of being taken up. Therefore, the present refutation proceeds by stating: "Furthermore, according to what is taught in the Hīnayāna teachings, the four [abodes] are refuted."
If one dwells in the exhaustion [of these states], one attains Buddhahood as well as the fruit of Arhatship; thus we know that the four dwellings (*catur-vāsa*) also have an initial arising.

Why, then, is it not said that they begin from the "cave" of the four dwellings? When the delusions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) arise, there is a Buddha who receives one and leads one to attain Buddhahood and the state of an Arhat and so forth.

Because these delusions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception are the lightest within the realm of existence (*dhātu*), their meaning is already incorrect; therefore, he concludes by saying:
Therefore, this is difficult to believe.
If that is so, the following section cites the opponent's position as the very point to be refuted by the present sutra.
"If that is so" means: even if one were to assume that those in the later stages of ignorance and within the four dwelling-places all possess a connection [to the path] leading to Buddhahood;
This would mean that the realization of both the Great and Small fruits is entirely attained spontaneously without depending on the cultivation of the path;
this point has already been refuted extensively in the "Chapter on the Great Lion’s Roar.

Below, the text provides the actual refutation: "If you claim that one attains [enlightenment] without cultivation by merely continuing [the process], then it would be the same as claiming that one attains Bodhi by mere indifference."
The two disciples of the Buddha are Ānanda and Devadatta; the two sons are Rāhula and Sunakṣatra.
The two disciples represent the provisional teaching, as already revealed in the *Lotus Sūtra*; by this analogy, the two sons are not actual persons.
Those who hear the non-definitive teachings and yet cling to them as definitive understandings fail to comprehend the Tathāgata’s skillful means;
instead, they dogmatically adhere to a single meaning to refute all others.

Regarding the seven points: the first four concern the ability to transform others—namely, being able to discipline those who cannot be disciplined and uprooting evil from its very beginning. The [fifth] concerns purifying that which is impure.

"Extricating evil" refers to the beginning of the rescue from suffering, wherein there was no refuge; "making a refuge" refers to the end of the rescue from suffering, wherein those not yet liberated are able to be liberated.
The latter three [perfections] are the virtues for transforming others, possessing the eight masteries. The virtue of rescuing from suffering is like a physician or a king of medicine;
the virtue of extricating evil is like a physician who knows the illness and cures it with medicine.
Rāhula was the son of his stepbrother born of a different mother; thus, he is called "stepbrother" (shùxiong) to clarify that Rāhula was born of Yaśodharā and was the Buddha’s legitimate son.
Master Huiyuan stated: "This must have been the Buddha’s younger cousin’s son, and for that reason he was spoken of as a son."

The "possession of the three virtues" refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). "Sla" (in its lower pronunciation, *si*) denotes a lowly servant.

Regarding the statement that there is a sequential order based on the depth or shallowness of conditions: for those whose conditions are deep, one first explains [the teachings]; for those whose conditions are shallow, one explains them later.
Below, the text first addresses the Bodhisattvas, then the Śrāvakas, and finally the *pratyekabuddhas* (or *icchantikas*) by means of interrogative inquiry.
The commentary explains that the response consists of three sections: first, clarifying the capacity of those with small faculties; second, addressing those with great faculties;
and third, revealing how the present sutra encompasses and unifies both the small and great vehicles. Within the first section, the cases of Tiwei and Wenlin are as previously described.

Regarding this teaching for those of lesser capacity (*hīnayāna-āśaya*), it is taught in sequence: the teachings for humans and devas as the beginning, the *Hīnayāna* as the middle, and the *Bodhisattva* path as the end.

Briefly stated, these suffice; however, to be fully exhaustive, one should say that the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras lead those of lesser capacity back to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), and thus they entirely constitute the teaching of bodhisattvas.
In this case, what is perceived by those of lesser capacity—first the small and subsequently the great—is not the same as the parable of the three sons in the present sutra.
Because they are the same, it is said that this is one particular path, and so forth.
If the first [passage] below is discussed in terms of the great-capacity [practitioners], it concerns the sequence [of teachings].
The first instance of "shining upon the mountain king" is a metaphor for the sun rising and shining first upon the high mountains; this refers to the *Avataṃsaka* being taught first.
This refers to the Bodhisattvas.
Next, "illuminating the level ground" refers to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) and subsequent periods, wherein the Mahāyāna teachings of the three samādhis are all taught to the Bodhisattvas.

It does not mention "illuminating the deep valley" because at the Deer Park, the teaching of the Small Vehicle was directed solely toward those with small-capacity faculties; therefore, this [subsequent period] concerns those with great capacity.
The view that the beginning and end are both "great" is also different from the analogy of the three sons in the present sutra;
therefore, it is said that this is another approach, because the analogies of the three sons and so forth in the present sutra all pertain to the later teaching concerning icchantikas.
Now, the following section reveals how these three metaphors encompass [the teachings].
Taking the King of Mountains as the first refers to the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, which primarily teaches Bodhisattvas.

Taking the scaled fish as the middle refers to those who were initially received and guided through the precepts, and subsequently taught the arising and ceasing of phenomena so that they might realize the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle; this is a provisional critique.

Those who were excluded and refined away until the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the small [vehicle] returns to the great and all are made into followers of the two vehicles—this refers to the Śrāvakas of the intermediate teaching.
As for those remaining at the Twin Trees, this scripture clarifies that even icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature; if they can reform their evil ways, they will certainly attain Buddhahood.

This refers to the subsequent teaching for the icchantikas; thus we know that these three metaphors span the teachings from the *Avataṃsaka* to the *Nirvāṇa*, encompassing all five periods of the Dharma in their entirety.

Question: Since these three metaphors already subsume the five periods, why does the Sūtra state that for the śrāvakas there is a progression beginning from the minor teachings of humans and devas up to the revelation and manifestation in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
For what reason is it said that [for them] there are only shallow and proximate meanings?

Question: Is this spoken by the Śrāvakas? Furthermore, since this present sutra discusses the eternal and reveals the nature that transcends the two deaths, why does it state that the meaning of the "world" is taught for the sake of icchantikas?
Answer: All [teachings] rely upon the initial exposition; therefore, it is said to be "shallow and near," and so forth.
Because those with the faculties of the Small Vehicle must first engage with the Small, persons who are icchantikas must first be led to have faith.
Regarding the cause and effect of good and evil: if one considers their ultimate convergence, this refers to the meaning of being subtle and refined;
for it is because both those of the Two Vehicles and the icchantikas alike become bodhisattvas.
Regarding "because of family affairs": the Buddhas take the transformation of sentient beings as their primary task; therefore, until the very end, they do not abandon the icchantikas.
"Jing-gao-cao" (經藁草) means "withered grain stalks" (古老反禾稈).
As for the meaning being "without discrepancy," although there are [teachings] earlier and later, they must be equal in their instruction.
Regarding "the elephant's power seems insufficient": the body of the elephant is massive, so when the lion kills it, its strength seems insufficient; the body of the rabbit is minute...
When a small lion kills [an elephant], its strength must have a surplus.

This is because when comparing their respective capacities, the elephant’s power is great while the rabbit’s power is weak; thus, there is a natural difference between the swiftness and slowness of their killing.

Now, as lions are of one kind, they all exert their full strength; they do not measure their power according to the size of the victim, nor do they distinguish between them as superior or inferior based on magnitude.
Regarding the subsequent scriptural passage, it merely combines the bodhisattvas and icchantikas while omitting the śrāvakas; the commentary provides them in full.
As for the phrase "the Buddha does not [act] twice or three times," this corresponds to the lion king.
Regarding "being seized in turn" (*jing fan bei juzu*), this refers to those who, in turn, don woolen garments (*maoyi*) and feign the appearance of demons.
"Seized" (*juzu*) refers to the *gubei chui maoyi* (woolen garments hanging from the *gubei* tree); this is what is described in the eleventh sutra.

Regarding the sūtra: Why does Sunakṣatra claim that both the Arhat and the one who has attained arhatship are Arhats, and why does he say that the Tathāgata is jealous of the Arhat who has attained arhatship?
As for the use of "Arhat" above and "Arahant" below, these terms are mutually illustrative of the same meaning; there is no need for a different explanation.
"Regarding 'one with a hunched spine,' this refers to a back that is massively curved backward.
By examining this, we know it is a provisional manifestation (*upāya*). As stated below, how could it be that only Śunakṣatra is provisional? That Nirgrantha was also a provisional manifestation.
If he were a real person, how could he have praised the virtues of the Tathāgata by [describing] the ghost body that had vomited food?"
One does not see a later successor who catches it, but only sees that rain is certain to fall; one does not see a later asura catching it with his hand and entering the sea.
For five reasons, even though dark clouds are spread, rain does not descend: first, the fire element scorches; second, the wind element blows away; third, it is caught by an asura;
fourth, it is governed by a wicked king; and fifth, it is due to the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
As stated in the *Sūtra-vinaya-vibhāga-lakṣaṇa*,
that which is the power of desire is the fifth among the ten powers; it refers to knowing the various desires and inclinations of other sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "like the untainted (anāsrava) and unimpeded [faculties]," if one follows our own school (jīngzōng), this is merely a partial analogy;

it does not serve as a complete analogy because while the untainted [faculty] arises once and never perishes, those with the nature of an icchantika (icchantika) can still give rise to wholesome thoughts when they encounter the right conditions.

However, if one relies on the school of the five natures (pañca-gotra), this serves as a complete analogy, for that school explains that icchantikas lack Buddha-nature and thus cannot attain Buddhahood. Thus we know that the Saṃkhya school...
The meaning accords with the five natures.
If this is so, [the text] below now cites and refutes the icchantikas; below, the present master clarifies the doctrine.
That "goodness does not arise simultaneously" means that good and evil are as contrary as water and fire; thus, one cultivates goodness here. If one discusses their nature...
Goodness is always inherently present.

When it is said that goodness cannot arise, it means that the cultivation of goodness does not arise; this is because the inherent goodness (xing-shan) is not manifest, and thus the cultivation of goodness fails to arise.

Therefore, we know that evil arises from the obscuration of the rational nature (li-xing), which thereby obstructs phenomenal goodness (shi-shan). If one understands the Buddha-nature, phenomenal goodness [will manifest].
"Because it arises again.
Regarding the phrase "later evil gradually ceases," etc.: because one understands the fundamental nature, the evil deeds cease; "gradually ceasing" means they diminish step by step.
In terms of the stages, this is called the cessation of what resembles the true through contemplation.
The answer is that it possesses two meanings: first, there is wholesome [karma] that can be severed; second, there is no wholesome [karma] that can be severed.
These will be explained in sequence below.

As for "no wholesome [karma] that can be severed," this actually establishes the meaning of severing wholesome [roots], because since the wholesome has not yet arisen, it cannot be produced. This is the principle.
Those "within the principle" (*neili*) are those who have attained realization of Buddha-nature at the stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) and above;
those "outside the principle" (*waili*) are those of the three preceding teachings who are in opposition to their original nature, and are thus called "outside the principle."
Those who are inverted and deluded seek a middle way apart from the two extremes; they wish to abandon birth-and-death and grasp at nirvana;
they take pleasure in the human and celestial realms and do not fear the evil paths. These nine realms are all termed "inverted" and do not accord with the true mark (dharmatā);
they are all termed "delusive. Therefore, they lack the five faculties such as perfect faith. Because this explanation is too diffuse, it is refuted by saying: "This meaning..."
Not so. This section below specifically explains that from the stage of "those outside the principle" (*li-wai*) down to humans and devas, each stage possesses the five faculties;
therefore, it says they "also possess faith and the others."

The following clarifies that even the three evil realms of those who have committed the acts of immediate retribution (icchantika) are severed; how much more so would the five faculties of the human and celestial realms, let alone the five faculties of the Buddha-realm, be severed?
This is because they deny the existence of cause and effect in both the mundane and supramundane spheres.
Regarding the phrase "since the Buddha-nature exists," it is because this nature is inherently complete that one is able to initiate cultivation;

for since the five faculties—both partial and perfect—are all intrinsically contained within principle, it is precisely due to this intrinsic containment of principle that they are skillfully activated upon encountering conditions.

That they have not yet [attained it] is due to the obstruction caused by the cultivation of evil; however, this "cultivation of evil" does not refer to the denial of [the Three Jewels], and thus differs from the case of an icchantika.
Regarding the non-interruption of the seeds of goodness and the nature of cultivated good and evil, these were explained extensively in the previous record.
The established tenet is that ultimately there is no wholesome dharma; this is the tenet of the icchantika.
It is said to be "weak" because it is merely weak itself, with goodness existing only in the future and not yet present, and thus providing no benefit at this time.
Regarding the passage "the sūtra [speaks of] seeds that are rotten and decayed," etc., this is explained based on the present;

however, if one considers the future, the fact that rotten seeds can still produce the Buddha-nature is "good" (until the point where it says) "it cannot be severed"—this is the question posed by Śāriputra.
When it is said that the Buddha-nature is good and eternal, this refers entirely to the *zhengyin* (direct cause).
"Entirely without a false self" means that there is no self as clung to by the non-Buddhist outsiders who hold to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*);

because all phenomena are empty, it is said that there is "entirely nothing. However, what they calculate for themselves is claimed not to be subsumed within the three periods of time; therefore, this "self" is cited as a metaphor for permanence.
When I say that the Buddha-nature is eternal because the force of the phrasing leads to it, this is merely due to the mutual implication [of the terms],
for the True Self is simply another name for the Buddha-nature.

Regarding the passage from "In the present world" to "the world of icchantikas," this is explained based on the *pratyaya-buddha-nature* (enabling Buddha-nature) and the *yuan-buddha-nature* (conditioning Buddha-nature).

If one fully cultivates and attains these two natures, how could one be an icchantika? Thus, we know that when it is said that "the roots of goodness are severed," this refers precisely to the *pratyaya* and *yuan* natures, and does not refer to the *zheng-yin* (direct cause) nature.
Because one who quickly poses such a question can bring great benefit and enable sentient beings of future generations to attain correct understanding;
as for the phrase "attaining [the fruit] in the future," it means that the nature of the true cause is ultimately manifested in the future.
Regarding "that which is visible is food": because one obtains life by means of food, food is the cause and life is the effect.
To speak of life as food is to state the cause within the effect. The latter part of the sutra text says, "seeing form is called contact": form is the cause and contact is the effect;
this is to state the effect within the cause.

The names for "contact" (*sparśa*) differ; below, the meaning of seeing color as contact will be explained in detail. Regarding the phrase "the treatise says," it refers to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

The question asks: since the preceding [discourse] arose from a prior cause, and the answer given was that "Buddha-nature is like space—neither past, nor future, nor present"—and since the scripture cites this by stating "the meaning is thus," if it does not belong to the three periods of time, why is it...?
In the preceding text, it was stated in various places that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;

yet, since it has also been said that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature [as something distinct], this would contradict the words of the Buddhas of the three periods. Therefore, he asks this question.
If sentient beings definitely possess this nature, then "sentient beings" is the delusion and "Buddha-nature" is the truth;

since delusion is itself truth, sentient beings possess this nature just as space does—what would it not encompass? How could it exclude grasses and trees, such that they alone would lack this nature?

One should know that just as those [grasses and trees] arise, so too is my mind; both "them" and "I" are deluded, and thus we equally establish the designation "arising. This is the arising of the mind.
Since this is so for all Buddhas, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are equally without distinction; each one universally pervades the others, yet they remain distinct from one another.

Because these are all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), even if there is the goodness of seeing, hearing, or feeling compassion, it cannot draw forth wholesome fruits, and thus they are categorized as such.
Regarding indeterminate karma:
since it lacks a lower basis and lacks the side of right faith in what is wholesome, it properly belongs to unwholesome karma;
thus, among the three natures, it possesses only two and definitely lacks the nature of the wholesome.
Regarding the action of grasping in relation to wholesome desire: one clings to the wholesome because of the presence of longing.
Regarding the action of seeking in relation to wholesome volition: all wholesome deeds of body and speech arise from the power of intention.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are the basis (*āśraya*) of karma.
Grasping at karma and seeking after karma are the association (*saṃprayoga*) with karma. The karma of giving and the karma of liberation are the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of karma.

Providing for friends and relatives is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of attachment; serving one's teachers and elders is merely a matter of human sentiment; and bestowing gifts upon outsiders is [merely] external.

Praying for blessings and repaying kindness through such acts as giving are all wrong actions (*mithyākarma*). Furthermore, the Commentary by Zeshou explains: "If an icchantika possesses bodily, verbal, or mental karma, it is categorized according to its nature:
karma created with a mind of views is called 'grasping karma' (*upādāna-karma*); karma created with a mind of craving is called 'seeking karma' (*paryeṣaṇā-karma*);

and the karma of giving and the karma of liberation are cited according to their respective characteristics. Even an icchantika may have the relinquishing of wealth, which is termed 'giving' (*dāna*)."
To recite and analyze [the scriptures] is called "understanding.
This concludes the preceding section clarifying the absence of goodness; the following section explains why this understanding is also pervasive.
Regarding those who do not seek cause and effect: they deny both mundane cause and effect and supramundane cause and effect.

Regarding the statement that "color and fragrance are not suffering," the Icchantikas possess only the goodness of compassionate affection; this is analogous to how color and fragrance are not suffering.
Regarding the interpretation of the "Adornment" (Vyūha) for the three families of inferior ordinary beings, each school relies upon one of the three natures (trisvabhāva) to explain the Adornment:

the Icchantikas are said to possess the nature of goodness (kuśala-svabhāva); Guangzhai claims it is the indeterminate nature (avyākṛta-svabhāva); and Kaishan claims it is the nature of evil (akuśala-svabhāva). These are the three.

Since the interpretation of the "House" (Jia) by Kaishan is superior, Daochang’s Huiguan likewise adopts this explanation, which accords with the established doctrine of the Master of the present [text].
While the doctrines of the former two masters are generally acceptable as well.
That which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is so called because the goodness of compassion cannot draw forth the wholesome fruits of humans or devas.

For example, playing chess with a compassionate heart is also subsumed under the indeterminate category of the "sphere of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*). Furthermore, there are four types of the indeterminate:

first, maturation (*vipāka*); second, the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*); third, the sphere of craftsmanship; and fourth, the fruit of liberation (*nairmāṇika*). Regarding maturation, it refers to the three... [text continues]

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that constitute the retribution of the five destinies within the realms (*dhātu*) are called "maturation" (*vipāka*) because they mature at a different time, mature as something transformed, and mature as a different category;

possessing these three meanings, they are thus termed maturation. Regarding the two types of deportment (*airyāpathika*), first is the matter of deportment, which has the four sense objects (*viṣaya*) as its nature—namely, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Second is the mind of deportment, which is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is predominant and capable of initiating deportment.

The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are by nature weak and inferior; although they take postures (*īryāpatha*) as their objects, they cannot give rise to the seventh manas-consciousness as a posture.
