However, when it further speaks of the "future" attainment, this is from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*): because the stages of cause and fruit are distinct, it is only in the future that realization occurs.
This refers precisely to the meaning of being neither identical with nor separate from [the dharmas].

The Tathāgata is not of the three periods of time because he has ultimately realized eternal abiding; whereas from the stage of the Golden Mind (*suvarṇacitta*) downward, although there is partial realization of eternity, there still remains impermanence, and thus they belong to the three periods of time.
The subsequent sutra clarifies that the nine stages of the final body (*paścima-kāya*) likewise all possess the six [perfections].
Regarding those things that possess constancy, one speaks of them in accordance with their nature.
As for those who have fully seen the future, upon reaching the stage of complete vision, this is precisely the state of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

If one is proficient in the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the fruits of the four stages (*catur-phala*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are the fruits of Bodhi; these are the ultimate fruits, as explained below in the commentary.
To further clarify: for one in a subsequent existence, both the true cause and the partial fruit belong to the three periods of time.

However, the statement that they are "visible" constitutes a difference from what was previously stated. This is distinguished by contrasting the six matters of the preceding and succeeding existences;
whereas previously it was said that the six were "slightly visible," now it is said they are "visible. To be "visible" means that one has not yet attained even slight visibility.

Regarding those who do not receive the name "Constant" (nitya): from the eighth stage down to the fifth stage, because the realization attained is inferior compared to that of the ninth stage and above, they are deprived of the name "Constant.

As for the distinction between the wholesome and unwholesome mentioned previously: from the fifth stage down to the first stage, the realization attained is again shallow and ignorance is still abundant.
Therefore it is said that the wholesome and the unwholesome are not the same; from the sixth stage upward, one attains the name of "purely wholesome," as will be explained in detail below.
The phrase "in subsequent lives" serves to distinguish this from what precedes it, thereby clarifying its meaning.
Those who have attained this through cultivation perceive the Middle Way within their respective stages.
Those who do not cultivate the unwholesome have not yet destroyed the ignorance of the higher realms;
thus, it is said that they "should also [realize] the true and the untrue. To state this fully, one should say: "They should also cultivate and attain what is true, and not cultivate what is untrue."

Regarding the statement that "losing mindfulness is unwholesome," if one refers to our own school’s system, from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Stage (*yuan-wei*) onward, one has already attained non-retrogression of mindfulness;
specifically, this applies even from the first ground (*bhūmi*). Therefore, this interpretation is incorrect.
Regarding "the objection has not yet been removed": if one wishes to remove the objection, it should be explained according to the text as annotated above.

Regarding "the sūtra definitely possesses Buddha-nature": if one says it definitely exists now but is not seen, or if one says it definitely does not exist but will certainly be attained in the future, such fixed adherence is not permitted;
this is termed a "set-aside answer" (*sthāpanīya-praśna*), which is set aside and not answered. This first [point] is a refutation.

The "rebuttal by counter-question" (*pratipraśna-vyākaraṇa*) refers to not becoming attached to a question; it is called a "set-aside answer" (*sthāpanīya-vyākaraṇa*) because one questions the meaning of the matter so as not to allow for attachment.
The Buddha used the term "not becoming attached" as a set-aside answer, which Kāśyapa challenged with a refutation.
I say that "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) means to cast away, to prohibit, and to refrain from attachment; all these are forms of setting aside what was asked.
Therefore, the answer is given simply by "setting aside," which encompasses both meanings. In the previous commentary, the Master explained the meaning separately according to two approaches;
when the general and the specific are related, the full significance becomes clear.
Regarding cause-within-cause: ignorance and afflictions are the causes within the cause; the four fruits and the ten stages are the fruits within the cause.
Furthermore, the sūtras state that the past, present, and future are likewise fruits within the cause.
"Nor is it equal" refers to the ultimate fruit.
"The two vehicles within the causal stage are themselves the three times" refers to the fruit within the causal stage.
"If [it is] great enlightenment and so forth" refers to the ultimate fruit.
The preceding passage reiterates the previous text to demonstrate the present explanation of its meaning.
"The nature of the fruit is not thus" means that because there is the fruit within the cause as well as the ultimate fruit.
"The wholesome five aggregates" refers to those that pervade both cause and fruit, namely all the wholesome qualities belonging to the four fruits and the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Regarding the statement that the five aggregates (skandhas) associated with the aspiration for Buddhahood are all causes while only the Buddha is the fruit, and that the five aggregates produced by wholesome states are themselves the nature of the fruit:
this is said in a general sense, because both the stage of partial realization and the ultimate stage—along with those of the Hīnayāna—are designated as "fruit."

In the preceding passage, the earlier text is cited below to corroborate the present meaning: that the three periods of time constitute the four fruits and the ten stages, whereas that which is not of the three periods of time is the ultimate.
"Someone" [in the following section] sets forth the interpretation of another; since the Master of the Commentary has already explained it in terms of cause and effect, we know it refers to others.
This interpretation is not appropriate.
If one were to take afflictions as the cause based on their identity with them, it is because afflictions are themselves Buddha-nature.

As for the nature of the "wholesome aggregates" (*śukla-skandha*) extending from the fruit to the cause, this is because the four fruits and the ten stages of the ultimate path are all termed "wholesome aggregates. As the Sūtra says:
Attaining the five aggregates of goodness is precisely the four fruits and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Yet, the Commentary states that they are "the fruits of the ten stages";

this is called "fruit" in relation to ordinary beings, while in relation to the Buddha, they are called "causes. As for the previous scripture stating that "fruits are also past and future," this was spoken in reference to ordinary beings.
Regarding the statement that "it exists only in the fruit," the Sūtra says: "To obtain bodhi is ultimate bodhi.
Because one attains the fruit of bodhi from the five aggregates of goodness (*kuśala-skandha*), they are called the "fruit of the aggregates" (*skandha-phala*).
It fully possesses both the fruit within the cause and the fruit of bodhi. Regarding the first dharma, the "wholesome five aggregates" are the fruit within the cause;
the fruit of bodhi is as stated in the text.

As for the phrase "like the body of sentient beings" in the sutra, the body of sentient beings is used as a metaphor for bodhi, while the semen and blood are metaphors for the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
And the wholesome aggregates (*skandha*).

The Buddha-nature mentioned in the sutras is also like this: the former four flavors are the fruit within the cause; this [Buddha-nature] is the fruit of *amṛta* (clarified butter) and *bodhi*, which does not belong to the three periods of time.
That which is combined with the present refers to the ability of afflictions to sever the roots of goodness; this combines the severing of goodness in the present with pleasant fruits.
That which must be traced to the past refers to past karma; because there was no faith in the past, one now severs the roots of goodness due to a lack of faith.
This refers precisely to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Now, regarding the subsequent explanation that resolves this objection: since it is stated that one severs the roots of goodness due to past delusions, why does the Sūtra speak of "present afflictions"?
This passage provides the explanation for that.
This corresponds to the second analogy (up to the point where it says "not producing fruit"): because if one cultivates the conditions and causes in the future, one is then able to attain the fruit;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha-nature, through causes and conditions, is able to produce [the fruit].
If one is stubbornly and rigidly attached, as if firmly holding that the true cause of Buddha-nature exists in a state of delusion without yet possessing the conditions and the wisdom,
it is like holding a lamp whose light has not yet emerged and thus cannot dispel the darkness.
If [phenomena] are merely conventional designations based on causes and conditions, then by understanding that when the future causes and conditions assemble, one will be able to see them—
just as one understands that although a lamp or the sun has not yet arrived or appeared, one must not definitively insist that they cannot dispel the darkness.
The sutra states that the future birth (*janman*) is able to produce sentient beings; however, this section of the sutra establishes two analogies:

first, the analogy of the lamp and the sun, and second, the analogy of the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The commentary (*śāstra*) explains only the analogy of the lamp, while the latter analogy is omitted, [the implication being] that within the twelve links of dependent origination, the future link of birth is able to produce sentient beings.
That which can produce the Buddha-nature is that which can produce the Buddha-nature of the first stage, the subsequent stages, and so forth.
If the sutra were to say that the five aggregates are the Buddha-nature, then if the aggregates were the nature, the nature would be within the body;
why then does it say that it is neither internal nor external?
When it is asked, "Did I not previously state in the sutra that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is the Middle Way?
this refers back to the "Lion's Roar" chapter, where the meaning of Buddha-nature as the Middle Way was explained in detail; therefore, it is being referred to here.

Regarding "not the six internal faculties" and so forth: the six internal faculties are the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*), while the six external objects are the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
These are taught to shatter the two attachments, namely, the attachment to the internal and the external.
That which is one yet three, and that which is the nature of the three virtues, means that the Middle is the nature of the Dharmakāya,
Emptiness is the nature of Prajñā, and Provisionality is the nature of Vimukti.
To possess these two meanings is to be three yet one, and one yet three.
How could there be a "middle" that is devoid of the true and the conventional? The perfectly interfused Middle Way is both negation and illumination; therefore, it possesses the two truths.

As for the omnipresence of Buddha-nature: since the Middle already encompasses the conventional, the conventional subsumes the three thousand phenomena—both principle and fact, as well as the environment and its inhabitants—leaving nothing unencompassed.
Therefore, it is said that "for this reason, the Buddha-nature reaches and pervades all.
As for the phrase "in many places," since the sources from which the discussion of pervasiveness originates are not one, they are called "many places.

Regarding the statement "it reaches these [levels] and so forth," the discussion of pervasiveness in many places constitutes a "double illumination" (shuangzhao), whereas the present statement of "double negation" (shuangfei) constitutes a "double exclusion" (shuangzhe).

One should know that although verbal expressions differ, the essence of the principle is without distinction. When various texts discuss "pervasiveness," this is precisely negation while illuminating;
when they state "neither internal nor external," this is precisely illumination while negating. Negation and illumination are identical, as is the case with the meanings of all such passages.
Furthermore, "should be dual" refers to simultaneous illumination.
As for the statement "one is still unable to calculate it, being like empty space," this means that one has not yet attained the level of the superior practitioners among the non-Buddhists;
how then could one understand the great meaning within the Perfect [Teaching]?
Regarding the phrase "the union of faculties and objects," the sutra merely states "the union of internal and external," which Jingxi explains by identifying them as the faculties and their objects.

Is it not the case that the three phrases beginning with "the identity of substance" serve to refute other teachers? If they are identical in substance, then the substance of the environment and the sentient being are one and mutually inclusive;

that is, the environment is the sentient being, and the sentient being is the environment. Since they are both one and mutually inclusive, one understands the relationship between the environment and the sentient being.

Since both [the nature and the object] are all-pervasive, one might ask: "Is it not the case that the nature is pervasive? Is it not the same as the view that the nature exists only within the bodies of sentient beings, like fruit inside a vessel?
Now, the following inquiry—based on the Sūtra’s statement that "the internal and external are conjoined"—proceeds through the faculties and their objects to interrogate and reveal that [position].

Contrary to the Sūtra, which first establishes [the four alternatives], if one were to employ "double negation" (ubhayābhāva), the following constitutes a formal refutation of those four alternatives.

First, I shall cite the double negation to dismantle it, fearing that others might see this clarification of the Middle Way as the Buddha-nature and cling to that interpretation, claiming that insentient things lack Buddha-nature because the Sūtra says they are "not the external six bases. Therefore, I now refute this by means of "not the internal."

Since these five aggregates of the self are the internal six sense organs, and it has already been stated that they are neither internal nor external, then the five aggregates of sentient beings likewise possess no Buddha-nature;

how much more so for walls and other insentient things which lack Buddha-nature? If one considers them from the perspective of dual illumination, then both the environment and its inhabitants possess [Buddha-nature].
"Alas! expresses a lamentation that serves as an exhortation; it is called "sorrowful suffering" because it pities those who are deluded and ignorant.
"Please examine carefully" below is the exhortation to clarify the intent of the sutra; the six gates are precisely the six sections on the Middle Way explained here.

Regarding the summary of this section: how could the text of this section ever be divorced from the Middle Way? Although the phrasing differs in its various explanations, the underlying principle remains eternally harmonious.

Because worldly people tend to cling to the literal meaning of the text as if it were a fixed wall, I have used this principle of mutual exclusion and illumination to unify and encompass all the passages.

Regarding the comprehensive integration of the entire period: since the principle discussed in this sutra is such that all the perfect sutras of the various schools are certainly without divergent tracks, they are nonetheless divided into five periods based on their relative emphasis on the "concurrent" (兼) and other aspects.

As for Śākyamuni’s aspiration to be equal [to the Buddhas of the past], his intent in appearing in the world was to point toward and take refuge in this very nature; thus, the path of the Buddhas is uniform across the five Buddhas.

Because there is no separate "one" that penetrates all, it is said that "principle is non-dual"; because the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching] have no distinction, it is said that "phenomena do not differ by even a hair’s breadth.

As for what was lost below, it is solely because worldly people do not understand the pervasiveness of nature (dharmatā) that they cause the Mahayana followers to vainly practice a "perfect cultivation" (pariniṣpanna-bhāvanā).
It is for this reason that he is called "Not-Light" (Adhimātra).
Śākyamuni and the others are the five Buddhas: one is Śākyamuni, and twenty directions, with the three periods of time, constitute the five.
First, regarding the two attachments mentioned at the outset, these refer to the attachments of non-Buddhists and Buddhists.

Next, concerning the four "subsequent turnings" (*paryāya*) and so forth, the sutra discusses Buddha-nature in terms of its fruition and its cultivation; however, cultivation arises from nature and fruition is attained through causes.

This is because it is precisely due to its original endowment that one can then discuss cultivation and fruition, thereby causing the principle of inherent possession to transform into actual cultivation.
One should possess each [aspect] of cultivation and possess that which is not devoid of principle; one should employ this intention to seek out the scriptural texts.

Although the Buddha-nature mentioned in the sutras exists, it is not like empty space, for while empty space is said to exist as a non-conditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta*), the Buddha-nature can actually be perceived.
The sūtra is like a lamp flame because it continues uninterruptedly from the initial flame to the subsequent flames.
Regarding the statement that "form is the Buddha-nature," this clarifies that the form outside of walls is itself the Buddha-nature. The *Jinpi* (Golden Needle) asks:
"Why is form pervasive? Because form is mind. It further states: "If it were not exclusively form, would form not be mind?"

If form and so forth do not exist, and if one were to claim that the Buddha-nature does not exist in the form of walls and such because it is form, then the form-body with its marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) would likewise lack this nature, since both are equally dharmas of form.
If both were non-existent, then sentient beings would also be non-existent; why then would it be only insentient things that are non-existent?

Regarding the second point, the "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*): the Sūtra states that this is a definitive teaching, not a dogmatic attachment; therefore, it is explained by means of provisional designation.

As for the phrase "because the mind is not equal": once one knows that curd arises from milk and thus curd exists within milk, why not likewise accept that milk arises from water-plants and thus milk exists within water-plants? Since both things would equally be inherently present, why [is there such partiality]?
To maintain that one exists while another does not is called "inequality of mind.

Regarding the statement that the four factors must harmonize, this clarifies that visual consciousness arises from four conditions; however, new sutras and treatises clarify that it arises from nine conditions, as recorded previously.
Regarding "the first [point] on different causes and different effects": because a single cause produces a single effect, it is called "different causes and different effects";
thus, it is clarified by means of a single character.
As for the phrase in the Sūtra, "departing from expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth: this refers to when milk remains for a long time and transforms into curd of its own accord, like a lion.
The Roaring Chapter.
Regarding the phrase "the sūtra requires skillful means" (*upāya*), this necessitates human effort.

As for the point that "the salt in the sūtra might also possess a subtle quality of not being salty," the intended difficulty is that since things which are not salty already possess [the potential for] salinity...

If the nature of salt is salty, should there not also be a non-salty nature? This is a mutual refutation: to refute existence by making it non-existent, and to refute non-existence by making it existent.
A scripture cannot be used in isolation; for if the salty and bitter nature of salt were used alone, people would find it unbearable to eat. If, however, [it is combined with other flavors]...
Why is it that there is a nature of blandness?
The Sūtra states that for those who do not follow skillful means, the internal [body] does not grow from the external four great elements.
As for "arising teachings based on principle," this refers to the Tathāgata’s arising of provisional and ultimate teachings based on the principle of Buddha-nature.

Second, "practice" (xi) refers to the fact that one establishes practice by receiving the teachings according to one's capacities and conditions; thus it is called "cultivating the cause. "Attainment" (cheng) refers to the fact that when practice is perfected, one realizes the principle; thus it is called "tending toward the fruit.

Third, "habituation" (xi) means that in cultivating the cause, one must habituate oneself to the perfect understanding (*yuanjie*); in tending toward the fruit, one must certainly eliminate the fetters and delusions (*jiehuo*). Therefore, these three—[cause, fruit, and habituation]—...
Regarding the classification: the first [section] corresponds to the response, while the latter two belong to the capacity of the audience.
To explain the specific intent of this treatise: since the "intent of the self" constitutes the primary meaning of the present sutra, it is explained separately.
According to the sutra, "knowing that liberation comes through killing" means knowing that one attains liberation by "killing" the mother of craving and the father of ignorance. Furthermore...

In the sūtra, the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) is used because, among the ten unwholesome actions, eight types [of wrong views] are omitted; hence it says "up to."
Regarding "knowing liberation from false views": one who knows that consciousness arises from false views and attains realization of the Right Path is said to have attained liberation.

As for "incurring immeasurable offenses," Zezhou says: King Prasenajit previously had a decree stating that anyone who committed an offense against the Buddha would be fined with their wealth confiscated by the state.

Upon hearing that [the monk] had incurred an offense, the King thought he was subject to this penalty; therefore, he requested to give him his wealth. (The character "坐" [zuò] is pronounced "cài" [cài-fuǎn] here.)

That which can be understood according to the intentions of both oneself and others is what the wise call "having a self" and also "following the self. According to the wise, this is following the other-self;
I myself also say it is following the self. Previously, when speaking according to the deluded, the illusion was said to be exclusively following the other.
The Sūtra does not state that all sentient beings definitely attain Bodhi; this is a teaching suited to those who have reached the stage of fulfillment (*yuanren*).

How could one who has attained the initial mind of fulfillment not certainly know this? Yet, while they do see it in comparison to those below, they are said not to see it in comparison to those above.
The meaning of this discourse on granting and withholding can thus be understood.
"When I have spoken thus, and you speak likewise," this mutual agreement is known as "speech according to the intentions of oneself and others.

Although it does not depart from the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), the immeasurable dharmas do not depart from these three categories, nor do these three categories depart from form (rūpa) and mind (citta).
Form is constructed by the mind; its entire substance is mind. In the practice established by our school, one can [only] take the aggregates, bases, and elements as the object.
This is where the beauty lies.

Regarding the seven types of discourse: to speak of the fruit within the cause is called "discourse on the cause" (*hetuvāda*); to speak of the cause within the fruit is called "discourse on the fruit" (*phalavāda*);

and to speak of present phenomena as being the fruit in relation to what precedes them and the cause in relation to what follows them is called "discourse on cause and fruit" (*hetuphalavāda*). These are established through the use of analogies to clarify [the meaning].

The term "dharma" refers to metaphorical speech (*upacāra-vāk*), which provisionally employs worldly conventions; it should not be considered a substantial entity, yet it is used to manifest the names of all phenomena.

This is called "conformable speech" (*anuvāda-vāk*), as it follows worldly distribution by employing names such as "man" or "woman. "Worldly-distributed speech" (*loka-prasiddha-vāk*) consists of what is proclaimed so as to transform the minds of other sentient beings according to one's own intent;
this is called "wish-fulfilling speech" (*yathā-ruci-vāk*). Although there are seven types of speech, here we clarify them primarily by means of the last one.
The intention of teaching "nature" (dhātu) for the sake of [understanding] birth is as follows:
when the sūtra speaks of the present six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) and contact (sparśa) as causes, it means that the present six bases and contact are the results of past karma;
furthermore, the karma currently being performed serves as the cause for the future. This is termed the "language of cause and effect."
The Sūtras state that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature (up to the point regarding those who are not heedless). The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:

"Because sentient beings give rise to a sense of cowardice within themselves, thinking they lack the nature [of Buddhahood] and thus sever their portion [of attainment], seeking nothing further, it is said that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. The meaning is the same as this.

First, regarding "non-existence" (wu suo you): because one realizes the principle of the true emptiness of the Dharma-body, external attributes such as powers, fearlessnesses, and the marks and signs of excellence are seen as being truly identical with the ultimate reality;
thus it is said that there is "non-existence," meaning that what was previously called by name has no abiding locus and is therefore non-existent.

Next, regarding "existence of non-existence" (you suo wu): this refers to that which is unwholesome or indeterminate, which existed in the past but is now absent; thus it is called the "existence of non-existence."

Furthermore, the former [of the two] reveals what is accomplished through the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while the latter clarifies what is abandoned through the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Regarding the statement "the icchantika indeed possesses [it]," etc., this is a discussion of the mutual presence or absence of cultivated good and cultivated evil;
it is like the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) that follows, which is why it is marked with "etc. (*yathā... tathā*).

Regarding the passage from "The sutra says sentient beings do not understand" to "their own intentional language": because sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) cling to partiality and doubt the perfect [teaching], it is said that they do not understand.

Regarding the passage from "The sutra says those in their final birth" to "are unable to understand": if one considers the final birth of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings, or the path of teaching and practice according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), then...
It has already been explained that those from the first stage upward, though they understand the teachings and the path, are still deluded regarding perfect enlightenment;

if viewed from the perspective of ultimate realization, even those in the final stage of the Perfect Teaching (Vairocana-nyorai) are said to be "not yet understanding," and all from the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) downward are termed "other bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, "shallow people" refers to those of the Two Vehicles and other bodhisattvas.

"Distinctions within the conventional truth" refers to the differences in the karma, conduct, causes, and effects of the ten dharma-realms within the conventional truths of the Separate and Complete Teachings;
thus, these are not understood by those of the Two Vehicles.

The manifestation of the physical body for the sake of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is a trace of transformation that is immeasurable and inconceivable; therefore, it cannot be understood by those of the Two Vehicles.
As stated in the preceding passage: "Manifesting illness is the realm of the Buddha, not something known by the Two Vehicles"—this is precisely such an example.

Regarding the point that there is something else related here: this refers to the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), which, among its elucidation of the seven kinds of two truths (*satyadvaya*), cites this scriptural passage to clarify the two truths of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*).
Thus, that text states: "Illusory existence and non-conditioned [reality] constitute the conventional;

neither being nor non-being constitutes the ultimate. This is because existence and non-existence are dual, and thus they form the conventional; the Middle Way, which is neither being nor non-being and is non-dual, is the ultimate. Duality is the conventional; non-duality is the ultimate.
Because those who hear this do not understand both the ultimate and the conventional truths, they are like the deaf and mute; as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"When I and Maitreya discussed the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the five hundred śrāvakas thought we were speaking of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)"—this is precisely that meaning.
As for its chronological period, it may belong to the *Avataṃsaka* or be common to both of the two "milk" periods (*kṣīra*).

Regarding the nature of the objective realm (*viṣaya-svabhāva*): even that which is evil and perverse and yet capable of being the object of the Buddha’s contemplation does not possess so much as a hair’s breadth of wisdom; this is called the nature of the objective realm.
Regarding the nature of the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu-svabhāva*): the revealing cause reveals all wholesome qualities; this is called the nature of the revealing cause.
That which is also called the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) refers to the aforementioned myriad wholesome deeds.
Alternatively, "the nature of sentient beings" refers to the nature of sentient beings as the conjunction of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Regarding the statement that "both possess the indeterminate nature of the five aggregates": since the body, which is the fruit of the aggregates, has already repaid past causes, it is therefore indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The manifestation of the wholesome and unwholesome that can act as causes for future lives is called the "wholesome and unwholesome aggregates" (*skandha*). This means that while the cause encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding the phrase "the words differ but the meaning is the same," the intent of the three sentences is identical; their significance is evident. As for the term "co-existent" (*sahabhū*), it is what was formerly referred to as "conjoined" (*ping*).

Question: There is the nature of correctness (samyaktva-niyāma) or the nature of sentient beings; how is it that this is now said to be identical to the nature of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) which are indeterminate (avyākṛta)?

Answer: The five aggregates are themselves Buddha-nature; is this not the direct cause (hetu)? Since the union of form (rūpa) and mind (citta) constitutes a sentient being, one knows that the meaning is the same as the traditional explanation.
Regarding the "one sentence up to seven sentences," this refers generally to the collective explanation of the current major section on the Middle Way, which consists of five parts in total:
first, one sentence; second, two sentences; third, three sentences; fourth, four sentences; and fifth, seven sentences. Therefore, it is said:
"from one sentence up to seven sentences."

Regarding the claim that the speech of both self and others is both existent and non-existent: it is called "non-existent" because the icchantika does not currently possess Buddha-nature, and it is called "existent" because they will certainly attain it in the future.
This interpretation by the ancients cannot be adopted, as the distinction between the cultivated (xiū) and the innate (xìng) aspects of good and evil resolves this "both-and" position;
since the doctrine of the cultivated and innate aspects of good and evil constitutes the present school's tenet, the seven types of sentient beings are discussed in the following section.
Each has its own side: the virtuous person has the side of goodness, while the icchantika has the side of evil; because these two are contrasted with one another, they are said to "both exist.
The same applies to their mutual non-existence; they exist only in relation to conditions.

"Attaining non-attainment" refers to the fact that those with deluded minds who grasp at attainment are said to "have attainment," while those with faith in the principle and realization of the mind are said to "have non-attainment.
Thus, as explained above, these two types of persons are contrasted to clarify how they both possess [these qualities] and so forth.
Regarding those within the principle alone, both Sunakṣatra and Rāhula were treated as ordinary persons; yet internally, they had already realized the principle.
As for the two modes of transformation—conformity and opposition—Sunakṣatra was transformed through opposition, while Rāhula was transformed through conformity.

That they all reside within the Ganges signifies that they equally possess the nature of the true cause (*tathāgatagarbha*).

As for the fact that the Buddha-nature is one, it is like the seven classes [of fish] which, though different, dwell together in a single river.
Regarding the *timitimiṅgila*: "ti" is pronounced "di" in the *Cangyin* (Sounds of the Cang Dictionary) with a low tone; "mi" is pronounced "mi";
the full term is *Timitimiṅgila*, which means "large-bodied fish. There are four species of this fish, and this is the fourth, the smallest.

Regarding the "concordance of analogies" (*paryāya-yukti*): this refers to the two types of analogies, general and specific, within the concordance itself.
In the latter part of the preceding chapter, differences are distinguished in contrast to the former.

Although the Sūtra states that those who have attained liberation are still mixed with afflictions, it is the realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth that constitutes their liberation.
Although the sutras state that the Buddha-nature exists within sentient beings, it does not necessarily mean that it is present in all of them without exception.

"Seeking only true benefit" refers to seeking bodhi.

The intended meaning here should be understood according to the sixth fascicle of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), which cites Dharmatrāta as saying that the six divisions [of the canon] are not believed in.
"Mutual non-communication" means that the *kṣudraka* lacks the *vaipulya*, while the *mahā* lacks the *praśna-vyākaraṇa*, *avadāna*, *ityuktaka*, *jātaka*, and *adbhuta-dharma*;

one merely believes in these six divisions. "Mutual communication" refers to the *sūtra*, *geya*, *gāthā*, *ityuktaka*, *jātaka*, and *adbhuta-dharma*, which, when applied to the present text, accord perfectly with reason.
The *Jingwan shou* (Skt. *Kāṅkṣāhasta*) bhikṣu [so named because] his hands were clasped; the meaning of this name is not yet detailed.

Regarding the "five expedients" (*pañca-upāya*) and the "thirty minds" (*triṃśac-citta*): in the Hīnayāna, the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) constitute one, while the four stages such as "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) and so forth constitute the five expedients.
In the Mahāyāna, the stages of practice—namely, the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the ten directions (*daśa-pratipatti*)—constitute the thirty minds.
Both are mundane ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the "seven stages of expedient means" (*saptavidha-upāya*), these are the seven [stages] of the Hīnayāna;

by adding five more to the five [previously mentioned], one further divides the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) into two—namely, general mindfulness and specific mindfulness—thus making seven.

Regarding those who penetrate the thirty minds, if we explain this according to the distinct stages: the stages of practice (caryā-bhūmi) and abiding (vihāra-bhūmi) correspond to the four levels of expedient means (prayoga-mārga), while the ten dedications (daśa-pariṇāmanā) correspond to the stage of supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma).
As for the phrase "due to the second [mind] and so forth," it means that the person of the second mind is used as a condition.
The interpretation that he "still remains as if in his original state" is correct.

Although the Elder Tiṣya (刁長者) leaped like a bird, he still remained in this life because he still possessed a body as the basis for suffering; therefore, he had not yet crossed over from birth and death.

Those who do not see this principle fail to recognize that within the principle there is a distinction between the "true" and the "middle. They hold that the nirvana of partial truth is not the Buddha-nature, while the middle-way nirvana is the Buddha-nature.
Since these three types of people have not yet seen the middle way, how could they see their nature?

Furthermore, if those who have not equally attained nirvāṇa are analogous to the case where the Buddha-nature is either seen or not seen, then it should likewise follow that there are cases where nirvāṇa is attained and cases where it is not.
Why, then, does the preceding text state that these four people equally constitute the seventh group who have reached the shore?
The phrase "there are differences in nirvana" refers to the distinctions within the ultimate truth (*tathatā*).
The phrase "birth and death are not the same" refers to the distinction between the two types: *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative).

Furthermore, the "seven persons of the Hīnayāna" results from expanding the four [śrāvaka fruits] into seven; that is, the śrāvakas are expanded into the four fruits, together with the pratyekabuddha.

Because the Bodhisattva is a Buddha, he knows that there are seven [aspects]; this knowledge of the preceding [passage] clarifies that *nirvāṇa* is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*).
Therefore, the *Śāstra* is cited to establish this shared meaning.

Regarding the mutual citation of the Shared and Distinct [teachings]: the present discussion of the river of *nirvāṇa* concerns the meaning of the Shared Teaching, whereas the previous discussion of the river of birth-and-death concerned the Distinct Teaching.
The meaning of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) arises solely because this present sutra applies the four teachings once again; thus, it is said to accord with the capacities of the four *siddhāntas*.

While the previous [teachings] spoke of the Common [Teaching], the present one clarifies the Separate [Teaching]; furthermore, because it ultimately converges back to the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), it differs from the preceding sections.
The Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues, Scroll Eighteen.
The Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues, Scroll Nineteen.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang.
The third section of the Kāśyapa Chapter:

Regarding the impurity as the causal condition for the preliminary practice of mindfulness of heat (*uṣmagata*). Impurity is the skillful means of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), while the causal condition is the skillful means of the dharma of heat.
Thus, one should know that when opened they constitute four dharmas, yet when combined they remain two; this refers to the causal condition of impurity.
It is not among the two [methods] within the five *sthāpanā* (meditative stabilizations).

As for the "gateways of crossing" (*taramukha*), they are so named because impurity, loving-kindness and compassion, and mindfulness of breathing serve as antidotes to greed, anger, and discursive thought,
thereby enabling one to enter into the principle.

Thus, for those who rely on the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, the "earth-holding" (*dharaṇī*) is as described; however, according to the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, there is no contemplation of the analysis of the eighteen realms (*dhātu-vibhaṅga*), and instead, mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is added to form the five methods of mental abiding (*pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*).

Since the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) has already been destroyed through the contemplation of the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) across the two periods of time within that [latter] method, the mention here of the "eighteen realms" refers specifically to the contemplation of the analysis of the realms. Nevertheless, the intent of this present sūtra does not concern these five methods of mental abiding.

Regarding the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), there are generally four types distinguished by being "deep in total but shallow in particulars": (1) both object and contemplation are distinct; (2) the object is distinct while the contemplation is general;

(3) the object is general while the contemplation is distinct; and (4) both object and contemplation are general. Of these, the first is shallow because one has not yet attained mastery; the latter three are [deeper].
Because it gradually matures to a deep degree, its explanation is as found in other texts.

Regarding the "attainment of the realization of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-adhimukti*): once the contemplation of the *uṣmagata* stage has been accomplished, the presence of a portion of the untainted (*anāsrava*) element is termed the "realization of emptiness at the *uṣmagata* stage.
The Sūtra itself explains this by saying: "It is like drilling for fire; first there is the heat of the smoke."
Regarding the "one lifespan, two faculties, and three consciousnesses," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that at the stage of the *kalala*, there are already these three things:

1. **Life-span (*āyus*)**: This refers to inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*). 2. **Warmth (*uṣman*)**: This is called warmth because it is sustained by the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) through karma;

thus, the physical matter (*rūpa*) of the earth, water, and other elements does not become putrid or decay. 3. **Consciousness (*vijñāna*)**: This refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) within this [embryo]. Thus, it is called consciousness.
This is the momentary cognition that knows [the mind]; it is the conjunction of the three factors which, from birth until growth, neither increases nor decreases.
The statement that "all sentient beings must first possess *uṣman*" is a challenge based on the identity of names.

Regarding what you have cited as being equivalent: you take the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) of sentient beings as heat, whereas I take the semblance-understanding (*nirbhāsa-buddhi*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*) as heat;
therefore, it is said that this is not my teaching.
As for the objection regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): desire is a distracted state of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
Regarding the contemplation of the six aspects: within the factors of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) of the first dhyāna, one becomes weary of and detached from them.

One regards the first dhyāna as suffering, coarse, and an obstacle, because these two factors disturb the concentrated mind; it is "suffering" because they arise from [the need for] joy and bliss, and "coarse" because these two factors obscure the higher concentrations and thus act as an obstacle.

The second dhyāna differs from this and is therefore called "excellent," "sublime," and "emerging. If one proceeds to the third dhyāna, the same principle as applied to the first may be followed by analogy.
One perceives the sixteen truths as previously seen.

Since the afflictions have not yet been abandoned, this stage of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) contemplation is still at the level of semblance (*sabhāga*); it should not be explained by means of the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), such as the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Regarding the second major section, "The General and the Particular," this refers to the analytical text of the preceding passage. Since the meaning encompasses both directions, it is divided accordingly.
Because the self-nature of the *uṣmagata* (heat) stage is not derived from another, the essence of heat is wisdom (*prajñā*); the nature of wisdom is heat. It is not that they are identical.

At that time, there was further discussion regarding the cause of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*). When the subsequent scripture speaks of "warmth," it refers to the characteristic of the fire of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
[Objection: If this is due to another, how can it be said not to be due to another's warmth? [Response: The explanation is as follows: the dharma of warmth has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.
The essence of wisdom is called "warmth" because it is caused by the fire of the Noble Ones; it is not called "warmth" simply because it is caused by another's warmth.
The name "Heated" (Tāpana) does not mean that it is caused by another;
rather, it means that one naturally attains this retribution of form because one has cultivated the cause of the untainted (anāsrava), and not because one sought birth in this heaven.
Thus it is said that one does not cultivate untainted karma for the sake of receiving a body, for by so doing, one will necessarily transcend birth and death.
It is said that the extinction of retribution occurs when an Anāgāmin is still born in the Form Realm; how then could the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) extinguish retribution?

It is simply because, looking toward the future until the time one attains Arhatship, [the retribution] will necessarily be extinguished along with everything else; therefore it is said that this is the extinction of retribution.

Furthermore, when one contemplates the retribution of the Form Realm through this dharma of "Heat," realizing its impermanence and so forth, and thus possesses a mind free from grasping, it is then called the extinction of retribution. As the sutra below states:
Because of craving one undergoes rebirth, and because of aversion one practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

As for the claim that only those established in the meditative concentration of form (*rūpa-dhyāna*) obtain retribution, this means that although one obtains the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma by relying on the concentration of form, the retribution is obtained through the concentration itself and not through the heat dharma;
for the contemplation of the sixteen truths does not serve as the cause for existence.
If one discusses the method, it refers to the sequence of practice. As for "merely the real dharma" (*vastu-dharma*):
in this initial stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one has not yet been able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, it is called "the real dharma.

Since this is at the very beginning, there is no prior concentration with which it could be continuous; therefore, it is said that "one does not yet rely on provisional designations" (*prajñapti*). "Does not yet rely" means...
This is because the latter must necessarily form a continuous series with the first category.
As for "drawing forth the first dhyāna," it means that the ninth category of the desire realm induces one category of the first dhyāna,
thereby jointly suppressing the afflictions of the ninth category of the desire realm along with the concentration of the desire realm itself.
Those who take the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as their basis can only sever the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);
because this stage is still with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and cannot produce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the nine grades of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself are not taken.
Rather, they are combined as one to complete the preceding count.

The citation of Āṛaḍa is intended to demonstrate that there are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who attain this meditative absorption; thus, including those in the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the total reaches seventy-three people.

Regarding the "obstacles to the future," when one attains the concentration of the future, the obstacles consisting of the body, bedding, and so forth are destroyed; therefore, it is called "the future."

This concentration has already abandoned desire for the Desire Realm and is directed toward the future First Dhyāna; therefore, it is called "future" (*anāgāmin*) and is also termed "not yet arrived" (*anāgamya*).
As for the "obstacle," it refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

According to the second interpretation, this master clarifies that the future concentration does not merely cease desire for the Desire Realm, but has already abandoned [desire] while still being at the stage prior to the First Dhyāna.
Reaching the second dhyāna, it is also called "future" (anāgāmin), and this applies to all stages from the third dhyāna upward; thus, the future concentration exists at every stage.

However, these views differ according to the various sectarian tenets: some say that the future [concentration] resides only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while others say that the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) exists in all four dhyānas;
still others say that the future [concentration] pervades all dhyānas. Therefore, let the Master [of the school] cite [the appropriate authority].
The application is different.

If you claim that the meaning of the text is not so, how can it be that—since five types of persons are listed in the text—one takes only those from the stage of "patience with suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) onwards?
As for the "one summit" (*mūrdhan*) and so forth: although this sutra clarifies the stages of practice of the Hīnayāna, they all ultimately return to the Buddha-nature. Thus one treads [the path].

Regarding the statement that "practice follows speech," while understanding is perfected, cultivation proceeds gradually; the stages of subduing and severing, such as the meanings of the Summits (*mūrdhan*) and Patience (*kṣānti*), cannot be explained in detail here as they are identical to those of the Hīnayāna.
These matters are already set forth in detail in the *Wēixuánjì* (Record of Analyzing the Profundities) according to other schools; students are requested to seek them there.

It is solely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), because during the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), when one first begins to practice contemplation and subsequently the contemplation increases, it is called the "summit" (*mūrdhan*);
since the practice of contemplation is superior to what preceded it, it is the aggregate of formations.

It cannot be avoided that what is covered by the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) consists of the determinate, the collective, and the unmanifest; the mind-king is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha);

the enumeration of feelings is the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha); the enumeration of perceptions is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha); and all other mental factors are called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
Contemplating the Four Truths is equivalent to contemplating the four directions.

Regarding the attainment of the "lowest stage of the supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), because different versions of the sutra text state either the "five faculties" (*pañcendriya*) or the "five aggregates" (*pañcaskandha*),
both interpretations are preserved as they each possess their own logical validity.
Regarding the most profound and supreme: the seven types of persons in the world who possess the stages of expedient means are all mundane because they are characterized by outflows (*āsrava*);
this seventh person is called "foremost" because he is the most excellent among those in the world.
Furthermore, regarding the term "aggregate" (*skandha*), its meaning is as explained previously in the *Dingfa ji* (Record of the Summit Dharma).
That which takes one truth as its object is the true emptiness realized through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); therefore, it is said that one attains the "Hall of True Equality.
It is also called "observing the four directions," because by observing the Four Noble Truths, one realizes true emptiness; thus, although it takes only one truth as its object, [it is so named].
They are called the four directions.

Regarding the eighty-eight [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*): because they can be severed by the vision of the truths, they are termed "afflictions of vision" (*darśana-heya*).

There are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) in total; when analyzed according to the three realms and the four truths, there are eighty-eight. As the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "In the stage of suffering, one is fully present..."
Having collectively gathered and eliminated the three views, and having removed the two views that do not function in the upper realms due to the absence of anger,
I shall now explain this again by means of a seven-character verse so that the names and meanings may be easily understood.
The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are fully present within the Truth of Suffering; the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises solely from the object of suffering.
Ignorance, karma, and the outflowing causes constitute the Truth of Origination; the essence of cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and an untainted fruit (*anāsrava-phala*).
Neither of these are objects of perception for the view of a self-identity, nor for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), nor for the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
These two do not arise even as they follow the body; therefore, the origin and cessation [of suffering] eliminate the three views.
Since the Truth of the Path is fundamentally the cause for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the view of self and extreme views likewise do not arise.
Once wrong view has already negated the Noble Path, the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) subsequently arises in accordance with that wrong view.
Grasping what is not the path as the true path—therefore, within the Truth of the Path, there is only the exclusion of the two [graspings of] accumulation and cessation.
Although wrong view exists, it merely negates the two truths;
it cannot conceive of what is not the path as being the path. Therefore, there is no grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The four truths possess afflictions that are either proximate or remote. Regarding the truth of suffering, there are three remote [afflictions] and seven proximate ones.

Grasping at self and what belongs to self constitutes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). From this view of identity, one calculates permanence or annihilation, which is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Denying the law of cause and effect is the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Grasping the inferior as superior is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Prohibiting the grasping of what is not a cause as being a cause; doubt is hesitation and indecisiveness;
ignorance is delusion and darkness because of a lack of understanding. These all arise based on the object of suffering;
therefore, these seven afflictions are called "intimate delusions. Greed, hatred, and pride—these three types of afflictions...
They do not arise from the objective sphere of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); rather, they are produced by taking the aforementioned seven as their object.

For this reason, they are also called "afflictions that take [the primary] afflictions as their object" (*paryavasthāna*). Greed has the nature of craving and attachment; pride has the nature of haughtiness;
and hatred has the nature of malice and resentment. All of these arise by taking the aforementioned seven afflictions as their objects.
Therefore, three are designated as "distant" delusions: The collection [of suffering] consists of the four [afflictions], while the three types of "distant" ones are:
Doubt regarding the cause, which is the denial of accumulation through wrong view; And attachment to inferior views, which is the confusion of ignorance.
The names of these three distant [delusions] are also as stated before. Greed and the others, however, arise based on the four [objects].
When [the truths] are extinguished, three are immediate and four are remote. Regarding "remote," the first three are added with the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
because one clings to what is inferior as being superior, the grasping at views is treated as immediate.
Now, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is a supreme and wondrous dharma; it cannot be further described as inferior and then superior.
Arising solely from the back of wrong view, the grasping of the inferior as superior is called the "view of attachment to views.
Therefore, regarding the Truth of Cessation, there are four indirect [afflictions], while the direct and indirect modes of activity are all as previously described.
Regarding the Path, there are eight [afflictions]: three are direct and five are indirect; the direct ones are doubt, delusion, and wrong view.
Compared to the preceding [factors], the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is added to the remote factors.

Since the fruit of the outflows is not the untainted path, yet one falsely clings to it as cause and fruit, there is a proximate condition for the origin of suffering consisting of precepts and observances; whereas the Truth of the Path is the true cause and the true path.
One cannot take as an object that which is not a cause or the Path;

since it arises only by taking wrong view as its object, the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is classified among the remote factors. Both the Path and Cessation are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas;
[the attachment to them] is not a case of grasping the inferior as superior. The attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is the same as before and is also classified as remote.
These arise solely from wrong views and constitute their grasping. In the higher realms, with the single exception of hatred (*dveṣa*), all other aspects of these formations are identical.

There are ten types of "thought-constructions" (*vitarka*); because one enters the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to sever these delusions, they are called "delusions of thought" (*vitarkakleśa*), and are also termed "cultivation-delusions" (*bhāvanākileśa*).

Because the delusions are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) common to the three realms. In the desire realm there are four: namely, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), ignorance (*moha*), and pride (*māna*).
In each of the two upper realms there are three, because hatred is absent; thus, three in each makes six, and together with the four [of the desire realm], they total ten.

Question: Why is there no doubt (*vicikitsā*) among those abandoned through cultivation? Answer: Since it has already been abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no longer any doubt regarding the principle.
The "forty-li water" refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which are vast and pervasive throughout the three realms, arising as attachments wherever they encounter objects;
thus, forty li is used as a metaphor. The Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) are set against these forty li because the delusions of view arise based upon the Four Truths.

Since the active outbursts of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) do not obstruct the principle of the Truths and do not arise perversely, they are slight and easy to sever, like a single drop of water.
The *Anupada-sūtra* (or *Dīgha Nikāya*, Sutta 33) has not yet been examined.
As for "that which can encompass all": because these three fetters (*saṃyojana*) give rise to the increase of delusion, they are able to universally encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Specifically, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) gives rise to the sixty-two [wrong] views; the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) gives rise to all ascetic practices (*duṣkaracaryā*); and doubt (*vicikitsā*) arises regarding all things in the past and future.
Because of doubt, these three are able to encompass all [defilements].
As for those that arise constantly, this explanation below applies generally to all sentient beings to clarify the three fetters; it does not pertain exclusively to non-Buddhists.

"Those who constantly maintain the notion of a self" refers to all sentient beings who grasp at the aggregates (*skandhas*) to form a body and perpetually establish a sovereign controller; therefore, it is said they "constantly maintain the notion of a self.
"All believe in heterodox deities" means that apart from the Buddha, everything else is termed a heterodox deity.
Next, regarding "difficult to recognize": it is not only difficult to recognize [the afflictions] in others; even those arising within one's own mind are not easily recognized.

As for the sutra stating that [afflictions] can serve as the cause for all defilements, this refers specifically to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which gives rise to the sixty-two [wrong views] and so forth, as previously explained.
Third, regarding the antidote to the enemy: "enemy" (dveṣa) signifies the act of harming; these three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are able to harm the three categories [of wholesome dharmas].

As for the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) being contrary to right wisdom (*samyagprajñā*): right wisdom realizes that persons and phenomena are fundamentally empty, whereas the view of self falsely establishes a sovereign master;
thus, it is contrary to right wisdom. The *Zhi guan fu xing* (Sub-commentary on the Calming and Contemplation) further states: "These three samādhis are the proximate antidotes to doubt."
This signless samādhi is the proximate antidote to the view of a self; this emptiness samādhi is the proximate antidote to the clinging to precepts and observances;
and this wishless samādhi is the proximate antidote to [the aforementioned] dharmas.

Because it is intended to lead those of limited capacity, [the teaching] is abbreviated; whereas in the extensive version there are eighty-eight *anuśayas*, and in the intermediate version twenty, while here the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abbreviated to three fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Since this is addressed to those of limited capacity, it speaks of the three fetters; yet even when providing pleasure through the extensive and intermediate versions, how could one not speak of them?

The "five faculties with faith as the foremost" refers to faith, diligence, and so forth; these are spoken of in terms of the horizontal classification of stages within the path (mārga-bhūmi). Thus, there are five faculties.
If classified vertically according to the sequence of stages, these are the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga).

Regarding "taking the three poisons as internal," this refers to the dullness within what is otherwise sharp; it does not refer to the three poisons within the context of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Next, the second part explains the term "flowing against the current" (*pratisrota*); the division of the sūtra should proceed from the phrase "furthermore, there must be...

[and so on], while the structural outline of the commentary follows for the sake of convenience. Question: *Srotāpanna* is a Sanskrit term; how can it be explained using terms such as "untainted" (*anāsrava*) and "cultivation"?
Answer: The general name *srotāpanna* contains various specific meanings. Translators have retained the general term in its Sanskrit form while following the Chinese for the specific meanings;
all such cases follow this principle. Regarding the phrase "because it is first attained":
it refers to the initial realization of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state and the initial reversal of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), even though [these states] may also occur later.

Since the realization also proceeds in reverse and is established as a distinct name based on a new meaning, it is said that one who has attained this "subsequently acquired" [realization] is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.

Regarding the phrase "having crossed once": "old" refers to the former state and "guest" refers to the latter state; this is explained by analogy with each stage, just as "Srotāpanna" is the old name and "Sakṛdāgāmin" is the guest name.
Therefore, although the second fruit also involves flowing against the stream, it is established as the "Once-returner" because one newly attains the state of coming back once more.
Alternative designations:
According to the Sūtra, there are two, namely liberation (*vimukti*) and nirvāṇa. Liberation is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while nirvāṇa is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Regarding the higher name being applied to the lower: although the name applies to the lower level, the distinction between delusion and awakening remains absolute; for one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) seeks the two types of wisdom.

Because "bodhi" (awakening) and "bodhisattva" share the same meaning of "seeking the supreme," they are called *bodhisattvas*; because "bodhi" and "buddha" share the same meaning of "awakened knowledge," he is called a "Buddha.
This is based on the identity of their meanings and does not refer to the equality of their underlying principle; nevertheless, it is used as a subtle indication to accommodate those of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the phrase "attaining perfect awakening through the vision of the path and so forth": it means that by correctly contemplating the principles of the truths (*satya*), one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding "perfectly awakening to cause and effect": it means being able to fully realize the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-phala*), the cause of its origination (*samudaya-hetu*), the fruit of cessation (*nirodha-phala*), and the cause of the path (*mārga-hetu*).

The noble practices observed by the Perfectly Awakened One, both those shared with others and those not shared, are viewed in relation to the aggregates (*skandha*) as being "shared" and in relation to the truths (*satya*) as being "unshared.
Because the meanings of their respective modes of practice within the four truths differ, they are called "unshared."
Regarding the first three truths, each and every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*) therein is said to be "common" because they all pertain to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

As for those who have slightly diminished their cycle of birth and death but lack the capacity for transcendence— those of dull faculties— this refers to those whose [defilements] have been reduced to six, five, or fewer, all of whom are included within the category of dull faculties.

One should not call [the practitioner before this stage] a "candidate" (pratipannaka). If it is said that one who first attains the Path is immediately called a Srotāpanna, for what reason are the first fifteen moments of mind still called a "candidate," while only at the sixteenth moment of mind is one called the "first fruit"?
Regarding the phrase "since it is the first fruit" and so forth: this objection is based on the notion of being the first attainment.

If one were to be called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) simply because of attaining [the fruit] for the first time, then non-Buddhist practitioners who have suppressed their afflictions and turned from the heterodox to the orthodox would also attain the third fruit for the first time; since they too attain it for the first time, they should likewise be called *srotāpannas*.

At that time, although the Buddha’s intention was to state that one who has attained the Dharma from the outset is called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) without yet discussing the person, he had not yet answered regarding those who are candidates for the three higher fruits; therefore, Kāśyapa subsequently raised another question.
The statement that "one also possesses the eight knowledges and sixteen modes of activity" is likewise based on the objection concerning the *sautkrāntika* (leap-over) *anāgāmin*.
When the Buddha replied with "the two kinds," etc., the sutra specifically addresses the *anupūrvaka* (gradual) *anāgāmin* to explain the meaning of the *srotāpanna* as the first fruit;
it does not discuss the *sautkrāntika* *anāgāmin* at all, because the latter does not follow the sequence of constant practice.
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is "semblance-understanding" (*tadākāra-jñāna*), referring to the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*);

that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is "true understanding" (*bhūta-jñāna*), referring to those from the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) upward. Regarding the one Abhidharma master: his interpretation is utterly irrational; while simultaneously observing what is correct, he instead says it is not.
The intention of this master is that viewing the single truth collectively does not apply to the others;
however, since viewing the sixteen truths collectively involves all four truths individually, it is ultimately unsatisfactory to call them "unshared."

The first three preparatory practices—namely, the stabilization of the mind and the general and specific applications of mindfulness—are shared [with the lower stages], because they still belong to the stage of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained semblance-understanding (*pratirūpaka-adhimukti*).

As for the latter four preparatory practices—namely, the four semblances of understanding such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth—they are no longer shared with external worldlings because semblance-understanding has already become manifest; therefore, it is said [that they are not shared].
It is not shared.

If one first correctly interprets the scriptural passage on abandoning the sixteen shared [factors] and attaining the unshared [factors], this refers to a practitioner following the gradual path who abandons the stage of an external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and enters the stage of an internal ordinary person;
this is called "abandoning the shared and attaining the unshared," and it is still within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*).
In the mind, one abandons them successively.
If one were to skip the lower stages—as is the case for those who attain *anāgāmin* by leaping over stages—it would not be thus; this is because it refers to those who practice by leaping.

However, one must cultivate only the latter four [stages], because within the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there are no such things as the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage and the others; therefore, they must be cultivated.
Since the defilements of the eighth stage have already been subdued, one enters the path of seeing and immediately realizes the three fruits.
The preceding [passage] explains the abandonment of the eight knowledges of the candidate and the fruit; this [passage] explains the attainment of the eight knowledges of the fruit.
Therefore, it is said that one who abandons the path and attains the fruit abandons fifteen minds and acquires sixteen minds.
This is not the case for the Anāgāmin explained below in the sutra;

because this sentence is a double conclusion regarding the two preceding categories—the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—I shall now follow the two texts and explain the passage by restating the terms.
All those who pass through the center do so with the swiftness of the untainted mind; yet, although they pass through the center, they do not grasp the fruit.
It is like a person with supernormal powers who flies through the air: though their speed is swift, the distance traveled is not without measure.
This is inconvenient because the Sūtra states that for an Anāgāmin it is not so;

if one were to interpret it as previously explained, then one would be abandoning the previous stage to attain the fruit, which would be identical to the case of a Srotāpanna—how then could such a person be one who has "leaped over"?

That [interpretation] is also inferior to this one; since its numerical meaning does not accord with the sūtra, the Master [Vasubandhu] provided a further explanation, first interpreting it according to the sequential order by correlating the first fruit with the third fruit.

Regarding the fact that the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is necessarily so: because there is no fruit prior to the first fruit, one must necessarily abandon the stage of the candidate (*pratipannaka*) to attain the fruit.
It is not so for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*); for the non-returner not only abandons the candidate stage to attain the fruit, but also abandons the fruit to attain the fruit.
This is because prior to the three fruits, there are two fruits.
If one skips the lower [fruit], it is explained by contrasting the person who transcends with the person who follows the sequential order.

"The transcender is likewise" means that upon entering the sixteen moments of mind, one immediately attains the three fruits; thus, it is still a case of abandoning the candidate stage and attaining the fruit.

As for the result (*phala*): since the subsequent section of the sūtra cites it to provide a concluding demonstration—because there are two different types of persons, those who transcend the stages and those who follow the sequence—the sūtra states, "it is not thus.
However, this interpretation is quite circuitous and is no better than the objection raised earlier by the master of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*), who said that such an explanation is inconvenient.
The statement is not false.
Each has its own "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) [knowledge] because there is *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) regarding each of the four truths of the desire realm; thus it is called "direct.
Each has its own "inferential" (*anumāna*) [knowledge] regarding the four truths of the two upper realms; thus it is called "inferential."

Of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), eight are excluded—namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-, samudaya-, nirodha-, mārga-jñāna*), along with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Thus, there are ten.
As for the fruit, it consists of only one knowledge; specifically, the knowledge of the path-category (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) is taken as the first fruit, being the sixteenth moment of mind.
The time of practicing skillful means while fully traversing the sixteen [stages] refers to the stage of the inner ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
If one follows this precedent, then since the four stages of approach (pratipannaka) belong to the three fruits of realization, the two stages of approach should likewise belong to the first fruit.
Regarding the clarification of the "Correct Position" (samyaktva-niyāma): the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) is the beginning of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the distinction between the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*): the first fruit is the very first realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*).

The two stages of "entering toward" (*pratipannaka*) involve repeated contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and thus are not included within the first fruit. The four delusions consist of the three poisons plus pride; in the two stages of entering toward, five grades of these delusions are severed.
The abandonment of the two fruits of delusion and the abandonment of the six and three stages toward the eight [stages] all pertain to the four delusions of the desire realm.
Accordingly, one should ask below: "If there are ten delusions of view and [ten] of cultivation, why are there only four?"
In explaining the lower [view] through reflection, it is because at the time of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*), the five views and doubt are all previously abandoned;
although residual traces remain, they are subsumed within pride (*māna*). Thus, there are only four [defilements] in reflection.
As for Piliṅga having the habit of pride due to his past life as a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), how could the five views and doubt not be included within pride?
Those who are "upward-bound practitioners" (ūrdhvaṃsrotas) are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the upper realms; they do not undergo further rebirth but attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.
Regarding the nine types of persons: seven are named as in the sūtra, and by adding the one who attains realization through the transformation of the body (kāyasākṣin), there are nine.
One who possesses faith-understanding (adhimukti) is precisely a person of faith; as they enter the path of cultivation, they are further termed a person of faith-understanding.
Because those of dull faculties rely upon faith to give rise to genuine understanding, they are called "those of faith-understanding."
Those who have "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) are practitioners of the Dharma who have entered the path of cultivation;

they are called "attainers through vision" because they are individuals of sharp faculties who, by means of their own wisdom, permeate their vision of the Dharma and thereby attain the principle. Therefore, Kaishan criticized this, saying:
