"This distinguishes between the sharp and the dull, but these are not two distinct types of persons; that is to say, these are not two kinds of Anāgāmins."
The body-witness (kāyasākṣin) is likewise either one who attains through faith (śraddhādhimukta) or one who attains through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

Entering the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), they employ untainted wisdom (anāsravajñāna) to sever the fetters of the lower and upper realms (avarabhāgīya- and ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana). They employ the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) to cultivate the eight liberations (vimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana).
They enter the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) and [sever] the two obstacles regarding the phenomena and nature of the three voids (triviveka). First.

Having already exhausted [the defilements] and further severed the obstacles of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the principle of the cessation of conditions through various mental states and mental factors;
because one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and attains this concentration, one is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) Anāgāmin. Why?

Because upon entering the meditative absorption of cessation, one abides in a state resembling *nirvāṇa* within the body, bringing to rest all the labors of the three realms. Since one has personally realized the cessation of perception and feeling, one is called a "body-witness. Furthermore—
It is said that because the body alone remains while the mind is like a fish in water or hibernating insects, one who attains this is merely designated a "Body-Witness" (kāyasākṣin).

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that when a Non-Returner (anāgāmin) cultivates and attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), they are further named a Body-Witness. Since the absorption of cessation is without mind, it is called a "Body-Witness" because it is realized through the body.
Having attained the fruit of Non-Returner, they cultivate the path toward Arhatship; they do not emerge from this contemplation again, but rather sever the eighth and ninth grades [of afflictions].
Even if one has abandoned the ten or twelve grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), one does not yet immediately realize arhatship.
Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are two types of "up-streamers" (*ūrdhva-srotas*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):

first, those who have practiced mixed meditation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvita*), who delight in wisdom and are reborn in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*); second, those who have not practiced mixed meditation, who delight in meditative concentration and are reborn in the [formless realms].
Regarding the term "mixed cultivation" (*miśrabhāvanā*) of form, it refers to the cultivation of multiple moments of both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states.
As for "in the present body," this means that within the very body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one attains both the fruit of *anāgāmin* and the fruit of *arhat*.

Regarding those who take birth pervading the four dhyānas, this refers to being completely submerged within them; for details on how they pervade the eighteen celestial realms, refer to the fifteenth commentary.
The present sutra, based on their major divisions, merely points to the four dhyānas.
Regarding those of sharp faculties who do not necessarily undergo many births, it is not the case that one with many births is necessarily of dull faculties;
even within a single lifetime, there are both sharp and dull faculties. For example, Śāriputra was sharp while Mahāmaudgalyāyana was particularly dull—was this due to the number of births?
If we consider it in terms of the number of births, then those with few births may be either sharp or dull, and those with many births may likewise be either sharp or dull.
Because [the faculties] are dull, the commentary concludes by stating: "This explanation is now made in reference to the four dhyānas.
This constitutes the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); that is, the two pairs of propositions are combined to form four propositions:
(1) having progress but no concentration; (2) having concentration but no progress; (3) possessing only the truth; and (4) possessing neither.

Regarding "lack of mastery over meditative concentration" (*samādhi-vaśitā*): it refers to the diligent cultivation of contemplative understanding, which is called diligence (*vīrya*). Because it does not manifest easily from the mind, it is termed "lack of mastery.

Its opposite, laziness (*kausīdya*), should be understood by reversing the preceding [definitions]. As for "possessing meditative concentration," it is the opposite of the former and can be understood accordingly.
The Sūtra states that there are those who perform actions but do not experience rebirth because they have extensively cultivated wisdom and understanding; thus it says they only perform actions.
Because their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is subtle within the higher realms, it says they lack the karma for rebirth.
Therefore, they do not reach the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); these are also people in whom wisdom is predominant and concentration is slight.
The Commentary states: "That which refers to 'dispersed karma' means that wisdom-understanding is considered dispersed karma.

My personal interpretation is as follows: "Below" refers to having already abandoned the desire realm; although one has not yet reached the form realm, this intermediate state (antarābhava) is already subsumed under the form realm.
This is precisely what the sutra below says: "Having departed from the desire realm and reached the edge of the form realm, one then attains nirvana."
"Already not receiving" means that one has not yet reached the state of taking birth in the Form Realm. One interpretation states:
the first phrase below provides the heading, while the subsequent "non-learner" (aśaikṣa) section provides the explanation.

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya-citta*): because conventional truth is not among the first three fruits [of the path], it is "neither learner" (*na śaikṣa*); because it is not among the four fruits, it is "not non-learner" (*na aśaikṣa*); and because it is not [the ultimate fruit], it is "not non-existent."
Regarding "learning" (*śaikṣa*): those whose minds take the True Truth (*satya*) as their object belong to the three fruits that are currently in the stage of learning (*śaikṣabhūmi*).
Thus, the "mind being guided" refers to the mind that is being guided; it is neither non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), nor the first fruit, nor is it beyond learning (*na-aśaikṣa*), nor is it the Arhat.
Han Zheng is an Anāgāmin who is able to lead the mind that previously realized the truths to the third fruit.
One who takes the true mind as their object further contemplates the principle and cultivates toward the realization of the fourth fruit; therefore, they are called a "learner" (śaikṣa).
Cultivating the mind of antiquity is the realization of truth within its own station, which is termed "beyond-learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding the "mind that loses mindfulness": first, it refers to regressing from the fruit, which is called losing mindfulness; second, it refers to emerging from meditative observation and becoming like a distracted mind, which is also called losing mindfulness.
Regarding the phrase "this interpretation cannot be seen" in the text, this interpretation refers to the subsequent interpretation.

Since the Sūtra states that there are four types of minds for an Anāgāmin, [the author] takes these four minds and explains them exclusively in relation to the Anāgāmin. This refutes the subsequent interpretation;
the preceding interpretation adopts the meaning of the first master’s explanation.
Furthermore, the statement that "two are [nirvāṇa] and two are not" refers to the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), wherein two positions are nirvāṇa and two are not nirvāṇa.
This meaning should be explained below.
Regarding the "two minds" of an Arhat: since both the mind of emptiness and the mind of existence are ultimate fruits, they constitute *nirvāṇa*. An Anāgāmin is the opposite of this.

If one explains the latter [verse] below, it clarifies that all four minds are present in the stage of an Anāgāmin; according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), these are the guiding minds that prevent the loss of mindfulness.
The ultimate truth of mind is the true mind as its object; the conventional truth consists of the old mind. Since these two minds can be extinguished, they are nirvana;
since the two minds cannot be extinguished [in their essential nature], they are not nirvana.

Regarding the "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon arising" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*): "arising" refers to being born [in the form realm], while "parinirvāṇa" means the final extinction; this is what is called a person who attains parinirvāṇa upon arising.
As for the "one who constantly practices": having been born in the form realm, they practice for a long time before finally attaining parinirvāṇa;
because they possess diligent cultivation but lack the path of rapid progress, the *Abhidharmakośa* calls this "attaining parinirvāṇa through effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*).
"Not depending on one's own exertion" means not waiting for the diligent cultivation of the path. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Having been born in the Form Realm, one attains parinirvāṇa without further undergoing the cultivation of effortless practice (*anabhisaṃskāra-pratipad*). Because both the path of diligent cultivation and the path of swift progress are absent, it is called "without practice.
However, the Commentary (*Śū*) explains that "the extinction of practice" refers to the dull [faculty] and "non-practice" refers to the sharp [faculty]; this is merely based on a single perspective.
Furthermore, these [faculties] may also be mutually sharp or dull.
Regarding those who are born in the Nirmāṇarati heaven and so forth: "Nirmāṇa" refers to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, and "Akiñcanya" refers to the Ākiñcanyāyatana (the Sphere of Nothingness).

Although they are born in the formless realm, they are not called "Parinirvāṇa-in-Formlessness," but are instead termed "Upstream-goers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), because they have traversed back through the form realm.

The answer states: "Regarding those not called 'Upstreamers' (ūrdhvasrotas): according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, these are precisely those among the Upstreamers who are 'Leapers' (*pluta*)—namely, those who leap entirely (*sarvacyuta*) to be born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
This is the leap of wisdom (*prajñā*). Those who leap to be born in the Abhāsvara heaven are leapers of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Those who have not yet reached [Akaniṣṭha] are half-leapers (*ardhapluta*)."
The third point establishes the first: because one is externally capable of debate and internally possesses wisdom and delights in tranquility, one is able to cultivate samādhi.

The fourth point further establishes that there are five distinctions among the aforementioned [practitioners]: because there are five grades of differentiation in the cultivation of *vāsanā-bhāvanā-dhyāna* (perfuming meditation), [the results] arise accordingly.
The five Pure Abodes differ.

Since this fourth category is established below the fourth [level], and because the preceding five distinctions have already been formed, one must explain its meaning in contrast to the former; only then will its significance be revealed.

Regarding the two interpretations in the text: first, the opinion of the Saṃkhyā masters is cited, and second, the opinion of the Śāstrakāra is cited. One should take the meaning of the Saṃkhyā as the basis.
Correct.
Regarding the statement that "the two untainted [attainments] intermingle with the perfuming, etc.," there should be five types of distinctions. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"By means of the five grades of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) are produced. As for the "five grades": first, inferior; second, middling; third, superior; fourth, superior-excellent; and fifth, supreme.
The five higher grades are likewise thus; the essential substance of the karma supported by these five grades is one and the same.

However, because the causal modes of the supporting practices differ, when each of these five grades of mind is supported, they all involve both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the fundamental (*maula*) stages.
First, regarding the support of the lower grade of mind: this practitioner first enters the fourth dhyāna, and within that concentration, first gives rise to many moments of thought.
When a succession of untainted (anāsrava) moments of mind manifests, followed by the manifestation of many moments of tainted (sāsrava) mind,
and then again a succession of untainted moments of mind manifests, and this process continues in such a way that they gradually decrease until there are two moments of untainted mind,
two moments of tainted mind, and then two moments of untainted mind— this is called the perfection of the preparatory stage (prayoga) of mixed cultivation. Furthermore...
To give rise to one thought-moment of outflow-free (anāsrava), one thought-moment of with-outflow (sāsrava), and one thought-moment of outflow-free—this is called the fundamental fulfillment.

Because the preceding and succeeding moments are outflow-free while the intermediate moment is with-outflow, and they are practiced in alternation, it is called "mixed cultivation" (vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā).
By means of this, one is supported by the Bṛhatphala Heaven; thus, when the karma [of that heaven] is exhausted and one passes away from Bṛhatphala, one is born in Avṛha. This is the lower [level].
This section classifies them according to their fragrance; the details regarding these middle classes and so forth are as explained extensively in the *Xuanji* (Record of Profound Analysis).
The Sūtra states that "No-Small Heaven" (*Anabhraka*) is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, "Good-to-See" (*Sudarśana*) is the Sudarśana Heaven, and "Small-Vast" (*Atapa*) is the Atapa Heaven;
the remaining names are identical [to those in other texts].

Having already explained the fifth person in conjunction with the preceding [discussion], that is, clarifying within the context of the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) those who delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) after entering the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), one should now also explain those who attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realms (*ārūpyopapadyaparinirvāyin*).
A detailed discussion of their essential characteristics is as found in the fifteenth commentary.
Regarding "Devadatta, Subhūti, and others," this refers to those who attain liberation through waiting for the right conditions (*samaya-vimukta*).
Because they obtain the fruit of the Path only when their requisite conditions are fully met, whether one is extravagant or frugal depends on the individual.

Thus, while the *kuṇḍala* robe was worth only five *kārsāpaṇas*, the chamber of Devadatta, Subhūti, was adorned with the seven treasures; though there was a difference in their abundance or austerity, both had realized the fruit of Arhatship. Since...
This principle follows what is appropriate to one's inclination; nevertheless, rather than being extravagant, it is better to be frugal.

Regarding this, the masters of the treatises also cite two teachers from within their own school whose explanations of the meaning differ, while there are also several who agree with the preceding view that there are no humans in the two upper realms, or that because they are humans [there], it is said that there are none. Thus, it is also the same as before when it says "none."
This is explained in the same manner as before.

Alternatively, it is said that this passage is cited by the Śāstra masters to demonstrate that there are individuals who first enter [the path] in the higher realms; thus, they quote the *Lalitavistara* as proof.

Regarding this passage, several scholars below have harmonized it with the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, asserting that those who practice through faith and Dharma (*śraddhā-dharmanusārin*) already abide in the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) while still in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Thus, it is said that they first engage in the preparatory means (*prayoga*), and after emerging from meditative observation (*vyutthāna*), they are born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu), where they encounter the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and slightly attain the fruits of the Path.
Therefore, one knows that the original inception of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) actually occurs within the desire realm.
The eighty thousand devas who attained the purity of the Dharma-eye were precisely these people.
Among the Arhats, those of the Middle Vehicle are the Pratyekabuddhas of the Middle Vehicle.
The sutras state that all are Buddha-nature; beginning from the icchantika, whose three obstructions are themselves the three virtues, they culminate in the Tathāgata’s ultimate realization.
In conclusion, although the three virtues differ according to the seven types of people—ranging from the virtuous to the evil—they do not depart from the water of Buddha-nature.

As for the question, "Nirvana has no cause; how can it be called a fruit? this is based on the fact that in the *Śānta-siṃhanāda-parivarta*, the Tathāgata extensively explained that Nirvana is a fruit and has no cause.
Now, taking this as a point of contention: if there is no cause, how can it be called a fruit?
Those who raise this objection desire to have the Tathāgata distinguish the cause and manifest the fruit so that people may practice and realize them.

The Sūtra also refers to the "śramaṇa" as the cause; the subsequent phrase refers to the fruit. As for the prior clarification of the seven fruits and so forth, it is intended to show that *nirvāṇa* is distinct from the preceding six.

Furthermore, throughout the Sūtra, the causes—whether distant or proximate—are all distinguished in relation to their respective fruits, with each being characterized by its direct and essential nature.
The proximate cause acts as an immediate condition, while the remote cause acts as a distant condition; "distant" and "near" are not defined by time.

Among the remaining fruits mentioned in the Sūtra, the third is the prolongation of years and increase of longevity, which constitutes the essential nature of the fruit. It is subsequently called the "remote cause," and it is further stated that this is itself the prolongation of years and increase of longevity;
this refers to the clothing [bestowed], because the food and clothing given can extend the years of others and augment their lifespan. Thus, it points specifically to the clothing.
Taking food as the remote cause—without regard for the substance of one's lifespan—the fruition of the *sūtra*’s impartiality is precisely the fruition of the Pure Land;

therefore, the ten wholesome actions serve as the proximate cause. Furthermore, the three calamities serve as the distant cause, for when the three calamities arise, sentient beings are able to reform their evils and cultivate goodness, thereby acting as the seed for the increasing eon (*vivarta-kalpa*).
Regarding the answer that the subsequent question possesses three meanings: these three meanings are contained within the text of the following questions and answers;
however, because Kāśyapa did not understand that they were already implied herein, he asked again, whereupon the Tathāgata revealed the three meanings.

Regarding the statement that the Sūtra refers to the Eightfold Noble Path and so forth: although names such as "śramaṇa" encompass both the partial and the small [vehicles], their ultimate destination does not exceed the single reality (ekayāna).
Therefore, the Eightfold Path is itself the category of the path of non-action (anabhisamskāra), which constitutes the perfect cause prior to abiding in the fruit.
The Sūtra states that by permanently severing all greed, hatred, and delusion, one breaks through ignorance and ultimately achieves its cessation; this is the relationship between cause and effect.

The Sūtra uses these two names as a double conclusion: "This is called a śramaṇa" concludes the preceding [discussion of] the eightfold right path, and "the fruit of a śramaṇa" concludes the preceding [discussion of] permanent [severance].
"Severing.
The Sūtra says that all beings in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) suffer from the deprivation of the wealth of the outflows-free (*anāsrava*).

By now practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one attains this outflows-free wealth and is able to sever this deprivation; therefore, it is said that "severing deprivation" means the Path is capable [of doing so].
"Cutting off lack" is that which is to be abandoned.
The sutra speaks of "cutting off all paths," specifically teaching the path capable of abandonment; now, one likewise abandons this [lack].

Thus, it is known that "cutting off lack" is the cutting off of birth and death, and the cutting off of the path is the cutting off of nirvana. This correctly reveals the Middle Way of non-action and the Eightfold Right Path.
Regarding the meaning of "śramaṇa," the Commentary states that it refers to severing all deficiencies and so forth, up to the point of being "neither of the two" (neither existent nor non-existent).

The phrase in the Sūtra, "permanently severing the causes and conditions for birth throughout the three periods of time," clarifies that the cause has perished; the phrase, "also severing the body of the five aggregates within the three realms," demonstrates that the fruit has been lost.

Regarding which category these [paths] belong to: although the Pratyekabuddha eliminates delusions in a single sitting, there is a distinction between the path of cultivation (*pratipannaka*) and the fruit (*phala*).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that the Pratyekabuddha first abandons the delusions of the eight stages and realizes awakening in a single sitting;

subsequently, they cultivate the nine stages in succession, further giving rise to the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Furthermore, even while not abandoning the delusions within the lower eight stages, they maintain their contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
This is because it is the natural order of successive stages (*dharmatā*). Since each stage (*bhūmi*) possesses eighteen minds, across the nine stages there are one hundred and sixty-two minds;
when combined with the sixteen minds of the prior path, there are one hundred and seventy-eight minds.

Thus, we know that when one first abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the eight stages, this is termed the "candidate for Pratyekabuddha" (*pratyekabuddha-pratipannaka*). Therefore, I now ask: among the seven types of persons (*pudgala*), to which category does this belong?
In the response, there are two parts: first, the previous text is cited by way of contrast; second, the phrase "this also" and following serves as an illustration to establish the present point.
Regarding the original selection of "abiding" (*sthiti*) as the sixth, this specifically refers to taking the fruit of *anāgāmin* (non-returner) as the sixth person.

Regarding the phrase "also being those who have attained the original fruit" (*mūlaphala*): previously, the *anāgāmin* was taken as the sixth example by virtue of having attained the original fruit; now, the *pratyekabuddha* is likewise taken as the seventh person because he has also attained the original fruit.

Therefore, the stage of the *pratyekabuddha* candidate (*pratipannaka*) is subsumed within the sixth category. Question: The sixth category consists of those who have attained the three fruits (*triphala*).

Since a *pratyekabuddha* eliminates all afflictions in a single sitting (*ekāsana*), how can there be three fruits for him? Answer: This is stated provisionally based on the fact that he eliminates [afflictions] in a single sitting.

When the afflictions of the middle realm are exhausted, it is explained that if one speaks in general terms, even those on the path toward Pratyekabuddhahood (Pratyekabuddha-abhimukha) belong to the third and fourth [stages] and so forth.

This answer does not resolve the objection; for although it is said that *pāramitā* means "reaching the other shore," the names of the six perfections are still designations based on their causes, and thus the objection remains unrefuted.

There is a distinct meaning here: since this is the stage common to the three vehicles, it refers to the stages of the *prativedha-saṃdhāna* (connecting the distinct and the perfect) and the stages of abiding in the grounds of the distinct and perfect teachings.
Because these are all termed "partial realization" (*pradeśa-prativedha*) of the three virtues (*tri-dharma*), they are called "reaching the other shore.

Thus, the Sūtra states that both Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are fully accomplished [in them], and it further says they obtain the fruit of the six *pāramitās*. From this we know that while Bodhisattvas possess the partial fruit, the Buddha possesses the ultimate fruit.

Ultimately, although those dwelling on the stages prior to the ultimate fruition, as well as bodhisattvas who have attained penetration, practice the six perfections, these are not called "fully accomplished" and are therefore not the fruition.

Regarding the Buddha-nature being both existent and non-existent: it is existent because it will certainly be obtained in the future; it is non-existent because it has not yet been realized and is not currently functioning.

Regarding the "breaking both": if one says that the icchantika attains bodhi is called "defiled attachment" and does not attain it is called "falsehood," this is because it breaks these two [extremes].
Regarding "breaking the particular by means of the universal":
because the particular and universal teachings are adjacent to one another, we shall first discuss breaking the universal by means of the particular in full detail.

This is also because the "Round" (the Perfect Teaching) subsumes the "Common" (the Shared Teaching). Since the meaning of the Path of Realization (*darśana-mārga*) in the Separate Teaching is identical to that of the Round Teaching, for the time being we shall treat it according to the Separate Teaching.

Thus, regarding the "seven types of persons" and so forth, these belong to the Common Teaching; not only do they not cultivate the immeasurable Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*) during their causal stages, but even the Buddhas have not yet cultivated them.

All must reform their views, which is why [the teaching] is refuted to cause them to reform their views. Although it is said that on the level of the fruit there is no person (*pudgala*), [this is still the case].

Because the teaching is presented as a literal exposition for the sake of those beginners who have first entered the path, even the Buddhas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) are included among those who have not yet completed their cultivation.

This is because the Nirvana of the Shared Teaching is described as a river; it clarifies that these seven types of persons have merely crossed the river of分段 (fen-duan, *bheda*) birth-and-death, but have not yet crossed the river of 變易 (bian-yi, *pariṇāma*) birth-and-death.

The Sūtra states that those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or violate the four grave precepts do so because they have not yet seen the Buddha-nature; thus, they fall into the path of transgression among the heinous crimes and the violation of the middle way among the precepts.
As for the seventh person, they have not yet emerged from the *vaivartika* (transformation) state and are collectively termed "sunk."
The second type of person who emerges is one who has transformed their perspective.
"Associating with virtuous friends" and so forth refers to associating with those who possess perfect knowledge;
they inspire the three perfect wisdoms, cultivate the three perfect practices, cross the river of change, and attain the three virtues, as described in the sutra.
This sūtra states that those who are "defiled and attached" are as follows: if one says that icchantikas do not practice yet naturally attain bodhi, such a person is called defiled and attached;
if one says that icchantikas will never become buddhas, such a person is called a liar.

"Defiled and attached" means to cling to principle while being deluded about phenomena, thus claiming that icchantikas naturally attain [enlightenment]; "liar" means to cling to the provisional while slandering the real, thus claiming they do not attain it.
If one says that icchantikas do not sever their wholesome nature, yet can attain bodhi by reforming and practicing evil, then one is able to avoid these two faults.
As for those who hold divergent views and speak divergently in the sutras, it is because their conceptions do not accord with correct principle that they cause their speech to be divergent.
Those who slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in the sutras are slandering the Three Jewels as a single entity within their own bodies.

Regarding the "last three phrases" and so forth, this refers to the commentary (*shu-wen*) which explains these by connecting them to the preceding section concerning whether sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature or not;
therefore, it is here specifically referred to as "the last three phrases."
To summarize the great principle: since the Buddha-nature is the presiding lord of this sutra, it is now concluded with a general summary.

As for the principle of Buddha-nature, if it were a numerical phenomenon (*saṃkhyeya-dharma*), it would belong to the three periods of time; because it is non-numerical (*asaṃkhyeya*), it is eternally abiding (*nitya*).
Regarding the phrase "encompassing all that is wholesome and unwholesome," etc.: while the causes include both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the results are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).
This refers to the fact that the cause and result of the nine realms are, in their essential nature, the Buddha-realm; therefore, it is said that they are all designated as "Buddha-nature."

Regarding the statement that "the cause may be spoken of as the result," this is said because the principle of cause and effect is identical and the arising of the Buddha is non-dual with [sentient beings].
Fourth, concerning the conclusion regarding speech according to one's own intention, it is indicated by the summary of the three names.
Regarding the initial clarification that the Buddha-nature is identical to space and so forth: first, clarifying their identity reveals that the essence of the mind-particle pervades all things.

Since all phenomena are subsumed within the mind and there is nothing remaining outside of it, how could there be any further distinction or separation? Therefore, the all-pervasiveness of empty space is used as a metaphor for this principle.

Next, to clarify how this differs from empty space: because this Buddha-nature is simply the true nature inherently possessed by sentient beings and is all-pervasive, it must be distinguished from wood, stone, and delusive afflictions, as well as from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

While this [Buddha-nature] might seem to differ from empty space in that there are things it does not pervade, delusive afflictions, the Small Vehicle, and even tiles and stones are all transformations of the mind; their very substance is the mind. Therefore, next...
Although it speaks of difference, it has never been that they were not identical from the beginning; although it speaks of identity, it has never been that they were not different.

Regarding the third point, the refutation of non-Buddhists and others: since they use empty space as a metaphor for the nature (dharmatā), one must know that the space used as the metaphor is not the same as that which outsiders cling to.

The *Jinbi lun* (Golden Scalpel) judges the passage in this sutra where it first says "identical to empty space" to be provisional, while the subsequent section on "different from empty space" is definitive.
The provisional nature of emptiness is the primary intent of the present commentary; whether they agree or differ, each possesses its own profound significance, as harmonized in the *Xianxing lu*.
This is because these are the authentic scriptures of the Dharma King, wherein both the points of agreement and difference are the Buddha’s own teaching.

Regarding the empty space seen by the eye, non-Buddhists fail to comprehend the nature of space; they falsely engage in speculative reasoning regarding this single manifest color of emptiness as seen, as in the following ten sections.
This is just like how figures in our own land, such as Qiu Guangting and others, speculated on the tides of the ocean entirely according to their own subjective views.
Because this is non-existent, the three periods of time cannot exist; since empty space is non-existent, there is no counterpart.
Because all counterparts are severed, the three periods of time do not exist.
That which is non-existent is eternal, for its essential nature is void and devoid of any transition or change.
The Buddha-nature is existent because, although space is eternal, one can never see it despite employing hundreds of thousands of skillful means; therefore, it is non-existent.
The Buddha-nature is also eternal, yet because one attains the vision of it through the skillful means of cultivating the path, it is existent.

Regarding the statement that "Buddha-nature is not entirely present": this is said to be "present" only in the sense that it can be realized; it is not a substantial dharma, and therefore it is not entirely present.
As for the scriptural analogy of "flowers in the sky," since the entirety of emptiness is the flower and the locus of the flower is itself emptiness, they do not belong to the three periods of time.
The reason for not further elaborating on this section is that it contains a thesis, an explanation, and a conclusion, which are already evident; thus, it is not analyzed in detail again.
Regarding the phrase "having attained Bodhi, one is unimpeded with respect to all dharmas," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"When the true source is realized, the empty space of the ten directions vanishes all at once. The *Golden Scalpel* says: "When a single Buddha attains enlightenment, there is nothing in the Dharma-realm that is not this."

The Buddha’s reliance [the environment] and his correctness [the body] are both the ultimate manifestation of buddha-nature. Furthermore, although these three passages equally reveal permanence, their meanings differ slightly:

the first clarifies permanence by way of the vertical, in terms of not being bound by the three periods of time; the second clarifies permanence by way of the horizontal, in terms of not being internal or external;
and the third clarifies permanence by way of that which is neither horizontal nor vertical, in terms of being unimpeded. Moreover, Kāśyapa, with the assembly...
The question concerns the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, yet the Buddha answers all three passages by referring exclusively to the stage of fruition.
The intention behind this is to clarify that cause and effect are non-dual and that sentient beings and Buddhas are without difference; thus, he asks about the cause but answers regarding the fruit.
This profound principle must be understood. As it is with this passage, so it is with all others.
Since space is not of the three periods of time yet is called "existent," one should say "is not" rather than "is called"; some characters are missing, or perhaps there is a textual error.
However, it is sufficient simply to change "existent" (有) to "space" (空), for its meaning becomes self-evident; this is not a case of missing characters.
This is because the preceding sutra states that space is non-existent and thus not of the three periods; therefore, the current statement that it is "called existent" is an error.

Regarding that which is called "eternal," the preceding sutra states: "Because the Buddha-nature is eternal, it is not subsumed within the three periods of time; because the Buddha-nature exists and is not of the world, it is eternal.
[The opponent] raises an objection based on parity with the following: "If both space and nirvana are equally non-existent within the three periods of time, why is space not identical to nirvana?"
"Because it exists, how can it not be different from existence?
This [question] is intended solely to preserve the meaning; this is Jingxi’s assistance in clarifying Zhanran’s intention.

Thus, one knows that the principle of the Buddha-nature being distinct from empty space was taught not only for the sake of those with perfect capacities, but also for the sake of those with distinct capacities after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the term "protection" (*parigraha*): this refers to those who rely on skillful means (*upāya*). If such individuals were to hear the truth, they would surely slander it; because they slander it, evil arises.
Therefore, the Buddha, in order to protect and guide these specific capacities and conditions, provisionally explains it through a different meaning.

If one were to say otherwise—just as it is said that tiles and stones are eternally non-existent—would the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the Two Vehicles also be eternally non-existent? For the world collectively acknowledges [the existence of] afflictions.
Because affliction (*kleśa*) is itself awakening (*bodhi*), and the Hīnayāna is itself the Mahāyāna;
when a sudden karmic opportunity arises, it is the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Since one must not fail to speak, once facing such a perfect capacity, one should say that "afflictions are themselves nirvāṇa," and so forth, even down to "tiles and stones."
This is precisely the Buddha-nature.
However, according to the answer provided below, the lower scripture states that there is nothing that is not space in relation to space.
Since space has no counterpart, this correctly elucidates that the Buddha-nature is the single suchness (*tathatā*).

It is not only the primary retribution (*vipāka*) that is discussed in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which encompasses both internal and external forms.
"Internal" refers to the six sense organs, which constitute the primary retribution; "external" refers to the six sense objects, which constitute the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Since worldly people already accept that the five aggregates are the Buddha-nature, to claim that tiles and stones lack this nature is to disbelieve that the aggregates possess Buddha-nature.

People of the world do not understand this intent; they perversely cling to the talk that tiles and stones lack *dharmatā* (nature) to reject the meaning of universal *cittamātra* (mind-only), as explained at length in the *Jinpi lun* (The Golden Needle).

By taking that which is "unconditioned by space" (*ākāśa-anapekṣa*) to mean that the sutras are nothing other than space, they treat "space" as being in opposition to "space," claiming that all things are [merely] space.
In the world, there is not a single place that is not empty space and yet stands in opposition to it;

therefore, it is said that "nothing is not [empty]," which serves as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature pervading all places—whether the environment or its inhabitants, nothing is not the Buddha-nature.

This uses the absolute non-relation of empty space to illustrate the absolute non-relation of the Buddha-nature. Thus, the *Fahua Wenju Ermen* (The Two Gates of the Lotus Sutra Commentary) states: "Ten..."

According to the Buddhadharma, the fundamental nature of the Buddha-realm and the sentient beings' nature are without distinction; they are all-pervasive. Who could speak of "internal" and "external," "matter" and "mind," or "self" and "other"?

However, regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and Buddha-nature (*buddhatva*), each possesses two meanings: the relative (*pratītya*) and the absolute (*atyanta*). These will be clarified in the following question-and-answer section.
Here, because the relative meaning of Buddha-nature is contrasted with the absolute meaning of empty space, there is a difference between them; thus it is said that "empty space has no dependence."

Regarding the statement that "nirvāṇa has conditions," if one follows the *Jinbi lun* (The Golden Needle Treatise), the preceding passage which judges that tiles and stones lack Buddha-nature is identified as the provisional teaching concerning the nature of the conditions and the aids (*pratyaya-bhūta-hetu* and *upakāra-hetu*).
This clarification that "empty space is all-pervasive" refers to the true cause (*dhātu-hetu*) according to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).

Thus, the resolution of the objection and the Master’s own commentary differ; there is no need to employ that [provisional] interpretation for this [definitive] context. Furthermore, regarding the passages by Zhangan and Jing...
The two masters of the Xi clan were both proficient [in this], so there was no superiority or inferiority between them, as clarified in the *Xianxing lu*.
Space (*ākāśa*) is also posited in contrast to that which is not empty; it is spoken of as the "Great Void" in relation to the myriad phenomena of the universe.
This is precisely the meaning of "relative dependence" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). How, then, can space be said to be "absolute and independent"? Therefore, it is asked: why is it not dependent?
The commentary states: Based on this interpretation, one can clearly see that Zhangan deeply understood the purport of the sutra.

Thus we know that *nirvāṇa* and empty space are fundamentally equal in their nature; it is only in response to the capacities of sentient beings (*jī*) that they are provisionally described as distinct. One should understand that *nirvāṇa* and empty space each possess both the aspects of "relativity" (*dai*) and "transcendence" (*jue*).

Because they are transcendent while being relative, they constitute "wondrous existence" (*miaoyou*); because they are relative while being transcendent, they are "wondrous non-existence" (*miaowu*). Since... [the text continues].

If the substantiality [of things] is severed by their dependence, how could Buddha-nature be excluded from a tile? If the substance of the tile is complete through its dependence, then that nature is pervasive and must still be pointed out as residing in sentient beings.
Thus we know that the commentary’s phrasing is subtle yet manifest, refined and well-structured; were it not for the Master, the Sage, who could have composed such a work?

Nirvāṇa is fundamentally transcendent, yet it is termed "dependent" because Nirvāṇa and the other two [vehicles] are entirely comprised of afflictions and the like; therefore, it is said to be "fundamentally transcendent.
Because one desires to cause the severing of delusions and the realization of principle, ordinary beings are refuted by saying that "afflictions are not Nirvāṇa.
Because one desires to prevent the arising of inferior aspirations and the denial of reality, those of the Two Vehicles and others are refuted by saying they are "icchantikas."
The Buddha is not like the Tathāgata who, wishing to urge sentient beings to turn back and contemplate their own minds, says that tiles and stones lack buddha-nature;
these are all intended as remedies, and thus it is said that they are "contingent."
"Space is fundamentally dependent" means that the great void exists in relation to the myriad phenomena; thus it is said to be "fundamentally dependent.

Now, based on the fact that the voidness of the myriad phenomena does not depart from space, it is called "absolute. Thus we know that both the Dharma (the teaching) and the analogy each possess the two meanings of dependence and absoluteness.

Because the Buddha adapted to the capacities of his audience, he treated the Dharma primarily in terms of dependence while treating the analogy solely in terms of absoluteness; therefore, *nirvāṇa* and space are both considered eternal.
As for "abiding," they are identical in being both existent and non-existent, yet they differ.
Regarding "wondrous existence" and so forth, it receives the name "wondrous" because it is based on the mutual identity of the relative and the absolute.
This is precisely what is meant by "not inverted"; the scriptural text provisionally clarifies this by using the metaphor of the absolute to contrast it with the relative.

Because their meanings differ, they cannot be treated as identical by way of analogy. Furthermore, one should know that the sūtra states that *nirvāṇa* and the other two are merely different names for the same essence.
Thus, the preceding sūtra says: "Nirvāṇa is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is Buddha-nature.
If one wishes to distinguish them, there is indeed no lack of difference; this clarifies that *nirvāṇa* is the fruit, the realization of quiescent extinction.

Because it is the Dharma, it is not a phenomenon agitated by afflictions; because the Tathāgata is one who has realized ultimate perfection, he is not a person of the partial and limited Two Vehicles.
Because Buddha-nature is the principle inherent within the causal state, it is not a matter of dull, obstructive objects such as tiles or stones.
This is the meaning of "relative" (相待). If explained through the lens of "transcending relativity" (絕待), Nirvāṇa is itself liberation.
That which comes is precisely Prajñā; the Buddha-nature is the Dharmakāya, and Nirvāṇa subsumes the three types of nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata subsumes the three bodies, and the Buddha-nature subsumes the three causes. Thus, whether considered sequentially or collectively, each possesses all three. These three are each one and three, and three and one;

cause and effect are both thus, and there is no distinction between the living and the Buddha. How could there be any difference between the primary (the Buddha) and the secondary (the environment)? Space is beyond all dependence.
This can be illustrated by seeking the meaning within this scriptural passage; one should understand its intent as follows:
when it says "nirvāṇa has a counterpart," it refers to nirvāṇa’s quiescence in contrast to conditioned phenomena and afflictions.

Regarding the phrase "that which is non-existent," it is simply because space is non-existent while the four great elements are existent. Although existence and non-existence differ, they both lack mutual dependence;
therefore, by means of this principle of non-dependence, the opponent challenges [the Buddha] to make them identical. First, the challenge seeks to make the four great elements identical to space;
next, the challenge seeks to make space identical to the four great elements. As for the initial statement, "The four great elements have no counterpart," if the Buddha were to proclaim:
There is not a single place in the world where emptiness (*śūnyatā*) does not exist; since there is nothing that can serve as its counterpart, one cannot say that emptiness exists.
Furthermore, all places in the world consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); there is not a single place where the four great elements do not exist.
Since there is nothing that can serve as their counterpart, one likewise cannot say that the great elements exist. Therefore, it is said that they too must be non-existent.
Regarding the statement that "the four great elements are non-obstructive" and so forth:
if one were to argue that although there is no place in the world devoid of the four great elements where they could be opposed by form, yet the four great elements can still be said to exist;

then even though there is likewise no place in the world devoid of space where it could be opposed by form, why should space not be said to exist? Therefore, it is said that space should also be considered existent.

This text is not easily understood because the meaning of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) being simultaneously empty is profound and obscure; it is said to be "not easy" because scholars are cautioned that they must investigate and examine it in detail.

Regarding the "formless four great elements" as contrasted with the [ordinary] four great elements: this means that all phenomena of form (*rūpadharma*) without exception are composed of the four great elements, and there are none that are not.
Not a single thing exists that is not composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and yet functions as a counterpart.

Although there is no external allowance [of such a thing], this refers to the locus of allowance; it means that there is no external location where a non-four-element object comes to serve as a counterpart to these four-element objects, because the four great elements are all-pervasive.
Regarding what are called "relative names": fire is opposed to heat, water to cold, wind to lightness, and earth to heaviness; these oppositions are perfectly distinct.
How could they be the same as empty space, which is merely a single entity?

There are fifteen phrases regarding nirvāṇa (up to the point where it is asked): "Why is it that [nirvāṇa] does not exist? This is precisely to demonstrate their difference by contrasting the meaning of nirvāṇa as being "dependent" with the meaning of space as being "absolute.
Question: Why not take the absolute meaning of nirvāṇa to make it equal to the metaphor?

And why not take the dependent meaning of space to make it accord with the dharma? Answer: By citing the dependent and the relative to contrast them with the absolute, one demonstrates that they are not the same.
This is likely because it is appropriate for the specific time and occasion, and by means of this, one gains benefit;
therefore, the Buddha posed this question of "waiting for emptiness" (*ākāśa-pratyaya*), the meaning of which is easy to understand. As for how to distinguish between the two meanings of *nirvāṇa*:

the meaning of "waiting" refers to cultivation and to phenomena, while the meaning of "separation from outflows" (*prahāṇa*) refers to nature and to principle, being all-pervasive. Through cultivation, one merges with nature; through nature, one attains [realization].
Although the cultivation of letters is divided into two parts, their principle is ultimately one and the same.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* generally clarifies that existence is not distinct from emptiness; it subsequently reveals this specifically:

that which is illuminated by wisdom is called "visible," and that which is harmonized with by the mind is called "verifiable. This refers to the body of the dharma-gate of perfect equality, as well as the inconceivable...
Because it is a body of transformation, it is said to be "form" (*rūpa*); because it can be sought and entered by practitioners, it is called a "trace" (*pada*);

because it can be expressed in speech, it is termed "phrases" (*vyañjana*); because its essence is complete with all virtues, it is called "possessing virtue" (*guṇavat*); because its manifestations are distinct and categorized, they are called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*);
because it is that which the mind grasps and traverses, it is named "condition" (*pratyaya*); and because sentient beings alike take refuge in it, it is called "refuge" (*śaraṇa*).

Abiding apart from worldly turmoil and agitation, it is called the essence of tranquility; being devoid of the obstruction of darkness, it is named luminosity; because all peril and fear are forever severed, it is termed peace and security;
and because it is the ultimate destination, it is called the "other shore" (*pāra*).

Therefore, it is named "not subsumed under the three periods of time" as a general conclusion; including the general and specific categories along with the concluding summary, there are fifteen propositions in total.
Third, refuting the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) reckoning of emptiness: the emptiness perceived by the eyes regarding the nature of the world is unfit to serve as a metaphor for Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is extensively refuted.
As for the claim that "emptiness is luminous form," this reveals that its numerical categories are entirely identical to the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) theories of space (*ākāśa*).
Although it is "unutterable" and "eternal," there are two interpretations of this: first, emptiness is actually eternal according to the non-Buddhists.
Because one fails to realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and falsely conceptualizes it as luminosity, it becomes impermanent.

Second, while the nature of vast empty space is considered permanent in the world, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is also impermanent. Why? Because it is constructed by the deluded mind and because it is discriminated by the deluded mind.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Due to delusive ignorance there is empty space; based on empty space, the world is established."

Furthermore, when a single person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions vanishes all at once; therefore, it is said that [space] is ultimately impermanent.
Although both interpretations are applicable, the former meaning is correct.
Regarding the phrase "may also be followed" (亦可下), fearing that others might interpret it as having the meaning of "permanently abiding" (常住), he demonstrates it once more by citing the *Shangshu*:
"Though one regrets, it may be pursued. This implies that [the opportunity] cannot be pursued, which accords with the present intent.
Regarding the "repeated layers" mentioned by Paramārtha, Guangzhai asserts that since what is realized in the Hīnayāna differs from what is realized in the Mahāyāna, these constitute repeated layers;
thus, where space is full, there is no space, yet it exists.
The sounding of the *xiāo* and *guǎn* flutes illustrates that the manifestation of phenomena reveals emptiness through a sequential process;

it is like the appearance of the characteristic of space as it gradually emerges once walls and partitions have been removed—is this not how emptiness is attained through succession? Regarding the *xiāo*, the *Fēngsú Tōng* states: "Shun invented the *xiāo*;
its form is jagged, imitating the wings of a phoenix. The *Wǔjīng Tōngjìng* says: "It is made by weaving bamboo; it is one foot and five inches long."
The *Erya* states: "The *xiao* [flute] has twenty-three tubes and no bottom when large; it has sixteen tubes and a bottom when small.
Regarding the term *xiàng*, it refers to a window; as the *Shijing* says: "Block the windows and seal the doors."

Regarding "emptiness exists within existence": because there is obstruction by material substance, one cannot obtain emptiness; thus we know that emptiness resides where there is space. Regarding "existence exists within emptiness":
it is like carving a cave out of stone, wherein emptiness is obtained; or like making a jar from clay, which encloses emptiness within. Is this not emptiness existing within existence?
As for "no place," since there is no way to grasp emptiness in a place devoid of material substance, it is called "no place."

Regarding "there is no emptiness," such as the example of being "moist and rotten" and so forth: this refers to the meaning that space (*ākāśa*) is subject to destruction; it is "non-existent" because it is destined to rot, yet "existent" because it has not yet rotted.
Thus, the meaning of emptiness is manifested through this object. If there were originally no object, what would there be to undergo destruction? If [the object] still...

Because solidity has not yet manifested the characteristic of disintegration, there is neither mere existence nor mere non-existence; thus, there is no emptiness. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because it is absent in both places.
Regarding the depiction of empty space reaching down to the ocean waters: this is a representation of empty space as having the appearance of vast, boundless ocean waters.
Since it is evident that empty space can be drawn, one knows that it can be produced.

Regarding "the conjunction of dissimilar activities" (*visabhāga-karmasaṃyoga*) and so forth: when two aggregates—one empty and still, the other material and moving—are situated together, this is called the conjunction of dissimilar activities.
The bird represents the activity of matter (*rūpa-karma*), while the tree represents the activity of space (*ākāśa-karma*).

Regarding "the conjunction of two karmas," etc.: when empty space and matter move together and both aggregates occupy the same location, it is called the conjunction of common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma-saṃyoga*).
Since empty space also conjoins with matter—whereby the prior space contracts as matter advances and matter recedes as space advances—one knows that it possesses both karma and motion;
therefore, it is illustrated by the analogy of two rams.
"Things are simply the substance (*tǐ*) and so forth" means that, for example, a human body is the substance, yet it possesses the function (*yòng*) of coming and going;
since there is substance, there is function. Therefore, it is said that these two matters—substance and function—are already unified.

Regarding the statement that "emptiness itself is the essence" and so forth: it is like the emptiness within a room; emptiness itself is the essence, yet it possesses the function of containing beds, couches, people, and objects.

When this essence and its function are already unified, then the essence and function of emptiness, as well as the essence and function of material objects—where there is emptiness, there is necessarily the capacity to contain.
Since that which possesses substance must be capable of movement, it is said to have already "joined.
When there is further mutual joining of pairs thereafter, these pairs constitute four fingers; this serves as a metaphor for how empty things each possess their own essence and function.
Just as a body enters a room, this constitutes the mutual joining of pairs—this is very easy to perceive if one reflects upon it.

Regarding the mind, consciousness, and so forth, the *Śata-śāstra*, Chapter One, states: The Outsider says: "There truly exists a self (*ātman*), as described in the *Sāṃkhya-sūtra* as having the characteristic of consciousness (*caitanya*).
The Insider asks: "Is the self and consciousness one, or are they different? The Outsider says: "The self and consciousness are one. The Insider says:
"If consciousness is the characteristic of the self, then the self would be impermanent; if the self is the characteristic of consciousness, then consciousness would be impermanent."
Therefore, the deity must be impermanent; for example, heat is a characteristic of fire, and because heat is impermanent, fire is also impermanent.
Since the present argument is identical in intent to that [example], it is cited here.

Regarding the refutation of the subsequent conjunction: since it is stated that "what was previously non-existent now exists," this refutes the mutual conjunction of two things, but does not refute the prior conjunction of the empty essence with its function, nor the self-conjunction of the substance with its function.
Regarding "existence at the same time": since space exists, it must necessarily be capable of containing; since material objects exist, they must necessarily be capable of being moved.
How can one say that there was first the time of space, but no capacity for containment or utility? Therefore, the previous synthesis cannot be refuted by the argument of impermanence.
Question: If this is so, should the previous synthesis not be permanent? Answer: Its essence is actually impermanent, and furthermore—

Since the refutation of the principle that "what was previously non-existent comes to exist later" by means of the simultaneous occurrence of essence and function is not clearly demonstrated, I shall set it aside for now.

However, according to those of shallow understanding who rely on worldly perspectives, because the functions of empty objects possess a sequence of before and after, they still fall under the category of impermanence;
thus, the statement that "what was previously non-existent now exists" also refutes the previous [position of] conjunction.
The phrase "as in worldly dharmas" is an illustration.
One cannot say that only one [element] can be understood; otherwise, as in the previous objection, there would have to be multiple emptinesses.

Regarding the statement that "the abiding of the five great elements is overturned and destroyed," this can be investigated: the "five great elements" consist of the four great elements plus space (*ākāśa*), yet in the sutra... [it is not so].
The *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states: "The great earth rests upon the water-circle; the water-circle rests upon the wind-circle; and the wind-circle rests upon space.
In these scriptures, the fundamental is cited to reveal the derivative, clarifying that because that which is supported is impermanent, that which supports it is also impermanent.
Among these, there are four pairs: first, grasses and trees rest upon the earth; second, the earth rests upon water; third, water rests upon wind; [and fourth, wind rests upon space].
The four winds depend upon space; this is to reveal the fourth [category].

Among the pairs of "raising" and "the rest," each first clarifies the derivative as depending on its basis, and subsequently, within the basis itself, it distinguishes the impermanence of the category to manifest it in the derivative.

Herein, it is taught that space is impermanent, causing the impermanence of the winds to be explained from the perspective of others' views rather than as the Buddha’s own definitive meaning. Regarding the Buddha’s own teaching: [it is as follows].
The principle of empty space is such that there is no phenomenon that does not rely upon it as its support.

If the Sūtra states that [space] is impermanent, this uses emptiness and impermanence to refute permanence and pervasiveness; this is merely a counter-objection and does not reveal the correct meaning.
If we discuss the correct meaning, emptiness is permanent and pervasive; therefore, it is not impermanent. Because it is not impermanent, it is not something that is an object of reliance.
Regarding the function of practicing the resolution of delusions, this is the third section within the extensive explanation of the Middle Way.
If one lacks this contemplation, the two vehicles and partial bodhisattvas, being devoid of the contemplation of the Middle Way, will be unable to shatter the great afflictions.
It is because of affliction that there is contention in the world.
First, regarding the Tathāgata and the two types of Bodhisattvas mentioned here, this indicates that both the ultimate fruit and its true cause are entirely free from contention.
"Worldly wise people" refers to those who have achieved perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*).
Therefore, those who harmonize with phenomena are called "harmonious" because they accord with the opportune moment and the assembly;
those who contravene the Buddha's intent are like the twenty-one pairs of disputations mentioned previously.
If even worldly people still dispute with the Buddha, how much more so would ordinary people not refrain from disputing?

Next, regarding the listing of the ten dharmas, the Sūtra clarifies that these ten must all be explained according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). One must understand that the three obstacles are themselves the three virtues (*tri-dharmadhātu*);

only then can they be called "non-contention" (*araṇā*). The same applies to the remaining nine. Furthermore, these ten dharmas have the same meaning as the cultivation of the ten marks within the previous section on the Lion’s Roar, though the phrasing may differ slightly;
that which is now termed "internal skillful reflection" was previously named "quiescence. This is the middle [stage].
Previously, wisdom was the tenth; now it is the seventh. Herein it is called "compassion for sentient beings.

Regarding what was previously termed "the destruction of the Dharma-body": because of delusion, the Dharma-body is not manifested, and thus it is called "destruction. The non-manifestation of the Dharma-body arises from the absence of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*);

this constitutes the destruction of the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). If the objects and wisdom are not manifested, how could there be the application [of the Buddha's activity]? This constitutes the destruction of the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Regarding the phrase "the three bodies are all destroyed," this refers to the distinction between contemplation and non-contemplation: "contemplation" corresponds to the first phrase, and "non-contemplation" corresponds to the second phrase.
When the sutra speaks of these two meanings, it refers to the two meanings of existence and non-existence.

Those who are free from all fetters and outflows (*āsrava*)—since the meaning of "outflows" as the objects to be remedied by the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) extends even beyond the realms (*dhātu*)—the "external conditions" refer to the five sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
Regarding the statement that "there may be minor differences," the verse says: "O Desire, I wish to know your faults; they all arise from conceptualization (*vitarka*). If...
One who is able to sever discursive thought knows that you have no involvement with it. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was staying in the city of Rājagṛha, Ānanda went on almsround.
A woman carrying her child approached a well to draw water; seeing Ānanda’s dignified and upright appearance, she conceived a heart of attachment and could not take her eyes off him.
Unconsciously, she tied her child with a rope, causing his death. Because she subsequently gave rise to a mind of remorse, she spoke thus.
When he returned from begging for alms, he recited this verse to the Buddha. The Buddha instructed Ānanda to receive and uphold this verse, saying:
"This was proclaimed by past Buddhas; she has heard it before. It is not through her own intellectual power that she is able to expound it.

Therefore, it is said that some minor details may differ. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The two characters 'yù-yù' (desire-desire) are words of inquiry and do not belong within the text of the verse itself."
Regarding the conjunction of ignorance (*avidyā*) with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*): ignorance is unified with the afflictions of the views of the three realms.

This distinguishes it from the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), clarifying that in the two upper realms, each stage of dhyāna can individually take objective spheres as its object and give rise to a mind of outflow.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Within the realm of desire, the causal conditions further constitute one mental factor as the internal [basis] for the four factors."

Regarding the phrase "as external," the *Sūtra* states that being unable to discern "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*) as distinct from internal and external correctly defines the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Master Zezhou says: "There are generally four ways of explaining 'self' and 'what belongs to self': first, the presiding spirit (*deva*) is the self, and the various aggregates (*skandha*) are [what belongs to it]..."

First, the two types of provisional persons are taken as the self, and provisional dharmas are taken as what belongs to the self (*mama*). Second, internal dharmas are called the self, and external dharmas are taken as what belongs to the self.
Third, the Buddha-nature is called the self, and the various distinctions of its virtuous qualities and meanings are spoken of as what belongs to the self. Therefore, the aforementioned sutra says:

"One who knows the self and what belongs to the self is a person who transcends the world; one who does not know the first three [types of self] fundamentally lacks this knowledge, while one who does not fail to recognize the fourth fundamentally possesses it."
This is called ignorance (*avidyā*). There are also many ways to explain "internal" and "external": 1. A single sentient being is called internal, while dharmas are called external; 2.
The phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth are external, while the characteristics of suffering, impermanence, and so forth are internal;

3. Phenomenal existence (*bhava*) is external, while the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is internal; 4. True dharmas are internal, while conceptualizations of sentient beings are external; 5. True nature (*tathatā*) is internal, while its true functioning is external.
When external factors do not recognize these [factors], it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
To first explain how they function as mutual cause and effect: when unwholesome reflection gives rise to ignorance, unwholesome reflection is the cause and ignorance is the effect;
when ignorance gives rise to unwholesome reflection, ignorance is the cause and unwholesomeness is the effect.
The explanation of "increase" (*vṛddhi*) is that these two factors are alike in their ability to produce and grow all afflictions (*kleśa*).

The analogy of the "knot" (*granthi*) is as follows: just as the seed is the proximate cause for the production of a sprout while the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the remote cause, so too is it with afflictions;

improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) serves as the proximate cause, while ignorance (*avidyā*) gives rise to afflictions as the remote cause. Furthermore, it is because of ignorance that [this occurs].
Improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) takes ignorance (*avidyā*) as its immediate cause; the same applies to the initial arising of reflection.
The sūtra that first mentions "the two" refers to internal ignorance, which is the *svatantra* (independent) sūtra.

From the cause of ignorance up to the internal and external causes, it is termed "associated" and is called the sūtra on external ignorance. If it speaks of reaching "non-self," this is the explanation of internal ignorance.

To directly obstruct the principle is called "independent ignorance" (*āveṇika-avidyā*); since it is said that one "does not recognize impermanence and so forth," is this not indeed an obstruction to the principle?

From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "If one speaks of... up to "my own," this explains external ignorance—that which arises in association with the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—and is thus termed "associated ignorance" (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*).
Since it serves as the causal condition for all afflictions (*kleśa*), is this not indeed "associated"?
The Commentary states: "That which arises from birth is external outflow (*āsrava*), etc. This merely explains the meaning of external ignorance (*avidyā*).
It means that while various afflictions arise from internal ignorance and subsequently receive the designation "external," ignorance itself is but one. Furthermore, the Commentary below states:
"The mind's failure to comprehend internally is called internal ignorance; not distinguishing external phenomena is external ignorance."
Regarding "binding two fruits": this refers to the two types of ignorance that induce the fruit of birth and death;
hence they are called "two fruits. Regarding "able to scorch the causal conditions": through the fire of the Middle Way contemplation, the wick of the causal conditions is scorched;

although *nirvāṇa* is beginningless, it is made to have a beginning, and thus the realization of the three virtues at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) occurs. Although *saṃsāra* is endless, it is made to have an end.
Therefore, because the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmi*) destroys that ignorance, it is said to "accomplish the beginning and end of existence.
This "end" (*zhōng*) which refers to returning from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to nirvāṇa is an error; it should instead be "returning to the principle of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, although the original text also reads "principle" (*lǐ*), since nirvāṇa has no end but does have a beginning, one should not say it has an "end."
Regarding "also attracting the fruit of the aggregates": the various outflows (āsrava) are the cause of delusion, capable of attracting the fruit of the aggregates of birth and death.
Regarding "desiring to produce their own characteristics": the character "yu" (欲) is an error; it should read "ge zì xiāng shēng" (各自相生).

Next, taking up the two meanings regarding "again taking up signs," the commentary first explains the sūtra by way of how grasping at signs of the beautiful and the ugly gives rise to greed and anger;
this is termed the "condition of craving.

Next, the passage beginning with "Or again" clarifies that while craving resides in the mind, it is not yet the act of taking up signs; rather, the delusion of taking up signs arises from internal craving.
Because they arise, the Sūtra says: "With craving as a condition, [existence] is able to grow and develop," and so forth.
Regarding "the untainted has no retribution": for one who cultivates the untainted, there is no retribution of birth and death. The following passage explains this itself:
"To speak of the effect within the cause" means that the mind is the cause and the body is the effect; by cultivating the meditative concentration of the initial sūtra, the mind serves as the cause.
Therefore, because the fruit of the Brahmā-body has been realized, the fruit is now spoken of within the context of the cause; thus, the first dhyāna is termed "the mind-and-body.
Consequently, when the Sūtra says, "From this mind-and-body I have gone to the realm of Brahmā," it simply means that by practicing the first dhyāna, one is born in the Brahmā heaven.
One should merely cite the name "mind-and-body" as proof that the fruit is spoken of within the cause, and one should carefully examine the commentary with this intent.
This is clearly and straightforwardly explained; however, some versions of the scripture include a commentary stating that because the mind moves the body, they are called "mind and body.
This is an erroneous annotation by a human master and is not a correct translation.
As for the phrase "and so forth" in the following sentence, it refers to what the scripture says: "the fruits and retributions of the path cultivated by all sages," and so on. Since...

It is said that the cultivation of the path primarily concerns the causal stage; because this very cause will inevitably realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the fruit is discussed within the context of the cause.
Therefore, the sutra concludes by stating: "This is called the outflow-free (anāsrava) retribution."
In the fourth fascicle of the *Kāśyapaparivarta*,
it says that those who follow evil afflictions possess an evil nature and are not virtuous. Regarding the word "nimbapa" (絍婆),
the *Jīngdì Shìwén* (經地釋文) records it as being pronounced with the second tone on the syllable "ní" (尼).

Regarding the phrase "when consciousness first arises," this is because when consciousness initially arises, it merely apprehends the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) such as blue and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "perception grasps the provisional name," this refers to the mental state of perception (saṃjñā-citta), which subsequently grasps the image of the object.

That which has not yet been differentiated is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); seeing [an object] impulsively without yet having differentiated it belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

As for the coarse and superficial nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is because the manifestation of the aggregate of form is easy to understand; however, this is merely an observation of the three aggregates.
This is an explanation given according to the capacities of beings.

For those in whom the three types of latent dispositions (anuśaya) are intensely active: first, the mental state of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is directed toward the Buddha; next, the mental state of feeling (*vedanā*) apprehends the preceding object;
and finally, the mental state of formations (*saṃskāra*) gives rise to afflictions such as craving.

Although all three [aggregates] are equally intense and powerful, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is predominant because feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) flow into the *saṃskāra-skandha* to constitute karma that invites retribution.
Therefore, they are categorized as "karma of desire" (*kāma-karman*), meaning that karma arises from craving for the five sensory objects;
thus, these two types both belong to the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
Regarding "merely the fruit of retribution," this is because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute the present retribution.

Regarding "the end of the five fruits," this refers to the fact that among these twelve links of dependent origination, the experience of the five fruits in the present life occupies the very last position;
hence they are called the "end."
"From this point" means that from the stage of the link of sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) arise again;

there are three causes. Regarding the phrase "causal condition," the Subcommentator has here extracted the passage concerning the three types of contact (*sparśa*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to explain and establish the meaning of the three causes arising again herein.
Regarding the sequential causes and conditions, this refers to the three causes that arise again from feeling (*vedanā*).
As for the statement "namely, the afflictions and the preceding mind," the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says: "Luminous, non-luminous, and neither of the two. Its commentary explains:

"Contact associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*) is called luminous contact (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*); contact associated with defilement (*kliṣṭa*) is called non-luminous contact (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*). And... [text continues]

Contact associated with tainted (sāsrava) wholesome or neutral states is called "contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance" (*na-vidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*); thus it is said to be "neither of the two.
Here, we are precisely clarifying that ignorance is the mental state preceding craving and grasping, whereas the eightfold noble path is untainted (*anāsrava*).
The tainted wholesome or neutral states preceding it refer to the wholesome minds of humans and devas.
Regarding what the Sūtra calls "internal and external outflows": ignorance and the three inversions are termed internal outflows, while the remainder are termed external.

As for the Sūtra’s statement that "feeling and so forth do not exist," this is because feeling cannot be found when sought through the fourfold analysis; it exists merely as a conventional designation.
