The sutra states that "severing conjunction" means to employ the three provisional designations and four propositions to investigate [phenomena] until they accord with the Middle Principle of Buddha-nature; this is called severing conjunction.
Regarding the three kinds of contact (*sparśa*): contact is a mental factor (*caitasika*) that gives rise to all dharmas; it is now categorized and divided according to what arises.
Third:

If one performs an unwholesome act (*akuśala*) with the mind during the fourth moment of mind, it reveals that the preceding three moments of mind were contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*).
The same principle applies to the performance of wholesome acts (*kuśala*) and so forth.
Furthermore, another interpretation is as previously stated, which refers to the preceding commentary concerning the prior moments of affliction and so forth.
The text states that "the meaning below" refers to the meaning of the sūtra, which applies to both interpretations.

As for the distinct presence of the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) within the mind of formations (*saṃskāra-citta*), it arises because the influxes of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) enter into the mind of formations, thereby causing the mind of formations to arise [with such perversions].

Regarding the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), there are those who do not attain the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), as this is because the third dhyāna lacks the mind of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-citta*).

Furthermore, while the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) extend only to the two spheres of space and consciousness where the perception of totality exists, they are absent in the sphere of nothingness; therefore, it is said "only."
The first two are all non-syllables (*akṣara*), while those following are mostly referred to as syllables.
The ten *sarvāyatanas* (all-bases) are identical to the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas* (all-bases), as explained in the *Fajie Cidi* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm).

Regarding those that largely agree with the numerical categories: although the followers of the Numerical School do not clarify the wisdom-mind, they nevertheless point to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as the objects of perception, namely name, concept, and feeling.
"Ear. When the Buddha sometimes speaks of them collectively, he refers to the two mental states of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) to encompass all other mental states.
When he sometimes speaks of them individually, he explains each of the various mental states one by one.
The phrase "the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) and so forth correctly refers to the present text as a general statement that encompasses the specific instances.

These two meanings directly respond to the preceding question: when one explains the Dharma by means of a person, one cites the person so that the Dharma may be known; when one explains the person by means of the Dharma, one cites the Dharma so that the person may be known.
By speaking of the cessation of perception and feeling through this method of analogy, one comes to know that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise [extinguished].
Because it is extinguished, it is said to "correctly answer" the previous question.
That which is the "gate of afflictions" refers to external objects and internal faculties, as they both enter into the category of afflictions.

That which is "precisely the internal mind" refers to desire—namely, the minds of greed, hatred, and delusion—which are precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); therefore, it is said to be "precisely the internal."
The mind is able to give rise to mental desires because the minds of the three poisons arise based on preceding objects.
To speak of the effect within the cause means that the three poisons achieve their accomplishment by depending on sensory objects; therefore, the objects themselves are the cause.

The "ten kinds of conceptions" (*daśa-saṃjñā*) refer to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) along with the conceptions of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and male and female; these ten conceptions arise based on the aforementioned inverted conceptions (*viparyāsa*).

Regarding the two interpretations of the *Sāṃkhya* school: the first is the interpretation of enumeration (*saṃkhyā*), and the second is the interpretation of discourse (*sāṃkhya*). However, both of these schools clarify the number of the King (*rāja*).
The identity and difference [of these categories] are as explained in the commentary on the twenty-first point of dispute mentioned previously.

Regarding the statement that "feeling" (*vedanā*) is the first of the "ten aggregates" (*daśa-skandha*) and yet it is called the "aggregate of sensation" (*vedanā-skandha*): in ancient translations, the term *vedanā* was rendered as "sensation" (*tòng*).

Regarding "karma that produces [rebirth] but does not produce [feeling]," Zezhou says: "The initial arousal of good or evil that is able to produce a subsequent fruit is called 'karma that produces [rebirth]' (*zàoshēng yè*);

when it has not yet moistened the experience of the fruit, it is called 'karma that does not produce feeling' (*bùzuòshòu yè*). The second explanation of the meaning of the terms in the commentary is not detailed;
the rest is self-evident.

Regarding the phrase "those with black-black retribution," the upper "black" character forms one clause referring to the cause—the karma; the lower "black" character forms another clause referring to the retribution—the fruit of that karma.
The same applies to the "white-white" and other examples. "Black" refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action; "white" refers to the ten wholesome paths of action;
"mixed" refers to performing good and evil deeds alternately; and "neither black nor white" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*). These four types together constitute two [categories].
Regarding the Dharma, the first three belong to the mundane realm while the last one is supramundane.

As for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) being the fruit of cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*), the Śrāvaka vehicle maintains that because one enters the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) where there is no further retribution,
there is therefore only the present fruit of cultivation.
The names of the four continents, such as Uttarakuru and the others, are explained by reversing the transliteration as previously recorded.

Regarding "heavy suffering" and "light suffering," the term for suffering should have been written with the character for "black" (黑); it was erroneously written as "heavy black. Since "heavy black" refers to the ten unwholesome actions of the highest grade, one enters hell.
"Each possesses four gates" refers to the four aspects of the cultivation of the essence, cause, and fruit.
Although it mentions "afflictions" and so forth— where "and so forth" includes karma, existence, and suffering— and thus also consists of four,
these differ in meaning from the previous four.
I say that when Jingxi [Zhiyi] presented this passage, it also fully contained the meaning of the preceding four gates;
his division of the sutra into these four sections is his own arrangement.

As for the phrase "provisionally relying on the extant text," this means that since the extant text clarifies the retribution of the fruit, one should follow the precedent of the previous four gates. However—

There are three [ways of categorizing this]. According to the Sūtra, which states, "clinging to the fruit of craving is called grasping," when one considers the words "craving" and "causes and conditions" (such as the head), based on this explicit text, it refers to the retribution;
for it is according to the phrase "when one considers it from the perspective of the wise. Therefore, it belongs to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Thus, we know that according to the text and the object, it belongs to the retribution; whereas according to the meaning and the subject, it belongs to the Path of Cultivation.

Regarding "attaining suffering through afflictions," this refers to what the Sūtra says: "Suffering arises from the causal conditions of afflictions," and also "suffering arises from the causal conditions of karma.

One should not say [that it refers to] "invoking retribution," because the Hīnayāna speaks only of karma invoking retribution; therefore, it is here said that one attains [suffering] through afflictions.
"Suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) refers to retribution (*vipāka*).
However, these four phrases below are all anticipatory explanations of the scriptural text.

The same applies to the latter two phrases: those beginning with "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta*) also possess four phrases, and those beginning with "suffering" (*duḥkha*) likewise possess four phrases.
The preceding two lines illustrate this.

Regarding the statement that "the current text contains only nine lines," all extant versions in circulation today contain twelve lines; it remains unclear which three lines are missing from the version consisting of nine.

According to the underlying principle, if one were to define it strictly according to the sequential arising of the twelve links of dependent origination—beginning from ignorance producing volitional formations and ending with birth producing aging and death—there would be only eleven factors. However, this sūtra does not adopt that interpretation;
rather, it establishes twelve factors by showing how the four dharmas of affliction, karma, existence, and suffering arise through mutual succession.

The wheel of dependent origination consists of twelve links; however, if one discusses them exhaustively according to the fourfold principles, there must necessarily be sixteen, as explained below in the commentary.

There are cases where the preceding arises from the succeeding, such as when it is said that "afflictions give rise to karma," which refers to ignorance giving rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
The subsequent arising of what precedes is like the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*) from formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth.

Regarding the mutual arising across the links, such as the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) based on ignorance, which bypasses the intermediate six links of formations and so on—the four sets of four propositions explaining the meaning of the mutual arising of the links do not go beyond this;
this is indicated here in advance so that it may be easily understood upon reading the text.
The text states, "internal and external craving, etc."; this anticipates and indicates the subsequent sūtra passage that clarifies the karmic retribution.

As for the phrase "all are applicable," although both meanings apply, it must be taken as suffering [itself] being the primary sense; therefore, the meaning of "craving" mentioned above is somewhat secondary.

Regarding the four aspects within the essence, since the essence of causes and conditions does not transcend cause and effect, these four passages first clarify their mutual production, thereby presenting both cause and effect together;
the subsequent three passages all speak from the perspective of the result.
Regarding the passage from "Contemplating Karma" up to "these two are retributions," one should know that this causal text primarily clarifies retribution.

Since retribution necessarily arises from causes, among the twelve links, two paths belong to the category of cause; because it primarily clarifies retribution, it explains the substance [of the result] first.
Consequently, the latter three are all situated within the result. By this analogy, although the result is mentioned within the text concerning the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it primarily...
Because this section was taught as an explanation of causes, the sutra concludes here by stating: "The wise, having contemplated karma and having contemplated afflictions...

In examining any scriptural text, one must recognize the context and its proper orientation to perceive the intended meaning; for when these elements are linked like hooks and chains, if one is ignorant of them, the purpose of the text will be lost the moment the passage ends.

As for "the substance itself being existence," the substance of sentient beings in the hells consists of form and mind; because these are designated as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) and so forth, it is said that they "exist.
Regarding the phrase "one hundred and thirty-six locations," there are eight great hells: first, Saṃjīva (Reviving); second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope); third, Saṃghāta (Crushing).
The four are the Screaming Hell, the Great Screaming Hell, the Hot Hell, the Greatly Hot Hell, and the Avīci Hell; these are the eight great hells.
Each has sixteen subordinate hells, which together with the primary ones total one hundred and thirty-six, as detailed previously in the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness."
Regarding the statement that "the three realms are all suffering," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house.
When the Mahāyāna identifies craving and ignorance as the causes of suffering, it specifically refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are capable of summoning retribution.
That is to say, beneath the character "love" (愛), there are many characters.

Regarding the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna): although it is said that karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) are the causes of suffering, because one specifically grasps that karma is what can summon retribution, it is stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is secondary.
Therefore, the following citation from the sutra establishes the great meaning; it is the text from the "Chapter on the Noble Practices" (Śrāvakabhūmi).
Regarding being both cause and fruit: when ignorance conditions formative action (*saṃskāra*), ignorance is the cause and formative action is the fruit;
when formative action conditions ignorance, formative action is the cause and ignorance is the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "capable of generating the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way": although the nature of goodness in icchantikas is inherently complete, it is only through this sutra that it is revealed;
therefore, it is said to be "generated anew.
Because it is based on the teachings and does not function within the limited or inferior vehicles, it is called "rare."
To praise the Three Jewels means that the teaching is the Dharma and practice is the Saṃgha.

Regarding what is meant by "the conditions for the holy life": the teaching is able to express the practice, and because one practices in reliance upon the teaching, the teaching is the condition for practice.
This indicates that Kāśyapa is correctly asking about the teaching, not about the practice itself; as for the essence of the practice, it consists of the four immeasurables.
"The mind is the essence of the Brahma-faring" clarifies that this refers to the actual substance of the practice itself, not the ontological essence of the principle to be realized.
In the sutra, when the "Good Son" asks, "All dharmas are this," Kāśyapa poses a general inquiry and the Buddha provides a general response;
though the words are general while the meaning is specific, pointing specifically to the present sutra, it is because the phrasing is general that it leads Kāśyapa through [the subsequent stages].
To answer in detail:

all [teachings] are capable of producing the provisional practices of the practitioner through provisional dharmas, and the real practices through real dharmas. Now, the Buddha specifically focuses on the dharma that reveals the Real by opening the Provisional;
because it produces the "one practice which is all practices"—namely, the Practice of the Tathāgata—it is said that the Perfect Teaching contains the One.

Regarding the statement that "the sūtra can give rise to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and so forth": since it should be this very sūtra alone that gives rise to the holy life, for what reason did the Buddha answer,
"all phenomena" (*sarvadharmāḥ*)?

This very nirvāṇa is all dharmas; thus, this present sutra reveals that the provisional teachings of the nine realms and the three vehicles of the past are now shown to be the reality of the perfect interfusion of the Buddha-realm.
Because the provisional is itself the real, all dharmas—whether good or evil—are entirely the Brahma-conduct (brahmacarya).
Regarding the phrase "now, severing the lightest [afflictions]," this refers to the fundamental, subtle ignorance outside the realms,
which is designated as "the lightest" to distinguish it from the coarse heaviness of the branches and secondary factors within the realms.

Regarding the simultaneous severance [of afflictions], although one contemplates that the three delusions are fundamentally non-existent, it is not precluded that the coarse impurities fall away first.
Kai Shan’s *Xia* (Lower Section) clarifies that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are cultivated by those outside the ordinary stages; thus it says they "pervade the ordinary stages.

In the text where it says "pervading both internal and external," the character "internal" (*nei*) is redundant; the original text read: "The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment pervade the ordinary stages outside [the path]."
Regarding the phrase "Because of practice," the Master [Hui]xia’s commentary below refutes it, saying: "How could an external ordinary person (*bāipin*) be able to contemplate this?

It is known that this term 'internal' (*neizì*) is incorrect. Master Kaishan says: "Externally, one universally cultivates all stages; from the internal ordinary person (*neipin*) onward, one cultivates them separately.
Therefore, it is said that the second and fifth [stages] of the third and fourth [dhyānas] are both internal ordinary persons, and so forth."
The section on the Eightfold Noble Path below clarifies that both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are truly noble.
Master Guan’s commentary below refutes the tenets of those two schools to clarify that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are exclusively practiced by supramundane noble ones (*ārya*).
Such an interpretation, however, represents only one perspective and is not a comprehensive teaching; for how could it be that ordinary beings do not cultivate the path?

If one does not cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), how can one transform the state of an ordinary person? Therefore, the teachings of Tiantai are cited to clarify that there are many types of *mārga* (paths) within the factors of enlightenment, so as to avoid narrow or dogmatic attachments.

The passage stating "fully explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, etc. refers specifically to the sixth section on the objects of meditation (*viṣaya*) within the *Bodhipākṣika-dharma* chapter of that same text. Thus, it says: [the text continues].

The text states that there are four aspects of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*): first, their respective domains (*pratyeka-bhāga*); second, their mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*); third, their correlation with stages (*avasthā*);

and fourth, their sequential generation (*anuloma*). First, regarding the clarification of their respective domains: it is not necessarily the case that one must possess all the factors to be able to attain the Path; rather, three, four, two, five, single, or even eight [factors] may constitute the Path in their respective domains.

Therefore, it is said that "one attains the Path by relying on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)," and it is further stated that "this is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)" and "this is the *māra*[-victory]."

Since it is thus for the Mahāyāna *smṛtyupasthānas*, it is likewise for the other categories; these are the path-factors (*mārga-aṅga*) according to their respective divisions, not as a harmonized synthesis.
Second, regarding mutual inclusion: just as the single dharma of the *smṛtyupasthānas* includes all categories, the *Śāstra* commentary states:

"Since the *smṛtyupasthānas* include the other categories, the other categories also include the *smṛtyupasthānas*. This constitutes mutual inclusion; these path-factors are also not [merely] distinct divisions.

Regarding the reconciliation by way of stages (*sthāna-viniyoga*): as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they correspond to the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*); the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) correspond to the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*); the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) correspond to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*);

the five faculties (*indriya*) correspond to the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); the five powers (*bala*) correspond to the stage of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*); the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) corresponds to the stage of seeing the truths;

and the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) correspond to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This is reconciliation by way of stages, yet it is not [the primary form of] reconciliation. Fourth, reconciliation by way of mutual production (*anyonya-janman*):...

Just as the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) can give rise to right effort (samyakprahāṇa), right effort gives rise to the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the bases of psychic power give rise to the five faculties (indriya), the five faculties give rise to the five powers (bala), the five powers give rise to the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the seven factors of enlightenment give rise to the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga)—this is the skillful method for harmonizing and adjusting them.
Precept, concentration, and wisdom are all called "right purity. When the mind is always one-pointed, one is then able to see Prajñā.
This constitutes both the arising of characteristics and their harmonious adjustment.
Kaishan bases his position on those who practice the path of cultivation in a general manner; this refers to the fourth stage of the arising of characteristics within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, since he relies on the fact that external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) generally cultivate all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he judges it thus. If one were to clarify the case of internal ordinary persons (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) and above, it would again appear similar [to the previous analysis].
Regarding the stages:

as for the claim that one cannot attain the fruit apart from the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "True dharmas are called the untainted factors of enlightenment;

these are tainted, yet they serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for the untainted. When these skillful means lose their proper object, the true principle is difficult to realize. This is clarified in the subsequent sutra.

The holy life (*brahmacarya*) exists solely within the untainted (*anāsrava*); this is stated from a specific perspective, though by principle it should be understood as applying to both [the path and the fruit].

One attains the "fruit of division" (*bhāga-phala*) because one partially realizes the ultimate truth, and one attains the "ultimate fruit" (*atyanta-phala*) because one completely realizes the ultimate truth. The Sūtra clarifies that both the small fruit and the great fruit arise from the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Within the context of the great fruit, the meaning encompasses both the partial and the ultimate; the Sūtra states that seeing the Buddha-nature is itself the fruit of Bodhi and the Buddha.
The fruit of nature is the fruit of the fruit of nirvāṇa.
The sūtra is able to destroy perversions; it destroys the eight perversions.
It is able to destroy evil views: the first two teachings destroy the views of the three realms, while the latter two teachings destroy the view of identity.
Those who can destroy fear enter the stages (*bhūmi*) and, having dwelt therein, become free from the five fears.
"Able to produce understanding" means they give rise to a semblance of untainted understanding (*anāsrava-adhimukti*).

"The continuity of the resolve for awakening" means that the teachings of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) cause sentient beings to seek upward from the initial generation of the resolve and [to apply themselves] downward.
The transformation continues in a succession of moments until reaching the ultimate fruit, at which point it is only then called "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*);

because there is only a single mind [at that stage], these [earlier stages] are not taken up. However, the latter three minds are treated lightly because the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) arises first; thus, although they involve the grasping of signs, they are considered minor compared to the former.
Regarding the three minds beginning with sensation (*vedanā*):

it clarifies that when the five consciousnesses first encounter an object, they merely perceive its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) in a state of sudden occurrence; at this stage, the three types of conceptual construction (*prajñapti*) have not yet been established.

It is only upon entering the second moment, when they merge and flow into the mind of perception (*saṃjñā-citta*), that they are termed "established through causes" (*hetu-siddha*), wherein the preceding moment continues into the subsequent one.

The subsequent thought is called "successive conventionality" (*saṃtāna-prajñapti*); depending on other moments of mindlessness, this state of having mind is called "relational conventionality" (*apekṣā-prajñapti*).
This clarifies that the three types of conventionality reside solely within these three moments of mind; this is also stated from the perspective of their primary significance.
Therefore, knowing that the mind of consciousness already possesses the grasping of signs, the previous question addressed the gravity of the three minds;

now, in response, it is stated that even the lighter consciousnesses possess inversion. This is to know that the mind of consciousness also possesses the three types of provisional existence (*prajñapti*).
To clarify the cause by citing the effect: taking the consciousness-mind as the cause and the perception-mind as the effect;
since perception already possesses attachment and perception arises from consciousness, one knows that consciousness also possesses attachment.

If one discusses their essential natures according to what each relies upon, they constitute thirty-seven because their natures are distinct; yet when examining their fundamental categories (*gotra*), there are only nine.
As for the six consisting of faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*):
the faculty of body (*kāyendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*) constitute these six.
Regarding those remaining as one each: among the seven factors of enlightenment, there are three remaining factors, namely the last three natures; "seven" refers to the factor of joy;
"eight" refers to the factor of tranquility; and "nine" refers to the factor of equanimity.
Regarding these nine meanings of the present sutra, although their names correspond to the nine numbers in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, their meanings differ eternally;
each of the nine [categories] in this sutra contains thirty-nine chapters.
"Reality is liberation" refers to the partial [attainment], namely the four fruits of śrāmaṇya; "ultimate" refers to the complete, distinct, and supreme fruit.
When the Sūtra states that the Tathāgata previously spoke of this in this very scripture, it refers to the *Guṇarājaparivarta*.
Regarding the phrase "the first among sentient beings who know [it]": because it is known through the Buddha’s teaching, the Buddha is the root.
The phrase "because contact is not fixed," etc., correctly demonstrates and explains that the term "contact" (sparśa) possesses multiple meanings.
The phrase "all can be explained" means that encountering a virtuous friend, hearing the true Dharma, and so forth are all instances of contact;
because they are all causes of bodhi, they are collectively termed "contact with illumination."

When one enters the stage of "True Entry" (*tathatā-praveśa*), having completely relinquished all conditioned wisdoms (*saṃskṛta-prajñā*) that existed within the causal stage, one then abandons the wisdoms of the preceding stages—such as those resembling the ultimate—which remain because they have not yet destroyed ignorance;
these are all termed "conditioned. One also abandons the provisional wisdoms regarding the four fruits of the śramaṇa and other dualistic extremes.
Regarding the statement that "nine factors constitute three intentions," one may consult the sutra for the corresponding explanation. However, the sutra says:

"By means of these four factors, one is able to produce and grow the desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) for the Path. Since the enumerated factors are too many, the word "desire" (*chanda*) is redundant.

It should be understood that "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) and "desire" (*chanda*) function together as companions; thus, they are mentioned collectively, which is why this "desire" resembles "recollection" (*smṛti*) among the factors of dhyāna.
That [text] correctly clarifies mindfulness as encompassing both recollection and application; this [passage] is likewise so.
Regarding "the mind attains liberation through the sutras," the mind is precisely in a state of concentration (*samādhi*).
Within the causal stage, those who are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) should emerge from the stage of the internal ordinary person by means of pure precepts and the cultivation of the four dhyānas.
The *jñapticaturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) of the household is precisely that of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

Since it applies to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it should also be said to apply to the fruits of both the Great and Small Vehicles, because the ninth [fruit] is ultimately *bodhi*.

Regarding the double occurrence of the "consciousness-link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*): the Sūtra states that ignorance increases consciousness; since it was already stated above that "desire is named consciousness," this constitutes a redundancy.

No variant characters appear in ancient or modern editions of the Sūtra, and the absence of the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in all subsequent passages is likely due to its excision by those who were ignorant of the text.
Therefore, in his commentary on this passage, Bei Yuan explains: "Because ignorance and delusion increase karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), it is so named."

To increase [the category of] "name," the mind is termed "ignorance" (avidyā), and consciousness (vijñāna) is likewise termed "ignorance. Verifying this through such analysis, one finds that the *Northern Version* of the Sūtra also contains the word "consciousness.
Second, regarding the statement that contact is consciousness: this refers to "contact associated with ignorance" as being consciousness. If one wishes to exhaustively analyze the text of the sūtra:

As the Commentary of Zhezhou states: "The mind-consciousness taking objects as its condition is explained in terms of 'desire' (*chanda*); the six sense bases encountering the six sensory realms is explained in terms of 'contact' (*sparśa*);

and because it is capable of experiencing [the object], it is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*). Because ignorance (*avidyā*) deludes and increases karmic formations (*saṃskāra*), it is called 'increase';
the mind of ignorance is termed 'ignorance-consciousness. Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the retributive body."

Because it is their nature, it is called the "primary"; because it can produce and lead all afflictions and fetters, it is called the "guide"; because it is particularly intense among the various forms of craving, it is called "grasping";

because its karmic activity regarding existence is not in vain, it is called "substantial"; and because it is the ultimate among the causal conditions for birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is called "final."
Regarding the fifth point of analysis: because these three factors increase from the fundamental cause and are both coarse and similar, they must be analyzed.
"Excluding only the Arhat" means that only the fourth fruit is excluded, while the second and third fruits both belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the statement that "when subsequent observation is accomplished (up to) it is also called 'perception'": although its accomplishment is designated as wisdom (*prajñā*), it is still termed "perception" because the name is established based on its cause;
the preparatory means (*upāya*) is precisely that cause.

Regarding the designation of the "nine perceptions" (*navasaṃjñā*) for those first practicing them, the *Śāstra* states: "The nine perceptions are like binding the thief; the ten perceptions are like killing the thief.

They are collectively called "perceptions" (*saṃjñā*) because they can transform the mind's thoughts. They are called "perceptions" because they can overturn various inverted perceptions, such as those that calculate [existence] as permanent or blissful.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is taught that the cultivation of the ten perceptions applies to three stages; among these, the first three perceptions are explained as being for the purpose of severing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

The first four contemplations (*saṃjñā*) are taught for the purpose of severing the afflictions of thought (*citta-kleśa*); the latter three are taught for those practicing the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

This is not the case here. As stated in the preceding commentary: "If one discusses their stages, they encompass both the shallow and the deep, because even those who are newly practicing are said to cultivate the ten contemplations.

Thus, we know that these ten are cultivated by beginners as well. Furthermore, the ten contemplations in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* apply to what is cultivated in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), whereas here [in this context], it is only...
Regarding the "Great" [Treatise]:
as for the "General Outline for Salvation," the term "general outline" (dàlüè) refers to the broad framework or main principles.

One who studies the ten visualizations (*daśa-saṃjñā*) within the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) should examine and compare them to understand their similarities and differences.
The Sūtra further observes that the various devas who hear the Dharma and those at the beginning of the kalpa all hear it from others rather than seeing it with their own eyes.
Regarding the clarification of the distinctions between the ten periods in the Sūtra: the first five occur within the womb. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are seven stages within the womb;
the first seven days are called the "impure stage," resembling solidified butter—this refers to what is here termed the "membrane stage. The second seven days are called... [text fragment ends].
The third week is called the "vesicle stage" (*arbuda*), which refers to the state resembling a blister; this is what is meant here by "the time of the vesicle.
The fourth week is called the "fleshy mass stage" (*peśī*), which refers to the state resembling congealed blood; this is what is meant here by "the time of the fleshy mass.
The fifth week is called the "stage of form," so named because the various sense organs and the four limbs begin to differentiate. The sixth week is called the "hair, body hair, and nails stage."
The stage of the teeth is called the stage of possessing the faculties (*indriya-samanvāgata*) because the five faculties are fully perfected.

Now, these three stages are collectively termed the "branch-time" (*aṅga-kāla*), as it takes the four branches to be complete. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, although the first five weeks possess the body faculty and the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are not yet perfected because the other four [faculties], such as the eye, are absent;
thus, within the ten links (*daśāṅga*), this period is included under "name" (*nāman*).
"Form" (*rūpa*) is subsumed [here].
"Wei-ye" (煒燁)—according to the *Fēi* (匪) and *Wéi* (為) dialects, it means "abundant"; according to the *Sāncāng* (三蒼), it means "radiant splendor.

The three aggregates (*skandha*) constitute form; as for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this refers to the aggregate of form, the aggregate of mind, and the aggregate of that which is neither form nor mind. These are the indeterminate.
This refers to the third category (*rāśi*).

Since it can be divided into segments, the character "you" (有) in the phrase "should be made into [segments]" is likely a scribal error; thus, *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* is also called "segmented food" (*kavaḍa-āhāra*).

Regarding the definitions and characteristics of the four types of nutriment, as previously cited at the beginning of the seventeenth [section], they have been briefly explained according to the *Tattvasiddhi* and the *Abhidharma*.

Now, based on the chapter on the four nutriments (*āhāra*) from another school, this shall be further clarified. "Four" refers to their number. "Nutriment" (*āhāra*) means that which provides sustenance and benefit.

Edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) refers to matter characterized by physical form and resistance; whenever it enters the mouth, it undergoes transformation and decay, sustaining the body and benefiting the spirit, and being capable of both promoting goodness and increasing evil, it is called edible food.
As for contact-nutriment (*sparśa-āhāra*), "contact" (*sparśa*) means the act of touching or encountering.
When the mind arises toward an object that is pleasing, it can produce the two sensations of joy and pleasure, which nourish the body and consciousness, providing satisfaction and tranquility;

because this fosters evil and incites good, it is called the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*). The commentary on the *Sparśāhāra* explains that this refers specifically to the nourishment of the body, following the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Thus, that treatise states: "Contact such as cold and heat is called the nutriment of contact. As for the nutriment of volition (*manahsañcetanāhāra*):

That which consists of mental volition (*manasikāra*) refers to the objects that are considered desirable; whether they be thoughts of evil, thoughts of good, or even insentient objects, these do not need to be present before one.

Rather, it is through mere mental reflection that joy and bliss arise, sustaining both the body and the spirit; therefore, it is called "food by volition" (*manaḥ-āhāra*). Regarding the fourth, "food by consciousness" (*vijñāna-āhāra*):

"consciousness" (*vijñāna*) means the mind that cognizes, with the sense of discerning and perceiving its objects. This refers to the fact that the aforementioned three types of food mutually sustain the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The function of maintaining continuity while abiding in the world—the continuous succession of matter and mind—is precisely what is meant by "nourishing and sustaining";

therefore, it is called the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Among these four nutriments, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the other three pervade all three realms.
Because all four are capable of providing nourishment and sustenance, they are collectively termed "nutriments."
The character for *jīng* (經) is pronounced as *zàn* (贊) with the rhyme *chū-luàn* (麤亂).

The character for *hǔ-xì* (虎兕) is pronounced as *xú-lǐ* (徐里). According to the *Erya*, the *rhinoceros* (*xì*) resembles an ox; Guo Pu states that it has a single horn, is blue-green in color, and weighs a thousand *qīn*.
"Those who practice this cultivation" refers to those who constantly contemplate impermanence and so forth without interruption; therefore, it is called "the constant cultivation of perception.

Regarding the passage in the sutra, "This is called a śramaṇa," etc., it first praises the true person (satpuruṣa) for being able to still evil, and thus names them a śramaṇa (one who strives). As for *brahman* (梵): [it denotes one who has transcended worldly defilement].
One whose conduct is untainted is called a *brāhmaṇa*; being free from the clamor and agitation of birth and death is tranquility; being rid of the defilement of afflictions is purity;
and being forever free from all suffering is called liberation.
This is called the wise person’s humble praise of their own practice; because they recognize their faults and seek liberation, they are called "wise.
Their discernment of what is right and what is wrong is termed "right view," and it should be understood as that which leads to the further shore.
The section beginning with "Named the Great Physician" and ending with "praising the virtue of benefiting others" is easily understood.

The section beginning with "This is called skillful understanding" refers to the understanding of the three types of speech of the Tathāgata mentioned above, such as speech according to one's own [nature] and so forth.

Regarding the seven kinds of speech of all Buddhas—from the speech of causes mentioned above up to the speech of fulfilling wishes—they are as explained in the preceding discussion of the three types of speech.

Regarding the present [text], among the seven types [of doubt], there are further two: first, one knows for oneself; second, regarding the net of doubts arising from the merit of the two kinds of abandonment, one cuts through the nets of doubt in others.

As for the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "the ultimate of the resolve for enlightenment," the initial dwelling's resolve is the cause, while perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) is the ultimate fruit; thus, the cause—

Since the principle of the fruition is the same, there is no distinction between the two; yet, it is easy for one who has already attained sagehood to enter further into sagehood, while it is difficult for one at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) to enter sagehood from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, Kāśyapa’s prostration to the Buddha is the true cause, and his words regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) may also apply generally to the stages prior to the [first] stage.
Regarding the Kātyāyanas of the Agniveśya lineage:
their ancestors served fire, and because they were named after this ancestral occupation, their clan name became Agniveśya.

Because they could discipline themselves and mortify their bodies to master the way of serving fire—just as a vessel receives objects—they established this honorable title; they are of the Brahmin caste.
Now, fire has two meanings: first, illumination; second, burning. Illumination means that darkness does not arise, which serves as a metaphor for the extinction of delusions.

Burning means that objects do not arise, which serves as a metaphor for the vanishing of karmic fruits. Since he first realized the principle of non-arising within the Buddha-dharma, auspicious signs were manifested in advance, and his surname was given the meaning of "non-arising" (*amṛta*).
On the contrary, "one who knows nothing" is precisely one who knows non-existence; this is because in the Western language (Sanskrit) the order is inverted.

It means that by means of the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), one knows the principle of non-arising; thus it is said, "knowing non-existence. Since the family name (*gotra*) represents non-arising, the given name (*nāman*) further indicates this same meaning.

The meanings herein are very numerous; according to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), they are fully explained through the fourfold interpretation of causes and conditions (*yinyuan*), provisional teaching (*jiaojie*), original and trace (*benti*), and contemplation of the mind (*guanchen*).

Because that text is extremely extensive, it is said that the meanings are "very numerous. Here, I shall provide only the single interpretation of causes and conditions; thus, it is stated: "I shall now set forth four points.
However, one must understand that Cunda was originally a bodhisattva who manifested as a follower of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); therefore, beginning from...

At the Deer Park, he guided those with karmic affinity to attain the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the four benefits, passing through the two flavors [of milk and cream] while employing censure and purification.
Upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, he revealed the secret treasury for those who had not yet entered; now, it is revealed once more.

Thus we know that the four *siddhāntas* benefit sentient beings throughout all five flavors. If this is so, although this passage specifically clarifies the causal conditions (*nidāna*), its fundamental and manifest aspects—
Regarding the teaching by way of categories, because "beauty resides within," the subsequent four *siddhāntas* are all explained in contrast between the Deer Park [teachings] and the present sutra;
thus, one knows that its meaning encompasses the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching.
The preceding four textual passages correspond precisely to these four *siddhāntas*.

Regarding those who first attained the Way: when the Buddha turned the Dharma-wheel of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing three times at the Deer Park, Cunda attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) during that initial turning.
As for the one on the left side, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 45, states: "Śāriputra was the Buddha’s disciple on the right side; Maudgalyāyana [was the disciple on the left]."
These two disciples on the left side—facing east toward the Most Honored One of that land—were positioned with the north to their left and the south to their right.
Since the south is the realm of Yang (Yang), Wisdom was placed on the right; since the north is the realm of Yin (Yin), Supernatural Powers were placed on the left.

This is because supernatural powers arise from meditative concentration. These two entered parinirvāṇa seven days prior to the Buddha; Kāśyapa, who maintained the Dharma, succeeded to the leadership of the Teaching.
Ānanda and Kāśyapa were on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered into *samādhi*, while Ānanda was ensnared by Māra outside the Twin Śāla Trees;

for these reasons, they were all not present at the assembly. Thus it is said: "From now until the future. As for the four senior disciples whose fame for voice and virtue is universally renowned, had they been present at the assembly, it would have been appropriate to address them directly.
Since they were not present at the assembly, the present entrustment of the final charge rightfully belongs [to others].
Venerable One,
one who is good at beginning and bringing to completion should preach the Dharma when first attaining realization and likewise address the assembly when entering final nirvana;
for only the Tathāgata possesses both beginning and end, and thus causes the minds of sentient beings to give rise to joy.

The "Puyan" (Spreading Down) refers to the Three Baskets (*Tripitaka*) of the True Dharma, which is likened to the descent of sweet dew (*amṛta*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Attaining the extinction of sweet dew, one realizes the Way.
Regarding the "Three Volumes" (*Sambon*): previously, for the sake of those on external paths (*tīrthika*), one first heard [the teachings] so that they might personally overturn their heterodoxy.

Now, by means of the "present," one establishes the "supreme" for the Elder; thus, one refutes heterodoxy and practices self-cultivation to transform others, breaking through evil from beginning to end.

First, the "past" was contrasted with realization where the small was made a skillful means for the great; now, the "present" is contrasted with manifestation, revealing that the provisional is the very substance of the eternal. Self-... (the text continues).

The practice of transforming others begins and ends with entering into the principle; however, these four intentions together encompass both self and others, which can be understood by reflecting upon them.

As for the statement regarding "five persons," it should actually be said to be "four persons. The initial realization is the person who leads, while the subsequent understanding of the four others constitutes the group being led.
Since both the leader and the led are mentioned together, it is referred to as "five persons."
If one were to discuss the entrustment of the Dharma according to the lower [vehicle], it should have been entrusted only to Ānanda, Kāśyapa, and Mañjuśrī;
however, because the others had already passed away, it was entrusted to Cunda. Question: Since Mañjuśrī was present in the assembly, why was he not entrusted with it? Answer:
It was for the sake of attracting those of the Lesser Vehicle and for the sake of revealing the provisional means; therefore, it was appropriate to entrust it to Cunda.
Regarding the "Brief Exposition Opening the School": in the first two chapters, "Cundā's Lament" and "The Two Chapters," the doctrine of permanence is briefly expounded;
from the section on "Long Life" (*dīrghāyuṣka*) onwards, it is explained in detail.

As for the phrase "attaining the former limited meaning, etc.": this refers to attaining only the preceding correct contemplation while losing the subsequent refutation of heterodoxy, according to the present master.
This constitutes a complete failure because it does not answer the question;

furthermore, it fails in other respects by omitting both the preceding correct contemplation and the subsequent refutation of heterodoxy, as it was only at the conclusion of the refutation of heterodoxy that Ānanda was addressed.

Since those who have attained both paths—from the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* onwards—employ both *prahāṇa* (subduing) and *saṃgraha* (gathering) as functions of *nirvāṇa*, there is no dispute regarding the correct teaching or its circulation;
let each person rely on their own [text], for in the end, it will fulfill the purpose of the chapter.
Regarding the fact that these two meanings do not conflict: these two chapters have already entered the "Chapter on Function" (*yòngzhāng*);

even if there were further texts, they would likewise be subsumed under "Function. Inferring from this, one knows that the latter portion belongs solely to the "Chapter on Function" and that a sixth chapter cannot be opened separately.

Regarding the previous chapter’s inclusion of "evil" and so forth: although the meanings of these two chapters—including evil and including the heterodox—are distinct, both are established as chapter titles based on the person being addressed, and both fully manifest the Tathāgata’s excellence from beginning to end.

While the previous chapter clarifies this beginning and end solely within the present sutra, since Kāśyapa has now initiated the various inquiries at the start of this assembly, [the present chapter follows].
At the end of the sutra, he again addresses them in this chapter to clarify the meaning of the beginning and the end, as explained previously.

Second, regarding "that which can be seen according to what is appropriate": this refers to those whose karmic conditions are such that they should hear that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are eternal; thus, this teaching was given.

Under the four words [of the verse], the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) of our own school contemplates only the realm of the aggregates, which is precisely the same as this. It is simply because sentient beings lack...
Because the five aggregates manifest before one, they are cited as objects of contemplation in various sūtras;
whereas afflictions, illnesses, and other such phenomena do not necessarily arise constantly, and thus are not discussed here.
As for the five aggregates being the starting point, the sūtra says: "Form is impermanent," and so forth.
Nirvāṇa is that which constitutes its culmination; as the Sūtra says, "attaining the eternal form" and so forth. Nirvāṇa is a synonym for the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñatā).
The Knowledge of All Modes arises from wisdom, while Nirvāṇa arises from abandonment. Furthermore, the Knowledge of All Modes is that which realizes Nirvāṇa, and Nirvāṇa is what is realized.

Since the essence of the wisdom—the agent—and the abandonment—the object—along with their respective functions, are non-dual, it is known that this passage is identical to that in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Furthermore, regarding the question of whether the "object-conditioning mind" (*ālambana-citta*) is considered form (*rūpa*), others say: "Discerning wisdom (*prajñā*) is clear and pure; it is likened to form, and this wisdom is precisely the object-conditioning mind.

As for the phrase "how could it be like the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and so forth," because the Lesser Vehicle involves the cessation of the ashes [of defilements], there is neither form nor mind; others say that the Buddha has no form.
If the mind were entirely identical to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) doctrine, how could one use the ashes from a cow’s footprint to contain the waters of the eternal ocean?
According to the facts, it should be stated that the Buddha has neither form nor mind; as for the claim that "it is not non-existent," this is a scribal error.

The citation of the sutra below serves as proof that the mind of the formless realm transcends the sphere of mind (*manodhātu*). Since even the mind itself is surpassed by it, how much more so for anything possessing form?

Although the citation below is intended as a refutation, it instead results in self-contradiction; for the sutra states that "transcending the sphere of mind" refers to being situated in the activity of wisdom (*jñānakarma*).

Since one abandons what is not common knowledge (*asaṃvṛti*) and attains what is common knowledge (*saṃvṛti*), it is known that the activity of wisdom (*jñānakarma*) is itself the Buddha-mind. Now, if it is admitted that there is mind, how could there be no form?
What does it mean to say that the Buddha lacks a mind with form? This master cites the phrase "the sphere of mental objects" (*dharmadhātu*) as proof that the Buddha lacks a mind with form;
however, he fails to realize that the subsequent clause—"abiding in the activity of wisdom"—actually establishes its existence. Thus, he harms himself.
Regarding the "prior meaning" mentioned above: that which was discussed at the Deer Park—the impermanence of the five aggregates—is called the prior meaning.
Although there are two types, the Distinct (Bie) and the Perfect (Yuan), the former states that by destroying impermanent form one obtains permanent form;

this refers to the Distinct Teaching, wherein before reaching the stages (bhūmi), one destroys the impermanent forms of the nine realms and, upon entering the stages, obtains the eternally abiding form of the Buddha-realm. Next...
It is said that impermanent form is itself permanent form; this means that in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), from beginning to end, one realizes that impermanence is itself permanence.
Although these two aspects differ, both clarify the existence of permanent form and so forth. How can others claim that the Buddha does not possess it?
To summarize the praise and censure: the initial passage is praise; the section beginning with "All non-Buddhists... is censure.

Regarding the five types of deliberation, the first four instances all follow the calculations of non-Buddhists to slander the Tathāgata, while the final instance contradicts the calculations of non-Buddhists to praise the Tathāgata.
These are all manifestations of great skillful means (mahopāya-kauśalya) appearing as either slandering or praising, acting together to mature the conditions of sentient beings.

Because the former [teachings] are considered actual practice (*satyavṛtti*), they are disparaged; because the latter is considered expedient practice (*upāyavṛtti*), it is praised. In the second section, it says: "Some say he was born into the family of King Śuddhodana;
others say he was not born," etc. This is likely due to a failure to understand that the Tathāgata gave diverse teachings according to the capacities of his listeners;
thus, one examines these apparent contradictions and treats them as slanders against the fundamental [truth].

"Coarse" (jīng) [is pronounced *gǔ* with the *mǎng* rhyme; according to the *Shuowen*, it means a dog that cannot be attached to]. "Not comprehensive" (*bù zōng*) [is pronounced *zǒng* with the *sòng* rhyme;

it means to practice]. This sutra is the Great Dharma-grindstone (*lì*); because its levelness is like a grindstone, it is the Great Dharma-scale (*chēng*); because it can determine lightness and heaviness, it is a grindstone (*lì*).
[The character for "grindstone" (*lì*) is pronounced *lì* with the *zhì* rhyme; it is a whetstone.]
Regarding the passage "the sūtra tames Kāśyapa and others": since Kāśyapa and the others were formerly all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), the sūtra [describes them] as being filled with derision.
According to the Cangjie pian, *chi* means to treat with contempt or to mock.
To be unable to feel compassion for their madness and confusion, yet instead to mock them lightly, is precisely what defines a fool.
The character for *biāo* (鉋) in "Mount Sumeru" is pronounced *pú* (蒲交反). The character for *chán* (齚) in "to bite" is pronounced *shì* (士白反); according to the *Tōngsùwén*, "to eat" is called *chán*.

The character for *lǔ* (鹵) in "brackish soil" is pronounced *lǔ* (魯). The *Zuǒzhuan* states: "It manifests as *chún-lǔ* (淳鹵). Du Yu’s commentary notes: "*Chún-lǔ* refers to land that is saline and infertile."
Regarding the passage stating that he went to where the Buddha was and prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet: "went" means he approached;
"prostrated" refers specifically to the act of bowing performed by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as they had not yet submitted. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because the non-Buddhists follow a different teaching, they came to where the Buddha was and sat down on their own. Since laypeople are like guests, he [the Buddha] commanded them to sit."
As for the question, "How could Nirvāṇa ever be permanent?"—it is because the three characteristics are mutually identical and thus all are indeterminate.
To refute the externalist attachment to impermanence, it is said that "it is permanent"; yet this essence of permanence is itself impermanent.
Thus, permanence is identical to impermanence, and impermanence is identical to permanence; it is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Regarding those who previously faced this objection, the ancient masters established the following thesis: [the Buddha] was specifically addressing this challenge from the non-Buddhists.
The Buddha’s initial question—namely, "Is your nature permanent or is it impermanent?"—is precisely what is recorded in the Sūtra.
Regarding those who initially resisted and opposed [the Buddha], one should ask: "Why did the Tathāgata not answer their challenge directly, but instead question them about the meaning?
Therefore, the Commentary answers: "They merely used the five challenges to resist the Buddha without presenting their own thesis;
since it was unknown whether their position held that [the self] is permanent or impermanent, he first questioned them."

Because the Buddha did not immediately refute the opponent's claim that the self-nature (*ātman*) is permanent, but instead questioned whether the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) produced by that [self] are permanent or impermanent,
it is called "further questioning" (*yuanan*).

When they subsequently brought forth their argument, they replied to the Buddha’s difficult question by asserting that all dharmas, such as the "great elements" (*mahābhūta*), are entirely impermanent;
thus it was known that their calculation held the cause to be permanent while the effect was impermanent.
Therefore, it is said that they "subsequently brought forth their argument," and because they had brought forth this argument, the Buddha established [his own response] to resolve their difficulty.
"If that were so," [the text] says, and this is precisely the subsequent correct explanation of this meaning.

Regarding the phrase "it is permanent" and so forth: in order to refute the non-Buddhists who claim that the nature of the cause is permanent while the fruit is impermanent, the Buddha provisionally employs the specific teaching (*pṛthag-dharma*)—that the cause is impermanent while the fruit is permanent—to overturn and refute them.
If one proceeds according to the perfect sense (*pariniṣpanna-artha*), the cause...

If both the fruits and the eternal [nature] are so, why are they not identical? The twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) elucidated in the *Śata-śāstra* are precisely the doctrine of Kapila;
why, then, do they differ from the present text?

The commentary explains that the intent here clarifies that the *Śata-śāstra* (Hundred Treatise) was established by the Original Patriarch himself, whereas the present sutra spoken by Jāti is a modification by his descendants;
therefore, there are differences between them. The names and meanings of the three masters are as recorded previously.

As in the *Zhuangyan* (Adornment), this citation serves as an example: these are all instances where disciples arbitrarily altered the names and meanings established by their teachers, following the precedent of changing "Jati" to the meaning of "Kapila.
Regarding the argument from the perspective of a single entity: it is because within the body of a single person there exist both feces and urine.

Regarding the sūtra’s reference to "two persons," since the male and female are distinct aspects of these two individuals, their meanings are mutually manifest; thus the commentary states "and so forth.
Question: The character "root" (根) in "equal root" (平等根) is an error; it should be the character "mind" (心).
Regarding the response to that third objection— that which challenges the claim that all things produced from causes are impermanent— if one were to answer according to your own tenet,
the intent of this refutation would temporarily employ a distinct teaching to dismantle it; for since they reckon that the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped) are distinct,
we now likewise refute them by means of the subject and the object.
The "actual dharmas of suffering and happiness" refer to the suffering of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the happiness of *nirvāṇa*.

That which ultimately uses the consciousness of suffering to cultivate this happiness refers to an ordinary person within [the realm of] internal experience who contemplates the continuity [of phenomena] as being the consciousness of suffering;
by contemplating it moment-to-moment as impermanent and refining it in this way, they enter *nirvāṇa*, which is then termed "happiness. This is what is attained.

"Joy is the realization of cessation. According to this master’s intention, suffering and its cessation are established as two in contrast; because one investigates suffering until reaching its cessation, they are treated as one.

If the Truth of the Path follows this same principle, then origination and the path are established as two in contrast; because one cultivates the path to remedy origination, they are treated as one—this is that master’s view.
The interpretation [of this passage] is not employed here.
Furthermore, there is a teacher who considers what follows this to be the correct exposition:
that which is called "attaining the Way" refers to the equality of the Four Noble Truths; this is the non-duality of cause and effect, wherein both object and wisdom have vanished.
This is for the sake of equality.
If one were to rely on Master Ai (愛師) to interpret this passage, it would merely serve to expose his error of contradicting the sūtras;

for how could he now claim that the Sage is one by interpreting "one" as referring to the internal succession of the paths of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), where they investigate suffering as being pleasure? Furthermore, [the Sage] is one.
Is this the meaning?

According to Kaishan, these are all manifest traces; that is to say, they were originally great powers who manifested the rapid attainment of realization. The passage beginning with "Adornment" refers to those of actual practice (*satyavādin*).

If one were to interpret this as referring to expedient means (*upāya*), how could it manifest the Buddha’s power and the merit of his preaching the Dharma? Thus, [the former interpretation] is correct.

Although there are these two interpretations, the meaning of the former teachings does not accord with this present sutra; one must know that the provisional reliance on the Lesser Vehicle to demonstrate the attainment of fruition is intended only to certify that the fundamental nature is perfect, eternal, and constant—this alone being the intent of the present teaching.
To say that the severance of afflictions constitutes *nirvāṇa* is to refute the obscuration of principle and reveal the manifest, originally existent, and eternally abiding *nirvāṇa*.
This is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).
As for the phrase "non-arising" and so forth, because afflictions are themselves nirvana, it is called "non-arising.
One who deems this explanation appropriate should instead provide an explanation of severing the afflictions.
If a phenomenon were non-existent through cessation, it would explain the sūtra which states that "having eliminated the afflictions is called nirvāṇa.
This is equivalent to mutual non-existence: just as there is no nirvāṇa where ordinary beings have their afflictions, like there being no horse among oxen;
and just as there are no afflictions where noble ones abide in nirvāṇa, like there being no ox among horses.
Now, to clarify that birth-and-death is inferior, the correct principle is shown: because birth-and-death is identical to nirvāṇa, it is said that "nirvāṇa is primordially present.
Since both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are mutually identical and thus properly possess one another, the mutual absence of oxen and horses cannot serve as a valid analogy.
Here, for the sake of addressing non-Buddhists, the explanation is given from a distinct perspective.
Although there is no mutual presence between the superior and inferior categories of oxen, this does not constitute the meaning of impermanence.

While there is no horse within the category of oxen, to say that there is a horse does not contradict the fact that although a horse is absent from the location of the ox, it exists separately outside of it;
this is not the same as the non-existence of a rabbit's horns.

"Ultimately, that which was originally non-existent now exists" means that while there is no horse where the ox is, this is "original non-existence"; that there is a horse outside the ox is "present existence.
Nirvana is also like this; one should likewise cite the analogy of birth-and-death to illustrate it, but for the sake of brevity it is omitted here. If one were to provide the full correspondence:
One should say that within birth-and-death there is no nirvana; this is "original non-existence," whereas birth-and-death exists now, and nirvana is an example of what exists now.
When the sūtra speaks of the "non-existence of different characteristics," it refers to mutual non-existence.

Regarding the difference in the suitability of the soil: because the nature of honey in the western lands is hot, it can treat cold conditions, which is not the case for the nature of honey in this region.

As for those who harbor doubts regarding existence and non-existence within the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), these doubts of existence and non-existence are precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), namely, the clinging to existence.

Because it is the unobstructed Middle Way, it is called "existence"; because the essence of the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), it is said that [defilements] such as those of existence truly exist.
As for the phrase "merely lacking the grasping of marks," this means that views and thoughts constitute the defilements of grasping marks.

Regarding the phrase "the true outflow-free [state] below the *cāturdīśa*": this refers either to the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) or, perhaps, it refers only to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
Since it says that one truly does not receive retribution, is this not the meaning of the Lesser Vehicle?

There is no need for laborious analysis; "resolving the essence" (*jiètǐ*) refers precisely to the essence of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Since it is outflow-free, there is no retribution.
There is no delusion within this understanding.
This passage from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is cited by Zhaoti to explain a difficulty; fearing that others might cite the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* to challenge his own doctrine, he provides this explanation.
"Similar outflow-free" refers to the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).
"Outflow-free as being led" refers to the first three fruits of the Hīnayāna and the stages prior to the Buddha-ground (*buddha-bhūmi*) in the Mahāyāna;

it is not [the grasping for] what is right, which is called the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*). Because views lead to the three miserable realms (*apāya*) that are to be feared, they are called the fear of views (*dṛṣṭi-bhaya*). Because views burn, they are called the heat of views (*dṛṣṭi-paridāha*).
Because they entwine the mind and do not leave it, they are called the entanglement of views (*dṛṣṭi-paryutthāna*).

Regarding "as for seeing the one who can speak," the sutra proceeds from the Tathāgata; that which is called "inferior" refers to the ability to see and the ability to speak without giving rise to the four attachments.
To "see" means to see according to the capacities of beings and to "speak" means to preach the four [truths] accordingly.
Regarding "as for seeing," it should be understood as the completion of the number one. As for "the perfection of the name," ten tens make a hundred, which is the perfection of the great number.
"Perfectly complete and upright" means being endowed with three thousand [realms]; thus it is called "perfectly complete. Because they are neither vertical nor horizontal, it is called "upright.

Furthermore, the hundred years may be used as a metaphor for the hundred worlds; since the hundred worlds necessarily comprise three thousand [realms] which are inherently possessed by the mind alone, it is said that the hundred years are "complete."
Regarding "whether together or separate": "together" refers to both before and after; "separate" refers to neither before nor after.

Having already refuted the four modes of existence (*catuskoṭi*), the four *siddhāntas* are provisionally taught as before and after according to the capacities of beings, so that those with such karmic conditions may realize there is no before or after.

In the second part of the *Cundī-varga*, regarding the statement "affection is present," the phrase "why speak of it as past? is a difficulty raised by the opponent himself.
This explanation was provided because [the author] forcibly introduced it out of fear of being further challenged by the opponent.
To claim that craving arises from formations means that this craving already belongs to the past and is not present craving;
thus, the meaning does not accord with the text, making such an interpretation forced.
To claim that ignorance and craving are "new" refers to the ignorance that moistens birth at the moment of initial conception in the womb, as well as present craving.
Since both arise in the present life, they both belong to the "new"; this is stated specifically with reference to the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).

However, when the Sūtra speaks of them as "old," it does so in relation to the path of karma (*karma-mārga*); because the delusions (*moha*) are able to augment karma and thus exist prior to the karma, they are termed "old."

Regarding the phrase "because it takes up the conditioned": if one were to interpret this directly as referring to the karmic paths themselves as being the cause that invites the fruit of suffering, then the cause would be old while the fruit is new.

However, when the Sūtra speaks of "new," it refers to karma in relation to the afflictions (*kleśa*); since karma arises subsequently, it is termed "new. This master’s interpretation of the meaning is extremely convoluted;
furthermore, he disregards the fact that "taking up" (*upādāna*) refers to the afflictions and erroneously judges it to be karma, thereby inviting [this confusion].
This is now refuted.
[The phrase] "That which is suddenly new" is an error; it should have been written as "not a cover. This is a critique of the ancients:
if you take afflictions, ignorance, and craving to be "new," then since they are also afflictions, how can they be considered "old"? Therefore, it says: "That which is not."
[The text] states:
"They are the 'conditioned' (*saṃskṛta*). Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—all these are refuted [as being the cause].

Since ignorance, craving, and grasping are both afflictions (*kleśa*), how can two [afflictions] suddenly become the 'grasping-link' (*upādānāṅga*) which belongs to karma? This is merely taking afflictions to be karma, suppressing the new [links] to be the old."
To contradict one's own statement—how could such an error be so? Therefore, it is said that this is most unacceptable.
As for "clinging arising from ignorance and craving," one should have stated "clinging arises from existence"; the character "existence" (有) has been omitted.
That which constitutes the branches and the secondary is ignorance and craving, as these are the root; thus, grasping and becoming are the branches and the secondary.
This rectifies the aforementioned errors: the first teacher’s error was in taking the present [existence] as a fault, while the second teacher’s error was in taking afflictions as karma.

Regarding those who agree with Master Guan, the present school adopts Master Guan’s interpretation.
