This refers to the beginning of manifest delusion; this refers to the end of manifest delusion. Because the initial delusion is separately received, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).

This refers to the final stage of the present cause, where the meaning of the "new" becomes self-evident. These meanings of "new" and "old," together with the four interpretations of the former masters, now total four.
The excellence of the present master’s [interpretation] is beyond praise; I shall now privately add one further explanation to clarify the intent of the Sūtra more fully.

The meaning can be understood from the statement that they "belong to" (*paryāpanna*) ignorance. Although craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is a manifest defilement, when compared to grasping (*upādāna*) and existence (*bhava*), it arises earlier;

therefore, it too belongs [to the past]. Since grasping and existence arise subsequent to craving, they are both termed "new. As for why only afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are cited to illustrate the "new" and the "old":
these two serve as the causes capable of summoning the fruit of suffering; since the cause ceases, the fruit perishes—it is with reference to this that [the distinction is made].
Second:
"Those who have mastered the classics" means those who possess benevolence (*ren*) and rectitude (*ya*).
Regarding "those who come to seek instruction through the classics," the *Zuozhuan* states: "To consult with the virtuous is called *zi* (inquiry)."
As for opening the inquiry, the Sūtra says: "In accordance with whatever you ask, I shall answer.

There are three kinds [of afflictions], namely the three poisons; ten kinds, namely the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*). The three poisons are delusion (*moha*), while the ten unwholesome actions are karma.

If one asks whether the three mental [unwholesome actions] among the ten unwholesome actions are not also delusion, the answer is: those that correspond to the physical and vocal [actions] belong to karma, whereas those that exist only in the mind...
The mental ground belongs to the afflictions; "all existences" refers to the twenty-five existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

Those who have attained deliverance in part are the *anāgāmins*, for they have exhausted the afflictions of the desire realm and partially realized *nirvāṇa*; thus, they are said to have attained it "in part."

The *Upāsaka-sūtra* clarifies that [the period of probation] must necessarily be four months; the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is the same. The Vinaya records that there was a naked ascetic named Poṣadha who debated with Śāriputra;
[Śāriputra] silenced him and he sighed, saying: "If even one as small as a *māṣa* bean is thus, how much more so one as majestic as this!
Subsequently, he went to where Upananda was and requested ordination; later, when questioned on the meaning [of the doctrine], he was unable to answer. Thus it is said.
He gave rise to the thought: "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are foolish, ignorant, and lacking in knowledge," and he immediately abandoned the path. A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"If a follower of another school comes to seek ordination, he must live together with the community for four months."
"Merely for one season" means that according to the Buddhist system, three seasons are established— spring, summer, and winter— and thus one season consists of four months.
Regarding "those whose faculties and dispositions differ," this refers to those with sharp faculties who do not necessarily require four months.
Some speak of "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*); *śamatha* is translated here as "stopping" or "concentration," while *vipaśyanā* is translated as "contemplation" or "wisdom.
As for Mafu and Beidu, they were both figures from the Eastern Jin period who had no recorded names; we only know that they constantly wore hempen tunics (*maju*).
Furthermore, he was able to cross waters by riding upon a bowl, and thus the people of the world established this as his title; his life story is related in the *Liang Zhuan*.
As for the character *rú* (襦), according to the *Shuowen*, it refers to a short tunic.

However, regarding the division of the text among individuals, these scriptural sections were not personally divided by the Buddha himself; since they pertain to human affairs, their principles are naturally explained [through such conventions].
Because it selects the excellent, it is divided into four sections based on the *Guanshi* (The Teacher of Contemplation).
Regarding the conclusion of the "Questions of Hongguang": Hongguang is the ninth non-Buddhist teacher in the subsequent scripture;
since all ancient masters maintain that this is related to the doctrinal positions established by this *Naiyi* (Robe-wearer), he raises a question to examine and distinguish the response below.
The question, "The beginning refers to the flow from [the source]," and so forth, employs the seven types of birth and death according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* to correlate with these words.
Regarding the seven types: first, flowing-in; second, emerging-back; third, segmented; fourth, expedient means; fifth, causal conditions;

sixth, having a subsequent existence; and seventh, having no subsequent existence. "Flowing-in" is the beginning of delusion regarding the True [Nature], while "emerging-back" is the turning away from the false.
Regarding the statement that "the beginning of the question is the end of the question," this means that the commencement of *nirvāṇa* is the conclusion of *saṃsāra*.
As for the Buddha’s frequent silence, it refers to his refusal to answer the fourteen difficult questions cited previously.
Furthermore, as for the question "from where does it come," this is refuted by the previous commentary regarding the meaning of the "cave of consciousness.

We know that the answer "it does not go" is given because the Buddha’s response—that it does not go—addresses the prior objection; thus, we know that the preceding question was not an objection concerning its flowing from elsewhere.
Therefore, the Tathāgata explains in accordance with the question: if the question were about flowing from elsewhere, the Buddha would certainly not have answered as he did.
The section "Under the *Nāṃśī* (Nan yi)" correctly demonstrates the meaning of the question. First, the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) and the citation of the text;
then, under "Explaining this," the divergent interpretations of two masters.

Regarding the statement that "one gives rise to craving before the birth-aggregate (*upapatti-skandha*)," this refers to seeing the hells and subsequently giving rise to craving while actually abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

"Clouds arise before the shadows" means that when there is a body and there are afflictions, both refer to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Furthermore, it refers to the arising of craving, or the very moment it arises.
"Immediately obtaining a body" means that by giving rise to craving for the body of the intermediate state, one obtains the body of the rebirth-linking aggregates (*pratisandhi-skandha*).
Regarding those whose afflictions prior to death arise subsequently:
because they give rise to craving for the aggregates of birth (*upapattibhava*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), craving moistens birth after the aggregates of death (*mṛtyubhava*).

This does not refer to the body of the intermediate state itself, but rather concerns the arising of delusion after death to undergo the aggregates of birth; thus the Sūtra says, "On the contrary, one again gives rise to craving and is born therein."
The following section cites the Buddha and others; the sutra begins from the words "For what reason? and so forth.

If it were the case that the afflictions existed first while the body and other aggregates did not exist at all, this would be an objection based on the non-Buddhist view that sentient beings have a beginning.
Since there was originally no body, from whom could the afflictions have arisen at that time? Therefore, below, Jingxi says: "All... [and so on].
A Mahāyāna sūtra states that "beginninglessness" refers not only to the body but also to afflictions (*kleśa*); for if one were to precede the other, that one would then have a beginning.

Thus we know that when ancient masters said, "The streams of existence do not come from a single path," they meant that while the origins are lost, there is the principle of performing wholesome and unwholesome deeds throughout immeasurable lifetimes;
this is why it was refuted by our present teacher. One should understand that this sūtra is indeed correct.
He challenges the Buddha’s teaching on dependent origination and the moistening of birth by raising a side-argument based on the non-Buddhist schools' view that there is a beginning.
He asks: "If afflictions are further caused by afflictions, then could it be said that when the body did not yet exist, there were afflictions?
If they do not arise from the body but instead arise from afflictions, and subsequent afflictions exist because of prior afflictions—if this were so..."

Afflictions cannot be the first; because the affliction of the preceding body further arises due to the affliction of the one before it, such a succession of mutual causality continues infinitely, meaning that the affliction of the preceding body cannot be the very first.
To summarize these three meanings, the Sūtra says: "prior, subsequent, and simultaneous. This refers to the case where one delusion is prior, while the two bodies are subsequent.
The afflictions of the three bodies arise simultaneously with the prior afflictions.
These ornaments, such as garlands and the like, are similar to the headgear, crowns, and sashes used here in this land to adorn the body.
"Craftsmen who measure wood" refers to taking measurements; the *Zuozhuan* states: "When there is timber in the mountains, the carpenter measures it.
"Wheels and carriage" (*jing cheyu*)—the character *jing* is pronounced as the opposite of *zhu*; according to the *Shuowen*, it means "carriage."
"Who carved the markings on the mussel? Who engraved the patterns on the clam? Who painted them? This serves as supporting evidence for the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Although the sūtras merely mention turtles and the like without referring to mussels or clams, the tenets of these non-Buddhists are quite similar to those held by Master Zhuang of this land;
thus, Zhuangzi says: "The crane is not whitened by daily bathing, yet it is white; the crow is not blackened by daily smearing, yet it is black."
Furthermore, Hei said: "Does the rain create the clouds, or do the clouds create the rain? Who bestows these [showers]? All of this is simply natural.
Regarding the term *jìngdiào* (經釣), Fú Qián stated that "to fish with bait is called *èr* (bait)."
"Nature is their thesis" means that the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is their tenet.
"The Buddha refutes them accordingly" means that because these non-Buddhists merely reckon the five great elements to be eternal while all other phenomena are impermanent,
and they claim both are devoid of causes and conditions, they are refuted together.
Regarding "that which should not be sacrificed to," the *Erya* states that the spring sacrifice is called *ci*; the commentary notes that the word *ci* signifies "to feed. The *Li* says:
"Praying and sacrificing, performing rituals, and providing offerings for the spirits and deities.
As for "transgression" (*zong*), the Sutra says: "One should know that all phenomena each have their own fixed nature (*dingxing*)," which constitutes transgression.
The Sūtra anticipates an objection:
if sugarcane merely maintains its own nature at all times, why does it produce juice, syrup, honey, and so forth? This serves as proof that all things arise from causes and conditions.
Regarding "if it has been kept for the duration of wine and is not drunk": this refers to fermented liquids such as grain syrup or honey that have stood long enough to transform into wine;

if one drinks them, one commits a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding "later becoming bitter wine" (*kaṣāya-kvātha*): "bitter wine" means vinegar, referring to wine that has transformed into vinegar; drinking it carries no offense.

Regarding the phrase "is immediately non-existent" (*jì wú*) in the context of the individual refutations: among the dual refutations, one merely refutes the sequence [of before and after], while the individual refutations merely refute the simultaneity;
because these three meanings are not complete, it is said that they are "immediately non-existent.

Regarding the phrase "it exists" in the context of the concluding refutation: this refers to what the Sūtra says—that the meanings of "before and after" and "simultaneity" are all impossible, and thus the three [meanings] are fully present.
This is the meaning.
Regarding the next section on "correctly answering the three difficulties," there is a textual error; it should read "next, answering the primary difficulties.

As for the phrase "coming in pairs," this clarifies that among the non-Buddhists' primary difficulties, the difficulty regarding afflictions comes first, followed by the difficulty regarding the body.
Because this is a lateral objection raised in contrast [to our position], it is said that it does not represent his original intent.

As for the statement "it still establishes my own thesis," this clarifies that the Buddha never taught that the body existed prior [to the afflictions]. If you claim it existed prior, that is merely your own assertion;
when it is refuted by me, it instead establishes the point I have established: that the afflictions are the cause of the body.
The "simultaneity" excluded here is not the simultaneity definitively asserted by non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) regarding the presence of the effect within the cause or the cause within the effect;
rather, it refers to that which they clearly assert as simultaneity, which is a false conception (mithyā-kalpanā), and thus it is said: "This, however, is untenable."

Regarding this "simultaneity of before and after": although afflictions serve as the cause and the body serves as the effect—such that the cause precedes and the effect follows—the afflictions and the body nonetheless exist at one and the same time; therefore, it is said to be "before and after yet simultaneous."
Furthermore, although there is a simultaneous occurrence [of cause and effect], it is only by depending on afflictions that a body can exist; thus, it appears as if the cause precedes the effect.

Therefore, one should know that from the perspective of principle (*li*), they are simultaneous, whereas from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), they follow a sequence of before and after. Since this is self-evident in the following text, the commentary states "and so forth" (*yunyun*).

Regarding "the establishment of conditions through the effect," the first chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "Examination of Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*), states: "The establishment of conditions depends upon the effect;

since the effect, in turn, depends on what precedes it, how can that which has no effect yet be called a condition? The verse of the treatise says: "Whether the effect exists or does not exist prior to the conditions, both are impossible.
If it does not exist beforehand, what could the conditions condition? If it already exists beforehand, what use are the conditions? This is the general [summary].
This refutes all [theories of] causes and conditions. Now, this sutra clarifies that "at one time" refers to the sequence of before and after;
since the meaning of that [previous text] which refutes and this [present text] which establishes differs, it is said that there is a distinct intention here.
It is not that only the body is beginningless, nor that only afflictions are beginningless; because sentient beings have no beginning, both afflictions and the body are likewise beginningless.
This is what is taught in the definitive teaching (siddhānta).

Now, in the following section of this sutra, because it is appropriate for those with such capacities to hear the provisional teaching, the intention is to provide an antidote to destroy delusions; therefore, it speaks of afflictions first.
Nevertheless, as it is spoken while still carrying the underlying principle, since the principle has no sequence while phenomena do have a sequence, it says "although."
Therefore, one should know that when the true principle and so forth do not accord with the capacities [of beings], they instead become other dharmas.
When the "true" is explained below in terms of the true principle, cause and effect are solely mind; how could there be a distinction between before and after?

This is not only the case for the past and present—it is likewise so for all—because everything is equally endowed with the three thousand [dharmas] by virtue of the inherent principle, causing them all to converge in non-duality.
Why is this? The following passage interrogates and explains the meaning of the absence of priority and posteriority.
Regarding the non-duality of cause and effect: how could the phenomena of cause and effect be separated from the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) of the realms?

Since the ten suchnesses of each realm coexist within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), and there is no distinction within that single thought-moment, how could there be any duality? Therefore, it is said they are "non-dual."
Regarding the identity of the substance of form and mind: whether in cause or effect, nothing exists apart from form and mind. Form is created by the mind; its very substance is mind.
Form is itself mind, for there is no phenomenon external to mind. Mind is itself form, for there is no phenomenon external to mind. Therefore, it is said that their substance is one.

Regarding the three paths being non-contradictory up to the ultimate: the path of suffering is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the path of afflictions is *prajñā*; and the path of karma is liberation (*vimukti*).
If the path is the fruit, then the two paths are the cause. The three paths within the ten realms are all identical to the three virtues (*triguṇa*);
they are neither vertical nor horizontal, for their principle is equal in a single instant (*kṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is said that in one thought-moment there is no contradiction.

Regarding "the five aggregates (up to) equality in principle": from the liberation of form through to the liberation of consciousness, the five aggregates of the hundred realms are all immediately liberation.
Because these five liberations mutually integrate as one and do not conflict within a single thought-moment, it is said that "in a kṣaṇa they are equal in principle.
To state the essential point: the three thousand realms are subsumed within a single thought-moment without exception; cause and effect are simultaneous. Why, then, should one harbor delusions?
The essential point lies in clarifying the intent of the sutra: in ultimate reality, there is fundamentally no sequence of before and after.
It is only because non-Buddhists cling to the notion that cause and effect do not exist that [the teaching] clarifies prior causes and subsequent effects in order to shatter their attachment.

Once these false attachments are destroyed, the single true nature is identical to the vast void; how could there then be any distinction between prior causes and subsequent effects, nor any differentiation between internal delusions and external bodies? Therefore...
It is said: "The void has no before or after, no inside or outside;
who is it that gives? (T.30, p. 296b). This passage generally reveals that the entire sutra shares this same nature.

One should know that although the names and characteristics of each fascicle and chapter differ, their ultimate destination does not transcend the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*). Therefore, by synthesizing the particulars to form a whole, the title of the work is established.

It is said that the thirty-six fascicles follow only from *nirvāṇa* and accord with it; they establish the designation "nirvāṇa" solely by conforming to the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) which are their expressed meaning.
As for the fifty-two [fascicles] below the thirty-six, these are the teachings that express [the meaning], while the fifty-two assemblies are those who receive the teachings.
When one who has realized this truth teaches others to realize it, how could it transcend this principle? What was called *nirvāṇa* above is here called *buddhadhātu*;

though the names differ, the essence of the principle is identical. The three extinctions and the three causes are precisely the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Those who understand this through the "beggar’s robe" are people for whom the teaching is timely;
those who remain deluded while guarding the stump are the assembly for whom the conditions for connection are being established.

The two sections consist of the first part, which clarifies the ultimate reality (*tattva*) at one time, and the second part, which encompasses both the provisional teachings and their subsequent refutation.
When the provisional is discarded and the ultimate alone remains, the single principle becomes increasingly manifest.
This is the essential method for resolving doubts; how could it be mere empty words?
The traditional explanation states that "lowering the mind" (下意) must refer to the very beginning of sentient beings for cause and effect to be simultaneous;
otherwise, it is merely a case of cause preceding and effect following.
Since the acquisition of a body through karma necessarily depends on afflictions (*kleśa*), once karma has been moistened by afflictions, it is further moistened by afflictions.
Because it moistens karma for its arising, it draws forth the fruit; because it moistens birth, one receives a body; thus it is said that [birth] must necessarily depend on these.
Therefore, within the text, two types are listed. Regarding "moistening karma": this refers to the performance of the three types of karma due to afflictions (*kleśa*).
Just as a sprout can grow and flourish when moistened by water, it is called "moistening karma. Regarding "afflictions moistening birth": this refers to the moment of first entering the womb.

Because one gives rise to attachment toward the mother and aversion toward the father, and by virtue of these afflictions subsequently receives the retribution of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, they are called "afflictions that moisten birth.
These delusions are precisely present at the very beginning of the aggregates of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
If the body as fruit is considered "distant," then moisture from past karma induces a retribution in the present, and moisture from present karma induces a retribution in a future life;
since the separation of births is remote, they are not simultaneous.

The passage from the Sūtra cited below—which states that one must rely on afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to obtain a body—precisely clarifies the afflictions that moisten rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*).
As the preceding commentary stated, when one first perceives hell as a result of evil conditions, one conversely gives rise to attachment; this is precisely of that same category.

If one follows the citations from various masters below, regarding the point at which the defilements that moisten rebirth arise, both Sengren and Lingwei maintain that these defilements arise at the very beginning of the *upapattibhava* (the state of birth);
thus, they establish the principle of the simultaneity of cause and effect.

Other masters, however, maintain that the defilements arise during the *maraṇabhava* (the state of death) to moisten the next life, which does not entail the principle of simultaneity; this latter view is not accepted here.

However, the present reliance on the "later interpretation" refers to the interpretation of the *Lingwei* (Flavor of the Spirit); thus, the concluding remark below states, "I have briefly gathered the teachings of the *Lingwei*.
The phrase "it may be said" below indicates the current meaning. Generally, when citing three passages, the first cites the *Kāśyapaparivarta*, followed by the *Daśabhūmika*.

The subsequent citations from the *Anupūrvasamudgata-sūtra* all serve as proof that the defilements which moisten rebirth and consciousness arise simultaneously; this is precisely the meaning of cause and effect being simultaneous.

Within the text, there is first the citation of the scriptural passage, followed by the explanation of the meaning under the heading "moistening rebirth. Regarding the initial citation, the phrase "craving, ignorance, etc.
refers to the fact that because one harbors feelings of aversion or attachment toward one's parents, one consequently takes conception in the womb; hence it is said, "one obtains [rebirth]."

Abiding in the life-span, the mind that possesses outflows (*āsrava*) and grasping (*upādāna*) is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*). The seeds of feverish affliction (*paritāpa*) are the delusions that moisten rebirth (*jāti*).

Because the mind of consciousness in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) gives rise to delusion, it causes the manifest consciousness to rely upon the womb; therefore, it is said that the seeds of feverish affliction and existence arise.
It is the seed of the outflows (*āsrava*).
This explains the meaning of "moistening birth" (*upapatti-sneha*) and its gradual preparation across the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the discrepancy [in the text], "異" (*yi*) should be "惑" (*huo*); it is an error. This means that although the delusions (*kleśa*) which moisten birth exist prior to the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), [they are nonetheless the seeds].

It arises precisely because the deluded consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is tainted (*sāsrava*); therefore, it gives rise to delusion, causing the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to take on a womb.
Thus, it is said that this [consciousness] "moistens birth," which concludes the point.

This constitutes the lower fetters; it clarifies that according to the two sūtras, because delusion arises from consciousness and causes consciousness to take up rebirth in a womb, it is said that "the mind with outflows and grasping produces the seeds of feverish affliction."
The phrase "already having the lower" (yǐ yǒu xià jí) clarifies that what is elucidated in the three sutras refers to the initial existence within the skandhas of birth;

since the defiled consciousness is precisely the fruition of retribution, is it not the case that the body and the delusions exist simultaneously? Therefore, it is said that this is the meaning of "attaining" (zhì).
The reading "three meanings" (sān yì) found in some editions is an error.
Those who briefly adopt the discourse on the *Lingwei* (The Mysterious Flavor) have already demonstrated this in the preceding text by following the *Lingwei*.
Although it is stated that "the former reaches [the latter]," one must not cite the previous objection regarding the *nāmakāya* (name-body).
Now, in answering the point that these meanings exist simultaneously: although cause and effect are simultaneous, there is still the state where the cause precedes and the effect follows.
How could this meaning be the same as the non-Buddhists' conceptualization of self-nature? Therefore, it is said that it is uniquely capable of overturning such heterodox objections.
As for the principle of "mutual causality," mutual causality refers to the sequence of before and after.
To clarify further that all phenomena truly possess causes and conditions is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on correct causes and conditions (*samyag-hetu-pratyaya*).
To state directly below [the opponent's view] is the heterodox cause and condition (*mithyā-hetu-pratyaya*) of the externalist; this is how the Buddha refutes them in return:
"Since you do not permit me to speak of correct causes and conditions, you likewise should not speak of heterodox causes and conditions."
Regarding the "three teachers of the non-Buddhists," they are as previously described: Kāpila, Sāṃkhya, and Lokāyata.
As for their school, it refers to the various non-Buddhist traditions.

Regarding those who assert that birth arises within the present single lifetime, these outsiders merely calculate that from *prakṛti* (the primal nature) arise the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, according to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
It states that having a "subject" (*yǔ zhǔ*) and having a "substratum" (*yǔ yī*) serve as the causes and conditions; it does not say they arise from the causal power of past karma.
For this reason, these causes and conditions differ from those of the Buddha.
"Subject" (*zhǔ dì*) and "substratum" (*yī dì*) are, in Sanskrit, called *dravya* (translated here as *zhǔ dì*) and *guṇa* (translated here as *yī dì*).
If form (*rūpa*) is a *guṇa* (quality) belonging to fire, then it stands in a reciprocal relationship of being both the primary subject and the support;

just as the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the primary subjects and the five sense organs (*indriya*) are the supports, so too, when objects are apprehended by means of the organs, the five organs are the primary subjects and the five objects (*viṣaya*) are the supports.
Therefore, it is said that "form is a *guṇa* belonging to fire."

The phrase "and so forth" means that the wind element creates the nose, the water element creates the tongue, and the earth element creates the body; the same applies to their respective primary supports.
Since the primary is the cause and the support is the condition, there is the principle of causal conditions for the mutual arising of the elements within a single lifetime.
Regarding the refutation of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*): they maintain that the nature of earth is solidity, and so on up to the nature of space being non-obstruction;

these essential natures are intrinsic and not produced by causes and conditions. Since the five great elements are thus, all things are likewise so, for this establishes the principle of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, the Buddha refutes such false attachments by showing that the five great elements follow conditions and do not maintain their own intrinsic nature.

Regarding "this earth-element of that house": because non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon substances such as ghee and wax to be the earth-element, the Buddha refutes their attachment to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by means of this.
Or, when it acts as water and so forth: when it encounters fire, it melts into water; when it is cold, it solidifies into earth.

Regarding the enumeration of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), the Buddha extensively refuted the two great elements of earth and fire; since these two lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the remaining three may be treated by analogy.

As for the statement that the three [remaining] great elements and so forth are not mentioned, this explains that the "nature of the five great elements" in the sutra refers precisely to the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If...

If there are no causes and conditions, why do you not say that the three great elements and the four great elements must necessarily be explained? Since the five great elements must certainly be explained, are they not causes and conditions?
When the Sūtra says "just as worldly people," etc., it cites an example to challenge you: if you take the five great elements as a category for all phenomena, what [fault] is there?

People of later generations say that when those who have left the household life maintain the precepts with diligence, one might as well say that even a *caṇḍāla* is diligent in maintaining the precepts.
Regarding these two pairs, this [text] employs the meaning of "non-Buddhists" (*bāhyaka*) from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Cheng lun) to explain this passage.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Fragrance," the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the initial question asks:

"Because various fragrances such as *tāmālapatra* are combined, their fragrance differs from the original; does this mean that these various fragrances further produce a different fragrance? The answer states:

"Due to the combination of fragrances, a different fragrance is further produced, just as when blue and yellow colors are mixed, green is further produced. There are those who hold [this view] based on the seed.

Due to the causal conditions of various karmic seeds, various fragrances arise. Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas claim that white arsenic, lead, tin, gold, silver, copper, and so forth are all substances of fire (*tejas*), yet because fragrance exists within them, they know that fragrance does not belong to earth alone;
thus it is said that fragrance is taught as belonging to earth.
From "As for the latter pair" onwards, the entire passage is from the third chapter of that treatise, the "Chapter on the Four Great Elements and Their Characteristics.
Regarding the statement, "That which does not follow the conditions of cold is earth": you claim it was originally water; therefore, why do you not say it is earth?
Is this not due to specific causes and conditions?

This refers to the "difficulties of the water chestnut" (jijiao nan), meaning the oblique difficulties of the water chestnut. It is so called because one uses the initial movement of the wind to challenge the subsequent freezing of the water;
challenging the latter by means of the former is termed "the difficulty of the water chestnut."

If one were to raise an objection by way of analogy—that is, a lateral, simultaneous objection—this would mean using the first [point] here to challenge the first there, and the latter [point] here to challenge the latter there;
this is called an "objection by analogy. It is only because the meaning of the scriptural text applies to both phrases that this is explained with such ease.
There must be things that do not move and yet are not called "wind"—this is likely a scribal error for "name";
for if a thing does not move, it is not named "wind. Why then can that which does not flow still be named "water"? This is a cross-examination using an analogy.
Now, the subsequent analysis of the term "ji-jiao" (angularity/corner) accords perfectly with the scriptural text.
The passage beginning with "Water originally... merely means that it is difficult for water to freeze after it has been moved by the wind.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent examples, they can all be seen by following the text itself.
When referring to that which is frozen as "frozen," one simply says "frozen water" and does not say it is "earth.

Regarding the statement that "wholesome or unwholesome vitarka and vicāra immediately give rise to greed and anger," one should have said "immediately gives rise to greed and anger [and] liberation," but this passage is missing from the *Śū* commentary.

This is like the analogy of a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold; its meaning can be understood thus: if there is internal wholesome thought, even if one encounters the Three Jewels, it is good. As for the objects [of experience], they merely increase evil because of slander and lack of faith.

Regarding the disparity in karmic results, one should know that sometimes the possession of intact faculties is a result in a future life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*), while poverty is a result in this life (*upapadya-vedanīya*);

or poverty is a result in a future life, while the possession of intact faculties is a result in this life. Thus, although one may currently have impaired faculties, they may later become intact; or although one is currently poor, [wealth may follow].
That one may become wealthy and noble after being impoverished is explained by means of the three types of retribution (*tri-vidha vipāka*) that accord with the sūtras.

This is because while causes may be fully present, the reception of their results varies; thus, there are differences such as being physically complete yet remaining poor. If one explains this in terms of partiality in the cultivation of causes:

wealth and nobility result from the practice of giving (*dāna*), while physical completeness results from the absence of anger and harm (*vyāpāda-vihiṃsā*). This is because within the causal stage, one practiced much giving while simultaneously harboring anger and harming others.
If one lacks the superior faculties despite being wealthy, all other cases are to be treated accordingly.
Regarding the "two kinds of non-existent dharmas," these refer to the previously mentioned two things: space and a rabbit's horn.

To "discard the general for the particular" means that the Dharma is bestowed according to the capacities of beings, with the Great and Small Vehicles suited to their needs throughout the entire dispensation; therefore, it is called "general" (pervasive).
Because the sequence of the five periods proceeds from small to great, they are called "distinct.

The initial arising refers to the lower [teachings] to demonstrate the sequential application of the Dharma throughout one period; within the text, it provisionally points to the beginning of the Small Vehicle, hence it says, "initially arising at the Bodhi Tree."

Regarding the frequent use of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to refute intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): for instance, when teaching the five precepts and so forth to Trapusa and Bhallika, these are called "correct dependent origination" as causes for human and celestial rebirths, used to refute the non-Buddhists' attachment to intrinsic nature.

Next, as for the teaching on impermanence: although one's own attachments have been destroyed, one still remains stagnant within the cycle of birth and death among humans and devas; therefore, the teaching of impermanence is proclaimed to cause others to attain liberation.
All of these occurred during the period at the Deer Park.

Regarding those who use the essence to perform analytical deconstruction: although the Vaipulya (fangdeng) discusses all four teachings together, its intent lies in transforming the Tripiṭaka into the Shared (tong).
Regarding those who use analytical deconstruction to examine the essence: the Prajñāpāramitā intends to transform the Shared into the Distinct (bie).

The Middle Way refutes the two [extremes]: because the *Lotus Sūtra*’s single reality sublates the three teachings, the sublation of analytical and intrinsic [emptiness] is the refutation of the extreme of emptiness (*śūnyatā-anta*), and the sublation of discrimination is the refutation of the extreme of existence (*bhāva-anta*).

The Perfect and Constant refutes the partial and gradual: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of the Perfect and Constant to refute the partiality and gradualism of the three teachings. This is the Perfect and Constant.

Thus, the Middle Way and the partial gradual [approach] share the same meaning despite differing names; this is why the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* Sūtras are said to have the "same flavor" throughout the sūtras and śāstras.

This is because each of the five periods of teaching has its own corresponding śāstra, and the bodhisattvas who composed these treatises interpreted the sūtras according to the specific principles of their respective schools.

Now, the Great Teacher reveals this present sutra according to the capacities of beings, which is not fixed; if one were to follow a strict sequential order, this sutra would only be appropriate for discussing the perfect and eternal to refute the partial and gradual.
Since there are externalist views, it employs the causal teachings of the initial vehicle to refute them;
hence it says, "It is merely according to their ailments," and so forth. This is precisely the meaning of the present sutra’s re-application [of the teaching].

Since this is the case for both the beginning and the end, as the later teaching already employs the medicine of the beginning, one may know by analogy that the initial teaching also employs the perfect and eternal;
it is simply that this [later teaching] is explicit while that [initial teaching] is implicit.

The same applies to the middle period: that is to say, with the exception of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* sutras are likewise so, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is exclusively of a single [perfect] nature.
This is because even in the Perfect [Teaching], there is still no lack of esoteric aspects.

The passage "In all [teachings]" below clarifies that in converting beings across the five periods, the Buddha adapts to the capacities of the four *siddhārtha* (fourfold purposes), employing the four teachings either manifestly or secretly as the occasion requires.

That the sequence remains perfectly intact refers to those of a certain class of capacity for whom the progression is from the small first and the great later; thus, the order of the five periods is not lost.
However, because there are those newly entering among the various flavors, it is necessary to employ them interchangeably.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, one must anticipate [the analysis]" (*kṣepa-vikalpa*): although this section lacks the preceding and following [context], because it already exists [within the text], one must apply the meaning here by anticipating it.

For example, in the "Chapter on Lamentation" (*parideva-parivarta*), when a bhikṣu speaks of the three inferior types of cultivation, he uses impermanence (*anityatā*) to perform analytical emptiness (*vibhāga-śūnyatā*) and thereby refute the correct causal conditions (*samyag-hetu-pratyaya*).
Similarly, as stated in various chapters, such as "like an illusion" (*māyopama*) or "like a transformation" (*nirmāṇopama*), one uses the essence (*svabhāva*) to perform analytical refutation.
The teaching of the five successive practices of the Bodhisattva dharma-gate is precisely the use of differentiation to break down the substantial body;
furthermore, there is another practice called the Tathāgata practice, which is the use of the perfect and eternal to break through the partial and gradual.
Such examples as these can all be understood by examining the sutras and contemplating their meaning; there is no need for prolixity of text.
The orthodox teaching and correct principle of our own school refers to the meaning of the true causes and conditions of the teachings for humans and devas.
Regarding "the worthy and sage-like ones of the Lesser Vehicle" and so forth: "teaching" refers to the Three Baskets (Tripitaka);
"practice" refers to the analysis of form, conduct, and stages—namely, the seven worthies and the seven sages; and "principle" refers to the partial truth of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "Mahāyāna" (the first character of the term): this refers to both the essence of the dharma (*dharmatā*) and its conceptual differentiation. Since both the universal and specific teachings are termed "Great," the teachings, practices, and so forth are explained in relation to these two teachings.

Regarding "encompassing" (the second character): this raises a comparison, meaning that they may be applied by successively refuting one another, or by following the sequence of the five periods, or [alternatively]...

If even the mutual use of various flavors according to specific ailments can disrupt established distinctions, how much more so would it disrupt external [views]? Thus it is said: "How much more so for the non-Buddhist outsiders who cling to an inherent nature?
Each must be converted; since all ten seers were outsiders who had newly entered [the path], the Tathāgata employed the initial teaching for them all.
The commentary sections that refute the meaning of "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) should all be fully recounted without fixed order;
however, for the sake of avoiding prolixity, I have described them here in their entirety as a model for the preceding seven and the subsequent two, which are all identical in this regard.

Furthermore, it should be understood that although these [teachings] employ partial and limited approaches, they all ultimately converge upon the Perfect; thus, their essential intent is forever distinct from the previous four flavors.
Regarding their foundation, the "four mindfulnesses" refer to the constant and the impermanent, the curved and the straight.

When the Buddha also employs the fourfold formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*), he merely remains silent regarding shallow matters such as begging for alms; however, he provides explicit answers concerning profound dharmas such as *nirvāṇa*.
This is because he uses the shallow to manifest the profound, desiring to cause others to abandon error and enter the correct path.
Those whose names are identical refer to the four terms such as "permanence" (*nitya*) and so forth;
yet their meanings differ, for while "self" (*ātman*) refers to constant alms-seeking, the Buddha takes *nirvāṇa* to be permanence— thus their meanings are different.
The Buddha is currently explaining for those who speak thus the meaning of their erroneous attachments.

As for "transgressing the sections" (*kua jie*): because they contemplate worldly affairs while the Buddha answers with the profound principles of the Mahāyāna, it is called "transgressing the sections.
The principle indicated by this is that the names of permanence, impermanence, crookedness, and straightness established by non-Buddhists secretly indicate the Buddha.
Because the Dharma possesses four meanings, the Buddha, by means of those [erroneous] names, reveals the correct meaning;
this is also the method for opening up the erroneous to reveal the correct, which may serve as a model for transforming sentient beings in future generations.

Regarding the term "hán-zhù" (函柱) for the lower bolt of a gate, the *Fāngyán* states that in the region east of the Pass it is called *jiàn* (鍵), while in the region west of the Pass it is called *yuè* (龠).
Both characters "hán" and "zhù" are erroneous. According to the *Shuowén*, *yuè* refers to the male pin at the bottom of a gate; "mǔ" (牡) is pronounced *wáng hòu*.
This male pin is used to seal and secure the gate so that it cannot be opened.
Within the ultimate principle, sentient beings are inexhaustible because the nature of the ten realms is inherently present and never diminishes from beginning to end.

Thus, while in the state of ordinary beings, the nature of goodness is not extinguished, so the four types of noble ones do not decrease; while in the state of the noble ones, the nature of evil is not extinguished, so the six classes of ordinary beings do not decrease.
Since ordinary and noble beings constantly manifest these ten births, how could they ever be exhausted?

I say that, according to the text, "fearing it may for now be based on phenomena" means that Jingxi, relying on the words of the sutra, states that "sentient beings are inexhaustible" is precisely a reference to phenomena;
it means that sentient beings are boundless and cannot be fully saved, rather than referring to the inherent completeness [of the principle].

Because I dare not suddenly contradict the meaning of the *Shu* (Commentary), I say "fearing it may for now," yet this does not conflict with it, for the immeasurability of phenomena must necessarily arise from...
Because principle is inexhaustible, the Master of the Commentary (Suzong) set aside the literal facts to follow principle, arranging the text to reveal the underlying intent.
If this is so, then the two interpretations of Zhang’an and Jingxi complement one another.
The phrase "the old usage below" is again the words of Zhang’an; it is not my own private opinion.
Subhadra was inherently obstinate, perverse, and disobedient to the Buddha’s transformation.
When the World-Honored One knew this—that the Tathāgata already knew Ānanda had been disturbed by Māra and intended to initiate the entrustment—He therefore questioned Cunda.
As for why the heavenly Māra disturbed only Ānanda, the answer is that it was Ānanda [who was targeted].
It was because those who transmitted the Dharma-treasury feared that the Buddha’s entrustment of the Dharma would be passed down to the final age, and thus they confused it.

This should be understood by comparing it with what is said in the "Shuoming" (Speech on Appointments) of the *Shangshu*: "Shuo bowed his head to the ground in homage, responding and extolling the glorious mandate of the Son of Heaven.
Kong Anqian’s commentary states: "Responding means answering; he answered the reception of the glorious mandate and extolled it."
The intention behind breaking Ānanda’s pride was that he might have presumed himself to be the Buddha’s personal attendant and thus superior to all others;
it was necessary to humble him.

When the Sūtra describes Maudgalyāyana entering meditative concentration and seeing that the Tathāgata’s mind was directed toward Ānanda, this was due to the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, for Maudgalyāyana occupied a lower station.
One can know the Buddha’s mind.

Regarding the sūtras being like lions and so forth: being fearless like a lion, sovereign like a dragon, and fierce and majestic like fire likewise symbolizes the Buddha’s three categories of ultimate perfection.
A lion kills beasts, which is like the precepts preventing what is non-virtuous; a dragon can submerge in water.

Just as fire within the Buddha’s meditative concentration can destroy darkness, and as wisdom cuts through delusions, so too does the Tathāgata internally realize the three kinds of purity and externally manifest the three virtues.
How could my internal impurities and external frailty possibly allow me to serve as his attendant?

Regarding the passage from "The Sūtra states that Ānanda was fully possessed of afflictions" up to "he did not give rise to a mind of desire": since Ānanda was a person who had attained only the first fruit (srotāpanna), his afflictions of desire were still entirely present;

therefore, it is asked why [the Buddha] praised him for not giving rise to a mind of desire. Some say: although Ānanda had already realized the third fruit (anāgāmin), and thus his afflictions of the higher realms were exhausted even though he still possessed those of the desire realm, why then praise him for not giving rise to a mind of desire?
The answer is: for one liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta), encountering favorable objects often leads to regression.
From those who attained the first fruit up to those who renounced the precepts to return home, Ānanda did not fall back; this is truly worthy of praise.

If there is mention of a "Shafu" (舍浮) who existed previously, it means that the character "Bi" (毗) was erroneously written as "You" (有). The names and meanings of the seven Buddhas are as recorded previously.
Regarding those who each have a heavy responsibility: their heavy responsibility consists in transforming sentient beings through compassion.
Those who were previously said to be "incapable" were so because they were originally followers of the Hīnayāna.
Those for whom it was said they were "capable" are now able to do so because they have already been opened to the Mahāyāna by abandoning the Lesser Vehicle.
This "younger brother from the same lineage" refers to a nephew (a son of one's paternal uncle).
However, when discussing those who are close, because they are near and familiar, anyone who speaks will necessarily believe and accept it;
thus, he concealed the title "from the same lineage" and simply said, "my younger brother," just as one would refer to one's own uterine brother.
The phrase "not being a non-Buddhist" refutes the first interpretation;
the phrase "not being a general exposition" refutes the second interpretation. Among these three interpretations, the second meaning is superior.
As for why certain passages do not appear here, it is because the Sanskrit manuscript had not yet arrived. During the Linde era of the Tang dynasty, the latter portion finally arrived.
The "One Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching" (*Yijiao*) is precisely its text.
Regarding the explanation for Ānanda: Ānanda was bound by the snares of Māra, and it was through a mantra that he was liberated from them.

As for the term "possessing both sound and meaning" (*fanyin jianyi*): it means that internally one possesses wisdom (*dhāraṇī-prajñā*) while externally one is endowed with eloquence (*pratibhāna*); hence, it is called "possessing both meaning."
Regarding the phrase "abandoning pungent flavors, etc.," this is because [the Buddha] was conforming to the common customs of the populace; therefore, he abandoned pungent flavors and so forth.

As for the term *vālamī*, it refers to those who are deluded or fearful; in ancient editions of the sutra, there is a character above the "婆" (*po*) that may be a name, or it may be an error for the character "恐" (*kǒng*).

Regarding this character "xié" (攜): those who pronounce it as "xié" should instead use the character [山/(夙-歹+圭)] (which is read as "lán"). The *Zuǎnwén* states that it is a surname and is distinct from the character "lán.
However, the text below states that the character "shān" (山) has both "oblique" and "correct" forms; the basis for this is unclear.

I suspect the meaning of this character was added arbitrarily by later generations rather than being personally authored by the Master of the Commentary (Jingxi). Since Jingxi followed the old tradition, I have retained it here for now.
Regarding the pronunciation "lán," Master Lì Hánxián remarked: "According to various character dictionaries, there is no such character. It appears only in the poem by Yìng Qú, which says:
'The cold of Mount Lán breaks one's bones. Thus, this character was created [based on that verse].
The *Shuowen* states that "xia" (夏) means virtue; some versions instead write it as "you" (憂), which is an error. It should be read with the phonetic compound *houzeng*.
Although the commentaries on the *Yun* (韻) clearly show this character to be erroneous, since the pronunciation of this character is entirely a Sanskrit term, what need is there for a Chinese gloss?

Nevertheless, in indicating its pronunciation and briefly pointing to its meaning, there should be no harm. A detailed explanation of the meaning of the mantra is as previously set forth in the commentary (*shu*).
Commentary:
"The new Jinming" refers to the seven-fascicle version translated by Paramārtha as the "new scripture.
It can be seen upon reflection that since the original ground and the initial realization both possess a physical body, the original ground likewise relies on the protection of mantras.
Therefore, it is said: "How can the fundamental and the manifested differ? Furthermore, although he has long since realized awakening, his ignorance is not yet exhausted;

thus, one might point to this ignorance as being like the "wolves and tigers" of fear and so forth. However, the present commentary does not adopt this interpretation, but explains it solely in terms of the manifested trace-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Thus, the commentary below states: "This is discussed in relation to the response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); here, it serves to demonstrate [the cause of] fear."
Therefore, many commentators explain the passage below as first demonstrating the difficulty and subsequently demonstrating the meaning.
Those who rely on the previous interpretation provide an explanation in terms of the manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*).
However, the section beginning with "But since ancient times" follows up to demonstrate the meaning of the mantra.
As for the various different names of the Three Jewels, although the various secret languages of the dhāraṇīs differ, they are all subsumed within the Three Jewels;
this is because they are esoteric expressions of the single essence of the Three Jewels.

Regarding the *mahāmucilinda* great fish, the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Five hundred merchants entered the sea to gather treasures and encountered the king of the *mucilinda* fish as he opened his mouth.
The boat sped away with great speed, whereupon the helmsman asked those on the upper deck, "What do you see?

They replied, "We see three suns and vast white mountains; the waters flow toward us as if rushing into a great pit. The helmsman said: [...]* *(Note: The source text provided appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra, specifically concerning the encounter with the Mucilinda fish.)*
"Three days hence, one thing will be real and two things will be false: the white mountain shall be the fish's teeth, and the rushing waters shall be its mouth;
we are finished. At that time, each person on the boat invoked their own deity, but none produced any sign or efficacy.
Among them was an upāsaka who said to the crowd, "We should all together invoke the name of the Buddha; the Buddha is the unsurpassed savior from suffering."

When those in peril all with one mind recited "Namo Buddha," the fish—having previously received the five precepts in a former life and thus possessed the knowledge of past lives—heard the name of the Buddha and immediately felt remorse.
The fish then closed its mouth, and the lives of the multitude were saved.
Regarding parrots reborn in the heavens, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:

When the householder Sudatta revered and believed in the Buddha-Dharma, he provided everything they required. At that time, the bhikṣus went there every day to preach the Dharma and offer instruction.
In Sudatta’s household, there were two parrots—one named Latthi and the other named Sallati—who were by nature clever and wise, and capable of understanding.
Whenever people spoke of the bhikṣus coming and going, they would always first inform the household so that they might prepare and arrange the bedding.
Later, Ānanda went to that house and saw two birds; he found them clever and took a liking to them in his heart, and said to them, "I wish to teach you the Dharma.
The two birds were delighted, and he bestowed upon them the verses of the Four Noble Truths: *duḥkha* (suffering), *samudaya* (origination).
Nirgrantha-mārga had two birds in a tree in front of his house that, having heard the Dharma, were filled with joy.
They flew up and down the tree seven times in succession, chanting and practicing it. That evening, they stayed overnight in the tree and were eaten by a wildcat.
Due to this wholesome mind, they were immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. The next day, Ānanda went to that house and heard how the two parrots had been eaten by the wildcat.
The person who had killed them returned and reported to the Buddha: "In the house of Sudatta there were two parrots;
yesterday they were taught to recite the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, and that night they passed away. I do not know where their consciousness has been reborn. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Because you bestowed the Dharma upon them, they have been born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and so on up to the Sixth Heaven. They will be reborn in the heavens seven times in succession, never meeting an untimely death. Ānanda spoke again.
Question: When the lifespans of those in the six heavens are exhausted, where will they be reborn? The Buddha said:
They will descend to Jambudvīpa, leave the household life, and become pratyekabuddhas—one named Dharma and the other named Sudharma.

Regarding the phrase "the true realm is nameless," etc.: the principle is fundamentally nameless, yet because one accords with the principle by means of names, various names are established based upon that single principle.
In the ninth chapter, the "Chapter on Great Illumination" (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*), it says: "Furthermore, Kauśika, this son of good family..."

When a virtuous woman hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receives and upholds it, draws near to it, recites it, and correctly contemplates it without departing from the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), she cannot be harmed by means of poisonous drugs, sorcery, fire-pits, deep waters, or attempts at assassination with blades and the like. Why is this? Because of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
This is the great vidyā-mantra; this is the unsurpassed mantra.

This is precisely the prajñā of the three wisdoms within a single mind, which is capable of universally sweeping away the poisons of the three delusions and two deaths; how much more so could it be harmed by worldly poisons?
Because its illumination of principle is not false, it is called "Great Brightness" (Mahā-vidyā); because there is nothing that surpasses it, it is termed "Unsurpassed."
Regarding "first, counting; second, following," and so forth: that sutra explains three mantras, the third of which is called the "Six-Syllable Phrase.

Following the mantra, it extensively explains the six destinies, the six sense organs, and the six wonders; thus one knows that the preceding mantra merely cryptically refers to these three kinds of sixfold dharmas, and is therefore named "Six Syllables.
Furthermore, the six destinies are the cycle of birth and death to be overcome, while the six sense organs are...
The afflictions to be destroyed are clarified in the sutras as arising from the three poisons when each of the six sense organs corresponds with its respective six objects;

therefore, the six wonders constitute the practice that destroys them. In this text, the meaning of "counting" (gaṇanā) is briefly presented to encompass the remaining two [methods]. Counting from one to ten while calming and regulating the breath is called the "gate of counting" (*gaṇanā-mukha*).

Focusing the mind on the object by following the breath as it enters and exits is called the "gate of following" (*anugama-mukha*). Not thinking of anything else... [is the gate of fixing] (*sthāpanā-mukha*).

When the mind follows counting and becomes still and tranquil, it is called the gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding). To discern with wisdom within the state of meditative concentration is called the gate of *vipaśyanā* (insight).

To reflect back upon the object of insight and find both the observer and the observed in tranquility is called the gate of "returning. When the mind does not give rise to any defilements and remains as originally pure, it is called the gate of "purity.
These six are the gates through which one can enter; when the subject and object are combined and designated, they are called the "six gates."
The wondrous gate is as extensively explained elsewhere.
Regarding the names of the ghost kings: by invoking the names of their respective kings, the chieftains of their tribes will respect them and be unable to cause harm.
This secret mantra is, in fact, a cryptic discourse on the Three Virtues; it should therefore possess five universal capacities, just as the *āgada* medicine universally cures all ailments.
If it were not for these various afflictions, how could the hosts of Māra, upon merely hearing [the teaching], give rise to the bodhicitta?

Since they have attained such states as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), this means that the meaning arises from the back of their shoulders—that is, they take what is not the fruit to be the fruit.

To conceive of the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as *nirvāṇa* is called the "view of grasping at a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); relying on what one has realized and looking down upon others.

Because those who have attained the lower stages [of meditative concentration] know that this pride arises from atop the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), for outsiders merely suppress the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) while the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) remain entirely intact.

Regarding the phrase "formerly in the Sphere of Nothingness" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and so forth, it refers to the old habits of Subhadra; thus it says "formerly. Furthermore, the Sphere of Nothingness itself possesses [these qualities].
The pride mentioned here is not the pride of the previously mentioned distracted mind; therefore, it is said that "pride still remains.
Furthermore, "those who have attained the lower concentrations" refers to others who have attained the concentrations of the lower eight stages.
"Those with particularly excessive pride" refers to those who, having attained the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*), look down upon others.

"Merely lacking present conditions" means that they do not understand that although sentient beings possess past life-span karma (*āyus-karma*), they must still rely on present conditions such as food and drink, as well as on present causes for suffering and pleasure, and the present experience of the retribution of suffering and pleasure; yet they merely say...
How is it that past karma, which brings about present results, becomes "perverse"?
Regarding the phrase "the present lacks causes" and so forth, the Sūtra states: "When one's original karma is exhausted, there are no causes in the present;
when all sufferings are extinguished, there are no results in the future."
Those with false views who repudiate [reality] refer to the *rājas* (or *lāntaka*), who deny the causes and effects of the three periods of time;
they also do not allow that past karma produces present results, which is why it is said that "karmic actions are not taught."
"Unfixed retribution" refers to indeterminate fruits.
When the sutra states that from the severing of karmic causes and conditions [up to] not attaining liberation, it refutes that [view] to reveal its error;
for since the creation of karma arises from the mind, one must sever delusions within the mind to attain liberation.

"Practicing many of the six modes of contemplation" refers to: loathing the suffering, coarseness, and obstacles of the lower [realms], while rejoicing in the cessation, subtlety, and detachment of the higher [realms]; this is also called "superior, subtle, and transcendent.

Practicing the eight modes of contemplation is also termed the "contemplation of the eight noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*). However, these eight contemplations have both general and specific aspects; here, they are presented generally.

In general, one contemplates those four aggregates (*skandha*) as being unreal through the eight contemplations; specifically, one treats the principle of the four aggregates with [the contemplations of] impermanence and so forth.

Regarding the contemplation of impermanence, this refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one contemplates feeling (*vedanā*), it is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); if one contemplates perception (*saṃjñā*), it is the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*);

and if one contemplates formations (*saṃskāra*), one treats these four aggregates with [the analogies of] an abscess, a wound, and so forth—namely, contemplating feeling as an abscess, perception as a wound, and formations as poison.

One contemplates consciousness as being like an arrow; if one cites this within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it says: "feeling is like a disease, perception is like an abscess, formations are like a wound, and consciousness is like a thorn.

Furthermore, one contemplates the sphere of infinite space as a disease, the sphere of infinite consciousness as an abscess, the sphere of nothingness as a wound, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a thorn.
Although their names differ, their treatment is largely the same, for these eight [realms] give rise to the mind easily.

One who is weary of [the lower realms] can abandon them and cultivate the untainted (anāsrava) practice of the four dhyānas; yet, if one uses only the "painful, coarse, and obstructive" aspects as the means for the first three, why must one employ all eight [aspects] for the four formless attainments, such as the sphere of infinite space?
Answer: Because the concentration of the sphere of infinite space is subtle, the eight faults are not mentioned there.

Furthermore, the afflictions (ādīnava) are difficult to recognize in the lower stages. Even ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) may rely on the six [lower] practices, yet they do not equal the swiftness of the noble lineages (ārya-gotra).
Regarding the passage "Now, this Subhadra... and so forth, this scriptural text is the explicit basis for the non-Buddhists' cultivation of the eight contemplations (*aṣṭau vipaśyanāḥ*).
As for the phrase "if one follows the analogy," if one were to follow the model of the Buddhist teaching, there ought to be eight [contemplations], yet here there are only seven;

because it lacks the contemplation of selflessness (*anātman*), the subsequent section on the non-Buddhists explains the reason for the absence of selflessness. Furthermore, the eight contemplations of the Buddhist teaching merely negate the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Now, its external application extends to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
As for "nirvāṇa without perception," true nirvāṇa is indeed a state of no-perceptual mind; yet you now falsely reckon non-perception to be nirvāṇa.
Therefore, while maintaining subtle perceptions, you will later fall into the Avīci hell.
Those who receive such an evil body emerge from hell to receive the body of a flying weasel; this was a prediction made by the Tathāgata regarding this very matter.
If this is so, what need is there to mention others, let alone inferior figures such as the non-Buddhist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa?
The "Return and Submission" (*Pratyāgama*) section is divided into three parts because it concerns the future; thus, there are only three sections.
Now that the "Final Part" (*Paryavasāna*) exists, there is a fourth: the ordination of Subhadra.

Regarding the phrase "thought is the name for wisdom" (*saṃjñā jñānasya nāmety-ādi*): wisdom is the subject that contemplates, while the objects of contemplation are the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*). These three truths...

When analyzed in detail, it severs both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) forms of the three realms of existence; thus, the Sūtra says, "It can sever all forms of existence.
Regarding the statement that "all dharmas lack self-nature," one employs the fourfold analysis of the Mahāyāna method to investigate them, thereby causing entry into ultimate reality.
The emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is the principle [of ultimate truth].
This emptiness dispels conventional existence by means of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), thereby sweeping away the existence of the two deaths (*dvividha-maraṇa*).
As for the "differentiated contemplations of the Three Vehicles," these refer to the analysis of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) regarding the Three Vehicles according to our own school.

Regarding "the three vehicles observing together," this refers to the Dharma-body of the Mahāyāna gate; thus, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is cited as an example, using the parable of the three animals crossing the river.
Regarding "observing the Middle Way together," because this present sutra equally realizes the perfect and eternal, observing the Middle Way together constitutes practice.

The gradual understanding is perfected; if one were to subsume it within the stage of perfection (*yuanwei*), then the bodhi of the *śrāvaka* would correspond to the seventh stage of faith (*xin*), the bodhi of the *pratyekabuddha* to the eighth stage of faith, and the bodhi of the *bodhisattva* to the first dwelling (*zhù*) and above.

Although they all equally contemplate the Middle Way, there are differences in the depth of their realization according to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties. This [gradual approach] must not be conflated with the aforementioned four types of wisdom that contemplate dependent origination (*yīnyuán*).

Following the previous analogy of the four types of partial and perfect liberation that establish the four teachings, these three now represent gradual practice with perfect understanding, both ultimately converging upon the single reality.
Thus, one knows that there is a specific reason why the former four and the current three do not differ in their underlying purpose.

As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those who "damage their lives" are explained by assigning each stage from the first to the eighth birth to the number of atoms in a world-system within the "Chapter on Distinctions.
However, in the present sutra, there are those who give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles because they have practiced with heavy [meritorious] giving;

thus, although they have given rise to a small mind, this is different from the three previous flavors. This [present case] is precisely the gradual practice of the Perfect [Teaching], which merely relies upon [the provisional].
Regarding the phrase "practicing within the Dharma of the Two Vehicles," it refers to generating the mind of a śrāvaka and so forth;
this may also be explained as a "Mahāyāna śrāvaka," as the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "By means of the sound of the Buddha-way, let all hear it."

Regarding Subhadra’s realization of the Way, the Northern Liang Sanskrit manuscript was incomplete; thus, these nine characters concerning his attainment of the Way were only present here [in the Chinese version].
Since the later editions have now arrived, these nine characters should be placed after the section on "Leaving Home" in the subsequent fascicle.
Regarding "Kaisan" (the Benevolent Goodness): Kaisan expresses his sorrow and fortune. This means that the Tathāgata’s final act of deliverance was for Subhadra alone, and immediately...
Because he has entered parinirvāṇa, it is said that from this point until the section on sorrow [is addressed].
However, as for the remainder below, although they have not yet attained liberation, they were fortunate enough to hear the Dharma and form karmic connections;

thus, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who transmitted the Dharma according to the four reliances and attained the holy path are exceedingly numerous—all of these are those who planted seeds and formed karmic connections in this assembly.
He was a human being.
Now, at the conclusion of this sutra, the Master has exhorted us regarding the five divisions of the *Nirvāṇa*;

the text for these is already complete, and what remains is merely a small portion of the chapters used for further application. Therefore, it is said that the scriptural teaching is fulfilled; thus he admonishes future generations to encounter this ultimate [teaching].
The Director should simply exert himself to practice this for himself and transform others; though he has not yet attained realization, it can certainly be said that he is close to it.

Should he, however, fail to encounter this scripture and thus fail to comprehend the perfect and eternal, then the three delusions will flow vast and deep, the two deaths will accumulate heavily, and he will be submerged in the sea of suffering—how then could he emerge? Hence it is said: "How could one emerge from suffering?"

The Layman [Daoxuan] below cites scriptures as evidence; according to what is discussed in those scriptures, it is known that this [text] is still lacking three sections. However, in the latter part [of the scripture], there are four sections:
the two sections "Bequeathing the Teachings" (*yùlèi*) and "Returning to the Source" (*huányuán*) correspond to the passage on the entrustment (*zhǔlì*) and the cremation (*chábī*);

the two sections "Broadly Benefiting" (*kuòrùn*) and "Building Stupas" (*qītá*) correspond to the text concerning self-immolation (*shāoshēn*) and the erection of stupas. Yet these have not yet been reached here. Furthermore, regarding the latter part...
The four categories [of the *Śrāvakabhūmi*] and these three categories [referred to here] differ both in number and in their arrangement;
this must be due to the translator’s arbitrary placement, resulting in such discrepancies, or perhaps because the Indic Sanskrit manuscripts themselves have always differed from one another.

For example, within the teachings of Confucius originating from this land, there are already the *Qilun* and *Lulun*, which differ in their opening chapters; how much more so, then, in the case of those [Indic texts]?
When the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa was distant, the two traditions of the councils diverged; how could what was transmitted from the Brahma Heaven be entirely identical?
Thus, whenever the translations of various sutras differ between earlier and later versions, they all follow this pattern. Alas!

Although the Patriarch Zhiyan did not encounter the latter portion [of the canon], I, though humble and inferior, have beheld the complete text. To extol it according to my ability is a most fortunate and great blessing.
Regarding this latter portion of the *Cundī-bhadravarga-parivarta*, the *Yijing tuji* (Records of the Translation of Scriptures) states:

"The śramaṇa Jñānabhadra—whose name means 'Wise and Virtuous' (Zhixian) in the language of Tang—was a native of Puliṅguo in the Southern Sea. During the year of Linde, the śramaṇa Huining of Chengdu in Yizhou [collated it]."
Therefore, while traveling through India to pay homage to the sacred sites, he sailed westward and passed through the kingdom of Pāṇḍu.

There, he collaborated with Zhi-xian to translate one section in two fascicles of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, specifically the "Section on the Cremation" (*Tepi-fen*). He sent these scriptures by ship to Jiaozhou, where they arrived during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
Later, in the early years of the Yifeng era, Liang Nan-di, the Governor-General (*Dudu*) of Jiaozhou, dispatched an envoy to deliver the scriptures [to the central government].
In the third year after entering the capital, the year Wuyin (698 CE), the monk Linghui of the Great Ci’en Monastery petitioned the Crown Prince for the implementation of this scripture.
The imperial decree stated: "The teacher who is a Brahmin is the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi-xian;
because among the four castes the Brahmins are taken as pure and noble, India is commonly referred to as the 'Brahmin Country,' and its monks are likewise called 'Brahmins.'"

The monk Faxian’s *Record of the Western Regions* (Xiyuji) has traditionally been divided by commentators into two volumes, which follow the preceding major sections to form volumes thirty-seven and thirty-eight.

This text still constitutes the fifth chapter; it begins with the half-chapter on Ājñātakauṇḍinya, who was among those who submitted through conversion, and proceeds to the fourth section on the renunciation of Subhadra.
Regarding the "profound and wondrous Dharma": when one hears the Buddha’s teaching above concerning the dharma of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*), this is indeed true wisdom and the true realm.

Although "realm" and "wisdom" are distinct in name, their essence is fundamentally identical; because the characteristics of the realm and wisdom are merged in mutual interpenetration as a single unity, it is called the "profound and wondrous Dharma."

Having attained the Dharma-eye, this refers to the first fruit (*prathama-phala*), the first of the noble fruits realized through direct experience. Regarding the initial section where the Master of the Sūtra (*sūtrakāra*) narrates the events:
