the phrase "the water of the wisdom of the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā-jñāna*) follows the narrative. Within the subsequent section where the Master of the Sūtra praises his virtues, the first three lines constitute the formal praise.

Of these, the first two lines praise the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). Within that, he first praises the object capable of eliciting wisdom; just as water flows from a source, so too does wisdom emerge from the source that is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because it is water, it is called the "water of the wisdom of dharma-nature. The second phrase praises the wisdom that can illuminate objects:

just as water flows from its source and returns to overflow the source, so too does wisdom arise from objects and return to illuminate those objects; therefore, it is said to "pour into the source of the mind. The final phrase praises the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*):
this is the profound union of object and wisdom, capable of severing the bonds of the three delusions and the two types of death; therefore, it is so described.
There is no further bondage or attachment.

With the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), he praises the virtue of wisdom and abandonment; with the severing of lower fetters, he praises the virtue of the liberation of mind and the virtue of knowledge of the severance of fetters.
Because he is endowed with these two virtues, he is called an Arhat. His practice gradually resolves and becomes perfected, as previously demonstrated.
"Receiving the grace of the Tathāgata" means that the Buddha commanded Ānanda to summon me and earnestly instructed me so that I might abandon what is heterodox;
thus it is called "grace.
"World-Honored One" below praises the virtues of the Buddha’s compassion and wisdom: because of his great wisdom, he has personally transcended birth and death; thus it is called "wisdom."
Because the great ocean of wisdom arises from great compassion, it causes me to abandon what is false; thus it is said that his loving-kindness and pity are immeasurable.
Regarding those "pressed by the shifting of conditioned suffering" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*): because suffering relies upon the body, one has not yet escaped being pressed by such shifting.

Regarding the "poisonous body" of a fragile vessel: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) lack solidity, being as easily broken as a clay pot; because the body is like a basket containing a venomous snake, it is called a "poisonous body.
As for "having no refuge, no reliance, and no destination": the Buddha is likened to a sovereign, a father, and a teacher; now that the Buddha has entered extinction, the subjects have none.
The Master has no son to rely upon, and there is no father to depend on; he has no patron to turn to, and no teacher to follow.

The first part briefly indicates the absence of a master, while the second part fully explains the three meanings. If it were to include all indicators, it should state: "no master, no father, and no teacher."
The eight kinds of voice are: first, extremely excellent; second, soft; third, harmonious and appropriate; fourth, noble and wise; fifth, not feminine; sixth, unerring;
seventh, profound and far-reaching; eighth, inexhaustible.

Regarding "universally taking objects as conditions" and so forth: this refers to giving rise to three types of delusion while taking the six sensory objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as conditions—namely, giving rise to craving toward beautiful forms.

Unpleasant forms give rise to anger, neutral forms give rise to delusion, and the same applies to sounds and so forth; because these delusions moisten karma and can induce birth and death, they are called "karma that creates birth and death.
It is the natural law that [the Buddha] should act thus: wishing to cause sentient beings to cultivate goodness and sever evil, he employs skillful means to manifest his passing into extinction.

Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is profoundly deep (*gambhīra*): because cessation is itself non-cessation and non-cessation is itself cessation—and furthermore, because it is neither cessation nor non-cessation—it is called "profoundly deep" (repeatedly).
Thus, when the Tathāgata manifests cessation, those of superior capacity understand his fundamental nature, while those of inferior capacity grieve for his traces.
Those of middling capacity dwell between this grief and understanding; both types of *śrāvakas* fall within the limit of grieving for his traces, and thus he manifests illness.
The chapter states: "Those of inferior and ignorant common views always speak of *nirvāṇa*, whereas only Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.

The phrase "sighing deeply" (*xū cháng tàn*)—*xū* meaning to exhale and *tàn* being pronounced in the level tone—refers to those who lack the conditions [for realization], who feel shame because they have not yet reached their own potential. Thus it is said.
He sighed deeply and proclaimed:
"Those who possess the capacity for awakening can see the worthy and strive to equal them; this is why it is called 'excellent.
The commentary states: "One should also give rise to the four grades [of aspiration]. Since Subhadra had attained the Way and entered parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata’s transformation...
Because the affairs were already complete, he left behind instructions for the assembly; thus there is the "Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching.

Since the entrustment was finished, the Sage’s mind was free from concern as he entered the secret treasury; thus there follows the "Chapter on Returning to the Source. Having returned to the source, it was necessary to cremate his physical remains;
thus there follows the "Chapter on the Cremation. Once the cremation was concluded, his sacred relics remained; thus there is the "Chapter on the Distribution [of Relics]."
Furthermore, because humans and devas are enabled to make offerings and thereby obtain benefit, there is the "Chapter on Broadening and Moistening" (*Korun pin*).

The "Chapter on Bequeathed Teachings" (*Yijiao pin*) and the four chapters below it constitute the fifth section, the "Chapter on Utility" (*Yongzhang*), which sequentially clarifies the utility of completing the transformation of beings and concealing one's traces. As the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Shu*) states:
It may also be called the sixth, the mind (*manas*), as previously noted; however, these four categories collectively form one pair.

The first category consists of "benefit through sound" (*śabda-anugraha*), because it benefits sentient beings by means of the *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (the Bequeathed Teachings). The latter three consist of "benefit through form" (*rūpa-anugraha*), as they all benefit sentient beings by means of the relinquishment of the body.
Regarding the explanation of the title of the chapter, the *Jíjiù zhāng* states: "Bequeathed (*yí*) means that there is a remainder. The *Fǎhuá xuányì* states: "As for 'teaching' (*jiào')..."
The Sage spoke these words as his final instructions, entrusting the remaining teachings to all capacities; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching" (Yijiao pin).
Question: Is this the same as the *Śāstrasaṃpūrṇa-sūtra* (Yijiao jing)? Answer: They are not the same. That is Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and this is Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

Thus, the *Fahua xuanyi* clarifies that the *Śāstrasaṃpūrṇa-sūtra* concludes the Āgama section and belongs to the Small Vehicle. Question: What about the *Upadeśa on the Bequeathed Teaching* (Yijiao lun) by Aśvaghoṣa?
Therefore, when it is judged as the Mahāyāna, the answer is: Aśvaghoṣa, relying on the "Great" within the "Small," judges it to be the Mahāyāna;
that is, within the Tripiṭaka Teaching, the Śrāvaka is the Small Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha is the Middle Vehicle, and the Bodhisattva is the Great Vehicle.
Since this Mahāyāna is still a teaching of the Small [Vehicle], one knows that the interpretations of Aśvaghoṣa and Tiantai do not conflict, and they both attain the Four Teachings.

One must certainly understand that there is no contradiction; the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra) does not discuss the permanent nature of reality, but rather serves as a verification for the initial teaching.
At that time, when the Buddha said, "Up to my Great Parinirvāṇa," he was indicating the inconceivable essence of the Dharma-body of the Great Parinirvāṇa and exhorting [the assembly].
To protect me, he resolved these difficulties in order to encourage practice for the benefit of both self and others.
As for the phrase "now already revealed," prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the provisional was used to cover the real, so it was not called a "revealed teaching.

Upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and this present sutra, the provisional was clearly and manifestly opened up, allowing all to enter the secret treasury; therefore, it is said, "now already revealed."

All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time are likewise like those in the *Lotus Sūtra*, who reveal the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means and lead the transformations of the five Buddhas to be identical.
Thus, every single Buddha of the ten directions and the three periods of time acts solely to cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*);
now it is also thus, for they are all identical to the Buddhas in abiding in Great Parinirvāṇa.

Regarding "complete and pervasive" (*zhōuyuán*): because birth and extinction are identical as one, and because the holy and the ordinary mutually possess [this nature], it is called "complete and pervasive.
Regarding "relinquishing body and life": this means relinquishing the manifested traces and casting off the physical form. This extinction is itself non-extinction;
it is neither extinction nor non-extinction, and is therefore named *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the Buddhas who stroke one’s head: if one practices according to the sutras, the Dharmakāya Tathāgata will stroke the crown of my head—which is the single mind of the three truths—with hands that are the non-duality of the provisional and the real.
One will not give rise to attachment to the names of the two extremes and shall not lose right mindfulness.
If one can do so, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas will constantly manifest before one, demonstrating entry into the methods of the heterodox paths.
The various Buddhas transform those of heterodox teachings by first appearing in accord with them and subsequently revealing their difference; thus they initially remain "outside.

As for the phrase "like dry grass and leaves," Subhadra was the foremost among the assembly of heterodox practitioners, yet upon a single transformation he returned [to the truth], just like dry grass cast into a great conflagration—how much more so would this apply to others who are inferior?
"Entering various realms" refers to not departing from the six teachers; therefore, it is said they "practice false teachings.
Regarding the term *yīn-yè*: the first character is pronounced as *jīn* (according to the *Qieyun*), meaning to weep without sound; the second character is pronounced as *jié*.
The Group of Six consists of Nanda and Upananda, who were well-versed in mathematics, astrology, and preaching the Dharma, yet were by nature prone to anger;
Kālodāyin and Channa, who were deeply skilled in the ways of wealth and proficient in Abhidharma, yet were by nature prone to delusion;
and Aśvakapada and Vatsa, who were well-versed in music and humor, yet were by nature prone to anger.

Dāyī was of the Brahmin caste, while the others were all of the royal (Kṣatriya) caste; because these six constantly formed a clique, they were called the "Six Groups" (Ṣaḍvargika). Regarding the term "weiyi" (唯然):

the *Book of Rites* states, "When a father calls, one does not say 'nuo' (諾); when an elder calls, one does not say 'nuo,' but rises with 'weiyi'. Zheng Xuan commented: [that one should respond with 'weiyi' rather than 'nuo'].
One’s responses should be respectful and compliant with the word "yes.

Now, this sutra clarifies that although the wording regarding Chandaka differs from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, their meaning is the same. That [treatise] states that because Chandaka spoke harsh words, he was subjected to the Brahma-penance (*brahmadanda*).
If his mind had become supple and submissive, then according to the *Nandika-katyayana-sutra*, he would have immediately attained entry into the Path.

The phrasing differs; however, what is now called "gradual subduing" (漸當調伏) actually employs the ritual of the Brahma-maṇḍala, wherein one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination before being able to enter the Path.
That [text] cites the teaching that expresses the meaning (能詮教), while this indicates the practice expressed by that teaching (所詮行).
This merely speaks of "subduing," whereas that provides the method for subduing; thus, their intent is the same. "Brahma-maṇḍala" refers to silent ostracism (默擯).
One who contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination realizes that the three paths are themselves the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is the realization that the practice of cessation is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness means to perfect the four foundations of mindfulness; this is precisely the application of the ten vehicles of contemplation to observe the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*). This is called [the practice].
One dwells with the mind adorned by the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If one lacks the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*), how can one reach the Path?

Regarding the offense of stealing property belonging to the Buddha, the Master of the Southern Mountain (Nanshan) said: "As for stealing property belonging to the Buddha, strictly speaking from the perspective of the Buddha, there is no offense of theft.

This is because the Buddha has no sense of 'mine' regarding objects and possesses no afflictive intent to harm; therefore, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense), as it is equivalent to [stealing from] a non-human being."
Regarding the category of objects, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that stealing the robes of a divine image constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also says that if one takes without asking jewelry or flower garlands used for the worship of a newly constructed Buddhist temple—whether one knows they belong to the Three Jewels or not—one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

If there is a guardian or owner, all property belonging to the Three Jewels incurs a grave offense; however, if there is no guardian or owner and the donor’s intention to give has been severed, it is not an offense.
This concludes the section on the offenses regarding merit.

The commentary states that the final point concerning the objection regarding the difficulty [of making offerings] means that even making an offering of the size of a mustard seed to the relics after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is no different from making an offering to the Buddha while he is present;
how much more so for making an offering to a greater quantity? Therefore, one should not raise an objection based on a distinction of superiority or inferiority.
Regarding the Cakravartin King possessing "slight merit," this is a eulogy of the Cakravartin.
In the context of worldly phenomena, that which acts as frost and hail refers to the causes and conditions for the arising of worldly suffering, such as the sprouts of grain;
the Noble Path, which serves as their antidote, is metaphorically compared to frost and hail.

Regarding the statement that although these wheel-turning kings have not yet attained liberation, the text does not mention them following [the Buddha] as Arhats because they have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for their all succeeding to the royal throne, it is because they performed the cremation within the city; having received this merit, they shall all become kings. Thus it is said.
First, it is not permissible that each king would inevitably wage war against one another, whereby the people would suffer its bitterness. Second,
it is not permissible that if the cremation were to take place within the city, the merit would be concentrated solely upon this city while being diminished for all other nations,
thereby causing the Tathāgata’s benefits to be distributed unequally.
Ānanda, it is sufficient that the merit [of this act] extends beyond the city walls to the four quarters.

Regarding the term "expedition" (*taofa*): the *Liji* (Book of Rites) states, "The ruler punishes those who rebel," and Zheng’s commentary explains that "punishing" (*tao*) means "executing" or "attacking. The *Zuozhuan* (Zuo’s Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals) further specifies that when bells and drums are used, it is termed an "expedition" (*fa*).
Regarding the statement that "A-luo-ta-cheng (Arthasiddhi) [uses] four layers," this refers to the successive reduction of the three lower fruits.

The commentary (*shu*) states: "The four Buddhas merely requested half-bodies. This should read "four" as "lower" (i.e., *xià*); the four characters immediately following are an error pointing forward to a later passage.

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'admitting a small portion,' Śakra is the Buddha’s *dānapati* (donor); because he obtained one tooth of the Buddha, he is distinguished from the rest of the assembly.
However, because [the Buddha] faced him with only half his body, he is said to 'admit a small portion.
The *Sūtra* also says that the meaning of *sūtra* is translated as 'thread' (*sūtra*), taking the sense of threading through and holding together."

*Naya* is also called *vinaya* or *vini*, which is translated as "Vinaya" (Discipline). *Abhidharma* is also called *ābhidharma* or *ābhidhamma*, which is translated as "Abhidharma" (Incomparable Dharma);
this refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, for among all forms of wisdom it is the most supreme.
Thus, it constitutes the Abhidharma Piṭaka, which elucidates the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*). "Sorrow and poison" (*choutu*) refers to the poison of suffering.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the benefit of extinguishing the previous body,' the preceding two sections both clarify the benefits realized after the extinction [of the body];
therefore, this single passage describes the entry into the third dhyāna at the time when the assembly is benefited by the emission of light and the manifestation of signs."
Regarding "difficult to be born therein," it is because the third dhyāna is the most difficult to attain birth in.
As for the "light of great nirvāṇa," because one internally realizes nirvāṇa, there is a great external function;

furthermore, it causes all sentient beings who are illuminated by this light to awaken to nirvāṇa, and is thus called the "light of nirvāṇa. This is, for example, as stated in the *Siddhārthabuddhi-paripṛcchā*, or as follows:
The light that comes forth is named "Able to Abandon"; by means of this light, one can destroy the stingy and greedy minds of sentient beings and cause them to practice giving and so forth.
Furthermore, the light emitted at the time of approaching *nirvāṇa* is named "Nirvāṇa Light. These constitute three explanations in total, each with its own intended meaning; reflect upon them.

In the "Chapter on Returning to the Source" (Huanyuan-pin), it is stated that because the two periods of transformation are completed, it is said that the response [body] should end; because it enters the secret treasury, it is called "returning to the source.

This is precisely the ultimate aim of subsuming the response body and the fundamental basis of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). However, since the dharma-body is eternally pervasive, how could there be a beginning to its "returning to the source," given that its spiritual transformations are ceaseless?

Since there is no fixed location [for the Buddha], how could one discuss his passing? It is simply that because the conditions and capacities [of the audience] were such that they should hear of his manifestation of extinction, he performed this act.

Regarding the passage "entering and exiting the second dhyāna from the first dhyāna," etc., it means that having already departed from the first dhyāna but not yet entered the second, it is called "exiting";

it does not mean exiting into a state of distracted consciousness. The same logic applies to "exiting from the third dhyāna," and so forth; this should be understood by analogy with the *Mahāyāna-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The *Ya jing* states that this is precisely the "uninterrupted samādhi" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), also called "refined dhyāna," which refers to the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

This is because the Tathāgata, through the mind of Great Nirvāṇa, penetrates the Dharma-realm of dhyāna; since it is not even the sequential order of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), how much less could it be shared with the two vehicles of the Shared Teaching?
Next, as for "entering and exiting in succession," this refers to the *vāsanā-dhyāna* (perfuming meditation), also known as the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s stretch samādhi).

It is called "stretching" because it involves entering and exiting [meditative states] in succession, in order to mature the settled mind and disperse the distracted mind—just as a lion shakes off dust from its body.
As for entering in forward order, one enters the nine meditative attainments starting from the first dhyāna up to the attainment of cessation.

As for entering in reverse order, one emerges from the attainment of cessation and re-enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; proceeding in this sequence back to the first dhyāna, both in reverse and forward order, one passes through each state and enters a single moment of distracted mind.
Regarding the three types of "transcendent entry and exit": this refers to entering the cultivation of dhyāna through the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (leap-over samādhi).

Having arisen from the first dhyāna, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); having arisen from that, one enters the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Having arisen from the cessation attainment, one enters the second dhyāna; having arisen from the second dhyāna, one enters the cessation attainment.

For all higher realms, the cessation attainment must serve as the primary vehicle; for the lower stages, one gradually enters cessation through the third, fourth, and formless spheres, excluding the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

From the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the perception of sorrow, one re-enters the attainment of cessation; this is "entry in forward order. As for "reverse order," arising from the attainment of cessation, one enters the first dhyāna;
arising from the first dhyāna, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; arising from that, one enters the first dhyāna.

This is when the first dhyāna is the primary focus, such that one gradually eliminates the higher stages down to two types and then re-enters the first dhyāna. There is also another sequence of reverse and forward order.

Regarding those who alternate [through the meditative attainments]: arising from the attainment of cessation, they enter the first dhyāna; arising from the first dhyāna, they enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they enter the second dhyāna; arising from the second dhyāna, they enter the sphere of nothingness; arising from the sphere of nothingness, they enter the third dhyāna;

arising from the third dhyāna, they enter the sphere of infinite consciousness; arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, they enter the fourth dhyāna; arising from the fourth dhyāna, they enter the sphere of infinite space; and arising from the sphere of infinite space, they proceed further.
Entering the fourth dhyāna, arising from the fourth dhyāna, entering the sphere of infinite consciousness; arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, entering the third dhyāna;

arising from the third dhyāna, entering the sphere of nothingness; arising from the sphere of nothingness, entering the second dhyāna; arising from the third dhyāna, entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, entering the first dhyāna;

arising from the first dhyāna, one again enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Since there are three ways of entering, there are likewise three ways of emerging, and all involve passing through the state of distracted mind.

To distinguish [the two], these characteristics are briefly extracted based on the *Māyājāla-sūtra*; however, since the wording in the present sūtra is concise while its general substance is identical, it should be understood as being extensive like that [sūtra].
Regarding the three stages of teaching the Dharma: first it is called "profound *prajñā*," next it is called "great (*mahā*) *prajñā*," and finally it is called the "Buddha-eye."

The former two [of the three wisdoms] pertain to knowledge (*jñāna*), while the latter one pertains to abandonment (*prahāṇa*). Because it thoroughly penetrates the three truths, it is called "profound" (*gambhīra*);

because it extends horizontally throughout the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "great" (*mahā*). Since abandonment is identical to knowledge, the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) should likewise possess both the meanings of profundity and greatness.

Thus, we know that when the three wisdoms are perfectly luminous and the five eyes are fully endowed, speaking from the perspective of what is preeminent, this is the Buddha of All-Knowledge (*sarvajña*).
The eye illuminates the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—within the very essence of emptiness.
As for reclining on his right side upon a bed of seven jewels: the left (yin) represents real wisdom (*jñāna*), while the right (yang) represents expedient wisdom (*upāya*).

The bed represents the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*); since the transformative functions of expedient wisdom have already reached their consummation, he ultimately abides in this land of quiescent light; therefore, he lies on his right side.
This refers to lying on one’s side.

Regarding the phrase “the head rests toward the north,” etc.: the east represents the origin of suffering (*samudaya*), the south represents suffering (*duḥkha*), the west represents the path (*mārga*), and the north represents cessation (*nirodha*). Having the head to the north and the feet to the south symbolizes the realization of cessation and the departure from suffering;
facing west and having one’s back to the east symbolizes practicing the path to sever the origin. This, however, symbolizes that which the Tathāgata has realized.
Ultimately, the Four Noble Truths are non-active; though four, they are not four. That is to say: the aggregates and sense bases are all suchness, so there is no suffering to be abandoned;
afflictions are themselves bodhi, so there is no origin to be severed; extremes and deviations are all the Middle Way, so there is no path to be cultivated;

birth and death are themselves nirvana, so there is no cessation to be realized. Because he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to this principle together, he rests his head toward the north and so forth.
This is indicated by the fact that because this truth of reality transcends both extremes and the eight inversions, it is situated amidst the eight trees.
As for the phrase "immediately becoming sorrowful and turning white," when the assembly gathered, the forest had already turned white; as stated in the Preface Chapter:
"The forest turned white like a white crane. That it is mentioned again here as "turning" refers to the previous statement regarding the near-summoning through compassion.

In the distant past, when the transformation into white occurred, the tree would return to green once the assembly had departed; therefore, now that [the Buddha] has entered extinction, the tree has changed forever.
Thus, the twin trees on all four sides grow in pairs, their branches hanging down to cover the precious couch, symbolizing the eight functions of *nirvāṇa*.
While the function is one with the essence, the two are also the essence; yet, even as the four withered and the four flourishing trees all turn white, they remain unified in this state.
This signifies that prosperity is not truly prosperous and decline is not truly declining.
As for "nirvāṇa in the interim," it signifies non-arising and non-ceasing while manifesting arising and ceasing. Question:

Previously, among the assembly listed above, both Brahmā and Śakra were already present in the gathering; why do they now only descend from the air? Answer: Previously, they were there to request [the Buddha] to remain and to present offerings.

Having come for the sake of making offerings and having already heard the discourse on the eternality of the nature [of reality], he was finally able to cross over; thus he returned to his own palace.
Now, hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, he has come once more.
"Puyin" (普飲)—the character for "yin" is pronounced with a departing tone (qùshēng), as is the case in the following passage—"zhòngjié" (眾劫) refers to many kalpas.

In this "Chapter on the Cremation," the theme of karmic resonance (*jigan*) pertains to the cremation performed while the Buddha was still alive. The various miraculous manifestations witnessed by the Buddha were truly due to karmic resonance; since the resonance of the capacity and the response of the teaching must be distinguished together, the chapter is so titled.

Furthermore, it is shown that manifesting birth, manifesting extinction, preaching the Dharma, and displaying supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) are all nothing other than matters of karmic resonance. Now, we shall set aside these supernatural powers.
Regarding "individually cremating" (*chāpī-chāpī*; also transcribed as *shājì* or *yáxún*, which translates to "cremation by fire"):
the commentary states that the first [section] is further divided into three parts; the latter two segments are anticipatory headings (*xuánkē*) without separate scriptural texts.

Next, the manifestation of signs upon exiting the coffin refers to the section on the actual cremation below, specifically "the profound kindness manifests the feet. Third, the disappearance of form upon entering the coffin refers to the section below.
Having completed the transformation, he covered his feet.
"Unable to overcome" (bùnéng shèng) means that "shèng" is pronounced in the level tone (*shēng*).
The commentary states, "The other cities were also like this," meaning that the sixteen cities and so forth were all likewise.
"Other times are also like this" means that throughout the seven days, it is exactly so every single day.
"Other traces are also like this" means that across ten billion Jambudvīpas, they all share these same characteristics.
That ground is the place where the transformative teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely identical;
their activities for the benefit of sentient beings are equal, and it is at this very spot that they are all cremated.
The Commentary states: "It is not the fire of humans or devas" because it illuminates the entire world; therefore, it is not an ordinary fire.
"Suddenly his heart was startled": "suddenly" (shu'er) means "instantly" (hu'er).
Regarding the intended instruction for the six kin: father and son, husband and wife, and brothers constitute the six kin.

It was only Kāśyapa who alone heard this; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa maintained and upheld the Buddha-dharma for the sake of such people as these, and for this reason he did not allow them to abandon the minor precepts. That Kāśyapa alone heard it is precisely due to this. As for the rest...
He did not allow others to hear it for fear they might be defiled by evil; thus, he knew that while others heard nothing so as to give rise to goodness, Kāśyapa alone heard it so as to destroy evil.
Furthermore, he placed the old felt upon the new felt without removing the old, so that both ordinary beings and sages might universally receive its merit; therefore, he did not remove it.

Regarding the fire within the heart: it is the fire of compassion based on the identity of self and others (*samatā-karuṇā*) that burns away the provisional traces of the body in order to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
thus, the following verse says: "From within one's own heart, the fire of compassion emerges."

The relics left behind by the *Kor-jun* (Pervasive Moistening) Chapter are called the "Sacred Body" (*shengqu*); because their blessings moisten all classes of beings, it is termed "pervasive and moistening. "Kuo" (pervasive) means broad.
One-tooth *śarīra*—here translated as "spiritual bone"—refers to the bone fragments left behind, which are collectively termed *śarīra*. As for these worldly people...

To burn only the small grains of rice while discarding the remaining bones—how mistaken this is! One should know that the substance of the grains and the large bones exist equally in both the holy and the mundane;
it is only because of the differences in cultivation and refinement that their solidity or decay differs, and thus their spiritual efficacy varies.
It is not merely the small grains of rice that should be considered marvelous.
"A thousand sheets of paper are not burned at all" (up to) "except for one pair"; everything in between is burned, which symbolizes that the Tathāgata constantly practices the Middle Way.
"Gold jar" (*jīn dǎn*): *dǎn* is pronounced as *tú hán*; it belongs to the category of *wǔ*.
"Peacock-feather *dào*" (雉毛纛) is read as *tú* (徒倒反); according to the *Erya*, *dào* means "screen" (*yì*). Guo Pu’s commentary states:
"It refers to the feathered canopy (*yùbǎodāng*) used by dancers today to shield themselves.
"Plundering" (*chāoliè*)—both characters are pronounced with the level tone (*qùshēng*)—means to seize by force. "Kǎidào" (慨悼) refers to lamentation and sorrowful mourning.
The Commentary states: "Alternatively, this is to exclude those without the requisite conditions, as described in the text;
that is, the eight kings were unaware of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and all returned without obtaining any śarīra.

Regarding the fact that the text is incomplete: it refers to the absence in the present sutra of a passage concerning the distribution of the śarīra, which implies that even the Sanskrit original had not yet reached [this point].
"Exhausted.
The commentary explains that "beginning" refers to King Kapila, who was of the Śākya clan; since King Pāñcika was the eighth, it is said to be "concluded."
Regarding the phrase "what I privately maintain" (*siwei*), which should refer to those who have already been invited:

according to the Japanese catalog, this is either called the *Houfen shu* (Commentary on the Later Part) or the *Houfen ke* (Outline of the Later Part), both of which were composed by Jingxi. Why, then, does it also use the term "what I privately maintain"? Answer:

To harmonize with the *Fofazang zhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma-Treasury), it says these are those who were first invited. This is not actually based on a textual passage stating they were first invited; rather, Jingxi applied this designation based on the underlying meaning.
Therefore, it is also referred to as a "private interpretation.

This should be understood as distinct from the eight kings mentioned in the *Biographies of the Dharma Transmission* (Fǎchuán zhōng). That is to say, this passage clarifies that these eight kings did not know of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
it is not the same as what is explained in the *Biographies of the Entrustment of the Dharma-treasury* (*Fǔfǎzàng chuán*), which describes the division of the relics into three portions by the gods.
The people of the ocean region were divided into eight nations: first, the Malla people of Kuśinagara;
second, the Mallika people of Pāvā; third, the Vṛji people of Cāla; fourth, the Koliya people of Magadha; fifth, the Brahmin people of Videha;
and sixth, the Śākya people of Kapilavastu. [The remaining two were: the Licchavi people of Vaiśālī and the Malla people of Uruvilvā.
1. The assembly of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī; 2. the assembly of the Mallas of Kuśinagara; 3. the assembly of the Sakyas of Kapilavastu; 4. the assembly of the Bulakas of Allakappa;

5. the assembly of the Koliyas of Rāmagrāma; 6. the assembly of the Brahmins and householders of Pāvā; 7. the assembly of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī; and 8. the assembly of King Ajātaśatru of Magadha—each declared, "I shall seek a portion of the relics from him.

Each then arrayed the fourfold army and commanded the Brahmin of the Gautama clan: "In my name, inquire after the welfare and health of the Mallas of Kuśinagara, asking if they are at ease and if their movements are vigorous."
"I have always held you all in mutual respect and reverence; our neighboring states have maintained righteousness and never engaged in dispute.

I have heard that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa within your kingdom. Since the Unsurpassed Honored One is truly my deity, I have come from afar to request a portion of his relics, hoping to return to my own country to erect a stūpa and offer worship.
Having received these instructions, the Malla chieftain addressed the Mallas.
"Truly as you say, since the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa here, the people of this country shall naturally provide for his offerings;
it is a great trouble for you all to have come from afar seeking a share of the relics, but in the end they cannot be obtained.

At that time, the various kings immediately assembled their ministers and said, "If [the Śākyas] do not grant them to us, we shall now take them by force with our fourfold army. Then the kingdom of Kuśinagara assembled its ministers and replied together in verse:
"The Tathāgata has left behind his physical remains; we dare not grant your request for them, yet you have raised an army, and we likewise have our own time [to do so].

The one of the Fragrant Clan addressed the multitude, saying: "Worthy elders, having received the Buddha’s instructions and reciting the words of the Dharma, your hearts submit to his benevolent transformation.
Why should you contend over the *śarīra* and slaughter one another? The *śarīra* are present here; let us simply divide them. The assembly all acclaimed this as excellent.
Soon after, he spoke again, asking, "Who is able to divide [the relics]? The assembly proposed the one of the Xiang clan, who was benevolent, wise, and impartial, saying, "He may divide the śarīra.
He then divided the śarīra into eight portions. The ninth portion was for the reliquary stupa of the urn;

the fifteenth remained as the hair-stupa, which the devas took up to heaven to erect a stupa and offer worship. When the morning star appeared, the division of the śarīra was completed, and there remained some ashes.
The people of Pipphalivana said to the assembly, "We beg for the remaining ashes to erect a stūpa as an object of veneration.
Everyone agreed, saying, "Give them to us," and each nation erected a stūpa at its own location to offer worship.

If one explains this from the perspective of what is symbolized by the lower [teachings], it should be understood that if a practitioner can penetrate the three truths as being "mind-only" and cultivate the practice of the eightfold path of non-action, entering higher and higher stages, then this is the constant portion of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body śarīra.
This is the legacy of his teaching and the legacy of his physical form; why then seek it elsewhere? Therefore, the interpretation of the meaning within our school opens only five chapters.
The "Assembly" (the multitude) refers to those who have realized the nature; "Giving" is the teaching that explains the nature; "Practice" is the contemplation capable of observing;

and "Meaning" is the principle that is the object of observation. When this principle is manifested, it functions to subdue evil, gather in the heterodox, and transform all beings until its traces are concealed.

These five chapters are summarized within the three virtues (*triguṇa*): Giving is liberation (*vimukti*), Practice is wisdom (*prajñā*), and Meaning is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Thus, they are one yet three.

All possess the three virtues; though they are three, they are one. Each maintains its own fundamental chapter, yet through the multitude, one realizes them for oneself. The function of the three virtues is the transformation of others.

Since these five chapters are identical to the three virtues, and the three virtues are identical to my single mind, the nature of the mind is universally fused, penetrating equally through both sentient beings and Buddhas.
That there is no distinction among the three—this is what is meant by this. To understand it in this way is what is called "opening the understanding."
If one wishes to practice, one must necessarily rely on the ten vehicles; that the ten vehicles are fully elucidated lies in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Thus, we know that the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) serves as the gateway for practice for all the sutras and teachings of the Perfect and Sudden Mahayana. Which of the four kinds of samādhis is not subsumed within it?
Which of the ten vehicles and ten objects is not employed by which teaching? Only when teaching and practice mutually support one another does there finally come a place of refuge.
Had it not been for this single school, such a teaching would never have been heard. How fortunate that I, a lowly and insignificant person, have encountered this supreme proclamation!
I shall now take this lamp of the night to augment its brilliance and illuminate the numinous.

Though my words are neither elegant nor my meaning worthy of note, I only pray that all Buddhas, the true Dharma of Nirvana, and the sages of the Three Vehicles will embrace me with compassion, endow me with merit and wisdom, and guide me through the cycles of the five realms of existence.

Wandering through the ten directions, I shall constantly expound this sutra to guide all sentient beings toward a common return to the secret treasury and a collective realization of the perfect *I* (the letter *i*).
May the void have its end, but may my vow never cease.
*Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary: Pointing to the Return of the Three Virtues*, Fascicle Twenty (End).
